norman-conquest.name: Norman Conquest of England
norman-conquest.blurb: William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066) and was crowned at Westminster, replacing the Anglo-Saxon ruling class and binding England to Norman France.

citations.label: Bates, William the Conqueror (Yale English Monarchs, 2016)

manzikert.name: Battle of Manzikert and the Turkish settlement of Anatolia
manzikert.blurb: The Seljuk victory over Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert (1071) collapsed Byzantine defense in Anatolia; within a decade Turkish beys held most of the plateau, and the Sultanate of Rum emerged at Nicaea, later Konya.

citations.label: Cambridge History of the Byzantine Empire, ch. by Cheynet

fourth-crusade.name: Fourth Crusade and the Sack of Constantinople
fourth-crusade.blurb: Diverted from Egypt, the Fourth Crusade stormed Constantinople, installed Baldwin of Flanders as Latin emperor, and partitioned Byzantine territory among crusader lords and Venice under the treaty Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae.

citations.label: Queller & Madden, The Fourth Crusade (Penn Press, 2nd ed.)
Geoffrey de Villehardouin, Memoirs of the Crusades (archive.org)

nicaea-reconquest.name: Nicaean reconquest of Constantinople
nicaea-reconquest.blurb: Michael VIII Palaiologos’s general Alexios Strategopoulos seized Constantinople from the Latins almost without a fight, restoring the Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologan dynasty.

citations.label: Geanakoplos, Emperor Michael Palaeologus and the West (Harvard UP, 1959; archive.org)

mongol-rus.name: Mongol invasion of the Rus’ principalities
mongol-rus.blurb: Batu Khan’s campaigns destroyed Riazan, Vladimir, and Kiev (1240), bringing the Rus’ lands under the tribute system of the Golden Horde for over two centuries.

citations.label: Cambridge History of Inner Asia: the Chinggisid Age

las-navas.name: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa and the great Reconquista advance
las-navas.blurb: The combined armies of Castile, Aragon, and Navarre broke Almohad power at Las Navas de Tolosa; within four decades Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248) fell to Castile, leaving Granada the last Muslim state in Iberia.

citations.label: O'Callaghan, Reconquest and Crusade in Medieval Spain (Penn Press)
Britannica: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa

norman-sicily.name: Norman conquest of southern Italy and Sicily
norman-sicily.blurb: The Hauteville brothers wrested Sicily from its Muslim emirs and Apulia and Calabria from Byzantium; Roger II united the conquests as the Kingdom of Sicily, crowned at Palermo in 1130.

citations.label: Loud, The Age of Robert Guiscard (Routledge)

treaty-of-tordesillas.name: Treaty of Tordesillas
treaty-of-tordesillas.blurb: On 7 June 1494, Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, brokered under papal authority, drawing a north-south demarcation line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands to divide newly discovered and future non-Christian lands between the two Iberian crowns. Portugal received everything east of the line — later underpinning its claim to Brazil — while Spain received the west, the legal basis for its American empire. Rival European powers never recognized its authority.

battle-of-waterloo.name: Battle of Waterloo
battle-of-waterloo.blurb: On 18 June 1815, near the village of Waterloo south of Brussels, the Duke of Wellington's Anglo-allied army and Gebhard von Blücher's Prussian army decisively defeated Napoleon Bonaparte's Armée du Nord, ending the Hundred Days and his second reign as Emperor of the French. Napoleon abdicated four days later and was exiled to Saint Helena; the restored Bourbon monarchy under Louis XVIII resumed control of France, formalized by the Second Treaty of Paris. The battle closed the Napoleonic Wars.

battle-of-cannae.name: Battle of Cannae
battle-of-cannae.blurb: On 2 August 216 BC, during the Second Punic War, Hannibal Barca's Carthaginian army encircled and annihilated a much larger Roman force near Cannae in Apulia, using a double-envelopment tactic still studied today. Roman losses of 50,000–70,000 dead made it one of antiquity's bloodiest single-day battles and Rome's worst defeat, yet Rome refused to negotiate, rebuilt its legions, and won the war at Zama in 202 BC.

cow-72-1839.name: Secession: Bolivia → Peru
cow-72-1839.blurb: In 1839 the Peru–Bolivian Confederation dissolved after its forces were crushed by a Chilean–Peruvian restoration army at the Battle of Yungay (20 January 1839). The Correlates of War dataset codes the breakup as Peru separating from the Bolivian-led union: on 25 August 1839 Agustín Gamarra formally abolished the North- and South-Peruvian Republics and reconstituted a unified Peru, ending Andrés de Santa Cruz's protectorate. The territory was thereby restored to Peruvian sovereignty rather than newly conquered.

cow-121-1854.name: Conquest: Khanate of Kokand → Russia
cow-121-1854.blurb: In 1854 Russia, advancing south of the Ili River, seized the Kokandian fortress of Alma-Ata and founded Fort Vernoye (later Verny, modern Almaty) on the site, securing control of the Trans-Ili region (Zailiysky Krai) at the expense of the Khanate of Kokand. The move followed the 1853 capture of Kokand's western stronghold Ak-Mechet and extended a chain of Russian forts into Semirechye, setting the stage for the decisive defeat of Kokandian forces at Uzun-Agach in 1860. It was an early step in Russia's piecemeal conquest of Central Asia.

cow-221-1874.blurb: In 1874 Turco-Egyptian forces under Khedive Isma'il completed the conquest of the Sultanate of Darfur, the great independent state of the western Sudan. Egyptian columns advancing through Kordofan, combined with the slave-trader al-Zubayr Rahma's army from Bahr al-Ghazal, defeated and killed Sultan Ibrahim in autumn 1874, after which Darfur was annexed to Turco-Egyptian Sudan. The conquered domain lay in the western Sudan, not in Ottoman Tripolitania, which Egypt never held.

cow-365-1898.name: Annexation: Republic of Hawai'i → United States of America
cow-365-1898.blurb: On 7 July 1898 the United States annexed the Republic of Hawai'i by the Newlands Resolution, a joint congressional resolution signed by President William McKinley after a treaty had failed to win a two-thirds Senate majority. The acquisition added the entire Hawaiian archipelago — roughly 16,600 km² — amid the Spanish–American War, when Pearl Harbor's strategic value to the Pacific was acute. Hawai'i was organized as a U.S. territory in 1900.

wd-Q2401276.name: Battle of Hamath
wd-Q2401276.blurb: The Battle of Hamath (604 BC) was fought in central Syria between the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II and the remnants of the Egyptian army of Necho II. Pursuing the Egyptian forces who had fled after their rout at Carchemish the previous year, the Babylonians annihilated them; the Babylonian Chronicle records that almost none returned home. The victory consolidated Babylonian control over the Levant. The Neo-Assyrian Empire, often listed as a participant, had already ceased to exist after the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC and the destruction of the Assyrian rump state at Carchemish in 605 BC, and played no part.

wd-Q815233.name: Siege of Tyre
wd-Q815233.blurb: The Siege of Tyre (332 BC; the dataset's 331 BC is off by a year) was a seven-month campaign in which Alexander the Great and the Macedonian Empire captured the island fortress of Tyre on the Phoenician coast. Tyre, ruled by King Azemilcus and aligned with the Achaemenid Empire, refused Alexander passage; he built a causeway from the mainland to the island and, after gaining naval superiority with Phoenician and Cypriot ships, breached the walls. The city was stormed and brutally sacked. The Ptolemaic Kingdom, listed as a participant, did not yet exist — it was founded by Ptolemy I only after Alexander's death in 323 BC.

wd-Q112016.name: Battle of the Persian Gate on the Mountain
wd-Q112016.blurb: The Battle of the Persian Gate (winter 330 BC, sometimes dated 329 BC) was fought in the Zagros Mountains as Alexander the Great advanced toward Persepolis. The Achaemenid satrap of Persis, Ariobarzanes, held a narrow mountain pass and ambushed the Macedonian column, halting it temporarily. Alexander, guided by local captives along a flanking path, encircled the defenders and broke through, opening the road to the Persian ceremonial capital. The opposing force was the Achaemenid Empire under Ariobarzanes; the Ptolemaic Kingdom, listed as a participant, did not exist until after Alexander's death in 323 BC.

wd-Q6744162.name: Mallian Campaign
wd-Q6744162.blurb: The Mallian Campaign (326–325 BC) was a series of operations by Alexander the Great and the Macedonian Empire against the Malli, an independent confederation in the Punjab region of the Indus valley. During the assault on a Mallian stronghold Alexander scaled the walls and was severely wounded by an arrow to the chest, an injury that nearly killed him. His enraged troops stormed the town and massacred its inhabitants. The campaign was conducted by Alexander's Macedonian Empire; the Ptolemaic Kingdom, listed as a participant, did not exist until after Alexander's death in 323 BC.

wd-Q123774059.name: War of Radagaisus
wd-Q123774059.blurb: The War of Radagaisus (405–406) was the invasion of Roman Italy by a large Gothic host under the pagan king Radagaisus. The Western Roman generalissimo Stilicho cornered and crushed the invaders near Faesulae (Fiesole), capturing and executing Radagaisus on 23 August 406. Stilicho's victorious army was itself a coalition that included Hunnic horsemen under Uldin and Gothic foederati under Sarus, so the Huns who appear in the record fought on the Roman side; the Vandals were not participants in this campaign.

wd-Q134734396.name: Hunnic War
wd-Q134734396.blurb: The Hunnic War of 426–427 was a campaign in which the Roman Empire moved against Hunnic groups that had settled in Pannonia, recovering part of the province for Roman control. Roman forces (drawing on both the Western and Eastern courts and on Gothic federate troops) confronted the Pannonian Huns in this little-documented episode of the broader Roman–Hunnic conflicts that preceded the rise of Attila. It is one of several friction points along the middle Danube as Roman and Hunnic power competed for the Pannonian frontier.

wd-Q4872170.name: Battle of Ravenna
wd-Q4872170.blurb: The Battle of Ravenna (2 September 476) was the engagement in which Odoacer, leading Heruli and other Germanic foederati, seized the imperial capital of Ravenna and destroyed the last remnants of the Western Roman field army. The victory let Odoacer depose the boy-emperor Romulus Augustulus and assume rule over Italy, an event conventionally taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire. The Kingdom of Soissons, the Gallic Roman rump under Syagrius, took no part in these events.

wd-Q131585304.blurb: The Franco-Gothic War (507–511) was the conflict in which Clovis I and the Franks invaded the Visigothic Kingdom of Toulouse. wd-Q15211574.name: Aksumite–Persian Wars
wd-Q15211574.blurb: The Aksumite–Persian Wars (c. 570–578) were fought in South Arabia between the Kingdom of Aksum, which then ruled Himyar (Yemen), and the Sasanian Empire under Khosrow I. Responding to an appeal from the Himyarite claimant Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, the Persian general Wahrez led seaborne expeditions that killed the Aksumite ruler Masruq ibn Abraha and expelled Aksumite forces from the peninsula. The wars ended with the Sasanians establishing direct control over Yemen as the province of Sasanian Yemen, displacing Aksumite hegemony in the region.

wd-Q4871254.name: Battle of Hulao
wd-Q4871254.blurb: The Battle of Hulao (621) was a decisive engagement of the wars that followed the collapse of the Sui dynasty, fought between the Tang dynasty and the rival warlord states of Xia and Zheng. The Tang prince Li Shimin, with a force of well under ten thousand, blocked and routed the much larger Xia relief army of Dou Jiande, who was captured; Wang Shichong, the Zheng ruler besieged in Luoyang, then surrendered. Often called the most decisive battle of the civil wars, Hulao gave the Tang control of the North China Plain and cleared the way for the reunification of China.

wd-Q1639459.name: Battle of Mu'tah
wd-Q1639459.blurb: The Battle of Mu'tah (629) was fought near the village of Mu'tah, east of the Jordan River in Byzantine Palaestina Salutaris, between an expeditionary force of the early Muslim state sent by Muhammad and the Byzantine Empire with its Ghassanid Arab allies. Heavily outnumbered, the Muslims lost their three appointed commanders—Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah—in succession before Khalid ibn al-Walid took command and withdrew the surviving troops. It was a Byzantine victory and the first major clash between Muslim forces and the Byzantines; the Sasanian Empire was not involved.

wd-Q887684.name: Muslim conquest of Persia
wd-Q887684.blurb: The Muslim conquest of Persia (633–654) was the campaign in which the Rashidun Caliphate overran and annexed the Sasanian Empire. Decisive victories at al-Qadisiyyah (636) and Nahavand (642) shattered Sasanian field armies and opened the Iranian plateau, while the last Sasanian shah, Yazdegerd III, fled eastward until his death in 651. The conquest ended more than four centuries of Sasanian rule and brought Persia into the expanding Islamic empire.

wd-Q173077.name: Battle of Tours
wd-Q173077.blurb: The Battle of Tours (732), also called the Battle of Poitiers, was fought between a Frankish and Burgundian army led by Charles Martel and the forces of the Umayyad Caliphate under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus. Charles's infantry held firm against the Umayyad cavalry, and al-Rahman was killed, after which the raiding army withdrew toward Iberia. wd-Q1369379.name: Battle of Bạch Đằng
wd-Q1369379.blurb: The Battle of Bạch Đằng was fought on 9 April 1288 on the Bạch Đằng River in present-day Quảng Ninh province, where Đại Việt forces of the Trần dynasty, led by Trần Hưng Đạo, destroyed the invading naval fleet of the Yuan dynasty during Kublai Khan's third campaign against Vietnam. The Vietnamese lured the Yuan ships in at high tide and trapped them on concealed iron-tipped stakes as the water receded, capturing or sinking some 400 vessels and taking the admiral Omar prisoner. The decisive victory ended Yuan ambitions to conquer Đại Việt and Champa. The Vietnamese side, not just the Mongol/Yuan invaders, was the central belligerent.

wd-Q11908715.name: Battle of Aulax
wd-Q11908715.blurb: The Battle of Aulax (1304) was a decisive victory of the Catalan Company, mercenaries from the Crown of Aragon led by Roger de Flor in Byzantine service, over a Turkish coalition during their Anatolian campaign. Marching to relieve the siege of Philadelphia, Roger de Flor's almogavars routed the army of Yakub bin Ali Shir, commanding the combined forces of the Germiyanid and Aydinid beyliks. The win briefly restored Byzantine momentum in western Asia Minor, though the Company's plundering soon turned it against its imperial paymasters.

wd-Q11908741.name: Battle of Cibistra
wd-Q11908741.blurb: The Battle of Cibistra (Kibistra, 1304) was fought during the Catalan Company's deep raid into the Anatolian interior on behalf of the Byzantine emperor Andronikos II. Near the Cilician Gates at the foot of the Taurus, Roger de Flor's Aragonese almogavars met and shattered a large regrouped Turkish force, an engagement chronicled by the eyewitness Ramon Muntaner. Like Aulax before it, the victory checked the Turks but did nothing lasting to restore Byzantine Anatolia, as the Company soon turned to plunder.

wd-Q2259304.name: Edwardian War
wd-Q2259304.blurb: The Edwardian War (1337–1360) was the opening phase of the Hundred Years' War, fought primarily between the Kingdom of England under Edward III and the Kingdom of France under Philip VI and John II, over Edward's claim to the French crown and the status of Aquitaine. English arms triumphed at Crecy (1346), Calais (1347), and Poitiers (1356), where John II was captured. The phase closed with the Treaty of Bretigny in 1360, which granted Edward an enlarged, fully sovereign Aquitaine in exchange for renouncing his claim to the French throne.

wd-Q2887879.name: Battle of Ardres
wd-Q2887879.blurb: The Battle of Ardres (8 June 1351) was a French victory over an English raiding force during the Hundred Years' War, fought near Ardres in the Pas-de-Calais. A French army under Edouard I de Beaujeu and Geoffroi de Charny defeated the Calais garrison led by John de Beauchamp; Beaujeu was killed in the fighting while Beauchamp and many of his men were captured after the English archers ran out of arrows. It was a rare French field success in the years between Crecy and Poitiers.

wd-Q3655510.name: Battle of Demotika
wd-Q3655510.blurb: The Battle of Demotika (October 1352), near Didymoteicho in Thrace, was a proxy engagement of the Byzantine civil war of 1352–1357. Serbian cavalry sent by Stefan Dusan to aid John V Palaiologos was routed by an Ottoman force supplied by Orhan I in support of John VI Kantakouzenos and his son Matthew, with the Byzantine rivals themselves largely spectators. Often counted as the first major battle fought by Ottoman troops on European soil, it foreshadowed their permanent foothold at Gallipoli in 1354.

wd-Q1631158.name: Battle of Nájera
wd-Q1631158.blurb: The Battle of Najera (3 April 1367) was a major engagement of the Castilian Civil War, drawn into the Hundred Years' War, fought in La Rioja. An Anglo-Gascon army under Edward the Black Prince, ruler of the Principality of Aquitaine, restored Peter I (Pedro the Cruel) of Castile by crushing the forces of his rival Henry of Trastamara, whose Franco-Aragonese host was led by Bertrand du Guesclin. The English-backed victory proved hollow: Peter failed to repay the prince, and Henry returned to kill him at Montiel in 1369, securing the Trastamara dynasty.

wd-Q124435128.name: Hungarian–Ottoman War
wd-Q124435128.blurb: The Hungarian–Ottoman War of 1375–1377 was the third Balkan clash between Louis I of Hungary and the rising Ottoman state under Murad I. After the Wallachian voivode Vladislav I leaked Hungarian plans and joined the Ottomans and Tsar Ivan Shishman's Second Bulgarian Empire, Hungarian armies campaigned through Wallachia and into Bulgaria, winning at Mezősomlyó and repelling an Ottoman raid on southern Transylvania. The fighting ended in a Hungarian success that temporarily checked Ottoman expansion north of the Danube, though it left Ottoman power in the Balkans intact.

wd-Q1112854.name: Ming–Hồ War
wd-Q1112854.blurb: The Ming–Hồ War (1406–1407) was the Ming dynasty's invasion of Đại Ngu (大虞), the Vietnamese realm proclaimed by the usurping Hồ dynasty after Hồ Quý Ly seized the Trần throne. Citing the restoration of the Trần line as pretext, Ming armies under Zhang Fu and Mu Sheng overran the country and shattered the Hồ defenses along the Red River. Hồ Quý Ly and his sons were captured and taken to Nanjing, and Đại Ngu was annexed as the Chinese province of Jiaozhi (Giao Chỉ), beginning two decades of Ming occupation.

wd-Q33570.name: Battle of Grunwald
wd-Q33570.blurb: The Battle of Grunwald (also Tannenberg), fought on 15 July 1410, pitted the allied Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania, under King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas, against the State of the Teutonic Order led by Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen. wd-Q135522442.name: Siege of Corinth
wd-Q135522442.blurb: The Siege of Corinth (1458) saw Sultan Mehmed II personally lead an Ottoman army into the Peloponnese against the fortress of Acrocorinth, the strongest citadel of the Despotate of the Morea, the last major Byzantine remnant ruled by the Palaiologos brothers Demetrios and Thomas. After a roughly three-month blockade the fortress surrendered in August 1458, and Acrocorinth, Patras, and the northern Morea passed under direct Ottoman rule, with the despots reduced to tributaries. The 'Crown of Aragon' attribution in the structured source is spurious; the belligerents were the Ottoman Empire and the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea.

wd-Q244980.name: Siege of Belgrade
wd-Q244980.blurb: At the Siege of Belgrade (1456), a Hungarian relief army under John Hunyadi and a peasant crusade rallied by the friar John of Capistrano, together with the Serbian Despotate of Đurađ Branković, repulsed Sultan Mehmed II's Ottoman assault on the fortress of Belgrade (Nándorfehérvár). Mehmed II was wounded and lifted the siege on 22 July 1456, a Christian victory that checked Ottoman expansion into Central Europe for decades. The structured source's 'Serbian Empire' is anachronistic — that empire had dissolved by 1371; the defenders were the Kingdom of Hungary and the Serbian Despotate against the Ottoman Empire.

wd-Q2403565.name: Battle of Chikhori
wd-Q2403565.blurb: The Battle of Chikhori (August 1463) was fought in western Georgia between King George VIII of the Kingdom of Georgia and a coalition of rebellious western lords led by Prince Bagrat (later Bagrat VI), backed by Imereti, Mingrelia, Guria, Abkhazia, and Svaneti. The rebels won decisively; George VIII withdrew to eastern Georgia and Bagrat took Kutaisi to be crowned King of Imereti, a turning point after which Georgian kings never again ruled the whole country. The structured source's 'Kingdom of Kartli' is mislabeled — that polity emerged only after this fragmentation; the contest was the unified Kingdom of Georgia against the western Imereti-led coalition.

wd-Q4871706.name: Battle of Meelick Island
wd-Q4871706.blurb: The Battle of Meelick Island was fought on 25 October 1650 on an island in the River Shannon, on the Connacht-Leinster border, during the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland. wd-Q2620862.name: Battle of Konotop
wd-Q2620862.blurb: The Battle of Konotop was fought on 8 July 1659 near Konotop in present-day Ukraine during the Russo-Polish War. A coalition led by the Cossack Hetman Ivan Vyhovsky, allied with the Crimean Khanate and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, ambushed and destroyed a large Russian cavalry force that had been besieging the town. Though a striking tactical victory for Vyhovsky, it proved politically hollow: internal Cossack opposition soon forced him from power and Russia retained the strategic initiative.

wd-Q4677341.name: Action of 2 May 1654
wd-Q4677341.blurb: The Action of 2 May 1654 was a naval engagement off Colombo, Ceylon, during the Dutch-Portuguese War. A Dutch East India Company squadron of eleven ships under Rijckloff van Goens intercepted and destroyed three Portuguese galleons, driving them aground and burning them along the Indian coast in the following days. The action stripped Portugal of a significant share of its remaining warships in the Indian Ocean and accelerated the Dutch conquest of Portuguese Ceylon.

wd-Q4871614.name: Battle of Lugos
wd-Q4871614.blurb: The Battle of Lugos was fought on 21 September 1695 near Lugos (Lugoj) in the Banat during the Great Turkish War. The army of Sultan Mustafa II, advancing from the recently captured Lippa (Lipova) and supported by the Crimean Khanate, overwhelmed a Habsburg corps of roughly 7,000 men under Field Marshal Federigo Veterani, commander of the imperial forces in Transylvania, who had been unable to link up with the main army of the Elector of Saxony. The Habsburgs were defeated and Veterani was captured and killed. Although his troops were styled the "Transylvanian" army, Transylvania was by then a Habsburg-administered principality (under the Diploma Leopoldinum of 1690), so the engagement pitted Habsburg imperial forces, not an independent principality, against the Ottomans.

wd-Q127257738.name: Afghan-Maratha War
wd-Q127257738.blurb: The Afghan–Maratha War (1758–1761) pitted Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghan Durrani Empire against the expanding Maratha Confederacy for control of northern India and the declining Mughal heartland around Delhi and the Punjab. After Maratha forces briefly seized Lahore and Attock, the conflict culminated in the catastrophic Maratha defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat in January 1761. The principal belligerents were the Durrani Empire and the Marathas (with Mughal and Rohilla allies on the Afghan side); the Sikhs were only a peripheral actor.

wd-Q2342985.name: Battle of Ponte Novu
wd-Q2342985.blurb: The Battle of Ponte Novu, fought on 8–9 May 1769 at a bridge over the Golo River in Corsica, was the decisive engagement that ended the Corsican War of independence. The forces of the Corsican Republic under Pasquale Paoli were defeated by the royal French army of the Comte de Vaux, after Genoa had ceded its claim to the island to the Kingdom of France in 1768. The defeat ended the fourteen-year-old Corsican Republic and led to French annexation of Corsica.

The belligerents were the Russian Empire and Habsburg Austria against the Ottoman Empire; Wallachia was the theater rather than a combatant.

wd-Q207318.name: French Revolutionary Wars
wd-Q207318.blurb: The French Revolutionary Wars (1792–1802) were a series of conflicts in which revolutionary France fought a succession of European coalitions. In the War of the First Coalition (1792–1797) and the War of the Second Coalition (1798–1802), France faced Austria, Prussia, Great Britain, the Dutch Republic, Spain, and other states across Europe, Egypt, and the seas. The principal adversaries were the French Republic and the coalition monarchies; the Russian Empire joined only the Second Coalition, and the Ottoman Empire was a peripheral participant rather than a leading belligerent as the blurb implies.

wd-Q140439.name: Battle of Markuszów
wd-Q140439.blurb: The Battle of Markuszów (9 July 1792) was fought near the village of Markuszów in the Lublin region during the Polish-Russian War of 1792, the war in defense of the May 3rd Constitution. Polish-Lithuanian cavalry under Prince Józef Poniatowski mounted a successful rearguard action against advancing Russian Imperial forces, screening the retreat of the Polish army toward the Vistula. The engagement was a tactical Polish success but could not reverse the Russian advance that led to the Second Partition of Poland.

wd-Q2887968.blurb: The Battle of Heliopolis (20 March 1800) was fought northeast of Cairo during the French campaign in Egypt and Syria. The French Army of the Orient under General Jean-Baptiste Kléber, though heavily outnumbered, routed a much larger Ottoman army, reasserting French control over Egypt after the abortive Convention of El-Arish. The Ottomans suffered thousands of casualties against only a few hundred French losses.

wd-Q124649.name: Second Battle of Algeciras
wd-Q124649.blurb: The Second Battle of Algeciras (12-13 July 1801) was a naval action in the Strait of Gibraltar during the French Revolutionary Wars. A British squadron under Rear-Admiral James Saumarez attacked a combined Franco-Spanish fleet escorting French ships toward Cádiz; in the confused night fighting two large Spanish ships of the line collided and exploded, while the British captured a French vessel. It was a British victory that avenged the British setback at the First Battle of Algeciras days earlier.

wd-Q1072889.name: Chilean War of Independence
wd-Q1072889.blurb: The Chilean War of Independence (Guerra de la Independencia de Chile) was the armed struggle, roughly 1810 to 1826, by which Chile broke from the Spanish Empire. Beginning with the formation of the First Government Junta in Santiago in September 1810, it passed through the Patria Vieja, the royalist Reconquista after the 1814 defeat at Rancagua, and the Patria Nueva inaugurated by the patriot victory at Chacabuco (1817) and secured at Maipú (1818). wd-Q235344.name: Battle of the Alamo
wd-Q235344.blurb: The Battle of the Alamo (23 February – 6 March 1836) was a pivotal siege of the Texas Revolution at the Alamo Mission in San Antonio de Béxar. A Mexican army under President-General Antonio López de Santa Anna overwhelmed a garrison of roughly 185–260 Texian and Tejano defenders, including James Bowie, William B. wd-Q4872300.blurb: The Battle of Santa Clara (2 January 1847), sometimes called the Battle of the Mustard Stalks, was a brief skirmish in northern California during the Mexican–American War. wd-Q254106.name: Crimean War
wd-Q254106.blurb: The Crimean War (1853–1856) was fought between the Russian Empire and a coalition of the Ottoman Empire, the United Kingdom, France, and the Kingdom of Sardinia. Sparked by disputes over the rights of Christians in the Holy Land and Russian pressure on the declining Ottoman state, the war centred on the allied siege of the Russian naval base at Sevastopol in Crimea. It ended with Russian defeat under the 1856 Treaty of Paris and is remembered for its costly battles, military mismanagement, and the nursing reforms of Florence Nightingale.

wd-Q616931.name: Battle of Caseros
wd-Q616931.blurb: The Battle of Caseros (3 February 1852) was fought near El Palomar on the outskirts of Buenos Aires. The Grand Army (Ejército Grande) led by Justo José de Urquiza — a coalition of the provinces of Entre Ríos and Corrientes with the Empire of Brazil and Uruguay — decisively defeated the forces of Juan Manuel de Rosas, governor of Buenos Aires and dominant figure of the Argentine Confederation. Rosas's defeat ended his long rule and he fled into exile in England, opening the way for Argentina's 1853 constitution.

wd-Q617772.name: Anglo-Persian War
wd-Q617772.blurb: The Anglo-Persian War (1856–1857) was fought between the United Kingdom (with the East India Company) and Qajar Iran over control of the city of Herat. After Persian forces seized Herat in October 1856, Britain — seeking to preserve Afghanistan as an independent buffer against Russian expansion toward India and allied with Dost Mohammad Khan's Emirate of Afghanistan — launched campaigns in the Persian Gulf. The war ended with the 1857 Treaty of Paris, under which Persia withdrew from Herat and renounced its claims over Afghanistan.

wd-Q3490568.name: Battle of Tirad Pass
wd-Q3490568.blurb: The Battle of Tirad Pass, fought on 2 December 1899 in the mountains of Ilocos Sur, was an engagement of the Philippine–American War, not the Spanish–American War. A rearguard of about sixty Filipino soldiers under Brigadier General Gregorio del Pilar held the narrow pass to cover the retreat of President Emilio Aguinaldo's First Philippine Republic, delaying the pursuing United States 33rd Infantry Regiment until nearly all defenders, including del Pilar, were killed. Spain played no part: it had ceded the Philippines to the United States by the December 1898 Treaty of Paris.

wd-Q135474658.name: Battle of Sokoto
wd-Q135474658.blurb: The Battle of Sokoto, fought on 15 March 1903 at the city of Sokoto, was the decisive engagement in the British conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate, not a clash with French forces. A British-led column of West African Frontier Force troops under Sir Frederick Lugard defeated the Caliphate's cavalry and infantry, after which Sultan Muhammadu Attahiru I fled and the territory was absorbed into the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria. The opponent was the British Empire; French Africa was not a participant.

wd-Q2889946.name: Battle of Sarantaporo
wd-Q2889946.blurb: The Battle of Sarantaporo, fought 9–10 October 1912, was the opening major engagement of the First Balkan War, in which the army of the Kingdom of Greece broke through Ottoman defensive positions in the Sarantaporo Pass of southern Macedonia. The Greek victory opened the road toward Thessaloniki, which the Greeks would enter weeks later. The Greek combatant was the Kingdom of Greece under King George I, not the First Hellenic Republic, which had existed only from 1822 to 1832.

wd-Q2499424.name: First Battle of Çatalca
wd-Q2499424.blurb: The First Battle of Çatalca, fought 17–18 November 1912 during the First Balkan War, saw advancing Bulgarian forces attack the Ottoman Empire's last fortified line defending Constantinople, the Çatalca lines roughly 30 km west of the capital. Bulgarian assaults against the entrenched Ottoman positions failed at heavy cost, halting the drive on the city. The attacker was the Tsardom (Kingdom) of Bulgaria, fully independent since 1908, not the earlier autonomous Principality of Bulgaria.

wd-Q1582511.name: Battle of Ctesiphon
wd-Q1582511.blurb: The Battle of Ctesiphon, fought 22–25 November 1915 during the Mesopotamian Campaign of the First World War, pitted the British 6th (Poona) Division under Major-General Charles Townshend against entrenched Ottoman forces at Ctesiphon, about 40 km southeast of Baghdad in Ottoman Iraq. The clash was tactically inconclusive but strategically costly for the British, whose heavy losses forced a retreat to Kut that led to the disastrous siege there. The combatants were the British Empire (with British India) and the Ottoman Empire; Qajar Persia was not a participant.

wd-Q4871557.name: Battle of Lida
wd-Q4871557.blurb: The Battle of Lida (16–17 April 1919) was an engagement of the Polish–Soviet War in which forces of the Second Polish Republic under General Józef Lasocki captured the town of Lida (now in Belarus) from the Red Army. Attacking from three sides, the Poles took the town along with an armored train, weapons stocks, and more than 350 prisoners. The action was a subsidiary operation supporting the larger Polish drive on Vilnius.

wd-Q994316.name: Battle of Maysalun
wd-Q994316.blurb: The Battle of Maysalun (24 July 1920) was fought near the Maysalun Pass in the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, about 25 km west of Damascus, between the French Army of the Levant and the forces of the Arab Kingdom of Syria. Syrian war minister Yusuf al-Azma led a heavily outnumbered defense of regulars, Bedouin cavalry, and volunteers against French troops backed by tanks and aircraft; al-Azma was killed and the Syrians were routed. The French victory ended King Faisal's short-lived kingdom and inaugurated the French Mandate over Syria.

wd-Q708217.blurb: The Battles of Narvik (9 April – 8 June 1940) were a series of naval and land engagements fought in and around the iron-ore port of Narvik in northern Norway during the German invasion of Norway. wd-Q154182.name: Battle of Berlin
wd-Q154182.blurb: The Battle of Berlin (16 April – 2 May 1945) was the final major offensive of the European theatre of the Second World War, in which the Soviet Red Army, supported by Polish forces, encircled and stormed the German capital. wd-Q137177468.name: Battle of Petaling
wd-Q137177468.blurb: The Battle of Petaling (14 February 1946) was a clash on Bangka Island during the Indonesian National Revolution, fought between Indonesian republican fighters of the People's Security Army (TKR) and Dutch forces of the Netherlands Indies Civil Administration (NICA). The Indonesians attempted to halt the Dutch advance on Pangkalpinang near the villages of Petaling and Cengkong Abang but were defeated, and the Dutch entered the town the same day. The twelve Indonesian soldiers who fell are commemorated locally as the 'Pahlawan 12' (Twelve Heroes).

wd-Q1667878.name: International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling
wd-Q1667878.blurb: The International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling was signed in Washington, D.C., on 2 December 1946 by fifteen whaling nations. The convention later became the legal basis for the 1986 global moratorium on commercial whaling.

wd-Q1413732.name: Kashmir conflict
wd-Q1413732.blurb: The Kashmir conflict is the territorial dispute over the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir that erupted in 1947 following the partition of British India into independent India and Pakistan. A UN-mediated ceasefire on 1 January 1949 left the region divided along a line of control, and the dispute has persisted ever since.

wd-Q796498.name: Third Indochina War

w4-200003.name: Sargon of Akkad's conquest of Sumer
w4-200003.blurb: Around 2334 BCE, Sargon of Akkad defeated Sumerian king Lugal-zage-si at the Battle of Uruk, unifying the Sumerian city-states under centralized Akkadian imperial rule and establishing the world's first multi-ethnic empire. This ~99,000 km² transfer from Sumerian city-states to the Akkadian Empire represents the core of that conquest.

w4-200004.name: Sargon of Akkad consolidates southern Mesopotamia
w4-200004.blurb: Following his initial conquests, Sargon of Akkad and his son Rimush conducted follow-up campaigns to suppress revolts in Sumerian cities including Ur, Umma, and Lagash, killing over 56,000 people across the region; these campaigns completed the absorption of remaining ~8,000 km² of independent Sumerian territory into the Akkadian Empire.

w4-200007.name: Elamite expansion during Akkadian collapse (Puzur-Inshushinak)
w4-200007.blurb: As the Akkadian Empire fragmented after Naram-Sin's death (~2218 BCE), Elamite king Puzur-Inshushinak exploited the power vacuum to expand westward, seizing regions in the Zagros foothills and lowland Mesopotamia (~90,000 km²) previously under Akkadian suzerainty. This is part of the broader Akkadian collapse driven by the 4.2-kiloyear climate event and internal dynastic strife.

w4-200009.name: Gutian invasion and collapse of the Akkadian Empire
w4-200009.blurb: Around 2154 BCE the Akkadian Empire finally collapsed under sustained Gutian pressure combined with the 4.2-kiloyear drought event; the Sumerian King List records that 'Uruk was smitten with weapons and its kingship carried off by the Gutian hordes.' The Gutians seized ~56,000 km² of the Akkadian heartland in central and southern Mesopotamia.

w4-200010.name: Collapse of Akkadian Empire: Sumerian city-states reassert independence
w4-200010.blurb: As the Akkadian Empire disintegrated after ~2154 BCE, southern Mesopotamian city-states such as Ur, Nippur, and Lagash reasserted local autonomy from former Akkadian provincial control, a process culminating in Ur-Nammu's founding of the Third Dynasty of Ur (~2112 BCE). This ~12,000 km² transfer back to Sumerian city-states reflects the break-up of Akkadian administrative territory.

w4-200011.name: Utu-hengal's expulsion of the Gutians (short chronology)
w4-200011.blurb: Uruk king Utu-hengal defeated the last Gutian king Tirigan (who had ruled only 40 days), capturing him and expelling Gutian rule from southern Mesopotamia per the Sumerian King List. The event is real, but the middle-chronology date (2119 BCE) used in the original entry falls before the atlas window opens (-2100); on the short chronology, Utu-hengal's victory over Tirigan is dated to c. 2050 BCE, which lands inside the -2100/-2000 window.

w4-200013.name: Reunification of Egypt by Mentuhotep II
w4-200013.blurb: The Eleventh Dynasty Theban king Mentuhotep II, who had ruled Upper Egypt as an independent polity, conquered the Heracleopolitan Tenth Dynasty around 2055 BCE and unified all Egypt under Theban rule, formally ending the First Intermediate Period and inaugurating the Middle Kingdom.

w4-200014.name: Reunification of Egypt by Mentuhotep II
w4-200014.blurb: Mentuhotep II of the Eleventh Dynasty (Thebes) defeated the rival Tenth Dynasty rulers at Heracleopolis around 2055 BCE, reunifying Upper and Lower Egypt and founding the Middle Kingdom; the decisive campaign exploited a revolt in the Thinite nome to strike north and consolidate control of Lower Egypt.

w4-200015.name: Amorite Babylonian rise under Sumu-abum and successors
w4-200015.blurb: From ~1894 BCE, Amorite rulers of Babylon (Sumu-abum and successors) gradually absorbed neighboring Sumerian city-states in central Mesopotamia, with Hammurabi completing the process by the 1760s BCE. This ~5,000 km² transfer from Sumerian city-states to Babylonia in the -2000 to -1800 window reflects the early Amorite consolidation of Babylonian power.

w4-200017.name: Hammurabi's conquest of southern Mesopotamia
w4-200017.blurb: Hammurabi of Babylon (r. 1792–1750 BCE) systematically conquered the remaining Sumerian city-states: he defeated Rim-Sin I of Larsa in 1762 BCE, then Eshnunna and Mari, unifying nearly all of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule. This ~48,000 km² transfer from Sumerian city-states to Babylonia corresponds to Hammurabi's campaigns in the -1800 to -1760 period.

w4-200018.name: Hammurabi's incorporation of Assyrian territories
w4-200018.blurb: After the death of Shamshi-Adad I (~1776 BCE), Hammurabi of Babylon exploited Assyrian weakness and pushed northward, incorporating parts of upper Mesopotamia previously held under Shamshi-Adad's kingdom into Babylonian control around 1760–1750 BCE. This ~25,000 km² transfer from Assyria to Babylonia corresponds to Hammurabi's northern expansion.

w4-200019.name: Shamshi-Adad I's expansion into upper Mesopotamia
w4-200019.blurb: Shamshi-Adad I (r. c. 1809-1776 BCE) forged the first great Upper Mesopotamian empire, the so-called Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, ruling from Ekallatum and then his royal seat at Shubat-Enlil (Tell Leilan) and styling himself "king of the universe." He brought the city of Ashur and much of the upper Tigris-Euphrates region under his control, capturing Mari around 1796 BCE and installing his sons as viceroys at Ekallatum and Mari. His realm was an Amorite-led conquest state rather than a transfer between settled "Babylonian" and "Assyrian" kingdoms; after his death around 1776 BCE it rapidly fragmented, with Mari recovered by Zimri-Lim and the rest later absorbed by Hammurabi of Babylon.

w4-200020.name: Hyksos seizure of Lower Egypt (Fifteenth Dynasty established at Avaris)
w4-200020.blurb: The Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty established control of the western Delta and central Lower Egypt around 1674 BCE; this polygon (centroid near modern Cairo/Faiyum) represents the Nile Valley territories of the Middle Kingdom that passed under Hyksos-aligned or Fifteenth Dynasty authority as unified pharaonic control collapsed.

w4-200022.name: Hyksos Conquest of Lower Egypt — Rise of Fifteenth/Sixteenth Dynasties
w4-200022.blurb: Following the weakening of the Egyptian Thirteenth Dynasty after ~1725 BCE, Canaanite-Semitic settlers (the Hyksos) who had established a base at Avaris in the eastern Delta gradually extended their power over Lower Egypt. By ~1650 BCE the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty and a parallel Sixteenth Dynasty controlled most of Lower Egypt, displacing Middle Kingdom authority in the region around the Nile Delta (lng ~31.8°E, lat ~30.4°N).

w4-200024.name: Expulsion of the Hyksos by Ahmose I
w4-200024.blurb: Ahmose I's military campaign (~1550 BCE) expelled the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty from Avaris and Lower Egypt, incorporating these territories into the newly founded Eighteenth Dynasty New Kingdom; Manetho records the Hyksos concluded a treaty and evacuated, while archaeological evidence shows Avaris was abandoned rather than destroyed.

w4-200025.name: Ahmose I unifies Egypt, absorbing the Seventeenth Dynasty into the New Kingdom
w4-200025.blurb: Ahmose I (~1550 BCE), himself a member of the Theban royal line that had ruled as the Seventeenth Dynasty, founded the Eighteenth Dynasty and New Kingdom upon expelling the Hyksos; the Seventeenth Dynasty's Upper Egyptian territories were thus subsumed into the new unified state he created.

w4-200026.name: Ahmose I's Expulsion of the Hyksos and Founding of the New Kingdom
w4-200026.blurb: Pharaoh Ahmose I (r. ~1550–1525 BCE), founder of the Eighteenth Dynasty, completed the military campaigns begun by Seqenenre Taa and Kamose to drive the Hyksos (Fifteenth Dynasty) from Egypt. After capturing Avaris (~1550 BCE) and pursuing the Hyksos into Canaan, Ahmose reunified Egypt under Theban rule, ending the fragmented Second Intermediate Period and inaugurating the New Kingdom. The area around the eastern Nile Delta (lng ~31.8°E, lat ~30.4°N) that had been held by the Sixteenth/Hyksos dynasties reverted to central Egyptian rule.

w4-200028.name: Mycenaean Conquest of Minoan Crete
w4-200028.blurb: Around 1450 BCE (Late Minoan IB/II transition), Mycenaean Greeks from the mainland overran Minoan Crete: most palace centers were destroyed, only Knossos survived under new administration, and Linear B (Mycenaean Greek) replaced Linear A as the bureaucratic script. The Minoan-controlled Aegean island zone (centroid ~24.9°E, 35.3°N, centered on Crete) passed under Mycenaean political and cultural authority.

w4-200029.name: Kassite conquest of the Sealand Dynasty under Ulam-Buriaš
w4-200029.blurb: Around 1460 BCE, Ulam-Buriaš, brother of Kassite Babylonian king Kashtiliash III, led a military campaign against the First Sealand Dynasty; the last Sealand ruler Ea-gâmil fled to Elam, and Ulam-Buriaš 'made himself master of the land,' absorbing ~17,000 km² of the southern Babylonian marshlands into the Kassite state.

w4-200033.name: Suppiluliuma I's Syrian Wars against Mitanni
w4-200033.blurb: Hittite king Suppiluliuma I (r. ~1344–1322 BCE) launched the 'One-Year War' and subsequent 'Six-Year War' against Mitanni, sacking the Mitanni capital Washukanni, crossing the Euphrates, and subjugating Mitanni's Syrian vassals — Aleppo, Qatna, Nuhashshi, Mukish, and others. He installed his son Piyashshili as viceroy at Carchemish (~1327 BCE), and the defeated Tushratta's successor Shattiwaza was reduced to a Hittite vassal king over a rump Mitanni state in the Khabur Valley, ceding the western and Syrian territories to Hittite control.

w4-200034.name: Battle of Kadesh and Egypt-Hittite Treaty
w4-200034.blurb: The Battle of Kadesh (1274 BCE) between Ramesses II and Muwatalli II of Hatti was fought on the Orontes River near Kadesh (lng ~36.2°E, lat ~35.6°N). Though the battle itself was a tactical stalemate, Egypt failed to recapture Kadesh and Amurru, which remained firmly under Hittite control; the subsequent Treaty of Kadesh (~1258 BCE) formally codified this frontier, with the Syrian coastal strip acknowledged as Hittite sphere.

w4-200035.name: Adad-nirari I subjugates Mitanni (vassalization of Shattuara I)
w4-200035.blurb: Early in his reign (c. 1305-1274 BCE), Adad-nirari I of Assyria defeated Mitannian king Shattuara I and reduced Mitanni (Hanigalbat) to vassal status, the first major step in Assyria's absorption of Mitannian territory. (Shalmaneser I's later, more complete destruction of Mitanni under Shattuara II, c. 1260s BCE, is a separate event outside this window and is not the basis for this change.)

w4-200036.name: Adad-nirari I's campaigns against Kassite Babylonia
w4-200036.blurb: Adad-nirari I of Assyria (c. 1305-1274 BCE) waged successful wars against Kassite Babylonia, defeating Nazi-Maruttash at the Battle of Kar-Ishtar and seizing northern Babylonian territory along the middle Tigris, later fixed by a border treaty. The precise year is not attested in sources; -1300 places the campaigns early in his reign, inside the accepted window, rather than the previously used -1295.

w4-200037.name: Assyrian Conquest of Mitanni under Adad-nirari I and Shalmaneser I
w4-200037.blurb: Adad-nirari I (~1307–1275 BCE) defeated Mitanni king Shattuara I, making him a tribute-paying vassal; when Shattuara's son Wasashatta rebelled (seeking Hittite aid that never came), Adad-nirari seized Washukanni and key Mitanni cities. Shalmaneser I (~1274–1245 BCE) then crushed a final revolt by Shattuara II around 1260 BCE, claiming to have destroyed 180 Hurrian cities and deporting the population, formally annexing the eastern Mitanni territories into the Middle Assyrian Empire.

w4-200038.name: Middle Assyrian expansion under Shalmaneser I into Babylonian territory
w4-200038.blurb: Shalmaneser I (r. c. 1274–1245 BCE) fought Kassite Babylonia as well as Mitanni, pushing Assyrian borders southward along the Tigris; border negotiations with Kassite kings stabilized some zones but left Assyria in control of formerly Babylonian territories in the middle Tigris region. This ~20,000 km² transfer represents Middle Assyrian encroachment on Kassite Babylonia in the -1300 to -1240 window.

w4-200039.name: Tukulti-Ninurta I's conquest of Babylonia
w4-200039.blurb: Assyrian king Tukulti-Ninurta I defeated Kassite king Kashtiliash IV in battle around 1225 BCE, sacked Babylon, demolished its walls, and ruled as 'King of Sumer and Akkad' — the first Assyrian to directly govern Babylonia. This enormous transfer (~133,000 km²) of southern Mesopotamia from Babylonian to Assyrian control corresponds precisely to this conquest.

w4-200040.name: Middle Assyrian Expansion into Northern Syria under Tukulti-Ninurta I
w4-200040.blurb: Tukulti-Ninurta I (r. ~1243–1207 BCE) campaigned aggressively westward into the upper Euphrates region, pushing into former Hittite-held territories in northern Syria at a time when the Hittite Empire was weakening. Assyrian advance into the territory around lng ~37.3°E, lat ~36.2°N (upper Euphrates / Taurus foothills) reflects this phase of Middle Assyrian imperial expansion, though the precise boundaries remain debated.

w4-200041.name: Kassite restoration and expulsion of Assyrian rule from Babylonia
w4-200041.blurb: Following Tukulti-Ninurta I's assassination around 1207 BCE and the ensuing Assyrian dynastic instability, Kassite leaders reasserted control over Babylonia. The Kassites reclaimed Babylon and southern Mesopotamia (~131,000 km²) from Assyrian occupation within a few years of his death, restoring the Kassite dynasty on the Babylonian throne.

w4-200042.name: Elamite Shutrukid sack of Babylon and conquest of Kassite Babylonia
w4-200042.blurb: Around 1158 BCE, Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte led a major raid into Babylonia, carrying off the Stele of Hammurabi and Stele of Naram-Sin; his son Kutir-Nahhunte then defeated the last Kassite king Zababa-shuma-iddin and briefly controlled Babylon. This Elamite conquest (~131,000 km²) accounts for the large transfer of southern Mesopotamia from Babylonia to Elam in the -1200 to -1150 window.

w4-200043.name: Bronze Age Collapse — Fall of the Hittite Empire
w4-200043.blurb: Around 1180 BCE, the Hittite capital Hattusa was sacked and burned by a coalition of Kaska peoples and Mycenaean-related Sea Peoples groups, ending the Hittite New Kingdom. The resulting power vacuum in southeastern Anatolia and upper Syria (centroid ~37°E, 37.5°N) was partially filled by the resurgent Middle Assyrian Empire under Tiglath-Pileser I, who campaigned aggressively westward into former Hittite territory in the early 12th century.

w4-200044.name: Bronze Age Collapse — Fragmentation of Hittite Empire into Neo-Hittite States
w4-200044.blurb: Following the destruction of Hattusa (~1180 BCE), the Hittite imperial dynasty fragmented into a series of successor Neo-Hittite (Syro-Hittite) city-states in southeastern Anatolia. Dynastic continuity has been traced at Carchemish and Melid, whose rulers preserved Hittite royal titulature and Luwian hieroglyphic script; the area around lng ~37.2°E, lat ~37.1°N (the Amanus / Islahiye region) falls within the northern Neo-Hittite zone (Palistin / Taita's kingdom).

w4-200045.name: Bronze Age Collapse — Assyrian Retreat and Rise of Neo-Hittite Successors in Northern Syria
w4-200045.blurb: In the aftermath of the Bronze Age Collapse (~1200–1150 BCE), the Middle Assyrian Empire contracted from its westernmost positions in the upper Euphrates / Orontes corridor. Neo-Hittite successor states, particularly Carchemish (lng ~37.4°E, lat ~37.1°N), filled the vacuum as Assyria faced internal pressure and the broader collapse of the palace-based trade system; Carchemish endured as an independent Neo-Hittite city-state through the Iron Age.

w4-200046.name: Bronze Age Collapse — Egyptian Withdrawal from the Levantine Coast
w4-200046.blurb: Following Ramesses III's defeat of Sea Peoples naval and land attacks (~1177 BCE, recorded at Medinet Habu), Egypt's imperial reach in the Levant collapsed. Egyptian garrisons and administrative centers along the Phoenician coast (lng ~35.7°E, lat ~33.9°N — the Byblos/Sidon area) were abandoned or overrun, and Phoenician city-states re-emerged as autonomous polities; the Onomasticon of Amenope records Sea Peoples groups (Tjeker, Peleset) occupying formerly Egyptian-controlled coastal cities.

w4-200048.name: Late Bronze Age Collapse / end of Mycenaean civilization
w4-200048.blurb: The Mycenaean palace civilization collapsed around 1200–1100 BCE as part of the broader Late Bronze Age Collapse. Palace centers at Mycenae, Tiryns, and Pylos were destroyed or abandoned, Linear B writing ceased, and the palatial economy gave way to the village cultures of the Greek Dark Ages. The worklist transfer Mycenaean Greece → Greek Dark Ages at lng 24.7, lat 37.4 in the 1150–1100 BCE window matches this collapse.

w4-300001.name: Division of the United Monarchy after death of Solomon
w4-300001.blurb: After Solomon's death (~930 BCE) the United Monarchy of Israel split into the northern Kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam I and the southern Kingdom of Judah under Rehoboam; the northern kingdom retained most of the territory of the tribal confederacy while Judah controlled only the tribe of Judah and part of Benjamin around Jerusalem.

w4-300002.name: Accession of Adad-nirari II and foundation of the Neo-Assyrian Empire
w4-300002.blurb: The Neo-Assyrian Empire is conventionally dated from the accession of Adad-nirari II in 911 BCE, who began a series of successful military campaigns that expanded Assyrian power and marked a new imperial phase. This change represents the atlas relabeling of the Assyrian core heartland from 'Assyria' to 'Neo-Assyrian Empire' reflecting the conventional historiographical periodization.

w4-300029.name: Assyrian conquest of Israel (Fall of Samaria)
w4-300029.blurb: In 724–722 BC, Shalmaneser V and then Sargon II of Assyria besieged and captured Samaria, the capital of the Kingdom of Israel. Sargon II deported roughly 27,290 Israelites and resettled the territory with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, and other regions, effectively ending the Kingdom of Israel.

w4-300031.name: Tiglath-Pileser III's Levantine campaign and Sennacherib's 701 BCE invasion
w4-300031.blurb: Tiglath-Pileser III's 734 BCE march through the Levant to the Egyptian border forced Judah to pay tribute and become an Assyrian vassal; Sennacherib's 701 BCE campaign further devastated Judah, with Hezekiah paying a heavy tribute after 46 Judahite towns were captured, reducing the kingdom's effective territory.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Sennacherib's campaign in the Levant

w4-300032.name: Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon II Assyrian campaigns in the Levant
w4-300032.blurb: Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727 BCE) campaigned through the Levant, forcing Phoenician cities into Assyrian vassalage; Sargon II's later campaigns (722–705 BCE) consolidated direct Assyrian control over the coastal Phoenician cities, replacing Phoenician autonomy with Assyrian provincial administration.

w4-300033.name: Neo-Assyrian conquest of the Levant under Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon II
w4-300033.blurb: Between 750 and 700 BC, the Neo-Assyrian Empire under Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon II conquered the Levantine coastal cities (Phoenicia, Philistia, and associated Greek trading colonies). The centroid corresponds to Cyprus and the northern Levantine coast, where Assyrian campaigns in 738, 732, and 709 BC forced submission of these Greek and Phoenician city-states.

w4-300034.name: Piye's conquest of Egypt — Kushite (25th Dynasty) takeover
w4-300034.blurb: Piye (Piankhi) of Napata launched a military campaign northward around 744 BCE, defeating the Libyan dynasts including the 22nd/23rd/24th Dynasties and reunifying Egypt under Kushite rule; his victory is recorded on the 'Victory Stele' now in Cairo. The 25th Dynasty he founded became the largest Egyptian empire since the New Kingdom.

w4-300035.name: Piye's Conquest of Egypt
w4-300035.blurb: The Kushite king Piye (Piankhi) launched a full-scale invasion of Egypt around 727–724 BCE, defeating the combined forces of the rival Egyptian dynasties including the Twenty-third Dynasty rulers, and founding the Twenty-fifth (Kushite/Nubian) Dynasty over all Egypt.

w4-300036.name: Cimmerian invasions destroy Phrygian power
w4-300036.blurb: Cimmerian nomadic raiders invaded Phrygia around 696–695 BCE, sacking Gordion and killing King Midas (who reportedly committed suicide); the destruction of Phrygian state power allowed Greek Ionian cities in western Anatolia to expand their hinterland control into formerly Phrygian-dominated territory.

w4-300040.name: Lydian expansion under Alyattes into Greek coastal cities of western Anatolia
w4-300040.blurb: By the mid-7th century BCE the Lydian Mermnad dynasty under Gyges (r. c. 680-644 BCE), not Alyattes, was pressing on the Ionian Greek cities of the Aegean coast. Exploiting the chaos left by the Cimmerian invasions, Gyges attacked Miletus, Smyrna and Colophon, seizing Colophon's lower town and bringing Magnesia and the Troad under Lydian control, though Miletus and Smyrna repelled him. Around 660 BCE Gyges was active enough to send aid to Egypt's Psamtik I and an embassy to Ashurbanipal, marking Lydia's emergence as the dominant power over the Greek hinterland of western Anatolia.

w4-300041.name: Assyrian Conquest of Egypt
w4-300041.blurb: Esarhaddon of Assyria invaded Egypt in 671 BCE, captured Memphis in half a day, seized Taharqa's family, and installed Necho I as a vassal king at Sais. Ashurbanipal followed up with campaigns in 667 and 663 BCE, sacking Thebes, establishing Assyrian suzerainty over Egypt for roughly a decade.

w4-300053.name: Babylonian revolt of Nabopolassar and the fall of Assyria
w4-300053.blurb: In 626 BC Nabopolassar led a Babylonian revolt against the Neo-Assyrian Empire, seizing Babylon and founding the Neo-Babylonian dynasty. The transfer of southern Mesopotamian territory (around Babylonia, near 46E/32N) from Assyrian control to Babylonia reflects the collapse of Assyrian authority in the region during the wars of 626-616 BC that culminated in the destruction of Assyria.

w4-300055.name: Consolidation of the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nabopolassar
w4-300055.blurb: Following Nabopolassar's seizure of Babylon in 626 BC, the region of Babylonia was consolidated into the formal Neo-Babylonian (Chaldean) Empire over the following decades. The transfer from generic 'Babylonia' to the 'Neo-Babylonian Empire' label reflects the maturation of Nabopolassar's and Nebuchadnezzar II's state into the dominant Mesopotamian power after the fall of Assyria.

w4-300059.name: Formation of the Peloponnesian League
w4-300059.blurb: Around 550 BC, Sparta began assembling the Peloponnesian League through a series of bilateral alliances, starting with a pact with Tegea after failing to conquer it militarily. The League, which the Greeks called 'the Lacedaemonians and their allies,' grew to encompass Corinth, Elis, Sicyon, and most Peloponnesian poleis, with Sparta holding effective veto power. It gave institutional form to Spartan hegemony over southern Greece and served as a counterweight to Argos and, later, Athens.

w4-300061.name: Cyrus the Great's conquest of Babylon
w4-300061.blurb: Cyrus the Great of the Achaemenid Empire conquered the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 539 BC, entering Babylon after the Battle of Opis. The transfer of Mesopotamian/Assyrian-region territory (around 43E/35N) from the Neo-Babylonian Empire to the Achaemenids reflects this conquest, which brought all of Babylonia and its dependencies under Persian rule.

w4-300062.name: Cyrus the Great's conquest of the Neo-Babylonian Empire
w4-300062.blurb: The former Urartian heartland (the Lake Van / Armenian highland region) passed to the Achaemenids not through Cyrus's 539 BCE capture of Babylon but through his earlier absorption of the Median realm. Urartu had already fallen to the Medes c. 590 BCE; when Cyrus II defeated Astyages and took over the Median Kingdom in 550 BCE, its northern dependencies including the old Urartian lands became Achaemenid, later organized as the Satrapy of Armenia. The Behistun Inscription (c. 522 BCE) explicitly equates this 'Armenia' with the former Urartu.

w4-300063.name: Median/Achaemenid conquest of Urartu
w4-300063.blurb: The Kingdom of Urartu was destroyed by the Medes under Cyaxares c. 590 BCE (or by Cyrus the Great c. 547 BCE under an alternative chronology); the Achaemenid Empire subsequently incorporated the territory as the Satrapy of Armenia, confirmed by the Behistun Inscription (~522 BCE) which equates 'Armenia' with the former 'Urartu.'

w4-300074.name: Cambyses II's conquest of Egypt (Battle of Pelusium)
w4-300074.blurb: Cambyses II of the Achaemenid Empire conquered Egypt by defeating Pharaoh Psamtik III at the Battle of Pelusium in 525 BC, ending the Twenty-sixth (Saite) Dynasty and founding the Twenty-seventh (First Persian) Dynasty. As recorded by Herodotus, this brought the entire Nile valley under Persian rule. The large transfer of Egyptian territory to the Achaemenids reflects this famous conquest.

w4-300075.name: Battle of Pelusium (525 BCE) — Cambyses II conquers Egypt
w4-300075.blurb: When Cambyses II of Persia conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, the Greek city-states of the eastern Mediterranean fell into the Achaemenid orbit rather than being taken by force. The kings of Cyprus, who had acknowledged the Egyptian pharaoh Ahmose II, submitted to Cambyses and supplied ships and crews for his Mediterranean fleet, while the Greek colonies of Cyrene and Barca in Cyrenaica voluntarily sent tribute. Cyprus was joined with Egypt and Phoenicia in the sixth Achaemenid satrapy, and Cyrene appears on Persian tribute lists thereafter.

w4-300077.name: Second Persian Invasion of Greece – Xerxes occupies Macedonia
w4-300077.blurb: Macedonia had been a Persian vassal since Megabazus extorted submission from king Amyntas I around 512 BC, and Mardonius re-subjugated it in 492 BC. In 480 BC Xerxes I marched through Macedonia and Thessaly with the cooperation of king Alexander I of Macedon, bringing Macedonia (lat 40.8, lng 23.5) under direct Achaemenid military control at the high-water mark of Persian reach in Europe. This matches the worklist transfer from the Macedonian realm to the Achaemenid Empire within the -500 to -480 window.

citations.label: Second Persian Invasion of Greece – Wikipedia

w4-300080.name: Wu-Yue Wars — Yue Final Conquest of Wu
w4-300080.blurb: After years of warfare, King Goujian of Yue completed the conquest of Wu in 473 BCE, forcing King Fuchai to commit suicide. Yue absorbed all of Wu's territory including the northern Jiangsu/Zhejiang coast (centroid ~119°E, 33°N). The atlas snapshot shows this region transferring from Wu to Yue between -480 and -450, consistent with the gradual military absorption of Wu territory culminating in 473 BCE.

w4-300084.name: Chu reconquest of upper Han River territories from Qin (mid-5th century BCE)
w4-300084.blurb: During the mid-5th century BCE, when Qin was internally weakened and focused on the Jin frontier, Chu regained control of territories in the upper Han River / Danjiangkou area (centroid lng 110.2 / lat 34.5, modern northwestern Hubei). This represents a reversal of earlier Qin gains in the region during the Spring and Autumn period.

w4-300085.name: Chu expansion into former Jin / Zheng borderlands in upper Yi River area (mid-5th century BCE)
w4-300085.blurb: During the 480–450 BCE period, as Jin fragmented into warring noble factions and weakened, Chu pushed northward into the upper Yi River and Luo River area (centroid lng 111.4 / lat 34.5, modern southwestern Henan). Chu exploited Jin's internal struggles between the Six Qing families to extend its influence into the southern edges of the Jin sphere.

w4-300086.name: Chu expansion into former Wu territories after Yue's conquest of Wu (473 BCE)
w4-300086.blurb: After Yue conquered Wu in 473 BCE, Chu gradually absorbed the Huai River basin territories that Wu had previously held (centroid lng 118.0 / lat 33.5, modern northern Jiangsu/Anhui). Chu had long competed with Wu for this zone and reasserted control over the eastern Jianghuai region as Yue's power remained concentrated further east and south.

w4-300087.name: Chu annexation of Chen (479 BCE)
w4-300087.blurb: Chu absorbed the state of Chen in 479 BCE, ending Chen's existence as an independent polity. The territory (centroid lng 114.7 / lat 34.6, modern eastern Henan) had long been under Chu's political pressure; Chu formally annexed it after a military campaign during the late Spring and Autumn period.

w4-300089.name: Ajatashatru's conquest of the Malla republics
w4-300089.blurb: Ajatashatru, the Haryanka king of Magadha, campaigned northward against the Malla republican confederacies (centered around Kushinara and Pava, near modern Gorakhpur/Deoria) as part of his broader war against the Vajji confederation c. 484–468 BCE. Buddhist sources record that the Malla republics, like the Licchavis, were absorbed into Magadha's growing empire during this period of Ajatashatru's expansionist reign.

w4-300090.name: Ajatashatru's absorption of the Chedi Janapada
w4-300090.blurb: The Janapada of Chedi (Cedi), centered in the Bundelkhand region (modern Madhya Pradesh/Uttar Pradesh border), was absorbed into the expanding Haryanka Magadha empire under Ajatashatru or his successors c. 475–450 BCE, as Magadha systematically eliminated the independent Janapadas of the Ganges basin. While the specific campaign against Chedi is not well-documented in surviving sources, the absorption fits the broader pattern of Magadhan consolidation during this period.

w4-300091.name: Ajatashatru's war against and conquest of Kosala
w4-300091.blurb: After Bimbisara was murdered by his son Ajatashatru c. 492 BCE, the Kosala king (Bimbisara's brother-in-law) demanded back the Kashi revenues that had been granted as dowry; war followed, and after initial reverses Ajatashatru ultimately defeated Kosala and absorbed its territory into Magadha by c. 475 BCE. Buddhist texts record that Ajatashatru also captured the Kosala crown prince, further cementing Magadhan dominance over the central Gangetic plain.

w4-300092.name: Ajatashatru's war against the Vajji confederacy
w4-300092.blurb: Ajatashatru of Magadha fought a prolonged 16-year war (c. 484–468 BCE) against the Vajji confederacy led by the Licchavis of Vaishali, ultimately defeating them and annexing their territory north of the Ganges. Buddhist and Jain texts record that Ajatashatru used novel military technology — a catapult (mahashilakantaka) and a scythed chariot — to defeat the republican Vajji forces, and the conquest ended the independence of the most powerful republic in northern India.

w4-300094.name: Magadhan conquest of the Vatsa kingdom
w4-300094.blurb: The Vatsa kingdom (Vamsa), centered at Kaushambi on the Yamuna River, was conquered by Magadha's Haryanka dynasty under Ajatashatru or his son Udayin c. 465–450 BCE; Puranic sources name Udayin as the king who moved the capital from Rajgir to Pataliputra (Patna) and record Vatsa's absorption into Magadha. The conquest gave Magadha control of the strategic Yamuna-Ganges confluence and access to the western Gangetic plain.

w4-300095.name: Greek victories at Salamis and Plataea (Persian withdrawal from Macedonia)
w4-300095.blurb: Following the Greek naval victory at Salamis in 480 BC and the decisive land victory at Plataea in 479 BC, Persian forces withdrew from Europe. Macedonia, which had been under nominal Persian suzerainty during the invasion, reverted to independent Macedonian control under Alexander I, who had served as a Persian vassal but now realigned with the Greek victors.

w4-300097.name: Partition of Jin — Zhao recognized as independent state
w4-300097.blurb: Following the Battle of Jinyang in 453 BCE, when Zhao, Wei, and Han defeated and eliminated the Zhi clan, the three families steadily divided Jin's territory. In 403 BCE, the Zhou king formally recognized Zhao, Wei, and Han as independent states. The territory around modern Hebei (centroid ~114.3°E, 37.0°N, near Handan) passed from the Jin polity label to Zhao.

w4-300099.name: Qi absorption of Zhu during the Tian clan consolidation period
w4-300099.blurb: The small state of Zhu in southern Shandong (centroid lng 117.7 / lat 35.2) was absorbed into Qi during the late 5th century BCE as the Tian clan consolidated its grip on Qi and expanded at the expense of minor surrounding polities. Zhu's formal extinction is traditionally dated to around 431–430 BCE.

w4-300101.name: Shishunaga's conquest of Avanti
w4-300101.blurb: Around 413 BCE, Shishunaga, founder of the Shaishunaga dynasty of Magadha, defeated the Pradyota dynasty of Avanti, ending centuries of rivalry between the two kingdoms and annexing Avanti into the Magadha realm; this significantly expanded Magadha's territory into central India.

w4-300102.name: Shishunaga's popular uprising and founding of the Shaishunaga dynasty
w4-300102.blurb: Around 413 BCE, Shishunaga, a minister (amatya) serving under the unpopular Haryanka king Nagadasaka, was chosen by the people of Magadha in a popular uprising that expelled the Haryanka line. Shishunaga then founded the second Magadhan dynasty named after himself, keeping Rajgir as capital and using Vaishali as a secondary base, while further consolidating power by defeating the rival Pradyota dynasty of Avanti.

w4-300103.name: Partition of Jin
w4-300103.blurb: After the three ministerial clans (Zhao, Wei, Han) destroyed the Zhi clan at the Battle of Jinyang in 453 BCE, they divided Jin's territories among themselves. In 403 BCE the Zhou king formally recognized Wei, Han (韓), and Zhao as independent states. The territory around 115°E, 38°N (southern Hebei corridor) passed to Wei, one of the 'Three Jins' that emerged from the partition of Jin.

w4-300106.name: Peace of Callias
w4-300106.blurb: The Peace of Callias (c. 449 BCE) ended the Greco-Persian Wars; Persia agreed to withdraw from the Aegean coast of Anatolia and not sail warships west of the Chelidonian Islands, effectively leaving Greek city-states in control of the coastal regions of Asia Minor that had been under Achaemenid suzerainty.

w4-300107.name: Partition of Jin / Rise of Han as independent state
w4-300107.blurb: Following the Battle of Jinyang (453 BCE) which eliminated the Zhi clan, Jin's territory was progressively absorbed by the Zhao, Wei, and Han ministerial clans. By 403 BCE, King Weilie of Zhou formally recognized Han, Wei, and Zhao as independent marquessates. The centroid (lng 112.4°E lat 35.3°N) in southern Shanxi/northern Henan corresponds to Han's core territory centered on Yidu, which was officially transferred from Jin sovereignty to Han.

w4-300109.name: Peace of Antalcidas (King's Peace)
w4-300109.blurb: The King's Peace (Peace of Antalcidas), dictated by the Persian king Artaxerxes II in 387/386 BCE, formally surrendered the Greek cities of Asia Minor — along with Cyprus and Clazomenae — to Achaemenid control, while declaring the other Greek states autonomous. The coastal and Cypriot communities near this point (lng 30.9, lat 35.9) thus passed firmly under the Persian King rather than to any Greek city-state hegemony. The settlement entrenched Persian authority over the Anatolian seaboard for a generation, with Sparta acting as the guarantor of the terms on the King's behalf.

w4-300110.name: Corinthian War and dissolution of Spartan hegemony
w4-300110.blurb: The Corinthian War (395–387 BCE) pitted a coalition of Thebes, Athens, Corinth, and Argos (backed by Achaemenid Persia) against Sparta, destroying Spartan naval supremacy at the Battle of Cnidus (394 BCE) and allowing Athens and other city-states to reassert independence from the Peloponnesian League's postwar hegemony.

w4-300112.name: Zhao-Han invasion of Wei after Marquis Wu's death (Battle of Zhuoze)
w4-300112.blurb: When Marquis Wu of Wei died in 370 BCE without naming an heir, Zhao and Han formed a coalition, invaded Wei, and defeated Wei's forces at the Battle of Zhuoze in 369 BCE, nearly partitioning the state during the succession war of the future King Hui. Zhao and Han's disagreement over how to divide Wei let it survive, but Zhao emerged with gains in the Wei-Zhao-Han borderlands (modern southern Hebei/northern Henan) from this campaign.

w4-300113.name: Zhao expansion into former Zheng territory during Zhao's eastward push
w4-300113.blurb: By 370 BCE the state of Zheng no longer existed: Han had annexed it in 375 BCE, absorbing its core around modern Xinzheng (northern Henan). The territory near this point (lng 114.5 / lat 35.3), on the southern Hebei / northern Henan border, was therefore part of Han, not Zheng, and any frontier loss to Zhao at this date reflects Zhao pressure on Han's northern marches during the early Warring States rivalry among the Three Jins. The Zheng label at -370 is anachronistic, as Zheng had already been extinguished five years earlier.

w4-300114.name: Peace of Antalcidas (King's Peace)
w4-300114.blurb: The King's Peace (Peace of Antalcidas) of 387/386 BC, brokered by Artaxerxes II, recognized Persia's sovereignty over all Greek cities in Asia Minor and Cyprus. Greek city-states on the Anatolian coast (lng ~31, lat ~35.7, consistent with Cilicia/Cyprus region) were formally handed to the Achaemenid Empire, ending their autonomy.

w4-300115.name: Foundation of the Second Athenian League
w4-300115.blurb: The Second Athenian League (Symmachy) was founded in 378/377 BC as a defensive alliance against Spartan imperialism, initially attracting over 60 member states across the Aegean. Athens organized formerly independent Greek city-states into the League structure, giving the alliance collective control of considerable territory across the Aegean littoral.

w4-300116.name: Battle of Leuctra and Theban hegemony
w4-300116.blurb: At the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BC, Epaminondas of Thebes shattered the Spartan army, killing around 400 Spartiates including the co-king Cleombrotus I. The Sacred Band's invincibility and Epaminondas's oblique tactics ended Spartan supremacy, allowing Thebes to dissolve the Peloponnesian League's effective control over central Greece and establish Theban hegemony.

w4-300117.name: Theban Hegemony — Battle of Leuctra and its aftermath
w4-300117.blurb: After the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE, where Epaminondas and the Theban Sacred Band led by Pelopidas broke Spartan power, Thebes rose to brief hegemony over central and northern Greece. Through the 360s BCE Theban influence extended into Boeotia, Phocis, and Thessaly (centered roughly 39.4 degrees N, 22.4 degrees E), with the elite Sacred Band serving as the spearhead of Theban arms until its destruction at Chaeronea in 338 BCE.

w4-300118.name: Zhongshan resurgence and expansion into Zhao territory
w4-300118.blurb: After Zhongshan regained independence from Wei around 381 BCE, it expanded into adjacent Zhao-controlled territory in the central Hebei region (lng 116.7°E lat 39.3°N, near modern Baoding). Zhongshan's aggressive expansion northward into Zhao lands is documented in sources from this period, and this location corresponds to the contested zone between Zhongshan's capital at Gu (Pingshan) and Zhao's territory.

w4-300119.name: Han annexation of Zheng
w4-300119.blurb: In 375 BCE the state of Han (韓) invaded and extinguished the state of Zheng (鄭), relocating the Han capital to Zheng's former capital at Xinzheng; this ended Zheng's centuries-long existence as a Zhou vassal and gave Han control of central Henan.

w4-300120.name: Death of Epaminondas at Battle of Mantinea and collapse of Theban hegemony
w4-300120.blurb: Epaminondas of Thebes was killed at the Battle of Mantinea (362 BCE), and with him the Theban hegemony over central Greece collapsed; the Sacred Band and other Theban political-military structures lost coherence as a separate entity, with territory reverting to generic 'Theban' civic control.

w4-300121.name: Wei-Zhao wars / Zhao gains northern Wei territory
w4-300121.blurb: During the 360s–350s BCE, Wei under King Hui and Zhao fought a series of border wars. The Battle of Guiling (353 BCE) saw Qi intervene on Zhao's behalf, ultimately weakening Wei and allowing Zhao to recover and expand in northern territory (centroid lng 114.4°E lat 37.4°N, south-central Hebei). This Zhao gain of former Wei territory in northern Hebei is consistent with Wei's strategic overextension during King Hui's reign.

w4-300123.name: Qin conquest of western Wei territories (Battle of Shaoliang / Wei cedes west-of-Yellow-River)
w4-300123.blurb: In the 360s-350s BCE, a reformed Qin under Duke Xiao and his minister Shang Yang pressed Wei for the Hexi region west of the Yellow River, building on victories at Shimen and Shaoliang (362 BCE). In 354 BCE, while Wei was committed against Zhao at Handan, Qin stormed the Wei fortress of Yuanli and seized part of Hexi (around 111.7 degrees E, 36.4 degrees N, on the modern Shanxi-Shaanxi border). The Cliopatria geometry tags this contested frontier zone as passing to Qin, reflecting Qin's westward consolidation rather than a direct Zhao cession.

w4-300124.name: Battle of Chaeronea
w4-300124.blurb: At the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, Philip II of Macedon and his son Alexander decisively defeated the allied Greek forces of Athens and Thebes. The Sacred Band of Thebes — 300 elite warriors — were annihilated, their remains later found beneath the Lion of Chaeronea monument, ending Theban military power and establishing Macedonian hegemony over Greece.

w4-300125.name: Philip II's subjugation of Thrace and the Odrysian Kingdom
w4-300125.blurb: Philip II of Macedon campaigned systematically into Thrace during the 350s BCE, subjugating the western Odrysian king Cetriporis and reducing Greek coastal cities along the Hebrus River, incorporating large swaths of Odrysian territory into the expanding Macedonian state.

w4-300126.name: Philip II's Macedonian conquests in Thessaly and central Greece
w4-300126.blurb: Philip II of Macedon seized Thessaly following the Battle of Crocus Field (352 BCE), destroying a Phocian force and becoming tagos (leader) of the Thessalian League; he simultaneously absorbed Amphipolis (357 BCE) and Pydna (357 BCE) from Athenian-aligned Greek city-states, transforming Macedonia from a peripheral kingdom into the dominant power in the Aegean north.

w4-300127.name: Philip II Subjugates Thrace
w4-300127.blurb: Philip II of Macedon campaigned against the Odrysian Kingdom of Thrace between 342 and 340 BCE, defeating and subjugating the Odrysian king Cersobleptes and annexing most of Thrace to the Macedonian sphere, consolidating Macedonian control over the northern Aegean hinterland.

w4-300128.name: Artaxerxes III's reconquest of Egypt
w4-300128.blurb: Artaxerxes III of Persia launched a three-pronged campaign against Egypt circa 343 BCE, defeating Nectanebo II (last pharaoh of the 30th Dynasty) at Pelusium and Bubastis. Nectanebo II fled to Nubia, and Egypt became the 31st (Achaemenid) Dynasty; Artaxerxes sacked temples and imposed a satrap (Pherendares).

w4-300129.name: Qin–Han war: Qin seizes Han territories in the Wei River / Fen River area
w4-300129.blurb: Following Shang Yang's military reforms and Qin's victory over Wei at the Battle of Shaoliang (364 BCE) and subsequent campaigns, Qin pressed Han for territories along the Wei and Fen River valleys (centroid lng 111.2 / lat 35, modern southern Shanxi). Han ceded border districts under military pressure from Qin during the 340s BCE as Qin systematically expanded eastward under Duke Xiao.

w4-300130.name: Wei attack on Zhao during the Wei-Zhao-Han wars
