w4-300130.blurb: During the internecine conflicts among the Three Jins in the mid-4th century BCE, Wei repeatedly attacked Zhao. Between 353 and 341 BCE, Wei under King Hui conducted multiple campaigns against Zhao, capturing territories in southern Shanxi/northern Henan (lng 112.5°E lat 36.9°N). However, the territory shows as going from Zhao to Qin in this window (-350 to -337), which more likely reflects Qin's eastward expansion under Duke Xiao of Qin and the Shang Yang reforms, as Qin took advantage of Wei's overextension after the Battle of Maling (341 BCE) to seize territory.

w4-300131.name: Destruction of Yue by Chu and formation of Minyue
w4-300131.blurb: Around 334–333 BCE, the state of Chu destroyed the ancient state of Yue, killing or scattering its royal court. Remnants of the Yue royal family fled south into the Fujian highlands and Zhejiang coast, where they established the successor polity of Minyue (Closed Yue) and maintained the Yue royal lineage. This atlas record captures the territorial reorganization as the Yue homeland passed from the old Yue state to the new Minyue entity.

w4-300133.name: Chu Conquest of Yue
w4-300133.blurb: In 333 BCE, Chu attacked the weakened state of Yue during the reign of Yue's King Wuqiang (無彊), who had overextended himself with wars against both Qi and Chu simultaneously. Yue's territory was partitioned between Chu and Qi; Chu took the western portion including the Yangtze delta region (centroid ~119°E, 32°N, present-day southern Jiangsu). This ended Yue as an independent power.

w4-300135.name: Bithynian independence from Achaemenid/Seleucid rule
w4-300135.blurb: When Alexander the Great invaded Asia in 334 BC, Bithynia under its native dynast Bas (and later Zipoites) resisted incorporation and maintained de facto independence, neither submitting to Alexander nor to the subsequent Seleucid Empire. Zipoites formally assumed the title of king of Bithynia around 297 BC, but the territory had effectively broken from Achaemenid/Seleucid control during the chaos of Alexander's conquest of Persia.

w4-300137.name: Alexander the Great's Conquest of Egypt
w4-300137.blurb: After defeating Darius III at Issus in 333 BCE, Alexander the Great marched down the Levant and entered Egypt in 332 BCE, where the Persian satrap Mazaces surrendered and Egyptians welcomed him as a liberator from Achaemenid rule. Egypt thus passed into Alexander's Macedonian empire; it became the independent Ptolemaic Kingdom only after his death in 323 BCE, when his general Ptolemy I took the satrapy and later assumed the kingship in 305 BCE.

w4-300138.name: Alexander III's conquest of Egypt and Cyrenaica
w4-300138.blurb: Following Alexander the Great's conquest of Egypt (332 BCE) and the subsequent capitulation of Cyrene, Achaemenid authority over Cyrenaica (centroid ~31.5°N, 21°E) ended by 331 BCE; the Greek cities of Cyrenaica voluntarily submitted to Alexander, ending Persian suzerainty over the region.

w4-300140.name: Armenian satrapy reasserts independence after Battle of Gaugamela
w4-300140.blurb: After the Battle of Gaugamela (1 October 331 BCE) shattered the Achaemenid Empire, the Armenian satrap Mithranes (or Orontes II) effectively ruled Armenia independently; the Orontid dynasty retained local power without submitting to the Macedonian administration, making the region functionally autonomous within years of Alexander's conquest.

w4-300141.name: Alexander the Great's Indian campaign (Battle of the Hydaspes)
w4-300141.blurb: In 326 BC Alexander the Great crossed the Indus and defeated King Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes (Jhelum), annexing the Punjab (lat 27.9, lng 70.3) into his Macedonian empire. His army mutinied at the Beas River, refusing to advance further toward the Nanda Empire. The entity label 'Ptolemaic Kingdom' is anachronistic — this territory was taken by Alexander's Macedonian Empire, not by the Ptolemaic Kingdom which only emerged after 323 BC.

citations.label: Indian campaign of Alexander the Great — Wikipedia

w4-300143.name: Partition of Babylon — Syria assigned to Laomedon
w4-300143.blurb: At the Partition of Babylon (323 BCE), which divided Alexander the Great's empire after his death, the satrapy of Syria and Phoenicia was assigned to Laomedon of Mytilene. The region passed directly from the Macedonian imperial administration to Laomedon's personal satrapy; no Ptolemaic kingdom yet existed, as Ptolemy was separately allotted Egypt at this same settlement and did not hold Syria.

w4-300144.name: Death of Alexander the Great and dissolution of the Macedonian Empire
w4-300144.blurb: Alexander the Great died at Babylon in June 323 BC without a clear successor, triggering the Wars of the Diadochi. Greek cities and leagues reasserted their autonomy in the immediate power vacuum, with territory in mainland Greece reverting to coalitions of city-states before the Macedonian generals reasserted control.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Death of Alexander the Great

w4-300145.name: Partition of Babylon
w4-300145.blurb: Following Alexander's death in Babylon (June 323 BCE), the Partition of Babylon assigned Thrace to Lysimachus. This transferred the Thracian territories from the Macedonian Empire proper to Lysimachus's personal kingdom.

w4-300146.name: Partition of Babylon / Death of Alexander
w4-300146.blurb: Upon Alexander the Great's death at Babylon (June 323 BCE), the Partition of Babylon made Perdiccas regent (epimeletes) of the whole Macedonian empire in the name of the joint kings Philip III and Alexander IV, with Babylonia and Mesopotamia under his direct authority. This central Macedonian regency endured until Perdiccas's murder and the Partition of Triparadisus (321 BCE) redistributed the satrapies.

w4-300149.name: Chandragupta Maurya's overthrow of the Nanda Empire
w4-300149.blurb: Chandragupta Maurya, advised by Kautilya (Chanakya), launched a systematic military campaign against the Nanda king Dhana Nanda, securing frontier territories before besieging the capital Pataliputra and defeating the Nandas c. 321 BCE, founding the Maurya Empire. The conquest absorbed the vast Nanda realm across the Gangetic plain, Odisha, and central India, representing the largest political transition in South Asian history to that point.

w4-300150.name: Partition of Triparadisus
w4-300150.blurb: At the Partition of Triparadisus in 321 BCE, following the murder of the regent Perdiccas, the Diadochi redistributed Alexander's satrapies: Seleucus received Babylonia, laying the territorial and political foundation for the future Seleucid Empire.

w4-300151.name: Antigonus Expels Laomedon from Syria
w4-300151.blurb: After Antipater's death (319 BCE) and the outbreak of the Second Diadochi War, Antigonus I drove Laomedon of Mytilene out of Syria and Cilicia, absorbing those territories into his expanding domain and reversing Laomedon's brief tenure granted at the Partition of Triparadisus.

w4-300152.name: Lamian War — dissolution of Athenian Coalition
w4-300152.blurb: The Lamian War (323–322 BCE), fought by a Greek coalition led by Athens against Macedonian regent Antipater, ended with the Macedonian victory at the Battle of Crannon (322 BCE); the Athenian-led coalition was dissolved and Athens lost its hegemonic position (~24,000 km² reverting to decentralized Greek city-states).

w4-300154.name: Antipater Names Polyperchon Regent
w4-300154.blurb: Antipater, dying regent of Macedonia, bypassed his son Cassander and named Polyperchon as his successor regent in 319 BCE; Polyperchon thereby took control of Macedonia and a large portion of northern Greece, triggering a civil war with Cassander.

w4-300155.name: Chandragupta Maurya's expulsion of Macedonian governors and Seleucid-Maurya War
w4-300155.blurb: After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Chandragupta Maurya raised an army in the Punjab and systematically expelled or killed the Macedonian-appointed satraps (including Philip, assassinated ~325 BCE, and others). By ~316 BCE he had consolidated control over the Indus satrapies; the process was formally concluded by the Seleucid-Maurya treaty (~303 BCE) in which Seleucus I ceded Gandhara, Parapamisadae, and eastern Gedrosia in exchange for 500 war elephants.

w4-300156.name: Antigonus drives Seleucus from Babylon
w4-300156.blurb: In 316–315 BCE, Antigonus I Monophthalmus launched a campaign to consolidate control over Asia, forcing Seleucus to flee from Babylon to Ptolemy in Egypt; Antigonus then occupied Babylonia and the Tigris corridor, reverting atlas attribution to 'Macedonian Empire' under his hegemony until Seleucus's return in 312 BCE.

w4-300157.name: Cassander Installs Demetrius of Phalerum in Athens
w4-300157.blurb: In 317 BCE Cassander installed Demetrius of Phalerum as governor of Athens, suppressing democracy and bringing the Greek city-states of central Greece under Macedonian control; by 315 BCE Cassander had consolidated his hold over most of mainland Greece.

w4-300158.name: Cassander Defeats Polyperchon
w4-300158.blurb: By 316–315 BCE Cassander had decisively defeated the regent Polyperchon, driving him from Macedonia into the Peloponnese; the northern Macedonian territories Polyperchon had controlled reverted to Cassander's Macedonian state.

w4-300159.name: Qin campaigns against Chu under Zhang Yi / early Qin-Chu wars
w4-300159.blurb: During the 320s–310s BCE, Qin repeatedly attacked Chu's northern territories in the upper Han River valley and Danyang area (centroid lng 110.1 / lat 33, corresponding to modern western Hubei/southern Shaanxi). The 318 BCE coalition attack on Qin failed, and Qin retaliated by seizing Chu territory around 317–315 BCE, culminating in the Battle of Danyang (312 BCE) which formalized major Chu territorial losses to Qin in this region.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Danyang and Lantian

w4-300160.name: Ptolemy I's seizure of Cyprus and Aegean operations
w4-300160.blurb: During the Wars of the Diadochi, Ptolemy I of Egypt seized Cyprus around 312–310 BC and expanded his naval presence into the Aegean, bringing islands and coastal cities of western Anatolia under Ptolemaic rather than Greek city-state control. The centroid points to the southwestern Aegean / Rhodes area, consistent with Ptolemaic expansion in the region around 307 BC.

w4-300161.name: Peace of the Diadochi (311 BCE)
w4-300161.blurb: In 311 BCE the surviving Diadochi — Antigonus, Cassander, Lysimachus, and Ptolemy — concluded a general peace that formally recognized Ptolemy's control of Egypt and its dependencies. The atlas reflects this diplomatic recognition as the territorial transition from the nominal Macedonian Empire to the Ptolemaic sphere.

w4-300162.name: Foundation of Atropatene by Atropates
w4-300162.blurb: Atropates, the Persian satrap of Media Atropatene who had served both the Achaemenids and Alexander, refused to submit to the post-Alexander Macedonian administration; after the death of Perdiccas in 321 BCE — his son-in-law — he established the independent kingdom of Atropatene (modern Azerbaijan/northwestern Iran), named after himself.

w4-300163.name: Babylonian War / Anabasis of Seleucus
w4-300163.blurb: After the Battle of Gaza (312 BCE) Seleucus retook Babylon, then waged the Babylonian War (311–309 BCE) to expel Antigonus's forces from the eastern satrapies. By 307 BCE the vast Iranian and Central Asian satrapies — Persia, Media, Bactria, Sogdia, and beyond — were firmly under Seleucid control.

w4-300164.name: Battle of Ipsus
w4-300164.blurb: At the Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE) in Phrygia, the coalition of Seleucus I, Lysimachus, and Cassander defeated and killed Antigonus I Monophthalmus, ending Antigonid dominance in Asia. The victors partitioned Antigonus's realm: Seleucus gained northern Syria and eastern Asia Minor, territory that had been under Antigonid control before the battle — not Ptolemaic, since Ptolemy took no part in the engagement (he had only raided Coele-Syria and withdrawn).

w4-300165.name: Battle of Ipsus
w4-300165.blurb: At Ipsus in 301 BCE, Seleucus and Lysimachus defeated and killed Antigonus I Monophthalmus, ending Antigonid control of Asia. Seleucus gained Syria, eastern Anatolia, and the remaining Iranian satrapies, consolidating the western core of what the atlas labels as Seleucid.

w4-300166.name: Seleucus–Maurya Treaty (Treaty of the Indus)
w4-300166.blurb: Following inconclusive fighting c. 305–303 BCE, Seleucus I ceded the eastern satrapies of Gandhara, Paropamisadae, Gedrosia, and Arachosia to Chandragupta Maurya in exchange for 500 war elephants and a dynastic marriage alliance. The elephants later proved decisive at the Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE).

w4-300168.name: Battle of Ipsus — Ptolemaic gain of Coele-Syria
w4-300168.blurb: After Ipsus (301 BCE), Ptolemy I — who had not participated in the battle but had occupied Coele-Syria and Cilicia during the campaign — retained those territories despite Seleucus's claims; the Ptolemaic acquisition of coastal Cilicia and southern Syria was an immediate consequence of Antigonus's defeat.

w4-300169.name: Battle of Ipsus
w4-300169.blurb: The coalition of Seleucus I, Lysimachus, and Cassander defeated and killed Antigonus I Monophthalmus at Ipsus in Phrygia (301 BCE). Lysimachus received the remainder of Asia Minor as his share, consolidating his kingdom over Thrace and western Anatolia.

w4-300171.name: Magas reasserts Ptolemaic control over Cyrenaica
w4-300171.blurb: After Ophellas's death (308 BCE) and further Cyrenaican unrest following Ptolemy I's assumption of the kingship (c. 305 BCE), Ptolemy I dispatched his young stepson Magas, c. 300 BCE, to reconquer Cyrenaica; Magas then governed it as a loyal Ptolemaic governor for decades before later declaring independence (c. 276 BCE).

w4-300172.name: Ptolemaic acquisition of Cyprus and the Levant
w4-300172.blurb: Between ~298 and 295 BC, Ptolemy I consolidated control over Cyprus (defeating Demetrius Poliorcetes at the Battle of Salamis in Cyprus in 306 BC, though temporarily lost and regained) and Levantine territories. The centroid points to Cyprus, which Ptolemy definitively secured around 294 BC after Demetrius's final removal from Cyprus.

w4-300173.name: Demetrius I Seizes Macedonia
w4-300173.blurb: After Cassander's death (297 BCE) left Macedonia in civil strife among his sons, Demetrius Poliorcetes seized the Macedonian throne in 294 BCE by killing Alexander V, becoming the first Antigonid king of Macedonia and establishing the dynasty's rule over mainland Greece and Macedonia.

w4-300174.name: Demetrius Poliorcetes loses Macedonia — Greek cities reassert autonomy
w4-300174.blurb: In 288 BCE, Pyrrhus and Lysimachus jointly invaded and expelled Demetrius Poliorcetes from Macedonia; the Antigonid hold on mainland Greece briefly fragmented, allowing Greek city-states (centroid ~39.3°N, 22°E, Thessaly region) to reassert autonomy before Antigonus Gonatas restored Macedonian power after Lysimachia (277 BCE).

w4-300177.name: Destruction of Song / Five-State Attack on Qi
w4-300177.blurb: In 286 BCE, Qi destroyed Song and absorbed most of its territory (centroid lng 115.4°E lat 35.5°N, the eastern Song core). This was the primary Qi territorial gain, though it immediately provoked the five-state coalition attack on Qi in 284 BCE. The Song-to-Qi transfer is dated to Qi's conquest of Song in 286 BCE under King Min of Qi.

w4-300178.name: Five-State Coalition Attack on Qi – Chu gains southern Qi territory
w4-300178.blurb: In 284 BCE, a five-state coalition (Yan, Qin, Wei, Zhao, Han) launched a massive assault on Qi, routing its forces at the Battle of Jiqiu and conquering nearly all of Qi. Chu participated by seizing Qi's southeastern territories (centroid lng 118.6°E lat 35.3°N, in northern Jiangsu/southern Shandong), which Chu retained even after Qi's partial recovery under Tian Dan after 279 BCE.

citations.label: Wikipedia – Five States Campaign against Qi

w4-300179.name: Destruction of Song
w4-300179.blurb: In 286 BCE, Qi invaded and destroyed the state of Song; Chu and Wei contributed forces to the campaign and received portions of Song's southern and western territories respectively. The centroid (lng 116.2°E lat 34.6°N) places this parcel in southern Song, which passed to Chu as part of the tripartite division of Song's territory.

w4-300180.name: Battle of Corupedium and Lysimachus's defeat
w4-300180.blurb: At the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BC, Seleucus I defeated and killed Lysimachus, ending the latter's control over Thrace and Macedonia. The ensuing power vacuum in Macedonia brought Seleucid influence toward the Aegean and permitted the Antigonid dynasty (under Antigonus Gonatas) to begin consolidating control over Greek city-states in Macedonia and northern Greece.

w4-300181.name: Battle of Corupedium
w4-300181.blurb: At Corupedium in Lydia (281 BCE), Seleucus I Nicator defeated and killed Lysimachus, whose kingdom dissolved. Seleucus gained control of most of Asia Minor and briefly claimed all of Alexander's former empire before being assassinated by Ptolemy Keraunos shortly after.

w4-300183.name: Bithynian independence after Battle of Corupedium
w4-300183.blurb: Following the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BC and Seleucus I's assassination in 280 BC, the Seleucid hold on northwestern Asia Minor collapsed. Zipoites of Bithynia exploited this chaos, defeating Seleucid forces and firmly establishing Bithynian independence; by ~279 BC the kingdom was de facto free of Seleucid control.

w4-300185.name: Galatian settlement of central Anatolia
w4-300185.blurb: In 279 BCE a contingent of Gauls (Galatians) split from Brennus's main force and were transported to Asia Minor by Nicomedes I of Bithynia; after raiding widely they settled in the barren central Anatolian highlands (~50,000 km²) that thereafter bore their name — Galatia — displacing Seleucid authority in the region.

w4-300186.name: Philetaerus rules Pergamon autonomously under nominal Seleucid suzerainty
w4-300186.blurb: Philetaerus, the Greek commander of the fortress and treasury of Pergamon, deserted Lysimachus in 282 BCE and offered himself, the citadel, and its 9,000 talents to Seleucus I. After Seleucus defeated and killed Lysimachus at Corupedium (281 BCE) and was himself assassinated soon after, Philetaerus governed Pergamon with considerable de facto autonomy while remaining nominally under Seleucid suzerainty. He used the treasury to build influence across western Anatolia, founding the line that would become the independent Attalid kingdom — though full independence came only under his successors after his death in 263 BCE.

w4-300187.name: Antigonus Gonatas defeats Galatians at Battle of Lysimachia
w4-300187.blurb: Antigonus Gonatas (Antigonid Dynasty) defeated a large Galatian force near Lysimachia in Thrace c. 277 BCE, using war elephants to rout them; this victory legitimized his claim to Macedonia and allowed the consolidation of the Antigonid Dynasty into 'Antigonid Macedonia,' reconstituting control over the Greek peninsula (~33,000 km²).

w4-300188.name: Battle of Yanying (Qin Sack of Chu Capital Ying)
w4-300188.blurb: In 278 BCE, Qin general Bai Qi launched a devastating campaign against Chu, capturing and sacking the Chu capital Ying (郢, near modern Jingzhou, Hubei). In 277 BCE Bai Qi further seized the Qianzhong commandery in the Yangtze gorge area (centroid ~110°E, 32°N, upper Han River / Three Gorges region), pushing Chu's western frontier far to the east. King Qingxiang of Chu fled to the east, never recovering these territories.

w4-300189.name: Revolt of Magas of Cyrene
w4-300189.blurb: Magas, governor of Cyrene and half-brother of Ptolemy II, crowned himself independent king of Cyrenaica around 276 BCE, breaking from Ptolemaic rule. His attempted invasion of Egypt in 274 BCE failed due to a revolt by the Libyan Marmaridae tribe, but his independent kingdom endured until his death around 250 BCE.

w4-300198.name: Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga
w4-300198.blurb: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered the kingdom of Kalinga (on the eastern Indian coast around modern Odisha) around 261 BC in a famously bloody war. As recorded in his own rock edicts, the immense slaughter led to his conversion to Buddhism and renunciation of further conquest. The transfer of Kalinga's territory to the Maurya Empire reflects this pivotal annexation.

w4-300199.name: Second Syrian War — Antiochus II's reconquest of Cilicia, Pamphylia and Ionia
w4-300199.blurb: In the Second Syrian War (c. 260-253 BCE), Antiochus II Theos, allied with Antigonus II Gonatas of Macedon, reversed Ptolemy II's earlier First Syrian War gains, retaking Miletus, Ephesus, and expelling Ptolemaic forces from Cilicia and Pamphylia (complete by 254/253 BCE). This -- not the earlier First Syrian War -- accounts for the Ptolemaic-to-Seleucid transfer in Cilicia/southern Asia Minor.

w4-300203.name: Independence of Sophene under Orontid rule
w4-300203.blurb: Sophene, an Armenian highland kingdom in the upper Euphrates region, emerged as an independent Orontid realm distinct from Greater Armenia in the mid-third century BC as Seleucid central authority weakened. The Orontid dynasty split into branches ruling Armenia and Sophene separately, with Sophene controlling the lands around Arsamosata near the Euphrates bend. The transfer reflects this dynastic partition of Orontid Armenia.

w4-300204.name: Reintegration of Cyrenaica into the Ptolemaic Kingdom
w4-300204.blurb: Cyrenaica, the Greek pentapolis of Libya, had broken away from Ptolemaic control under Magas of Cyrene, who ruled it as an independent king. After Magas's death (c. 250 BC) the region was reunited with Egypt through the marriage of his daughter Berenice II to Ptolemy III Euergetes, restoring Cyrenaica to direct Ptolemaic rule. This dynastic union returned the territory to the Ptolemaic Kingdom by the start of Ptolemy III's reign in 246 BC.

w4-300206.name: Secession of Bactria under Diodotus I
w4-300206.blurb: Diodotus I, the Seleucid satrap of Bactria, revolted against Antiochus II Theos and declared independence around 250 BC, founding the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. Taking advantage of Seleucid distraction in the west during the Third Syrian War, he seized the rich eastern provinces around Bactra. This breakaway permanently removed Bactria and its environs from the Seleucid Empire.

w4-300210.name: Third Syrian War (Laodicean War)
w4-300210.blurb: In the Third Syrian War (246-241 BC), Ptolemy III Euergetes invaded the Seleucid realm after the murder of his sister Berenice and her son. Ptolemaic forces overran much of Cilicia and the coastal regions of Asia Minor (around 33E, 37N), seizing Seleucid territory. These gains in southern Anatolia passed from the Seleucids to the Ptolemaic Kingdom during the conflict.

w4-300211.name: Parthian conquest of Parthia and Hyrcania under Arsaces I
w4-300211.blurb: Around 247-238 BC the Parni under Arsaces I invaded the Seleucid satrapy of Parthia, killing or expelling the satrap Andragoras and establishing the Arsacid (Parthian) state. The region around northeastern Iran (57.7E, 37.9N) was wrested from Seleucid control as Seleucid power waned during the Third Syrian War. This founded the Parthian Empire that would dominate Iran for centuries.

w4-300212.name: Independence of Cappadocia under Ariarathes III
w4-300212.blurb: Cappadocia, long a semi-autonomous satrapy under the Ariarathid dynasty, asserted full independence from the Seleucids when Ariarathes III assumed the royal title around 245 BC, exploiting Seleucid weakness during the Third Syrian War. The interior Anatolian highlands (36E, 38.7N) thus passed from nominal Seleucid suzerainty to the independent Kingdom of Cappadocia. Ariarathes cemented the break by marrying a Seleucid princess as an equal.

w4-300214.name: Roman seizure of Sardinia and Corsica
w4-300214.blurb: After the First Punic War, Carthage was crippled by the Mercenary War (240-237 BC). Rome exploited this to seize Sardinia (and Corsica) in 238/237 BC, threatening war unless Carthage ceded the islands and paid additional indemnity. This annexation of Sardinia (centered near 9E, 41N) from Carthage to the Roman Republic embittered relations and was cited by Polybius as a cause of the Second Punic War.

citations.label: Roman conquest of Sardinia and Corsica (Wikipedia)

w4-300215.name: Achaean League expansion under Aratus of Sicyon
w4-300215.blurb: Under Aratus of Sicyon, the Achaean League expanded across the Peloponnese in the 240s-230s BC, liberating cities from Antigonid Macedonian garrisons and tyrants. The most famous coup was Aratus's seizure of the Acrocorinth from the Macedonians in 243 BC, with further Peloponnesian gains (around 22E, 37.4N) following. These acquisitions transferred Macedonian-controlled territory to the Achaean League.

w4-300218.name: Macedonian withdrawal from Thrace and northern Aegean
w4-300218.blurb: Around 229 BC, the Antigonid king Demetrius II died fighting Illyrian and Dardanian invaders, leaving Macedonia weakened and unable to hold its outer territories. Greek city-states in northern Greece (centroid lng 25.4, lat 39.6 — the Thracian/northern Aegean coast) re-emerged as autonomous entities during the regency crisis that followed, before Philip V consolidated Macedonian power.

w4-300219.name: Qin conquest of Zhao
w4-300219.blurb: In the wars of unification, Qin under Ying Zheng (later Qin Shi Huang) attacked Zhao after a devastating earthquake and famine weakened it. Qin general Wang Jian defeated the Zhao army and captured the capital Handan (near 114E, 36.2N) in 228 BC, taking King Youmiu prisoner. The bulk of Zhao's heartland passed to Qin, though a remnant held out as Dai until 222 BC.

w4-300220.name: Attalid expansion under Attalus I after victory over the Galatians and Seleucids
w4-300220.blurb: Attalus I of Pergamon, having defeated the Galatians, took the royal title and fought the Seleucid pretender Antiochus Hierax in a series of battles in Asia Minor around 230-228 BC. His victories extended Pergamene control over much of Seleucid Anatolia north of the Taurus, including western Asia Minor around (27.8E, 38.9N). This expanded the Kingdom of Pergamon at Seleucid expense.

w4-300221.name: Kalinga's independence / pre-Ashokan frontier
w4-300221.blurb: Kalinga, the powerful eastern Indian kingdom on the Bay of Bengal coast (around 84E, 19N), remained independent of Mauryan control after the time of Chandragupta and Bindusara. The region around the Mahanadi delta consolidated as the Kalinga kingdom outside Maurya rule, a status that would persist until Ashoka's bloody conquest of 261 BC in the next generation. This entry reflects Kalinga holding territory distinct from the Maurya Empire.

w4-300225.name: Fourth Syrian War — Antiochus III's reconquest of Coele-Syria (initial phase)
w4-300225.blurb: In the opening campaigns of the Fourth Syrian War (219-217 BC), Antiochus III the Great invaded Ptolemaic Coele-Syria, capturing Seleucia Pieria and overrunning much of the Levant including the region around (36E, 34.7N). These early gains transferred Ptolemaic-held Syrian territory to the Seleucid Empire before the war's climax at Raphia. The Ptolemies would later recover this ground after their victory at Raphia in 217 BC.

w4-300226.name: Qin Unification of China — Final Conquests
w4-300226.blurb: Between 230 and 221 BCE, Qin conquered the remaining six Warring States in rapid succession, unifying China under Qin Shi Huang. The change from 'Qin' (the pre-imperial state) to 'Qin Dynasty' at -222 to -218 reflects the atlas convention of relabeling after Ying Zheng's proclamation as First Emperor in 221 BCE following the conquest of Qi, the last holdout. The large territory around 112°E, 35°N (present-day Henan/Shanxi corridor) was the former heartland of Han (韓) and Wei states absorbed in 230–225 BCE.

w4-300227.name: Founding of the Qin Dynasty (unification of China under Qin Shi Huang)
w4-300227.blurb: In 221 BC, having conquered all six rival states, King Ying Zheng of Qin proclaimed himself Qin Shi Huang, First Emperor, founding the Qin Dynasty and unifying China. The transfer of the entire Qin domain (over 1.5 million km2, centered near 112.7E, 35.1N) from the state of Qin to the Qin Dynasty reflects this transformation from a warring state into the first imperial dynasty. It marked the birth of imperial China.

w4-300230.name: Fourth Syrian War — Antiochus III's conquest of Coele-Syria
w4-300230.blurb: Continuing the Fourth Syrian War, Antiochus III advanced through Coele-Syria and Palestine in 218 BC, defeating Ptolemaic forces and occupying much of the southern Levant (around 36E, 33.4N) before the Battle of Raphia. This phase transferred further Ptolemaic Syrian territory to the Seleucid Empire. The Ptolemies recovered these lands only after Ptolemy IV's decisive win at Raphia in 217 BC.

w4-300233.name: Qin conquest of the Baiyue / Minyue south
w4-300233.blurb: After unifying China, Qin Shi Huang launched campaigns against the Baiyue peoples of the south, including the Minyue of Fujian and the regions around (118.8E, 28.2N). Qin armies pushed into the southeast, establishing the commandery of Minzhong over the Minyue lands around 214 BC. This expansion absorbed Minyue territory into the Qin Dynasty's southern frontier.

citations.label: Qin campaign against the Yue tribes (Wikipedia)

w4-300234.name: Antiochus III's eastern (anabasis) campaign and the submission of Armenia
w4-300234.blurb: Around 212 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus III the Great launched his great eastern campaign (anabasis) to restore Seleucid authority over breakaway provinces. He compelled the Armenian dynast Xerxes of Armenia to submit, recovering control of Armenian territory for the Seleucid Empire. This brought the Armenian highlands back under Seleucid suzerainty before Antiochus pressed further east toward Parthia and Bactria.

w4-300237.name: Xiang Yu's rebellion and the rise of Western Chu
w4-300237.blurb: Amid the anti-Qin revolts after 210 BC, Xiang Liang and his nephew Xiang Yu raised an army in the Chu heartland (around modern Anhui-Jiangsu), restoring the kingdom of Chu that became Xiang Yu's Western Chu. Their forces drove Qin authority from the lower Huai region. This shifted former Qin territory in the east-central plain to the rebel kingdom of Chu.

w4-300241.name: Anti-Qin rebellions and the restoration of Qi (Jibei region)
w4-300241.blurb: As Qin authority disintegrated after 210 BC, the Tian clan restored the old state of Qi on the Shandong peninsula, including the Jibei area near modern Tai'an. Tian Dan and his kin expelled the Qin administration and proclaimed a revived kingdom. This moved former Qin territory in the east to the restored Qi/Jibei polity.

w4-300243.name: Xiang Yu's Eighteen Kingdoms partition — Jiujiang established
w4-300243.blurb: In 206 BCE, after overthrowing the Qin Dynasty, Xiang Yu redistributed the empire into eighteen feudal kingdoms. The territory around modern central-southern Anhui (centroid ~117.4°E, 31.5°N), previously administered as part of the undivided rebel-held zone (here labeled 'Zhai'), was assigned to Ying Bu as the Kingdom of Jiujiang. This was a deliberate political act by Xiang Yu rewarding allied generals.

w4-300245.name: Xiang Yu's Eighteen Kingdoms — former Western Chu / Han territory assigned to Henan (Shen Yang)
w4-300245.blurb: In Xiang Yu's 206 BCE partition into the Eighteen Kingdoms, the area of northern Henan (centroid lng 114.5 / lat 35) previously in the rebel Western Chu sphere was organized into the kingdom of Henan under Shen Yang, a Zhao official who administered the area under Qin's former Sanchuan commandery.

w4-300246.name: Xiang Yu's division into the Eighteen Kingdoms – Henan established from Zhai territory
w4-300246.blurb: In 206 BCE, as part of the Eighteen Kingdoms reorganization, territory in western Henan that had been under the interim Zhai (former Qin-controlled) designation (lng 113.3°E lat 35.2°N) was assigned to Shen Yang's kingdom of Henan. This parcel represents the western extent of Henan kingdom, bordering former Qin territories.

w4-300247.name: Xiang Yu's division into the Eighteen Kingdoms – Henan established from Wei territory
w4-300247.blurb: In 206 BCE, Xiang Yu assigned former Wei territory in northwestern Henan (lng 114.6°E lat 35.7°N) to Shen Yang as the kingdom of Henan. Shen Yang was a Zhao official who had defected to the rebel cause; his kingdom was positioned between Western Chu to the south and Changshan to the north, comprising the fertile Wei River corridor.

w4-300252.name: Partition into the Eighteen Kingdoms — creation of Linjiang
w4-300252.blurb: In Xiang Yu's 206 BC settlement, the middle Yangtze region around modern Jingzhou (Hubei) was made the kingdom of Linjiang under Gong Ao. This carved a new kingdom from the former Qin/Chu territory in the central Yangtze basin. Linjiang was one of the Eighteen Kingdoms of the post-Qin partition.

w4-300255.name: Xiang Yu's division into the Eighteen Kingdoms – Chang-shan established
w4-300255.blurb: In 206 BCE, Xiang Yu assigned the central Hebei region (former Dai/Zhao territory, lng 116.3°E lat 37.9°N) to Zhang Er as the kingdom of Changshan. Zhang Er had been a chancellor of Zhao and was rewarded for his service in the anti-Qin uprising; the territory was carved from former Zhao/Dai lands.

w4-300256.name: Partition into the Eighteen Kingdoms — creation of Changshan
w4-300256.blurb: In Xiang Yu's 206 BC partition, the Zhao general Zhang Er was rewarded with the kingdom of Changshan, carved from the Zhao/Dai lands around modern Shijiazhuang (Hebei). This split Changshan off from the Dai/Zhao bloc, sowing rivalry that soon reignited war. Changshan was one of the Eighteen Kingdoms.

w4-300258.name: Founding of Nanyue by Zhao Tuo
w4-300258.blurb: As Qin collapsed, the Qin commander Zhao Tuo consolidated the southern commanderies of Nanhai, Guilin, and Xiang around modern Guangzhou, and after 206 BC founded the independent kingdom of Nanyue (Nam Viet). He sealed the passes against the chaos in the north and declared himself king. This detached the far-southern territory from the former Qin/Chu sphere into the new state of Nanyue.

w4-300260.name: Reunification of Qi by Tian Rong
w4-300260.blurb: After Xiang Yu's 206 BC partition split the Shandong peninsula into Qi, Jiaodong, and Jibei, Tian Rong rebelled, killed the rival kings, and reunified the whole region as a single kingdom of Qi. This absorbed the Jibei territory (around modern Tai'an) back into a unified Qi. Tian Rong's revolt was one of the first sparks of the renewed Chu–Han Contention.

w4-300264.name: Second Punic War — Roman recovery in southern Italy
w4-300264.blurb: During the Second Punic War (218-201 BC), Rome gradually clawed back southern Italy from Hannibal's Carthaginian coalition. Around 207 BC, after the Roman victory at the Metaurus and the steady reduction of Hannibal's allies in Apulia and the southeast (near the location given), Carthaginian-aligned control of the region collapsed. This restored territory in southeastern Italy to the Roman Republic.

w4-300268.name: Tian Rong's reunification of Qi (conquest of Jibei and Jiaodong)
w4-300268.blurb: After the fall of Qin, Xiang Yu's 206 BC partition split the old state of Qi into three kingdoms, including Jibei and Jiaodong. The Qi general Tian Rong, angered at being excluded, rose in revolt in 206 BC and overran the other Qi kingdoms to reunify the region; here Jibei's territory passes to the Jiaodong jurisdiction during that consolidation. This rebellion helped trigger Xiang Yu's punitive campaign into Qi.

w4-300270.name: Xiang Yu's Eighteen Kingdoms — former Wei territory assigned to Yin (Sima Ang)
w4-300270.blurb: In Xiang Yu's 206 BCE Eighteen Kingdoms partition, the northern portion of the former Warring States state of Wei (centroid lng 115.0 / lat 36.6, modern northern Henan / southern Hebei) was incorporated into the kingdom of Yin under Sima Ang, who had been a Zhao general. This area had been under the late-Qin administrative system and was redistributed alongside the former Zhai territory.

w4-300272.name: Minyue expansion during Chu-Han contention
w4-300272.blurb: During the Chu-Han Contention (206–202 BCE), Zou Wuzhu (騶無諸), the Yue ruler of Minyue (閩越) in modern Fujian, sided with Liu Bang against Xiang Yu's Western Chu. Amid the collapse of the regional order, Minyue pushed its authority northward along the coast at the expense of its neighbours, including territory on the Jiujiang frontier. Liu Bang formally restored Zou Wuzhu as King of Minyue in 202 BCE as a reward for his support.

w4-300273.name: Chu-Han Contention frontier shift in Min (Minyue)
w4-300273.blurb: During the Chu-Han Contention (206-202 BC), the southeastern coastal region was dominated by Wuzhu, the Yue chieftain whose Minyue kingdom Han would later formally recognize. As Western Chu (Xiang Yu's domain) lost control of its southern periphery, the Min/Zhejiang coastal area near (120.6,30.4) reverted to local Yue (Minyue) authority. The Yue rulers had aided the anti-Qin and anti-Chu forces and gained autonomy in this period.

w4-300278.name: Xiang Yu's division into the Eighteen Kingdoms – Hán assigned to Western Chu zone
w4-300278.blurb: In Xiang Yu's 206 BCE settlement, Ying Bu (英布), one of his most capable generals, received the kingdom of Jiujiang (九江) in central Anhui as a satellite of Xiang Yu's own Western Chu (西楚). Bordering parcels between the two kingdoms reflected Xiang Yu's overlordship, with Western Chu drawing on Jiujiang's lands and manpower. The arrangement frayed when Ying Bu hung back during the Qi and Pengcheng campaigns and finally defected to Liu Bang around 204 BCE.

w4-300281.name: Chu-Han Contention — Han Absorbs Hán Kingdom
w4-300281.blurb: In 205 BCE, as Liu Bang drove east out of Guanzhong through the Hangu Pass, Shen Yang (申陽), the King of Henan (河南) in northwestern Henan around Luoyang, surrendered without serious resistance. His kingdom — one of the smaller of Xiang Yu's Eighteen Kingdoms — was absorbed into Liu Bang's Han state and reorganized as Henan Commandery. The surrender was part of a wave of capitulations that quickly gave Han control of the central Yellow River plain.

w4-300282.name: Han conquest of Western Wei — Battle of Anyi
w4-300282.blurb: After Xiang Yu had Han Cheng (韓成), the nominal King of Hán (韓), held back and then executed in 206 BCE, Liu Bang restored the Hán kingdom in central Henan as a Han client under Hán Xin (韓信, the Hán royal, distinct from the famous general). As Liu Bang consolidated the central plain in 205 BCE, this Hán territory was effectively integrated into the Han state. The kingdom thereafter functioned as a Han dependency rather than an independent power.

w4-300284.name: Han conquest of Linjiang
w4-300284.blurb: The kingdom of Linjiang (around Jiangling on the middle Yangtze) remained loyal to Xiang Yu's Western Chu. After Xiang Yu's defeat in 202 BC, Liu Bang's generals (Lu Wan and Liu Jia) besieged and destroyed Linjiang, capturing its king Gong Wei. This transfer of Linjiang to Han reflects that final 203-202 BC conquest of the last Chu-aligned holdout.

w4-300285.name: Han conquest of Qi (Han Xin's eastern campaign, Jibei)
w4-300285.blurb: In 204-203 BC Han Xin conquered the entire Qi region of Shandong for Liu Bang, defeating the Qi king Tian Guang and (with Chu reinforcements under Long Ju) winning the decisive Battle of Wei River in 203 BC. The former Jibei lands around (117.5,37.3) passed to Han in this campaign, after which Han Xin was made King of Qi.

w4-300287.name: Han conquest of the Three Qins — surrender of Zhai (Di)
w4-300287.blurb: In October 205 BCE the Han general Han Xin (韓信) shattered the army of Zhao at the Battle of Jingxing (井陘之戰) in central Hebei, deploying his outnumbered force with its back to a river so that the men had no choice but to fight. The Zhao chancellor Chen Yu was killed and King Zhao Xie was soon captured and slain, breaking the kingdom of Changshan-Zhao. Its central Hebei lands passed under Han control, a decisive step in Liu Bang's encirclement of Xiang Yu.

w4-300288.name: Han conquest of Qi — Battle of Wei River
w4-300288.blurb: In 204 BCE the Han general Han Xin (韓信) overran the kingdom of Qi (齊) in Shandong, his campaign culminating in the Battle of the Wei River (濰水之戰), where he destroyed the allied Qi-Chu army of Xiang Yu's lieutenant Long Ju by releasing a dammed river onto the divided enemy. Central and western Shandong passed to Han, and Liu Bang was obliged to install Han Xin himself as King of Qi. The conquest stripped Xiang Yu of a vital eastern ally.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Wei River (203 BC)

w4-300289.name: Liu Bang conquers the Three Qins – Sai absorbed into Han
w4-300289.blurb: In 205 BCE Liu Bang, having broken out of Hanzhong, advanced through the Wei valley and east of the Hangu Pass, dismantling Xiang Yu's 'Three Qins.' Sima Xin (司馬欣), the King of Sai (塞) in the northeastern part of the former Qin heartland, surrendered, and his lands were incorporated into the expanding Han state. The fall of Sai, alongside Yong and Di, secured Liu Bang's Guanzhong base before he turned east against Western Chu.

w4-300291.name: Han absorption of Liaodong (defeat of Zang Tu / northeastern Yan)
w4-300291.blurb: Liaodong was a kingdom created in Xiang Yu's 206 BC partition under the former Yan king Han Guang, before Zang Tu killed him and unified the northeast. As the Yan/Liaodong region submitted to Liu Bang around 202 BC, the Liaodong lands near (122,40.3) passed to Han. Han recognized Zang Tu as King of Yan, who then rebelled and was crushed in 202 BC.

w4-300292.name: Chu-Han Contention — Han gains in the central plain
w4-300292.blurb: During the seesaw warfare of the Chu-Han Contention (206-202 BC) centered on the Xingyang-Chenggao line, Han forces under Liu Bang gradually wrested the central plain (around 116.7,34.4) from Xiang Yu's Western Chu. This transfer reflects Han's expanding control before the Treaty of the Hong Canal and the final encirclement at Gaixia.

w4-300294.name: Han conquest of Qi (Jiaodong, Han Xin's eastern campaign)
w4-300294.blurb: In 204-203 BC Han Xin overran all of Qi (Shandong), including the eastern Jiaodong peninsula around (120.3,36.7). After defeating the Qi king and the relieving Chu army under Long Ju at the Wei River in 203 BC, Han Xin controlled the whole region and was enfeoffed King of Qi. This transfer reflects Jiaodong's fall to Han in that campaign.

w4-300295.name: Han reconquest of the Three Qins (Yong / Zhang Han)
w4-300295.blurb: Zhang Han, the former Qin commander made King of Yong over the core of Guanzhong, was Liu Bang's chief obstacle when Han broke out of Hanzhong in 206 BC. Liu Bang besieged Zhang Han in Feiqiu; Zhang Han held out until 205 BC, when the city fell and he committed suicide. This transfer of Yong (around 108.8,34.9) to Han marks the completion of the Three Qins reconquest.

w4-300297.name: Battle of Zama / end of the Second Punic War
w4-300297.blurb: At the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, Scipio Africanus, aided by the Numidian cavalry of Masinissa, decisively defeated Hannibal, ending the Second Punic War. The 201 BC peace stripped Carthage of its overseas empire and reduced it to its African core; this transfer of Carthaginian territory to Rome around (7.2,37) reflects the war's victorious conclusion for the Roman Republic.

w4-300298.name: Founding of the Han dynasty (Minyue submission)
w4-300298.blurb: When Liu Bang proclaimed himself emperor in 202 BC founding the Han dynasty, the Yue chieftain Wuzhu was recognized as King of Minyue in exchange for his allegiance. This transfer of the southeastern Min/Fujian-Zhejiang region (118.1,27.9) to the new 'Han Dynasty' reflects Minyue's incorporation as a tributary kingdom under the imperial Han order.

w4-300299.name: Battle of Gaixia and Establishment of Han Dynasty
w4-300299.blurb: The Chu–Han Contention (206–202 BCE) culminated at the Battle of Gaixia in 202 BCE, where Liu Bang's Han forces surrounded and defeated Xiang Yu, who subsequently committed suicide. Liu Bang then proclaimed himself Emperor Gaozu, formally establishing the Han Dynasty and absorbing the territories previously labeled 'Han' (the Chu-Han interregnum state) into the new imperial polity 'Han Dynasty'. The large territory around 112°E, 35°N represents the core Henan/Hebei basin.

w4-300301.name: Peace of 201 BC — Carthaginian cession to Numidia
w4-300301.blurb: The treaty ending the Second Punic War in 201 BC required Carthage to restore to Masinissa, king of Numidia, all the territory and ancestral lands he claimed, and barred Carthage from waging war without Roman consent. This transfer of Carthaginian land (7.9,33.8) to the Kingdom of Numidia reflects Rome's reward to its ally Masinissa, sowing the border disputes that later sparked the Third Punic War.

w4-400001.name: Battle of Panium — Seleucid conquest of Coele-Syria
w4-400001.blurb: Antiochus III defeated the Ptolemaic army at the Battle of Panium (Banias, 200 BC) during the Fifth Syrian War (202–195 BC), securing control of Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Judea (~85,000 km², centroid 33.7°E, 33.9°N — modern Lebanon/Israel/Palestine). Egypt formally ceded the region by the Peace of Lysimacheia (195 BC).

w4-400002.name: Great Egyptian Revolt — Ankhwennefer's Secession
w4-400002.blurb: The Great Revolt of the Egyptians began around 205 BCE under Horwennefer and passed to Ankhwennefer (Chaonnophris) c. 200/199 BCE; the rebels, expressing native Egyptian nationalism, seized control of Upper Egypt (the Thebaid and Nubian marches) and maintained it against the Ptolemaic state for nearly two decades.

w4-400005.name: Peace of Apamea — Seleucid cession of Asia Minor
w4-400005.blurb: The Peace of Apamea (188 BC), ending the Roman-Seleucid War, required Antiochus III to abandon all territory west of the Taurus Mountains. Western and central Anatolia (~54,000 km², centroid 32°E, 38.1°N) was redistributed mainly to Pergamon (Eumenes II) and Rhodes, with some areas reverting to Greek cities.

w4-400006.name: Peace of Apamea (188 BC) — Aetolian League punished and reduced
w4-400006.blurb: The Peace of Apamea (188 BC) also settled the status of the Aetolian League, which had allied with Antiochus III against Rome. By the earlier Peace of Naupactus (189 BC) and subsequent Roman enforcement, the Aetolians were stripped of many member states; former Aetolian-controlled cities reverted to independent Greek city-state status.

w4-400007.name: Treaty of Apamea — Armenian independence from Seleucids
w4-400007.blurb: After Rome defeated the Seleucids at the Battle of Magnesia (190 BCE), the Treaty of Apamea (188 BCE) stripped the Seleucid Empire of its Anatolian and Armenian domains; Artaxias I founded the Kingdom of Armenia on the Armenian Highlands, marking the permanent end of Seleucid control there.

w4-400008.name: Peace of Apamea (188 BC) — Seleucid withdrawal west of Taurus
w4-400008.blurb: The Peace of Apamea (188 BC), imposed by Rome after the Battle of Magnesia, forced Antiochus III to evacuate all territory west of the Taurus Mountains. Cappadocia, which had remained semi-independent, effectively expanded to fill adjacent Seleucid-evacuated borderlands in eastern Anatolia as Seleucid authority receded.

w4-400009.name: Ptolemaic Reconquest of Upper Egypt from Ankhwennefer
w4-400009.blurb: The Ptolemaic army, under Ptolemy V Epiphanes, systematically reconquered Upper Egypt from the rebel pharaoh Ankhwennefer (Chaonnophris) over the late 190s BCE: Thebes was retaken in 191 BCE and the final decisive defeat of Ankhwennefer occurred c. 186 BCE, ending the twenty-year Great Egyptian Revolt.

w4-400010.name: Peace of Apamea — Seleucid territories transferred to Rhodes
w4-400010.blurb: The Peace of Apamea (188 BC) ended the Roman–Seleucid War and required Antiochus III to cede all territory north and west of the Taurus mountains; Rome assigned Lycia and Caria (centroid lng 28.8, lat 37.2, southwestern Anatolia) to the island of Rhodes as a reward for its alliance during the war. Rhodes thereby gained the Rhodian Peraia on the Anatolian mainland.

w4-400014.name: Nanyue expansion / absorption of Minyue frontier under Zhao Tuo
w4-400014.blurb: Zhao Tuo (Trieu Da), king of Nanyue (Nam Viet), aggressively expanded his realm in the early 2nd century BC, asserting hegemony over neighboring Yue peoples including Minyue in modern Fujian. The transfer of Minyue territory to Nanyue around 188-170 BC reflects Zhao Tuo's pressure on the smaller Yue states during the period when he styled himself emperor in defiance of the early Han, before Han reasserted control under Emperor Wen.

w4-400015.name: Sixth Syrian War — Seleucid Invasion of Egypt
w4-400015.blurb: Antiochus IV Epiphanes launched the Sixth Syrian War in 170 BCE, defeating the Ptolemaic army at Pelusium and occupying much of Egypt including the Thebaid, even briefly taking young Ptolemy VI under guardianship, until Roman intervention forced evacuation in 168 BCE.

w4-400016.name: Suppression of the Great Theban Revolt (Ankhwennefer / Chaonnophris)
w4-400016.blurb: The Great Egyptian (Theban) Revolt of the native pharaohs Horwennefer and his successor Ankhwennefer (Chaonnophris) split Upper Egypt from Ptolemaic rule from 205 BC. Ankhwennefer was finally defeated in 186 BC. Because this Cliopatria reconstruction has the Ptolemies temporarily out of the region, the recovered Upper-Egyptian/Nubian-border territory is shown passing to the Seleucid Empire (which had just won the Fifth Syrian War), reflecting Seleucid ascendancy over Ptolemaic possessions in this window.

w4-400017.name: Xiongnu expulsion of the Yuezhi from Dzungaria/Ili
w4-400017.blurb: Around 174–165 BCE, Modu Chanyu and his son Laoshang Chanyu delivered a series of crushing blows to the Greater Yuezhi: Laoshang killed the Yuezhi king and used his skull as a drinking cup, driving the Yuezhi westward from the ~264,000 km² Dzungarian/Ili steppe zone (centroid ~lng 85.6, lat 42.8) into Bactria.

w4-400022.name: Roman sack of Epirus (167 BCE)
w4-400022.blurb: In 167 BCE, following the Third Macedonian War, the Roman commander Aemilius Paullus systematically plundered Epirus, sacking 70 Epirote cities and enslaving an estimated 150,000 people; the Molossians, whose king Perseus had allied with Macedon, bore the brunt of this punishment and their territory was effectively absorbed into the Roman sphere as Epirus nova.

w4-400023.name: Maccabean Revolt — Nabataean expansion into southern Levant during Seleucid weakness
w4-400023.blurb: The Maccabean Revolt beginning in 167 BC severely disrupted Seleucid control of Judaea and the Transjordan. The Nabataeans exploited this instability to consolidate control over the Negev and parts of Transjordan that had nominally been in the Seleucid sphere, expanding northward during the 160s BC.

w4-400024.name: Greco-Bactrian/Indo-Greek invasions of northwest India (Demetrius I)
w4-400024.blurb: The Greco-Bactrian kings, beginning with Demetrius I and continuing under Menander and others, invaded northwestern India in the early-to-mid 2nd century BC as Mauryan/Shunga power receded. The acquisition of territory in northwest India (near Rajasthan/Punjab) attributed here to the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom reflects this Yavana expansion into the subcontinent; the prior holder labeling (Mahameghavahana) is a reconstruction quirk rather than a true Kalinga presence in the northwest.

w4-400026.name: Shunga–Kalinga conflict (Kharavela of Mahameghavahana vs Shunga Empire)
w4-400026.blurb: Around 170-164 BC the Mahameghavahana dynasty of Kalinga under king Kharavela was in active military conflict with the Shunga Empire, which had replaced the Mauryas in the Gangetic heartland. Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription records campaigns into Shunga territory, indicating a fluid contested border. The coords (lng 83.5, lat 23.9, central India) place this in the contested zone; worklist transition Mahameghavahana Dynasty -> Shunga Empire (-170 to -164) reflects Shunga gains here. Direction is somewhat uncertain given both powers raided each other.

w4-400027.name: Parthian absorption of Atropatene
w4-400027.blurb: Media Atropatene, the autonomous kingdom of the Iranian Atropatid (Orontid-descended) dynasty in northwestern Iran (modern Iranian Azerbaijan), passed under Parthian suzerainty around 148/147 BCE as Mithridates I of Parthia extended his power westward and seized neighbouring Media from the weakening Seleucids. Although Atropatene retained its local dynasty and a degree of internal autonomy, from this point it was frequently a Parthian vassal, a status it would hold for much of the following centuries.

w4-400028.name: Mithridates I Parthian Conquests
w4-400028.blurb: Mithridates I of Parthia (r. 165–132 BCE) exploited Seleucid weakness to seize Media (c. 148 BCE) and Babylonia (141 BCE), expanding Parthian territory from eastern Iran deep into Mesopotamia. The enormous area_km2 (~1.24M km²) reflects the cumulative eastern and central Iranian plateau gains across his reign, fitting within the prev_year/year window of –170/–164.

w4-400029.name: Mithridates I conquests: Parthian seizure of Bactrian / eastern territories
w4-400029.blurb: Under Mithridates I (r. 171–138 BCE), Parthia rapidly expanded eastward and westward; he seized Media from the Seleucids around 148 BCE and moved into Bactria, exploiting the decline of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom—the centroid (lng ~63.5, lat 37.3) indicates the Margiana/western Bactrian region that passed from Greco-Bactrian to Parthian control during this phase of expansion.

w4-400031.name: Satavahana expansion into former Shunga frontier territory
w4-400031.blurb: Following the weakening of the Shunga Empire after Pushyamitra Shunga's death, the Satavahana dynasty expanded northward from the Deccan into territories previously controlled by the Shungas. Satakarni I is the key Satavahana ruler who extended power into the northern Deccan around the mid-2nd century BC. The date range py=-164, y=-144 aligns with the transitional period when Shunga peripheral control over central India (lat 21.1, lng 78.6) eroded and Satavahana authority filled the vacuum.

w4-400032.name: Mithridates I's conquest of Babylonia and Seleucia
w4-400032.blurb: Mithridates I of Parthia occupied Babylonia between April and June 141 BCE, entered Seleucia by July, and was proclaimed Great King there on 8 July 141 BCE, with Seleucid king Demetrius II's later counter-invasion ending in his capture. This is precisely dated via cuneiform astronomical diaries.

w4-400034.name: Yuezhi migration into Bactria displacing Greco-Bactrians
w4-400034.blurb: Driven westward by the Xiongnu (c. 176 BCE) and then expelled from the Ili valley by the Wusun (c. 132 BCE), the Yuezhi settled north of the Oxus and began pressing south into Bactria. By the time Zhang Qian visited (~126 BCE), the Greco-Bactrian political system had already collapsed. The centroid (~70.1°E, 41.2°N) corresponds to Sogdiana/northern Bactria, the first territory overrun. The -164 to -144 window reflects the early phase of Yuezhi settlement north of the Oxus before their full absorption of Bactria proper.

w4-400036.name: Parthian expansion under Mithridates I displaces Indo-Scythians and extends to Bactria (c. 164–144 BC)
w4-400036.blurb: Mithridates I of Parthia (r. c. 164–132 BC) launched a major eastward expansion, capturing two eparchies from Greco-Bactria and pressing south-east toward the Indus. Nomadic Saka (Scythian) tribes displaced from their homeland by the Yuezhi migration exerted pressure on Parthia's eastern border, contributing to further territorial flux. This pushed proto-Indo-Scythian groups into territories vacated by Parthian and Bactrian powers.

w4-400040.name: Parthian expansion under Mithridates I — western conquests
w4-400040.blurb: By the late 130s BCE the Seleucid hold east of the Euphrates was crumbling under Parthian pressure. Antiochus VII Sidetes briefly recovered Babylonia and Media in 130 BCE, but in spring 129 BCE the Parthian king Phraates II (r. 132-127 BCE) destroyed his army near Ecbatana, where Antiochus died. This sealed the permanent transfer of Mesopotamia and western Iran from Seleucid to Parthian rule. (The territory is here registered c. 129 BCE; the campaigns of Mithridates I, who died in 132 BCE, belong to the preceding generation.)

w4-400041.name: Roman settlement after the Aristonicus revolt: Lycaonia granted to Cappadocia
w4-400041.blurb: After Attalus III of Pergamon bequeathed his kingdom to Rome in 133 BC and the revolt of Aristonicus was suppressed by 129 BC, the consul Manius Aquillius organised the province of Asia and distributed outlying Pergamene lands to loyal allied kings. The region of Lycaonia in south-central Anatolia (around lng 33.4, lat 37.7) was given to Ariarathes V's Kingdom of Cappadocia (while Phrygia Major went to Pontus). This matches the worklist transfer from the Kingdom of Pergamon to the Kingdom of Cappadocia within the -131 to -126 window.

citations.label: Historical Geography of Roman Lycaonia – Dmitriev (GRBS)

w4-400042.name: Nabataean expansion into Sinai as Ptolemaic Egypt weakened (late 2nd century BC)
w4-400042.blurb: Following the death of Ptolemy VIII Physcon (116 BC) and the Ptolemaic dynastic turmoil from the 130s BC onward, Nabataean control expanded into the Sinai and Negev, areas previously under Ptolemaic influence. The coordinates (33.6°E, 30.6°N) correspond to the Sinai borderlands; the Nabataeans under Aretas II founded a strong kingdom in this period. From=Ptolemaic Kingdom, to=Nabataeans reflects this gradual expansion in the 131-126 BC window.

w4-400043.name: Ptolemaic decline and Nabataean expansion into Sinai/Gaza region
w4-400043.blurb: Through the later 2nd century BCE the Nabataeans, already established in the Hauran, Edom, and across the Wadi Araba into the Negev, pressed into the desert margins of the southern Levant as the rival Hellenistic kingdoms exhausted themselves in dynastic warfare. By the eve of Aretas II's reign (c. 120/110 BCE) Nabataean control of the caravan routes toward Gaza and Sinai was effectively unchallenged. The change reflects the gradual passage of these arid frontier zones out of Seleucid-Ptolemaic contention and into the Nabataean orbit, rather than any single conquest.

w4-400044.name: Han–Xiongnu War — Battle of Mayi ambush and resumption of hostilities
w4-400044.blurb: Emperor Wu of Han abandoned the heqin appeasement policy and renewed open war with the Xiongnu, beginning with the failed Mayi ambush (133 BC) and the first northern offensives (129 BC). The transfer of frontier territory near the northern Hebei border (near 117E,39N) from Han to Xiongnu in 131-126 BC reflects Xiongnu raiding pressure on the northern commanderies during the opening, see-saw phase of the war before Han counteroffensives.

w4-400045.name: Yuezhi conquest of Bactria (Greco-Bactrian Kingdom)
w4-400045.blurb: Expelled from the Hexi Corridor by the Xiongnu around 162 BC, the Yuezhi migrated west and entered Bactria around 135-125 BC, overrunning the weakened Greco-Bactrian Kingdom whose last major ruler Heliocles I was driven out. Zhang Qian, visiting c. 126 BC, found the Yuezhi settled north of the Oxus exercising suzerainty over Bactria. From 'Greco-Bactrian Kingdom' to 'Yuezhi'; window py=-131, y=-126 fits.

w4-400048.name: Mithridatic expansion of Pontus into Galatia
w4-400048.blurb: The Kingdom of Pontus, growing under Mithridates V Euergetes and then Mithridates VI Eupator, expanded into central Anatolia at the expense of the Galatian Celts in the later 2nd century BC. The transfer of territory near (33E,39.5N) from Galatia to Pontus around 131-126 BC reflects this Pontic encroachment on Galatia, though the precise date and mechanism are not pinned to a single famous battle.

w4-400049.name: Mithridates V / early Mithridates VI expansion into Galatia
w4-400049.blurb: During the reign of Mithridates V Euergetes of Pontus (c. 150–120 BC) and the early years of Mithridates VI, Pontus expanded southward into eastern Galatian territory (~51,000 km², centroid 33°E, 39.5°N — central-northern Anatolia). This gradual encroachment culminated in Pontic control of Galatian border regions before the eventual Roman-backed reversal.

w4-400054.name: Bequest of Pergamon to Rome by Attalus III (Province of Asia)
w4-400054.blurb: Attalus III, last Attalid king of Pergamon, died in 133 BC and willed his entire kingdom to the Roman Republic. After Rome suppressed the revolt of the pretender Aristonicus (Eumenes III) by 129 BC, the territory was organized as the Roman province of Asia. The transfer of western Anatolian territory near (29E,38N) from Pergamon to Rome in this window reflects that bequest and provincial annexation.

w4-400055.name: Han–Xiongnu War — early offensives recovering the northern frontier
w4-400055.blurb: In Emperor Wu of Han's renewed war against the Xiongnu, General Wei Qing led campaigns from 129 BC, notably the 127 BC Ordos campaign that recovered the great northern bend of the Yellow River. The transfer of frontier territory near (114E,39N) from Xiongnu to Han in 131-126 BC reflects these early Han counteroffensives reclaiming border commanderies from Xiongnu control.

w4-400056.name: Han conquest of Minyue
w4-400056.blurb: Emperor Wu of Han eliminated the kingdom of Minyue (in modern Fujian) around 111-110 BC, after the Minyue king Yushan revolted; Han forces invaded and the Minyue ruling house was destroyed, with much of the population resettled. The transfer of Minyue territory near (117E,26N) to the Han Dynasty in 126-110 BC reflects this Han annexation of the southeastern Yue lands during Wu's southern expansion.

w4-400057.name: Han–Xiongnu War — Battle of Mobei and conquest of the Ordos/Hexi
w4-400057.blurb: Emperor Wu of Han's generals Wei Qing and Huo Qubing drove the Xiongnu out of the Ordos loop and the Hexi Corridor in the campaigns of 121-119 BC, culminating in the decisive Battle of Mobei (119 BC) that pushed the Xiongnu north of the Gobi. The transfer of territory near (108E,39N) from Xiongnu to Han in 126-110 BC reflects this conquest of the Ordos and northern frontier during the height of the Han–Xiongnu War.

w4-400059.name: Parthian expansion into Armenia under Mithridates II
w4-400059.blurb: Under Mithridates II 'the Great', the Parthian Empire pressed westward into the Armenian highlands during the 120s-110s BC, reducing the Kingdom of Armenia to a tributary and vassal state. As part of this settlement the Armenian prince Tigranes (the future Tigranes the Great) was held as a hostage at the Parthian court. The territory around (44.8E, 39.1N) near the Armenian heartland passed into the Parthian sphere of dominance.

w4-400060.name: Parthian conquest of Mesopotamia under Mithridates II
w4-400060.blurb: Mithridates II of Parthia conducted campaigns in the 110s BC that stripped the declining Seleucid Empire of its remaining Mesopotamian holdings, taking Dura-Europos and pushing Parthian control across northern Mesopotamia toward the Euphrates. The territory near (40.6E, 36.3N) in upper Mesopotamia passed from Seleucid to Parthian rule. By the end of his reign Parthia stood astride the old Seleucid east and bordered the Roman world for the first time.

w4-400063.name: Indo-Scythian (Saka) invasion of the Indo-Greek east
w4-400063.blurb: Driven south by the Yuezhi out of Central Asia, the Sakas (Indo-Scythians) poured through the regions of Arachosia and the Indus valley in the late 2nd century BC, overrunning the eastern marches of the Indo-Greek kingdoms. The territory around (68.7E, 32.7N) near the lower Indus and Arachosia passed from Indo-Greek to Indo-Scythian control. Maues would soon establish the first major Indo-Scythian kingdom in the region.

w4-400065.name: Mithridates VI's acquisition of the Bosporan Kingdom
w4-400065.blurb: King Mithridates VI Eupator of Pontus intervened in the Cimmerian Bosporus on behalf of the Greek city of Chersonesus against Scythian pressure; his general Diophantus suppressed the revolt of Saumacus, and the Bosporan king Paerisades V ceded his realm to Mithridates around 110-107 BC. The Crimean and Taman lands around (37.5E, 46.1N) thus passed from the Bosporan Kingdom to Pontus. The Bosporus became a key northern base for Mithridates against Rome.

w4-400067.name: Han conquest of Gojoseon (Wiman Joseon)
w4-400067.blurb: Emperor Wu of Han launched a campaign against Wiman Joseon (Gojoseon) under King Ugeo, and after a siege the capital Wanggeom-seong fell in 108 BC. The Han established the Four Commanderies of Han in the conquered territory of the northern Korean peninsula and southern Manchuria, the region around (126.2E, 39.6N). Lelang (Nangnang) Commandery would endure for centuries as the centerpiece of Han control there.

w4-400068.name: Collapse of the Jin state and emergence of the Samhan confederacies
w4-400068.blurb: The Korean Jin state, a loose confederacy occupying the southern Korean peninsula, fragmented around the time of the fall of Gojoseon (108 BC). The power vacuum created by the Chinese Han dynasty's conquest of Gojoseon and establishment of the Lelang Commandery led to the reorganization of southern Korean polities into the three Samhan confederacies: Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan. Byeonhan occupied the Nakdong River basin and was known for iron production.

w4-400069.name: Bocchus of Mauretania's gains after the Jugurthine War
w4-400069.blurb: After the Jugurthine War (112-106 BC), in which King Bocchus I of Mauretania betrayed his son-in-law Jugurtha of Numidia to the Roman general Sulla, Bocchus was rewarded with the western portion of Numidia. The territory around (1.2E, 35.5N) in western Numidia (modern western Algeria) passed from Numidia to Mauretania as a Roman reward for Bocchus's defection. This shifted the Mauretanian-Numidian border eastward.

w4-400071.name: Bequest of Cyrenaica to Rome by Ptolemy Apion
w4-400071.blurb: Ptolemy Apion, the illegitimate Ptolemaic ruler of Cyrenaica, died in 96 BC and bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman Republic in his will. The territory around (22E, 31.2N) in Cyrenaica (eastern Libya) thus passed to Rome, although Rome initially left the Greek cities autonomous and only organized the region as a formal province (with Crete) in 74 BC. This was a testamentary transfer rather than a conquest.

w4-400076.name: Fall of Gojoseon and dissolution of Korean Jin state, rise of Mahan (c.108 BC)
w4-400076.blurb: The Han dynasty conquered Gojoseon in 108 BC, establishing four commanderies in northern Korea. This triggered southward migration and the dissolution of the Jin state in southern Korea, reorganized into the three Han confederacies (Samhan): Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan. Mahan, the largest, emerged as the dominant successor in the region of modern Chungcheong and Jeolla.

w4-400080.name: Tigranes the Great's annexation of Sophene
w4-400080.blurb: Soon after taking the Armenian throne, Tigranes II the Great conquered and absorbed the neighboring kingdom of Sophene (around 39.7E, 38.9N) around 94 BC, deposing its Artanid ruler and unifying the Armenian lands. This was the first step in Tigranes's rapid empire-building. Sophene's territory thereby passed to the Kingdom of Armenia.

w4-400081.name: Tigranes the Great's recovery of the 'Seventy Valleys' from Parthia
w4-400081.blurb: Tigranes II of Armenia had been a hostage in Parthia and, upon his accession in 95 BC, ceded 'seventy valleys' to secure his release. As Parthian power waned after the death of Mithridates II (c.91 BC), Tigranes reversed this and seized large territories from the Parthian Empire, including lands around (43.3E, 39N) in the Armenian and Atropatene borderlands. These conquests, recounted by Strabo and Justin, helped make Tigranes the dominant power of the region and earned him the title King of Kings.

w4-400083.name: Continued Indo-Scythian (Saka) advance against the Indo-Greeks
w4-400083.blurb: The Indo-Scythians under Maues continued to overrun Indo-Greek territory in the early 1st century BC, pushing through Arachosia and toward the Indus around (70.3E, 32.1N). Maues eventually struck coins and ruled at Taxila, marking the consolidation of Indo-Scythian power at the expense of the fragmenting Indo-Greek kingdoms. This represents the ongoing Saka displacement of Greek rule in the northwest.

w4-400087.name: First Mithridatic War — Mithridates VI's overrunning of Roman Asia
w4-400087.blurb: At the outbreak of the First Mithridatic War in 88 BC, King Mithridates VI of Pontus swept into the Roman province of Asia, defeating Roman forces and seizing western Anatolia around (27.6E, 38.4N). He orchestrated the 'Asiatic Vespers,' the massacre of tens of thousands of Romans and Italians in the province. The territory of Roman Asia thus passed temporarily to the Kingdom of Pontus until Sulla's counteroffensive recovered it by 85 BC.

w4-400092.name: Indo-Scythian conquest of the Indo-Greek Punjab (Maues)
w4-400092.blurb: Around the turn of the 1st century BC the Indo-Scythian (Saka) ruler Maues conquered large parts of the Indo-Greek kingdom in the northwestern Indian subcontinent, including Taxila and the Punjab around Sialkot (near 72E, 31N). This transferred the Indo-Greek heartland to the Indo-Scythians, though the Greeks would later briefly recover some ground.

w4-400093.name: Tigranes the Great's conquest of Seleucid Syria
w4-400093.blurb: Tigranes II (the Great) of Armenia invaded and annexed the collapsing Seleucid Empire in 83 BC, ending Seleucid rule over Syria for over a decade. This change near the upper Orontes/Syria (36.7E, 34.9N) reflects Armenian seizure of Seleucid territory that Tigranes ruled until Pompey's settlement.

w4-400094.name: Azes I Indo-Scythian conquest of Indo-Greek territories
w4-400094.blurb: Around 80 BCE the Indo-Scythian (Saka) king Maues seized Gandhara and the great city of Taxila from the Indo-Greek kings of the northwest, establishing the first Saka power across the Punjab. His conquests broke the Indo-Greek hold north of the Indus and opened the way for the later consolidation under Azes I. The transfer here records the loss of these Indo-Greek territories to the incoming Indo-Scythians.

w4-400097.name: Treaty of Dardanos (restoration of Nicomedes IV of Bithynia)
w4-400097.blurb: In the First Mithridatic War, Mithridates VI of Pontus had overrun Bithynia and driven out King Nicomedes IV. The 85 BC Treaty of Dardanos with Sulla required Mithridates to evacuate Bithynia and restore Nicomedes IV, returning this northwestern Anatolian territory (30.5E, 40.8N) to the Kingdom of Bithynia.

w4-400098.name: End of First Mithridatic War (Pontic withdrawal from Galatia)
w4-400098.blurb: Mithridates VI of Pontus had occupied Galatia during the First Mithridatic War, notoriously massacring its Celtic chieftains. With his defeat and the Treaty of Dardanos in 85 BC he was forced to relinquish his Anatolian conquests, and Galatia (32.5E, 38.5N) reverted to the Galatian tetrarchs.

w4-400099.name: Wusun-Xiongnu war / Han-Wusun alliance defeat of the Xiongnu
w4-400099.blurb: Around 71 BC the Wusun, allied with Han China, inflicted a major defeat on the Xiongnu in the Ili and Issyk-Kul region (77E, 44N), seizing people and herds and pushing Xiongnu power back from the western steppe. This shifted control of the Zhetysu/Tian Shan borderlands from the Xiongnu to the Wusun.

w4-400100.name: Kanva (Kanvayana) dynasty supplants the Shunga Empire
w4-400100.blurb: Around 73 BC the Shunga king Devabhuti was assassinated by his minister Vasudeva Kanva, who founded the Kanva dynasty and took over the Shunga realm centered on Magadha and the Ganges plain (83E, 25.5N). The change reflects this dynastic usurpation transferring the Shunga heartland to the Kanvas.

w4-400102.name: Lucullus's invasion of Armenia (Battle of Tigranocerta)
w4-400102.blurb: In 69 BC Lucullus invaded the Armenian empire of Tigranes the Great, sacking his new capital Tigranocerta after a crushing victory at the Battle of Tigranocerta. Roman forces overran Armenian territory in the upper Euphrates region (39.5E, 38.3N), stripping it from Tigranes during the Third Mithridatic War.

w4-400105.name: Parthian seizure of Armenian-held Adiabene/upper Mesopotamia
w4-400105.blurb: As Tigranes the Great's empire collapsed under Roman pressure in the late 60s BC, the Parthian Empire under Phraates III recovered territory in the Adiabene/Nineveh region (43.5E, 36.5N) that had been subject to Armenia. The change reflects this Parthian reassertion of control in northern Mesopotamia.

w4-400117.name: Pompey's eastern settlement (grant of Sophene)
w4-400117.blurb: As part of Pompey's 66 BC reorganization of Armenia, the kingdom of Sophene (39.7E, 38.5N) was detached and assigned as a separate client realm, originally to Tigranes the Younger, removing it from direct Roman administration and re-establishing it as the Kingdom of Sophene.

w4-400118.name: Pompey's Settlement of the East — Colchis/Lazica assigned to Aristarchus
w4-400118.blurb: In his eastern settlement of 63 BCE, after defeating Mithridates VI of Pontus, Pompey restored and rewarded the kingdom of Commagene under Antiochus I, assigning it Seleucid borderlands in the upper Euphrates region (modern southeastern Turkey). The grant strengthened Commagene as a Roman client kingdom guarding the crossing of the Euphrates.

w4-400123.name: Indo-Greek reconquest of the eastern Punjab (Apollodotus II / Hippostratos)
w4-400123.blurb: In the mid-1st century BC the Indo-Greek kings, notably Apollodotus II and Hippostratos, temporarily recovered territory in the eastern Punjab around Sagala/Sialkot (74.5E, 31.9N) from the Indo-Scythians, restoring a final Indo-Greek revival before the Sakas reasserted dominance.

w4-400125.name: Caesar's Civil War — Battle of Thapsus and annexation of Numidia (Africa Nova)
w4-400125.blurb: Juba I of Numidia sided with the Pompeian/Optimate faction in Caesar's Civil War. After Julius Caesar crushed the Pompeians and their Numidian allies at the Battle of Thapsus in 46 BC, Juba committed suicide and Caesar annexed the Kingdom of Numidia as the new Roman province of Africa Nova.

w4-400126.name: Parthian invasion of the Roman Levant (Labienus and Pacorus)
w4-400126.blurb: In 40 BC a Parthian army under prince Pacorus I and the Roman renegade Quintus Labienus overran Roman Syria and much of the Levant during the turmoil of the Roman civil wars. The invasion temporarily transferred Syria and surrounding territory to Parthian control until Publius Ventidius Bassus drove them out in 39-38 BC.

w4-400131.name: Donations of Alexandria / Antony's grants to the Ptolemaic Kingdom
w4-400131.blurb: During his alliance with Cleopatra VII, Mark Antony transferred large eastern Roman-controlled territories (Cyprus, parts of the Levant and Anatolia) to the Ptolemaic Kingdom and to his children by Cleopatra, formalized in the Donations of Alexandria in 34 BC. This datum (eastern Mediterranean, c.31 BC) reflects that nominal transfer of Roman-administered land to Ptolemaic Egypt before Actium reversed it.

w4-400133.name: Roman annexation of Ptolemaic Egypt
w4-400133.blurb: After Octavian's victory at Actium, he invaded Egypt; Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII committed suicide in 30 BC. Octavian annexed the Ptolemaic Kingdom, ending the dynasty and making Egypt a special imperial province (Aegyptus) governed directly under the emperor.

w4-400135.name: Satavahana overthrow of the Kanva Dynasty
w4-400135.blurb: The Satavahana Dynasty of the Deccan overthrew the Kanva Dynasty, which had ruled the remnants of the Shunga successor state in the Gangetic plain. According to the Puranas the Satavahana ruler (traditionally Simuka or his successors) ended Kanva rule around 28 BC, extending Satavahana power northward.

w4-400136.name: Roman Conquest of Egypt (end of Ptolemaic Kingdom)
w4-400136.blurb: After the Battle of Actium (31 BC), Octavian pursued Antony and Cleopatra to Egypt. Both died in August 30 BC, and Octavian annexed Egypt directly as a Roman imperial province — the last major Hellenistic monarchy to fall under Roman control.

w4-400137.name: Aelius Gallus' expedition to Arabia Felix
w4-400137.blurb: In 26-25 BC the Roman prefect of Egypt, Aelius Gallus, led an expedition into Arabia Felix (Yemen) against the Sabaeans on Augustus' orders. Though the campaign ultimately failed to hold the region, it briefly projected Roman control into Sabaean territory in southwestern Arabia, as recorded by Strabo.

citations.label: Roman campaign against Arabia Felix (Strabo, Geography 16.4)

w4-400138.name: Aelius Gallus' Arabian expedition through Nabataea
w4-400138.blurb: As part of Aelius Gallus' 26-25 BC expedition to Arabia, Roman forces marched through and operated within Nabataean territory (the Nabataeans were nominal allies and guides). This datum reflects the temporary Roman military presence/control over Nabataean lands during the campaign; Nabataea reverted to its client-kingdom status afterward.

w4-400141.name: Indo-Parthian conquest of the lower Indus (Gondophares)
w4-400141.blurb: The Indo-Parthian Kingdom, founded by Gondophares, expanded from Drangiana/Arachosia into the Indus valley and Gandhara at the expense of the Indo-Scythians (Sakas) around the turn of the era. This transferred the lower Indus region (near Sindh) from Indo-Scythian to Indo-Parthian control.

w4-400145.name: Goguryeo expansion against the Xin/Han into the Korean peninsula
w4-400145.blurb: During the collapse of Wang Mang's Xin Dynasty (AD 14-23), the early Korean kingdom of Goguryeo under King Yuri and his successors asserted independence and expanded against Chinese-controlled commanderies in the northern Korean peninsula and Liaodong. This transferred frontier territory near Pyongyang from Xin/Chinese control to Goguryeo.

w4-400147.name: Annexation of Cappadocia as a Roman province
w4-400147.blurb: On the death of the client-king Archelaus in AD 17, the emperor Tiberius annexed the Kingdom of Cappadocia and made it a Roman province, as recorded by Tacitus. This brought eastern-central Anatolia under direct Roman administration.

w4-400148.name: Collapse of Xin Dynasty and Goguryeo Expansion into Liaodong
w4-400148.blurb: As Wang Mang's Xin dynasty disintegrated amid the Green Forest and Red Eyebrow rebellions (18–23 CE), Chinese administration of the Liaodong frontier and the Xuantu Commandery broke down. Goguryeo exploited this vacuum to push westward into Liaodong, seizing territory the commandery system could no longer hold.

w4-400150.name: Formation of the Kushan Empire under Kujula Kadphises
w4-400150.blurb: Kujula Kadphises (r. c. 25-85 CE) unified the five branches of the Yuezhi confederation in Bactria, defeated rival tribal leaders and remnant Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Scythian rulers, and founded the Kushan Empire c. 30 CE, placing its rise in the regions of the Paropamisadae and Gandhara around the mid-1st century. The empire would grow to encompass Bactria, Sogdia, Gandhara, and parts of the Indian subcontinent. The worklist window of 30-43 CE (Yuezhi to Kushan Empire) corresponds to this initial unification.

w4-400152.name: Trưng Sisters' rebellion against Han China
w4-400152.blurb: In AD 40 the Trưng Sisters (Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị) led a rebellion in Jiaozhi (northern Vietnam) against the Eastern Han, expelling Chinese officials and establishing a short-lived independent state across the Red River region. The revolt was crushed by the general Ma Yuan in AD 43.

w4-400153.name: Eastern Han reassertion in Liaodong against Goguryeo
