w4-400153.blurb: After Emperor Guangwu restored the Han Dynasty (Eastern Han) by AD 25-36, Han forces reasserted control over the Liaodong/northern Korean frontier that Goguryeo had seized during the Xin collapse. This datum reflects the Han recovery of territory near the Korean border (around Pyongyang/Liaodong) from Goguryeo.

w4-400155.name: Kushan unification of Bactria under Kujula Kadphises
w4-400155.blurb: In the mid-1st century AD Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Kushan (Guishuang) clan of the Yuezhi confederation, united the five Yuezhi principalities of Bactria and Sogdiana and expanded Kushan rule over the Ferghana/Sogdian frontier. The 'Great Yuan' label here is an anachronistic mapping artifact for the Yuezhi/Da Yuezhi territory in the upper Syr Darya region, which was absorbed into the consolidating Kushan state.

w4-400156.name: Kujula Kadphises' conquest of Gandhara and the Kabul valley from the Indo-Scythians
w4-400156.blurb: Kujula Kadphises, founder of the Kushan Empire, pushed south through the Hindu Kush and seized Kabul, Arachosia and Gandhara from the declining Indo-Scythian (Saka) and Indo-Parthian rulers in the mid-1st century AD. This conquest, recorded in the Hou Hanshu, moved the region around modern Kabul/Ghazni from Indo-Scythian to Kushan control.

w4-400157.name: Roman annexation of the Thracian Kingdom (Province of Thracia)
w4-400157.blurb: The client Odrysian Thracian Kingdom was annexed by Emperor Claudius in AD 46 after the murder of the Roman-installed king Rhoemetalces III, becoming the Roman province of Thracia. This transferred the lands south of the lower Danube from the Thracian Kingdom to direct Roman rule.

w4-400158.name: Division of the Xiongnu into Southern and Northern Xiongnu
w4-400158.blurb: In AD 48 a succession dispute split the Xiongnu confederation when eight southern tribes proclaimed Bi (Huhanye II) as chanyu, breaking away from the Northern Xiongnu and submitting to the Han as the Southern Xiongnu. The southern group settled in the Ordos/Inner Mongolia region, transferring control of the Yellow River loop lands from the unified Xiongnu to the Southern Xiongnu.

w4-400159.name: Han suppression of the Trưng Sisters' rebellion (Ma Yuan's campaign)
w4-400159.blurb: The Trưng Sisters (Hai Bà Trưng) led a Vietnamese uprising against Han rule in Jiaozhi from AD 40, briefly establishing an independent realm. The Han general Ma Yuan crushed the revolt by AD 43, defeating and killing the sisters and restoring direct Han control over the Red River delta region of northern Vietnam.

w4-400161.name: Roman–Parthian War over Armenia / Corbulo's campaigns
w4-400161.blurb: During the Roman–Parthian War of AD 58–63 over the Armenian succession, the general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo invaded Armenia, captured and sacked the capital Artaxata in 58 and Tigranocerta in 59, and installed the Roman client Tigranes VI. This brought the Kingdom of Armenia under Roman control during the late 50s before the later compromise settlement.

w4-400170.name: Han conquest of the Northern Xiongnu / campaigns of Dou Xian and reopening of the Western Regions
w4-400170.blurb: In the late 80s AD the Han general Dou Xian, allied with the Southern Xiongnu and Xianbei, smashed the Northern Xiongnu (notably at the Battle of Ikh Bayan, AD 89–91), while Ban Chao restored Han authority over the Tarim Basin. This transferred the Hami/Turfan region of the eastern Tarim from Xiongnu to Han control.

w4-400171.name: Kushan conquest of northwestern India under Vima Takto/Vima Kadphises
w4-400171.blurb: In the later 1st century AD the Kushan rulers Vima Takto and Vima Kadphises extended Kushan power deep into northwestern India, displacing the remaining Indo-Scythian (Western Kshatrapa/Saka) holdings in the Indus and Punjab region. This absorbed the area around the lower Indus into the expanding Kushan Empire.

w4-400173.name: Roman annexation of Nabataea (creation of Provincia Arabia Petraea)
w4-400173.blurb: In AD 106 Emperor Trajan annexed the Nabataean Kingdom after the death of its last king Rabbel II Soter, organizing it as the province of Arabia Petraea with its capital at Petra and Bostra. This brought the region around Petra and the southern Levant under direct Roman rule, executed by the governor of Syria, Cornelius Palma.

w4-400174.name: Kushan Conquest under Kujula Kadphises
w4-400174.blurb: In the later 1st century CE, Kujula Kadphises, who united the Yuezhi clans of Bactria into the Kushan Empire, expanded southeast across the Hindu Kush into the Indus region and Punjab. He overran the Indo-Parthian successor states of Gondophares (rulers such as Abdagases and Sases) and absorbed adjacent Indo-Scythian (Saka) holdings, bringing the northwestern Indian subcontinent under Kushan control. This change records the Kushan takeover of these territories from the residual Indo-Parthian/Indo-Scythian polities of the region.

w4-400175.name: Xianbei expansion into the Hexi/northern frontier after the collapse of the Northern Xiongnu
w4-400175.blurb: After the Han and Southern Xiongnu destroyed the Northern Xiongnu (AD 89–91), the Xianbei surged west to occupy the vacated steppe and frontier zones. Around the turn of the 2nd century the Xianbei encroached on the Han northwestern frontier in the Hexi corridor region, taking territory the Han could no longer hold.

w4-400176.name: Xianbei occupation of the former Northern Xiongnu lands in Mongolia
w4-400176.blurb: Following the rout of the Northern Xiongnu at the Battle of Ikh Bayan (AD 89–91) and their flight westward, the Xianbei moved into and absorbed the abandoned Xiongnu heartland across Mongolia. The Hou Hanshu records that the remaining Xiongnu 'all called themselves Xianbei,' marking the large-scale transfer of the Mongolian steppe from Xiongnu to Xianbei dominion.

w4-400177.name: Trajan's Parthian campaign and annexation of upper Mesopotamia
w4-400177.blurb: Emperor Trajan invaded Armenia in 114 CE and annexed it as a Roman province, then in 115-116 overran northern Mesopotamia including Gordyene (between the Tigris tributaries southeast of Lake Van). Gordyene, long a borderland between Rome and Parthia, passed into Roman hands as part of the new province of Mesopotamia. The data window 106-114 captures the campaign's onset in 114; the conquest itself was largely 115-116 and was partly relinquished by Hadrian after 117.

w4-400178.name: Trajan's Parthian War – annexation of Armenia
w4-400178.blurb: In AD 114 Emperor Trajan opened his Parthian War by invading and annexing Armenia, deposing the Arsacid client king Parthamasiris and organizing Armenia as a Roman province. This converted the Kingdom of Armenia into direct Roman territory at the start of Trajan's eastern campaign.

w4-400179.name: Trajan's Parthian War – subjugation of Osroene (Edessa)
w4-400179.blurb: During Trajan's Parthian War, the kingdom of Osroene under Abgar VII submitted to Rome in AD 114–116, bringing the region around Edessa into the Roman sphere as a vassal/annexed territory. The city of Edessa and northern Mesopotamia thus passed from Osroene to Roman control during Trajan's eastern advance.

w4-400181.name: Xianbei raids and seizure of the Han northwestern frontier under Tanshihuai's precursors
w4-400181.blurb: In the early 2nd century AD the Xianbei intensified raids on the Han northwestern frontier in the Hexi corridor (around modern Gansu), wresting border districts from a Han state increasingly unable to defend its outer commanderies. This continued the steppe transfer of frontier lands from Han to Xianbei control.

w4-400182.name: Kushan expansion into the Tarim Basin / conflict with Han over the Western Regions
w4-400182.blurb: In the early 2nd century AD the Kushan Empire, at its height under Kanishka's predecessors, contested and gained influence over the southwestern Tarim Basin (around Khotan/Kashgar) as Han authority in the Western Regions waned after Ban Chao's death. This shifted control of the area near modern Khotan from the Han protectorate toward the Kushans.

w4-400183.name: Han reassertion over the Tarim Basin / Western Regions under Ban Chao
w4-400183.blurb: Following Ban Chao's campaigns (73-102 AD), the Eastern Han re-established firm control over the city-states of the Tarim Basin and reconstituted the Protectorate of the Western Regions (Xiyu Duhu), with Ban Chao named Protector-General in 91 AD. The territory near Kucha/the central Tarim (85.4E, 39.2N) thus passed from direct Han administration into the renewed Protectorate framework. This consolidation expelled the Xiongnu from the oasis kingdoms and secured the Silk Road.

w4-400185.name: Trajan's Parthian War (capture of Mesopotamia)
w4-400185.blurb: In his Parthian War (114-117 AD), the Roman emperor Trajan invaded the Parthian Empire, captured the capital Ctesiphon in 116 AD, and annexed Mesopotamia, reaching the Persian Gulf. The territory around central Mesopotamia/Babylonia (44.3E, 33.6N) thus passed from Parthia to Rome at the empire's greatest territorial extent. The Roman provinces of Mesopotamia, Assyria, and Armenia were briefly organized before being abandoned under Hadrian.

w4-400187.name: Trajan's Parthian Campaign – Conquest of Adiabene
w4-400187.blurb: During Trajan's Parthian campaign, a Roman division crossed the Tigris into Adiabene in 115–116 CE, sweeping south and capturing Adenystrae; Adiabene was incorporated into the Roman province of Assyria, with its last independent king Meharaspes offering the chief Parthian resistance in the region.

w4-400188.name: Trajan's Parthian War — conquest of Mesopotamia and Armenia
w4-400188.blurb: Emperor Trajan invaded Parthian territory in 114 CE, annexing Armenia (114), overrunning northern Mesopotamia and Babylonia (115–116), and reaching the Persian Gulf. Coins issued in 116 CE proclaimed Armenia and Mesopotamia under Roman authority; this ~348k km² transfer matches the Mesopotamian and Armenian core of the conquest.

w4-400189.name: Hadrian withdraws from Trajan's Mesopotamian conquests
w4-400189.blurb: On becoming emperor in 117 CE, Hadrian reversed Trajan's eastern expansion, withdrawing Roman forces from the newly created provinces of Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia, including the Gordyene region, and restoring the Roman-Parthian boundary roughly to the Euphrates. Parthian-aligned local rulers, including Gordyene, reasserted their authority. The data window 117-127 captures this relinquishment from the Roman Empire back to the Kingdom of Gordyene.

w4-400190.name: Hadrian's restoration of Osroene as a client kingdom under Parthamaspates
w4-400190.blurb: After Trajan's death in 117, Hadrian abandoned Trajan's new province of Mesopotamia and reversed his eastern conquests. Rather than hold Osroene directly, Hadrian installed the deposed Parthian prince Parthamaspates -- who had briefly been Trajan's client king in Ctesiphon before being ousted by Osroes -- as client king of Osroene at Edessa in 118 AD, restoring it from direct Roman rule to a buffer client kingdom.

w4-400191.name: Hadrian abandons Trajan's Parthian conquests
w4-400191.blurb: Upon succeeding Trajan in August 117 CE, Hadrian immediately relinquished Armenia, Mesopotamia, and Assyria — all territories Trajan had conquered in 114–116 CE — restoring the Euphrates as the Roman–Parthian frontier. This large transfer (~569k km²) directly corresponds to Hadrian's deliberate strategic withdrawal.

w4-400193.name: Satavahana reconquest of Western Satraps territory under Gautamiputra Satakarni
w4-400193.blurb: The Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni (reigned c. 86–130 CE in the prevailing chronology) defeated Nahapana of the Kshaharata Western Satraps and expelled them from Malwa, northern Maharashtra, and the Konkan. His Nashik Prashasti records the reconquest of Saurashtra, Aparanta, Anupa, and Vidarbha from the Sakas. The 127–154 window captures Gautamiputra's gains and subsequent partial Satrap recovery under Rudradaman I, consistent with the Western Satraps→Satavahana transfer.

w4-400195.name: Parthian seizure of Armenia (start of the Roman-Parthian War of 161-166)
w4-400195.blurb: In 161 AD the Parthian king Vologases IV invaded the Kingdom of Armenia, expelled the Roman client king, and installed his own nominee, triggering the Roman-Parthian War of 161-166 under Lucius Verus. The territory of Armenia (43.9E, 39.3N) thus passed into the Parthian sphere at the war's outset. Rome later recovered Armenia, but the initial Parthian offensive moved this region from the Roman client kingdom to Parthia.

w4-400196.name: Parthian invasion of Syria (Roman-Parthian War of 161-166)
w4-400196.blurb: At the outbreak of the Roman-Parthian War of 161-166, Vologases IV's forces destroyed a Roman legion at Elegeia and invaded Roman Syria in 161-162 AD, defeating the governor and overrunning border territory. The land around the upper Euphrates/Syrian frontier (38.8E, 37.6N) thus briefly passed from Rome to Parthia. Lucius Verus's generals (notably Avidius Cassius) subsequently drove the Parthians back and sacked Ctesiphon.

w4-400198.name: Parthian seizure of Armenia — Vologases IV
w4-400198.blurb: The Parthian king Vologases IV invaded and occupied Armenia in 161 CE, defeating the Roman-backed client ruler and prompting the Roman counter-campaign of 162–165 CE. This ~221k km² transfer (same centroid as other Armenia changes) is well attested as the start of the Roman-Parthian War of 161–166.

w4-400199.name: Parthian invasion of Syria — Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
w4-400199.blurb: In 161 CE Vologases IV of Parthia invaded Roman Armenia and Syria, annihilating a Roman legion under Sedatius Severianus at the Battle of Elegeia. The centroid (38.8°E, 37.6°N, northern Syria/upper Euphrates) corresponds to the initial Parthian advance into Roman Syria before Marcus Aurelius's counter-offensive under Lucius Verus (162–166 CE) recovered the territory.

w4-400200.name: Gautamiputra Satakarni's reconquest of the Deccan from the Western Satraps
w4-400200.blurb: The Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni (r. c. 106-130 AD) defeated the Western Satrap Nahapana, recovering Maharashtra, Malwa, and the western Deccan, as celebrated in the Nasik prashasti inscription of his mother Gautami Balasri. The territory near central India (78E, 22.8N) thus reverted from the Western Satraps to the Satavahanas. He restruck Nahapana's coins, marking a decisive reversal of Saka gains.

w4-400201.name: Han/Protectorate reassertion over the Tarim against Kushan influence
w4-400201.blurb: After Ban Yong (son of Ban Chao) restored Han authority in the Western Regions in the 120s AD, the oasis states of the Tarim Basin were reorganized under the Protectorate of the Western Regions, displacing Kushan overlordship that had briefly extended into the region (the Kushans had been rebuffed by Ban Chao c. 90 AD). The territory near the central/northern Tarim (81.9E, 40.1N) thus passed from Kushan to the Protectorate. This reflects the renewed Han-aligned control of the Silk Road oases.

w4-400202.name: Roman counter-offensive restores Osroene — Lucius Verus's Parthian campaign
w4-400202.blurb: During the Roman counter-offensive of 163–166 CE under Lucius Verus, Roman forces under Avidius Cassius recovered Mesopotamia and sacked Ctesiphon (165 CE). Osroene's Abgarid dynasty was confirmed as a Roman client kingdom (~50,000 km², centroid 39.7°E, 36.8°N — upper Euphrates/Edessa region), removing direct Parthian control.

w4-400203.name: Hadhramaut annexation of Qataban
w4-400203.blurb: The Kingdom of Qataban was partitioned between Hadhramaut and Himyar in the late 1st–2nd century CE; Hadhramaut annexed the eastern portion in the second half of the 2nd century CE, reaching its greatest extent. The worklist window (165–184) fits this dating of the Qataban→Hadhramaut transfer.

w4-400205.name: Lucius Verus's Parthian War — Roman conquest of northern Mesopotamia
w4-400205.blurb: In the Roman–Parthian War of 161–166 CE, Lucius Verus's generals (notably Avidius Cassius) sacked Ctesiphon and Seleucia in 165 CE, forcing the Parthians to cede Dura-Europos and much of northern Mesopotamia to Rome (centroid ~42.6°E, 34.2°N). This was Rome's first permanent foothold in Mesopotamia, establishing a new frontier on the Euphrates.

w4-400212.name: Sun clan's consolidation of the lower Yangtze (rise of Eastern Wu)
w4-400212.blurb: Sun Ce and then Sun Quan (from 200 AD) consolidated control over the Jiangdong region and the lower/middle Yangtze, the territorial base that became Eastern Wu. The lands of southeastern China around Jiangxi/Hunan (113.8E, 27.8N) thus passed from nominal Han authority to the Sun regime. This established one of the three powers whose rivalry defined the Three Kingdoms period.

w4-400214.name: Roman annexation of Osroene under Caracalla
w4-400214.blurb: In 213-214 AD the emperor Caracalla deposed King Abgar IX of Osroene and annexed the kingdom, converting the client state centered on Edessa into a Roman province. The territory of Osroene in northern Mesopotamia near Edessa (39.7E, 36.8N) thus passed from the Kingdom of Osroene to the Roman Empire. This eliminated one of the last buffer kingdoms on the Roman-Parthian frontier.

w4-400215.name: Ardashir I's rebellion against Parthia (rise of the Sasanians in Fars)
w4-400215.blurb: Beginning around 205-212 AD, Ardashir I, ruler of Istakhr in Persis (Fars), rebelled against Parthian overlordship and conquered neighboring territories of Fars, founding the nascent Sasanian state. The core region of Fars/Persis near Persepolis-Istakhr (52.7E, 29.7N) thus passed from the Parthian Empire to the rising Sasanians. This was the opening stage of the revolt that culminated in the overthrow of the Parthians at the Battle of Hormozdgan in 224.

w4-400218.name: Cao Wei inheritance of Han authority over the Western Regions
w4-400218.blurb: When Cao Pi forced the abdication of Emperor Xian and founded the state of Cao Wei in 220 AD, Wei inherited the Han claim to the Western Regions, appointing officials and a Wuji colonel to oversee the Tarim oasis states. The territory of the central Tarim Basin (83.5E, 39.7N) thus passed from the (now-defunct) Protectorate/Han framework to Cao Wei. Wei maintained nominal suzerainty over the Silk Road kingdoms.

w4-400219.name: Xianbei tribal leaders submit to Cao Wei
w4-400219.blurb: Following Cao Cao's defeat of the Wuhuan at White Wolf Mountain (207), Xianbei chiefs paid tribute to Cao Cao and his successor Cao Pi. When Cao Pi proclaimed Cao Wei in 220 CE, Kebineng dispatched horses as tribute and received the title Prince Fuyi, and Budugen also pledged allegiance and sent tribute. This diplomatic submission (rather than outright conquest) is the mechanism for Xianbei territory appearing under Wei. The data window 215-224 captures the 220 submission.

w4-400222.name: Fragmentation of the Kushan Empire / Sasanian pressure (rise of the Eastern Kushans)
w4-400222.blurb: In the early-to-mid 3rd century the Kushan Empire fragmented under internal division and the rising pressure of Ardashir I's Sasanians, splitting into western (soon Kushano-Sasanian) and eastern branches. The large bloc of territory across northwestern India/Punjab (75.3E, 29.1N) thus passed from the unified Kushan Empire to a distinct Eastern Kushan polity. This decline ended the era of pan-Kushan dominance over the northwest.

w4-400223.name: Sasanian invasion splits the Kushan Empire (Western Kushans)
w4-400223.blurb: After the collapse of Parthia in 224 AD, the Sasanian Empire under Ardashir I expanded eastward into Kushan territory, reaching Bactria around 230 AD. The death of Kushan emperor Vasudeva I (c. 225) had already weakened the empire; Sasanian pressure accelerated the split, with the western territories becoming the Kushano-Sasanian sphere c. 224-238. Matches worklist transition Kushan Empire -> Western Kushans (224-238); coords lng 68.6 lat 36.4 confirm Bactria.

w4-400225.name: Aksumite expansion into Yemen under king GDRT (Gedara)
w4-400225.blurb: Under King Gedara (GDRT, r. c.200-230) the Kingdom of Axum intervened in South Arabia, allied with Saba against Himyar and Hadramawt, and held territory in western Yemen including the Tihama coast (lat 16.4, lng 43.2). South Arabian inscriptions record Aksumite forces in western Yemen in the first quarter of the 3rd century. Window 224-238.

w4-400228.name: Sabaean–Himyarite counter-offensive expels Axum from Yemen
w4-400228.blurb: After Axum briefly held parts of Yemen under GDRT, a Himyarite-Sabaean coalition counter-attacked in the 230s-240s, retaking interior territory and pushing Aksumite forces back from the Tihama (lat 16.4, lng 43.2). South Arabian inscriptions record the Himyarites reasserting control by c.238-247. This mirrors id 400225's earlier Aksumite advance. Window 238-247.

w4-400229.name: Sasanian conquest of Caucasian Iberia under Shapur I
w4-400229.blurb: During the Roman-Persian wars of the mid-3rd century, Shapur I of the Sasanian Empire extended Persian suzerainty over the Caucasus. His Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription (Res Gestae Divi Saporis) lists Iberia (Virzan/Wiruzan) among the lands subject to his empire, reflecting the imposition of Sasanian overlordship on the kingdom of Caucasian Iberia (Kartli) around 252.

citations.label: Res Gestae Divi Saporis (Naqsh-e Rostam inscription)

w4-400230.name: Sasanian subjugation of Caucasian Albania under Shapur I
w4-400230.blurb: Shapur I brought Caucasian Albania (Arran) under Sasanian control during his campaigns of the 250s, listing 'Albania' among the territories of his realm in the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription. The Albanian kingdom became a Sasanian vassal, securing the empire's northern Caucasus frontier against nomadic incursions through the Derbent passes.

w4-400231.name: Sasanian annexation of Armenia under Shapur I
w4-400231.blurb: After the assassination of the Arsacid king Khosrov II of Armenia (engineered by the Sasanians) and the flight of his heir Tiridates to Roman territory, Shapur I overran Armenia and installed his own son Hormizd-Ardashir as its king around 252. Armenia was effectively absorbed into the Sasanian sphere, a key prize cited in Shapur's inscription, until Roman intervention later restored the Arsacids.

w4-400232.name: Shapur I's conquest of Caucasian Iberia
w4-400232.blurb: Shapur I's early Sasanian campaigns brought Caucasian Iberia (centroid ~44.1°E, 42.2°N — modern Georgia) under Sasanian suzerainty c. 252–260 CE. Shapur I's Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription lists Iberia among his territorial holdings, reflecting Sasanian absorption of the Caucasian kingdoms as a buffer against Rome.

w4-400235.name: Vakataka expansion against the Western Satraps under Rudrasena/Vindhyashakti-Pravarasena
w4-400235.blurb: In the mid-3rd century the rising Vakataka dynasty of the Deccan, founded by Vindhyashakti and expanded by Pravarasena I, pushed northward into Malwa and the upper Deccan at the expense of the declining Western Kshatrapas (Saka Western Satraps). This brought the region around Vidisha/Malwa under Vakataka control as the Satrap state contracted.

w4-400238.name: Foundation of the Gallic Empire by Postumus
w4-400238.blurb: In 260, amid the Crisis of the Third Century, the general Postumus rebelled against Emperor Gallienus, killed the heir Saloninus at Cologne, and established a breakaway Gallic Empire (Imperium Galliarum) comprising Gaul, Britain, and Hispania. This severed the western provinces, including northern Gaul around Lutetia, from central Roman authority.

w4-400239.name: Rise of Palmyrene autonomy under Odaenathus
w4-400239.blurb: After Shapur I captured Emperor Valerian at Edessa in 260, Septimius Odaenathus of Palmyra rallied the Roman East, defeated the Persians, and became de facto ruler of the eastern provinces (Syria, the Levant) as corrector totius Orientis. This created the autonomous Palmyrene power, nominally Roman but independent in practice, around the Levant.

w4-400241.name: Odaenathus's Persian campaigns against the Sasanians
w4-400241.blurb: Following Valerian's capture, Odaenathus of Palmyra led campaigns against the Sasanian Empire in 262-263, recovering Mesopotamian territory and twice advancing to the gates of Ctesiphon. This pushed Sasanian forces back and brought borderlands of northern Mesopotamia/Osroene under Palmyrene-Roman control.

w4-400242.name: Sima Yan's usurpation founding the Western Jin
w4-400242.blurb: In 265 Sima Yan forced the abdication of the last Cao Wei emperor, Cao Huan, and proclaimed himself Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty. This dynastic usurpation transferred all Cao Wei territory to the new Western Jin, completing the Sima family's takeover begun by Sima Yi.

w4-400243.name: Western Satrap resurgence in Rajasthan under Rudrasena II / late Kshatrapas
w4-400243.blurb: In the later 3rd century the Western Kshatrapas reasserted control over parts of northwestern India (Rajasthan/Marwar) against the declining Kushan presence in the region. This frontier shift returned territory around Ajmer/Marwar to Saka Satrap rule as Kushan power in the northwest fragmented.

w4-400247.name: Western Jin conquest of Eastern Wu
w4-400247.blurb: In 280 the Western Jin under Emperor Wu launched a massive multi-pronged offensive down the Yangtze against Eastern Wu. Wu's last ruler Sun Hao surrendered, ending the Three Kingdoms period and reunifying China; the southern and southeastern lands passed to Jin.

w4-400249.name: Aurelian's reconquest of the Gallic Empire
w4-400249.blurb: In 274 Emperor Aurelian defeated Tetricus I, the last Gallic emperor, at the Battle of Chalons, ending the breakaway Gallic Empire and reuniting Gaul, Britain, and Hispania with the Roman Empire. Northern Gaul around Lutetia thus reverted to central Roman rule.

w4-400253.name: Sasanian restoration of control over Caucasian Albania (Bahram II era)
w4-400253.blurb: During the reign of Bahram II, the Sasanians reasserted authority over Caucasian Albania in the Caucasus after the disruptions of the early 280s and the death of Carus. Albania returned to its position as a Sasanian vassal kingdom guarding the northern frontier.

w4-400254.name: Tiridates III restored to the Armenian throne under Roman protection (traditional date 287)
w4-400254.blurb: In 283 CE Emperor Carus invaded the Sasanian Empire, advancing down the Tigris and capturing Ctesiphon, briefly restoring Roman control over upper Mesopotamia (centroid ~42.6°E, 36.9°N) and the Adiabene region. Carus died suddenly during the campaign — reportedly struck by lightning — and the offensive halted, leaving these gains tenuous and largely reversed under his short-lived successors. Durable Roman dominance over the trans-Tigrine zone would not be secured until the Peace of Nisibis in 299, a separate settlement under Diocletian and Galerius.

w4-400255.name: Bahram II installs Mirian III as king of Iberia, founding the Chosroid dynasty
w4-400255.blurb: In 284 the Sasanian king Bahram II secured the Iberian throne for the young Mihranid prince Mirian III, founder of the Chosroid dynasty, to strengthen Persian influence in the Caucasus. The installation re-established Caucasian Iberia as a distinct kingdom -- initially a Sasanian client that later realigned toward Rome -- after a period of direct Sasanian dominance.

w4-400259.name: Li Xiong's founding of Cheng-Han
w4-400259.blurb: Amid the chaos of the War of the Eight Princes and the great Ba-Di and Sichuanese refugee migrations, Li Te and his son Li Xiong led the Liu people of Ba and Di stock in revolt against Western Jin authority in Yi Province (Sichuan). Li Xiong took Chengdu in 304 and proclaimed himself King of Cheng, then Emperor in 306, founding the Cheng-Han state and stripping Jin of the Sichuan basin around modern Chongqing.

w4-400260.name: Pallava expansion into the Tamil country under the early Pallavas
w4-400260.blurb: During the obscure post-Sangam interval, the rising Pallava dynasty based at Kanchipuram pressed southward into the lands of the older Chera (and Chola) crowned kings of the deep south. The Cheras of the Kerala coast lost frontier territory as Pallava power radiated out across the Tamil country. The attribution rests on the general Pallava ascendancy of c. 300 rather than a single named battle.

w4-400262.name: Pallava ascendancy over the early Cholas
w4-400262.blurb: In the centuries between the Sangam-age Cholas and the imperial Cholas, the Chola country fell into eclipse as the Pallavas of Kanchipuram dominated the northern Tamil region. The early Cholas around the Kaveri lost territory to the expanding Pallava state. This reflects the broad Pallava supremacy of the period rather than one documented engagement.

w4-400267.name: Western Jin loses the Western Regions during the War of the Eight Princes
w4-400267.blurb: The War of the Eight Princes (291–306 CE) devastated Jin's military capacity; by 304 the dynasty had lost effective control of the Western Regions protectorate as the court collapsed inward. The atlas reassignment of this Tarim Basin territory (~694,000 km²) to a nominally independent 'Protectorate of the Western Regions' reflects the de facto end of Jin suzerainty in that window.

citations.label: Wikipedia: War of the Eight Princes

w4-400269.name: Shi Le's conquest of Former Zhao
w4-400269.blurb: The Later Zhao warlord Shi Le, a former subordinate of the Xiongnu Han-Zhao, turned on his overlords and destroyed Former (Han) Zhao. His forces crushed Liu Yao at the Battle of Luoyang in 328 and captured the Former Zhao capital Chang'an in 329, transferring the Guanzhong and central plain heartland from Former Zhao to Later Zhao.

w4-400271.name: Fall of Kush and rise of Alodia
w4-400271.blurb: By the mid-4th century the Kingdom of Kush at Meroe had collapsed, weakened internally and struck by the Aksumite king Ezana around 350. In the power vacuum along the Blue Nile and Gezira the Nubian successor kingdom of Alodia (Alwa), centered on Soba, emerged to inherit the southern Kushite lands.

w4-400272.name: Fall of Kush and rise of Makuria
w4-400272.blurb: With the disintegration of Meroitic Kush in the 4th century—hastened by the campaign of Aksum's King Ezana around 350—new Nubian kingdoms arose from its ruins. Makuria, centered on Dongola in the Nile's great bend, succeeded Kush in the northern-central Nubian lands.

w4-400276.name: Baekje's absorption of the Mahan confederacy
w4-400276.blurb: Under King Geunchogo (r. 346–375), the kingdom of Baekje consolidated its hold over the southwestern Korean peninsula by absorbing the remaining statelets of the Mahan confederacy. This brought the Mahan territory of the lower Geum and Yeongsan basins firmly under Baekje rule.

w4-400282.name: Former Qin's conquest of Later Zhao's western lands
w4-400282.blurb: After the collapse of Later Zhao following Shi Hu's death and the Ran Min massacres (349–352), the Di chieftain Fu Jian (Fu Hong's son Fu Jiàn) seized Guanzhong and founded Former Qin in 351. Former Qin took the western heartland around Chang'an from the disintegrating Later Zhao.

w4-400283.name: Samudragupta's southern (Dakshinapatha) campaign
w4-400283.blurb: Samudragupta's famed southern expedition, recorded in the Allahabad Pillar inscription, carried Gupta arms deep into the Deccan and the eastern coast, subduing a string of southern kings. Gupta pressure extended into the northern Tamil/Andhra frontier at the expense of the Pallava sphere, whose ruler Vishnugopa of Kanchi was among those defeated.

w4-400285.name: Former Qin emerges from Later Zhao's collapse and seizes Guanzhong
w4-400285.blurb: Later Zhao disintegrated after Shi Hu's death in 349, with Ran Min's coup and ethnic massacres destroying the regime by 350–351. Amid the collapse the Di chieftain Fu Hong led his people toward Guanzhong but was killed before completing the march; his son Fu Jian (苻健) seized the Guanzhong basin around Chang'an and in 351 proclaimed himself Heavenly King, founding the Former Qin and absorbing the ~388,000 km² formerly held by Later Zhao.

w4-400286.name: Samudragupta's Southern Campaign and Submission of Vishnugopa of Kanchi
w4-400286.blurb: The Allahabad (Prayagraj) Pillar inscription of Samudragupta records his defeat of twelve kings of the Dakshinapatha during his great southern campaign (c. 350 CE), among them Vishnugopa, the Pallava king of Kanchi (Kanchipuram, in modern Tamil Nadu). Following the policy of grahana-moksha-anugraha, Samudragupta captured then released and reinstated these rulers as tributaries rather than annexing the far south. The episode established Gupta paramountcy over the Pallava realm without direct administration of the distant Tamil country.

w4-400293.name: Former Qin's conquest of Former Yan
w4-400293.blurb: Fu Jian's Former Qin, guided by the statesman Wang Meng, invaded the Murong state of Former Yan and destroyed it. Wang Meng won the decisive Battle of Lupi/Luchuan in 370 and captured the Yan capital Ye, annexing all of Former Yan's territory in the eastern plain and bringing northern China close to unification under Former Qin.

w4-400294.name: Ardashir II as Vassal King of Adiabene under Shapur II
w4-400294.blurb: The territory near Nineveh was the heartland of Adiabene, a vassal kingdom of the Sasanian Empire. Ardashir II served as vassal king of Adiabene c. 344-376 CE under his brother Shapur II. The window 367-371 spans a period of Romano-Sasanian conflict over Armenia; Adiabene was already under Sasanian suzerainty, so the apparent transfer from 'Kingdom of Adiabene' to 'Sasanian Empire' likely reflects a data-model boundary adjustment of its semi-autonomous client status rather than a distinct conquest. Adiabene was converted to a province only after Ardashir II became shah in 379.

w4-400296.name: Hunnic conquest of the Ostrogothic kingdom (Gothia)
w4-400296.blurb: Around 370–375 AD the Huns swept westward, overrunning the Alans east of the Don and then the Ostrogothic kingdom north of the Black Sea; King Ermanaric was defeated and reportedly died c.375. Surviving Goths submitted to Hunnic rule or fled across the Danube into Rome in 376. The conventional date is c.375; the dataset's 371-373 window captures the early phase of the Hunnic advance and matches the Gothia → Huns transfer.

w4-400297.name: Hunnic conquest of the Cimmerian Bosporus (c. 375 AD)
w4-400297.blurb: Around 375-376 AD, the Huns swept westward from the Pontic steppe, defeating the nearby Alans and overrunning the Gothic-allied territories north of the Black Sea. The Bosporan Kingdom (Cimmerian Bosporus), centred on the Kerch Strait at Panticapaeum, succumbed to Hunnic pressure in the final quarter of the fourth century. Modern scholarship debates whether the political end was clean (an inscription of a ruler Douptounos survives from c. 483), but the kingdom's independence effectively ended with the Hunnic invasion of 375/376, with a Gothic-then-Hunnic-vassal realm succeeding it.

citations.label: Crimea in the Roman era - Wikipedia

w4-400298.name: Former Qin's conquest of Eastern Jin's Yi Province (Sichuan)
w4-400298.blurb: In 373 Fu Jian's Former Qin generals invaded the Eastern Jin's western provinces, capturing Yi and Liang provinces (the Sichuan basin and Hanzhong). This wrested the southwest from Jin and brought Former Qin to its territorial peak before the Battle of Fei River. (The 'Western Jin' label is the dataset's continuation of the Jin state, by then Eastern Jin.)

w4-400299.name: Hunnic Conquest of the Greuthungi (Eastern Goths)
w4-400299.blurb: Around 370–372, the Huns crossed the Volga and Don rivers, first subjugating the Alans and then defeating the Greuthungi (Eastern Goths) under King Ermanaric, who reportedly killed himself in despair. The centroid at 30°E/49°N (Ukrainian steppe) places this in the Pontic steppe — the initial zone of Hunnic conquest of Gothic territory.

w4-400300.name: Samudragupta's subjugation of the Yaudheya republic
w4-400300.blurb: The Allahabad Pillar inscription names the Yaudheyas among the frontier tribal republics (atavika/gana states) that submitted to Samudragupta and paid tribute. The martial Yaudheya republic of the eastern Punjab and Rajasthan was absorbed into the Gupta sphere during this consolidation of the north.

w4-400301.name: Gothic crossing of the Danube and occupation of Moesia/Gothia (376–378)
w4-400301.blurb: In 376, pushed by Hunnic pressure from the east, the Tervingi Goths under Fritigern and Alavivus crossed the Danube with imperial permission and settled in Moesia. Roman mismanagement provoked a rebellion; at the Battle of Adrianople (9 August 378), Emperor Valens was killed and the Eastern Roman army destroyed. The Goths thereby came to control much of the Balkan territory previously administered as Roman provinces.

w4-400303.name: Silla's absorption of the Jinhan confederacy
w4-400303.blurb: The Saro/Silla state, centered on Gyeongju (Seorabeol), gradually subjugated and absorbed the small statelets of the Jinhan confederacy in southeastern Korea during the 4th century, a process consolidated under King Naemul (r. 356-402). By the 370s the Jinhan polities had effectively become Silla, accounting for this transfer of territory in the Nakdong River basin.

w4-400304.name: Gothic settlement (foedus) of 382
w4-400304.blurb: After the catastrophic Roman defeat at Adrianople (378) where Emperor Valens was killed, his successor Theodosius I fought the Goths to a stalemate and concluded a treaty (foedus) on 3 October 382. The Goths were settled as federates within the Roman Empire south of the Danube in Thrace/Moesia, retaining autonomy under their own leaders in exchange for military service, returning the region near the lower Danube to nominal Roman sovereignty.

w4-400305.name: Hunnic invasion of Gothia - Goths flee across the Danube
w4-400305.blurb: In approximately 372-375 CE the Huns swept westward from the Pontic steppe and overwhelmed the Greuthungi and Thervingi Goths north of the Danube (the region historians call Gothia, modern Romania/Moldova). Driven from their lands, the Goths appealed to Emperor Valens and crossed the Danube into Roman territory in 376, precipitating the Gothic War that culminated in the catastrophic Roman defeat at the Battle of Adrianople (9 August 378). By 383 the Huns had consolidated control over the former Gothic territories north of the Danube.

w4-400307.name: Kidarite conquest of Bactria/Tokharistan
w4-400307.blurb: The Kidarites (Kidarite Huns), a Hunnic people, pushed into Sasanian-held Bactria and the eastern provinces during the later 4th century, wresting Tokharistan and the region around Balkh from Sasanian control. Exploiting Sasanian distraction, they established a kingdom straddling the Hindu Kush, displacing Persian authority near Balkh (the location here).

w4-400308.name: Founding of Western Qin after the Battle of Fei River
w4-400308.blurb: The Former Qin's crushing defeat at the Battle of Fei River (383) against the Eastern Jin shattered Fu Jian's unified northern empire. In the collapse, the Xianbei Qifu clan leader Qifu Guoren broke away and founded the Western Qin in 385 in the Longxi/Gansu region (around the upper Yellow River), seizing this territory from the disintegrating Former Qin.

w4-400310.name: Murong rebellion and founding of Western Yan after Fei River
w4-400310.blurb: After the Former Qin's defeat at Fei River (383), the Murong Xianbei nobles who had been resettled in Former Qin territory rose in revolt. Murong Hong proclaimed the Western Yan in 384 in the Shanxi region (around Taiyuan/Chang'an's hinterland), tearing this territory away from the collapsing Former Qin.

w4-400311.name: Partition of Armenia between Rome and Sasanian Persia (387)
w4-400311.blurb: In 387 Theodosius I and the Sasanian shah Shapur III formally partitioned the Kingdom of Armenia between their empires, ending decades of contest over the buffer kingdom. The larger eastern portion (Persarmenia) came under Sasanian suzerainty; this transfer reflects Sasanian-backed Armenian authority being established in the eastern Armenian highlands around Lake Van/Ararat.

citations.label: Peace of Acilisene / Partition of Armenia — Wikipedia

w4-400314.name: Murong Chui's founding of Later Yan after Fei River
w4-400314.blurb: In the wake of the Former Qin's defeat at Fei River (383), the Murong Xianbei general Murong Chui rebelled and restored the Yan state, founding the Later Yan in 384 with its base in the northeast (around Zhongshan/Hebei and the old Yan heartland near Beijing). This transferred the northeastern territory from the Former Qin to the new Later Yan.

w4-400317.name: Roman-Sasanian peace and partition of 387 (Mesopotamian frontier)
w4-400317.blurb: The settlement between Theodosius I and Shapur III in 387, best known for partitioning Armenia, also adjusted the Roman-Persian frontier in upper Mesopotamia. This small transfer near the upper Tigris/Tur Abdin region reflects the Roman gains/frontier rectification arising from that diplomatic settlement.

w4-400319.name: Xionite displacement of the Kidarites in Sogdiana/Bactria
w4-400319.blurb: The Xionites (Chionites) and Kidarites were competing Hunnic powers in 4th-century Central Asia, and the Xionites overran Kidarite-held lands in Sogdiana and the Oxus region (around Samarkand/Balkh latitude). This transfer reflects Xionite ascendancy over the Kidarites in Transoxiana during the late 4th century.

w4-400321.name: Eastern Jin northern recovery in the North China Plain after Fei River
w4-400321.blurb: Continuing the Eastern Jin (rendered Western Jin) counteroffensive after the Battle of Fei River (383), Jin forces pressed into the central plain. This area around the Shandong/Hebei border passed from the collapsing Former Qin into Jin hands in the later 380s, though such gains proved short-lived against the resurgent Xianbei states.

w4-400322.name: Goguryeo conquest under Gwanggaeto the Great
w4-400322.blurb: Goguryeo's King Gwanggaeto the Great, who took the throne in 391, launched vigorous campaigns that absorbed neighboring polities in the Korean peninsula. The Dongye, a small chiefdom on the east-central coast, fell under Goguryeo control during this expansion, transferring the region around the east Korean coast.

w4-400323.name: Later Qin conquest of the Guanzhong and final fall of Former Qin
w4-400323.blurb: The Later Qin under Yao Chang and his son Yao Xing destroyed the rump Former Qin, which finally collapsed in 394 when its last emperor Fu Deng was defeated and killed. This large transfer in the Guanzhong/Wei River region marks the Later Qin's consolidation of the former Qin heartland around Chang'an.

w4-400325.name: Later Yan annexation of Western Yan
w4-400325.blurb: In 394 the Later Yan emperor Murong Chui invaded and destroyed the rival Murong state of Western Yan, killing its ruler Murong Yong and absorbing its territory in modern Shanxi. This reunited most of the Murong Xianbei holdings under Later Yan. The campaign eliminated the last independent Murong rival in the north.

w4-400328.name: Death of Theodosius I and final division of the Roman Empire
w4-400328.blurb: On the death of Theodosius I in January 395, the Roman Empire was divided between his sons: Arcadius received the East and Honorius the West. This was the last division of a unified Roman state, never to be reunited. The eastern provinces, including this region, passed to the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) administration under Arcadius.

w4-400330.name: Hunnic invasion of the Caucasus and Near East (395-396)
w4-400330.blurb: In 395-396 the Huns burst through the Caucasus passes (the Caspian/Darial gates) and raided Armenia, the Roman East, and Sasanian territory. The Armenian highlands around Lake Van and Ararat were overrun by the Hunnic onslaught described by Jerome and Claudian. This great raid temporarily stripped Armenia from settled control.

w4-400333.name: Duan Ye's installation by the rebelling Juqu clan founds Northern Liang
w4-400333.blurb: In 397, after Later Liang's ruler Lü Guang executed the Xiongnu chieftain Juqu Luochou following a military defeat, Luochou's nephews Juqu Mengxun and Juqu Nancheng rose in revolt and installed the Han Chinese administrator Duan Ye as founding ruler of Northern Liang in the Hexi Corridor, detaching the western Gansu region around Zhangye from Later Liang control. Juqu Mengxun remained the power behind the throne until 401, when he killed Duan Ye and took direct rule himself.

w4-400334.name: Establishment of Southern Liang
w4-400334.blurb: In 397 the Tufa Xianbei chieftain Tufa Wugu broke away from Later Liang and founded the Southern Liang state in the eastern Gansu region around modern Lanzhou. The secession stripped Later Liang of its southeastern territory. Southern Liang became a rival Xianbei power in the Hexi-Longxi area.

w4-400335.name: Alaric's First Invasion of Greece
w4-400335.blurb: In 395–396 Alaric led the Visigoths from Thrace southward through Thermopylae into Greece proper, sacking Corinth, Argos, and Sparta and effectively occupying much of the Peloponnese (centroid lng 22.6, lat 37.5). The Eastern Roman general Stilicho briefly interposed but allowed Alaric to escape; Arcadius then granted Alaric the title of magister militum per Illyricum in 397, effectively legitimizing Visigothic presence.

w4-400336.name: Withdrawal of the Huns from Armenia after the 395-396 raid
w4-400336.blurb: After their devastating raid of 395-396, the Huns withdrew back through the Caucasus, and Armenia reverted to its prior status under Roman-Sasanian partition arrangements. The transient Hunnic occupation of the Armenian highlands ended as the raiders returned north of the Caucasus. Armenian territory was thus restored from Hunnic control.

w4-400338.name: Kidarite ascendancy over the Xionites in Bactria/Sogdia
w4-400338.blurb: Around 400 the Kidarites (Kidarite Huns), under their eponymous leader Kidara, rose to dominance over the earlier Xionite groups in Bactria, Sogdiana, and Transoxiana. They supplanted the prior Xionite/Chionite power in the region between the Oxus and the Jaxartes. This transition established the Kidarite kingdom that would later clash with the Sasanians and Gupta India.

w4-400342.name: Rise of the Rouran Khaganate on the northern steppe
w4-400342.blurb: In 402 Shelun unified the Rouran tribes and proclaimed himself Qaghan, establishing the Rouran Khaganate as the dominant steppe power north of Northern Wei. As Wei consolidated in China proper, the Mongolian steppe and Inner Asian frontier zone passed to Rouran control. The Rouran became Northern Wei's principal northern rival for the next century.

w4-400345.name: Later Qin expansion into former Later Yan/Western Yan territory
w4-400345.blurb: As Later Yan disintegrated after Canhe Slope, the Qiang-led Later Qin under Yao Xing expanded eastward in the late 390s, seizing territory in the southern Hebei/Henan border region around the upper Yellow River. Yao Xing's Later Qin became the dominant power in the central plains west of Northern Wei. This brought former Yan lands under Qin control.

w4-400346.name: Later Qin subjugation of Western Qin
w4-400346.blurb: In 400 the Later Qin of Yao Xing defeated and annexed the Tuoyuhun/Xianbei-led Western Qin of Qifu Gangui, who submitted as a Later Qin vassal and lost his independent state around modern Gansu (Longxi). This absorbed Western Qin's territory into Later Qin. Western Qin would later be re-established in 409 after Later Qin weakened.

w4-400350.name: Alaric I appointed Magister Militum per Illyricum; Visigoth withdrawal from Greece
w4-400350.blurb: After ravaging Greece in 395–396, Alaric I of the Visigoths was appointed Magister Militum per Illyricum by the Eastern Roman court (c. 397–401), effectively ceding Illyricum's administration to him. Between 401 and 407, Alaric repeatedly invaded Italy, while the Eastern Empire regained administrative control of Illyricum and Greece. By around 407, the Visigoths were militarily focused on Italy, leaving the Balkans to return to Eastern Roman governance.

w4-400351.name: Later Qin annexation of Later Liang
w4-400351.blurb: In 403 the Later Liang ruler Lü Long, pressed by the rival Liang states and unable to hold the Hexi Corridor, formally surrendered his state to Yao Xing of Later Qin. This brought the Wuwei/Guzang region of Gansu under Later Qin control and ended the Later Liang. The submission marked Later Qin's peak extent in the northwest.

w4-400353.name: Establishment of Western Liang by Li Gao
w4-400353.blurb: In 400 Li Gao, a Han Chinese governor under Northern Liang, declared independence at Dunhuang and founded the Western Liang in the far western Hexi Corridor (Jiuquan/Dunhuang region). The secession detached the western oases from Northern Liang control. Li Gao is traditionally claimed as an ancestor of the later Tang imperial house.

w4-400355.name: Suebic settlement in Gallaecia (Crossing of the Rhine / invasion of Hispania)
w4-400355.blurb: Following the Crossing of the Rhine on 31 December 406, the Suebi, Vandals, and Alans poured into Gaul and then crossed into Hispania in 409. By treaty/lot the Suebi (along with the Hasding Vandals) were allotted Gallaecia in the northwest of the peninsula, founding the Kingdom of the Suebi with its capital at Bracara Augusta (Braga). This stripped the region around Braga from Roman control.

w4-400357.name: Chandragupta II's conquest of the Western Satraps
w4-400357.blurb: The Gupta emperor Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) campaigned against the Western Kshatrapas (Saka Western Satraps) of Malwa, Gujarat, and Saurashtra, defeating and annexing them around 409 and giving the Guptas access to the western seaports. The conquest is commemorated by Chandragupta's silver coinage struck in the Saka style. This transferred the large Malwa-Gujarat region to the Gupta Empire.

w4-400360.name: Helian Bobo's Xia expansion in the Ordos
w4-400360.blurb: Helian Bobo, a Tiefu Xiongnu leader, founded the Xia (Hu Xia) state in 407 in the Ordos region and aggressively raided his neighbors. His consolidation of the Ordos plateau brought territory that had been within the steppe sphere of the Rouran Khaganate under Xia control around the Ordos loop of the Yellow River.

w4-400361.name: Hephthalite (White Hun) supplanting of the Kidarites in Transoxiana
w4-400361.blurb: During the early 5th century the Hephthalites (White Huns) rose in Central Asia and progressively displaced the Kidarite Huns from Transoxiana and the regions around Sogdia and the Ferghana corridor. This power shift transferred the area around the upper Syr Darya/Sogdiana to the emerging White Hun confederation. The displacement culminated in the Hephthalites driving the Kidarites south into Gandhara later in the century.

w4-400362.name: Liu Yu's destruction of Southern Yan
w4-400362.blurb: The Eastern Jin general Liu Yu (later founder of the Liu Song dynasty) invaded Southern Yan, besieged its capital Guanggu (modern Qingzhou, Shandong), and captured and executed the Southern Yan emperor Murong Chao in 410. This annexed the Shandong peninsula region to Eastern Jin (rendered here as Western Jin), eliminating Southern Yan.

w4-400363.name: Vandal-Alan-Suebic invasion of Hispania (division of 411)
w4-400363.blurb: After crossing into Hispania in 409, the barbarian confederation divided the peninsula by lot in 411: the Hasding Vandals took part of Gallaecia, the Siling Vandals took Baetica, the Alans took Lusitania and Carthaginiensis, and the Suebi took the rest of Gallaecia. This stripped the central-southern interior of Hispania (around the Meseta) from Roman control to the Vandals.

w4-400364.name: Vandal departure from Gaul into Hispania (Roman recovery of the Rhine/Danube frontier zone)
w4-400364.blurb: When the Vandals and their allies left Gaul to cross the Pyrenees into Hispania in 409, the lands they had ravaged in the upper Danube/Rhine borderlands (around modern Bavaria/Raetia) reverted nominally to Western Roman control. The reverse direction here reflects the Vandals vacating territory in southern Germania that returned to Rome's sphere.

w4-400367.name: Vandal migration into Gaul and Spain — Roman reoccupation of former Vandal territory
w4-400367.blurb: The Vandals, along with Alans and Suebi, crossed the frozen Rhine on 31 December 406 and swept through Gaul, crossing into Hispania in October 409. Their former territory in central Germania (~53,000 km², centroid 10.2°E, 49.3°N — Thuringia/central Germany) was left largely undefended and reverted nominally to Roman or neighboring Germanic control.

w4-400368.name: Division of Hispania by lot among Vandals, Alans, and Suebi (411)
w4-400368.blurb: In the 411 partition of Hispania, the Alans under King Respendial received the large provinces of Lusitania and Carthaginiensis, the most extensive allotment. This transferred the central-western interior of the peninsula (around modern Extremadura/La Mancha) from the Hasding/Siling Vandal sphere to the Alans. The Alans were later crushed by the Visigoths in 418, after which survivors merged with the Vandals.

w4-400369.name: Western Qin expansion against Southern Liang
w4-400369.blurb: The Western Qin, restored in 409, expanded against its Hexi-corridor rivals. Western Qin attacked Southern Liang (the Tufa Xianbei state), and in 414 Western Qin's forces destroyed Southern Liang, killing its last ruler Tufa Rutan's line and annexing its territory around the Huangshui valley near modern Xining/Lanzhou.

w4-400370.name: Western Qin gains in Gansu at Later Qin's expense
w4-400370.blurb: As Later Qin (Yao dynasty) weakened in the 410s under pressure from Eastern Jin and Xia, the resurgent Western Qin recovered and expanded its holdings in the upper Yellow River region of Gansu around modern Lanzhou. This change reflects Western Qin annexing former Later Qin territory in the Hexi/Longxi region between 410 and 414.

w4-400374.name: Visigothic settlement in Aquitania (foedus of 418)
w4-400374.blurb: After Athaulf and then Wallia led the Visigoths through Gaul and Hispania, the Visigoths were settled by Roman treaty (foedus) in Aquitania Secunda around 418, with their capital at Toulouse, forming the Visigothic Kingdom. This transferred the region around the Garonne in southwestern Gaul from direct Roman administration to the Visigoths.

w4-400375.name: Suebic-Vandal conflict in Gallaecia (Battle of the Nervasos Mountains)
w4-400375.blurb: The Hasding Vandals and the Suebi, both settled in Gallaecia, came into conflict; the Suebi under Hermeric were besieged by the Vandals in the Nervasos Mountains around 419, but Roman intervention forced the Vandals south, leaving the Suebi to dominate northwestern Gallaecia. This transferred the area around modern Lugo/Galicia from Vandal to Suebic control.

w4-400376.name: Treaty between Wallia and Constantius III — Visigoths as Roman foederati (416–418)
w4-400376.blurb: Visigothic king Wallia concluded a foedus with the Roman patrician Constantius III in early 416, agreeing to campaign in Hispania against the Vandals, Alans and Suebi in exchange for grain; the Visigoths were settled as foederati in Aquitaine in 418. This restored nominal Roman authority over territories the Visigoths held in southern Gaul. From=Visigoths, to=Western Roman Empire matches the foederati settlement in the 414-417 window.

w4-400379.name: Foedus of 418 — Visigoths settle in Aquitaine as Roman federates
w4-400379.blurb: Emperor Honorius formalized a treaty in 418 granting the Visigoths lands in Gallia Aquitania (Aquitaine Secunda) as federates. This followed years of raiding through Gaul and Spain; the settlement around Tolosa (Toulouse) marked the foundation of the Visigothic Kingdom within nominal Roman suzerainty.

w4-400380.name: Xia capture of Chang'an from Eastern Jin
w4-400380.blurb: After Liu Yu withdrew east to claim the throne in 418, Helian Bobo's Xia attacked the weakened Jin garrison in Guanzhong, defeated them, and captured Chang'an in 418, where Helian Bobo proclaimed himself emperor. This transferred the Guanzhong region around modern Xi'an from Eastern Jin (Western Jin here) to Xia.

w4-400381.name: Rouran encroachment on the Ordos as Xia turned south
w4-400381.blurb: As Helian Bobo's Xia shifted its focus south to capture Chang'an and contest Guanzhong with Jin and Northern Wei, the Rouran Khaganate pressed on Xia's northern steppe frontier in the Ordos. This transferred the northern Ordos region back into the Rouran sphere between 417 and 426, before Northern Wei later destroyed Xia.

w4-400382.name: Tuyuhun expansion as Western Qin declined
w4-400382.blurb: The Tuyuhun, a Murong Xianbei nomadic state in the Qinghai region, expanded eastward against the weakening Western Qin in the 420s as Western Qin came under pressure from Xia. This transferred territory in the upper Yellow River / Tao river region around modern southern Gansu-Qinghai border from Western Qin to the Tuyuhun before Western Qin was finally destroyed by Xia in 431.

w4-400388.name: Suebi conquest of Lusitania under King Rechila
w4-400388.blurb: As the Vandals and Alans departed Iberia (the surviving Alans having merged with the Hasding Vandals who crossed to North Africa in 429), the Suebi under King Rechila (r. 438–448) expanded into the vacuum. In 439 Rechila invaded Lusitania and captured the provincial capital Mérida (defeating residual Alan forces), then took Seville in 441. This swept the last Alan territorial identity from Lusitania (lat 40, lng -7.3, modern Portugal/western Spain) by the late 430s.

w4-400389.name: Sasanian abolition of the Armenian monarchy (Marzpanate established)
w4-400389.blurb: In 428 the Sasanian king Bahram V deposed the last Arsacid king of Armenia, Artaxias IV, at the request of the Armenian nobility (nakharars), abolishing the Kingdom of (Persian) Armenia and converting it into a Sasanian province governed by a marzpan (margrave). This brought the bulk of Armenia, around the Ararat plain and Lake Van, under direct Sasanian rule. The change reflects the consolidation of this marzpanate in the following years.

w4-400394.name: Vandal capture of Carthage
w4-400394.blurb: On 19 October 439 Geiseric's Vandals seized Carthage, the rich capital of Roman Africa, after they had earlier been granted Numidia by the 435 Treaty of Hippo Regius and then broke the peace. The location near eastern Sicily/the central Mediterranean reflects the Vandal seizure of the African proconsular province and the beginning of Vandal naval raids; Rome formally ceded Africa Proconsularis by the treaty of 442.

w4-400395.name: Anglo-Saxon settlement of lowland Britain
w4-400395.blurb: The Gallic Chronicle of 452 records for 441 that the British provinces were 'reduced to Saxon rule.' Following the Roman withdrawal, Angles, Saxons, and Jutes settled the eastern lowlands, displacing Brythonic authority over the Midlands plain by around 441. A gradual process rather than a single battle, but attested within the 439-441 window.

w4-400398.name: Burgundian settlement in Sapaudia (Savoy)
w4-400398.blurb: After the Huns devastated the first Burgundian kingdom centered on Worms in 436-437, the Roman general Aetius resettled the surviving Burgundians as foederati in Sapaudia (the Savoy/Lake Geneva region) in 443. This transfer reflects the Western Roman Empire ceding control of the territory around modern Geneva/Savoy to the new Burgundian Kingdom along the upper Rhone.

w4-400399.name: Treaty of 442 between Geiseric and Valentinian III
w4-400399.blurb: By the treaty of 442 the Western Roman Empire formally recognized Vandal sovereignty over the wealthiest North African provinces, ceding Africa Proconsularis, Byzacena and part of Numidia to Geiseric in exchange for the Vandals returning the poorer Mauretanian provinces. The location around the Gulf of Sirte/Tripolitania reflects this formal cession of the African core to the Vandal Kingdom.

w4-400403.name: Hephthalite (White Hun) expansion into the Wusun lands of the Ili/Issyk-Kul region
w4-400403.blurb: During the mid-5th century the Hephthalites (White Huns) expanded across Central Asia, pressing the Wusun out of their homeland in the Ili valley and around Issyk-Kul (the location here, in modern Kyrgyzstan/SE Kazakhstan). Under steppe pressure the Wusun were driven into the Pamirs, and the Hephthalites came to dominate the Tian Shan approaches and Transoxiana.

w4-400405.name: Narendrasena's Vakataka expansion into Malwa, Kosala and Mekala amid Gupta turmoil
w4-400405.blurb: Around 450 AD, exploiting the turmoil of Kumaragupta I's last years -- when the Gupta Empire was strained by Pushyamitra attacks -- the Vakataka king Narendrasena, son of Pravarasena II, seized the central Indian territories of Malwa, Kosala and Mekala from Gupta control, extending Vakataka power over the Deccan region shown here. Skandagupta later reclaimed these territories for the Guptas.

w4-400406.name: Northern Wei southern campaign against Liu Song (Yuanjia northern expeditions)
w4-400406.blurb: In 450-451 Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei launched a massive counter-offensive against the Liu Song dynasty, whose Yuanjia-era northern expedition had failed, driving Wei armies all the way to the Yangtze near Guabu opposite Jiankang. Wei devastated and seized Liu Song territory in the Huai-Yellow River region (around modern Shandong/northern Jiangsu shown here), consolidating the contested frontier under Northern Wei.

w4-400407.name: Battle of Avarayr (Vardanants) — Armenian revolt against Sasanian rule
w4-400407.blurb: In 451 the Armenian nakharars under Vardan Mamikonian rose against Sasanian king Yazdegerd II's attempt to impose Zoroastrianism, fighting the Battle of Avarayr. Although the Armenians were defeated militarily, the rebellion forced the Sasanians to relent on forced conversion and tolerate Christianity, restoring effective Armenian autonomy over the Ararat region; this reversion (Sasanian -> Armenia) reflects that restored Christian Armenian self-rule.

w4-400409.name: Attila's invasion of Italy
w4-400409.blurb: In 452 Attila led the Huns across the Julian Alps into northeastern Italy, sacking Aquileia and ravaging Venetia and the Po valley (the location here, around modern Veneto/Friuli). The Western Roman Empire lost control of these regions during the invasion until Attila withdrew, famously after meeting Pope Leo I, with plague and supply problems also forcing the retreat.

w4-400410.name: Collapse of Hunnic Empire after Attila's death — Saxon expansion in northern Germany
w4-400410.blurb: After Attila's death in 453 and the Hunnic defeat at the Battle of Nedao in 454, the Hunnic Empire disintegrated and its subject and peripheral peoples reasserted themselves. In the northwest (around modern Lower Saxony/Westphalia shown here), the Saxons expanded into the power vacuum left by the collapsing Hunnic hegemony.

w4-400413.name: Ostrogothic settlement in Pannonia as Roman foederati
w4-400413.blurb: After the collapse of Hunnic power following Attila's death (453) and the Battle of Nedao (454), the Ostrogoths under the Amali brothers were settled in Pannonia (the location here, around modern Slavonia/the Sava valley) as foederati of the Western/Eastern Roman state. The Western Roman Empire's nominal control of Pannonia thus passed to the now-independent Ostrogoths.

w4-400415.name: Roman recovery of Venetia after Attila's withdrawal and the Hunnic collapse
w4-400415.blurb: After Attila withdrew from Italy in 452 and the Hunnic Empire fragmented following his death in 453, the Western Roman Empire reasserted control over the northeastern Italian territory (Venetia, around modern Veneto/Friuli shown here) that the Huns had overrun during the invasion. This reversion (Hunnic -> Western Rome) reflects the end of the Hunnic threat in Italy.

w4-400422.name: Burgundian expansion after the death of Majorian
w4-400422.blurb: Following the murder of Emperor Majorian in 461 and the resulting collapse of Western Roman authority in Gaul under Ricimer's puppet emperors, the Burgundians under Gundioc again expanded into the Rhône valley and Sapaudia (around lng 5.8, lat 46). The lands Majorian had briefly recovered reverted to Burgundian control.

w4-400426.name: Visigothic expansion after Majorian's assassination
w4-400426.blurb: After Majorian's assassination by Ricimer in 461 CE, which had been partly instigated by Visigothic king Theodoric II, the Visigoths expanded their territory in southern Gaul (Narbonensis and parts of Aquitaine) that Majorian had temporarily contested. The centroid at ~3.1°E, 43.7°N (Languedoc/Narbonne region) confirms this is Visigothic territorial expansion in Mediterranean Gaul.

w4-400430.name: Rise of the Maitraka dynasty of Vallabhi amid Gupta decline
w4-400430.blurb: As the Gupta Empire weakened under Hephthalite (White Hun) invasions in the later 5th century, the Maitraka general Bhatarka, a former Gupta governor, established an independent dynasty at Vallabhi in the Saurashtra/Gujarat peninsula (around lng 71.2, lat 22.4). The region passed from nominal Gupta control to the Maitrakas around 470.

w4-400432.name: Visigothic conquest of Hispania Tarraconensis under Euric
w4-400432.blurb: Under King Euric the Visigoths threw off federate status and conquered the remaining Roman territories in Gaul and Spain. In the early-mid 470s Euric's forces seized the Tarraconensis and the lands around the eastern Pyrenees, completing the absorption of Roman Hispania into the Visigothic Kingdom by the time of the Western Empire's fall in 476.

w4-400433.name: Formation of the Kingdom of Thuringia (c. 470s-500 AD)
w4-400433.blurb: The Thuringii, a Germanic people that emerged from the late Migration Period amalgamation of Angles, Warni, and Hermunduri remnants, established an independent kingdom centred in central Germania south of the Harz Mountains from around the late 5th century. Their first attested king, Bisinus, ruled at the turn of the 5th-6th centuries, and the kingdom grew to be the most powerful Germanic state outside former Roman borders, extending from the Harz to the Danube. The data entry (Thuringian states to Kingdom of Thuringia, py=469, y=476) records the coalescence of these tribal polities into a unified kingdom around the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

w4-400437.name: Anglo-Saxon settlement and conquest of the West Midlands
w4-400437.blurb: Following the Roman withdrawal from Britain, Germanic Anglo-Saxon groups — Angles, Saxons, and Jutes — progressively pushed Brythonic (Celtic British) populations westward from the late 5th century onwards. Around lat 52.4, lng -2.3 (the West Midlands / English Midlands), this transition from Brythonic to Anglo-Saxon control occurred during the late 470s–480s, coinciding with the earliest organised Saxon coastal settlements (Aelle of Sussex, 477 AD). The region eventually became part of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia. The exact attribution is imprecise since conquest was gradual.

w4-400438.name: Goguryeo expansion into Manchuria under Jangsu
w4-400438.blurb: Under King Jangsu, Goguryeo reached its territorial peak, expanding northwest into Manchuria and contesting the steppe frontier with the Rouran (Ruanruan) Khaganate. Around 479 Goguryeo and the Rouran jointly partitioned the Khitan-held lands, with Goguryeo absorbing territory around southern Manchuria.

w4-400441.name: Hephthalite defeat of the Sasanians / death of Peroz I
w4-400441.blurb: The Hephthalites (White Huns) inflicted catastrophic defeats on the Sasanian Empire, culminating in 484 when Shah Peroz I was killed and his army destroyed. The eastern Sasanian provinces of Khorasan and the lands around Sistan/eastern Iran fell under Hephthalite domination, and Persia was forced to pay tribute.

w4-400442.name: Hephthalite (Alchon Hun) invasion of northwest India
w4-400442.blurb: The Hephthalite/Alchon Huns under leaders such as Toramana invaded the northwestern Gupta Empire in the 480s, overrunning the Punjab and Rajasthan (around lng 72.2, lat 29.1). These conquests stripped the Guptas of their northwestern provinces and hastened the empire's decline.

w4-400444.name: Lombard occupation of Rugiland after the fall of the Rugii kingdom
w4-400444.blurb: After Odoacer defeated the Rugii kingdom in 487 and killed King Feletheus, Rugiland (the Rugii territory in modern Lower Austria north of the Danube) was left without central authority. The Lombards moved into and occupied this territory around 488 CE, absorbing the surviving Rugii population. The data window 480-490 captures the Lombard takeover following Odoacer's campaigns.

w4-500001.name: Xiao Yan's usurpation and founding of the Liang Dynasty
w4-500001.blurb: Xiao Yan, a Southern Qi royal and military strongman, deposed the last Southern Qi emperor Xiao Baorong in 502 and founded the Liang Dynasty (502–557), absorbing all Southern Qi territory. The transition was a palace coup by an insider of the ruling clan rather than an external conquest.

w4-500003.name: Ghassanid recognition as Byzantine foederati / phylarchs
w4-500003.blurb: Around 500–502, the Ghassanid Arab dynasty was formally recognised by the Eastern Roman Empire as foederati and frontier phylarchs, consolidating their control over the semi-arid zone east of the Jordan River (lat 31.3, lng 37.4). The atlas shift from 'Eastern Roman Empire' to 'Ghassanids' reflects formalisation of client-state status under Emperor Anastasius I, who reorganised the Arab frontier defence.

w4-500004.name: Sasanian reassertion of control over Caucasian Albania (c. 510)
w4-500004.blurb: Following the death of Peroz I in 484 and the severe Hephthalite pressure that disrupted Sasanian authority in the Caucasus, Caucasian Albania had functioned with increased autonomy. Under Kavad I (r. 488–531), the Sasanians stabilized and reasserted direct control over Caucasian Albania by around 510, subordinating its ruling Arsacid dynasty to Sasanian governors.

w4-500005.name: Gepid seizure of Sirmium from the Eastern Roman Empire
w4-500005.blurb: After the Ostrogoths withdrew from Pannonia, the Gepids seized the strategically vital city of Sirmium (modern Sremska Mitrovica, Serbia; lat 44.3, lng 21.6) around 504–510, wresting it from Eastern Roman/Ostrogothic control. The Eastern Roman Emperor Anastasius attempted but failed to reclaim the city, leaving it as the Gepids' royal centre.

w4-500006.name: Gepid consolidation of Pannonia after Theoderic's focus on Italy
w4-500006.blurb: After the Ostrogoths under Theoderic the Great left Pannonia for Italy (488–493) and then reasserted control at Sirmium circa 504, the Gepid Kingdom nonetheless consolidated its hold on the broader Pannonian territory (centroid at lng 19.5, lat 46.0) east of the Drava river; the atlas reflects this Gepid territorial consolidation in the Pannonian basin during the first decade of the 6th century, even as Sirmium itself remained contested.

w4-500008.name: Clovis I Consolidates the Kingdom of the Franks
w4-500008.blurb: Between 507 and 509, Clovis I defeated the Visigoths at Vouillé (507), annexed Aquitaine, and then eliminated rival Frankish kings (Chararic, Sigobert, Ragnachar), becoming sole king of all the Franks around 509 — transforming the Salian Frankish tribal polity into the unified Kingdom of the Franks.

w4-500009.name: Clovis I conquers the Ripuarian Franks
w4-500009.blurb: Around 508-509 Clovis I of the Salian Franks engineered the elimination of the Ripuarian Frankish royal line at Cologne. According to Gregory of Tours, he secretly incited Chloderic (the "Parricide") to murder his father, King Sigobert the Lame, then had Chloderic himself killed by his agents, after which the Ripuarian Franks accepted Clovis as their king and their middle-Rhine territory (centered on Cologne, ~6.7°E / 51.6°N) was absorbed into the unified Kingdom of the Franks.

w4-500010.name: Sasanian reconquest of Hephthalite border territories
w4-500010.blurb: After the disastrous defeat and death of Peroz I at Hephthalite hands in 484, the Sasanians paid tribute to the Hephthalites for decades. Under Kavad I the Sasanians gradually recovered and, with renewed military pressure in the early 6th century, reestablished control over the Merv oasis and adjacent western Khorasan territories by around 510–520.

w4-500011.name: Frankish conquest of Ostrogothic Burgundy and Raetia
w4-500011.blurb: During the early Gothic War, the Ostrogothic kingdom shed its trans-Alpine and Provence holdings to the Franks. King Vitiges ceded Provence to the Frankish kings Childebert I and Theudebert I in 536-537 to secure Frankish neutrality against Justinian, and the Ostrogothic-held Alpine and Raetian districts (centered ~8.3°E / 46.4°N) passed to Frankish control in the same period. This transfer involved former Ostrogothic territory, not the Burgundian kingdom, which had its own separate conquest.

w4-500012.name: Frankish conquest of Thuringia (531–534)
w4-500012.blurb: The Frankish kings Theuderich I and Chlothar I destroyed the Kingdom of Thuringia at the Battle of the Unstrut (ca. 531), killing King Hermanafrid and absorbing Thuringia into the Frankish realm. The Saxons also participated, receiving the northern portion as reward.

w4-500013.name: Frankish Conquest of the Burgundian Kingdom
w4-500013.blurb: In 534 the Franks under Childebert I and Chlothar I completed the conquest of the Burgundian Kingdom, which had been weakened by internal dynastic strife. The last Burgundian king Godomar was defeated and killed; the entire Burgundian realm (centroid ~5.8°E, 46.1°N, corresponding to the Rhône-Saône corridor) was absorbed into the Frankish kingdom.

w4-500014.name: Dissolution of Northern Wei and Formation of Eastern Wei
w4-500014.blurb: When Northern Wei split in 534, the warlord Gao Huan installed the puppet Emperor Xiaojing and founded Eastern Wei, which inherited the larger eastern realm including its northern frontier marches facing the steppe. Rather than annexing the Rouran Khaganate, Gao Huan actively sought a marriage alliance with the still-formidable Rouran to secure his northern flank against the rival Western Wei. The Rouran's decline came later, in the 550s, at the hands of the rising Göktürks, not through absorption by Eastern Wei.

w4-500015.name: Partition of Northern Wei into Eastern Wei
w4-500015.blurb: When Emperor Xiaowu fled west to Yuwen Tai's territory in 534 after losing his power struggle with eastern warlord Gao Huan, Gao Huan installed a new emperor at Ye and relocated 400,000 families, creating Eastern Wei as the eastern successor state to Northern Wei.

w4-500016.name: Treaty of Eternal Peace confirms Sasanian control over Iberia (532)
w4-500016.blurb: The 523 Gurgen revolt predates this window entirely. The datable event that fits 527–534 is the 532 Treaty of Eternal Peace ending the Sasanian–Byzantine Iberian War (526–532), in which Byzantium recognized Sasanian control of Caucasian Iberia (retaining only Lazica). The later 'reduction to nominal monarchy' the original blurb describes actually belongs to 580, a different, much later episode.

w4-500017.name: Partition of Northern Wei into Western Wei
w4-500017.blurb: Emperor Xiaowu's flight west to warlord Yuwen Tai's domains in 534 created Western Wei as the western successor state of Northern Wei, with Yuwen Tai as the de facto ruler controlling the territories west of the Taihang Mountains and in the Wei River basin.

w4-500031.name: Khosrow I's Invasion and Sack of Antioch
w4-500031.blurb: In 540 CE, Sasanian King Khosrow I broke the Eternal Peace of 532 and launched a massive invasion of Syria and Mesopotamia, capturing and sacking Antioch. This opened decades of Byzantine-Sasanian conflict and transferred large swaths of northern Syria and upper Mesopotamia (centroid ~38.7°E, 36.1°N) temporarily to Sasanian control.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Lazic War (covers the 540 invasion context)

w4-500033.name: Ostrogothic cession of Provence to the Franks (536)
w4-500033.blurb: In 536, the Ostrogothic king Vitiges ceded Provence to the Frankish kings Childebert I and Theudebert I in exchange for Frankish neutrality during the Byzantine–Gothic War. This transferred control of the Alpine and Provençal region (centroid ~lng 6.7, lat 44.9) from the Ostrogoths to the Franks.

w4-500034.name: Ostrogothic Withdrawal from Noricum / Frankish-Bavarian Takeover
w4-500034.blurb: As Justinian's Gothic Wars (535–554) forced the Ostrogoths to cede Noricum and Raetia to secure Frankish neutrality (Treaty of 536), the Bavarians—a Frankish client people—occupied the former Ostrogothic territories north of the Alps (centroid ~12°E, 47.7°N). By 540 the region was firmly under Bavarian/Frankish control rather than Ostrogothic.

w4-500037.name: Champa Reclamation During Lý Bí Revolt
w4-500037.blurb: During the chaos of Lý Bí's revolt against Liang (541–546), Chinese administrative control over the southernmost districts of Jiaozhou (centroid 106.3°E, 17.6°N, near modern Quảng Bình/Quảng Trị) collapsed, allowing Champa to reclaim or reoccupy the territory it had historically contested with Chinese-controlled Vietnam.

w4-500038.name: Revolt of Lý Bí and Foundation of Vạn Xuân
w4-500038.blurb: Lý Bí (Lý Nam Đế) rose against Liang rule in 541, expelled Liang forces from Jiaozhou, and in February 544 proclaimed the kingdom of Vạn Xuân ("Eternal Spring"), effectively ending Liang administration over northern Vietnam. The Liang counterattack under Chen Baxian from late 544 eventually reclaimed much of the delta by 546, but the initial 540–546 snapshot captures the revolt's peak territorial hold.

w4-500039.name: Lazica defects to Persia (Lazic War begins)
w4-500039.blurb: In 541 CE King Gubazes II of Lazica, angered by Byzantine trade restrictions imposed by official John Tzibus, secretly invited Khosrow I of Persia into the country; Khosrow captured the Byzantine fortress of Petra, and Lazica passed under Sasanian suzerainty, initiating the Lazic War (541–562).

w4-500040.name: Lombard occupation of Pannonia following Ostrogothic collapse
w4-500040.blurb: Following the destruction of the Ostrogothic power in the Gothic Wars (535-554), the Lombards under King Audoin moved into Pannonia (modern Hungary/Croatia) by c. 546, filling the power vacuum left by the retreating Ostrogoths who had held the region since the late 5th century. Byzantine Emperor Justinian had encouraged Lombard settlement as a buffer against other peoples.

w4-500041.name: Gao Yang proclaims Northern Qi, replacing Eastern Wei
w4-500041.blurb: Gao Yang, son of the Eastern Wei strongman Gao Huan, forced the last Eastern Wei emperor to abdicate in 550 and proclaimed himself the first emperor of Northern Qi, with all Eastern Wei territories transferring to the new dynasty.

w4-500042.name: Göktürk Destruction of Rouran and Northern Qi Expansion
w4-500042.blurb: In 552–555, the Göktürk confederation under Bumin and his successor Muqan Qaghan crushed the Rouran Khaganate; the territory at centroid lng 116.8, lat 40.2 (near modern Beijing) fell not to the Göktürks but was absorbed by the Northern Qi as the Rouran client polities in southern Inner Mongolia collapsed into Chinese warlord control.

w4-500043.name: Chalukya Pulakesi I subjugates Kadamba territories
w4-500043.blurb: Chalukya king Pulakesi I (r. c. 543–566), who performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice at Badami, expanded Chalukya power over the declining Kadamba kingdom of Banavasi in northern Karnataka around 550. The Kadambas had been weakening since the 5th century and the Chalukyas absorbed their core territories in this period.

w4-500045.name: Byzantine (Eastern Roman) conquest of Spania
