w4-500045.blurb: In 551–554 Emperor Justinian I intervened in a Visigothic civil war at the invitation of the pretender Athanagild, and Byzantine forces under general Liberius seized a substantial strip of southern Iberia (Baetica and part of Carthaginensis), establishing the province of Spania which remained Byzantine until the early 7th century.

w4-500047.name: Justinian I's reconquest: Lombard-Byzantine victory over the Gepids
w4-500047.blurb: Emperor Justinian I allied with the Lombards under King Audoin (and his son Alboin) to crush the Gepids; a joint Lombard-Byzantine army defeated the Gepids at the Battle of Asfeld around 551–552, with Alboin slaying the Gepid prince Turismod. This allowed Eastern Roman forces to reassert nominal control over the Sirmium region (lat 44.3, lng 21.6) temporarily, though the Gepids retained Sirmium itself until their final destruction in 567.

w4-500048.name: Byzantine expulsion of Persians from Lazica (Lazic War)
w4-500048.blurb: In the Lazic War (541–562), after the Lazi king Gubazes switched allegiance to Byzantium (541), Byzantine armies gradually drove Persian forces from Lazica. By the early 550s, major Persian strongholds like Onoguris and Petra fell or were bypassed; the area at lng 41.2/lat 42.1 (eastern Lazica/Egrisi) passed under Byzantine control roughly by 555.

w4-500050.name: Lombard–Gepid War (551–552)
w4-500050.blurb: In 551–552 the Lombards, allied with Byzantium, defeated the Gepids in a major campaign; Alboin killed the Gepid prince Turismod (551) and the Lombards inflicted a decisive defeat on King Thurisind (552). The Gepids lost territory in the Pannonian plain to Lombard control, prefiguring their final destruction in 567.

w4-500051.name: Maukhari expansion into Gupta territories amid Gupta collapse
w4-500051.blurb: As the Gupta Empire fragmented under the pressure of Alchon Hun invasions in the mid-6th century, the Maukhari dynasty of Kannauj — who had borne much of the military burden against the Huns — expanded into the Ganges plain, with Ishanavarman adopting the title Maharajadhiraja and effectively annexing former Gupta territory in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

w4-500053.name: Byzantine Gothic War — collapse of Ostrogothic Noricum
w4-500053.blurb: The Gothic Wars (535–554) ended with the Pragmatic Sanction of 554 dissolving the Ostrogothic Kingdom. In the Alpine Noricum/Raetia region (modern Tyrol/Trentino, centroid ~lat 46.7, lng 11.5), Ostrogothic garrisons collapsed and the Bavarians moved in to fill the power vacuum, establishing control over territory they would hold throughout the Merovingian period.

w4-500054.name: Göktürk Conquest of the Rouran Khaganate
w4-500054.blurb: Bumin Khan of the Göktürks allied with Western Wei and crushed the Rouran at Huaihuang in 552, causing Rouran khagan Anagui to commit suicide; by 555 Muqan Qaghan annihilated remaining Rouran remnants, ending the khaganate entirely.

w4-500055.name: Silla Seizure of the Han River Basin from Goguryeo (King Jinheung's Expansion)
w4-500055.blurb: Under King Jinheung (진흥왕, r. 540–576), Silla allied with Baekje to attack Goguryeo in 551, seizing the upper Han River valley. In 553, Silla then treacherously turned on Baekje and seized the lower Han River basin as well, giving Silla direct access to the Yellow Sea and a critical strategic advantage. This expansion is confirmed by the four Jinheung border steles found across the region.

w4-500057.name: Completion of Justinian's Gothic War: remaining Ostrogothic holdouts surrender (561–562)
w4-500057.blurb: The general Narses completed the Byzantine reconquest of Italy; the last Ostrogothic forces and holdout cities in Venetia, Noricum, and the Alpine foothills surrendered by 561–562. The centroid corresponds to northeastern Italy and the Veneto, the final areas to fall.

w4-500058.name: Battle of Casilinum: Byzantine expulsion of Frankish–Alamannic forces from Italy (554)
w4-500058.blurb: Justinian I's Pragmatic Sanction of 13 August 554 reorganized the administration of Italy following the Byzantine reconquest of the Ostrogothic kingdom, restoring confiscated property and confirming imperial control. It was not a cession of land to the Franks: during the same Gothic War the Franks and their Alemannic allies under Leutharis and Butilinus, who had pushed into northern Italy, were driven back, with the survivors defeated at Casilinum in 554. The frontier around the western Alps thus moved in the Empire's favour rather than toward the Frankish king Theudebald, making the original capsule's account of an Alpine cession to the Franks inaccurate.

w4-500059.name: Byzantine reconquest of Lazica in the Lazic War
w4-500059.blurb: During the Lazic War (541–562), the Lazi rebelled against Persian suzerainty and requested Byzantine aid; Byzantine forces under Bessas and later Martinus progressively expelled Persian garrisons from Lazica through the early 550s. By around 555 Byzantine control over Lazica (western Georgia) was firmly established, a status ratified by the Fifty-Year Peace of 562.

w4-500062.name: Göktürk-Sasanian destruction of the Hephthalite Empire
w4-500062.blurb: In a coordinated campaign, the Göktürk Khaganate under Istämi and the Sasanian Empire under Khosrow I crushed the Hephthalite (White Hun) state in a pincer movement c. 557–560. The Göktürks seized the Hephthalite lands north of the Oxus — roughly Sogdia, Bactria, and parts of the Ferghana corridor — while the Sasanians absorbed the territories south of the Oxus.

w4-500063.name: Chen Baxian's founding of the Chen Dynasty
w4-500063.blurb: Chen Baxian, a Liang general who had accumulated power after defeating Western Wei attacks and eliminating rival regent Wang Sengbian, forced the last Liang emperor to abdicate in 557 and established the Chen Dynasty, inheriting the rump Liang territories in the lower Yangtze region.

w4-500064.name: Northern Zhou succeeds Western Wei as suzerain over the Western Liang puppet state (557)
w4-500064.blurb: Xiao Cha's Western Liang puppet regime was installed by Western Wei at Jiangling in 555, but its suzerain only became Northern Zhou when Yuwen Jue took the Western Wei throne and founded Northern Zhou in 557 — that succession, not a direct 555 event, is what moved this territory into Northern Zhou's column, and 557 sits comfortably inside 555–561.

w4-500065.name: Yuwen Jue's proclamation of Northern Zhou replacing Western Wei
w4-500065.blurb: Yuwen Jue (son of Yuwen Tai), having consolidated military control after his father's death in 556, deposed the last Western Wei emperor in 557 and proclaimed the Northern Zhou dynasty, inheriting all Western Wei territories intact.

w4-500066.name: Establishment of Western Liang under Xiao Cha
w4-500066.blurb: In 555, Xiao Cha, a grandson of Emperor Wu of Liang, established the Western Liang (later called 'Later Western Liang') as a puppet state under Western Wei at Jiangling, splitting from the main Liang dynasty realm and effectively partitioning the central Yangzi territory.

w4-500067.name: Lazic War settlement / Fifty-Year Peace of 562
w4-500067.blurb: The Lazic War between the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) and Sasanian Empires over Lazica/Colchis ended with the Fifty-Year Peace of 562, in which Persia recognized Roman control of Lazica. The Caucasian/western Georgian territory around lng 41.5, lat 42.4 was secured in the Byzantine sphere, here recorded as passing to Georgia/Lazica.

w4-500068.name: Visigothic reconquest of Byzantine Spania under Leovigild
w4-500068.blurb: The Visigothic king Leovigild waged sustained campaigns to roll back the Byzantine province of Spania along Iberia's southern and southeastern coasts. In 570-571 he recovered part of the Byzantine enclave in the southeast (around Baza and the Granada region), and in 572 he seized Córdoba, which had stood outside Visigothic control. These advances pushed the Eastern Roman holdings back toward a coastal rump in Baetica and the southeast.

w4-500069.name: Avar-Lombard Destruction of the Gepid Kingdom
w4-500069.blurb: In 567, Lombard King Alboin allied with the Avar Khaganate to destroy the Gepid Kingdom. The joint assault killed the last Gepid king Cunimund at the Battle of Asfeld, and former Gepid territories in the Carpathian basin (centroid ~22.5°E, 45.9°N, roughly modern Vojvodina/Transylvania) passed to Avar control while the Lombards moved into Italy in 568.

w4-500070.name: Silla Absorption of the Gaya Confederacy
w4-500070.blurb: King Jinheung of Silla completed the absorption of the Gaya (가야) confederacy in 562 CE by conquering Daegaya (대가야), the last major Gaya polity, after a series of earlier annexations of smaller Gaya statelets beginning in 532 (Geumgwan Gaya). The change from 'Byeonhan' to 'Silla' in the atlas reflects the atlas's treatment of late Gaya territory as the successor of the ancient Byeonhan confederacy.

w4-500072.name: Lombard-Avar Destruction of the Gepid Kingdom
w4-500072.blurb: In 567, the Lombard king Alboin allied with the Avar Khagan Bayan I to launch a two-front assault on the Gepid kingdom; the Gepid king Cunimund was killed in battle, his kingdom was extinguished, and its territory in the Carpathian Basin was divided between the Lombards and Avars.

w4-500074.name: Lombard Migration to Italy — Avars Occupy Pannonia
w4-500074.blurb: In spring 568, the Lombards under King Alboin departed Pannonia and invaded Italy, ceding their Pannonian homeland to the Avars, with whom they had allied in 567 to destroy the Gepid kingdom; the Avar Khaganate thereupon expanded into the vacated Danubian basin, which became the Avar heartland.

w4-500075.name: Byzantine–Sasanian War of 572–591: Sasanian gains in Armenia and Mesopotamia
w4-500075.blurb: In 573 Khosrow I captured Dara, the main Byzantine stronghold in Mesopotamia, while Sasanian forces raided deep into Syria and Armenia. The centroid points to the Armenian/eastern Anatolian front where Byzantine border territories shifted to Persian control in the early phase of this war.

w4-500077.name: Lombard invasion of Tuscany and establishment of Duchy of Tuscia
w4-500077.blurb: During the Lombard invasion of Italy beginning in 568, the Lombards under King Alboin swept into Tuscia (Tuscany, lat 43.2, lng 10.9) around 570–572, displacing Byzantine provincial administration. A separate Lombard Duchy of Tuscia (Tuscia Langobardorum) was established, distinct from the Roman-controlled Tuscia Romanorum further south, marking the Lombard seizure of the region from the Eastern Roman Empire.

w4-500078.name: Northern Zhou conquest of Northern Qi
w4-500078.blurb: Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou launched a decisive campaign against Northern Qi in 577; the Northern Qi regime disintegrated within a month as armies and court officials defected en masse, and both the reigning and last emperors were captured, ending Northern Qi and unifying northern China under Northern Zhou.

w4-500079.name: Visigothic reconquest of Byzantine Spania in Córdoba region
w4-500079.blurb: Visigothic King Leovigild (r. 568–586) systematically dismantled the Byzantine enclave of Spania in southern Iberia; the centroid near Córdoba/Seville corresponds to the territories he recovered from the Eastern Roman Empire through campaigns c. 569–577, reducing Byzantine holdings to a coastal rump before Suinthila finally expelled the Byzantines c. 624.

w4-500081.name: Lombard conquest of Apulia (Duchy of Benevento expansion)
w4-500081.blurb: Following the Lombard invasion of Italy in 568–569, Zotto founded the Duchy of Benevento c. 571 and its forces progressively overran Byzantine Apulia through the 570s. The centroid at 16.1°E / 41°N (Apulia) reflects this gradual Lombard takeover of Byzantine territory in the heel of Italy.

w4-500082.name: Lombard establishment of the Duchy of Spoleto
w4-500082.blurb: During the Lombard invasion of Italy (568–572), Lombard warlord Faroald I established the Duchy of Spoleto around 571, seizing central Italian territory from Byzantine control. The duchy controlled the Via Flaminia, severing Byzantine land communications between Ravenna and Rome; the territory (lat 42.9, lng 13.3) remained nominally a separate Lombard duchy rather than being absorbed directly into the Lombard kingdom.

w4-500083.name: Battle of Dyrham
w4-500083.blurb: The Battle of Dyrham (577) saw the West Saxons under Ceawlin kill three British kings and capture Gloucester, Cirencester, and Bath, opening the Severn valley to Anglo-Saxon settlement; the Hwicce kingdom subsequently emerged in this zone, absorbing territory formerly held by Brythonic peoples.

w4-500084.name: Consolidation of Duchy of Tuscia into the Lombard Kingdom under Authari
w4-500084.blurb: The semi-autonomous Duchy of Tuscia (lat 43.2, lng 10.9), established during the Lombard invasion, was brought under firmer Lombard royal authority when King Authari (r. 584–590) centralised Lombard governance. Cliopatria renders this as a transfer to 'Kingdom of Italy,' reflecting the duchy's absorption into the unified Lombard polity rather than remaining a quasi-independent entity.

w4-500087.name: Integration of the Duchy of Spoleto into the Lombard Kingdom under Authari
w4-500087.blurb: The autonomous Duchy of Spoleto, which had operated semi-independently since its foundation around 571, was brought under firmer Lombard royal control when King Authari (r. 584–590) consolidated Lombard territories. The territory (lat 42.9, lng 13.3) is here rendered as 'Kingdom of Italy,' reflecting Cliopatria's representation of the Lombard kingdom proper absorbing the duchy into a unified polity label.

w4-500088.name: Division of the Göktürk Khaganate into Eastern and Western Khaganates
w4-500088.blurb: The death of Taspar Qaghan in 581 triggered a succession crisis when the ruling council bypassed his designated heir; Tardu in the west declared independence while Sui Dynasty diplomacy exploited the resulting civil war, cementing the permanent split into Eastern and Western Göktürk Khaganates by 583.

w4-500090.name: Yang Jian's Usurpation and Foundation of the Sui Dynasty
w4-500090.blurb: Yang Jian, regent and father-in-law of the child Northern Zhou emperor, seized power on the death of Emperor Xuan in 581, deposed young Emperor Jing, massacred the Yuwen imperial clan, and proclaimed the Sui Dynasty, inheriting all Northern Zhou territory.

w4-500091.name: Sui abolition of Western Liang
w4-500091.blurb: In 587, the Sui Dynasty under Emperor Wen abolished the Western Liang puppet state, whose last ruler Xiao Cong was forced to abdicate. The Jiangling region was directly incorporated into Sui administration, ending over three decades of Liang puppet rule.

w4-500093.name: Visigothic conquest of the Kingdom of the Suebi
w4-500093.blurb: In 585 Visigothic king Leovigild invaded Gallaecia, defeated and captured the Suebian king Audeca, and annexed the Kingdom of the Suebi — the last independent Germanic kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula — to the Visigothic Kingdom.

w4-500094.name: Division of the First Turkic Khaganate
w4-500094.blurb: Following the death of Taspar Qaghan in 581, civil war erupted between rival claimants across the eastern and western wings of the Göktürk empire. The western territories under Istämi's line (governed separately since 553) emerged as a distinct political entity — the Western Göktürk Khaganate — under Tardu by c. 581–584, formally separating what had been a unified administrative structure.

w4-500095.name: Byzantine gains in Armenia during the War of 572-591
w4-500095.blurb: During the Byzantine-Sasanian War of 572-591, Eastern Roman forces under generals such as Maurice campaigned successfully in Armenia, capturing Sasanian-held territory around the upper Euphrates/Armenian highlands. These gains were consolidated and ultimately confirmed by the treaty of 591 that ceded much of Persarmenia to Byzantium.

w4-500096.name: Karkota dynasty establishes control over Gandhara/northwest Kashmir (c. 590)
w4-500096.blurb: The Karkota dynasty, founded by Durlabhvardhana around 625 CE (though earlier traditions place Karkota roots to ~590), consolidated control over territories in northwestern Kashmir and adjacent Gandhara (lng 68.6, lat 36.9 = Gandhara region) previously within the Western Göktürk sphere of influence. The collapse of Göktürk power in Bactria and Gandhara circa 588–590 created a vacuum the Karkota kingdom filled.

w4-500098.name: Sui conquest of Chen Dynasty
w4-500098.blurb: In 589, Emperor Wen of Sui launched a massive three-pronged invasion across the Yangtze River, overwhelming the Chen Dynasty's disorganized defenses. Emperor Chen Shubao was found hiding in a well and surrendered; the general submission of Chen forces ended the last southern Chinese dynasty and reunified China under Sui.

w4-500100.name: Pandya king Kadungon defeats Kalabhras
w4-500100.blurb: Pandya king Kadungon (also Kadunkon) defeated the Kalabhra rulers of the Tamil region around 575–590 CE, ending the so-called 'Kalabhra interregnum' and restoring orthodox Brahmanical Hindu dynastic rule in southern Tamil Nadu. The Velvikudi inscription describes Kadungon as the destroyer of the Kalabhra kings.

w4-500102.name: Death of Childebert II and Partition between Theuderic II and Theudebert II
w4-500102.blurb: When Childebert II died in 595/596, his realm was divided between his sons: Theuderic II received Burgundy and Theudebert II received Austrasia, re-establishing Burgundy as a distinct sub-kingdom that the atlas records as separating from the broader Frankish realm.

w4-500103.name: Early Chalukya–Pallava wars
w4-500103.blurb: The Badami Chalukyas under Pulakesi I and Kirtivarman I (r. 566–597) fought a series of campaigns against the Pallavas, capturing territory in the Tungabhadra–Krishna doab and northern Andhra; the 592–602 snapshot captures the Chalukya territorial gains in the Rayalaseema / Vengi corridor at the expense of the Late Pallavas.

w4-500104.name: Western Göktürk resurgence and loss of Sui/Tang control of Tarim Basin
w4-500104.blurb: After the Göktürk split of 583, the Western Göktürks under Niri Qaghan and successors reasserted control over the Tarim Basin and Central Asian oases; Sui Dynasty's nominal protectorate in the Western Regions collapsed by c. 601-603 as Western Göktürk power consolidated in the region.

w4-500105.name: Sui Conquest of Vietnam (Liu Fang's Campaign)
w4-500105.blurb: In 602 CE Sui Dynasty general Liu Fang led an army south and crushed the kingdom of Vạn Xuân under Lý Phật Tử (successor of Lý Bí), reincorporating northern Vietnam into the Chinese empire as Giao Chỉ commandery. The campaign was swift and the Sui immediately reinstated direct administration.

w4-500106.name: Simhavishnu expels the Kalabhras
w4-500106.blurb: Pallava king Simhavishnu (r. ~575–600 CE) drove the Kalabhra interlopers out of northern Tamil Nadu, extending Pallava control south to the Kaveri; the atlas snapshot captures the completed reconquest in the 592–602 window.

w4-500107.name: Shashanka's Expansion and Absorption of Maukhari Borderlands
w4-500107.blurb: Shashanka of Gauda (r. c. 590–625) expanded aggressively from Bengal westward and southward, absorbing Maukhari borderlands. The centroid at 88.3°E, 22.1°N is in lower Bengal/Gangetic delta area, consistent with early Gauda expansion before Harsha's rise; Shashanka is attested as having eliminated the Maukhari king Grahavarman (husband of Harsha's sister) around 605 CE.

w4-500111.name: Abolition of the Lakhmid Kingdom by Khosrow II
w4-500111.blurb: In 602 CE Sasanian shah Khosrow II deposed and executed the last Lakhmid king al-Nu'man III, dissolving the Arab client buffer state and incorporating its territory (centered on al-Hira in lower Mesopotamia) under direct Sasanian provincial administration. The removal of the Lakhmid frontier guard weakened Persian border defense against Arab tribes and contributed to Sasanian vulnerability during the subsequent Muslim conquests.

w4-500112.name: Sasanian conquest of Yemen from Aksum
w4-500112.blurb: By the 590s southern Arabia was firmly under Sasanian control, the end-state of two campaigns led by the veteran general Wahrez (Vahrez): an initial expedition c. 570 that expelled the Aksumite Ethiopian governor and installed the Himyarite prince Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan as a Persian vassal, and a second campaign c. 575-578 that crushed a renewed Aksumite rising and brought Yemen under direct Sasanian administration. A standing Persian garrison and governor remained for over fifty years, so the 597 snapshot near highland Yemen (lng 47.4, lat 15.2) records territory long since transferred from the Kingdom of Aksum to the Sasanian Empire rather than a fresh conquest in that year.

w4-500113.name: Khosrow II's invasion of the Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine–Sasanian War)
w4-500113.blurb: Using the murder of Emperor Maurice (602) as pretext, Khosrow II launched a massive offensive that by 610–612 had captured Dara (605), Amida and Edessa (609–610), Theodosiopolis, and swept into Cappadocia, seizing all Roman territories east of the Euphrates and Armenia. The centroid corresponds to eastern Anatolia/upper Mesopotamia, the primary zone of Sasanian conquest in this phase.

w4-500116.name: Visigothic conquest of Basque/Pyrenean territories under Sisebut
w4-500116.blurb: Around 612, at the start of his reign, the Visigothic king Sisebut (r. 612-621) extended royal authority into the western Pyrenean borderland of Cantabria, a frontier zone contested among Franks, Visigoths and Basques. The Frankish-allied duke Francio, who had earlier sworn allegiance to the Merovingians in Cantabria, was displaced, and the territory passed into the Visigothic sphere. Sisebut's better-attested military successes, recorded by Isidore of Seville, came against the Asturians and the mountain-dwelling Ruccones rather than the Franks directly, so this entry reflects a shift of frontier allegiance more than a pitched Frankish defeat.

w4-500117.name: Æthelfrith's union of Bernicia and Deira into Northumbria
w4-500117.blurb: Around 604 Æthelfrith of Bernicia seized the kingdom of Deira, expelling the Deiran prince Edwin and uniting the two Anglian kingdoms under his rule to form the composite kingdom later known as Northumbria.

w4-500118.name: Æthelfrith unites Bernicia and Deira into Northumbria
w4-500118.blurb: Around 604, Æthelfrith of Bernicia killed or expelled the Deiran royal family and seized control of Deira, uniting the two kingdoms into what later sources call Northumbria; Bede describes Æthelfrith as the first king to rule both peoples, with the merger consolidating territory at the centroid in present-day Yorkshire.

w4-500120.name: Theuderic II Defeats Theudebert II and Briefly Unifies Burgundy and Austrasia
w4-500120.blurb: In 612, Theuderic II of Burgundy defeated and killed his brother Theudebert II of Austrasia at the Battle of Toul (or Zülpich), reuniting Burgundy and Austrasia temporarily under his rule; the atlas records the consolidation as Burgundian territory expanding at the expense of the broader Frankish realm.

w4-500121.name: Harsha's Campaigns Against Gauda
w4-500121.blurb: After Shashanka of Gauda murdered Harsha's brother Rajyavardhana (c. 605/606), Harsha launched repeated campaigns into Gauda territory. Although the conflict was inconclusive and Gauda remained independent under Shashanka, Harsha consolidated hegemony over much of northern Bengal by c. 606–612, reflected in the atlas showing Gauda territory nominally assigned to Harsha's sphere.

w4-500122.name: Harsha inherits Maukhari realm and founds empire
w4-500122.blurb: After the Maukhari king Grahavarman (Harsha's brother-in-law) was killed by King Devagupta of Malwa around 605–606, and Harsha's brother Rajyavardhana was treacherously murdered by Shashanka of Gauda, Harsha inherited both the Pushyabhuti kingdom of Thanesar and the Maukhari realm, uniting them as he launched campaigns to rescue his sister and avenge his family.

w4-500123.name: Battle of Chester and Mercian expansion into Brythonic territory
w4-500123.blurb: At the Battle of Chester (c. 613-616) Aethelfrith of Northumbria annihilated a combined British army drawn chiefly from the Welsh kingdoms of Powys and Gwynedd, killing Selyf Sarffgadau of Powys among many others and reportedly massacring monks from Bangor-is-coed beforehand. The victory drove a Northumbrian wedge through the Brittonic world of the northwest near Chester (lng -2.4, lat 53.2), severing the land link between Wales and the British kingdoms of the Old North. Mercia did not gain here; its king Cearl appears to have been on the losing British-allied side, his power in the region collapsing after the battle.

w4-500124.name: Avar exploitation of Byzantine–Persian War — Avar Balkan expansion
w4-500124.blurb: With Byzantine forces fully committed against the Sassanid Persians from 613 onward, the Avars enjoyed a free hand in the undefended Balkans. In 617, during a parley near Constantinople, Avars launched a surprise attack, seizing 270,000 captives and overrunning much of the Balkan interior formerly under Byzantine administration, consolidating Avar Khaganate control over the region.

w4-500125.name: Eastern Göktürks Seize Ordos During Sui Collapse
w4-500125.blurb: As the Sui Dynasty imploded under the weight of the Goguryeo campaigns and internal rebellions (617–618), Eastern Göktürk Qaghan Shibi Khan seized the strategic Ordos region and northern Shaanxi, where multiple Chinese warlords including Liu Wuzhou and Liang Shidu became Turkic vassals; the Turks effectively controlled the northern frontier zone by 617.

w4-500126.name: Sassanid conquest of the Levant (614)
w4-500126.blurb: During the Byzantine-Sassanid War of 602-628, Sassanid Persian forces under Shahrbaraz and Khosrow II overran Syria and Palestine in 613-614, sacking Jerusalem in 614 and capturing the True Cross. This destroyed the Ghassanid client kingdom, which had served as Byzantium's Arab buffer state in the Levant, with the territory passing to direct Sassanid control.

w4-500127.name: Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 — Sasanian Conquest of Syria and Anatolia
w4-500127.blurb: Between 613 and 617, Sasanian general Shahrbaraz conquered Damascus, Antioch, and all of Syria, while general Shahin swept through Anatolia and reached Chalcedon by 617, bringing Persian forces within sight of Constantinople and stripping the Byzantine Empire of its eastern provinces.

w4-500128.name: Goguryeo Repulse of the Sui Invasions
w4-500128.blurb: Emperor Yang of Sui launched three massive invasions of Goguryeo (612, 613, 614 CE), all of which failed catastrophically. The 612 invasion alone lost perhaps 300,000 troops. Goguryeo not only held its territory but recovered control of the Liaodong frontier. The Sui dynasty collapsed by 618 partly because of the ruinous cost of these campaigns.

w4-500131.name: Clotaire II's Conquest and Reunification of the Frankish Realm
w4-500131.blurb: In 613, Clotaire II of Neustria defeated and captured the Austrasian regent Brunhilda, had her executed, and reunified all Frankish sub-kingdoms — including Burgundy — under his sole rule, effectively absorbing the Burgundian sub-kingdom back into a unified Frankish realm.

w4-500132.name: Byzantine recovery in the Balkans / decline of Avar pressure (early 620s)
w4-500132.blurb: Around 617-623 the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire under Heraclius recovered ground in the central Balkans (near the Morava valley) against the Avar Khaganate. Following the failed Avar surprise attack on Heraclius near Constantinople (c. 623) and the focus of Heraclius on the Persian war, frontier zones in the Danubian interior shifted hands. This reflects the volatile Avaro-Byzantine frontier of Heraclius's early reign rather than a single decisive battle.

w4-500134.name: Samo's revolt against the Avars
w4-500134.blurb: Around 623 the Frankish merchant Samo led a Slavic ('Wendish') uprising against Avar overlordship in Bohemia, Moravia, and Slovakia. His battlefield victories allowed him to be elected king, and his polity effectively ended Avar control over this central-European Slavic zone.

w4-500135.name: Sui-Eastern Türk frontier conflict in the Ordos (Yanmen and aftermath)
w4-500135.blurb: In the late Sui period the Eastern Göktürks (under Shibi Khan) raided deep into the Ordos region, even besieging Emperor Yang at Yanmen in 615. The territory near the Ordos loop marks the contested Sui-Türk steppe frontier in the dynasty's collapsing final years before 618. The shift here reflects this turbulent frontier rather than a clean Sui conquest, as the Eastern Türks were actually ascendant.

w4-500136.name: Visigothic reconquest of Byzantine Spania under Sisebut and Swinthila
w4-500136.blurb: Between c.615 and 621 Visigothic kings Sisebut (612–621) and then Swinthila progressively expelled Byzantine forces from their remaining Iberian enclaves; Swinthila completed the conquest of all Byzantine territory in Spain by c.625, making him the first king of all Iberia.

w4-500137.name: Sasanian conquest of Egypt (Byzantine–Sasanian War)
w4-500137.blurb: During the climactic phase of the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628, the Persian general Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt and captured Alexandria in June 619, routing the Byzantine defense led by Heraclius' cousin Nicetas. Persian forces then extended control southward along the Nile, completing their occupation of the entire province by approximately 621 CE.

w4-500138.name: Gao Kaidao Seizes Beiping and Yuyang During Sui Collapse
w4-500138.blurb: Rebel leader Gao Kaidao, allied with the Eastern Göktürks, besieged and captured Beiping (modern Beijing region) around 619 and subsequently seized Yuyang, establishing himself as Prince of Yan with his capital at Huairong; this transfer of the northeastern Hebei coast from nominal Sui/Tang authority to Gao Kaidao's control occurred in the context of the Sui collapse.

w4-500139.name: Karkota expansion displacing Göktürk influence in western Himalayas
w4-500139.blurb: Durlabhavardhana (c. 625–661), founder of the Karkota dynasty, extended his authority into the Gilgit/Dardistan area (lng 74.3/lat 35.2), a frontier zone previously under nominal Western Göktürk suzerainty. As Göktürk power fragmented after internal strife, the Karkotas filled the vacuum in the western Himalayan foothills.

w4-500140.name: Edwin of Northumbria's conquest of eastern Mercia
w4-500140.blurb: By 627 Edwin ruled 'Bernicia, Deira and much of eastern Mercia,' meaning Northumbrian control over territory previously in Mercian hands was established during the mid-620s through Edwin's military expansion following his victory at the Battle of the River Idle (616).

w4-500142.name: Edwin of Northumbria's absorption of Lindsey
w4-500142.blurb: Edwin of Northumbria expanded his realm to include Lindsey by c. 625, as evidenced by Paulinus of York's presence in Lindsey (Lindum/Lincoln) that year; the kingdom was absorbed into Northumbria in the early 7th century during Edwin's consolidation of Anglian power.

w4-500143.name: Edwin of Northumbria's absorption of sub-Roman British kingdoms
w4-500143.blurb: Edwin of Northumbria absorbed several small sub-Roman British kingdoms including Dunoting (located in the Pennines/Lancashire area) during his consolidation of power in the 620s, extending Northumbrian control northward through annual campaigns that pushed out British rulers.

w4-500144.name: Heraclius's counter-offensive in the Byzantine–Sasanian War
w4-500144.blurb: Emperor Heraclius launched a bold counter-offensive in 624, marching through Armenian highlands and into Persian-held Anatolia (Cappadocia, Pontus), recovering substantial eastern Anatolian territory from the Sasanians by 624–626 before the decisive campaigns further east. The centroid corresponds to northeastern Anatolia/Armenian highlands, the zone of Heraclian reconquest in this phase.

w4-500145.name: Xuanwu Gate Incident consolidates Tang rule (626)
w4-500145.blurb: The Tang founding (618) predates this window by five years and cannot explain a 623–626 change. The event that actually falls inside the window and the blurb already describes is the 626 Xuanwu Gate Incident, in which Li Shimin killed his brothers and forced Gaozu's abdication, consolidating undivided Tang control right as the snapshot closes.

w4-500146.name: Coup Against Gao Kaidao and Surrender to Tang
w4-500146.blurb: In spring 624, Gao Kaidao's own general Zhang Jinshu staged a coup — disabling weapons and attacking Gao's mansion — after which Gao committed suicide by hanging; Zhang then surrendered the territory around Beiping/Huairong to Tang, completing Tang's absorption of the northeastern Hebei coast.

w4-500148.name: Eastern Göktürk Raids and Weishui Crisis
w4-500148.blurb: In 626, Illig Qaghan of the Eastern Göktürks led a major incursion deep into Tang territory, reaching the Wei River outside Chang'an. Emperor Taizong (newly enthroned after the Xuanwu Gate Incident) negotiated the humiliating Weishui Bridge Covenant, paying tribute and effectively conceding border territories in present-day Gansu/Ningxia (centroid ~lng 105, lat 36) to Göktürk dominance.

w4-500152.name: Göktürk–Byzantine invasion of Sasanian Caucasus (627)
w4-500152.blurb: In 627 CE, the Western Göktürk Qaghan Tong Yabghu allied with Byzantine Emperor Heraclius and launched a massive invasion of the Sasanian Caucasus, temporarily seizing territories in Azerbaijan and Caucasian Albania. The Göktürk forces advanced as far south as Tbilisi and Albania while Heraclius devastated Sasanian Mesopotamia, stripping Sasanian control from the northern Caucasian buffer zone.

w4-500153.name: Battle of Cirencester and Mercian expansion under Penda
w4-500153.blurb: In 628, Penda of Mercia clashed with the West Saxon kings Cynegils and Cwichelm at Cirencester; the subsequent settlement gave Mercia control over lands along the lower Severn formerly held by Brythons (via West Saxon intermediaries), marking Mercia's decisive westward expansion into British territory.

w4-500154.name: Penda of Mercia absorbs Hwicce — Battle of Cirencester
w4-500154.blurb: Following the Battle of Cirencester in 628, Penda of Mercia secured control of the southwestern Midlands including the territory that became the sub-kingdom of Hwicce, absorbing it from West Saxon and residual Brythonic control into the Mercian sphere.

w4-500155.name: Tang Consolidation of the Ordos and Northern Shaanxi from Sui Remnants
w4-500155.blurb: Following the destruction of rival warlords and the submission of the last Sui-loyalist commanders, Emperor Taizong completed the consolidation of the Ordos plateau and northern Shaanxi by 628, absorbing the final remnants of Sui-era administrative territory that had survived under various local strongmen after the Sui collapse in 618.

w4-500156.name: Battle of Nineveh and Byzantine reconquest of upper Mesopotamia
w4-500156.blurb: Heraclius's decisive victory at the Battle of Nineveh (December 12, 627) enabled Byzantine forces to sweep through Mesopotamia and recover territories Persia had seized since 614. The subsequent peace agreement of 628 with Kavad II restored Byzantine borders in southeastern Anatolia and upper Mesopotamia.

w4-500157.name: Göktürk-Byzantine alliance and Caucasus campaign against Sasanians
w4-500157.blurb: Following the Byzantine victory at the Battle of Nineveh (December 627) and their alliance with the Western Göktürks (Khazars), Göktürk forces under Ziebel (Jibghu Khagan) campaigned into the Caucasus and Azerbaijan in 627–628, seizing territory the weakened Sasanians could not hold. Heraclius personally negotiated this alliance as a second front against Persia.

w4-500160.name: Peace of 628 / Sasanian retention of upper Mesopotamia zones
w4-500160.blurb: The peace agreement of 628 between Heraclius and Kavad II (Sheroes) ended the Byzantine-Sasanian War; while Byzantium recovered most Levantine territories, portions of upper Mesopotamia (the area around lng 42/lat 37, Tur Abdin/Nisibis region) remained or reverted to Sasanian hands under the negotiated settlement, before the Arab conquests swept all away a decade later.

w4-500161.name: Dagobert I Grants Aquitaine as Sub-kingdom to Charibert II
w4-500161.blurb: In 629, Dagobert I became sole king of the Franks and granted his half-brother Charibert II the sub-kingdom of Aquitaine (centroid ~1.1°E, 44.1°N) as an appanage, separating it from direct Frankish royal control. This established Aquitaine as a semi-autonomous entity, reflecting the standard Merovingian practice of partition among royal heirs.

w4-500162.name: Sasanian collapse after Khosrow II and reversion of the Lakhmid (Hira) lands
w4-500162.blurb: After the murder of Khosrow II (628) the Sasanian Empire fell into a chaotic interregnum of rapidly succeeding monarchs. Central control over the Arab frontier client zone of al-Hira (the former Lakhmid Kingdom, near lng 44, lat 30.5) lapsed, leaving the Lakhmid/Hira region effectively detached from direct Sasanian rule on the eve of the Muslim invasion. This reflects the disintegration of Sasanian authority rather than a formal grant.

w4-500163.name: Tang Destruction of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate
w4-500163.blurb: Emperor Taizong launched six Tang armies across a 1,200-km front against Illig Qaghan, whose power had been devastated by famine and internal rebellions among the Xueyantuo, Uyghurs, and other subject peoples; Illig was captured in 630, and the Eastern Turkic Khaganate dissolved, with its core Mongolian and Ordos territories brought under Tang control.

w4-500164.name: Sasanian reoccupation of Caucasian Albania / Atropatene after Göktürk collapse
w4-500164.blurb: With the collapse of Western Göktürk power around 628–630, the Sasanian Empire under Khosrow II's successors reoccupied the Transcaucasian territories (centroid lng 47.4, lat 40.8 = Azerbaijan/Caucasian Albania) that had been contested with or nominally under Göktürk influence, coinciding with the Göktürk civil war that ended active Turkic presence south of the Caucasus.

w4-500165.name: Fragmentation of the Western Göktürk Khaganate and emergence of Khazaria
w4-500165.blurb: The Western Türk (Göktürk) Khaganate fractured during the Interregnum of 628-634, when civil war among the Ashina lineages and Tang pressure shattered its authority over the western steppe. Out of the wreckage of the western Türk confederation the Khazars (Хазары / Хазарское каганат / Khazars) gradually rose to dominance over the Pontic-Caspian steppe (centroid lng 45.8, lat 44.8, North Caucasus and lower Volga); they had become effectively independent by the mid-7th century, but a distinct Khazar Khaganate is not securely attested until the latter half of the 7th century, well after 630. The c. 630 date marks only the collapse of Western Türk power, not the foundation of Khazaria.

w4-500166.name: Dagobert I reunifies the Frankish realm and subjugates Thuringia (631–632)
w4-500166.blurb: Dagobert I reunified the Frankish kingdom by 629 and launched campaigns to bring peripheral peoples under direct royal control. By 631–632, he suppressed Thuringian autonomy, reintegrating it under the Frankish crown and replacing its duke with royal officials.

w4-500167.name: Death of Charibert II and Reintegration of Aquitaine
w4-500167.blurb: Charibert II died in 632 and his infant son Chilperic died shortly after. Dagobert I, who had reunited the Frankish realm, reabsorbed Aquitaine (centroid ~1.1°E, 44.1°N) directly into the Frankish kingdom, ending its brief existence as a distinct sub-kingdom. Merovingian Aquitaine would only re-emerge as a separate duchy later in the 7th century.

w4-500168.name: Battle of Hatfield Chase
w4-500168.blurb: At the Battle of Hatfield Chase (October 633), the Northumbrian king Edwin was defeated and killed by the combined forces of Penda of Mercia and Cadwallon of Gwynedd; the kingdom immediately fragmented, with Eanfrith reclaiming Bernicia and Osric taking Deira separately.

w4-500169.name: Rashidun invasion of Sasanian Arabia (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign)
w4-500169.blurb: In 633 Khalid ibn al-Walid (خالد بن الوليد) led the first Rashidun campaign against the Sasanian frontier, winning the Battle of Chains (Dhat al-Salasil), al-Madhar, al-Walaja and Ullais before taking al-Hira. While those battles lay in lower Mesopotamia (Iraq), this transfer's centroid (lng 50.8, lat 20.5) falls on the eastern Arabian coast near Bahrain and al-Hasa, a region under loose Sasanian suzerainty that had already been brought into the Islamic state during the Ridda wars of 632-633 under commanders such as al-Ala al-Hadrami. By 633 this eastern Arabian littoral was absorbed into the Rashidun Caliphate as Khalid's forces simultaneously stripped the Sasanians of their Mesopotamian and Gulf marches.

w4-500171.name: Battle of Hatfield Chase — Northumbria splits into Bernicia and Deira
w4-500171.blurb: At the Battle of Hatfield Chase (12 October 633), Penda of Mercia allied with Cadwallon of Gwynedd killed Edwin of Northumbria; Northumbria immediately fragmented, with Osric taking Deira and Eanfrith taking Bernicia, dissolving the unified Northumbrian kingdom that Edwin had created.

w4-500172.name: Northumbrian unification under Edwin — Deira expansion against Mercia
w4-500172.blurb: During Edwin of Northumbria's reign (616–633), Deira expanded at Mercian expense in the southern Vale of York and adjacent areas; the broader Northumbrian–Mercian conflict, culminating in the Battle of Hatfield Chase (633) where Edwin was killed, defined these boundary shifts.

w4-500174.name: Foundation of Old Great Bulgaria under Kubrat
w4-500174.blurb: Around 632, Khan Kubrat of the Onogur Bulgars united the Kutrigur and Utigur Bulgar tribes, expelling Avar overlordship and establishing Old Great Bulgaria centred on Phanagoria (Taman Peninsula, lat 45.4, lng 34). Emperor Heraclius of the Eastern Roman Empire recognised Kubrat with the title of patrician, effectively ceding the northern Black Sea steppe region to Bulgar control.

w4-500175.name: Kubrat's Revolt and Foundation of Old Great Bulgaria
w4-500175.blurb: Around 630–632, Kubrat of the Dulo clan led a successful uprising of the Onogur-Bulgars against Avar domination, expelling Avar authority from the Pontic steppe north of the Black Sea (centroid ~35.4°E, 48.2°N). Old Great Bulgaria was thus established, and Kubrat concluded a peace with Byzantine Emperor Heraclius, receiving imperial recognition.

w4-500176.name: Battle of Narmada — Chalukya Pulakesi II defeats Harsha
w4-500176.blurb: The Chalukya emperor Pulakeshin II (ಇಮ್ಮಡಿ ಪುಲಿಕೇಶಿ / Immadi Pulikeshi, r. c. 610-642) halted the southward advance of the northern emperor Harshavardhana at the Battle of Narmada, fought on the banks of the Narmada River in the winter of 618-619 CE, not 634. The defeat forced Harsha to accept the Narmada as the boundary between the 'Lord of the North' and the 'Lord of the South,' securing the northern Deccan frontier (centroid lng 77.2, lat 22.0) for Chalukya control for the rest of Pulakeshin's reign.

w4-500177.name: Tang Campaign against the Eastern Turks
w4-500177.blurb: Emperor Taizong launched six Tang armies on a 1,200 km front in early 630, exploiting Göktürk famine and vassal revolts (Xueyantuo, Uyghurs); Illig Qaghan was captured in the spring of 630, ending the Eastern Göktürk Khaganate and bringing its territory under Tang suzerainty.

w4-500178.name: Battle of Wogastisburg — Samo's empire expands against Bavarians
w4-500178.blurb: In 631/632 King Dagobert I sent three Frankish armies against Samo's Slavic empire; the decisive Frankish defeat at Wogastisburg allowed Samo to go on the offensive and assert control over borderland territories previously under Frankish/Bavarian nominal suzerainty in the Bohemian-Bavarian frontier zone, reflected in this polygon transfer near lng 13.7, lat 47.5.

w4-500179.name: Emergence of an autonomous Duchy of Aquitaine from Frankish/Visigothic borderlands
w4-500179.blurb: In the early 7th century the region of Aquitaine and the Pyrenean marches (near lng 0.4, lat 42.8) emerged as a semi-autonomous Frankish duchy under Charibert II (king of Aquitaine 629-632) and his successors. Border zones formerly under Visigothic control in the Pyrenees shifted into the Aquitanian orbit. This reflects the carving out of Aquitaine as a distinct polity under the late Merovingians.

w4-500180.name: Creation of the sub-kingdom of Aquitaine for Charibert II (629)
w4-500180.blurb: On the death of Chlothar II, his son Dagobert I granted his half-brother Charibert II a sub-kingdom centered on Aquitaine (capital Toulouse) in 629-631. This partition transferred a large swath of the Frankish realm (over 500,000 km2 in the Aquitanian south, near lng 3.4, lat 48.3) into a separate Aquitanian kingship. It is a classic Merovingian dynastic division of the Frankish lands.

w4-500181.name: Muslim conquest of al-Hira / Battle of the Chains and Hira (633)
w4-500181.blurb: In 633 Khalid ibn al-Walid led the Rashidun Caliphate's invasion of Sasanian Iraq, defeating frontier forces and capturing the former Lakhmid capital al-Hira, which surrendered and agreed to pay tribute. This transferred the Lakhmid (Hira) territory near lng 44, lat 30.5 to the Rashidun Caliphate. It was the opening phase of the Muslim conquest of Persia.

w4-500182.name: Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign in lower Mesopotamia (633-634)
w4-500182.blurb: During Khalid ibn al-Walid's 633-634 campaign in Iraq, the Rashidun Caliphate seized Sasanian territory in the lower Euphrates region (near lng 44.3, lat 31.5) through battles such as Ullais, Walaja, and the Chains. This stripped the Sasanian Empire of its southern Mesopotamian frontier before Khalid was redeployed to Syria. It is part of the early Muslim conquest of Persia.

w4-500186.name: Battle of Heavenfield — Oswald unites Northumbria
w4-500186.blurb: After Edwin of Northumbria fell at Hatfield Chase in 633 and his realm split into Bernicia and Deira, Oswald of Bernicia (Northumbria) defeated and killed the British king Cadwallon ap Cadfan of Gwynedd at the Battle of Heavenfield, near Hexham on Hadrian's Wall, in 634. The victory destroyed Cadwallon's army, ended his ravaging of Northumbria, and allowed Oswald to reunite Bernicia and Deira under a single Northumbrian crown. The defeated power was Gwynedd, not Mercia, which was not a combatant at Heavenfield.

w4-500188.name: Battle of Heavenfield: Oswald of Bernicia defeats Cadwallon and reunites Northumbria
w4-500188.blurb: After Edwin of Northumbria was killed at Hatfield Chase (12 October 633), the united kingdom split back into Bernicia and Deira. Oswald of Bernicia, returning from exile in Iona, defeated and killed Cadwallon of Gwynedd at the Battle of Heavenfield near Hexham in 634. Both Bernicians and Deirans recognized Oswald as king, reuniting Northumbria under Bernician dominance and absorbing the Kingdom of Deira.

w4-500189.name: Caucasian principalities (Balasagan) breaking free amid Sasanian collapse
w4-500189.blurb: As the Sasanian Empire disintegrated in the 630s under the pressure of the Arab conquest and internal civil war, peripheral Caucasian Albanian/Balasagan territory in the eastern Caucasus (near lng 47.5, lat 40.6) slipped from Sasanian control. The principality of Balasagan asserted autonomy as central Sasanian authority evaporated. This reflects the unraveling of the Sasanian northern frontier.

w4-500192.name: Armenian autonomy amid Sasanian collapse (630s)
w4-500192.blurb: With the Sasanian Empire collapsing after 628 and under Arab assault, Persarmenia (the Sasanian-held part of Armenia, near lng 45.3, lat 40.1) reverted to local Armenian princely rule. Armenian nakharars reasserted control as Persian authority disintegrated before the Arab conquest of Armenia. This reflects the dissolution of Sasanian rule in the Caucasus.

w4-500193.name: Restoration of Armenian autonomy after Byzantine-Sasanian settlement (630s)
w4-500193.blurb: Following Heraclius's victory over Persia and the chaos of the 630s, Byzantine-held western Armenia (near lng 42.9, lat 40.3) passed back into the hands of local Armenian princes. As both Byzantium and Persia were exhausted by their long war and the onset of the Arab invasions, the Armenian principality consolidated autonomy. This reflects the post-war reshuffling of the Armenian highlands.

w4-500195.name: Tibetan Empire's subjugation of the Tuyuhun (637-638)
w4-500195.blurb: Under Songtsen Gampo the expanding Tibetan Empire attacked the Tuyuhun (Azha) kingdom around 637-638, seizing their grazing lands on the northeastern Tibetan plateau (near lng 97.5, lat 35.1). This pressure on the Tuyuhun also brought Tibet into direct conflict with Tang China and led to Songtsen Gampo's demand for a Tang princess. It marks the Tibetan Empire's rise as a major Inner Asian power.

w4-500197.name: Iberian/Georgian autonomy in the wake of the Byzantine-Persian war (630s)
w4-500197.blurb: After the Byzantine-Sasanian war and the onset of the Arab conquests, Byzantine-influenced territory in the Caucasus near Iberia/Lazica (near lng 43.7, lat 42.1) reverted to local Georgian princely control. The exhaustion of the great empires allowed the Georgian principality of Kartli/Iberia to assert itself. This reflects the realignment of the Caucasus before the Arab arrival.

w4-500200.name: Chenla's conquest and absorption of Funan (early-mid 7th century)
w4-500200.blurb: During the early-to-mid 7th century the rising Khmer kingdom of Chenla, originally a vassal, overthrew and absorbed its former overlord Funan in the lower Mekong region (near lng 105.3, lat 11.3). Kings such as Isanavarman I completed the conquest, ending Funan as an independent state. This was the foundational territorial consolidation preceding the later Khmer Empire.

w4-500201.name: Tang conquest of the Tuyuhun (635) and annexation of the Tarim/Qinghai frontier
w4-500201.blurb: The Tang Dynasty under Emperor Taizong campaigned against the Tuyuhun in 634-635, defeating their khagan and reducing the kingdom to a Tang vassal, with much of its western territory (near lng 88.7, lat 38.9, toward the Tarim Basin) falling under Tang control. This opened the Hexi corridor and the road to the Western Regions for Tang expansion. The Tuyuhun were caught between Tang and Tibetan pressure.

w4-500202.name: Arab conquest of Mesopotamia (Battle of Qadisiyyah and fall of Ctesiphon)
w4-500202.blurb: The Rashidun Caliphate's conquest of Mesopotamia from the Sasanian Empire culminated at the Battle of Qadisiyyah in 636 CE, after which Ctesiphon fell in 637. By 638 Arab forces had cleared Sasanian resistance from Mesopotamia west of the Zagros. Central Mesopotamia (lat 33°N, lng 47°E, near modern Kut) passed from Sasanian to Rashidun control in this period; the data window 638-641 captures the consolidation.

w4-500204.name: Emergence of an autonomous Duchy of Thuringia after Dagobert I (c. 640)
w4-500204.blurb: Following the death of Dagobert I (639), Frankish central authority weakened and the Duchy of Thuringia (near lng 10.7, lat 50.6) gained autonomy under Duke Radulf, who rebelled against the Frankish king Sigebert III around 641-642. Radulf defeated the royal army and ruled Thuringia as a quasi-independent prince. This reflects the fragmentation of Merovingian power on the eastern frontier.

w4-500206.name: Rise of the autonomous Dabuyid dynasty in Tabaristan amid Sasanian collapse
w4-500206.blurb: As the Sasanian Empire collapsed under the Arab conquest after the Battle of Nahavand (642), the mountainous Caspian region of Tabaristan (near lng 51.7, lat 37.6) came under the independent Dabuyid dynasty, founded by Gil Gavbara. The rugged terrain allowed local Iranian princes to resist Arab rule and detach from Sasanian central authority. The Dabuyids would hold Tabaristan as a refuge of Sasanian-style rule for over a century.

w4-500207.name: Battle of Strathcarron - Strathclyde Defeats Dál Riata
w4-500207.blurb: In December 642, Owain ap Beli (Eugein I), king of Alt Clut (Strathclyde), defeated and killed Domnall Brecc of Dál Riata at the Battle of Strathcarron, recorded in the Annals of Ulster and the Y Gododdin 'Strathcarron interpolation'. This decisive Brittonic victory facilitated Strathclyde expansion at the expense of Dál Riata in the Forth/Clyde zone, consistent with the dataset transfer from 'Brythons' to 'Strathclyde' near lng -4.1, lat 55.4 within the 641-644 window.

citations.label: Eugein I of Alt Clut - Wikipedia

w4-500211.name: Turk Shahi consolidation in Kabul/Gandhara region (mid-7th century)
w4-500211.blurb: In the mid-7th century the Turk Shahi dynasty consolidated control over the Kabul-Gandhara region (near lng 68.5, lat 36.9), wresting frontier territory from Indian (Karkota) and other neighboring powers. The Turk Shahis became the dominant Buddhist-Hindu Turkic power of the Hindu Kush. This reflects the shifting frontier between the Kashmiri Karkota state and the Turk Shahis.

w4-500212.name: Merovingian division: Burgundy under Sigebert III / Clovis II (c. 639-642)
w4-500212.blurb: On the death of Dagobert I in 639 the Frankish realm was partitioned among his heirs, with the kingdom of Burgundy joined to Neustria under Clovis II while Austrasia went to Sigebert III. The large block near lng 3.4, lat 47 reflects the reconstitution of the Burgundian kingdom as a distinct sub-realm. This is a standard Merovingian dynastic partition.

w4-500213.name: Reabsorption of Aquitaine into the Frankish/Burgundian realm after Charibert II (632)
w4-500213.blurb: After the death of Charibert II in 632 and the murder of his infant son, the sub-kingdom of Aquitaine was reabsorbed into the wider Frankish realm under Dagobert I, with its lands (near lng 3.4, lat 47) reattached to the Burgundian/Neustrian bloc. This ended the brief independent Aquitanian kingship. It reflects the recombination of the Merovingian partitions.

w4-500214.name: Tang campaigns into the Western Regions and submission of the Western Türks (640s)
w4-500214.blurb: Following the Tang conquest of Gaochang (640) and campaigns into the Tarim Basin, the Tang Dynasty under Emperor Taizong extended control into Dzungaria and the Tian Shan region (near lng 86.3, lat 43.9) at the expense of the Western Göktürks. Tang protectorates and the Anxi garrisons projected power deep into Central Asia. This was a key stage in the Tang absorption of the Western Turkic Khaganate, completed in 657.

w4-500215.name: Emergence of the Khazar Khaganate from the Western Turkic Khaganate
w4-500215.blurb: The Western Turkic Khaganate fragmented following the death of Tong Yabghu Qaghan in 630 and subsequent Tang Chinese military pressure (630–657 CE). From the remnants, the Khazar people — a Turkic group long subordinate to the Göktürks and associated with the Ashina clan — coalesced into an independent Khaganate on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, conventionally dated to c. 650 CE. The dataset window 644–647 falls within this prolonged 630–650 transition period as the Western Göktürks disintegrated and Khazar independence solidified.

w4-500216.name: Arab conquest of Balasagan and the Caucasus (644–647)
w4-500216.blurb: During the early caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, Arab forces under Salman ibn Rabi'a al-Bahili advanced into Caucasian Albania and Balasagan between 644 and 648 CE, subjugating the region. This campaign extended the Rashidun Caliphate's control over the southern Caucasus territories previously held by surviving Sasanian client states.

w4-500218.name: Muslim conquest of Caucasian Albania / Arran
w4-500218.blurb: During the Rashidun conquest of the Caucasus, Arab armies under commanders such as Salman ibn Rabiah and Habib ibn Maslama pushed north from newly conquered Iran into Caucasian Albania (Arran) and the region of Balasagan in the eastern Caucasus. The local principalities submitted to the Rashidun Caliphate by the mid-640s, transferring this territory south of the Caucasus (47.3E, 40.6N) to Arab control.

w4-500219.name: Muslim conquest of Armenia
w4-500219.blurb: Rashidun forces under Habib ibn Maslama campaigned into Armenia in the early-to-mid 640s, capturing Dvin in 640 and progressively subduing the Armenian principalities. By the mid-640s much of Armenia (around 44E, 40.7N) had passed under Rashidun suzerainty, ending Byzantine and local autonomy in the region.

w4-500220.name: Collapse of Harsha's Empire and rise of regional dynasties in Bengal
w4-500220.blurb: After Emperor Harsha of Kannauj died without an heir in 647, his loosely held north Indian empire rapidly disintegrated. In eastern Bengal the Khadga dynasty emerged as an independent regional power, taking over territory (around 89.5E, 23.5N in the Bengal delta) that had nominally fallen within Harsha's orbit.

w4-500223.name: Formation of Old Great Bulgaria under Kubrat
w4-500223.blurb: Around 632 Khan Kubrat united the Onogur-Bulgar tribes north of the Black Sea and threw off Avar overlordship, establishing Old Great Bulgaria in the Pontic-Caspian steppe. The transfer of steppe territory north of the Black Sea (33E, 47.6N) from the Avar Khaganate reflects Kubrat's consolidation of this independent Bulgar realm.

w4-500227.name: Establishment of the Umayyad Caliphate by Mu'awiya
w4-500227.blurb: Following the assassination of Caliph Ali and the abdication of his son Hasan, Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, became sole caliph in 661, founding the Umayyad Caliphate with its capital at Damascus. The large transfer centered on Syria (37E, 34.7N) reflects the dynastic succession from the Rashidun to the Umayyad Caliphate in the heartland of Mu'awiya's power base.

w4-500228.name: Unification of Nobatia and Makuria
w4-500228.blurb: In the mid-7th century the Nubian kingdom of Nobatia was absorbed into its southern neighbor Makuria, forming a single unified Christian Nubian state with its capital at Dongola. The transfer of the Nile Valley territory around Lower Nubia (32.4E, 21.7N) from Nobatia to Makuria reflects this merger, which left a unified Makuria to face the Arab armies at the First Battle of Dongola (641-642).

w4-500229.name: Battle of the Winwæd and Northumbrian control of Mercia
w4-500229.blurb: At the Battle of the Winwæd (15 November 655) King Oswiu of Northumbria killed the pagan Mercian king Penda, ending Mercian dominance. Oswiu partitioned Mercia, taking the northern half outright; when Peada was murdered in 656 he assumed direct control of all Mercia (lat 52.6, lng -1.1) for three years. Window 647-656.

w4-500231.name: First Fitna and Byzantine reoccupation in Anatolia
w4-500231.blurb: During the First Muslim Civil War (656-661) the Caliphate's pressure on Byzantine Anatolia slackened, and Mu'awiya agreed to a truce and tribute with Constantinople to secure his rear. This allowed the Byzantine Empire to recover frontier territory in eastern Anatolia (around 37.2E, 38.4N) that had been contested with the Caliphate.

w4-500233.name: Tang-Silla conquest of Baekje
w4-500233.blurb: In 660 a combined Tang-Silla campaign led by the Tang general Su Dingfang and Silla's forces invaded and destroyed the Korean kingdom of Baekje, capturing its capital Sabi and King Uija. The Tang established the Ungjin Commandery over former Baekje territory in the southwest Korean peninsula (127.1E, 35.7N), the area shown transferring to the Tang Dynasty.

w4-500234.name: Tang conquest of the Western Turkic Khaganate
w4-500234.blurb: In 657 the Tang general Su Dingfang decisively defeated the Western Turkic qaghan Ashina Helu, ending the Western Turkic Khaganate. The Tang Dynasty established protectorates over the vast Central Asian steppe and Tarim/Tian Shan region (around 74.4E, 40.3N), absorbing the enormous Western Turk domain shown here.

w4-500236.name: Mercian recovery after the Battle of the Winwaed
w4-500236.blurb: At the Winwaed (15 November 655) Oswiu of Northumbria defeated and killed Penda of Mercia, but a Mercian revolt in 657-658 expelled Oswiu, and by c. 661 Mercia under Wulfhere had regained its territory and extended control over the adjacent midlands. The Northumbria-to-Mercia shift falls within the 656-661 window. Well attested.

w4-500237.name: Dissolution of Samo's realm and emergence of Carantania (c.658–660)
w4-500237.blurb: Samo, the Frankish merchant-king who united Slavic tribes against the Avars and Franks, died around 658 and his confederation dissolved for want of a stable succession. The Alpine Slavs of the Eastern Alps then organised as the independent Principality of Carantania around 660, centred near modern Klagenfurt — the principal successor to Samo's realm in the Alpine region.

w4-500239.name: Early Umayyad campaigns into Khorasan and Kabul region
w4-500239.blurb: Under Caliph Mu'awiya I (معاوية بن أبي سفيان), Arab armies based in newly consolidated Khurasan pushed eastward toward the Kabul region c. 661-666, pressing against the Turk Shahi rulers who held the former Sasanian and Hephthalite marches of what is now northern and eastern Afghanistan. The territory ceded in these frontier campaigns came from the Turk Shahis and the residue of Sasanian-successor holdings, not from the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire, which had no presence east of the Iranian plateau. Khurasan itself had already passed from Sasanian to Arab hands in the 650s, and Mu'awiya's governors used it as the springboard for these eastern raids.

w4-500240.name: Umayyad Conquest of Byzantine Cilicia and Syria
w4-500240.blurb: Following Muawiya I's consolidation of the Umayyad Caliphate after 661, Arab forces continued the advance into Byzantine territories in Cilicia and southern Anatolia. The centroid at ~30.2°E, 35.5°N (southern Anatolia/Cyprus region) reflects Umayyad raids and annexations of frontier zones between 661 and 666, part of the sustained Byzantine-Arab wars that eroded Byzantine control of the eastern Mediterranean littoral.

w4-500241.name: Tibetan Empire's conquest of the Tuyuhun and expansion into the Tang frontier
w4-500241.blurb: In 663 the Tibetan Empire under minister Gar Tongtsen conquered the Tuyuhun kingdom around Kokonor, bringing Tibetan power up against the Tang frontier in the Qinghai/Amdo region. The transfer of territory around 96.2E, 36.8N from the Tang Dynasty to the Tibetan Empire reflects this Tibetan advance into the Tang-aligned northeastern Tibetan plateau.

w4-500245.name: Merovingian fragmentation and reunification under Ebroin/Chlothar III
w4-500245.blurb: After Dagobert I's death (639), Frankish authority fragmented among rival sub-kings and Mayors of the Palace; around 660-661 Ebroin reunified the kingdom for Chlothar III, while Aquitaine and Austrasia repeatedly asserted autonomy. The coordinates point to the Burgundy/Rhine area rather than Aquitaine proper, a likely dataset anomaly, but the Aquitaine-to-Kingdom-of-the-Franks transfer in the py661-y666 window reflects this reunification.

w4-500246.name: Tang-Silla conquest of Goguryeo
w4-500246.blurb: In 668 Tang armies under Li Ji, allied with Silla, captured Pyongyang and destroyed the kingdom of Goguryeo after the death of the strongman Yeon Gaesomun and ensuing succession strife. The Tang established the Protectorate General to Pacify the East over former Goguryeo territory in the northern Korean peninsula and Manchuria (around 126.5E, 40.5N).

w4-500247.name: Arab conquest of Crete/Aegean during the siege of Constantinople era
w4-500247.blurb: During the Umayyad naval offensive against Byzantium in the late 660s and early 670s (the campaigns culminating in the first Arab siege of Constantinople, 674-678), Muslim fleets raided and seized Byzantine Aegean territory. The transfer around 22E, 35.8N (Crete/southern Aegean) reflects Umayyad maritime expansion at Byzantine expense in this period.

w4-500249.name: Turk Shahi reconquest of Kabul/Zabulistan from the Umayyads
w4-500249.blurb: The Turk Shahis of Kabul repeatedly resisted Arab expansion, and in the late 660s-670s they recovered territory around the Hindu Kush (66.5E, 36.7N) after Umayyad forces overextended. The transfer back from the Umayyad Caliphate to the Turk Shahis reflects this successful resistance that kept Kabul and Zabulistan outside firm Arab control for generations.

w4-500250.name: Succession of Tarusbawa and founding of the Sunda Kingdom
w4-500250.blurb: The last king of Tarumanagara, Linggawarman, died around 669 CE. His son-in-law Tarusbawa succeeded him but renamed the realm after his home domain, effectively replacing Tarumanagara with the Kingdom of Sunda in western Java. The Citarum River became the border between Sunda (west) and the breakaway Kingdom of Galuh (east), marking the end of Tarumanagara as a unified polity.

citations.label: Kingdom of Sunda and Galuh – New World Encyclopedia

w4-500251.name: Tibetan Empire expansion into the western Himalaya / Kashmir region (c. 670s)
w4-500251.blurb: Under Mangsong Mangtsen, the Tibetan Empire expanded dramatically westward in the 660s–670s, consolidating Zhang Zhung, seizing the Tang Four Garrisons of Anxi after the Battle of Dafei River (670), and pressing into Central Asia and the western Himalayas adjacent to Kashmir. The coordinates (77.5°E, 35.6°N) lie in the Karakoram/Ladakh zone, consistent with Tibetan dominance there in the 666–674 window.

w4-500252.name: Tibetan expansion into Gilgit-Baltistan
w4-500252.blurb: Tibet's aggressive westward expansion in the 660s–670s, which saw the seizure of Khotan (665–670) and the Four Garrisons of Anxi (670), extended into the Gilgit-Baltistan / Little Balur region at the expense of local rulers aligned with Kashmir. Tibetan forces brought the upper Indus valley and surrounding highlands into their sphere of control during this period.

w4-500253.name: Khazar conquest of Old Great Bulgaria
w4-500253.blurb: After the death of Khan Kubrat (c. 665), Old Great Bulgaria fragmented among his sons, and the rising Khazar Khaganate overran the Pontic-Caspian steppe. The transfer of the steppe north of the Sea of Azov (37.6E, 47.1N) from Old Great Bulgaria to Khazaria reflects the Khazar conquest that scattered the Bulgar hordes, driving Asparukh's followers toward the Danube.

w4-500257.name: Frankish reassertion over Aquitaine after the Battle of Autun (Neustria-Austrasia conflicts)
w4-500257.blurb: In the turbulent late Merovingian period, the semi-autonomous duchy of Aquitaine was drawn back under Frankish royal authority amid the wars between Neustria, Austrasia and Burgundy. The transfer of central Gaul territory (around 3.4E, 47.2N) from Aquitaine to the Kingdom of the Franks reflects this reassertion of Merovingian overlordship over the Aquitanian/Burgundian frontier.

w4-500259.name: Tang Withdrawal from the Korean Peninsula after Silla–Tang War
w4-500259.blurb: Following a series of Silla military victories (670–676), Tang China evacuated its administrative headquarters from the Korean peninsula and relocated the Protectorate General to Pacify the East to Liaodong, effectively ceding all territory south of the Taedong River to Unified Silla. The formal cession was confirmed by Tang Emperor Xuanzong's recognition of Silla's king over the peninsula in 735.

w4-500260.name: Iberian (Kartli) resistance to Umayyad rule in the Caucasus
w4-500260.blurb: Amid the disorder of the Second Fitna (680-692), Umayyad control over the Caucasus weakened, allowing the Principality of Iberia (Kartli) in eastern Georgia to recover autonomy. The transfer of territory around 44.1E, 42.1N from the Umayyad Caliphate to the Principality of Iberia reflects this reassertion of local Georgian princely power during the Arab civil war.

w4-500262.name: Umayyad campaigns in Tokharistan and Zabulistan against the Turk Shahis
w4-500262.blurb: During the late 7th century the Umayyad Caliphate, expanding eastward from Khurasan under governors such as Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad and Salm ibn Ziyad, pushed into Tokharistan and the Hindu Kush region around Kabul and Zabulistan, then ruled by the Turk Shahis. The area near Bamiyan repeatedly changed hands as Arab raiders extracted tribute and briefly occupied territory. This reflects the Umayyad seizure of Turk Shahi land in the 670s-680s.

w4-500263.name: Asparukh's migration and founding of the First Bulgarian Empire
w4-500263.blurb: After the collapse of Old Great Bulgaria following Khan Kubrat's death and Khazar pressure, his son Asparukh led the Bulgars westward across the Danube. The First Bulgarian Empire was established in 681 when Byzantium recognized the new state after the Battle of Ongal. This transfer reflects the Bulgar successor state inheriting the old Great Bulgaria heartland north of the Black Sea.

w4-500265.name: Bulgar settlement of the lower Danube under Asparukh
w4-500265.blurb: When Asparukh's Bulgars crossed the Danube and founded the First Bulgarian Empire in 681, they occupied the lands of Moesia and the lower Danube (near lng 25, lat 44) that had been on the periphery of the Avar Khaganate. The new Bulgar state pushed back Avar influence and Byzantine control in the region, taking territory in present-day Romania/Bulgaria from the Avar sphere.

w4-500268.name: Tang reconquest of the Four Garrisons of Anxi from Tibet
w4-500268.blurb: After the Tibetan Empire had seized the Tarim Basin and the Four Garrisons of Anxi in 670, the Tang Dynasty under Empress Wu Zetian launched a major counteroffensive led by general Wang Xiaojie, who decisively defeated the Tibetans in 692 and recovered the Four Garrisons (Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar, Karashahr). This restored Tang control over the Tarim Basin (near lng 83, lat 39).

citations.label: Protectorate General to Pacify the West (Anxi)
Tang campaigns against the Western Turks/Tibet

w4-500270.name: Türgesh ascendancy in the Western Turkic lands under Wuzhile
w4-500270.blurb: As the Western Turkic Khaganate fragmented, the Türgesh confederation under Wuzhile (Üch-Elig) rose to dominance over the Semirechye and the western steppe (near lng 76, lat 41) around 699, establishing their own khaganate centered on Suyab and Talas. This transfer reflects the Türgesh supplanting the older Turkic (Western Turk) authority in Central Asia.

w4-500272.name: Move of the capital to Heijo-kyo (Nara), beginning of the Nara period
w4-500272.blurb: In 710 Empress Genmei moved the Japanese imperial capital from Fujiwara-kyo (in the Asuka region) to the new city of Heijo-kyo (Nara), marking the formal start of the Nara period. This is a periodization change of the same Yamato Japanese state rather than a conquest; the territory of the Japanese home islands (near lng 135, lat 34) passed in the dataset from the 'Asuka' to the 'Nara' label.

w4-500273.name: Merovingian Frankish realm relabeling (dynastic continuity)
w4-500273.blurb: The transfer from 'Kingdom of the Franks' to 'Merovingian Empire' near the Rhone reflects a dataset relabeling of the same Merovingian-ruled Frankish state rather than a discrete conquest. In this era the Frankish kingdom remained under nominal Merovingian kings while real power lay with the Pippinid mayors of the palace; no single battle moved this land.

w4-500275.name: Division of Chenla into Land Chenla and Water Chenla
w4-500275.blurb: Early in the 8th century the Khmer kingdom of Chenla fragmented into two parts: Land Chenla (upper, inland) and Water Chenla (lower, in the Mekong delta region near lng 105, lat 11), as recorded in Chinese sources around 706-717. This entry reflects the southern delta portion passing to the Water Chenla successor polity.

w4-500279.name: Division of Chenla into Land Chenla and Water Chenla
w4-500279.blurb: The same early-8th-century fragmentation of the Khmer kingdom of Chenla produced Land Chenla (Upper/inland Chenla, in the region near lng 105, lat 15 in modern Laos/northern Cambodia). This entry reflects the inland northern portion passing to the Land Chenla successor polity around 706-717.

w4-500280.name: Carolingian (Pippinid) ascendancy after Battle of Vincy
w4-500280.blurb: After Pippin of Herstal's death the mayoralty of the palace passed to Charles Martel, who consolidated Frankish power by defeating the Neustrians at the Battle of Vincy in 717. The transfer of Frankish land (near lng 5.9, lat 44) from 'Kingdom of the Franks' to 'Carolingian Empire' reflects the rise of the Carolingian (Pippinid) house to effective control of Francia.

w4-500283.name: Battle of Covadonga and founding of the Kingdom of Asturias
w4-500283.blurb: Around 718-722, the Visigothic nobleman Pelayo (Pelagius) led a revolt against Umayyad authority in the mountains of Asturias, defeating a Muslim force at the Battle of Covadonga, and established the Kingdom of Asturias — the first Christian polity to survive the 711 Islamic conquest of Hispania. The dataset transfer (Visigothic Kingdom -> Kingdom of Asturias, py710/y718) at lng-6.1/lat42.7 (NW Iberia) reflects the emergence of this remnant Christian state.

w4-500284.name: Türk (Western Turk/Türgesh) gains in the western Tibetan-Pamir frontier
w4-500284.blurb: In the 710s the resurgent Turks/Türgesh under Suluk and the Tang-allied western steppe powers contested the Pamir and Wakhan corridor (near lng 74, lat 38) with the Tibetan Empire, which had been expanding toward the western Tarim and Gilgit. This entry reflects Turkic forces wresting borderland from Tibetan control in the western mountains.

w4-500285.name: Khazar counteroffensive in the Second Arab-Khazar War
w4-500285.blurb: In 721–722 a Khazar army of ~30,000 invaded Armenia and crushed the Arab garrison at Marj al-Hijara, recovering significant territory from the Umayyad Caliphate in Dagestan and the eastern Caucasus. Though al-Jarrah ibn Abdallah subsequently retook Derbent in 722, Khazaria regained much of the frontier zone in Azerbaijan and Dagestan during the period 718–724.

w4-500287.name: Charles Martel's conquest of Neustria (Battles of Amblève, Vincy and Soissons)
w4-500287.blurb: Following the Frankish civil war between Austrasia and Neustria, Charles Martel defeated the Neustrians and their ally King Chilperic II, decisively at Soissons in 719. The transfer of northern Frankish territory (near lng 1, lat 48.5, the Neustrian heartland around Paris) to the 'Kingdom of Neustria' label reflects this Neustrian polity's distinct status before Charles' final subjugation of it.

w4-500289.name: Charles Martel's subjugation of Thuringia (720–724)
w4-500289.blurb: Charles Martel conducted campaigns against the Saxons and Thuringians in the early 720s, reasserting Frankish royal authority over Thuringia. By ca. 724 he had suppressed the Thuringian duchy and brought the region under direct Carolingian-Frankish control.

w4-500291.name: Umayyad conquest of Septimania
w4-500291.blurb: Following the collapse of the Visigothic kingdom at the Battle of Guadalete (711), Umayyad governor Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani crossed the Pyrenees and captured Narbonne in 719, bringing Septimania (northeastern Iberia and southern Gaul near lat 43.4, lng 3.1) under Umayyad control. Frankish forces eventually halted Umayyad expansion at the Battle of Toulouse (721) and ultimately recovered Narbonne in 759.

w4-500293.name: Sanjaya's Campaign — Galuh Absorbed into Mataram / Sunda Gains Territory
w4-500293.blurb: In 723 CE, Sanjaya of Mataram killed Purbasora, the usurper who had seized the Galuh throne around 716 CE with support from Indraprasta. After Purbasora's death, Galuh came under Mataram's suzerainty, and the Carita Parahyangan credits Sanjaya with redistributing some western Sundanese territories. The Cliopatria map convention records this as Galuh-to-Sunda in the 718–724 window.

w4-500297.name: Arab raids destabilize Maitrakas; early Chalukya encroachment
w4-500297.blurb: The Arab governor of Sind, Junaid ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Murri, launched raids into Gujarat around 724–730 CE that severely weakened the Maitraka kingdom of Vallabhi; the Chalukyas of Gujarat (Chalukyas of Lata) appear to have absorbed portions of southern Maitraka territory during this period of Maitraka vulnerability.

w4-500300.name: Arab defeat of Maitraka Kingdom and Gurjara-Pratihara expansion into Gujarat
w4-500300.blurb: The Arab governor of Sind al-Junaid ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Murri attacked the Maitraka kingdom of Valabhi around 725–726, severely weakening it. The Gurjara-Pratiharas under Nagabhata I exploited this disruption, expanding into the vacuum left in Gujarat and Rajputana and driving back the Arab advances. The Maitraka kingdom never recovered and Gurjara-Pratihara control over the region followed.

w4-500301.name: Charles Martel subdues Alamannia
w4-500301.blurb: Charles Martel, after securing his grip on the Frankish realm following the Battle of Tours (732), had already been incorporating Alamannia into the Carolingian sphere in the late 720s–730s, suppressing the semi-independent Alemannic dukes. The atlas window 724–732 captures this Frankish absorption of Alamannia, completed definitively by Carloman's blood court at Cannstatt (746) but administratively under Frankish control from around 730.

w4-500307.name: Lombard campaigns of Liutprand in the Exarchate
w4-500307.blurb: Lombard King Liutprand seized large portions of the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna between 727 and 740, including territories around Perugia and the Duchy of Spoleto, exploiting Byzantine distraction with the Iconoclast controversy. By 740 the Exarchate was reduced to scattered enclaves, effectively transferring central Italian territory from Byzantine to Lombard (Kingdom of Italy) control.

citations.label: Wickham, C. Early Medieval Italy (1981) — Lombard expansion under Liutprand

w4-500309.name: Mercian seizure of Somerton and northern Wessex under Æthelbald
w4-500309.blurb: Æthelbald of Mercia seized the royal manor of Somerton in Somerset in 733, extending Mercian political control over the northern Wessex border zone; Bede wrote in 731 that all southern kingdoms were subject to Æthelbald, and the ASC records his dominance as effectively uncontested in this period.

w4-500311.name: Umayyad conquest of Iberia (Kartli)
w4-500311.blurb: Umayyad commander Marwan ibn Muhammad ('Marwan II') launched a major campaign into the Caucasus around 735–737 CE, conquering much of Caucasian Iberia (Kartli/Georgia) from the local Principality of Iberia and imposing Arab suzerainty over the region.

w4-500313.name: Tang offensives against Tibet in the Tarim/Kunlun frontier under Emperor Xuanzong
w4-500313.blurb: During the 740s the Tang Dynasty under Emperor Xuanzong pressed the Tibetan Empire along the southern Tarim and Kunlun frontier (near lng 80, lat 37, the Khotan/Karakoram region), culminating in Gao Xianzhi's famous 747 campaign over the Pamirs against Tibet and its allies. This entry reflects Tang recovery of borderland from Tibet on the eve of the Battle of Talas era.

citations.label: Tang campaigns against the Western Regions

w4-500314.name: Tang expansion into the Türgesh lands after the Türgesh collapse
w4-500314.blurb: After the assassination of the Türgesh khagan Suluk in 738 the Türgesh confederation fell into civil war and decline, allowing the Tang Dynasty under Gao Xianzhi and the Anxi Protectorate to extend control deep into Semirechye and the Ili/Issyk-Kul region (near lng 83, lat 44). Gao Xianzhi captured Suyab/Talas areas around 748, transferring vast Türgesh steppe to Tang authority just before the Battle of Talas (751).

w4-500315.name: Aistulf brings Duchy of Benevento under Lombard royal influence
w4-500315.blurb: King Aistulf of the Lombards (r. 749–756), after his brother Ratchis abdicated, pursued an assertive policy of bringing the semi-independent southern duchies under royal authority.
