He ruled Spoleto directly without a duke (751–756) and exercised indirect control over the Duchy of Benevento (lat 41.1, lng 16.1), though the duchy retained considerable autonomy. His expansionism alienated the Papacy and invited Frankish intervention, and after his death Spoleto and Benevento broke away again.

w4-500316.name: King Aistulf subjugates the Duchy of Spoleto (c. 750–751)
w4-500316.blurb: King Aistulf of the Lombards, after seizing Ravenna and ending the Byzantine Exarchate in 751, brought the semi-autonomous Duchy of Spoleto under direct Lombard royal control, removing its independent duke. This incorporated Spoleto into the Lombard Kingdom of Italy as part of Aistulf's expansion across central Italy.

w4-500317.name: Bavarian protectorate over Carantania against the Avars (c.743–745)
w4-500317.blurb: Around 740–743 Avar attacks on the Alpine Slavic principality of Carantania prompted Prince Boruth to appeal to Duke Odilo of Bavaria. Odilo intervened, defeated the Avars, and established Bavarian overlordship, taking hostages and beginning Christianisation. This subordination of Carantania to Bavaria (and through it the Frankish realm) is the transfer recorded here; sources date it variously 743–745.

w4-500319.name: Aquitanian autonomy under Duke Hunald/Waiofar resisting Carolingian Francia
w4-500319.blurb: After Charles Martel's death in 741, the Duchy of Aquitaine under Hunald I (and later Waiofar) reasserted its independence from the Carolingian Frankish kings Pepin and Carloman, leading to renewed war in southwestern Gaul (near lng 0.6, lat 44.8). This entry reflects Aquitaine breaking away from Frankish control in the 740s before Pepin the Short's later reconquest.

w4-500320.name: Fihrid seizure of Ifriqiya during the collapse of Umayyad authority
w4-500320.blurb: As the Umayyad Caliphate disintegrated amid the Berber Revolt (740-743) and the Third Fitna, the Fihrid family of Arab governors seized effective independent control of Ifriqiya (North Africa, near lng 12, lat 33, around Tunisia/Tripolitania). Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib al-Fihri established autonomous Fihrid rule from Kairouan in 745, transferring the province out of central Umayyad control on the eve of the Abbasid Revolution.

w4-500322.name: Ibadi Kharijite takeover of Tripolitania from the Fihrids
w4-500322.blurb: Around 750-751 CE, as the Abbasid revolution overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate and the Fihrids asserted independence in Ifriqiya, Ibadi Kharijite missionaries who had been active in Tripolitania since the 720s organised Berber tribes (especially the Hawwara and Nafusa) into an Ibadi imamate. The Ibadis took Tripoli and then pushed into Tunisia, capturing Kairouan from the Sufri Kharijites around 757-758 CE. The coordinates (14 degrees E, 31 degrees N) point to Tripolitania/Libya, the heartland of the Ibadi uprising. This briefly created an Ibadi state stretching from Tunisia to Tripolitania until Abbasid reconquest in 761.

w4-500324.name: Abbasid Revolution
w4-500324.blurb: The Abbasid Revolution (747-750), led from Khurasan by Abu Muslim under the black banners and culminating in the Battle of the Zab (750) where Marwan II was defeated, overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate. The victorious Abbasids, descended from the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas, took control of the vast caliphal heartland from the Umayyads. This transferred the empire's core territory across Arabia, the Levant, Iraq and beyond to the new dynasty.

w4-500326.name: Rashtrakuta overthrow of the Chalukyas of Vatapi (Dantidurga's conquest)
w4-500326.blurb: The Rashtrakuta ruler Dantidurga overthrew his Chalukya overlords, defeating Kirtivarman II of the Badami (Vatapi) Chalukyas around 753. His successor Krishna I completed the conquest, ending Chalukya dominance in the Deccan. This transferred the Chalukya core in the western Deccan to the rising Rashtrakuta Dynasty based at Manyakheta.

w4-500327.name: Fihrid recovery of Tripolitania from the Kharijites
w4-500327.blurb: After the Fihrids lost control of Tripolitania to Kharijite (Ibadi) forces around 750-751 CE, Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib al-Fihri briefly reasserted Fihrid influence before internal family strife in 755 caused the dynasty's definitive collapse. The Fihrids' brief recovery of Tripolitanian territory (c. 751-755) preceded their final overthrow by Kharijite forces and the subsequent Abbasid reconquest of the region in 761. The coordinates (14 degrees E, 31 degrees N) again indicate Tripolitania. The Fihrid political situation was highly fluid in this period, oscillating between Fihrid and Kharijite control.

citations.label: Umayyad rule in North Africa – Wikipedia

w4-500329.name: Battle of Talas
w4-500329.blurb: At the Battle of Talas (751) the Abbasid Caliphate, with its Karluk Turkic allies, defeated a Tang expeditionary army under Gao Xianzhi in the Talas River valley of Transoxiana/the Jaxartes region. The victory ended Tang westward expansion and secured Central Asian Turkic-held lands within the Islamic sphere. The territory in the Syr Darya region passed from Turkic control toward the Abbasid orbit.

w4-500330.name: Uyghur ascendancy in the Tarim/Beshbalik after Tang collapse in the west
w4-500330.blurb: Following the Battle of Talas (751) and the outbreak of the An Lushan Rebellion (755), the Tang withdrew forces from the western frontier, allowing the Uyghur Khaganate to expand into the Beshbalik and eastern Tarim region around Turfan. The Uyghurs, soon to be Tang allies against An Lushan, filled the vacuum left by collapsing Tang authority. This shifted the Turfan area from Tang to Uyghur control.

w4-500331.name: Uyghur expansion into the Tian Shan/Semirechye after the fall of the Second Turkic Khaganate
w4-500331.blurb: The Uyghur Khaganate, having destroyed the Second Turkic (Gokturk) Khaganate in 744 under Kutlug Bilge Kol, continued absorbing former Turkic lands across the Tian Shan and Semirechye into the 750s. The remaining Turkic-held steppe west toward the Chu River fell under Uyghur sway. This represents the Uyghur takeover of residual Gokturk territory.

w4-500333.name: Donation of Pepin – Exarchate of Ravenna granted to the Papacy
w4-500333.blurb: The Lombards under King Aistulf captured the Exarchate of Ravenna in 751, severing Byzantine control of central Italy. Pope Stephen II appealed to Frankish King Pepin the Short, who campaigned in Italy in 754 and 756. After defeating Aistulf, Pepin issued the Donation of Pepin (754–756), granting the former Byzantine exarchate and Pentapolis to the papacy rather than returning them to Constantinople. This act founded the temporal Papal States.

w4-500334.name: Battle of Burford (752) – Cuthred of Wessex Defeats Aethelbald of Mercia
w4-500334.blurb: In 752, Cuthred of Wessex defeated Aethelbald of Mercia at the Battle of Burford, temporarily halting Mercian supremacy over southern England and restoring Wessex's control over contested border territories. Aethelbald had dominated most of southern England since 716, but this defeat cost Mercia significant influence. Aethelbald was murdered by his own bodyguards in 757 and succeeded by Offa.

w4-500337.name: Tibetan expansion into the Pamirs/Wakhan after Tang withdrawal
w4-500337.blurb: After the An Lushan Rebellion (755) forced the Tang to recall its western garrisons, the Tibetan Empire expanded into the Pamir and Wakhan corridor, absorbing former Turkic-held mountain principalities. Tibet had long contested this strategic region with the Tang and Arabs. The collapse of Tang power let Tibet seize these passes.

w4-500338.name: Tibetan seizure of the Tang western frontier during the An Lushan Rebellion
w4-500338.blurb: When the An Lushan Rebellion (755) drained Tang garrisons from the northwest, the Tibetan Empire under Trisong Detsen overran the Hexi Corridor approaches and the western reaches toward the Tarim and Qinghai. The Tibetans exploited the Tang military collapse to seize vast frontier territory, a process that culminated in their brief capture of the capital Chang'an in 763. This large transfer reflects Tibet's wartime conquest of Tang western lands.

w4-500339.name: Kharijite Berber uprising overthrows Fihrid rule in Ifriqiya (756-757)
w4-500339.blurb: The Fihrid rulers of Ifriqiya collapsed after an internal family conflict in 755, allowing the Warfajuma Berbers under Kharijite (Sufrite) ideology to rebel; Habib ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri was defeated and the Warfajuma entered Kairouan in early 757, ending Fihrid rule. The from->to (Fihrids -> Kharijites) at 12.1, 33.2 in the 755-757 window matches this uprising.

w4-500340.name: Rashtrakuta consolidation of the Deccan under Krishna I
w4-500340.blurb: Continuing Dantidurga's overthrow of the Badami Chalukyas, Krishna I of the Rashtrakuta Dynasty completed the conquest of the southern Deccan from the remnants of Chalukya power by the mid-750s. This extended Rashtrakuta rule deeper into Karnataka. The territory passed from the defunct Chalukya state to the Rashtrakutas.

w4-500342.name: Establishment of the Emirate of Córdoba by Abd al-Rahman I
w4-500342.blurb: Abd al-Rahman I, a surviving Umayyad prince who fled the Abbasid massacre of his family, reached al-Andalus and defeated the governor Yusuf al-Fihri at the Battle of Musarah near Córdoba in 756. He established the independent Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba, breaking Iberia away from caliphal authority. This transferred al-Andalus from the (now Abbasid-claimed) Umayyad realm to the new Cordoban emirate.

w4-500343.name: Uyghur takeover of the Turfan/Beshbalik region during the An Lushan Rebellion
w4-500343.blurb: As the An Lushan Rebellion (755) gutted Tang frontier defenses, the Uyghur Khaganate extended its authority over the Turfan and Beshbalik region of the eastern Tarim. The Uyghurs were simultaneously sending armies to rescue the Tang in the interior, gaining influence and territory in the northwest. This shifted the Turfan region from Tang to Uyghur control.

w4-500344.name: Tibetan advance toward the Wei/Han valley during the An Lushan Rebellion
w4-500344.blurb: Exploiting the chaos of the An Lushan Rebellion, the Tibetan Empire pushed into the upper Han River and southern Gansu frontier by 763, the same year Tibetan forces briefly sacked the Tang capital Chang'an. The Tang, with its armies tied down in the east, could not defend these western marches. This transferred the borderland from Tang to Tibetan control.

w4-500347.name: Suppression of the Ibadi/Kharijite revolt in Ifriqiya (Abu Hatim's rebellion) and Abbasid reconquest
w4-500347.blurb: After a series of Kharijite (Ibadi and Sufri) revolts seized Ifriqiya and Tripolitania in the 750s, the Abbasid general Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath crushed the Ibadi imamate and retook Kairouan around 761, defeating Abu Hatim al-Malzuzi. This restored Abbasid control over the North African coast around Tripoli. The territory passed from Kharijite rebels back to the Abbasid Caliphate.

citations.label: Ibadi Imamate of Tripolitania / Kharijite revolts

w4-500348.name: Uyghur subjugation of the Yenisei Kyrgyz
w4-500348.blurb: Around 758 the Uyghur Khaganate under Bayanchur Khan (Moyan Chur) campaigned north and defeated the Yenisei Kyrgyz, bringing their lands along the upper Yenisei under Uyghur suzerainty. This expansion is recorded in the Uyghur runic inscriptions. The territory passed from the Kyrgyz to the Uyghur Khaganate until the Kyrgyz overthrew them in 840.

w4-500349.name: Second Arab–Khazar War (Khazar invasion of the Caucasus, 762-764)
w4-500349.blurb: In the early 760s the Khazars, under the general Ras Tarkhan, launched a major invasion across the Caucasus into Abbasid Caucasian Albania/Arran, exploiting unrest in the region. The Khazars overran territory south of the Caucasus before being pushed back. This temporary Khazar advance transferred the Caucasian borderland from the Abbasids to Khazaria.

w4-500350.name: Tang recovery of the Han valley frontier after the end of the An Lushan Rebellion
w4-500350.blurb: After the An Lushan Rebellion was finally suppressed in 763 and the brief Tibetan occupation of Chang'an was reversed, the Tang under Emperor Daizong with general Guo Ziyi recovered parts of the western frontier in the upper Han/southern Gansu region. This reversed the Tibetan gains of 763. The borderland returned from Tibet to the Tang.

w4-500351.name: Frankish conquest of Aquitaine and Gascon submission to Pepin the Short
w4-500351.blurb: Pepin the Short's long war (760-768) against Duke Waioffre of Aquitaine ended with Waioffre's death in 768 and the collapse of independent Aquitaine. The Gascons (Vascones) of the southwest submitted, with Duke Lupus II of Gascony acknowledging Frankish overlordship. The Gascon lands passed out of the Aquitanian duchy to a distinct Duchy of Gascony under Frankish suzerainty.

citations.label: Pepin the Short – conquest of Aquitaine

w4-500352.name: Abbasid recovery of Caucasian Albania after the Second Arab–Khazar War
w4-500352.blurb: After the Khazar invasion of 762-764, the Abbasids under Caliph al-Mansur reorganized the Caucasian frontier and drove the Khazars back beyond the Caucasus, restoring control over Arran. The recovery reversed the temporary Khazar occupation. The territory returned from Khazaria to the Abbasid Caliphate.

w4-500353.name: Frankish conquest of Aquitaine under Pepin the Short
w4-500353.blurb: Pepin the Short's eight-year war against the independent Duchy of Aquitaine culminated in 768 with the death of Duke Waioffre and the annexation of Aquitaine into the Kingdom of the Franks. This ended Aquitaine's autonomy and incorporated its heartland into the Carolingian realm. The large transfer reflects this final Frankish conquest.

w4-500354.name: Aquitanian War of Pepin the Short (frontier fluctuation, 760-768)
w4-500354.blurb: During the protracted Frankish–Aquitanian war (760-768), control of border districts in the Quercy/Périgord region shifted repeatedly as Duke Waioffre's forces resisted Pepin the Short. This small reverse transfer reflects a temporary Aquitanian recovery of contested borderland during the campaign before the final Frankish victory in 768. It is part of the same war that ended Aquitanian independence.

w4-500355.name: Karkota Kashmir's subjugation of Kannauj under Lalitaditya (c. 768–772)
w4-500355.blurb: The Varman (Ayudha) dynasty of Kannauj was overthrown around 770 CE amid the tripartite struggle for Kannauj. Kashmiri sources (the Rajatarangini) record that Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir defeated and subjugated the ruler of Kannauj. The transition reflects the turbulent frontier between Kashmir's expanding power and the northern Indian plains.

w4-500358.name: Gurjara-Pratihara ascendancy at Kannauj under Vatsaraja
w4-500358.blurb: Around 768-772 a large block of the Ganges-Yamuna doab passed from the Kannauj-Varman line to the Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty. Under Vatsaraja the Pratiharas pushed eastward from Rajasthan toward Kannauj, displacing the local Varman/Ayudha rulers in the contest for the imperial city that became the centerpiece of the tripartite struggle. The attribution is plausible but the exact dynastic mechanics in this narrow window are model-driven.

w4-500359.name: Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard kingdom
w4-500359.blurb: Pope Adrian I appealed to Charlemagne against the Lombard king Desiderius. Charlemagne invaded northern Italy in 773-774, capturing Pavia after a nine-month siege in June 774, deposing Desiderius, assuming the Lombard crown, and confirming the Donation of Pepin securing the Papal States. The data window 772-775 captures Frankish sovereignty over former Lombard territory adjacent to the Papal States.

w4-500360.name: Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard Kingdom
w4-500360.blurb: In 773-774 Charlemagne, king of the Franks, invaded Italy at the appeal of Pope Adrian I against the Lombard king Desiderius, besieged and took Pavia in 774, and assumed the Iron Crown as King of the Lombards. This brought the Kingdom of Italy (the Lombard realm) under direct Frankish rule, exactly the Italy-to-Franks transfer dated 772-775 here.

w4-500361.name: Charlemagne's Saxon Wars (first campaigns, 772-775)
w4-500361.blurb: The Saxon Wars opened in 772 when Charlemagne invaded Saxony, stormed the Eresburg, and destroyed the pagan Irminsul sanctuary. Campaigns in 774-775 pushed Frankish control over Saxon lands between the Rhine and Weser, matching this Saxons-to-Franks gain near Lower Saxony in 772-775.

w4-500362.name: Charlemagne's Conquest of the Lombard Kingdom and Confirmation of the Donation of Pepin
w4-500362.blurb: Charlemagne invaded the Lombard Kingdom in 773–774, deposed King Desiderius, and assumed the title King of the Lombards; he then confirmed Pepin's Donation, asserting Frankish suzerainty over central Italian territories formerly contested between the Lombards, Papacy, and Byzantium. The centroid (lat 43.7, lng 12, Umbria) reflects territories that passed under Frankish nominal authority following this conquest.

w4-500363.name: Charlemagne's 778 Iberian campaign; Abbasid-aligned revolt against Umayyad Córdoba
w4-500363.blurb: In 777 the governor of Zaragoza, Sulayman al-Arabi - aligned with the Abbasids against the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba - invited Charlemagne to intervene. In 778 Charlemagne campaigned across the Pyrenees; the coordinates (2.2, 41.9) point to Catalonia, where Carolingian/Abbasid-aligned influence supplanted Umayyad control and the Spanish March was later organised. The window (775-778) fits this realignment away from the Emirate of Córdoba.

w4-500364.name: Charlemagne's campaign into the Ebro valley (778)
w4-500364.blurb: In 778 Charlemagne led a two-pronged Frankish invasion into the Ebro valley at the invitation of dissident Muslim governors opposed to the Emirate of Córdoba, briefly seizing Pamplona and advancing on Zaragoza. Zaragoza refused to surrender, and Charlemagne withdrew; Pamplona was razed on the retreat, and the rearguard was destroyed at Roncevaux Pass. The data window 775-778 captures brief Frankish control of upper Ebro territory.

w4-500365.name: Charlemagne conquers Lombard Kingdom; Arechis II of Benevento asserts independence
w4-500365.blurb: When Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom and deposed Desiderius in 774, Duke Arechis II of Benevento alone refused to do homage, adopting the title princeps (Prince of Benevento) as a gesture of defiance and even legislating in the manner of the former Lombard kings. Too distant to be easily reached, Benevento was left unmolested and remained an autonomous Lombard principality outside Carolingian suzerainty; Arechis held it independently until Charlemagne finally forced his submission at Capua in 787. The atlas accordingly keeps this southern Italian territory under Benevento rather than transferring it to the Franks in 774.

w4-500366.name: Lombard Duke Hildeprand of Spoleto asserts autonomy
w4-500366.blurb: Amid the crisis of Charlemagne's invasion of 773-774, the Lombard Duchy of Spoleto broke from the collapsing Lombard kingdom of Desiderius: after Duke Theodicius fell at the siege of Pavia, the Spoletans elected Hildeprand and, rather than remain under the Lombard crown, sought Frankish and papal protection. The duchy thus asserted itself independently of Lombard royal authority during 773-775 before Hildeprand formally submitted to Charlemagne. The atlas marks Spoleto separating from the Lombard Kingdom of Italy, not its absorption by the Franks at this date.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Fall of the Lombard Kingdom

w4-500367.name: Saxon revolt under Widukind (Frankish reversal, 775-778)
w4-500367.blurb: While Charlemagne was occupied in Italy and Spain, the Saxons led increasingly by Widukind rose in repeated revolts, raiding Frankish positions and recovering Saxon territory in the later 770s. This Franks-to-Saxons reversal in 775-778 reflects that backlash before Charlemagne's renewed offensives of 779-780.

w4-500368.name: Pala expansion under Dharmapala (tripartite struggle for Kannauj)
w4-500368.blurb: Around 775-778 territory in the central Ganges plain shifted from the Gurjara-Pratiharas to the Pala Empire. Under Dharmapala the Palas advanced westward from Bengal into the doab during the tripartite struggle among Palas, Pratiharas, and Rashtrakutas for control of Kannauj. The direction fits Dharmapala's rise, though the precise year is model-approximated.

w4-500369.name: Leon II of Abkhazia annexes the Kingdom of Lazica
w4-500369.blurb: Around 778, Leon II of Abkhazia (Egrisi) exploited dynastic claims to Lazica and used Khazar support to expel Byzantine garrisons from western Georgia, absorbing the Kingdom of Lazica, assuming the title 'King of the Abkhazians,' and moving his capital to Kutaisi (42.1E, 42.4N). This created the Kingdom of Abkhazia as successor to Lazica, marking a decisive shift from Byzantine suzerainty to local independence.

w4-500370.name: Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard Kingdom
w4-500370.blurb: After the fall of the Lombard kingdom in 774, the Duchy of Spoleto under Duke Hildeprand passed into the Frankish sphere: Hildeprand submitted formally to Charlemagne around 775-776, dating his charters by the regnal years of Charles, 'king of the Franks and Lombards.' Spoleto retained its administrative identity as a vassal duchy under Frankish suzerainty, and on Hildeprand's death in 789 Charlemagne replaced him with his own appointee, the Frank Winigis. The territory thus moved from the former Lombard Kingdom of Italy into the Carolingian realm.

w4-500371.name: Frisian–Saxon rebellion against Charlemagne (782–785)
w4-500371.blurb: In 782 the Frisians east of the Lauwers joined the Saxon uprising under Widukind, temporarily expelling Carolingian authority from eastern Frisia. Charlemagne campaigned through 783–784, and the rebellion ended in 785 with Widukind's surrender. The 778–783 window captures the onset of this rebellion that briefly reversed Frankish control, matching the Franks→Frisia change at (6.9°E, 53.2°N).

w4-500374.name: Córdoba recovers the upper Ebro after Charlemagne's withdrawal
w4-500374.blurb: After Charlemagne's 778 withdrawal (his rearguard annihilated at Roncevaux Pass), the Emirate of Córdoba reasserted control over the upper Ebro valley and Pyrenean foothills that had briefly deferred to Frankish authority. Abd al-Rahman I's forces consolidated the region by the early 780s, pushing the Frankish frontier back to the Pyrenees. The data window 778-783 captures this reversion to Córdoba.

w4-500377.name: Charlemagne's subjugation of Aquitaine / creation of the sub-kingdom
w4-500377.blurb: Aquitaine, conquered earlier by Pepin the Short, was consolidated under Frankish rule when Charlemagne erected it as a sub-kingdom for his infant son Louis the Pious in 781. This Aquitaine-to-Franks transfer in 778-783, in the Gascon/Garonne region, reflects that formal incorporation following the 778 Spanish campaign and Roncevaux.

w4-500378.name: Nagabhata I / Vatsaraja defeats Dharmapala (Pala-Pratihara conflict)
w4-500378.blurb: Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja defeated Pala king Dharmapala in battle in the late 770s–780, seizing contested territory in the middle Gangetic plain (Kannauj region). The Rashtrakutas then intervened, defeating both parties, but the Pratiharas had temporarily displaced Pala territorial control.

w4-500381.name: Charlemagne's annexation of Bavaria / deposition of Tassilo III
w4-500381.blurb: In 788 Charlemagne deposed Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria, accusing him of treason (harisliz) and conspiracy with the Avars, and absorbed the previously autonomous duchy directly into the Frankish realm. This Bavarians-to-Franks transfer dated 783-788 is precisely that annexation, ending Agilolfing ducal independence.

w4-500383.name: Charlemagne's Saxon Wars (renewed conquest, 782-785)
w4-500383.blurb: After the 782 disaster at the Suntel and the Massacre of Verden, Charlemagne crushed Saxon resistance; Widukind submitted and was baptized in 785, bringing much of Saxony under Frankish control. This Saxons-to-Franks gain in 783-788 reflects that decisive phase of the Saxon Wars.

w4-500384.name: Offa of Mercia's Domination of Wessex (c. 787–788)
w4-500384.blurb: King Offa of Mercia (r. 757–796) extended Mercian supremacy over Wessex in the 780s through military pressure and diplomatic alliance. Around 787–788, Offa arranged the marriage of his daughter Eadburh to Beorhtric, King of Wessex, effectively placing Wessex under Mercian political control. This consolidated Offa's dominance over southern England south of the Humber.

w4-500385.name: Dharmapala's conquest of Kannauj and the Ganges valley
w4-500385.blurb: A large block of the lower-middle Ganges plain passed from the Gurjara-Pratiharas to the Pala Empire around 783-788. The Pala emperor Dharmapala became the dominant power in northern India in the late 8th century, taking Kannauj and installing his client Chakrayudha while the Pratiharas were checked by the Rashtrakutas. The direction and era match Dharmapala's high tide.

w4-500386.name: Pala recovery after Rashtrakuta withdrawal (tripartite struggle)
w4-500386.blurb: Around 788-793 a parcel near Kannauj passed from the Rashtrakuta Dynasty to the Pala Empire. After Dhruva Dharavarsha's Rashtrakuta raid into the north receded back to the Deccan, Dharmapala's Palas filled the vacuum in the Ganges-Yamuna doab. This reflects that swing within the tripartite struggle rather than a single named battle.

w4-500387.name: Reassertion of Beneventan autonomy under Grimoald III
w4-500387.blurb: This Franks-to-Benevento reversal in 788-793 reflects the loosening of Carolingian control over the southern Lombard duchy after 787. Grimoald III, installed as duke by Charlemagne, soon pursued an independent course, dropping Frankish formulas and resisting Carolingian campaigns, so Benevento effectively slipped back out of direct Frankish authority.

w4-500389.name: Tibetan conquest of Beshbalik/Tarim from the Uyghurs
w4-500389.blurb: Around 788-793 a vast tract of the eastern Tarim/Beshbalik region in the Tian Shan passed from the Uyghur Khaganate to the Tibetan Empire. In the wars of 789-792 the Tibetans, allied with the Qarluqs, defeated the Uyghurs and Tang around Beshbalik (Beiting) and seized control of much of the northern Silk Road, matching this transfer.

w4-500392.name: Qarluq expansion in Semirechye during the Tibeto-Uyghur wars
w4-500392.blurb: Around 788-793 a large region of the Ili/Semirechye (near Lake Balkhash) passed from the Uyghur Khaganate to the Qarluqs. Allied with the Tibetan Empire against the Uyghurs in the Beshbalik wars of c.790-792, the Qarluqs expanded their power across the western Tian Shan and Zhetysu steppe, consolidating the hold that later made them a major Central Asian power.

w4-500396.name: Charlemagne's Avar Wars (opening campaigns, 791)
w4-500396.blurb: In 791 Charlemagne launched a major offensive against the Avar Khaganate, advancing down the Danube into Pannonia and forcing the Avars back. This Avar-to-Franks transfer in 788-793 in the western Carpathian Basin marks the first phase of the Avar Wars that culminated in the sack of the Avar Ring in 795-796.

w4-500397.name: Move of the Japanese capital / start of the Heian period
w4-500397.blurb: This Nara-to-Heian Japan transfer dated 788-793 marks Emperor Kanmu's relocation of the imperial capital, briefly to Nagaoka-kyo (784) and then definitively to Heian-kyo (Kyoto) in 794, ending the Nara period and inaugurating the Heian period. It is a continuity-of-state succession of regimes rather than a conquest, so the whole realm is re-labeled.

w4-500398.name: Great Saxon revolt of 792-793
w4-500398.blurb: This Franks-to-Saxons reversal in 788-793 reflects the widespread Saxon uprising of 792-793, when the Saxons rose again against Frankish rule and forced conversions, killing Frankish officials and missionaries. The revolt prompted Charlemagne's brutal renewed campaigns and mass deportations later in the 790s.

w4-500399.name: Frankish destruction of the Avar Ring (795-796)
w4-500399.blurb: This Franks-to-Avar entry labeled 793-800 corresponds to the climactic phase of the Avar Wars: in 795-796 Frankish forces under Eric of Friuli and King Pepin of Italy stormed the Avar Ring, seizing its legendary treasure and shattering the Khaganate. The from/to ordering in the worklist appears reversed, but the territory in the central Carpathian Basin was conquered by the Franks from the Avars.

w4-500400.name: Foundation of the Aghlabid emirate of Ifriqiya
w4-500400.blurb: In 800 the Abbasid governor Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab obtained from Caliph Harun al-Rashid hereditary governorship of Ifriqiya, founding the Aghlabid Dynasty as an autonomous emirate paying nominal tribute to Baghdad. This Abbasid-to-Aghlabid transfer dated 793-800 around Tripolitania/Tunisia is exactly that grant of de facto independent rule over North Africa.

w4-500405.name: Bulgar conquest of the Avar lands / Krum's expansion
w4-500405.blurb: Following Charlemagne's destruction of the Avar Khaganate in the 790s, the First Bulgarian Empire under Khan Krum overran the eastern Avar territories in the Carpathian Basin and Transylvania around 803-805. The Avar state collapsed, and the Bulgars annexed the lands east of the Tisza/Danube, the region around (22.6E, 46.2N). This left the rump Avars as Frankish vassals while Bulgaria absorbed the rest.

w4-500407.name: Post-Offa decline of Mercian overlordship; Egbert restores Wessex independence
w4-500407.blurb: Offa of Mercia (d. 796) had dominated the southern English kingdoms including Wessex. After Offa's death, Egbert — exiled in Francia — returned and became King of Wessex in 802, ending Mercian hegemony over Wessex. Coords (-2.1, 50.9) lie in core Wessex. The decisive expansion came later at Ellandun (825), but the shift in the balance of power began with Egbert's 802 accession, within the window [801,806].

w4-500408.name: Rashtrakuta campaigns of Govinda III in Gujarat/Malwa
w4-500408.blurb: The Rashtrakuta emperor Govinda III, having defeated the Gurjara-Pratihara king Nagabhata II, extended Rashtrakuta power into Gujarat and western India in the early 9th century as part of the tripartite struggle for northern India. The territory near (71.8E, 22.2N, the Saurashtra/Gujarat region) passed from Pratihara to Rashtrakuta control. Govinda III established a Rashtrakuta branch in Gujarat (Lata).

w4-500409.name: Rashtrakuta-Pallava conflict under Govinda III
w4-500409.blurb: Govinda III of the Rashtrakuta Dynasty campaigned into the Tamil-Telugu south, defeating the Pallava king Dantivarman and exacting tribute around 803-804. The borderland near (78.6E, 14.2N) in the northern Pallava/Rayalaseema zone shifted to Rashtrakuta suzerainty. The Pallavas were forced to acknowledge Rashtrakuta overlordship.

w4-500410.name: Founding of the Khmer Empire by Jayavarman II
w4-500410.blurb: In 802 CE Jayavarman II proclaimed himself chakravartin (universal monarch) on Phnom Kulen, founding the Khmer Empire and unifying the fragmented polities of Cambodia. He absorbed Water Chenla (the lower Mekong/delta region near 105.4E, 11.3N), ending the period of Chenla division. This act is conventionally dated as the start of the Angkorian era.

w4-500411.name: Founding of the Khmer Empire by Jayavarman II
w4-500411.blurb: Jayavarman II's unification of Cambodia in 802 CE also incorporated Land Chenla, the upper/inland Chenla polity in the middle Mekong region near (105.1E, 14.9N). Declaring independence from Javanese (Sailendra) overlordship and ritual universal kingship, he merged the divided Chenla realms into the new Khmer Empire centered on the Angkor region.

w4-500413.name: Frankish subjugation of Dalmatian Croatia
w4-500413.blurb: In the early 9th century Charlemagne's Kingdom of the Franks extended its overlordship over the Duchy of Croatia in Dalmatia, which was confirmed in the 812 Pax Nicephori between Charlemagne and Byzantium. The Croatian lands near (15.7E, 44.4N) came under Frankish suzerainty, ruled through Frankish-appointed dukes such as Borna. This brought Croatia into the Carolingian orbit.

w4-500414.name: Frankish capture of Barcelona (801) and establishment of the Spanish March
w4-500414.blurb: By 806 the Carolingians had consolidated the Marca Hispanica (Spanish March), the belt of trans-Pyrenean territory between the mountains and the Ebro that Charlemagne's forces had wrested from the Umayyad Emirate of Cordoba in a series of campaigns culminating in the capture of Barcelona in 801. Governed from the subkingdom of Aquitaine under Louis the Pious, these counties formed a fortified frontier facing al-Andalus, and in Charlemagne's 806 partition plan the March and Aquitaine were assigned together to Louis. The change records this Pyrenean frontier territory passing from the Emirate of Cordoba to Frankish control.

w4-500415.name: Gurjara-Pratihara recovery against the Palas (Nagabhata II)
w4-500415.blurb: After recovering from his defeat by Govinda III, the Gurjara-Pratihara king Nagabhata II pushed eastward against the Pala Empire in the Ganges plain, in the ongoing Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj. The territory near (81.1E, 26.4N) in the central Doab/Awadh region passed from Pala to Pratihara control. The Pratiharas would soon seize Kannauj itself.

w4-500417.name: Nagabhata II defeats Dharmapala and advances into eastern territories
w4-500417.blurb: Nagabhata II of the Gurjara-Pratiharas (r. c.800-833) reversed his dynasty's earlier setbacks by driving into the eastern Gangetic plain: he defeated the Pala king Dharmapala, reportedly facing his elephant army at Munger in Bihar, and seized Kannauj from the Pala client Chakrayudha (c.816), making it his imperial capital. These campaigns wrested territory in the central and eastern Gangetic plain from Pala control and made the Pratiharas the dominant power of northern India. The change therefore records land passing from the Pala Empire to the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

w4-500418.name: Ashot I Bagratuni's rise / Bagratid principality in Iberia
w4-500418.blurb: Amid Abbasid weakness during the civil war between al-Amin and al-Ma'mun, the Bagratid prince Ashot I (Ashot Kuropalates) consolidated Christian power in Tao-Klarjeti, restoring a Georgian (Iberian) principality around 813. Territory near (41.9E, 40.9N) in the upper Kura/Tao region passed from Abbasid Caliphate control to the Kingdom/Principality of the Iberians. This founded the Georgian Bagratid line.

w4-500423.name: Pala resurgence under Devapala
w4-500423.blurb: The Pala emperor Devapala (r. c. 810-850) expanded the Pala Empire at the expense of the Gurjara-Pratiharas in the central Gangetic and Malwa regions during the Tripartite Struggle. The large territory near (77E, 25.1N) shifted from Pratihara back to Pala control. Devapala marked the peak of Pala power in northern India.

w4-500424.name: Nominoe unifies Breton kingdoms under Frankish suzerainty (c. 820-825)
w4-500424.blurb: Around 820-825, Louis the Pious appointed Nominoe as imperial emissary (missus imperatoris) to govern Brittany, beginning the process of unifying the formerly separate Breton sub-kingdoms (Domnonia, Cornouaille, Broërec) into a single entity. The rebellion of Wihomarc (822-825) and its suppression by Lambert I of Nantes was a parallel development, with the broader administrative consolidation occurring under Nominoe. The formal Kingdom of Brittany emerged under Nominoe's son Erispoe in 851.

w4-500427.name: Establishment of the Shirvanshah state under the Mazyadids
w4-500427.blurb: As Abbasid central authority weakened, the Arab Mazyadid governor Haytham ibn Khalid took the title Shirvanshah around 820-861, establishing a hereditary, effectively autonomous dynasty in Shirvan. The eastern Caucasus region near (47E, 40.3N) passed from direct Abbasid Caliphate control to the autonomous realm of Shirvan. This founded the long-lived Shirvanshah polity.

w4-500430.name: Basque/Gascon revolt and restored Duchy of Gascony
w4-500430.blurb: Following the Basque victory at the second Battle of Roncevaux (824), which defeated a Frankish army, Gascon autonomy revived under a hereditary ducal line. Territory in the Garonne/Gascony region near (-0.3E, 44.1N) passed from direct Frankish royal control to the Duchy of Gascony. This reasserted Basque self-rule south of the Garonne.

w4-500432.name: Battle of Ellendun: Ecgberht of Wessex defeats Mercia
w4-500432.blurb: In 825 Ecgberht of Wessex defeated Beornwulf of Mercia at the Battle of Ellendun, seizing Sussex, Kent, and Essex; the battle decisively ended Mercian supremacy over southern England and transferred these territories to Wessex.

w4-500433.name: Battle of Ellendun
w4-500433.blurb: In 825, King Egbert of Wessex defeated Beornwulf of Mercia at the Battle of Ellendun (near Swindon). Egbert then sent his son Æthelwulf to expel the Mercian client king Baldred from Kent; the entire kingdom of Kent (along with Sussex and Surrey) submitted to Wessex, ending Mercian overlordship.

w4-500434.name: Nanzhao raids and occupation of parts of Jiannan (Sichuan)
w4-500434.blurb: In 829 Nanzhao forces under Wang Cuodian attacked Chengdu in Tang's Jiannan circuit, exploiting the chaos caused by corrupt governor Du Yuanying; they withdrew the following year but retained some border areas. The atlas records Nanzhao's transient occupation of southern Sichuan border territories in this snapshot window.

w4-500435.name: Bulgaria under Omurtag expands into Pannonian Slavic territories
w4-500435.blurb: Khan Omurtag of Bulgaria (814–831) pushed westward into the Slavic principalities of Pannonia that had been under loose Frankish suzerainty, replacing local Slavic chiefs with Bulgarian governors around 827–829. The centroid at 17.3°E / 46.3°N (middle Pannonia) reflects Bulgarian consolidation at Frankish expense.

w4-500437.name: Gurjara-Pratihara Mihira Bhoja I recaptures central India from Palas
w4-500437.blurb: Mihira Bhoja I (r. 836–885), the greatest Gurjara-Pratihara emperor, reconquered Kannauj and surrounding territories soon after his accession, reversing earlier Pala gains and establishing Pratihara hegemony over the Indo-Gangetic plain. His reign marks the apogee of Pratihara power.

w4-500438.name: Mojmír I expels Pribina and annexes Nitra
w4-500438.blurb: Around 833, Mojmír I, duke of the Moravians, expelled Prince Pribina from the Principality of Nitra, forcing him to flee to the Frankish court; this annexation merged Nitra into Mojmír's realm and is traditionally regarded as the founding act that created Great Moravia.

w4-500439.name: Abbasid reassertion of control over Shirvan under al-Mu'tasim
w4-500439.blurb: The Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim (r. 833–842) conducted military campaigns in the Caucasus and reasserted central authority over the region (centroid lng 47, lat 40.3 = Shirvan/Azerbaijan) around 833–838, temporarily suppressing autonomous Shirvanshah rule before it re-emerged in subsequent decades. The nearly identical area (114,430 km²) to change 500429 suggests the atlas records a symmetric reversal.

w4-500441.name: Siconulf proclaims himself Prince of Salerno amid the Beneventan civil war (840)
w4-500441.blurb: The formal partition of Benevento was only ratified by Emperor Louis II's mediated division around 849, well after this window closes (the row's 851 date is also wrong). But the de facto split began in 839–840, when Siconulf, opposing Radelchis's coup at Benevento after Sicard's assassination, established himself as a rival prince at Salerno — the earliest datable moment the two principalities existed as separate polities, fitting the window's close at 840.

w4-500442.name: Wiglaf restores Mercian independence from Wessex
w4-500442.blurb: After Ecgberht of Wessex briefly became overlord of all England in 829, Mercian king Wiglaf reasserted independence in 830, recovering much of Mercia's former territory; the atlas geometry reflects this Mercian recovery of lands that had briefly been counted under Wessex.

w4-500443.name: Yenisei Kyrgyz Destruction of the Uyghur Khaganate
w4-500443.blurb: In 840, the Yenisei Kyrgyz under their qaghan invaded the Uyghur Khaganate with roughly 80,000 horsemen, sacking the Uyghur capital Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon River and beheading the ruling Qasar Qaghan, ending Uyghur dominance over the Mongolian steppe and its surrounding territory.

w4-500444.name: Kara-Khanid Khanate formation after Uyghur collapse
w4-500444.blurb: When the Yenisei Kyrgyz destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in 840, the Karluk confederation in Semirech'ye — already dominant in the region — transitioned into the Kara-Khanid (Qarakhanid) Khanate under Bilge Kul Qadir Khan, inheriting Uyghur legitimacy and territory in the Ili/Chu valley basin.

w4-500445.name: Yenisei Kyrgyz Destruction of Uyghur Khaganate and Karluk/proto-Kara-Khanid expansion
w4-500445.blurb: Following the Yenisei Kyrgyz destruction of the Uyghur Khaganate in 840, the Karluks and allied Turkic groups (ancestors of the Kara-Khanids) expanded into former Uyghur territory in Semirechye (centroid ~lng 81, lat 45, eastern Kazakhstan). The atlas labels this territory as Kara-Khanid because these Karluk groups became the nucleus of the later Kara-Khanid confederation.

w4-500447.name: Viking Raids on the Seine and Sack of Paris (845)
w4-500447.blurb: Under Ragnar Lothbrok, a Danish Viking fleet of 120 ships sailed up the Seine and sacked Paris in March 845, with Charles the Bald paying 7,000 pounds of silver as ransom; Viking raiders effectively controlled Seine valley approaches (lat 48.6, lng 3.4) and maintained seasonal presence in northern Francia through the 840s–850s.

w4-500448.name: Bulgarian expansion into Macedonia under Khan Presian I (836–852)
w4-500448.blurb: Khan Presian I of Bulgaria (r. 836–852) conquered most of Macedonia, with Bulgarian borders reportedly reaching the Adriatic near Valona and the plain around Thessaloniki. Byzantine sources record no effective resistance, and the region (centroid lng 22.9, lat 41.0 = northern Macedonia/Thessaloniki hinterland) passed from Byzantine to Bulgarian control.

w4-500449.name: Treaty of Verdun (Middle Francia to Lothair I)
w4-500449.blurb: The Treaty of Verdun in 843 divided the Carolingian Empire among the three surviving sons of Louis the Pious after the civil war ended by the Battle of Fontenoy (841). Lothair I received Middle Francia, a long strip from the Low Countries through Burgundy and the Alps into Italy, including the region near (9.1E, 47.2N). This partition is a foundational event in European history.

w4-500453.name: Treaty of Verdun
w4-500453.blurb: The Treaty of Verdun (843) partitioned the Carolingian Empire among Louis the Pious's three sons; the County of Barcelona and the Spanish March were assigned to Charles the Bald's West Frankish kingdom. The Cliopatria snapshot window of 840–850 captures the formal transfer of the march's overlordship from the undivided Frankish realm to the West Frankish (future French) crown.

w4-500455.name: Treaty of Verdun (Aquitaine to West Francia)
w4-500455.blurb: The 843 Treaty of Verdun assigned the western third of the Carolingian Empire, West Francia, to Charles the Bald, incorporating the Kingdom of Aquitaine (near 1.2E, 44.9N). Though Aquitaine had its own sub-kings (Pepin II contested it), it fell within Charles's West Frankish realm. This is part of the threefold division of Charlemagne's empire.

w4-500456.name: Treaty of Verdun (Gascony to West Francia)
w4-500456.blurb: Under the 843 Treaty of Verdun, the Duchy of Gascony (near -0.3E, 44.1N) fell within Charles the Bald's West Frankish kingdom along with Aquitaine. The western Pyrenean and Garonne lands thus passed to West Francia in the threefold partition of the empire. Gascony remained a frequently autonomous duchy under nominal West Frankish overlordship.

w4-500459.name: Treaty of Verdun (East Francia to Louis the German)
w4-500459.blurb: The 843 Treaty of Verdun granted the eastern third of the Carolingian Empire, East Francia, to Louis the German, comprising the lands east of the Rhine including the region near (12.8E, 49.7N, Bavaria/Franconia). This kingdom became the nucleus of the future Holy Roman Empire and Germany. The treaty ended the Carolingian civil war that followed Louis the Pious's death.

w4-500462.name: Classic Maya collapse – Terminal Classic city abandonment
w4-500462.blurb: The Terminal Classic period (c. 800–900 CE) saw the widespread abandonment of major southern Maya lowland city-states, including Palenque, Tikal, Copán, and Calakmul. A combination of prolonged drought, environmental degradation, warfare, shifting trade routes, and dynastic collapse caused political authority to disintegrate across the region around 840–850 CE. Political control transferred to or was assumed by successor polities (referred to in the dataset as 'Later Mayan City-States') often in the northern lowlands.

citations.label: The Classic Maya Collapse – World History Encyclopedia

w4-500463.name: Collapse of the Tibetan Empire (assassination of Langdarma)
w4-500463.blurb: The assassination of King Langdarma (Glang Darma) around 842 triggered a succession dispute between rival heirs Yumten and Osung, fracturing the Tibetan Empire. Central authority disintegrated, and the vast plateau near (89.9E, 32.5N) passed from the unified Tibetan Empire to a fragmented patchwork of local Tibetan rulers. This ended the imperial period and began Tibet's Era of Fragmentation.

w4-500465.name: Gurjara-Pratihara reconquest of Gujarat from the Rashtrakutas
w4-500465.blurb: Under Mihira Bhoja, the Gurjara-Pratiharas reasserted control over Gujarat/Saurashtra (near 71.8E, 22.2N) against the Rashtrakuta Dynasty in the mid-9th century. The region reverted from Rashtrakuta to Pratihara rule as part of the long contest over western India. This consolidated Pratihara power at its height.

w4-500467.name: Collapse of the Karkota dynasty and accession of the Utpala dynasty in Kashmir
w4-500467.blurb: The Karkota dynasty of Kashmir, which had peaked under Lalitaditya Muktapida, disintegrated amid factional strife in the mid-9th century. Around 855, the warlord Avantivarman founded the Utpala dynasty, ending Karkota rule over the Kashmir valley. The transfer from 'Karkota Dynasty' to a generic 'Kashmir' polity reflects this dynastic replacement rather than a foreign conquest.

w4-500468.name: Death of Lothair I and partition of Middle Francia (Treaty of Prüm)
w4-500468.blurb: On the death of Emperor Lothair I in 855, his Middle Frankish realm was divided among his sons by the Treaty of Prüm, and over the following years its components were contested by his uncles. The transfer of large Middle Frankish territory toward the West Frankish sphere reflects the breakup of Lothair's central kingdom and Charles the Bald's encroachment on the disputed middle realm during the 850s.

w4-500470.name: Treaty of Prüm and division of Lothair I's realm (Italy)
w4-500470.blurb: After Lothair I died in 855, the Treaty of Prüm assigned the Kingdom of Italy to his son Louis II while the rest of Middle Francia was split. The reassignment of the northern Italian/Lotharingian frontier toward the western Carolingian sphere stems from this partition and the ensuing rivalry among Lothair's brothers Charles the Bald and Louis the German.

w4-500478.name: Rise of the autonomous Habbari emirate of Sindh
w4-500478.blurb: As Abbasid central authority weakened, the Arab Habbari family established a de facto independent emirate in Sindh, with Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Habbari taking control around 854 with Mansura as capital. The transfer from the Abbasid Caliphate to the Habbari dynasty marks Sindh's detachment from direct caliphal rule into a tributary-only autonomy.

w4-500479.name: Tang–Nanzhao frontier wars in Sichuan
w4-500479.blurb: Nanzhao and the Tang dynasty fought intermittently over the Sichuan frontier through the mid-9th century, with control of border prefectures shifting repeatedly before Nanzhao's major invasions of the 860s–870s. This 850s transfer back to Tang reflects a temporary Tang recovery of contested Sichuan territory near Chengdu before renewed Nanzhao offensives.

w4-500480.name: Foundation of the Ziyadid dynasty in Yemen
w4-500480.blurb: The Ziyadid dynasty, founded by Muhammad ibn Ziyad with Abbasid sanction at Zabid, governed Yemen as an effectively autonomous emirate that paid only nominal allegiance to Baghdad. During the Abbasid 'Anarchy at Samarra' in the 860s, Ziyadid control over Yemen became fully independent in practice, accounting for the transfer of this large southern Arabian territory from caliphal to Ziyadid hands.

w4-500482.name: Carolingian contest over the kingdom of Provence/Lower Burgundy after Charles of Provence
w4-500482.blurb: The kingdom of Lower Burgundy/Provence, created at the Prüm partition for Charles of Provence, was disputed after his death in 863 between Louis II of Italy and the western Carolingians. The shift of part of Lower Burgundy toward the West Frankish sphere reflects Charles the Bald's claims and the redistribution of the defunct sub-kingdom in the 860s.

w4-500483.name: Lambert I of Spoleto's revolt against Louis II
w4-500483.blurb: After Lothair I's death (855), the Italian portion of Middle Francia (including Spoleto) passed to Louis II. During Louis II's 860s southern campaigns, Lambert I of Spoleto rebelled (860), introducing West Frankish factional influence into the duchy before reconciliation. The contested Spoleto region near lng 13.5 E / lat 42.8 N fits the [860,866] window, though the framing is medium-confidence.

w4-500484.name: Unification of Norway under Harald Fairhair (consolidation of petty kingdoms)
w4-500484.blurb: During the second half of the 9th century the petty kingdoms of Norway were progressively subjugated by Harald Fairhair, traditionally culminating in the Battle of Hafrsfjord (c. 872). This transfer from 'Scandinavian minor kingdoms' to the emerging Old Kingdom of Norway reflects Harald's early campaigns absorbing the central and southern Norwegian petty kingdoms.

w4-500488.name: Great Heathen Army campaigns in Mercia — Danish seizure of East Midlands
w4-500488.blurb: Between 866 and 870, the Great Heathen Army seized Nottingham (867) and progressively stripped Mercia of its eastern territories; by 870 Danish forces controlled much of what became the East Midlands Danelaw, with the Mercian king driven out by 874.

w4-500489.name: Tang–Nanzhao frontier wars in southern Sichuan/Yunnan borderlands
w4-500489.blurb: The Tang dynasty and Nanzhao fought repeatedly over the Sichuan-Yunnan frontier in the 860s; Nanzhao's invasions and Tang counter-offensives caused control of border prefectures to oscillate. This transfer to the Tang reflects a Tang reassertion of contested southern Sichuan territory amid the broader Tang–Nanzhao wars that culminated in fighting over Chengdu.

w4-500490.name: Saffarid conquest of Khurasan/Herat region by Ya'qub ibn al-Layth
w4-500490.blurb: Having consolidated Sistan, Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar expanded westward and northward, capturing Herat and pushing into Khurasan in the late 860s at the expense of Abbasid-aligned governors. This large transfer from the Abbasid Caliphate to the Saffarids reflects Ya'qub's seizure of the Herat region and central Afghan lands.

w4-500491.name: Saffarid conquest of Kabul and the Turk Shahis by Ya'qub ibn al-Layth
w4-500491.blurb: In 870 Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar marched on Kabul and decisively defeated the Turk Shahis, capturing the city and looting its temples; idols were reportedly sent to Baghdad. This transfer of Turk Shahi territory around Kabul to the Saffarid dynasty corresponds to that campaign, which broke Turk Shahi power in the region.

w4-500498.name: Abbasid reconquest of Tabaristan, expelling Hasan ibn Zayd
w4-500498.blurb: Hasan ibn Zayd, founder of the Zaydi emirate in Tabaristan (est. 864), was twice expelled by Abbasid military forces — once in 869 and again in 874. The 870–875 boundary shift reflects an Abbasid military campaign that temporarily restored caliphal control over Tabaristan before the Zaydis returned.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Alid dynasties of northern Iran

w4-500500.name: Treaty of Meerssen (partition of Lotharingia)
w4-500500.blurb: The Treaty of Meerssen (870) split the lands of the deceased Lothair II between Charles the Bald and Louis the German. The western share of Lower Burgundy/Lotharingia, including territory toward the upper Burgundian frontier, passed to Charles the Bald, matching this transfer to the West Franks.

w4-500501.name: Unification of Norway under Harald Fairhair (northward consolidation)
w4-500501.blurb: Harald Fairhair's campaigns to unify Norway absorbed petty kingdoms across the country in the late 9th century, with northern Tröndelag and adjacent regions brought under a single crown. This transfer from the Scandinavian minor kingdoms to the Old Kingdom of Norway reflects the extension of Harald's consolidation into central-northern Norway.

w4-500505.name: Cham–Khmer frontier conflict and Cham resurgence under Indravarman II
w4-500505.blurb: Champa reasserted itself under the new Indrapura (Dong Duong) dynasty founded by Indravarman II around 875, recovering and expanding territory along the central Vietnamese coast and its hinterland against neighboring powers. This transfer from the Khmer Empire to Champa reflects Cham expansion at Angkorian expense during this period of Cham revival.

w4-500506.name: Lambert II of Spoleto's expansion into Carolingian Italy
w4-500506.blurb: After Emperor Louis II died in 875 without a male heir, the Duchy of Spoleto under the Guideschi (the dukes Lambert and Guy) expanded its control over central Italian territory amid the contest for the Italian crown between Charles the Bald (West Frankish king) and the East Frankish Carolingians. The Spoletan dukes were major power-brokers in this succession crisis, extending Spoleto's reach in the central Apennine region near Rome.

w4-500514.name: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth's conquest of Kabul and the Turk Shahis
w4-500514.blurb: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, founder of the Saffarid dynasty, campaigned into the Kabul valley around 870-871, defeating the Turk Shahi (Kabul Shahi) rulers and capturing Kabul. This brought the Hindu Kush region near Kabul under Saffarid control, displacing the long-standing Turk Shahi dynasty from its heartland.

w4-500515.name: Saffarid conquest of Sistan, Khurasan and the east under Ya'qub ibn al-Layth
w4-500515.blurb: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar rose from Sistan and seized vast eastern Abbasid provinces, notably overthrowing the Tahirid governors and capturing Nishapur in 873, ending nominal Abbasid authority over Sistan and Khurasan. This transferred a huge swath of the eastern caliphate to the Saffarid dynasty, which Ya'qub ruled as a de facto independent power.

w4-500521.name: Council of Troyes (878): Louis the Stammerer invests Wilfred the Hairy with his counties
w4-500521.blurb: At the Council of Troyes in August 878, presided over by Pope John VIII and West Frankish king Louis the Stammerer, Wilfred the Hairy was formally invested with the counties of Urgell and Cerdanya (around lng 2.3, lat 41.9), which he had administered since 870; in the same year, following the dispossession of the rebel Bernard of Gothia, he also received Barcelona, Girona, and Besalú. Because Wilfred made these counties hereditary, the act is regarded as the founding of the de facto autonomous Catalan counties. This matches the worklist transfer from the West Franks to the County of Urgell within 876-878.

w4-500524.name: Battle of Dayr al-Aqul
w4-500524.blurb: In April 876 the Abbasid army under the regent al-Muwaffaq defeated Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar at Dayr al-Aqul, about 80 km from Baghdad, halting the Saffarid advance on the capital. The Abbasids consequently recovered western Iranian territory (around the Jibal/Isfahan region) that the Saffarids had threatened or occupied.

w4-500525.name: Ahmad ibn Tulun's expansion into Syria (Bilad al-Sham)
w4-500525.blurb: Ahmad ibn Tulun, the autonomous Abbasid governor of Egypt and founder of the Tulunid dynasty, marched into Syria in 877-878 and took control of its main cities (Damascus, Homs, Aleppo) while the Abbasid central government was distracted by the Zanj Rebellion and the Saffarids. This brought the southern Levant under Tulunid rule, detaching it from direct Abbasid control.

w4-500529.name: Principality of Salerno shifts to Byzantine alignment under Guaimar I (c. 880)
w4-500529.blurb: Prince Guaimar I of Salerno seized power from his father in 880 and shifted toward Byzantine protection amid Saracen raids, against the backdrop of Basil I's reconquest campaigns in southern Italy (Nikephoros Phokas the Elder reconquered much of the region c.880-885). Guaimar later travelled to Constantinople in 886 to do homage to Leo VI/Basil I. From=Principality of Salerno, to=Byzantine Empire reflects the c.880 Byzantine alignment; note the formal homage came in 886, slightly after the 878-880 window.

w4-500531.name: Treaty of Ribemont — Lotharingia ceded to East Francia
w4-500531.blurb: The Treaty of Ribemont (February 880) transferred the whole of Lotharingia from West Frankish to East Frankish control; the West Frankish kings Louis III and Carloman II formally recognized East Frankish possession of both halves of Lotharingia in exchange for recognition of their own kingship.

w4-500533.name: Boso of Provence's foundation of the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy (Provence)
w4-500533.blurb: Following the death of West Frankish king Louis the Stammerer in 879, Boso of Provence, a powerful magnate, had himself elected king at Mantaille (October 879), creating the independent Kingdom of Lower Burgundy/Provence in the Rhone valley. This detached the southeastern provinces from the West Frankish realm.

w4-500534.name: Consolidation of the Duchy of Burgundy after Louis the Stammerer's death
w4-500534.blurb: During the West Frankish succession crisis after Louis the Stammerer died in 879, Richard the Justiciar consolidated the Duchy of Burgundy as a largely autonomous principality, partly in reaction to Boso of Provence's usurpation. The duchy emerged as a distinct territorial bloc separate from direct royal control.

w4-500536.name: Treaty of Ribemont
w4-500536.blurb: By the Treaty of Ribemont in 880, the East Frankish king Louis the Younger renounced East Frankish claims to the western part of Lotharingia in favor of the West Frankish kings Louis III and Carloman II. This was the last frontier settlement between the East and West Frankish realms; the direction here (East to West Franks) reflects the western Lotharingian lands passing to West Francia.

w4-500537.name: Carolingian suppression of Boso of Provence
w4-500537.blurb: In 880-882 the united Carolingian kings (Louis III and Carloman II of West Francia, with Charles the Fat) campaigned against Boso of Provence, besieging Vienne in 880-882 and recovering much of the northern part of his usurped Kingdom of Lower Burgundy. This returned Rhone-valley territory to West Frankish control.

w4-500538.name: Oleg of Novgorod's Southern Expansion and Magyar Displacement
w4-500538.blurb: Oleg of Novgorod seized Kyiv in 882 and rapidly expanded Rus' control southward along the Dnieper, pushing Magyar semi-nomadic groups from the right-bank Ukraine (lat 50.7, lng 28.5); the Magyars themselves migrated westward in phases, completing their departure to the Pannonian Basin by 895.

w4-500539.name: Oleg's seizure of Kiev and founding of Kievan Rus'
w4-500539.blurb: According to the Primary Chronicle, in 882 the Varangian prince Oleg the Wise moved south from Novgorod, captured Kiev (killing Askold and Dir), and made it his capital, uniting the northern and southern Rus' lands into the state known as Kievan Rus'. This is the traditional foundation of Kievan Rus'.

w4-500542.name: Alfred the Great's absorption of western Mercia (c. 883-884)
w4-500542.blurb: After the Danes seized eastern Mercia as part of the Danelaw settlement (c. 877-880), western Mercia came under the rule of Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians, who acknowledged Alfred the Great's overlordship around 883. Alfred extended his control over Mercia following the deposition of the last Mercian king Ceolwulf II and the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum that divided Mercia along Watling Street. By 884, Alfred had secured western Mercia and began styling himself 'King of the Anglo-Saxons.'

w4-500544.name: Coronation of Ashot I and restoration of Bagratid Armenian kingdom
w4-500544.blurb: In 884-885 the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tamid recognized Ashot I Bagratuni as king of Armenia, sending him a crown and formally restoring an independent Armenian monarchy after centuries of foreign rule. This detached the Armenian highlands (around Ararat/Lake Sevan) from direct Abbasid administration into the Bagratid kingdom.

w4-500545.name: Saffarid reassertion in Khurasan under Amr ibn al-Layth
w4-500545.blurb: After Ya'qub's death in 879, his brother Amr ibn al-Layth ruled the Saffarids and continued to dominate Khurasan; in the mid-880s he was confirmed as governor of Khurasan and reasserted Saffarid control over the region around Nishapur. This reflects eastern Iranian territory passing from nominal Abbasid authority to the Saffarids.

w4-500546.name: Samanid consolidation of Transoxiana under Nasr I
w4-500546.blurb: In 875 the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tamid invested Nasr ibn Ahmad with the governorship of Transoxiana, and through the 880s the Samanids consolidated autonomous rule over the region around Samarkand and Bukhara. This brought Transoxiana under effective Samanid control as a hereditary realm, detaching it from direct Abbasid administration.

w4-500549.name: Louis the Blind's restoration of the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy (Provence)
w4-500549.blurb: Amid the collapse of the empire after Charles the Fat's deposition in 887, Louis the Blind, son of Boso of Provence, was established (with Carolingian backing) as king of Lower Burgundy/Provence in 887-890. This re-detached the Rhone-valley/Provence lands from the Frankish royal domain into the revived southern Burgundian kingdom.

w4-500550.name: Election of Arnulf of Carinthia and the breakup of Charles the Fat's empire
w4-500550.blurb: When Charles the Fat (who briefly reunited the whole Carolingian empire) was deposed in November 887, Arnulf of Carinthia was elected East Frankish king, and the empire fragmented into separate kingdoms. The large block here moving from West to East Frankish control reflects the reversal of Charles the Fat's brief reunification, with Lotharingian/eastern lands reverting to the East Frankish (Arnulf) realm.

w4-500552.name: Guy III of Spoleto seizes the Kingdom of Italy
w4-500552.blurb: After Charles the Fat's deposition (887) dissolved unified Carolingian rule, Guy III of Spoleto contested and won the Iron Crown (crowned King of Italy 889), uniting Spoleto and the Italian crown under his family. The Spoleto region near lng 13.5 E / lat 42.8 N effectively merged into the contested Kingdom of Italy from 888, matching the [887,888] window.

w4-500554.name: Adarnase IV's assumption of the Georgian (Iberian) kingship under Bagratid rule
w4-500554.blurb: In 888 Adarnase IV (Adarnase II of Iberia) of the Bagrationi dynasty took the title 'king of the Georgians/Iberians,' restoring a royal title in Iberia (Kartli) that had lapsed since the Sasanian-era abolition of the Iberian monarchy. This reflects the Caucasian Iberian/Georgian heartland near Tbilisi passing from nominal Abbasid overlordship into an autonomous Georgian Bagratid kingdom.

w4-500555.name: Abbasid/Samanid suppression of the Zaydi Alids of Tabaristan
w4-500555.blurb: The Zaydi Alid emirate in Tabaristan, founded by al-Hasan ibn Zayd, was disrupted after his death in 884 and the troubled reign of Muhammad ibn Zayd; around this period Abbasid and Samanid forces pressed into the Caspian region of Tabaristan, briefly recovering territory from the Alids. This reflects the Caspian coastlands near the Elburz passing back from Zaydi Alid to Abbasid control.

w4-500556.name: Gyeon Hwon's revolt and founding of Hubaekje (Later Baekje)
w4-500556.blurb: As Unified Silla disintegrated in the late 9th century (the Later Three Kingdoms period), the general Gyeon Hwon led a revolt in the southwest of the Korean peninsula and proclaimed the state of Hubaekje (Later Baekje) around 892. This carved the southwestern region away from Silla's control into a new rebel kingdom.

w4-500559.name: Magyar conquest of the Carpathian Basin (Hungarian Honfoglalás)
w4-500559.blurb: Between 892 and 896 the Magyars, pushed west out of the Pontic steppe, crossed the Carpathians and seized Transylvania and the eastern plains then held by the First Bulgarian Empire under Simeon I. The Bulgarians, recently victorious over the Magyars in 895, nonetheless lost their trans-Danubian and Transylvanian holdings as the Magyars settled the Carpathian Basin (the Honfoglalás). This location near 26.7E/46.2N corresponds to former Bulgarian-held Transylvania/Moldavia.

citations.label: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin

w4-500560.name: Magyar conquest of the Carpathian Basin (Honfoglalás), fall of Great Moravia
w4-500560.blurb: As the Magyars under Árpád entered the Carpathian Basin in 895-896, they overran the eastern territories of Great Moravia in the upper Tisza region. The location near 21.3E/48.6N is the Upper Tisza/eastern Slovak plain, among the first Moravian lands lost to the invading Magyars. This was the opening phase of the conquest that would destroy Great Moravia within a decade.

citations.label: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin

w4-500561.name: Arnulf of Carinthia's Italian campaign / contest for the Kingdom of Italy
w4-500561.blurb: In 894-896 Arnulf of Carinthia, king of East Francia, invaded Italy against Guy and Lambert of Spoleto, capturing northern Italy and being crowned emperor in Rome in 896. The transfer near 10.7E/44N (Po valley/Emilia) reflects East Frankish control imposed over the Kingdom of Italy during these campaigns. Arnulf's gains proved short-lived after he fell ill and withdrew north of the Alps.

w4-500562.name: Abbasid recovery of Khurasan from the Saffarids (rebellion of Amr ibn al-Layth)
w4-500562.blurb: The Saffarid Amr ibn al-Layth held Khurasan as a nominal Abbasid governor, but the caliph al-Mu'tadid resisted Saffarid expansion and worked to reassert authority. Around 892-896 Abbasid pressure and the rivalry with the Samanids eroded Saffarid control of eastern Khurasan near 60.6E/35.7N. The contest culminated in 900 when Amr was defeated and captured by the Samanids, who then governed Khurasan for the caliph.

w4-500563.name: Zaydi Alid state of Tabaristan (al-Hasan al-Utrush / Alid resurgence)
w4-500563.blurb: The Zaydi Alids established and expanded an independent Shia state in the Caspian provinces of Tabaristan and Daylam, near 51.7E/36.6N, resisting Abbasid authority. In the 890s the Alids reasserted control over Tabaristan against the caliphate and its Samanid allies. This persistent Caspian Zaydi polity, later consolidated by al-Hasan al-Utrush, removed the region from effective Abbasid rule.

w4-500565.name: Bohemian secession from Great Moravia (submission to Arnulf, 895)
w4-500565.blurb: At the Diet of Regensburg in 895 the Bohemian dukes, led by the Přemyslids Spytihněv I and Vitislav, broke from the declining Great Moravia and submitted to Arnulf of East Francia. This detached Bohemia (near 14.1E/49.9N) from Moravian overlordship, establishing the autonomous Duchy of Bohemia. It marked a decisive fragmentation of Svatopluk's former Moravian realm after his death in 894.

w4-500566.name: Magyar migration from the Pontic steppe to the Carpathian Basin (895–896)
w4-500566.blurb: Pressed by Pecheneg attacks, the Magyar confederation under Árpád crossed the Carpathians and occupied the Pannonian Basin in 895–896, vacating their prior territories in the Etelköz steppe (modern Ukraine, around lng 33.3, lat 50.3). Eastern Slavic peoples under the nascent Kievan Rus' then extended into the abandoned steppe lands (Magyars -> Kievan Rus'), matching the [892,896] window.

w4-500568.name: Samanid expansion into Ferghana/Semirechye against the Turks
w4-500568.blurb: In 893 the Samanid amir Isma'il ibn Ahmad campaigned against the Karluk/Qarluq Turks of the steppe, capturing Talas (Taraz) and converting its great church into a mosque. The transfer near 72.4E/42.6N (Talas/Ferghana frontier) reflects Samanid annexation of these frontier marches from the Turkic tribes that later formed the Kara-Khanid confederation. This was a celebrated victory expanding Islam into the Syr Darya steppe.

w4-500569.name: Rise of the Sajid dynasty in Azerbaijan (889–898)
w4-500569.blurb: Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj was appointed Abbasid governor of Azerbaijan around 889 CE and progressively consolidated autonomous power, with the Sajid dynasty minting coins in his name by 898–900. The family effectively transformed their governorship into a hereditary emirate as Abbasid central authority weakened during the late 9th century.

w4-500571.name: Simeon I's Pecheneg alliance drives Magyars west — Bulgaria recovers eastern territories
w4-500571.blurb: After negotiating a truce with Byzantium, Simeon I secretly dispatched envoys to the Pechenegs, who attacked Magyar homelands from the east while Magyar warriors were absent on campaign. The combined Pecheneg–Bulgarian pressure routed the Magyars, forcing them permanently west over the Carpathians into the Pannonian Basin; Bulgaria recovered the Wallachian and Moldavian lowlands they had lost to Magyar occupation in 895.

w4-500572.name: Establishment of the Sajid emirate of Azerbaijan (Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj)
w4-500572.blurb: Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj, an Abbasid commander of Sogdian origin, was appointed governor of Azerbaijan and Armenia in 889-890 and made the post hereditary, founding the autonomous Sajid dynasty. By the late 890s the Sajids ruled Azerbaijan near 46.9E/38.7N as semi-independent emirs only nominally subject to Baghdad. This transfer reflects the consolidation of Sajid autonomy out of the Abbasid province.

w4-500573.name: Berengar I reasserts rule of Italy after Arnulf of Carinthia's departure
w4-500573.blurb: Arnulf of Carinthia (East Franks) invaded Italy in 894–896 and briefly held the region, but left Italy in 896 due to illness and died in December 899. Berengar I, king of Italy, reasserted control over northern Italy in 896–898, restoring the Kingdom of Italy's independent authority over the Po valley (centroid ~11.7°E / 45.8°N).

w4-500574.name: Bulgarian victory over the Magyars (Pechenegs invade Etelköz, 896)
w4-500574.blurb: In 894-896 Simeon I of Bulgaria, after initial defeats by Byzantine-allied Magyars, allied with the Pechenegs who attacked the Magyar homeland of Etelköz, forcing the Magyars to flee west into the Carpathian Basin. This allowed Bulgaria to recover steppe lands near 30.9E/46.3N (the Pruth/Dniester region) vacated by the departing Magyars. The episode is recorded by Byzantine sources including the Annals and Constantine Porphyrogenitus.

citations.label: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin

w4-500576.name: Restoration of Lambert of Spoleto / collapse of Arnulf's Italian rule
w4-500576.blurb: After Arnulf of Carinthia fell ill and withdrew from Italy in 896, the Spoletan claimant Lambert (and after his death in 898, Berengar) reasserted native control of the Kingdom of Italy. The transfer near 11.7E/45.8N (the Veneto/Po plain) back from the East Franks reflects the collapse of Arnulf's brief imperial authority over northern Italy. Italian rule reverted to local kings.

w4-500578.name: Civil war among Svatopluk's sons / fragmentation of Great Moravia (Principality of Nitra)
w4-500578.blurb: After the death of Svatopluk I in 894, his sons Mojmír II and Svatopluk II fought a civil war (897-898) that split Great Moravia, with the younger Svatopluk II ruling the appanage Principality of Nitra near 18.3E/48.6N. East Frankish intervention exacerbated the division. This internal partition fatally weakened Great Moravia on the eve of the Magyar conquest.

w4-500579.name: Lotharingia (Middle Francia) passes to Zwentibold / death of Arnulf's arrangements
w4-500579.blurb: In 895 Arnulf of Carinthia made his illegitimate son Zwentibold king of Lotharingia (the old Middle Frankish realm) near 6E/50.6N, detaching it from direct East Frankish rule. The transfer from East Franks to Middle Franks reflects the creation of this separate Lotharingian sub-kingdom around 898-899. The region had long been the contested Carolingian 'middle kingdom.'

w4-500580.name: Qarmatian revolt in eastern Arabia (Bahrayn)
w4-500580.blurb: In 899 the Qarmatians under Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi seized al-Hasa and Bahrayn in eastern Arabia near 52E/26.6N, establishing an independent Ismaili state in open revolt against the Abbasid Caliphate. The Qarmatians would terrorize the caliphate for decades, even sacking Mecca in 930. This transfer marks their founding conquest of the Persian Gulf coast.

w4-500581.name: Death of Lambert II and Collapse of Spoletan Dominance in Italy
w4-500581.blurb: Lambert II of Spoleto, who had ruled as emperor and de facto King of Italy since 891, was killed in 898. His death allowed Berengar I of Friuli to reassert control as King of Italy, drawing the Spoletan-dominated central Italian lands (coords 10.7E/43.9N) into the broader Kingdom of Italy and ending the Guideschi dynasty's dominance.

w4-500582.name: Abbasid recovery of Fars from the Saffarids
w4-500582.blurb: As Saffarid power waned under Amr ibn al-Layth, the caliph al-Mu'tadid reasserted Abbasid authority over Fars and central Iran near 54.4E/32.6N in 898-899. Caliphal forces and rival governors reclaimed these provinces ahead of the Saffarids' catastrophic defeat by the Samanids at Balkh in 900. The large transfer reflects the Abbasid reconquest of the Iranian plateau heartland.

w4-500583.name: Donald II becomes first 'rí Alban', Kingdom of Alba emerges
w4-500583.blurb: Around 900 Donald II became the first ruler recorded with the title rí Alban ('King of Alba'), marking the formal emergence of the Kingdom of Alba from the earlier Dál Riatan and Pictish political structures; his reign saw ongoing Viking pressure that accelerated the consolidation of the Gaelic–Pictish kingdom.

w4-500585.name: Death of Zwentibold / Lotharingia reabsorbed by East Francia under Louis the Child
w4-500585.blurb: Zwentibold, the unpopular king of Lotharingia, was abandoned by his nobles and killed in battle in 900, after which Lotharingia (near 6E/50.6N) was reattached to East Francia under the boy-king Louis the Child. This reversed the 895 separation of the Middle Frankish realm. The transfer back to the East Franks reflects this reunification.

w4-500586.name: Death of Donald II and accession of Constantine II — consolidation of the Kingdom of Alba (900)
w4-500586.blurb: King Donald II, the first ruler styled rí Alban (King of Alba), died at Dunnottar in 900, marking the emergence of the Kingdom of Alba from the earlier union of Picts and Dál Riata under Kenneth MacAlpin's line. His successor Constantine II (r. 900–943) consolidated Alba, absorbing the residual Dál Riata territorial identity and effectively ending it as a separate polity.

w4-500588.name: Magyar conquest of the Pannonian Basin / consolidation as Principality of Hungary
w4-500588.blurb: By 900 the settled Magyars under Árpád had consolidated their conquests into the Principality of Hungary, seizing the Banat and lands along the Tisza/Maros (near 21.2E/45.9N) from the First Bulgarian Empire. Bulgaria's former trans-Danubian holdings in the central Carpathian Basin were absorbed into the new Hungarian polity. This completed the core of the Honfoglalás.

citations.label: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin

w4-500589.name: Consolidation of the Principality of Hungary (Magyar tribal state)
w4-500589.blurb: Around 900 the loose Magyar tribal confederation in the Carpathian Basin formalized into the Principality of Hungary under the Árpád dynasty. The transfer near 21.1E/47.9N (the Tisza plain) from 'Magyars' to 'Principality of Hungary' reflects this political consolidation of the conquered lands into a single principality rather than a new conquest. It is the cartographic relabeling of the maturing Hungarian state.

w4-500596.name: Formation of the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy (Cisjurane Burgundy / Provence) under Louis the Blind
w4-500596.blurb: Around 900 the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy (Provence/Cisjurane Burgundy) under Louis the Blind, who was crowned King of Italy and briefly Holy Roman Emperor, expanded its reach over northwestern Italian and Provençal lands amid the collapse of effective Carolingian royal authority in Italy. Louis the Blind's bid for the Italian crown (he was crowned in 900-901) shifted control of these territories from the Kingdom of Italy to his Burgundian/Provençal realm. The change reflects the dynastic struggle over the Italian crown in the post-Carolingian power vacuum.

w4-500597.name: Hungarian (Magyar) departure from the Etelköz and Rus' expansion under the early Rurikids
w4-500597.blurb: After the Magyars migrated westward into the Carpathian Basin (the Hungarian conquest, c.895-900), their former steppe lands north of the Black Sea in the Etelköz/Pontic region fell under the influence of the expanding Kievan Rus' under Oleg of Novgorod. With the Magyars gone, Rus' authority extended over the Dnieper-region territories near (28.6E, 50.1N). The change records the filling of the vacuum left by the Hungarian westward migration.

citations.label: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin

w4-500599.name: Liu Shouguang declares the Yan empire at Youzhou
w4-500599.blurb: Liu Shouguang, military governor of the Lulong (Youzhou/modern Beijing region) and Yichang circuits, exploited the Tang dynasty's collapse (907) and proclaimed himself Emperor of Yan in 911, breaking Hebei away from the fallen Tang order. His short-lived Yan state was crushed by Li Cunxu of Jin in 913-914.

w4-500600.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and rise of Min during the Ten Kingdoms period
w4-500600.blurb: The Tang Dynasty fell in 907 when the warlord Zhu Wen deposed Emperor Ai and founded the Later Liang, triggering the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era. In Fujian, the Wang family under Wang Shenzhi established the Min kingdom, which became a fully autonomous state (Wang Shenzhi was made Prince of Min in 909). The territory in coastal Fujian thus passed from the defunct Tang to Min.

w4-500601.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and rise of the Shatuo Jin regime (Later Jin / Li Keyong's domain)
w4-500601.blurb: With the Tang Dynasty's fall in 907, the Shatuo Turkic warlord Li Keyong, Prince of Jin, refused to recognize Zhu Wen's Later Liang and ruled an independent power base in Shanxi centered on Taiyuan. This 'Jin' state (the precursor that his son Li Cunxu would turn into the Later Tang, and ancestral to the later Later Jin) controlled the territory near (113.2E, 39.6N). The change reflects the breakup of Tang authority among rival warlords.

w4-500602.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and establishment of Southern Han under the Liu family
w4-500602.blurb: After the Tang collapse in 907, Liu Yin and his brother Liu Yan consolidated control over Lingnan (Guangdong, Guangxi, and Hainan), founding what became the Southern Han kingdom (Liu Yan declared himself emperor in 917).
