The territory of far-southern China near (110.7E, 21.6N) thus passed from the fallen Tang to the Southern Han regime during the Ten Kingdoms period.

w4-500603.name: Samanid conquest of Tabaristan from the Zaydid (Alid) emirs
w4-500603.blurb: In 900 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad defeated the Saffarid Amr ibn al-Layth and then moved against the Zaydid Alid rulers of Tabaristan along the Caspian coast. Samanid forces seized control of Tabaristan from the Zaydid dynasty around 900, extending Samanid authority to the region near (51.7E, 36.6N). The Alids would later recover the area, but at this snapshot it passed to the Samanids.

w4-500604.name: Samanid victory over the Saffarids and Abbasid investiture of Khurasan
w4-500604.blurb: In 900 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad crushed the Saffarid amir Amr ibn al-Layth at the Battle of Balkh, after which the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tadid invested Isma'il with the governorship of Khurasan and much of the Iranian east. This formalized de facto Samanid sovereignty over the vast region of eastern Iran and Central Asia near (56.3E, 36.1N), transferring it from nominal Abbasid administration to the autonomous Samanid Empire.

w4-500605.name: Fatimid takeover of the Aghlabid Emirate of Sicily
w4-500605.blurb: In 909 the Fatimid Caliphate, founded by Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah with the help of the Kutama Berbers led by Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, overthrew the Aghlabid dynasty in Ifriqiya, and with it Aghlabid Sicily passed under Fatimid suzerainty. The Emirate of Sicily near (14E, 37.1N) thereby came under Fatimid control as part of their North African empire.

w4-500608.name: Division of Alfonso III's kingdom: Ordoño II receives Galicia
w4-500608.blurb: In 910 Alfonso III of Asturias divided his realm among his three sons: Ordoño II received Galicia as a separate kingdom, while García I took León; this partition of Asturias created the short-lived autonomous Kingdom of Galicia alongside the Kingdom of León.

w4-500610.name: Collapse of the Tang Dynasty and emergence of the Later Liang
w4-500610.blurb: Zhu Wen, warlord of Xuanwu circuit, forced the last Tang emperor to abdicate in 907 and proclaimed the Later Liang, inaugurating the Five Dynasties period; most of central China's Tang territories passed under Later Liang control at this transition.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period

w4-500612.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and founding of Former Shu by Wang Jian
w4-500612.blurb: When the Tang Dynasty fell in 907, the warlord Wang Jian, who controlled Sichuan, refused to submit to the Later Liang and declared himself emperor, founding the Former Shu kingdom. The territory of the Sichuan Basin near (105.7E, 30.9N) thus passed from the defunct Tang to Former Shu during the Ten Kingdoms era.

w4-500613.name: Zhu Wen's usurpation of the Tang and founding of the Later Liang Dynasty
w4-500613.blurb: In 907 the warlord Zhu Wen (Zhu Quanzhong) deposed the last Tang emperor, Ai, and proclaimed himself emperor, founding the Later Liang Dynasty and ending the Tang. As the dominant successor regime he inherited the Tang heartland in the Central Plain near (114.9E, 35.6N), the largest single transfer of former Tang territory in this snapshot.

w4-500617.name: Byzantine-Bulgarian frontier conflict under Simeon I (early reign)
w4-500617.blurb: During the reign of Simeon I of Bulgaria, the First Bulgarian Empire pressed against Byzantine Macedonia; following the Arab sack of Thessalonica in 904, the Treaty negotiations and Simeon's pressure shifted the Byzantine-Bulgarian boundary, with Bulgaria gaining territory in Macedonia near (22.5E, 40.9N). The change reflects Simeon's expansion at Byzantine expense in the years around 904-911.

w4-500618.name: Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin (establishment of the Principality of Hungary)
w4-500618.blurb: Following the Magyar migration into the Carpathian Basin (c.895-900), the Hungarian tribal confederation consolidated into the Principality of Hungary, with the Battle of Pressburg (907) destroying East Frankish resistance and securing the conquest. The Magyar-held lands near (21.6E, 47N) in the Pannonian plain were thus formalized as the territory of the settled Principality of Hungary.

w4-500621.name: Gung Ye's rebellion and founding of Taebong (Later Goguryeo)
w4-500621.blurb: In 901 the rebel monk-warlord Gung Ye proclaimed the state of Later Goguryeo (later renamed Majin and then Taebong) in central Korea, breaking away from Unified Silla during the Later Three Kingdoms period. The territory of central Korea near (127E, 37.7N) thus passed from the declining Unified Silla to Gung Ye's Taebong.

w4-500622.name: Power transfer within Lower Burgundy to Hugh of Arles (c. 911)
w4-500622.blurb: By 911 Louis the Blind, King of Lower Burgundy, blinded after his failed 905 bid for the Italian crown, had transferred most royal powers to Count Hugh of Arles. The data shift from 'Kingdom of Lower Burgundy' to 'Lower Burgundy' at lng 5.8, lat 45 reflects this internal reorganisation rather than external conquest; the two Burgundies were not formally unified until 933 under Rudolph II. Matches the [900,911] window.

w4-500623.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and founding of Wuyue under Qian Liu
w4-500623.blurb: After the Tang fell in 907, the warlord Qian Liu was enfeoffed as King of Wuyue, ruling the wealthy region of modern Zhejiang and parts of Jiangsu. The territory near (120.3E, 29.8N) thus passed from the defunct Tang to the Wuyue kingdom, one of the most stable of the Ten Kingdoms.

w4-500625.name: Abbasid reconquest of Egypt from the Tulunids
w4-500625.blurb: In 905 the Abbasid general Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Katib led an army that overran Egypt, destroying the autonomous Tulunid dynasty founded by Ahmad ibn Tulun and sacking the capital al-Qata'i. Egypt and its dependencies near (29.4E, 30.1N) were thereby restored to direct Abbasid Caliphate control, ending Tulunid rule.

w4-500628.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and founding of Chu (Southern Chu) under Ma Yin
w4-500628.blurb: With the Tang's fall in 907, the warlord Ma Yin was enfeoffed by the Later Liang as King of Chu, ruling the Hunan region. The territory near (111.1E, 26.8N) thus passed from the defunct Tang to the Chu (Southern Chu) kingdom during the Ten Kingdoms period.

w4-500632.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and rise of Yang Xingmi's Wu (Southern Wu)
w4-500632.blurb: After the Tang collapse in 907, the domain built by Yang Xingmi in the Huai and lower Yangtze region became the autonomous kingdom of Wu (Southern Wu), refusing submission to the Later Liang. The territory near (117.9E, 29.6N) thus passed from the defunct Tang to Wu during the Ten Kingdoms era.

w4-500633.name: Lotharingia (Lorraine) reverting to West Frankish allegiance after Louis the Child's reign
w4-500633.blurb: On the death of the East Frankish king Louis the Child in 911, the duchy of Lotharingia (Lorraine), near (6E, 50.6N), rejected the new East Frankish king Conrad I and submitted instead to the West Frankish Carolingian Charles the Simple. This shifted the contested middle-kingdom territory from East Francia to West Francia.

w4-500634.name: Fall of the Tang Dynasty and Li Maozhen's Qi (Kingdom of Qi)
w4-500634.blurb: After the Tang fell in 907, the warlord Li Maozhen, governor of Fengxiang, refused to recognize the Later Liang and ruled an effectively independent state in the Guanzhong/Gansu region, styled the Kingdom of Qi. The territory near (106.4E, 36.2N) thus passed from the defunct Tang to Li Maozhen's Qi.

w4-500636.name: Fatimid conquest of the Idrisid realm (Fez)
w4-500636.blurb: After founding their caliphate in Ifriqiya in 909, the Fatimids under al-Mahdi Billah pushed westward through the Maghreb. Their general Masala ibn Habus campaigned against the Idrisids of Fez, defeating them and bringing northern Morocco under Fatimid (and their Miknasa allies') suzerainty around 921. This transferred the central Maghreb territory from the Idrisids to the Fatimid Caliphate.

w4-500637.name: Edward the Elder's reconquest of the southern Danelaw
w4-500637.blurb: In 917 King Edward the Elder of Wessex and his sister Æthelflæd launched the decisive phase of the reconquest of the Danelaw. Æthelflæd took Derby, Edward captured Tempsford and Colchester, and Danish leaders in East Anglia and the Midlands (lat 52.6, lng -0.1) submitted by year's end; by 918 Leicester and East Anglia had fallen. Window 911-922.

w4-500641.name: Rognvald's Viking conquest of Brittany
w4-500641.blurb: By 919 Breton defenses had collapsed and the Norse warlord Rognvald seized Nantes, renaming it his capital and ruling all of Brittany; the exiled Breton nobility (including the young Alan) fled to Francia and England. In 921 Robert of Neustria made peace with Rognvald, ceding Brittany to Norse control - the first full Viking domination of the former Breton kingdom, lasting until Alan II's reconquest in the late 930s.

w4-500643.name: Ordoño II Inherits León, Uniting Galicia and León
w4-500643.blurb: On Alfonso III's death (910) his realm was divided: García I received León, Ordoño II Galicia, Fruela II Asturias. García I died childless in 914 and Ordoño II inherited León, uniting it with Galicia (~-7.6E/42.7N) and moving the royal seat permanently to León. Window [911,922], date 914.

w4-500645.name: Hasan al-Utrush's establishment of Zaydi rule in Tabaristan
w4-500645.blurb: The Zaydi Alid leader al-Hasan al-Utrush (al-Nasir li'l-Haqq) reconquered Tabaristan and Daylam from the Samanids around 914, restoring Alid (Zaydi) rule on the Caspian coast after the Samanids had earlier expelled them. This wrested the Caspian region near the Alborz from the Samanid Empire to the Zaydi Alid dynasties.

w4-500646.name: Li Cunxu's conquest of the Yan Kingdom
w4-500646.blurb: Liu Shouguang declared himself emperor of Yan in 911, provoking war with the Jin (Later Tang) ruler Li Cunxu. Jin forces besieged and captured Youzhou (Beijing), executing Liu Shouguang in 914 and absorbing the Yan Kingdom into the Jin domain. This transferred the northeastern territory around modern Beijing from Yan to the Jin (Former Jin).

w4-500647.name: Jin–Later Liang war (Hedong consolidation under Li Cunxu)
w4-500647.blurb: During the protracted Jin–Later Liang conflict, Li Cunxu's Jin (Former Jin) expanded its control across Hedong and the northern plain near Taiyuan/Shanxi at the expense of rival regimes. The territory recorded here as 'Later Jin' to 'Former Jin' reflects Jin consolidation in northern Shanxi during the wars of the 910s under Li Cunxu against the Liang and local warlords.

w4-500648.name: Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy acquires Italy (922)
w4-500648.blurb: Rudolf II, King of Upper Burgundy since 912, was offered the crown of Italy in 922 by Italian nobles rebelling against King Berengar I of Friuli. He was crowned King of Italy at Pavia and fought and defeated Berengar near Piacenza. From 922 until 926, Rudolf thus jointly ruled both Upper Burgundy and Italy, creating a composite 'Upper Burgundy and Italy' realm. The data entry (Upper Burgundy to Upper Burgundy and Italy, py=911, y=922) captures the moment Rudolf added the Italian crown to his Burgundian title.

w4-500649.name: Invitation of Rudolph II of Burgundy to take the Italian crown (922)
w4-500649.blurb: Disaffected Italian nobles, opposed to King Berengar I, invited Rudolph II of Upper Burgundy to assume the Italian throne. Rudolph crossed the Alps in 922, was crowned King of Italy at Pavia, and his forces defeated Berengar near Piacenza in 923; Berengar was murdered in 924. The Kingdom of Italy thus passed under the rule of Upper Burgundy, uniting the two crowns until Rudolph returned to Burgundy in 926.

w4-500651.name: Chola conquest of the Pandya country under Parantaka I
w4-500651.blurb: The Chola emperor Parantaka I (r. 907-955) invaded the Pandya kingdom early in his reign, capturing Madurai around 910 and taking the title Madurai-konda ('capturer of Madurai'). He defeated the Pandya king Maravarman Rajasimha II, bringing the southern Tamil country under Chola control and transferring Pandya territory to the Chola Empire.

w4-500653.name: Wang Geon's overthrow of Gung Ye and founding of Goryeo
w4-500653.blurb: In 918 the general Wang Geon (Taejo) overthrew the tyrannical Gung Ye, ruler of Taebong (Later Goguryeo), and founded the Goryeo dynasty, taking over Taebong's territory in central Korea. This transferred Taebong's domain to the new Goryeo state, which would go on to unite the peninsula.

w4-500654.name: Gurjara-Pratihara Mahipala I recovers territories after Rashtrakuta withdrawal
w4-500654.blurb: After Rashtrakuta Indra III withdrew his forces southward, Gurjara-Pratihara Mahipala I (r. 912–944) reoccupied central Indian territories that had been raided, including around Kannauj. The Rashtrakutas did not maintain permanent northern occupation, so territorial reversion was rapid once their army retired.

w4-500655.name: Tomislav crowned first King of Croatia (c. 925)
w4-500655.blurb: Around 925, Duke Tomislav of Croatia was addressed as 'king' (rex Croatorum) in a letter from Pope John X, marking the elevation of the Duchy of Croatia to the Kingdom of Croatia. Tomislav had built a powerful realm by defeating Bulgarian invasions and uniting Dalmatian Croatia with Pannonian Croatia. The Council of Split (925) formalized the ecclesiastical organization of his kingdom. The dataset records a transition from 'Duchy of Croatia' to 'Kingdom of Croatia' around 922-926, consistent with this transformation.

w4-500657.name: Rashtrakuta–Pratihara wars (Pratihara recovery under Mahipala I)
w4-500657.blurb: After the Rashtrakuta king Indra III sacked Kannauj around 916, the Gurjara-Pratiharas under Mahipala I recovered their central Indian territories as Rashtrakuta forces withdrew south. The reassertion of Pratihara control over Malwa and the central Deccan frontier in the 920s transferred the contested region from the Rashtrakutas back to the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

w4-500659.name: Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte
w4-500659.blurb: By the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte in 911, the West Frankish king Charles the Simple granted the Viking leader Rollo lands around Rouen along the lower Seine, creating what became the Duchy of Normandy. This ceded West Frankish territory in northern France to Rollo's Norse settlers, founding Normandy.

w4-500660.name: Idrisid restoration in Fez against the Fatimids
w4-500660.blurb: Fatimid (and Miknasa) control over Fez proved unstable, and the Idrisids reasserted authority over northern Morocco in the mid-920s amid shifting allegiances of the Berber Miknasa. This temporarily returned the central Maghreb territory from Fatimid suzerainty back to the Idrisids, reversing the earlier conquest.

w4-500661.name: Transformation of the Kingdom of Asturias into the Kingdom of León
w4-500661.blurb: After the death of King Ordono II of León in 924, his brother Fruela II briefly reunited Asturias with León but died in 925, triggering civil conflict. In 926 Sancho Ordonez carved out a separate Galicia while Alfonso IV ruled León and Asturias, completing the transition of the old Asturian kingdom into the Kingdom of León. The from=Kingdom of Asturias / to=Kingdom of León and the 922-926 window reflect this dynastic reorganisation.

w4-500662.name: Later Tang Conquest of Later Liang
w4-500662.blurb: Li Cunxu of Later Tang (Shatuo Turks) launched a final offensive in 923, crushing the Later Liang forces; the last Liang emperor committed suicide and the Later Tang unified control over central China, ending the Later Liang.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period

w4-500663.name: Khitan (Liao) conquest of Balhae (Bohai)
w4-500663.blurb: In 926 the Khitan emperor Abaoji (Taizu of Liao) destroyed the kingdom of Balhae (Bohai), capturing its capital and ending the Manchurian state. He reorganized its territory as the puppet kingdom of Dongdan, transferring Balhae's vast domain in Manchuria and northern Korea to the Liao dynasty.

w4-500664.name: Absorption of Qi Principality by Later Tang
w4-500664.blurb: Li Maozhen, ruler of the Qi principality at Fengxiang (Shaanxi–Gansu area), submitted to Later Tang before his death in 924; his son Li Congyan continued governing Fengxiang until 926, when Later Tang's Emperor Li Cunxu removed him and formally absorbed Qi's territory into Later Tang.

w4-500665.name: Li Cunxu's destruction of Later Liang and founding of Later Tang
w4-500665.blurb: In 923 the Jin ruler Li Cunxu proclaimed himself emperor of the Later Tang and launched a decisive campaign that captured the Liang capital Daliang (Kaifeng), driving the last Later Liang emperor Zhu Zhen to suicide. This destroyed the Later Liang and transferred the bulk of the North China Plain to the Later Tang.

w4-500666.name: Conversion of Jin into the Later Tang under Li Cunxu
w4-500666.blurb: When Li Cunxu proclaimed the Later Tang in 923, the former Jin state's own core territory in the north (around Hebei/Shanxi) became part of the new Later Tang empire. This records the transfer of the Jin (Former Jin) heartland to the Later Tang as Li Cunxu's regime was elevated to imperial status.

w4-500668.name: Hugh of Arles crowned King of Italy, expelling Rudolph II
w4-500668.blurb: In 926 Hugh of Arles, Count of Provence (Lower Burgundy), was invited by Italian magnates to take the throne after they tired of Rudolph II of Upper Burgundy. Hugh crossed the Alps, and Rudolph withdrew to Burgundy; the atlas reflects this as Lower Burgundy (Hugh's territorial base) absorbing Italy while Rudolph's Upper Burgundy and Italy combination dissolved.

w4-500669.name: Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy loses Italy (922-926)
w4-500669.blurb: Rudolf II, King of Upper Burgundy, was invited to Italy by nobles disaffected with King Berengar I of Friuli. Crowned King of Italy at Pavia in 922, Rudolf briefly united Upper Burgundy and Italy under one crown. His hold on Italy was tenuous; after Berengar was murdered in 924, Italian nobles eventually transferred their allegiance to Hugh of Provence in 926, forcing Rudolf to return to Burgundy. The data entry (Upper Burgundy and Italy to Upper Burgundy, py=922, y=926) records the loss of Italy, restoring just Upper Burgundy to Rudolf.

w4-500670.name: Reunification of the Burgundian kingdom under Rudolf II / Hugh of Arles arrangements
w4-500670.blurb: The Kingdom of Lower Burgundy (Provence/Cisjurane Burgundy) was consolidated in the 920s amid the rivalry of Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy and Hugh of Arles. This entry reflects the reorganization of the Lower Burgundian kingdom in this period, transferring the Provencal/Rhone territory into the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy.

w4-500671.name: Hugh of Arles's departure to Italy and Burgundian realignment
w4-500671.blurb: In 926 Hugh of Arles left Provence to become King of Italy, and the dynastic arrangements between him and Rudolf II of Burgundy reshaped control of the Burgundian-Italian borderlands. This records the territory of Upper Burgundy and Italy passing into the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy (Provence) as part of these realignments.

w4-500672.name: Henry the Fowler's acquisition of Lotharingia (Lorraine)
w4-500672.blurb: In 925 the East Frankish (German) king Henry the Fowler annexed the Duchy of Lotharingia, which had wavered between West and East Frankish allegiance. Taking advantage of West Frankish weakness under Charles the Simple's deposition, Henry brought Lorraine firmly into the Kingdom of Germany, transferring the Rhineland duchy from West Frankish to German control.

w4-500673.name: Bulgarian conquest of Serbia under Simeon I
w4-500673.blurb: Tsar Simeon I of the First Bulgarian Empire, at war with Byzantium, turned on Serbia in 924, deposing and capturing Prince Zaharije and annexing the Serbian principality directly into Bulgaria. This transferred the Serbian lands in the western Balkans from the Principality of Serbia to the First Bulgarian Empire.

w4-500674.name: Revolt of Časlav Klonimirović — Serbian independence from Bulgaria
w4-500674.blurb: Around 933, Prince Časlav Klonimirović escaped captivity in the Bulgarian capital Preslav and, backed by Byzantine Emperor Romanos I, organized a successful revolt against Bulgarian overlordship. Serbia recovered its independence and much of its former territory, accounting for the large transfer from the First Bulgarian Empire to the Principality of Serbia in the 929–936 window.

w4-500675.name: Abd al-Rahman III's proclamation of the Caliphate of Córdoba
w4-500675.blurb: In 929 the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman III, having consolidated his authority over al-Andalus, proclaimed himself Caliph, elevating the Emirate of Córdoba into the Caliphate of Córdoba. This transformed the Andalusian state into a caliphate, transferring the realm from emirate to caliphal status.

w4-500676.name: Fatimid reconquest of Morocco after Musa's defection
w4-500676.blurb: After the Miknasa leader Musa ibn Abi al-Afiya defected to the Umayyads of Córdoba c.931, the Fatimid caliph al-Qa'im sent Humayd ibn Yasal, who defeated Musa in 933; al-Qasim al-Gannun then ruled northern Morocco for the Fatimids from 938, as reflected in the atlas geometry shifting back to Fatimid by 936.

w4-500677.name: Serbian restoration under Caslav Klonimirovic
w4-500677.blurb: After Simeon I's death in 927, Bulgarian control of Serbia collapsed. Caslav Klonimirovic, who had been held in Bulgaria, escaped around 933 and restored the Principality of Serbia, now under Byzantine protection. This transferred the Serbian lands back from the First Bulgarian Empire to a revived Principality of Serbia.

w4-500678.name: John Kourkouas's Byzantine reconquest in the east (capture of Melitene)
w4-500678.blurb: The Byzantine general John Kourkouas led a sustained offensive against the Abbasid frontier, capturing the emirate of Melitene (Malatya) in 934. This pushed the Byzantine frontier eastward into upper Mesopotamia/eastern Anatolia, transferring Abbasid-aligned border territory to the Byzantine Empire.

w4-500680.name: Shi Jingtang's rebellion and founding of the Later Jin
w4-500680.blurb: In 936 the Later Tang general Shi Jingtang rebelled and, with crucial military aid from the Khitan Liao (to whom he ceded the Sixteen Prefectures), overthrew the Later Tang and established the Later Jin dynasty with himself as emperor. This transferred the Later Tang's core territory on the North China Plain to the new Later Jin.

citations.label: Shi Jingtang / Emperor Gaozu of Later Jin (Wikipedia)

w4-500681.name: Founding of the Althing at Þingvellir
w4-500681.blurb: Around 930, at the close of the roughly 60-year Age of Settlement (landnám), Iceland's chieftains and free farmers established the Alþingi at Þingvellir along with the goðorð system, adopting a common law code. This event marks the transition from scattered, unorganized Norse settlement to the structured Icelandic Commonwealth (Free State), which endured until 1262.

w4-500683.name: Athelstan's unification of England — end of Wessex as distinct kingdom
w4-500683.blurb: Athelstan of Wessex conquered York in 927, the last Viking (Scandinavian) kingdom in England, becoming the first ruler of a unified Kingdom of England. By 929 he had consolidated this unification; the title shifted toward 'King of the English.' Wessex as a separate political entity ceased to exist, absorbed into the new unified kingdom, which Athelstan further confirmed by defeating a coalition of rivals at the Battle of Brunanburh in 937.

w4-500684.name: Æthelstan's Annexation of York and Northumbria
w4-500684.blurb: After the death of Sihtric, the Danish King of York, in 927, Æthelstan of Wessex seized the Viking Kingdom of York and annexed Northumbria, becoming the first King of a unified England. The window 929-936 reflects Æthelstan consolidating and governing the newly absorbed north during his reign (924-939). Northumbria changed hands several more times after his death, with final permanent incorporation into England only under Eadred in 954.

w4-500685.name: Khitan (Liao) annexation of the Sixteen Prefectures
w4-500685.blurb: When Shi Jingtang rebelled against the Later Tang and founded the Later Jin (936), he secured military aid from the Khitan Liao emperor Abaoji's successor Yelü Deguang by ceding the Sixteen Prefectures (Yan-Yun region around modern Beijing). The collapse of the Later Tang in 936 transferred this strategically vital northern frontier, including Youzhou/Yanjing (~115.6, 40), to the Liao Dynasty, which they held for nearly two centuries.

w4-500687.name: Merger of Upper and Lower Burgundy into the Kingdom of Arles (933)
w4-500687.blurb: King Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy (r. 912–933) reached a treaty with Hugh of Italy in 933, renouncing his Italian claims in exchange for Lower Burgundy (Provence). This united the two Burgundian kingdoms under Rudolf, forming the Kingdom of Arles (Kingdom of Burgundy) with its capital at Arles, encompassing the Alpine Burgundian realm at these coordinates.

w4-500688.name: Union of Upper and Lower Burgundy into the Kingdom of Arles
w4-500688.blurb: In 933 Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy and Hugh of Arles (Hugh of Italy) agreed that Rudolf would cede his Italian claims in exchange for Lower Burgundy (Provence/Cisjurane Burgundy). This merged Upper and Lower Burgundy into a single realm, the Kingdom of Arles (Kingdom of the Two Burgundies), transferring the Rhône valley region (~5.8, 45) under Rudolf's rule.

w4-500689.name: Hugh of Arles–Rudolf II accord (Hugh's consolidation of the Kingdom of Italy)
w4-500689.blurb: Hugh of Arles became King of Italy in 926 and in 933 reached an accord with Rudolf II of Burgundy whereby Rudolf renounced his claims to Italy in return for Lower Burgundy. This consolidated the northern Italian territories (~10.7, 44) under Hugh's Kingdom of Italy, ending Burgundian contestation of the Italian crown.

w4-500690.name: Hamdanid seizure of the Jazira and Mosul
w4-500690.blurb: As Abbasid central authority disintegrated in the 930s, the Hamdanid dynasty under Nasir al-Dawla al-Hasan consolidated control over the Jazira (Upper Mesopotamia) and Mosul (~42.4, 36.1), formally recognized by the Caliphate. The Hamdanids became the effective independent rulers of northern Iraq and Syria, detaching this large region from direct Abbasid rule.

w4-500691.name: Fall of the Sajid dynasty in Azerbaijan
w4-500691.blurb: The Sajid dynasty, a vassal governorship of the Abbasids in Azerbaijan, collapsed in 929 after the death of Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj and the rebellion of his commanders. The Caliphate briefly reasserted nominal control over the Azerbaijan/Aran region (~46.9, 39.4) before it passed to local powers such as the Sallarids; this window reflects the Abbasid reclamation following the Sajid demise.

w4-500692.name: Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth unify Denmark
w4-500692.blurb: Gorm the Old, the first historically recognised king of Denmark, began unifying the petty kingdoms of Jutland and the Danish islands around 936 CE; his son Harald Bluetooth completed the unification, as commemorated on the Jelling Stones. The worklist transfer Scandinavian minor kingdoms → Kingdom of Denmark at lng 10.4, lat 56 (Jutland) in the 929–936 window matches the establishment of recognised kingly authority over the previously fragmented realm.

w4-500693.name: Mardavij ibn Ziyar conquers Tabaristan and founds Ziyarid dynasty
w4-500693.blurb: After the Samanids ended the second Zaydi Alid emirate of Tabaristan (928), Mardavij ibn Ziyar seized Tabaristan around 929-931 and founded the Ziyarid dynasty. The Caspian coast passed from the Zaydi Alid dynasties to the Ziyarids within the 929-936 window. Well attested.

citations.label: Alid dynasties of northern Iran – Wikipedia

w4-500694.name: Goryeo Conquest of Later Baekje and Unification of Korea
w4-500694.blurb: In 936 CE, Wang Geon of Goryeo — aided by the defection of the deposed Later Baekje founder Kyeon Hwon himself — led a coalition army of roughly 87,500 soldiers that crushed Later Baekje, completing Korea's reunification under Goryeo. The last Unified Silla king had peacefully submitted to Goryeo in 935, making this the final military act of the Later Three Kingdoms period.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Later Three Kingdoms of Korea

w4-500697.name: Surrender of Silla to Goryeo
w4-500697.blurb: In 935 King Gyeongsun, the last ruler of Unified Silla, peacefully surrendered his kingdom to Wang Geon (Taejo) of Goryeo, ending nearly a millennium of Silla rule. This transferred the Gyeongju heartland of southeastern Korea (~128.5, 36.1) to Goryeo, a key step in Wang Geon's reunification of the Later Three Kingdoms (completed with the defeat of Later Baekje in 936).

w4-500698.name: Battle of Bạch Đằng (939) and Vietnamese independence
w4-500698.blurb: At the Battle of Bạch Đằng River in 938, the Vietnamese leader Ngô Quyền decisively defeated the naval fleet of the Southern Han using iron-tipped stakes hidden in the tidal river. The victory ended a thousand years of Chinese domination over Vietnam; Ngô Quyền proclaimed himself king in 939, founding the Ngô Dynasty and detaching the Red River delta region (~106.1, 19.8) from Southern Han.

w4-500699.name: Reconquista frontier campaigns of Ramiro II of León
w4-500699.blurb: King Ramiro II of León inflicted a major defeat on Caliph Abd al-Rahman III at the Battle of Simancas (939), checking Umayyad northward expansion. The campaign secured the Duero frontier zone (~-5.1, 40.8), allowing León to consolidate and repopulate territory along the Christian-Muslim border at the expense of the Caliphate of Córdoba.

w4-500701.name: Otto I's subjugation of the Obotrite Slavs
w4-500701.blurb: Otto I of Germany, through his lieutenants Margrave Gero and Margrave Hermann Billung, subjugated the Polabian Slavs including the Obotrites from 939 onward, with Hermann Billung extracting tribute from the Obotrite tribal federation north of the Elbe. By the late 940s the Obotrite region near the Elbe had been brought under tribute-paying vassalage to the Kingdom of Germany. The data window 939-947 captures this subjugation.

w4-500704.name: Buyid capture of Baghdad
w4-500704.blurb: In 945 Ahmad ibn Buya (Mu'izz al-Dawla) of the Buyid dynasty entered Baghdad and took control of the Abbasid government, reducing the caliph to a figurehead. The Abbasid heartland of central Iraq (~46.3, 32.5) became a Buyid-administered condominium, with the caliph retaining nominal religious authority while the Buyids held real power.

w4-500705.name: Buyid capture of Baghdad (shared Abbasid-Buyid condominium)
w4-500705.blurb: Following Mu'izz al-Dawla's seizure of Baghdad in 945, the Buyid-held lands of southwestern Iran (~50.8, 31.9, around Khuzestan/Fars) were formally integrated into the new Abbasid-Buyid condominium under nominal caliphal sovereignty. The change reflects the reclassification of Buyid territory as jointly held with the Abbasid Caliphate after the Buyids assumed the office of amir al-umara.

w4-500707.name: Southern Tang (Wu) conquest of Min
w4-500707.blurb: The Kingdom of Min collapsed amid internal civil war in the 940s, and in 945 the Southern Tang (successor to Southern Wu, here labeled Southern Wu) conquered the Min heartland of Fujian (~118.3, 26.1), capturing the capital Jianzhou. This brought most of Fujian under southern Chinese control during the Ten Kingdoms period, though Min's coastal areas later fragmented.

w4-500708.name: Founding of the Later Han after the Khitan sack of Later Jin
w4-500708.blurb: In 946–947 the Khitan Liao destroyed the Later Jin, sacking its capital Kaifeng; but the Khitan soon withdrew, and the Jin general Liu Zhiyuan proclaimed the Later Han dynasty in 947. The North China Plain centered on Kaifeng/Luoyang (~113.5, 34.7) passed from the defunct Later Jin to the new Later Han, the fourth of the Five Dynasties.

w4-500710.name: Chaulukya (Solanki) expansion in Gujarat amid Rashtrakuta decline
w4-500710.blurb: Mularaja founded the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty of Gujarat around 940–942, carving out a kingdom centered on Anhilwara as Rashtrakuta power waned. The southern Gujarat/Lata region near Surat (~73.4, 21.2) passed from Rashtrakuta overlordship to the rising Chaulukyas during this period of Deccan political fragmentation.

w4-500711.name: Idrisid recovery of Fez during Fatimid–Umayyad rivalry
w4-500711.blurb: Amid the contest between the Fatimid Caliphate and Umayyad Córdoba over Morocco, and following the great Kharijite revolt of Abu Yazid (944) that shook Fatimid Ifriqiya, the Idrisids reasserted control over northern Morocco around Fez (~-4.1, 33.6). The Fatimids' inability to hold the far Maghreb allowed the Idrisid line to recover their ancestral domains.

w4-500712.name: Fatimid annexation of Cyrenaica/Barqa
w4-500712.blurb: During the reign of Caliph al-Mansur and al-Mu'izz, the Fatimid Caliphate consolidated and expanded its control eastward across Cyrenaica (Barqa, ~22, 31), the frontier between Ifriqiya and Abbasid Egypt. This eastward push set the stage for the Fatimid conquest of Egypt in 969, drawing Barqa firmly out of the Abbasid sphere.

w4-500713.name: Founding of the Southern Tang from Southern Wu
w4-500713.blurb: In 937 Li Bian (Xu Zhigao) deposed the last ruler of Southern Wu and proclaimed the Southern Tang dynasty, inheriting Wu's territories in the lower Yangtze (~117.3, 27.9). This dataset records the transfer of the Jiangxi/Jiangnan heartland from Southern Wu to its successor state Southern Tang, the strongest of the southern Ten Kingdoms.

w4-500714.name: Southern Tang conquest of Chu
w4-500714.blurb: In 951 the Southern Tang invaded and conquered the Kingdom of Chu (Southern Chu), which had collapsed into civil war among the sons of Ma Yin. Southern Tang annexed the Hunan region (~111.1, 26.8) centered on Changsha, though it soon lost much of it to the warlord Liu Yan and the Later Zhou.

w4-500718.name: Battle of Lechfeld and the end of Hungarian raids
w4-500718.blurb: At the Battle of Lechfeld in 955, Otto I of Germany decisively defeated the Magyar (Hungarian) raiding army near Augsburg, ending decades of Hungarian incursions into Central Europe. The victory secured the eastern marches and pushed Hungarian power back, transferring the frontier region around the Eastern March/Styria (~15.2, 47.6) from the Principality of Hungary to the Kingdom of Germany.

w4-500720.name: Guo Wei's Coup and Foundation of the Later Zhou
w4-500720.blurb: General Guo Wei, commander of Later Han armies, led a coup against the Later Han emperor in 951, proclaimed himself emperor, and founded the Later Zhou, inheriting Later Han's territory; the Later Zhou then expanded through military campaigns under Chai Rong.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period

w4-500721.name: Later Zhou conquest of Huainan from Southern Tang
w4-500721.blurb: In a series of campaigns from 956 to 958, Emperor Shizong (Chai Rong) of the Later Zhou conquered the Huainan region between the Huai and Yangtze rivers (~118, 32.6) from the Southern Tang. The defeated Southern Tang ruler ceded fourteen prefectures and acknowledged Zhou suzerainty, a major step toward the reunification later completed by the Song.

w4-500723.name: Death of Eric Bloodaxe; Danelaw absorbed into England
w4-500723.blurb: Eric Bloodaxe, the last Norse king of York, was killed in 954 at Stainmore (per Symeon of Durham, by Earl Maccus), ending the last Viking kingdom in England; Earl Oswulf then recognised King Eadred's overlordship, ending the political Danelaw. Coord 1.5W/54.1N is in Northumbria, core of the former Danelaw. The dataset's 947–960 window brackets Eric's reigns (947–948, 952–954) and subsequent consolidation. Event real and correctly dated.

w4-500731.name: Burman (Mranma) settlement of Upper Burma and decline of the Pyu city-states
w4-500731.blurb: Around the mid-9th to 10th centuries the Pyu city-states of central Burma collapsed after raids by the Kingdom of Nanzhao (notably the sack of Halin in 832) and were gradually absorbed as the Burman people founded Pagan (Bagan), traditionally dated 849, which expanded across the dry zone of Upper Burma. This change captures the transfer of the Pyu heartland around the Irrawaddy to the rising Pagan Kingdom by 960. The process was a migration-and-absorption rather than a single battle, but it is the well-known origin of Pagan as successor to the Pyu.

w4-500734.name: Borrell II inherits the County of Urgell from his uncle Sunifred II (948)
w4-500734.blurb: Count Fernan Gonzalez of Castile progressively consolidated autonomous rule over the County of Castile through the 930s-950s. By around 960, exploiting Leonese dynastic crises, he had reduced his obligations to the Kingdom of Leon to nominal fealty, establishing the de facto independence of the county; Castile remained a county under Leonese suzerainty in name and would not be elevated to a kingdom until 1065.

w4-500735.name: Otto I invades Italy and assumes the crown as King of Italy (961)
w4-500735.blurb: Pope John XII appealed to Otto I of Germany for protection against Berengar II, who held the Kingdom of Italy. In August 961, Otto descended through the Brenner Pass, and by Christmas 961 he had assumed the title King of Italy at Pavia. He was subsequently crowned Holy Roman Emperor by the Pope on 2 February 962, permanently uniting the Kingdom of Germany and the Kingdom of Italy under a single sovereign.

w4-500736.name: Fernan Gonzalez's de facto independence of Castile from Leon (c. 960-961)
w4-500736.blurb: Count Fernan Gonzalez of Castile progressively asserted Castile's independence from the Kingdom of Leon through the mid-10th century. In 960, Garcia Sanchez I of Navarre defeated and captured Fernan at Cirueña, releasing him on territorial concessions and a pledge to drop his support for the Leonese pretender Ordoño IV. By 961 Castile's hereditary and increasingly autonomous status was consolidated, with the county acting de facto as an independent entity that merely acknowledged nominal Leonese suzerainty. Territory around lat 42.2, lng -3.1 in the Castilian heartland reflects this autonomy.

w4-500738.name: Founding of the Song dynasty / Chenqiao Mutiny
w4-500738.blurb: In 960 the general Zhao Kuangyin (Emperor Taizu of Song) was acclaimed emperor by his troops at Chenqiao, supplanting the Later Zhou dynasty whose throne was held by the child emperor Gong. This bloodless coup transferred the entire Later Zhou realm in the North China Plain (centered on Kaifeng) to the new Northern Song dynasty, beginning the reunification of China after the Five Dynasties period.

w4-500740.name: Alp Tigin's seizure of Ghazna / founding of the Ghaznavid dynasty
w4-500740.blurb: In 962 the Turkic Samanid commander Alp Tigin, having fallen out with the Samanid court, captured the fortress city of Ghazna in present-day Afghanistan and established an autonomous power there, the nucleus of the Ghaznavid dynasty. This carved the Ghazna region out of nominal Samanid authority, beginning the Ghaznavid breakaway that his successor Sebuktigin and especially Mahmud of Ghazni would expand into an empire.

w4-500742.name: Coronation of Otto I and union of the Kingdom of Italy with the Holy Roman Empire
w4-500742.blurb: On 2 February 962 Otto I was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope John XII, formally re-establishing the (Holy Roman) Empire. Otto had already taken the Iron Crown of the Lombards in 961, bringing the Kingdom of Italy under his rule; the imperial coronation joined the Italian kingdom to the empire, transferring northern Italy (the Po valley) into the Holy Roman Empire.

w4-500743.name: Coronation of Otto I and formation of the Holy Roman Empire
w4-500743.blurb: Otto I, King of Germany (East Francia) since 936, was crowned Roman emperor by Pope John XII on 2 February 962, transforming his German kingdom into the core of the Holy Roman Empire. This change reflects the German realm becoming the Holy Roman Empire under Otto, the conventional starting point of the empire that endured until 1806.

w4-500745.name: Buyid expansion into Jibal and the Samanid-Buyid frontier
w4-500745.blurb: The Buyid emir Rukn al-Dawla, ruling Ray and Jibal, pushed his frontier eastward into areas formerly under Samanid nominal suzerainty in the mid-960s. The centroid indicates northern Fars/Jibal; the Buyids had seized Ray in 943 and consolidated their control over the Caspian-adjacent provinces during this decade.

w4-500747.name: Buyid expansion into Samanid-held Kerman / central Iran
w4-500747.blurb: During the 960s the Buyid dynasty, dominant over western Iran and Iraq, contested control of central and southeastern Iran (the Kerman region) with the declining Samanid Empire. Under 'Adud al-Dawla the Buyids consolidated Kerman and Fars, pushing the Samanid frontier back eastward. This change reflects the Buyid absorption of Samanid-held territory in central/southeastern Iran by 970, though it was a frontier struggle rather than one decisive battle.

w4-500749.name: Harald Bluetooth's overlordship of Norway after the death of Haakon the Good
w4-500749.blurb: Around 961 King Haakon the Good of Norway was killed at the Battle of Fitjar against the sons of Eric Bloodaxe, who were backed by Harald Bluetooth of Denmark. The Danish king thereby gained suzerainty over Viken and southeastern Norway (the Oslofjord region around 59.6N), placing parts of Norway under Danish overlordship, as recorded in this transfer.

w4-500751.name: Byzantine reconquest of Apulia/Lucania under Nikephoros II Phokas
w4-500751.blurb: In the late 960s, as Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas reasserted Byzantine power in southern Italy and clashed with Otto I, Byzantine forces under the catepan of Italy strengthened control over the Apulia-Lucania frontier at the expense of the Lombard principalities including Salerno. This change reflects Byzantine absorption of territory in the heel of Italy (around 16.7E, 40.5N) in this period of renewed Byzantine assertiveness.

w4-500752.name: Byzantine eastern reconquests under Nikephoros II Phokas (fall of Antioch, 969)
w4-500752.blurb: Under Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas and his general John Tzimiskes the Byzantines drove deep into northern Syria and the Jazira at the expense of the Hamdanid emirate of Aleppo, capturing Antioch in 969 and reducing Aleppo to tributary status. This change reflects the seizure of Hamdanid territory in the upper Mesopotamia / northern Syria region (around 39E, 36.8N) during this decisive phase of the Byzantine reconquest.

w4-500753.name: Sviatoslav I's destruction of Khazaria
w4-500753.blurb: Kievan Rus' prince Sviatoslav I, employing Oghuz and Pecheneg auxiliary forces, destroyed the Khazar fortress of Sarkel c. 965 and subsequently sacked the Khazar capital of Atil (968/969). The combined Rus'-Oghuz pressure shattered Khazar imperial power, with Oghuz tribes overrunning former Khazar steppe territories around lat 46.3, lng 53.6 (north Caspian steppe). By 970 the Khazar Khaganate had ceased to function as a political entity.

w4-500754.name: Song conquest of Later Shu
w4-500754.blurb: In 964-965 Emperor Taizu of Song launched a two-pronged invasion of Later Shu in Sichuan; the Shu ruler Meng Chang surrendered after only about 66 days of campaigning. This brought the wealthy Sichuan basin (around 105.7E, 30.9N) into the Northern Song, a major step in the Song reunification of China.

w4-500755.name: Song annexation of Jingnan (Nanping)
w4-500755.blurb: In 963 the Northern Song, using passage through Jingnan (the small Nanping state on the middle Yangtze) as a pretext during a campaign against Hunan, occupied Jingnan and forced its ruler Gao Jichong to submit. This absorbed the strategic middle-Yangtze territory (around 111.7E, 31.6N) into the Song, an early step in Taizu's reunification wars.

w4-500759.name: Otto I grants Duchy of Spoleto and Camerino to Pandulf Ironhead
w4-500759.blurb: On 4 May 967, Emperor Otto I granted the vacant Duchy of Spoleto and March of Camerino to Pandulf Ironhead, Prince of Benevento and Capua, charging him with the war against Byzantium. The Spoleto/Benevento border region near lng 13.4 E / lat 42.8 N thus passed from the Kingdom of Italy's administration to Pandulf of Benevento, matching the [962,970] window.

w4-500760.name: Otto I's campaigns against Byzantium and the Lombard principalities of southern Italy
w4-500760.blurb: After his imperial coronation, Otto I intervened in southern Italy (967-969), seeking to bring the Lombard principalities and Byzantine territories under imperial overlordship. In the resulting reshuffle the Duchy of Benevento came under Otto's suzerainty but retained/regained control of territory in the central-southern Apennines (around 13.4E, 42.8N) as an imperial vassal, which this change records as a transfer from direct imperial holding to Benevento.

w4-500762.name: Buyid annexation of Hamdanid Mosul / the Jazira under 'Adud al-Dawla
w4-500762.blurb: By 978-979 the Buyid amir 'Adud al-Dawla extinguished the Hamdanid emirate of Mosul, driving out the last Hamdanid rulers and bringing the upper Tigris / Jazira region (around 44.5E, 35.8N, near Mosul) under Buyid control. This change reflects that absorption of Hamdanid territory by the Buyids in the 970s.

w4-500763.name: Buyid Adud al-Dawla Expels Ziyarid Qabus and Seizes Tabaristan
w4-500763.blurb: Qabus ibn Wushmgir of the Ziyarid dynasty sheltered the rebel Buyid prince Fakhr al-Dawla, who had fled his brother Adud al-Dawla. In retaliation, Adud al-Dawla (via his brother Mu'ayyad al-Dawla) invaded Ziyarid territory: Qabus lost Tabaristan in 980 (369 AH) and was expelled from Gurgan in 981. The southern Caspian region (~51.6E/36.6N) came under direct Buyid rule for 17 years until Qabus returned in 998. Window [970,980], date 980; territory from Ziyarid to Buyid.

w4-500764.name: Rise of Haakon Sigurdsson (Jarl Hákon) and Norwegian recovery of Viken
w4-500764.blurb: After the death of Harald Greycloak around 970, Haakon Sigurdsson became the effective ruler of Norway, nominally as a vassal of Harald Bluetooth of Denmark but in practice asserting Norwegian autonomy; he eventually threw off Danish overlordship. This change records southeastern Norway (the Oslofjord region around 59.6N) reverting from Danish to Norwegian control in the 970s as Norwegian power revived under Jarl Hákon.

w4-500765.name: Sebuktigin's expansion of the Ghaznavid realm
w4-500765.blurb: In 977 Sebuktigin became ruler of Ghazna and greatly expanded the Ghaznavid domain, pushing into the regions of Bost, Zabulistan, and toward the Indus (around 67.8E, 30.2N) at the expense of nominal Samanid authority and local rulers. This change reflects the Ghaznavid absorption of further Samanid-frontier territory in the lower Helmand / Balochistan-Sindh borderlands under Sebuktigin.

w4-500766.name: Croatian recovery of Dalmatian territory under Stephen Drzislav
w4-500766.blurb: In the 970s-980s the Kingdom of Croatia under Stephen Drzislav strengthened its position along the eastern Adriatic; amid the Byzantine difficulties following the death of John Tzimiskes (976) and Bulgarian wars, Croatia expanded its control over Dalmatian hinterland territory (around 17.8E, 43.9N). Byzantium subsequently recognized Drzislav with imperial insignia. This change reflects the transfer of Dalmatian/inland territory from Byzantine to Croatian control in this period.

w4-500768.name: Tailapa II's overthrow of the Rashtrakutas and founding of the Western Chalukya Empire
w4-500768.blurb: Around 973, Tailapa II, a Chalukya feudatory of the Rashtrakutas, rebelled against the last effective Rashtrakuta king Karka II in the Deccan, exploiting the dynasty's collapse after the Paramara sack of Manyakheta. Tailapa overthrew the Rashtrakutas and established the Western Chalukya (Kalyani) Empire, absorbing the bulk of Rashtrakuta territory in the central Deccan around modern Karnataka and Maharashtra.

w4-500770.name: Córdoban (Almanzor) expansion into Idrisid/Maghreb Morocco
w4-500770.blurb: In the 970s the Caliphate of Córdoba under Caliph al-Hakam II, and increasingly the hajib Almanzor (al-Mansur), extended Umayyad authority into northern Morocco at the expense of the declining Idrisid dynasty, whom the Fatimids had already shattered. Córdoban forces and allied Zenata Berbers ended Idrisid power, bringing the Fez/Rif region under Córdoban suzerainty by the late 10th century.

w4-500771.name: Song Conquest of Northern Han
w4-500771.blurb: In 979, Song Emperor Taizong personally led an army to besiege Taiyuan, the Northern Han capital; after defeating a Liao relief force, the last Northern Han emperor surrendered, ending the final holdout of the Ten Kingdoms era and completing Song reunification of northern China.

w4-500773.name: Northern Song conquest of Southern Tang
w4-500773.blurb: Emperor Taizu of Song launched a campaign in 974-975 against the Southern Tang ruler Li Yu, part of the Song reunification of China. After besieging and capturing the capital Jinling (Nanjing) in 976/975, the Song annexed the Southern Tang's wealthy lower-Yangtze and Jiangxi territories, ending one of the largest Ten Kingdoms states.

w4-500774.name: Northern Song conquest of Northern Han
w4-500774.blurb: In 979 Emperor Taizong of Song besieged Taiyuan and conquered the Northern Han, the last of the Ten Kingdoms, which had survived under Liao protection. Taizong defeated a Liao relief army and captured the Northern Han ruler Liu Jiyuan, completing the Song reunification of China proper and adding the Shanxi region around Taiyuan to the empire.

w4-500775.name: Unification of Sweden under Eric the Victorious
w4-500775.blurb: Eric the Victorious (r. c. 970–995) is traditionally regarded as the first historically attested king of a unified Sweden, having consolidated both Svealand and Götaland under his rule and defeating rivals at the Battle of Fýrisvellir. The c. 970–980 window in the atlas captures the consolidation of formerly independent Scandinavian petty kingdoms under Swedish royal authority, completed definitively under his son Olof Skötkonung.

w4-500779.name: Consolidation of the County of Toulouse under the Capetian accession (1987)
w4-500779.blurb: With the extinction of the Carolingian (West Frankish) line and the accession of Hugh Capet in 987, royal authority in the far south collapsed and the County of Toulouse under the Raymondine dynasty became effectively autonomous. The cartographic shift from 'West Franks' to the County of Toulouse reflects this de facto independence of Languedoc rather than a single conquest.

w4-500781.name: Polish–Bohemian War of 990 — Mieszko I annexes Silesia
w4-500781.blurb: After the death of Mieszko I's Bohemian wife Dobrawa (977) the Polish-Bohemian alliance ended. In 990 Bohemian Duke Boleslaus II contested Polish actions in Silesia; both sides fought there, with the Holy Roman Empire backing Poland. Mieszko I defeated the Bohemians and annexed Middle Silesia (around Niemcza and Krosno), transferring this borderland from Bohemian to Polish control.

w4-500784.name: Emergence of the County of Maine at the Capetian accession (987)
w4-500784.blurb: The replacement of the West Frankish (Carolingian) crown by Hugh Capet in 987 formalized the autonomy of the principalities, including the County of Maine under the Hugonides. The map's transfer represents Maine's standing as an independent comital state between Normandy and Anjou rather than a battlefield conquest.

w4-500787.name: Autonomy of the County of Rouergue at the Capetian accession (987)
w4-500787.blurb: After the Carolingian West Frankish line ended and Hugh Capet was crowned in 987, the County of Rouergue (held by the house of Toulouse) in southern Aquitaine became effectively independent of the crown. The shift reflects this fragmentation of royal authority in the south rather than a discrete military event.

w4-500792.name: Autonomy of the Duchy of Aquitaine at the Capetian accession (987)
w4-500792.blurb: The accession of Hugh Capet in 987 ended the Carolingian West Frankish monarchy, and the powerful Duchy of Aquitaine under William IV/Poitou became a virtually independent principality only nominally subject to the new Capetian kings. The transfer marks this de facto autonomy of southwestern France rather than a conquest.

w4-500794.name: Accession of Hugh Capet and founding of the Kingdom of France (987)
w4-500794.blurb: On the death of the last Carolingian king Louis V in 987, the nobles elected Hugh Capet, founder of the Capetian dynasty, ending the West Frankish (Carolingian) realm and inaugurating the Kingdom of France. The change centered on the Île-de-France royal domain around Paris reflects this dynastic succession.

w4-500795.name: Hamdanid (Marwanid) recovery of the Jazira/Mosul from the Buyids
w4-500795.blurb: In the 980s the Buyid grip on the upper Mesopotamian Jazira and Mosul, briefly seized from the Hamdanids, slipped as Kurdish and Hamdanid successor forces reasserted themselves around Mosul and Diyar Bakr. The territory around Mosul reverted from Buyid control to Hamdanid (and allied Marwanid) hands amid the fragmentation of the region in the late 10th century.

w4-500796.name: Western Chalukya consolidation of the southern Deccan under Tailapa II
w4-500796.blurb: Following Tailapa II's overthrow of the Rashtrakutas (c. 973), the Western Chalukyas continued absorbing residual Rashtrakuta-aligned territory in the southern Deccan around the Tungabhadra region into the 980s. This change reflects the final extinction of Rashtrakuta authority in southern Karnataka as Chalukya rule was consolidated.

w4-600003.name: Byzantine Emperor Basil II conquers northwestern Bulgaria
w4-600003.blurb: Emperor Basil II ('the Bulgar-Slayer') launched systematic campaigns against the First Bulgarian Empire from 1000 onward: in 1001 he retook Preslav and Pliska, and progressively conquered the Danubian Bulgaria region (~42.4°N, 24.9°E). The large 62,927 km² bloc reflects Byzantine absorption of northeastern Bulgaria before the final annihilation of the empire in 1018.

w4-600004.name: Bolesław I the Brave gains Milsko and Lusatia at the Congress of Gniezno / Treaty with Otto III
w4-600004.blurb: At the Congress of Gniezno (March 1000), Emperor Otto III granted Duke Bolesław I the Brave of Poland significant dignities and territorial concessions in the Lusatia/Milsko region (~50.3°N, 14.1°E) on the Bohemian-Polish border. Bolesław subsequently seized additional border territories from the Holy Roman Empire during 1002–1003, formalizing Poland's control of what had been imperial march territory.

w4-600005.name: Bolesław I the Brave conquers Moravia and Bohemian borderlands
w4-600005.blurb: In 1003, Bolesław I the Brave of Poland exploited succession disputes in Bohemia to seize Moravia and parts of Silesia (the area at lng 15.6, lat 49.8), briefly bringing Bohemian-held lands under Polish control during the German-Polish wars.

w4-600006.name: Bolesław I Chrobry conquers Moravia from Hungary
w4-600006.blurb: In 1003, Bolesław I Chrobry of Poland seized Moravia and parts of Slovakia from Hungary's Stephen I during the broader Polish-German conflict; this temporary Polish expansion shifted the region (centroid ~lng 19.1, lat 48.6) from Hungarian to Polish control.

w4-600007.name: Succession from Utpala to Lohara dynasty in Kashmir
w4-600007.blurb: The Lohara dynasty succeeded the Utpala dynasty in Kashmir around 1003 CE when Didda, the Utpala queen-regent, designated her nephew Sanggramaraja of the Lohara clan as heir. Sanggramaraja founded the Lohara dynasty, and the large Kashmir/Kabul region passed to the new ruling house without military conquest.

w4-600008.name: Establishment of the Taifa of Valencia during the fitna
w4-600008.blurb: The Taifa of Valencia emerged around 1010–1011 as the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba disintegrated during the fitna. Effective independence was established not by Mujahid al-Amiri (who founded the neighboring Taifa of Dénia) but by two saqaliba former slaves of the Amirid household, Mubarak and Muzaffar, who had served as irrigation officials in the city. After their fall the city briefly accepted other saqaliba rulers, and from about 1021 the Amirid prince Abd al-Aziz al-Mansur, a grandson of Almanzor, took power and ruled Valencia for some four decades.

w4-600010.name: Unification of Georgia under Bagrat III
w4-600010.blurb: Bagrat III of the Bagrationi dynasty unified the Georgian kingdoms by inheriting Kakheti and Hereti (c. 1003) and Tao-Klarjeti (1001-1008), completing the consolidation of a Kingdom of Georgia distinct from its predecessor polities by approximately 1008. The atlas shift from 'Georgia' to 'Kingdom of Georgia' between 1005 and 1010 reflects this dynastic unification.

w4-600011.name: Chola Invasion of Chalukya Territories under Rajendra Chola I
w4-600011.blurb: Around 1007 the Chola assault on Western Chalukya territory was directed by Rajaraja Chola I, who had already overrun Gangapadi and Nolambapadi (in present-day Karnataka) and defeated Satyashraya at Annigeri. Follow-up raids into the Bijapur–Donur region and Banavasi were pressed in this period, though Satyashraya recovered ground up to the Tungabhadra. Rajendra Chola I, then crown prince, took part in these northern campaigns, but his own great expansions came only after his accession in 1014; the contest with the Chalukyas was bound up with the long struggle over the Vengi succession.

w4-600012.name: Henry II of Germany recovers Lusatia/Silesia from Poland (Peace of Merseburg context)
w4-600012.blurb: Henry II of Germany launched a campaign against Bolesław I the Brave of Poland in 1005, recovering control of territories (including the Silesia/Bohemia borderland at lng 14.1, lat 50.4) that Bolesław had seized during the German-Polish wars; the campaign was part of the series of conflicts ultimately settled by the Peace of Merseburg (1013) and Peace of Bautzen (1018).

w4-600014.name: Fitna of al-Andalus — emergence of the Taifa of Toledo
w4-600014.blurb: The Fitna (civil war) that destroyed the Caliphate of Córdoba began in 1009 and led to the rapid fragmentation of al-Andalus into independent taifa kingdoms. The Dhunnunid rulers established the Taifa of Toledo as an independent entity circa 1010–1018, taking control of the central meseta territory around Toledo, Cuenca, and Ciudad Real that had been Caliphal lands. The centroid is exactly the Toledo region.

w4-600015.name: Kara-Khanid conquest of Khotan
w4-600015.blurb: Yusuf Qadir Khan of Kashgar (Kara-Khanids) conquered the Kingdom of Khotan in 1006, ending Khotan's existence as an independent Buddhist state and completing the Islamization of the Tarim Basin. This event falls squarely in the atlas window 1005–1010.

w4-600016.name: Founding of the Taifa of Dénia during Caliphate collapse
w4-600016.blurb: Mujāhid al-'Āmirī, a freed Slavic slave (saqaliba), established the Taifa of Dénia around 1010 during the fitna (civil war) that destroyed the Caliphate of Córdoba. He seized Dénia and its hinterland in the Valencian region, and by 1015 had extended his realm to the Balearic Islands.

w4-600018.name: Foundation of the Taifa of Tortosa during the Fitna of al-Andalus
w4-600018.blurb: The Taifa of Tortosa was established around 1009–1010 by the Slavic warlord Labib al-Fata al-Saqlabi as the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed during the Fitna civil war. The territory (centroid lng 1.1, lat 41.2, the lower Ebro valley around Tortosa) broke away from central caliphal control, establishing an independent taifa.

w4-600019.name: Henry I of Burgundy acquires Nevers but it separates as a distinct county
w4-600019.blurb: When Henry I of Burgundy (Henry the Venerable, brother of Hugh Capet) died without an heir in 1002, the Duchy of Burgundy was disputed between King Robert II of France and Otto-William, Henry's adopted stepson. The County of Nevers, already a hereditary comital lordship since about 989–990 under Landry of Nevers (Otto-William's son-in-law), stood apart from the ducal succession. Landry backed Otto-William and seized Auxerre, before making peace with Robert II in 1005, leaving Nevers as a distinct county rather than part of the royal duchy.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Henry I, Duke of Burgundy

w4-600022.name: Founding of the Taifa of Almería
w4-600022.blurb: Khayran al-'Āmirī, a saqaliba (Slavic freed slave) official, established independent control of Almería around 1012-1015 during the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba. He developed Almería into a major Mediterranean trading port and naval power.

w4-600023.name: Cnut's conquest of England — Battle of Assandun and subsequent treaty
w4-600023.blurb: Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside at the Battle of Assandun (18 October 1016) and the subsequent Treaty of Olney divided England, with Edmund retaining Wessex; Edmund died on 30 November 1016, giving Cnut all of England and creating the Danish-English union. The atlas records territory shifting from 'Kingdom of England' to 'Kingdom of Denmark' in the 1014–1015 snapshot, likely reflecting the earliest phase of Cnut's invasion (1013–1014 conquest by Sweyn Forkbeard, followed by Cnut's own conquest 1015–1016).

w4-600024.name: Emergence of Taifa of Saltés during collapse of Caliphate of Córdoba
w4-600024.blurb: During the fitna (civil war) that destroyed the Caliphate of Córdoba after 1009, local governors and Berber leaders seized power across Al-Andalus. The Taifa of Saltés and Huelva emerged around 1012–1018 as an independent principality from the caliphal wreckage, likely under Berber Siqlabi leadership.

w4-600025.name: Reassertion of Swedish control over Götaland after Cnut's English conquest
w4-600025.blurb: Following Sweyn Forkbeard's death in February 1014 and Cnut's renewed but initially unsuccessful English campaign, Denmark's grip on disputed Swedish borderlands (Götaland/Scania) loosened. Anund Jakob of Sweden exploited Danish preoccupation with the English succession struggle to reassert control over these contested territories around 1014–1015.

w4-600026.name: Mujahid al-Amiri's conquest of Sardinia for the Taifa of Dénia
w4-600026.blurb: Mujahid al-Amiri, ruler of the Taifa of Dénia, launched a seaborne invasion of Sardinia around 1015–1016, conquering most of the island from the Giudicati including Arborea (centroid ~9°E, 40.4°N). Dénia held parts of Sardinia until expelled by a Pisan-Genoese fleet around 1016–1022, making this a short-lived but dateable conquest.

w4-600027.name: Mujahid al-Amiri's invasion of Sardinia
w4-600027.blurb: In 1015, Mujahid al-Amiri, ruler of the Taifa of Dénia, launched a large naval invasion of Sardinia with 120 ships, seizing coastal territory from the Giudicato of Cagliari and defeating the Cagliari army. He fortified his conquests before internal mutiny and Pisan-Genoese naval resistance ultimately forced his withdrawal.

w4-600028.name: Mujahid al-Amiri's naval conquest of the Balearic Islands
w4-600028.blurb: Mujahid al-Amiri, the Slavic-origin ruler of Dénia (independent since 1010), used his fleet to seize control of the Balearic Islands in 1015, extending his taifa's maritime reach ahead of a subsequent failed invasion of Sardinia. This corresponds to the Balearic/Valencian-coast centroid recorded for the change.

w4-600029.name: Collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba and emergence of Taifa of Murcia
w4-600029.blurb: After the fitna (civil war) that destroyed the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba beginning in 1009, local governors and strongmen carved out independent principalities (taifas). By around 1011–1015, the Murcia region broke away from Córdoban control under local leadership, with the area around the centroid initially falling under Almería's sphere before a Murcian taifa coalesced.

w4-600032.name: Founding of the Taifa of Carmona during Caliphate collapse
w4-600032.blurb: The Taifa of Carmona was established around 1013 by the Banu Birzal Berber clan during the disintegration of the Caliphate of Córdoba. The centroid (lat 37.4, lng -5.1) corresponds to the Carmona/Seville hinterland that the new taifa controlled.

w4-600035.name: Collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba and emergence of Taifa kingdoms
w4-600035.blurb: The Caliphate of Córdoba fragmented during the Fitna (civil war) of 1009–1031; the Taifa of Zaragoza under the Tujibid dynasty emerged as an independent principality by c. 1018, after local governors asserted autonomy during the chaos of the Hammudid counter-caliphate. The ~41,275 km² shift records this formal separation of the Upper March from Córdoba.

w4-600036.name: Battle of the Bug River and Polish seizure of Red Ruthenia
w4-600036.blurb: Boleslaw I of Poland defeated Yaroslav the Wise at the Battle of the Bug River in 1018 and captured Kiev, during which he re-annexed the Cherven cities (Red Ruthenia, centroid ~23.3°E, 51.2°N) from Kievan Rus'. This is the mirror-image companion change to 600062, which shows Yaroslav's reconquest of the same territory in 1031.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Bug River (1018)

w4-600037.name: Expulsion of Mujahid al-Amiri's forces from Sardinia
w4-600037.blurb: Following Mujahid al-Amiri's 1015 invasion, a combined Pisan-Genoese fleet destroyed his remaining ships and forces in 1016, while mutiny undermined his land troops. His mother and son were captured; Mujahid fled back to Dénia, and the seized territory reverted to the Giudicato of Cagliari.

w4-600038.name: Reversion of Sardinian territory to Giudicato of Cagliari after Dénia expulsion
w4-600038.blurb: After the Pisan-Genoese destruction of Mujahid al-Amiri's fleet in 1016 forced the Dénia forces off Sardinia, territory in the border zone between the Giudicato of Arborea and Giudicato of Cagliari that had been disturbed by the invasion reverted to Cagliari's control. The neighboring Arborea giudicato also ceded or lost ground to Cagliari in the post-invasion settlement.

w4-600040.name: Cnut the Great's conquest of Sweden's Baltic territories
w4-600040.blurb: Cnut the Great (Canute), after consolidating England (1016) and Denmark (1019), created the North Sea Empire that exercised overlordship over parts of Scandinavia. In Swedish territory (centroid ~14°E, 56.6°N, corresponding to Scania/Blekinge), Cnut imposed Danish suzerainty by around 1018–1026 through military campaigns and treaties, reflected in the Cliopatria transfer from Sweden to the North Sea Empire.

w4-600043.name: Rajendra Chola I's conquest of Sri Lanka
w4-600043.blurb: In 1017 Rajendra Chola I completed his father's conquest of the island by overrunning the Kingdom of Polonnaruwa, capturing the Sinhalese king Mahinda V and carrying him back to India; the Anuradhapura kingdom ceased to exist as an independent polity, absorbed into the Chola Empire.

w4-600044.name: Peace of Bautzen (1018) — Poland cedes Moravia/Slovakia to Hungary
w4-600044.blurb: Around 1018 the Kingdom of Hungary under Stephen I (István) recovered the northwestern Upper Hungarian (Slovak) lands between the Morava and Vág rivers that Bolesław I Chrobry of Poland had occupied since the early 11th century. Stephen had allied with Emperor Henry II against Poland during the Boleslavian wars, and as that conflict wound down — culminating in the Peace of Bautzen (30 January 1018) between Bolesław and the Empire — Bolesław gave up his Hungarian-frontier conquests, restoring Hungarian control of the region. (Note: the Peace of Bautzen itself concerned Lusatia and Meissen, not a direct Polish cession to Hungary; the earlier blurb conflated the two.)

w4-600048.name: Byzantine annexation of Vaspurakan (bequest of Senekerim-Hovhannes)
w4-600048.blurb: Around 1021-1022, the Armenian Artsruni king Senekerim-Hovhannes of Vaspurakan, harassed by Turkic raids, ceded his kingdom around Lake Van to Emperor Basil II in exchange for estates at Sebasteia (Sivas). The Byzantine Empire thereby annexed Vaspurakan, advancing its eastern frontier into Armenia.

w4-600050.name: Jingkang Incident / Jin conquest of Northern Song
w4-600050.blurb: The Jurchen Jin besieged Kaifeng and captured Emperors Huizong and Qinzong in the Jingkang Incident (January 1127); the Song court fled south and Prince Zhao Gou proclaimed the Southern Song on 12 June 1127. The dataset's [1018,1028] window is a ~100-year date artifact in the Cliopatria source; the true event date is 1127, corrected here. The named transition 'Northern Song' to 'Southern Song' is genuine and well-attested.

w4-600051.name: Abbadid founding of the Taifa of Seville amid the Caliphate's collapse
w4-600051.blurb: As the Caliphate of Córdoba disintegrated during the Fitna civil wars, the qadi Abu al-Qasim Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Abbad was appointed to head Seville's governing council in 1023 and soon established the independent Abbadid Taifa of Seville, absorbing former caliphal territory in the lower Guadalquivir basin as central authority in Córdoba collapsed and the Caliphate was formally abolished by 1031.

w4-600055.name: Suryavarman I's incorporation of Lavo (Lopburi) into the Khmer Empire
w4-600055.blurb: Khmer king Suryavarman I (r. 1002-1050), who had already installed a Khmer-appointed governor over Lavo (Lopburi) in 1006, completed the political absorption of the Chao Phraya (Menam) basin into Angkor's administrative structure by around 1025, ending Lavo's separate existence as a Dvaravati Mon polity and giving the Khmer Empire a western frontier province controlling the overland route toward the Kra Isthmus trade corridor.

w4-600059.name: Odo II of Blois acquires Champagne
w4-600059.blurb: After the heirless death of his cousin Stephen I (1019/1020), Count Odo II of Blois seized Troyes, Meaux, and Champagne c. 1019–1023, uniting Blois and Champagne into one powerful domain. The coordinates are the Champagne plateau,

citations.label: Odo II, Count of Blois – Wikipedia

w4-600062.name: Malcolm II Places Duncan on Strathclyde Throne - Absorption into Kingdom of Alba
w4-600062.blurb: In his final years Malcolm II of Alba arranged for his grandson Duncan to rule Strathclyde after Owen the Bald died without an heir. When Malcolm died on 25 November 1034, Duncan I succeeded to both Alba and Strathclyde, uniting them under a single Scottish crown. The coordinates point to the Clyde valley heartland of Strathclyde. This dynastic manoeuvre effectively extinguished Strathclyde as a separate polity, within the 1028-1034 window.

w4-600064.name: Death of Rudolf III of Burgundy and Conrad II's annexation of the Kingdom of Arles
w4-600064.blurb: When the childless King Rudolf III of Burgundy (Arles) died in September 1032, Emperor Conrad II claimed the kingdom under a succession pact Rudolf had made with Conrad's predecessor Henry II in 1016. After putting down a rival claim from Count Odo II of Blois-Champagne, who invaded and briefly held parts of Burgundy before being defeated by 1034, Conrad had himself crowned King of Burgundy at Peterlingen (Payerne) in 1033, formally uniting the Kingdom of Arles with the Holy Roman Empire as one of its constituent realms.

citations.label: Conrad II, Holy Roman Emperor — Wikipedia

w4-600065.name: Conrad II's inheritance of the Kingdom of Arles (Burgundy)
w4-600065.blurb: On the death of the childless King Rudolph III of Burgundy in 1032, Emperor Conrad II of the Holy Roman Empire enforced his prior inheritance claim and was crowned king of Burgundy/Arles in 1033, defeating rival claimant Odo II of Blois. The Kingdom of Arles (Lower Burgundy/Provence) was thereby incorporated into the Holy Roman Empire.

w4-600066.name: Chalukya-Chola wars: Jayasimha II's recovery of the Tungabhadra Deccan
w4-600066.blurb: During the long Chalukya-Chola wars, the Western Chalukya king Jayasimha II contested the Tungabhadra-Raichur Doab frontier with the Cholas under Rajendra Chola I around 1028-1034. This change reflects Chalukya recovery of the contested Deccan borderland from Chola occupation in the early 1030s.

w4-600068.name: Seljuk capture of Merv and conquest of Khorasan
w4-600068.blurb: In 1037 Chaghri Beg's Seljuk forces captured Merv, the first great city of Khorasan to fall, with the khutba read in Chaghri's name - the de facto beginning of Seljuk rule in Khorasan. The Ghaznavid field army was then routed near Sarakhs in May 1038, after which Tughril was proclaimed ruler at Nishapur, and the decisive Battle of Dandanaqan (1040) finally extinguished Ghaznavid power in the region.

w4-600070.name: Ferdinand I's unification of León-Castile and annexation of Galicia
w4-600070.blurb: Ferdinand I of Castile defeated and killed his brother-in-law Bermudo III of León at the Battle of Tamarón on 4 September 1037. Bermudo left no heirs, and Ferdinand - through his wife Sancha, Bermudo's sister - was crowned King of León in June 1038, uniting Castile and León. His forces then extended raids into and annexed Galicia by 1040, completing the union of the three realms under one crown.

w4-600071.name: Fernando I Defeats Bermudo III at Tamarón – Union of Galicia and León
w4-600071.blurb: Fernando I of Castile defeated and killed Bermudo III of León at the Battle of Tamarón on 4 September 1037, claiming León through his wife Sancha and being crowned King of León in 1038. Galicia, held within Bermudo's Leonese realm, was permanently united under Fernando (~-7.6E/42.7N). Window [1037,1040], date 1037.

w4-600072.name: Taifa of Valencia conquers Almería (c. 1038)
w4-600072.blurb: Around 1038, Abd al-Mālik ibn Abd al-Azīz, ruler of the Taifa of Valencia, conquered the Taifa of Almería, holding it until approximately 1041-1044. Almería was a prosperous trading city with a major silk and textile industry, making it an attractive prize among the competing taifa kingdoms that emerged after the fragmentation of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031. The Taifa of Almería eventually regained independence under the Banū Sumādih dynasty before being absorbed by the Almoravids in 1091.

w4-600073.name: Partition of Odo II's domains – Champagne separated from Blois (1037)
w4-600073.blurb: On the death of Count Odo II of Blois (15 Nov 1037), who had united Blois and Champagne, his domains were divided: Theobald III took Blois/Chartres/Tours while Stephen II received the Champagne counties of Troyes and Meaux. This split of Champagne away from Blois matches the recorded Blois → Champagne transfer in the 1037–1040 window.

citations.label: Odo II, Count of Blois – Wikipedia

w4-600082.name: Harthacnut unites Denmark and England
w4-600082.blurb: Harthacnut became King of England in 1040 (after Harold Harefoot's death) while already holding Denmark, uniting the two crowns. The from→to (Kingdom of Denmark → Denmark-England) at southern Scandinavia (12.1,56) reflects this personal union in the 1037–1040 window.

w4-600083.name: Ferdinand I of León-Castile campaigns against Badajoz and expansion into Galicia (c. 1037-1040)
w4-600083.blurb: After Ferdinand I defeated and killed Bermudo III at the Battle of Tamarón (4 September 1037), he united Castile with León and soon extended his control to Galicia (annexed by 1040). Ferdinand's early campaigns pressured the Taifa of Badajoz, extracting tribute and seizing territory in the Douro and Mondego river valleys. The dataset records Badajoz territory passing to the Kingdom of Galicia around 1037-1040, consistent with Ferdinand's annexation of Galicia after 1037 and his subsequent raids on Badajoz lands.

w4-600084.name: Airlangga's Division of Kahuripan into Janggala and Kediri
w4-600084.blurb: King Airlangga of Kahuripan in East Java divided his kingdom between his two sons in 1042, creating the Kingdom of Janggala in the east (centered on Kahuripan) and the Kingdom of Panjalu/Kediri in the west (centered on Daha). The Ngantang inscription and other contemporaneous sources record this event. Airlangga himself abdicated and became a hermit in 1045, leaving the two successor states to engage in prolonged rivalry.

w4-600089.name: Magnus the Good's union of Norway and Denmark
w4-600089.blurb: Magnus the Good (Magnus den gode), king of Norway since 1035, inherited Denmark on the death of Harthacnut in 1042 under an earlier mutual-succession pact, uniting the two crowns. This personal union placed Norway (here the Trøndelag/western Norway region near 6.1E, 62.6N) under the combined Norway-Denmark monarchy. The arrangement lasted until Magnus's death in 1047.

w4-600090.name: Magnus the Good inherits Denmark, uniting Norway and Denmark (1042)
w4-600090.blurb: In 1042, Magnus I (Magnus the Good), already King of Norway since 1035, inherited the Danish throne under a succession pact with Harthacnut: each king had agreed that whoever outlived the other would inherit both kingdoms. When Harthacnut died childless in 1042, Magnus united Norway and Denmark in a personal union that lasted until his death in 1047. The dataset records the border region of Scania/Götaland (coords 13.8E, 57.6N) transitioning to a Norway-Denmark label around 1040-1046, consistent with Scania belonging to the Danish realm now joined under Magnus's combined crown.

w4-600092.name: Magnus the Good inherits Denmark; Norway-Denmark union
w4-600092.blurb: On Harthacnut's death in 1042, Magnus the Good of Norway inherited Denmark per their succession treaty, creating a Norway-Denmark union that he held against Sweyn Estridsson into the mid-1040s. The from→to (Kingdom of Denmark → Norway-Denmark) at (12.1,56) matches this in the 1040–1046 window.

w4-600093.name: Division of the Kara-Khanid Khanate into Eastern and Western branches
w4-600093.blurb: Around 1041 the Kara-Khanid Khanate formally split into Eastern and Western branches when Muhammad ʿAyn al-Dawla took over the western family. The Western Karakhanid Khanate, centred at Samarkand and Bukhara, controlled Transoxiana (coordinates lng 68.1, lat 40.6); the Eastern Khanate held Kashgar and Semirechye. The split was crystallised partly by the Battle of Dandanaqan (1040). Window py=1040, y=1046 brackets it.

w4-600094.name: Battle of Tamarón and Union of León and Castile
w4-600094.blurb: Ferdinand I of Castile defeated and killed Bermudo III of León at the Battle of Tamarón on September 4, 1037, claiming León by right of his wife Sancha, and was crowned King of León and Castile in 1038. This territorial shift over the León region (coords ~-6.3E/41.9N) reflects Castilian control spreading over Leonese territory across the [py=1040, y=1046] window.

w4-600095.name: Ferdinand I unites Galicia/León under Castile
w4-600095.blurb: Ferdinand I of Castile became King of León after defeating Bermudo III at Tamarón (1037) and ruled Galicia as well, consolidating the northwestern Iberian kingdoms under his royal authority. The transition Kingdom of Galicia → Kingdom of Castile at (-7.6,42.2) in the 1040–1046 window reflects this consolidation.

w4-600097.name: Partition of Kahuripan into Kediri and Janggala
w4-600097.blurb: In 1045 King Airlangga of Kahuripan divided his kingdom between two sons to prevent civil war over succession. The sage Mpu Bharada ritually delineated the boundary, creating Kediri (Pañjalu) in the south and Janggala in the north. Kediri eventually absorbed Janggala and became the dominant kingdom in East Java (lat -7.4, lng 110.7). Window 1040-1046.

w4-600099.name: Valencian annexation of the Taifa of Almería
w4-600099.blurb: After the death of Almería's ruler Zuhayr in 1038, a power vacuum drew in Abd al-Aziz of the Taifa of Valencia, whose forces occupied Almería around 1038-1041. Valencian control was brief: the governor installed by Abd al-Aziz declared independence and the Banu Sumadih dynasty re-established Almería's autonomy by the early 1040s.
