The data window 1040-1046 (from Valencia to Almería) reflects Almería throwing off this brief Valencian control.

w4-600101.name: Seljuk westward expansion into the Jazira / Azerbaijan after Dandanaqan
w4-600101.blurb: Following their decisive victory over the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040, the Great Seljuks under Tughril Beg pushed west across Iran into Azerbaijan and the Jazira, overrunning the local dynasties. The territory near 46.4E/37.8N (Azerbaijan/upper Mesopotamia, associated with Hamdanid/Marwanid-era successor emirates) fell under Seljuk overlordship as Tughril advanced toward Baghdad. This was part of the rapid Turkmen conquest of western Iran in the 1040s.

w4-600105.name: Accession of the Lohara dynasty in Kashmir
w4-600105.blurb: The Lohara dynasty came to rule Kashmir when Samgramaraja founded the line after the death of Queen Didda in 1003, succeeding the Utpala/older Kashmir kingship. By the mid-11th century the Vale of Kashmir (75.3E/33.7N) was firmly under Lohara rule as chronicled in Kalhana's Rajatarangini. The transfer reflects the consolidation of the Lohara house over the Kashmir realm.

w4-600106.name: Lohara/Kashmiri recovery of the northwest frontier from the Ghaznavids
w4-600106.blurb: After Mahmud of Ghazni's failed campaigns against Kashmir, Ghaznavid power on the upper Indus and Kashmir's western marches receded, and the Lohara rulers of Kashmir held the mountainous frontier near 72.3E/36N (the region toward Gilgit/Chitral). Ghaznavid attention turned to internal crises and India proper after 1040, leaving these highlands to Kashmir. The shift marks Lohara/Kashmiri control over former Ghaznavid borderlands.

w4-600109.name: Gruffydd ap Llywelyn's conquest of Deheubarth and unification of Wales
w4-600109.blurb: Gruffydd ap Llywelyn, king of Gwynedd and Powys, killed his southern rival Gruffydd ap Rhydderch in 1055 and seized Deheubarth, then drove out the rulers of Gwent and Brycheiniog in the southeast, becoming sole ruler of all Wales by 1057 — the only time the country was united under one native king.

w4-600110.name: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn subjugates Brycheiniog and unifies Wales (1055–1057)
w4-600110.blurb: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn, King of Gwynedd and Powys, killed his rival Gruffudd ap Rhydderch in 1055 and asserted overlordship over all Welsh kingdoms including Brycheiniog, becoming the only Welsh king ever to rule the whole of Wales until his death in 1063. From=Kingdom of Brycheiniog, to=Kingdom of Gwynedd reflects this unification in the 1046-1056 window.

w4-600112.name: Geoffrey Martel of Anjou conquers the County of Maine (c. 1051-1056)
w4-600112.blurb: After Count Hugh IV of Maine died in 1051, Geoffrey II Martel of Anjou invaded Maine, took Le Mans, and Hugh's son Herbert II fled to Normandy in 1056. The window (1046-1056) captures this Angevin conquest of Maine.

citations.label: Herbert II, Count of Maine - Wikipedia

w4-600117.name: Kipchak conquest of the Oghuz Yabgu State along the Syr Darya
w4-600117.blurb: From the early 11th century the Kimek-Kipchak confederation expanded into the Oghuz Yabgu State's lower Syr Darya heartland. The Oghuz state, already weakened by the Seljuk rebellion (the 1040 Battle of Dandanaqan and the 1041 defeat of the last yabgu Shah Malik), could not resist; by the mid-11th century the Kipchaks had seized the Aral and lower Syr Darya region (the steppe becoming 'Dashti-Kipchak'), with the Oghuz state ending c. 1055 and displaced Oghuz groups migrating toward Anatolia and Persia. The worklist window of 1046-1056 (Oghuz Turks to Kimek-Kipchak confederation) matches.

citations.label: UNESCO Silk Road: States of the Oghuz, Kimek and Kipchak

w4-600120.name: Tughril Beg's capture of Baghdad and the end of Buyid rule
w4-600120.blurb: In December 1055 the Seljuk sultan Tughril Beg entered Baghdad at the invitation of the Abbasid Caliph al-Qa'im, who sought relief from the Shi'a Buyid amirs and the rebellious general al-Basasiri. Tughril deposed the last Buyid ruler, al-Malik al-Rahim, ending over a century of Buyid dominance over the Abbasid caliphate and transferring Iraq and western Iran to the Great Seljuk Empire; the Caliph invested Tughril with the title of Sultan.

w4-600121.name: Seljuk conquest of the Buyid territories in Fars/western Iran
w4-600121.blurb: The Great Seljuks under Tughril Beg dismantled the Shia Buyid (Buwayhid) confederation in western Iran during the 1040s-1050s, culminating in Tughril's entry into Baghdad in 1055 and the end of Buyid power. The southern Iranian region of Fars and the Persian Gulf coast (50.8E/29.3N) passed from the Buyids to the Seljuks. This established Seljuk dominance over Iran.

w4-600122.name: Seljuk advance into the Jazira (upper Mesopotamia)
w4-600122.blurb: As Tughril Beg's Seljuks expanded westward toward Baghdad in the early-to-mid 1050s, they extended overlordship over the upper Mesopotamian/Jazira region near 42.6E/35.4N (around Mosul and the Khabur), formerly tied to Hamdanid/Uqaylid-era successor emirates. The Turkmen pressure brought these lands under Seljuk authority. This was part of the broader Seljuk takeover of the eastern Abbasid heartland.

w4-600123.name: Duklja's consolidation of independence from Byzantium under Mihailo Vojislavljević
w4-600123.blurb: Stefan Vojislav's Dukljans annihilated a Byzantine army at the Battle of Bar (1042), securing de facto independence for Duklja from Constantinople. After Vojislav's death in 1043, his son Mihailo (r. from 1046) consolidated this autonomy through the 1040s-50s, ruling Duklja and its dependencies (Travunija, Zahumlje, Raška) while only nominally acknowledging Byzantine authority.

w4-600127.name: Fragmentation of Kievan Rus' — Chernigov appanage to Sviatoslav Yaroslavich
w4-600127.blurb: Under Yaroslav the Wise's 1054 testament, his third son Sviatoslav Yaroslavich received Chernigov together with the left-bank Dnieper lands, Murom, and Tmutarakan, establishing the Principality of Chernigov (c. 31.3°E/51.5°N) as a separate appanage carved from the unitary Kievan Rus' realm under the new rota succession system.

w4-600132.name: Yaroslav the Wise's death and testamentary partition of Kievan Rus' — Pereyaslavl to Vsevolod
w4-600132.blurb: Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise died on 20 February 1054. In his testamentary partition of Kievan Rus' among his sons, the Pereyaslav (and Rostov) lands were assigned to his son Vsevolod as a separate appanage, detaching the Pereyaslavl region from unitary Kievan rule and founding the Principality of Pereyaslavl.

w4-600139.name: Ghaznavid campaigns in the Punjab/Rajputana frontier
w4-600139.blurb: In the mid-11th century the Ghaznavid Empire, ruling Punjab from Lahore after Mahmud of Ghazni's earlier raids, pressed against the Chauhan (Chahamana) dynasty of Shakambhari along the Thar/Rajputana frontier. The territory around 74.8E,29.3N (the Hisar-Sirsa area) shifted to Ghaznavid control during these frontier campaigns. The frontier remained contested for decades.

w4-600141.name: Fragmentation of Kievan Rus' / Principality of Polotsk autonomy
w4-600141.blurb: On the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054, Kievan Rus' was divided among his sons, accelerating the rise of autonomous principalities. The Principality of Polotsk, long restive under the Rurikid Iziaslavich line of Vseslav, asserted effective independence from Kiev around this time. The lands near Polotsk (27.8E,55.1N) thus passed from the Kievan center to the Polotsk principality.

w4-600142.name: Re-establishment of the independent Taifa of Murcia (1065)
w4-600142.blurb: Through the mid-11th century Murcia had been ruled by or subject to neighboring taifas -- Almería, Valencia, and Dénia. In 1065 -- the same year the Taifa of Valencia was itself seized by Toledo -- Murcia broke free of this overlordship and re-emerged as an independent taifa, a phase of independence that lasted until 1078.

w4-600149.name: Raymond IV inherits the County of Rouergue
w4-600149.blurb: Around 1066 Raymond IV of Saint-Gilles inherited the County of Rouergue through familial succession, while his elder brother William IV held the County of Toulouse. Raymond, of the Toulouse house, reunited Rouergue with Toulouse upon William IV's death in 1094. The from=County of Rouergue / to=County of Toulouse and the 1056-1066 window reflect Rouergue passing into the Toulouse dynastic sphere.

citations.label: Raymond IV, Count of Toulouse - Wikipedia

w4-600150.name: Karakhanid border shift — Ferghana attached to the Western Khanate
w4-600150.blurb: The Kara-Khanid Khanate had split into Eastern and Western branches by 1041, with Ferghana–Semirechye a contested border zone. Around 1059–1060 Ibrahim b. Nasr of the Western (Alid) branch attached Ferghana to his domain, striking coins in his name in the region; the border between the two khanates ran along the Syr Darya. The dataset records 'Eastern Kara-Khanids → Western Karakhanid Khanate' near lng 72, lat 40.4 (Ferghana Valley) in the 1056–1066 window — i.e. Ferghana passing to the Western Khanate, consistent with Ibrahim's conquest.

w4-600151.name: Partition of the Kingdoms of Fernando I of León–Castile
w4-600151.blurb: When Fernando I (Ferdinand the Great) died on 24 December 1065, he partitioned his realm among his three sons: Sancho II received Castile, Alfonso VI received León, and García I received Galicia. This division caused Castile and León to become separate kingdoms again for about a decade, until Sancho II conquered León in 1071 and was assassinated in 1072, after which Alfonso VI reunited both crowns. The territorial shift from Castile to León in the 1056–1066 window reflects the boundary changes surrounding Fernando's reign and final partition.

w4-600153.name: Union of Gascony and Aquitaine under Guy-Geoffrey (William VIII)
w4-600153.blurb: Following a succession crisis in Gascony after the extinction of the native ducal line around 1039, Guy-Geoffrey of the Poitevin house won control of Gascony by 1052 and became Duke of Aquitaine in 1058, merging both titles. The absorption of Gascony (lat 44.1, lng -0.3) into the Duchy of Aquitaine is traditionally dated to 1058, within the 1056-1066 window.

w4-600156.name: Almoravid Conquest of the Barghawata
w4-600156.blurb: The Almoravid movement swept northward into Morocco after 1056 and encountered the Barghawata, a long-independent Berber confederation on the Atlantic coast practicing a syncretic Islam. Almoravid leader Abdullah ibn Yasin launched a jihad against the Barghawata and fell in battle against them in 1059. His successor Abu Bakr ibn Umar continued the campaign and subdued the Barghawata, forcing conversion to orthodox Sunni Islam. The dataset window 1056–1066 captures this decisive Almoravid absorption of Barghawata territory.

w4-600157.name: Collapse of Byzantine authority in Dalmatia under Mihailo I of Duklja
w4-600157.blurb: Continuing the consolidation begun by his father Stefan Vojislav's 1042 victory at Bar, Mihailo I of Duklja pressed Byzantine authority on the Dalmatian coast during the 1050s-60s, absorbing neighbouring Slavic lands (Travunija, Zahumlje, Raska) and reducing effective Byzantine control outside Dubrovnik and the southern tip.

w4-600158.name: Rise of Duklja under Stefan Vojislav / Mihailo I
w4-600158.blurb: Duklja (Zeta), under Stefan Vojislav and his son Mihailo Vojislavljevic, threw off Byzantine suzerainty after Vojislav's victory over a Byzantine army at the Battle of Bar (1042), and expanded in the following decades. The Serbian Adriatic hinterland around 19.6E,43.1N passed from Byzantine to Dukljan control, with Mihailo later recognized as king (c.1077).

w4-600159.name: Reunification of Blois and Champagne under Theobald III
w4-600159.blurb: Odo II had united Blois and Champagne, but on his death in 1037 the domains were divided: Blois to Theobald III, Champagne (Meaux/Troyes) to his brother Stephen. After Stephen died (c.1048) Theobald acted as regent for his minor nephew Odo, and from 1063 formally held the Champagne counties as Theobald I, reuniting them under the comital authority of Blois.

citations.label: Theobald III, Count of Blois — Wikipedia
Odo II, Count of Blois — Wikipedia

w4-600160.name: Theobald III of Blois seizes the County of Champagne
w4-600160.blurb: In 1066 Theobald III of Blois exploited his nephew Odo's departure to England with William the Conqueror to seize Odo's Champagne holdings (Troyes, Meaux), uniting Blois and Champagne. Eastern Champagne near lng 4.3 E / lat 48.8 N passed from the County of Champagne (Troyes line) to the County of Blois, matching the [1056,1066] window.

citations.label: Theobald III, Count of Blois – Wikipedia

w4-600169.name: Norman Conquest of England
w4-600169.blurb: On 14 October 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated and killed Harold II at Hastings, was crowned king on Christmas Day 1066, and by 1072 had suppressed major resistance. Normandy (lat 49.7, lng 0) thereby became the base of the new Norman English realm, merging the Duchy of Normandy with the Norman kingdom of England. Window 1066-1072.

w4-600178.name: Elevation of Duklja to a kingdom under Mihailo I
w4-600178.blurb: Mihailo I (Michael I) of Duklja, after aiding the 1072 Slavic uprising against Byzantium and seeking papal support, was recognized by Pope Gregory VII as Rex Docleae (King of Duklja) c. 1077, raising the Great Principality to the Kingdom of Duklja. The coordinates are the Montenegro/Adriatic region. (The elevation slightly postdates the dataset's 1066–1072 window, which captures the broader transition under Mihailo.)

w4-600182.name: Abbadid Seville's absorption of Caliphate remnant territories
w4-600182.blurb: Under Abbad II al-Mu'tadid (r. 1042–1069) and his son al-Mu'tamid (r. 1069–1091), Seville systematically annexed neighboring taifas and former Caliphate lands; the centroid points to the Córdoba hinterland area absorbed when al-Mu'tamid seized Córdoba in 1071.

w4-600190.name: Henry IV's 1081 diploma grants Pisa communal autonomy
w4-600190.blurb: Amid the Investiture Controversy, Emperor Henry IV, seeking Pisan support against Pope Gregory VII and Countess Matilda of Tuscany, issued a diploma (1081) recognizing Pisa's self-governing consular commune and releasing it from the lordship of the Margraves of Tuscany, formalizing Pisa's practical independence from direct imperial administration.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor

w4-600197.name: Rise of Duklja under Mihailo Vojislavljević
w4-600197.blurb: In the 1070s-1080s, the Principality of Duklja (Zeta) under Mihailo Vojislavljević expanded its influence along the Dalmatian coast at the expense of the weakened Croatian kingdom. Croatia suffered from internal succession crises following King Petar Krešimir IV's death around 1074-1076, and Duklja exploited this to extend control over coastal territories between 1072 and 1085. Mihailo received a royal crown from a papal legate in 1077, formalizing Duklja's status as a kingdom.

w4-600198.name: Norman conquest of the Emirate of Sicily (fall of Syracuse and southern Sicily)
w4-600198.blurb: The Norman brothers Robert Guiscard and Roger I conquered Palermo in 1072, ending Kalbid rule and establishing Norman control over the western island. Roger I then steadily reduced the remaining Muslim-held cities; Syracuse fell in 1085, the same year Robert Guiscard died. The period 1072–1085 represents the transition from the Emirate of Sicily to Norman Italy across most of the island's territory.

citations.label: Norman conquest of southern Italy – Wikipedia
Roger I of Sicily – World History Encyclopedia

w4-600203.name: Hudid (Banu Hud) conquest of Denia (1076), uniting it with the Tortosa-Lérida-Zaragoza realm
w4-600203.blurb: The Hudid ruler al-Muqtadir of Zaragoza, who had already taken Tortosa in 1061 and Lérida earlier, conquered the Taifa of Dénia in 1075-76, absorbing its territory into the same Hudid domain that held Tortosa -- ending Dénia's independent existence. Under his son Mundhir, Dénia, Tortosa, and Lérida formed the realm's eastern portion from 1081.

w4-600206.name: Rostislavichi Partition - Establishment of Principality of Terebovlia
w4-600206.blurb: Around 1084-1085, Grand Prince Vsevolod I of Kiev enabled the three sons of Rostislav Vladimirovich to reclaim their father's lands in southwestern Rus'. The territories were divided into the principalities of Przemyśl, Zvenyhorod, and Terebovlia, carving them out of land previously administered as Kievan Rus'. Vasylko Rostyslavych received Terebovlia, confirmed at the Council of Liubech in 1097. This partition shifted the region from direct Kievan control to a semi-independent appanage; it falls at the late end of the dataset window (1072-1085).

w4-600207.name: Rostislavichi Partition - Border of Peremyshl and Terebovlia Established
w4-600207.blurb: The Rostislavichi partition of c. 1084-1085 divided southwestern Rus' into three principalities and drew a border between Peremyshl (Volodar) and Terebovlia (Vasylko). Territory previously in Peremyshl's orbit was allocated to Terebovlia in the Galicia/Podolia borderlands. Grand Prince Vsevolod I enabled the three Rostyslavych brothers to reclaim their father's lands; the grants were confirmed at the Council of Liubech (1097). Falls at the late end of the dataset window (1072-1085).

w4-600211.name: Alfonso VI of Castile Captures Toledo (1085)
w4-600211.blurb: Alfonso VI of León and Castile besieged and captured Toledo, the capital of the Taifa of Toledo, on 25 May 1085 after the Dhulnunid ruler Yahya al-Qadir surrendered. This was the most significant territorial gain of the Reconquista to that point, returning the ancient Visigothic capital to Christian rule. Alfonso proclaimed himself 'Emperor of All Spain' and Toledo became a major center of cultural exchange.

citations.label: Alfonso VI of León and Castile – Wikipedia

w4-600213.name: Alfonso VI reunites León and Castile (1072)
w4-600213.blurb: The blurb originally described the 1085 conquest of Toledo, which does not match the recorded from=Kingdom of León / to=Kingdom of Castile. The event matching this direction is the 1072 reunification: after Sancho II of Castile (who had defeated and exiled Alfonso in early 1072) was assassinated at Zamora in October 1072, Alfonso VI recovered León and inherited Castile, joining the two realms in personal union (1072-1157). The 1072-1085 window opens on this union; the coordinates near Toledo reflect territory subsequently consolidated under the combined Leonese-Castilian crown.

citations.label: Alfonso VI of León and Castile - Wikipedia
Sancho II of Castile and León - Wikipedia

w4-600217.name: Almoravid annexation of the Denia region
w4-600217.blurb: After their 1086 victory at Sagrajas, Yusuf ibn Tashfin's Almoravids systematically absorbed the remaining Andalusi taifas (Granada, Cordoba, Seville, Almeria). The Denia/Valencian coastal region — whose mainland had earlier passed to the Taifa of Zaragoza in 1076 — was brought under Almoravid control around 1092.

w4-600218.name: Almoravid conquest of Almería
w4-600218.blurb: The Almoravids, having crossed into al-Andalus to halt the Christian advance, turned on the Muslim taifa rulers they had come to defend. The Taifa of Dénia, a coastal Valencian principality centered on its namesake port and the Balearic-facing Levante, lost its independence to Almoravid forces around 1091–1092 as Yusuf ibn Tashfin absorbed the eastern Iberian taifas. Dénia's harbor and shipyards made it a valuable maritime asset for the consolidating Almoravid state.

w4-600219.name: Almoravid conquest of the Taifa of Badajoz
w4-600219.blurb: In 1094 Almoravid forces under Sir ibn Abu Bakr captured Badajoz, killing the Aftasid ruler al-Mutawakkil and absorbing the Taifa of Badajoz (covering much of modern Portugal and Extremadura, -7.1,38.9). This matches the from→to (Taifa of Badajoz → Almoravid Dynasty) in the 1085–1094 window.

w4-600220.name: Almoravid conquest of the taifa kingdoms including the Toledo region (1086–1094)
w4-600220.blurb: After Alfonso VI of Castile captured Toledo in 1085, Andalusian taifa rulers appealed to the Almoravid emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin. The Almoravids defeated Alfonso at Sagrajas (1086) then between 1090 and 1094 annexed the taifas one by one, absorbing most of al-Andalus including the territories formerly in the Taifa of Toledo's orbit by 1094.

w4-600221.name: Almoravid conquest of the Taifa of Granada (1090)
w4-600221.blurb: In September 1090 Almoravid emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin besieged and captured Granada, forcing the last Zirid ruler Abdallah ibn Buluggin into exile in Aghmat, justified by Maliki fatwas against tribute to Christian kings. This ended the Zirid taifa's ~77-year independence, matching the Taifa of Granada→Almoravid transfer at (−3.7°E, 37.2°N) in the 1085–1094 window.

w4-600225.name: Ladislaus I of Hungary's conquest of Croatia
w4-600225.blurb: After King Zvonimir died in 1089 and his ineffectual successor Stephen II died without an heir in early 1091, a Croatian noble faction invited Zvonimir's brother-in-law King Ladislaus I of Hungary to intervene. Ladislaus crossed the Drava in 1091 and occupied all of Slavonia and much of Croatia (halted only at Mt. Gvozd by loyalist noble Petar Svacic), installing his nephew Almos as administrator and founding the Diocese of Zagreb — the opening move of the Hungarian-Croatian union.

w4-600229.name: Secession of Raska (Serbia) from Duklja under Vukan
w4-600229.blurb: After a Byzantine campaign against Bodin of Duklja (c.1089-1091) and ensuing civil war, outlying Duklja territories including Bosnia, Rascia (Raska) and Hum broke away. Bodin's kinsman Vukan, previously his vassal zupan in Raska, became a self-governing Grand Prince and began expanding independently of Duklja from around 1090-1091.

citations.label: Vukan, Grand Prince of Serbia — Wikipedia

w4-600230.name: Vukan of Rascia breaks from Duklja and founds the Grand Principality of Serbia
w4-600230.blurb: When King Bodin of Duklja was captured by the Byzantines around 1090, his vassal Vukan of Rascia (Raška) seized the opportunity to declare independence, taking the title of Grand Župan. He founded the Grand Principality of Serbia centered at Ras (near modern Novi Pazar), raided Byzantine territory in the Balkans, and concluded a peace with Emperor Alexios I Komnenos in 1094. This marks the transfer of Serbian political dominance from coastal Duklja to inland Rascia.

w4-600231.name: Emergence of the Principality of Ryazan (Murom-Ryazan)
w4-600231.blurb: Amid the continuing fragmentation of Kievan Rus' formalized at the Council of Liubech (1097), the Murom-Ryazan lands became a distinct appanage principality. The southeastern frontier territory around 40.3E,54.1N passed from the Kievan center to the Principality of Ryazan.

w4-600234.name: Welsh revolt of 1094 -- Gruffudd ap Cynan recovers Gwynedd from Norman control
w4-600234.blurb: As the First Crusade passed through the upper Euphrates, Baldwin of Boulogne broke from the main army and in 1098 took control of Edessa, an Armenian-populated city under the local ruler Thoros, founding the County of Edessa as the first of the Crusader states. The county extended Latin authority across the Euphrates frontier into former Byzantine and Seljuk-contested lands. It became a buffer protecting the later Crusader principalities to the south and west.

citations.label: Wikipedia: History of Gwynedd in the High Middle Ages

w4-600240.name: Welsh revolt of 1094 -- Cadwgan ap Bleddyn recovers Powys from Norman control
w4-600240.blurb: In 1097 the armies of the First Crusade, marching alongside Byzantine contingents, besieged and took Nicaea (June 1097) and routed the Seljuk forces of Kilij Arslan I at Dorylaeum (July 1097). These victories stripped the Seljuks of their hold over northwestern and central Anatolia, opening the plateau to renewed Byzantine authority under Alexios I Komnenos. The centroid in west-central Anatolia falls within the corridor the Seljuks lost in this campaign.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Wales in the High Middle Ages

w4-600242.name: Kulottunga I captures Vengi from the Western Chalukyas
w4-600242.blurb: The Chola emperor Kulottunga I, who also held a claim to the Eastern Chalukya throne of Vengi, pressed his advantage against the rival Western Chalukyas of Kalyani and secured control of the contested Vengi region (the Krishna-Godavari deltas) by 1099, though the Western Chalukyas would recapture it in 1118.

w4-600243.name: Byzantine recovery of western Anatolia after the First Crusade (Siege of Nicaea)
w4-600243.blurb: Aided by the armies of the First Crusade, Emperor Alexios I Komnenos besieged and recovered Nicaea (Iznik), the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum's capital, in June 1097. Byzantine forces then swept through western Anatolia in 1097-1099, retaking Smyrna, Ephesus, Sardis and the Maeander valley from Sultan Kilij Arslan I. This reversed two decades of Seljuk expansion since Manzikert (1071) and pushed the Rum frontier back onto the central Anatolian plateau, forcing Kilij Arslan to make Konya his new capital.

w4-600244.name: Siege of Antioch and founding of the Principality of Antioch
w4-600244.blurb: During the First Crusade, a Crusader army besieged Antioch, then held by the Seljuk governor Yaghi-Siyan, from October 1097. On 3 June 1098 the city fell through the treachery of the guard Firouz, who let Bohemond of Taranto's forces in; after repelling Kerbogha's relief army on 28 June, Bohemond proclaimed himself Prince of Antioch, founding the Crusader Principality of Antioch on former Seljuk territory.

w4-600247.name: Almoravid conquest of Zaragoza
w4-600247.blurb: After Ahmad II al-Musta'in fell at Valtierra (January 1110), the Almoravid general Muhammad ibn al-Hajj entered Zaragoza on 30 May 1110, ending the last independent taifa in al-Andalus. The Ebro valley near lng -0.6 E / lat 41.5 N passed from the Taifa of Zaragoza to the Almoravid dynasty, matching the [1102,1111] window.

w4-600249.name: Almoravid conquest of the Taifa of Albarracín (1104)
w4-600249.blurb: The Taifa of Albarracín (Banu Razin), a Berber-ruled taifa in eastern Iberia, was conquered by the Almoravids in 1104 under its last ruler Yahya Husam ad-Dawla. The Almoravids absorbed the fragmented taifas through the 1090s-1110s. From=Taifa of Albarracín, to=Almoravid Dynasty matches the 1102-1111 window.

w4-600252.name: Fragmentation of Kievan Rus' into appanage principalities
w4-600252.blurb: Following the Council of Liubech (1097), which formalized the partition of Kievan Rus' among the descendants of Yaroslav the Wise, lands fragmented into hereditary appanage principalities. The Principality of Drutsk emerged as a distinct polity carved from the Polotsk-Smolensk borderlands in the early 12th century. This reflects the dynastic subdivision of Rus' rather than a foreign conquest.

w4-600253.name: Partition of Polotsk after Vseslav's death
w4-600253.blurb: Upon the death of Prince Vseslav of Polotsk (24 April 1101), his realm was divided among his six sons in the customary Rus' apanage system. The Principality of Drutsk emerged as one of several sub-principalities carved from Polotsk, awarded to Rogvolod-Boris and centred on the upper Drut River in what is now central Belarus. This fragmentation mirrors the broader dissolution of Kievan Rus' following the end of strong central rule.

w4-600254.name: Fulk V of Anjou inherits Maine through marriage to Eremburge (1110)
w4-600254.blurb: Fulk V became Count of Anjou in 1109 and married Eremburge of Maine in 1110; when her father Elias I died, Fulk inherited Maine by right of his wife, restoring Angevin control after the Norman interlude. The window (1102-1111) and shift toward Angevin control fit this acquisition around 1110.

w4-600255.name: Rise of the Hoysalas under Vishnuvardhana
w4-600255.blurb: The Hoysalas, originally feudatories of the Western Chalukya Empire, asserted independence in the Gangavadi (modern southern Karnataka) under Vishnuvardhana in the early 12th century. He expanded from his hill capital and seized Chalukya-held districts in the Malnad and Mysore plateau. This marked the beginning of the Hoysala kingdom's territorial breakaway from its Chalukya overlords.

w4-600260.name: Partition of Polotsk among Vseslav's sons — Minsk to Gleb Vseslavich
w4-600260.blurb: Following the 1101 partition of Polotsk among the sons of Vseslav Bryachislavich, the Principality of Minsk emerged under Gleb Vseslavich, who aggressively expanded his appanage against neighboring Rus' lands. In the early 1100s Gleb raided into the Dnieper basin and clashed repeatedly with Kiev, drawing Minsk into open conflict with the senior Rus' princes. The atlas records the resulting territorial shift from Kievan Rus' to the assertive Minsk principality.

w4-600263.name: Tancred's conquest of Cilicia and the Orontes valley for Antioch
w4-600263.blurb: The northern Lebanese coast around Tripoli was held in the late 11th century by the Banu Ammar, a local qadi dynasty, not by the Hamdanids. The Crusaders, having besieged Tripoli since 1102 under Raymond IV of Toulouse, captured the city on 12 July 1109 and established the County of Tripoli. The atlas's Hamdanid label reflects an older layer of Levantine political geography rather than the city's actual early-12th-century rulers.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Timeline of the Principality of Antioch

w4-600264.name: Fragmentation of the Principality of Polotsk — founding of Vitebsk
w4-600264.blurb: Between 1101 and 1110, King Baldwin I of Jerusalem, supported by Genoese, Pisan and other Italian fleets, methodically reduced the Levantine coastal cities held by Muslim garrisons: Arsuf and Caesarea (1101), Acre (1104), and Beirut (1110). The political fragmentation of the Great Seljuk realm under the rival brothers Barkiyaruq and Muhammad Tapar left these ports without coordinated relief. The captured coast was annexed to the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

w4-600266.name: Partition of the Principality of Polotsk after Vseslav's Death
w4-600266.blurb: On the death of Vseslav the Seer of Polotsk on 24 April 1101, his principality was divided among his six surviving sons. Sviatoslav Vseslavich received the volost of Vitebsk, founding the Principality of Vitebsk as an appanage of the Polotsk dynasty. The dataset records 'Principality of Polotsk → Principality of Vitebsk' for the region near lng 29.1, lat 56, in the window 1102–1111 — directly consistent with this post-Vseslav partition.

w4-600274.name: Alfonso I 'the Battler' of Aragon's control of former Castilian territory and Peace of Támara
w4-600274.blurb: Alfonso I 'El Batallador' of Aragon married Urraca of Castile-León in 1109, using the union to exercise royal power over Castile. After Urraca's death in 1126, Alfonso refused to relinquish control of territories in the Rioja and upper Ebro region (lat 42, lng -3) he effectively ruled. Alfonso VII of Castile pressed his claim, and the two settled with the Peace of Támara (1127), by which Alfonso the Battler recognised Castilian sovereignty. The dataset window 1111–1126 reflects the period of Aragonese dominance over Castilian border territories.

w4-600275.name: Georgian conquest of Shirvan under David IV the Builder
w4-600275.blurb: David IV of Georgia campaigned repeatedly against the Muslim emirates on Georgia's southeastern border: he crushed the Seljuk field army at Didgori (1121), then invaded Shirvan in 1123 (capturing Gulustan) and again in 1124 (capturing Shamakhi and Derbent), bringing large stretches of the Shirvan/Ganja borderlands under Georgian control.

w4-600278.name: Almoravid reconquest of the Balearic Islands (1116)
w4-600278.blurb: The Balearic Islands -- the maritime remnant of the old Taifa of Dénia -- were assaulted by a Pisan-Catalan crusading expedition in 1113-15. In 1116 an Almoravid fleet expelled the remaining Christian (Pisan) garrisons and reconquered the islands, installing Almoravid governors (the Banu Ghaniya) who ruled in the Almoravids' name.

w4-600280.name: Absorption of County of Berga into County of Barcelona
w4-600280.blurb: The counties of Champagne and Blois were united under Count Theobald II of Champagne (Theobald IV of Blois), who inherited Blois and Chartres in 1102 and Champagne in 1125, joining the two great Loire-and-Marne lordships under a single Thibaudian count. The atlas records the resulting reorganization of these northern French comital territories in the early 12th century. The combined holdings made Theobald one of the most powerful magnates in the Kingdom of France.

w4-600284.name: Fulk V's rule of Anjou and Angevin dynastic consolidation
w4-600284.blurb: Fulk V the Young succeeded as Count of Anjou in 1109 and consolidated Angevin holdings (Maine, Anjou, Touraine) under a strong personal rule that the atlas labels 'Angevins' as distinct from the earlier County of Anjou designation. The ~29,446 km² shift between 1111–1126 likely reflects this atlas reclassification of the same territory under a new polity label corresponding to the Angevin dynastic identity.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Fulk V, Count of Anjou

w4-600285.name: Fulk V of Anjou inherits Maine through marriage to Eremburge (1110)
w4-600285.blurb: After Fulk V became Count of Anjou in 1109 he married Eremburge, heiress of Maine, in 1110; her father Elias I died shortly after, making Fulk count of Maine by right of his wife and restoring Angevin control after the Norman interlude. The window (1111-1126) reflects Angevin consolidation of Maine following this marriage.

w4-600286.name: Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth — Creation of Duchy of Silesia
w4-600286.blurb: Upon his death in 1138, Duke Bolesław III Wrymouth of Poland divided his realm by testament into principalities under a seniorate system. Silesia (coords 18E/52N) was assigned to his eldest son Władysław II the Exile, who also held Kraków as senior duke. This fragmentation created the Duchy of Silesia as a separate political unit; the [py=1130, y=1139] window brackets the partition.

w4-600287.name: Battle of Ourique and Afonso Henriques' Declaration of Independence
w4-600287.blurb: Afonso Henriques had warred against his suzerain León since the Luso-Leonese War (1130–1137). After his victory over Almoravid forces at Ourique on 25 July 1139, his army proclaimed him King of Portugal and he renounced Leonese suzerainty. Formal recognition came with the Treaty of Zamora (1143), but León lost effective control over Portugal's core by 1139. Window [1130,1139], date 1139; territory from León to County of Portugal.

w4-600289.name: Partition of Aragon and Navarre after Alfonso I's death (1134)
w4-600289.blurb: Alfonso I 'the Battler' of Aragon died childless on 7 September 1134, triggering a succession crisis. The Navarrese nobility refused Ramiro II and elected their own king Garcia Ramirez, restoring the independent Kingdom of Navarre after 58 years of union with Aragon. Ebro valley territories were divided between the two newly separate kingdoms, with peace formalized around 1135–1139.

w4-600290.name: Jin–Song Wars and the Jingkang Incident
w4-600290.blurb: After conquering the Liao, the Jurchen Jin turned on the Northern Song, sacking the capital Kaifeng in 1127 (the Jingkang Incident) and capturing Emperors Huizong and Qinzhong. The Song court fled south to reestablish as the Southern Song, ceding all of north China above the Huai River to the Jin. This catastrophe transferred the entire North China Plain to Jin control.

w4-600292.name: Kara-Khitan conquest of Eastern Kara-Khanid territories
w4-600292.blurb: In the early-to-mid 12th century the Western Chalukya Empire of Kalyani and the Chola Empire of the south contested the Tungabhadra-Krishna doab and the eastern Deccan in a prolonged frontier struggle. The atlas records a transfer of territory between the two great peninsular powers as Chola fortunes recovered against Chalukya pressure. This Deccan rivalry defined South Indian politics until both dynasties declined later in the century.

w4-600293.name: Kara-Khitan subjugation of Qocho (Turfan Uyghur Kingdom)
w4-600293.blurb: The Kara-Khitan (Western Liao) khanate, expanding rapidly after its foundation by Yelü Dashi c. 1124, incorporated the Qocho (Turfan) Uyghur kingdom as a vassal in 1128, during the reign of Bilge Tekin. The change appears in the atlas in the 1130–1139 snapshot, reflecting the Cliopatria data resampling a submission that actually occurred in 1128.

w4-600295.name: Death of Bolesław III Wrymouth and fragmentation of Poland
w4-600295.blurb: In the early 12th century the maritime Republic of Pisa and the Holy Roman Empire contended over authority in Tuscany and the Tyrrhenian coast, where imperial claims pressed against the autonomy of the rising Italian communes. The atlas records a transfer of territory in this Italian zone between Pisan and imperial control. Pisa's growing naval and commercial power made it a key player in the contest between commune and empire in northern Italy.

w4-600296.name: Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth (fragmentation of Poland)
w4-600296.blurb: On Bolesław III Wrymouth's death (28 October 1138) his Testament fragmented Poland; Polish suzerainty over the Duchy of Pomerania ended and the duchy became independent (soon drawn toward the Empire and Denmark). The Pomeranian region near lng 15.3 E / lat 53.9 N passed from the Kingdom of Poland to an independent Pomerania, matching the [1130,1139] window.

citations.label: Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth – Wikipedia

w4-600297.name: Demetrius I of Georgia restores Shirvan vassalage under Manuchihr
w4-600297.blurb: In 1129–1130, Demetrius I of Georgia reached a compromise (aided by his sister) whereby eastern Shirvan was returned to the Shirvanshah Manuchihr II as a Georgian vassal/client-state, while the Christian western strip remained annexed to Georgia. Eastern Shirvan near lng 48.1 E / lat 40.1 N thus passed from direct Georgian control to the (vassal) Shirvanshahs, matching the [1130,1139] window.

w4-600301.name: Seljuk counteroffensive against Georgia (post-David IV)
w4-600301.blurb: After David IV's death in 1125, his successor Demetrius I of Georgia faced Seljuk and local Muslim counterattacks along the southern frontier. Seljuk-aligned forces recovered some borderlands south and east of Tbilisi in the 1130s, partially reversing David's gains around the Kura valley. This reflects the back-and-forth Georgian-Seljuk frontier warfare of the period.

w4-600302.name: Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth – fragmentation of Poland
w4-600302.blurb: Bolesław III Wrymouth (d. 28 Oct 1138) issued a testament dividing Poland among his sons, assigning Greater Poland (Poznań, Gniezno) to Mieszko III the Old as a hereditary duchy and launching Poland's period of feudal fragmentation. The coordinates are Poznań / Greater Poland.

citations.label: Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth – Wikipedia

w4-600303.name: Alfonso VII of Castile annexes Aragonese border territory after the 1134 succession crisis
w4-600303.blurb: The worklist codes a transfer from the Kingdom of Aragon to the Kingdom of Castile in py 1130, y 1139. After Alfonso I of Aragon died heirless in 1134, his brother Ramiro II took a weakened throne; Alfonso VII of León-Castile exploited Aragon's vulnerability and annexed Aragonese (and Navarrese) border districts, becoming the leading Christian ruler in Iberia. This — not the Petronilla / Ramon Berenguer IV betrothal (which formed the Crown of Aragon and actually checked Castilian influence) — is the event that attests the Aragon-to-Castile shift. Direction matches; the betrothal originally cited was the wrong event.

w4-600305.name: Testament of Bolesław III Krzywousty — partition of Poland
w4-600305.blurb: The 1138 testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth divided Poland among his sons, inaugurating the period of feudal fragmentation. Among the resulting appanages was the Duchy of Sandomierz, carved from the Polish kingdom and assigned to one of Bolesław's sons (Henry of Sandomierz). The atlas records Sandomierz's separation from the unified realm as a distinct duchy.

w4-600307.name: Srivijaya's loss of Kedah amid Chola raids and imperial decline
w4-600307.blurb: Srivijaya's control of the Malay Peninsula weakened sharply after the Chola raids of 1025 and following decades. Around 1130–1139 Kedah effectively separated from Srivijayan suzerainty as the empire fragmented; the (disputed) Kedah Annals record the Sultanate of Kedah's foundation in 1136. Whether a sharp discontinuity or gradual disintegration, the Srivijaya→Kedah change at (100.4°E, 5.9°N) is real in broad strokes.

w4-600308.name: Almohad conquest of the Almoravids (rise of Ibn Tumart/Abd al-Mu'min)
w4-600308.blurb: The Almohad movement, founded by the Mahdi Ibn Tumart and led after his death by Abd al-Mu'min, revolted against the Almoravid Dynasty in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco. From the late 1120s the Almohads seized the Almoravid heartland in the High Atlas and Sus, beginning the conquest that would topple Marrakesh in 1147. This transferred large areas of southern Morocco from Almoravid to Almohad control.

w4-600309.name: Kediri's Conquest of Janggala under King Jayabaya
w4-600309.blurb: King Jayabaya of Kediri (r. c. 1135–1159) conquered the rival kingdom of Janggala around 1135, as recorded in the Ngantang inscription bearing the motto 'Panjalu jayati' (Panjalu triumphs). This reunified the territory of the former Kahuripan kingdom under Kediri, ushering in a golden age of Javanese culture.

w4-600310.name: Rubenid expansion in Cilicia under Leo I
w4-600310.blurb: The Armenian Rubenid prince Leo I (Levon) expanded the principality of Cilicia at Byzantine expense in the 1130s-1140s, capturing plains cities such as Mamistra, Adana, and Tarsus. Despite Emperor John II Komnenos's campaign of 1137-1138 that temporarily restored Byzantine rule, Armenian control over much of Cilicia was reasserted by the mid-1140s. This moved Cilician territory from Byzantium to the Armenian principality.

w4-600311.name: Geoffrey Plantagenet becomes Count of Anjou; consolidation into Angevin Empire
w4-600311.blurb: Geoffrey V Plantagenet, count of Anjou by 1129 and husband of the Empress Matilda, invaded Normandy during the Anglo-Norman civil war and completed its conquest by 1144, when he was recognized as Duke of Normandy. Joining Normandy to the Angevin patrimony built the continental core of what would become the Angevin Empire under his son Henry II. The atlas relabels the territory accordingly as the cross-Channel realm took shape.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Geoffrey V, Count of Anjou

w4-600312.name: Formation of the Angevin Empire under Geoffrey Plantagenet
w4-600312.blurb: This change reflects the consolidation of the Angevin domains (the County of Anjou and associated Plantagenet lands) into the larger Angevin Empire. Geoffrey Plantagenet, count of Anjou, conquered Normandy by 1144 and merged it with Anjou and Maine, and through his marriage to Empress Matilda set the stage for the cross-Channel Angevin realm later ruled by Henry II. This is a dynastic/cartographic consolidation of Angevin core lands.

w4-600313.name: Geoffrey Plantagenet consolidates Maine within the Angevin domain
w4-600313.blurb: Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou and Maine, consolidated his Angevin holdings in the 1140s, completing his conquest of Normandy by 1144-1145 and suppressing baronial revolts (he was also long at odds with his brother Elias, whom he held captive until Elias's death in 1151). Through this period Maine remained firmly within the Angevin domain, passing to his son Henry II in 1151-1154. The data window 1139-1147 captures Maine's consolidation under Angevin control.

citations.label: Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou – Wikipedia

w4-600314.name: Incorporation of Anjou into the Angevin Empire
w4-600314.blurb: The County of Anjou, the Plantagenet patrimony, was absorbed into the broader Angevin Empire during the consolidation of Geoffrey Plantagenet's domains in the 1140s. Geoffrey's conquest of Normandy (completed 1144) joined Anjou to the larger cross-Channel realm that his son Henry II would inherit. This represents the dynastic merger of the Angevin core county into the imperial agglomeration.

w4-600315.name: Seljuk suzerainty over Khwarazm (Sanjar's campaigns)
w4-600315.blurb: The Khwarazmian rulers (Khwarazmshahs) were vassals of the Great Seljuk Empire under Sultan Ahmad Sanjar in this period. Sanjar repeatedly campaigned against rebellious Khwarazmshahs such as Atsiz, reasserting Seljuk control over Khwarazm and the lower Oxus region in the 1130s-1140s. This reflects Seljuk overlordship being imposed (or reimposed) over the Khwarazmid lands, though Seljuk power collapsed soon after the Battle of Qatwan (1141).

w4-600318.name: Almoravid collapse and re-emergence of Taifa of Badajoz (Second Taifas)
w4-600318.blurb: As Almoravid authority in al-Andalus collapsed after 1140, the Second Taifa period saw local powers reassert independence. Around the port of Almería, a renewed taifa briefly emerged from Almoravid control before the Almohads and, in Almería's case, a Christian-led coalition intervened later in the decade. The atlas records the breakaway of the Almería region from the disintegrating Almoravid state.

w4-600319.name: Afonso Henriques captures Santarém and Lisbon
w4-600319.blurb: Afonso Henriques, having proclaimed himself King of Portugal, pressed south in the Reconquista, taking Santarém by surprise in March 1147 and Lisbon in October 1147 with Northern European crusaders. These conquests roughly doubled the young kingdom and shifted its frontier toward the Tagus. Window [1139,1147], date 1147; territory moved from County to Kingdom of Portugal (~-7.6E/40.9N).

w4-600320.name: Fall of Marrakesh and Fez to the Almohads
w4-600320.blurb: In the final stage of their conquest of the Almoravid realm, the Almohads under Abd al-Mu'min took Fez after a long siege in 1146 and stormed Marrakesh, the Almoravid capital, in 1147, killing the last Almoravid ruler Ishaq ibn Ali. The centroid in northern Morocco lies within this Almoravid core that passed to the Almohads. The conquest extinguished the Almoravid dynasty and made the Almohads masters of the Maghreb.

w4-600321.name: Collapse of Almoravid rule and re-emergence of Second Taifa of Saltés
w4-600321.blurb: When Almoravid power in al-Andalus disintegrated in the early 1140s, the Second Taifa of Badajoz re-emerged around 1144 under local rulers, breaking free of the collapsing Almoravid state. This revived Extremaduran taifa, centered on Badajoz on the Guadiana, survived only briefly before the Almohad advance. The atlas records its separation from Almoravid control.

w4-600322.name: Almoravid collapse and re-emergence of the Taifa of Córdoba (1145)
w4-600322.blurb: As the Almoravid dynasty disintegrated in al-Andalus, the Córdobans expelled the Almoravid governor in early 1145 and raised Ibn Hamdin as emir, re-establishing the Taifa of Córdoba at the start of the second taifa period. The coordinates (-4.2, 38) point to Córdoba; the window (1139-1147) captures this transitional flux before the Almohads absorbed the city.

w4-600323.name: Almohad capture of Fez from the Almoravids
w4-600323.blurb: After defeating the Almoravids at Oran and killing their king Tashfin ibn Ali in 1145, Abd al-Mu'min's Almohad forces besieged and captured Fez in 1146 after a nine-month siege, before turning south to besiege Marrakesh, which fell in 1147. This transferred northern Morocco (Fez and the surrounding Rif/Sale/Tangier region) from the Almoravids to the Almohad Caliphate.

w4-600326.name: Fragmentation of Poland under Bolesław III Wrymouth's Testament
w4-600326.blurb: On the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138, his Testament divided Poland among his sons into hereditary provincial duchies, beginning the period of fragmentation. Silesia passed to Władysław II while Masovia was assigned to Bolesław IV the Curly; the redistribution of lands and the 1146 civil war that exiled Władysław II shifted territory and influence toward Masovia and the junior dukes. This dataset change reflects that partition of the Piast realm.

w4-600329.name: Collapse of Almoravid power; second taifa period begins
w4-600329.blurb: From the early 1140s the Almoravid dynasty in al-Andalus collapsed amid the Almohad advance and internal revolts; a second wave of taifa statelets emerged c. 1144–1147. The Taifa of Dénia / eastern al-Andalus (coord 1.9W/38.3N, Murcia-Alicante coast) reasserted local autonomy before Ibn Mardanish incorporated it c. 1147. The dataset's 'Almoravid → Taifa of Dénia' shift in 1139–1147 reflects this fragmentation; event real and correctly dated.

w4-600331.name: Establishment of the Principality of Halych under Volodymyrko
w4-600331.blurb: Around 1141 Volodymyrko Volodarovych united the small Rurikid principalities of southwestern Rus' (Przemyśl, Zvenyhorod, Terebovlia) into a single Principality of Halych (Galicia) with its capital at Halych. This consolidated a major autonomous principality out of the disintegrating Kievan Rus', and the territory near the upper Dniester passed under Halych's distinct rule. The change marks Halych's emergence as a power independent of Kiev.

w4-600332.name: Volodymyrko Volodarovych unifies Peremyshl into the Principality of Halych
w4-600332.blurb: Prince Volodymyrko Volodarovych consolidated the Galician principalities of Zvenyhorod, Peremyshl, and Terebovlia into a unified Principality of Halych between 1124 and 1141–1144, with his capital at Halych, laying the foundation for Galicia-Volhynia. The worklist transfer Principality of Peremyshl → Principality of Halych at lng 24, lat 49.5 in the 1139–1147 window matches the final stage of this consolidation.

w4-600333.name: Consolidation of Galicia under Volodymyrko Volodarovych
w4-600333.blurb: Volodymyrko Volodarovych (Vladimirko), prince of the Zvenyhorod branch of the Rostyslavych dynasty, systematically absorbed the fragmented western Rus' principalities. He took control of Peremyshl (1129) and by 1141 had incorporated the Principality of Terebovlia into his expanding domain, moving his residence to Halych in 1141 (some sources 1144) and establishing it as the unified capital. This consolidation created the Principality of Galicia, which became one of the most powerful states in Kievan Rus'. The dataset window 1139–1147 reflects this absorption of Terebovlia into the Halych polity.

w4-600334.name: Battle of Qatwan
w4-600334.blurb: At the Battle of Qatwan (near Samarkand) in September 1141, the Kara-Khitan (Western Liao) under Yelü Dashi crushed the army of the Great Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar, who was allied with the Khwarazmian ruler Atsiz. The victory gave the Kara-Khitans suzerainty over Transoxiana and reduced Khwarazm to tributary status, transferring control over the lands east of the Aral and along the lower Syr Darya. This change reflects Kara-Khitan dominance over former Khwarazmian frontier territory.

w4-600337.name: Almohad conquest of Badajoz
w4-600337.blurb: Amid the Almohad conquest of al-Andalus, the short-lived Second Taifa of Carmona, ruled by the Berber Darddusid emir Darddus, held out in the lower Guadalquivir before falling to the Almohad Caliphate in 1150. The Almohads' systematic reduction of the second-period taifas brought Carmona under their authority as they consolidated control of the peninsula's interior. The atlas records the absorption of the Carmona region into the Almohad realm.

w4-600338.name: Almohad conquest of Córdoba
w4-600338.blurb: During the Almohad takeover of al-Andalus in the late 1140s, the short-lived second taifas of the Levante were drawn under Almohad sway. The Taifa of Valencia, which had reasserted local autonomy amid the Almoravid collapse, came into the Almohad orbit as Abd al-Mu'min's forces extended their authority over eastern al-Andalus. The atlas records the transfer of the Valencia region from Almoravid-era rule into the Almohad fold.

w4-600339.name: Almohad conquest of the Hammadid dynasty under Abd al-Mu'min
w4-600339.blurb: The Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min marched east against the Hammadid dynasty in 1151-1152, seizing Algiers and then the capital Béjaïa; the last Hammadid ruler Yahya ibn Abd al-Aziz surrendered on 10 November 1152. The conquest extinguished the Hammadid dynasty and incorporated its central Maghrib territories into the Almohad Caliphate. The centroid in northern Algeria lies within the absorbed Hammadid heartland.

w4-600340.name: Almohad conquest of Carmona
w4-600340.blurb: As the Almohads reduced the Second Taifas of al-Andalus, the revived Taifa of Badajoz on the Guadiana lost its brief independence and was absorbed into the Almohad Caliphate around 1150, ending the Extremaduran taifa's short second life. The Almohad reduction of the peninsula's western marches followed their landing in Iberia in the late 1140s. The atlas records the transfer of the Badajoz region into Almohad control.

w4-600341.name: Almohad conquest of al-Andalus (capture of Córdoba)
w4-600341.blurb: After overthrowing the Almoravids in the Maghreb, the Almohad Caliphate under Abd al-Mu'min crossed into Iberia and absorbed the fragmented taifa states that had re-emerged in al-Andalus. Córdoba and its surrounding territory fell under Almohad control around 1148-1149 as the caliphate suppressed the local taifa rulers. This change reflects the Almohad takeover of the Córdoba region.

w4-600342.name: Almohad conquest of the Hammadid dynasty
w4-600342.blurb: Abd al-Mu'min, first Almohad caliph, launched his eastern North African campaign in 1151, defeating the Hammadid dynasty of northeastern Algeria. In August 1152 he captured Béjaïa (the Hammadid capital), and Yahya, the last Hammadid emir, surrendered on 10 November 1152. This completed Almohad control of the Maghreb. The data window 1147-1152 captures the transfer from the Hammadid dynasty to the Almohad Caliphate.

w4-600344.name: Lohara expansion into the northwest (Ghaznavid frontier) — data-adjacent frontier shift
w4-600344.blurb: The Lohara dynasty ruled Kashmir in the mid-12th century, and the dataset records adjacent Ghaznavid frontier lands near the upper Indus/Gilgit passing to Lohara control as Ghaznavid power collapsed under Ghurid pressure. The waning of Ghaznavid authority in the trans-Indus mountain regions allowed neighboring Kashmiri/Lohara authority to extend into them. This frontier shift is plausibly real but lacks a single named battle.

w4-600346.name: Lohara consolidation of the Kingdom of Kashmir
w4-600346.blurb: The Lohara dynasty was the ruling house of the Kingdom of Kashmir in this period, so this change reflects the equivalence/relabeling of Lohara-ruled lands as 'Kashmir' rather than an external conquest. Under rulers such as Jayasimha the core Vale of Kashmir remained firmly under Lohara administration. The shift is best read as a dynasty-to-realm reassignment within the same polity.

w4-600353.name: Khwarazmian independence and seizure of Khorasan after Sanjar's fall
w4-600353.blurb: The defeat of the Great Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar and his capture by the rebellious Oghuz Turks in 1153 shattered Seljuk authority in Khorasan. The Khwarazmshahs, who had grown autonomous after Qatwan (1141), expanded westward to seize the now-ungoverned Seljuk lands around the Kara Kum and Khorasan frontier. This large transfer reflects the collapse of Seljuk power and Khwarazmian takeover of its eastern provinces.

w4-600354.name: Norman conquest of Ifriqiya (Kingdom of Africa)
w4-600354.blurb: Roger II of Sicily sent his admiral George of Antioch with a fleet to capture the Zirid capital of Mahdia in June 1148, exploiting famine and the internal collapse of the Zirid dynasty. With Mahdia, Sousse and Sfax taken, Roger II established the short-lived 'Kingdom of Africa' (Regnum Africae) over the Tunisian coast. By 1152 the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min began the eastward advance that would end Norman rule there by 1160.

w4-600356.name: Ghurid sack of Ghazni (Ala al-Din Husayn 'Jahansuz')
w4-600356.blurb: In 1151 the Ghurid ruler Ala al-Din Husayn, nicknamed Jahansuz ('World-Burner'), sacked and burned Ghazni in revenge for the Ghaznavid execution of his brothers. The campaign broke Ghaznavid power in the Afghan highlands and transferred core territory around Ghazni and Zamindawar to the Ghurids. This change reflects the Ghurid seizure of Ghaznavid heartland.

w4-600357.name: Zengid conquest of the County of Edessa (final fall to Nur al-Din)
w4-600357.blurb: The Crusader County of Edessa fell to Imad al-Din Zengi in 1144 (sparking the Second Crusade), and the remaining western Edessene territory was extinguished when Nur al-Din captured the last fortresses around 1150-1151 after Joscelin II's capture. The Zengid dynasty absorbed the county's lands in the Euphrates region. This change reflects the final Zengid annexation of Edessa.

w4-600359.name: Ibn Mardanish expands Taifa of Murcia northward into Valencian territory
w4-600359.blurb: As effective Almoravid authority in al-Andalus collapsed after 1145, Muhammad ibn Mardanish (the 'Wolf King', r. 1147–1172) built an independent realm centered on Murcia and Valencia in the Sharq al-Andalus. By the early 1150s his domain absorbed the former Almoravid territory of this eastern frontier (centroid near the Valencia–Murcia border), which he held against the rising Almohads until his death. The atlas records the passage of this zone from the disintegrating Almoravid sphere to Ibn Mardanish's Taifa of Murcia.

w4-600361.name: Ibn Mardanish incorporates Dénia into Taifa of Murcia
w4-600361.blurb: After the Almoravid collapse, Muhammad ibn Mardanish (the 'Wolf King') established the Taifa of Murcia c. 1147 and expanded over Dénia, Valencia and parts of Jaén. Coord 1.9W/38.3N (Murcia/Alicante coast) matches the territory shifting from Dénia's orbit to Murcia. Ibn Mardanish ruled until 1172, when the Almohads absorbed his realm. The dataset's 1147–1152 'Taifa of Dénia → Taifa of Murcia' shift matches; event real and correctly dated.

w4-600362.name: Ibn Mardanish unifies Taifas of Valencia and Murcia
w4-600362.blurb: Following the collapse of Almoravid power in al-Andalus by 1147, Ibn Mardanish (Muhammad ibn Sa'd) emerged as dominant ruler of eastern al-Andalus, taking control of both Valencia and Murcia. He ruled the two jointly until his death in 1172, when the Almohads absorbed them. The worklist transfer Taifa of Valencia → Taifa of Murcia at lng -1, lat 40 in the 1147–1152 window matches this consolidation of the eastern taifas under one ruler.

w4-600367.name: Restoration of Silesian Piasts (sons of Władysław II the Exile)
w4-600367.blurb: In 1163, with imperial backing from Frederick Barbarossa, the sons of the exiled Władysław II returned to Poland and recovered the Duchy of Silesia from the junior Piasts who had held it after 1146. This restored Silesia as a distinct Piast duchy, shifting territory back from the Masovian/senior branch. The change reflects that return of Silesia to Władysław's line.

w4-600368.name: Byzantine–Hungarian War and Treaty of 1167 (Battle of Sirmium)
w4-600368.blurb: During the Byzantine–Hungarian wars under Manuel I Komnenos, the Byzantines decisively defeated Hungary at the Battle of Sirmium in 1167, securing Croatia, Dalmatia, and the Syrmia/Srem region around the Sava. Hungary ceded these contested borderlands to the Byzantine Empire. This change reflects Byzantine acquisition of the trans-Sava territory.

w4-600370.name: Mahdid/Ayyubid era collapse of the Najahids in Yemen — Nabhani frontier shift
w4-600370.blurb: The Najahid dynasty of Zabid (Tihama, Yemen) was in decline in the mid-12th century, falling to the Mahdids by 1158, while inland and eastern Arabian territory came under other local dynasties. This large transfer to the Nabhanids (of Oman) reflects the reassignment of southern/eastern Arabian lands as Najahid authority collapsed. The exact attribution is uncertain and may partly reflect base-map generalization of poorly controlled desert interior.

w4-600373.name: Frederick Barbarossa compels restoration of Silesia (including Wrocław) to sons of Władysław II
w4-600373.blurb: After Władysław II 'the Exile' was expelled from Poland in 1146 by his brothers including Bolesław IV, Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa applied diplomatic and military pressure. In 1163 Bolesław IV was compelled to restore the Duchy of Silesia — including Wrocław — to Władysław's sons Bolesław the Tall and Mieszko Tanglefoot. The Piast fragmentation meant Masovia and Silesia/Wrocław were now governed as formally separate duchies.

w4-600375.name: Mahdid rise in Yemen after the fall of the Najahids
w4-600375.blurb: The Mahdids, a Yemeni dynasty based at Zabid, supplanted Najahid and residual Seljuk-aligned authority in the Tihama and southwestern Arabia around 1159. This change reflects former Seljuk-nominal Arabian frontier territory passing to Mahdid control as central authority receded. The attribution to a precise event is weak given the region's fragmented politics.

w4-600376.name: Almohad conquest of the Norman Kingdom of Africa (fall of Mahdia)
w4-600376.blurb: Silves (Xelb), capital of a short-lived second taifa in the western Algarve, fell to the advancing Almohads around 1150–1151 as they extended their control across al-Andalus following their entry into the peninsula in 1147. Its absorption ended the town's brief renewed independence and placed the Algarve under Almohad authority. The Algarve had been an Andalusi, not a Norman ('Kingdom of Africa'), territory; the Norman holdings in Ifriqiya never reached this region.

w4-600379.name: Union of Aragon and County of Barcelona (Crown of Aragon)
w4-600379.blurb: When Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona died in 1162, his son Alfonso II inherited both Aragon and Barcelona, formally creating the Crown of Aragon. The ~37,672 km² shift from Kingdom of Aragon to Crown of Aragon in the 1152–1169 window reflects the atlas's recording of this dynastic union, which took effect upon Alfonso II's accession in 1162.

w4-600380.name: Aragonese Reconquista expansion into Valencia/Ebro frontier
w4-600380.blurb: Under Alfonso II of Aragon (r. 1162–1196), the Crown of Aragon systematically pushed south into the Ebro valley and Valencia frontier regions previously controlled by the Taifa of Murcia and other Muslim taifas. The centroid corresponds to the Maestrazgo/southern Aragon borderland that passed under Aragonese control during the mid-12th century Reconquista.

w4-600382.name: Inheritance of Vermandois by Philip of Alsace
w4-600382.blurb: Count Raoul II of Vermandois, afflicted with leprosy, resigned his title around 1163, and died without heirs on 3 June 1167. The county passed to his sister Elisabeth and her husband Philip I of Alsace, Count of Flanders, dramatically expanding Flemish power southward into northern France. Philip administered Vermandois jure uxoris until his death in 1191.

citations.label: Philip I, Count of Flanders — Wikipedia

w4-600383.name: Piast partition — Sandomierz lands and Masovia under Bolesław IV/Casimir II
w4-600383.blurb: Within the fragmented Piast realm, the Duchy of Sandomierz changed hands among the brothers; after Henry of Sandomierz died in 1166 his duchy was redistributed, with portions falling to Bolesław IV the Curly (also duke of Masovia). This change reflects that reallocation of Sandomierz territory toward the Masovian line. The shift is internal Piast dynastic politics rather than a war of conquest.

w4-600386.name: Ghurid annexation of Khorasan frontier after Seljuk collapse
w4-600386.blurb: Following the death of the Oghuz-captured Seljuk Sultan Sanjar (1157) and the disintegration of Great Seljuk authority, the expanding Ghurids under Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad pushed into the former Seljuk lands of Khorasan, taking Herat in 1175 and adjacent territory toward Sistan. This change reflects the Ghurid seizure of ungoverned Seljuk Khorasan frontier. It brought the Ghurids into rivalry with the Khwarazmshahs over the region.

w4-600387.name: Saladin's abolition of the Fatimid Caliphate and takeover of the Hejaz
w4-600387.blurb: After Saladin abolished the Fatimid Caliphate in September 1171 and restored Sunni allegiance to the Abbasid caliph, the Hejaz and its holy cities passed into the orbit of the new Ayyubid power. The Sharifs of Mecca, formerly Fatimid appointees, shifted their recognition toward Saladin, and by around 1200 the Ayyubid sultan formally invested the Sharif Qatada ibn Idris. This brought the Hejaz (centroid in western Arabia) under Ayyubid suzerainty in place of the defunct Fatimid claim.

w4-600388.name: Ayyubid Conquest of Yemen under Turanshah
w4-600388.blurb: In 1174 Saladin sent his brother Turanshah to conquer Yemen, then divided among local dynasties — the Mahdids at Zabid on the Tihama, the Zurayids at Aden, and the Hamdanids at Sanaa. Turanshah overran the Tihama and captured Zabid and Aden by 1174–1175, ending the Mahdid emirate and bringing the region under Ayyubid rule. These polities, not the long-defunct Fatimid Caliphate (abolished 1171), were the powers actually displaced.

w4-600389.name: Ayyubid Conquest of Yemen (1174-1175)
w4-600389.blurb: In 1174 CE Saladin sent his brother Turan-Shah to conquer Yemen and secure the Red Sea trade. Turan-Shah took Zabid (May 1174), Aden, and Sanaa (1175), uniting the fragmented Yemeni polities under Ayyubid rule. The coordinates (45.8E, 15.6N) fit Yemen, and the 1169-1177 window captures the conquest. The dataset's loser label 'Nabhani Dynasty' is an error (the Nabhanis ruled Oman, not Yemen; the displaced parties were Hamdanid remnants and local rulers), but the Ayyubid conquest of Yemen is well attested, so the underlying event stands.

citations.label: Ayyubid entry into Yemen - Yemen Corner

w4-600390.name: Kakatiya assertion of independence from the Chola Empire
w4-600390.blurb: The Kakatiya ruler Rudradeva (r. c. 1158–1195), based at Hanamkonda and later Warangal, was originally a feudatory of the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani. Exploiting the Chalukya collapse, he subdued rival Chalukya subordinates and declared full sovereignty around 1163, ending Chalukya overlordship in the Telangana region. The atlas records this passage of the Krishna–Godavari uplands from Western Chalukya suzerainty to the independent Kakatiya dynasty.

w4-600392.name: Casimir II the Just gains Sandomierz (Kraków congress / seniority crisis)
w4-600392.blurb: When Casimir II the Just seized the senior throne at Kraków in 1177 during the breakdown of Bolesław III's seniority system, the partition of the Polish duchies was reshuffled, and Casimir's own appanage of Sandomierz was reattached to the Kraków seniorate. The arrangements were confirmed at the Congress of Łęczyca (1180). This snapshot reflects the redrawing of boundaries among the fragmented Piast duchies in the late 1170s.

w4-600393.name: Piast reorganization under Casimir II the Just (Sandomierz restored)
w4-600393.blurb: After the death of High Duke Bolesław IV the Curly in 1173, the Sandomierz lands reverted to Casimir II the Just, reversing the earlier consolidation under the Masovian duke. This change reflects Sandomierz being restored as its own duchy out of Masovian-held territory. It is part of the ongoing reshuffling of provinces among the Piast dukes.

w4-600395.name: Danish conquest of the Wends (capture of Rügen and the Mecklenburg coast)
w4-600395.blurb: Under King Valdemar I and Bishop Absalon, Denmark conquered the pagan Wendish (Rani) stronghold of Arkona on Rügen in 1168 and extended control over the southern Baltic coast at the expense of imperial/Saxon and Slavic lordships. The Pomeranian and Rügen coastal territory came under Danish overlordship in this period. This change reflects Danish expansion along the Holy Roman Empire's Baltic frontier.

w4-600396.name: Almohad conquest of Murcia (end of Mardanish's realm)
w4-600396.blurb: Muhammad ibn Mardanish, the 'Wolf King' who ruled the independent taifa of Murcia and Valencia in resistance to the Almohads, died in 1172. After his death his sons submitted to the Almohad Caliphate, and Murcia was absorbed into Almohad al-Andalus. This transferred southeastern Iberia from the last major independent taifa to Almohad rule.

w4-600397.name: Kilij Arslan II conquers the final Danishmendid territories
w4-600397.blurb: Through the 1170s Kilij Arslan II of the Sultanate of Rum steadily absorbed the lands of the rival Danishmendid emirates of central and eastern Anatolia, exploiting their fragmentation among quarrelling branches. By around 1175–1178 the principal Danishmendid centers had fallen to Rum, consolidating Seljuk Turkish authority over the Anatolian interior. The atlas records this transfer of Danishmendid territory to Rum.

w4-600398.name: Battle of Myriokephalon and subsequent Byzantine collapse in Anatolia
w4-600398.blurb: After routing Manuel I Komnenos at the Battle of Myriokephalon (17 September 1176), Kilij Arslan II of Rum ended Byzantine hopes of recovering the Anatolian plateau. Following Manuel's death in 1180 and amid Byzantine internal turmoil, Rum pressed forward and absorbed contested borderlands of the central Anatolian uplands that the empire had held or claimed. The atlas records this passage of Byzantine-held interior Anatolia to the Sultanate of Rum.

w4-600399.name: Kilij Arslan II of the Sultanate of Rum absorbs the Danishmendid territories (1174-1178)
w4-600399.blurb: Kilij Arslan II of the Sultanate of Rum systematically dismantled the Danishmendid principality through a series of campaigns from the 1160s to 1178. He captured Sivas and deposed the last independent Danishmendid ruler Dhu'l-Nun around 1168-1174, and by 1178 had taken Malatya, ending Danishmendid independence. The Danishmendid territories in central and eastern Anatolia around lat 38.8, lng 37.1 were thus absorbed into the Rum Sultanate, unifying most of Anatolia under Seljuk rule for the first time.

w4-600400.name: Serbian independence under Stefan Nemanja
w4-600400.blurb: Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja of Raška (Serbia), exploiting the collapse of Byzantine authority after the death of Emperor Manuel I Komnenos in 1180, threw off Byzantine suzerainty and expanded his realm. Allied at times with Hungary, he annexed Byzantine territory in the central Balkans, founding the independent medieval Serbian state. This moved interior Balkan lands from the Byzantine Empire to the Serbian principality (later Kingdom).

w4-600401.name: Jayavarman VII's northern expansion into Haripunjaya region
w4-600401.blurb: Under Jayavarman VII (acc. c. 1181), Angkorian power reached its widest extent and the Mon kingdom of Lavo (Lopburi) in the central Chao Phraya basin was firmly drawn into the Khmer sphere as a tributary. Khmer administration and Buddhist building activity radiated from Angkor into Lavo's territory during his reign. The atlas records this region passing from the Lavo kingdom into the Khmer Empire at the peak of Jayavarman VII's authority.

w4-600402.name: Jayavarman VII's Khmer expansion into Mekong valley after defeating Cham
w4-600402.blurb: After Cham forces sacked Angkor in 1177, Jayavarman VII seized power around 1181 and expanded Khmer authority across the empire's northern and eastern marches, including the middle Mekong corridor (centroid in present-day southern Laos). Angkorian inscriptions and temple foundations attest Khmer overlordship reaching deep into this region at the height of his reign. The atlas records the area coming under Khmer suzerainty during the 1177–1188 window.

w4-600404.name: Geoffrey II of Brittany's Angevin lordship
w4-600404.blurb: Henry II of England (the Angevin Empire) secured control of Brittany by marrying his son Geoffrey to Constance, heiress of Duke Conan IV. Geoffrey became Duke of Brittany and held it as a vassal of his father, bringing the duchy firmly under Angevin overlordship in the 1180s. This integrated Brittany into the Angevin domains.

w4-600405.name: Uprising of Asen and Peter (founding of the Second Bulgarian Empire)
w4-600405.blurb: In 1185 the brothers Peter and Asen led a revolt of Bulgarians and Vlachs against Byzantine Emperor Isaac II Angelos, sparked by new taxes. Their rebellion succeeded in expelling Byzantine authority north of the Balkan Mountains and re-established an independent Bulgarian state, the Second Bulgarian Empire, with its capital at Tarnovo. This transferred Moesia and adjacent Balkan lands from Byzantium to the new empire.

w4-600408.name: Kievan Rus' fragmentation — Turov-Pinsk separation from Kiev
w4-600408.blurb: During the disintegration of Kievan Rus' in the 12th century, the Principality of Turov and Pinsk became independent of Kiev (under Yuri Yaroslavich c.1162) and continued to consolidate its hold over the Pripyat region (28,52.2). The window py=1177/y=1188 reflects ongoing reallotment of these borderlands away from Kiev, matching the from→to (Principality of Kiev → Principality of Turov and Pinsk).

w4-600409.name: Casimir II the Just seizes power — Congress of Leczyca
w4-600409.blurb: Casimir II the Just seized the senior Polish throne at Kraków in 1177 and consolidated power; the Congress of Leczyca (1180) recognized new territorial arrangements, with Casimir acquiring influence over parts of Masovia and reducing its duke's authority, resulting in the atlas's depiction of this territory shifting to Sandomierz's sphere.

w4-600410.name: Partition of Poland under the testament of Bolesław III (Piast fragmentation)
w4-600410.blurb: This reflects the dynastic reshuffling among the fragmented Piast duchies of Poland in the late 12th century. Following the death of Casimir II the Just's relatives and the redistribution of provinces, territory shifted between the duchies of Masovia and Sandomierz, both held by branches of the Piast dynasty. The change is a succession/partition within fragmented Poland rather than a conquest by an outside power.

w4-600411.name: Genpei War and establishment of Kamakura Shogunate
w4-600411.blurb: The Northern Fujiwara of Hiraizumi, who had ruled Mutsu and Dewa provinces in northern Honshu since 1087, fell to Minamoto no Yoritomo in 1189. After their head Fujiwara no Yasuhira had Yoritomo's brother Yoshitsune killed, Yoritomo launched the Battle of Ōshū (autumn 1189), destroying the dynasty and annexing the north. This completed Yoritomo's nationwide dominance and the consolidation of the Kamakura shogunate.

w4-600412.name: Genpei War and establishment of the Kamakura Shogunate
w4-600412.blurb: The Genpei War (1180–1185) between the Minamoto and Taira clans ended with Minamoto no Yoritomo's decisive victory at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185. Yoritomo established military government, gaining the right to appoint stewards and constables across Japan and being named shogun in 1192, founding the Kamakura Shogunate. This transferred effective rule of Japan from the imperial Heian court to the shogunate.

w4-600414.name: Treaty of Boves - partition of Vermandois (1185)
w4-600414.blurb: The Treaty of Boves (July 1185), confirmed at Gisors (May 1186), resolved the conflict between Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders, and King Philip II Augustus of France over the County of Vermandois. Under the treaty the disputed territory was partitioned: Philip II gained Amiens and 65 castles in Vermandois, while Philip of Alsace retained the core county of Vermandois proper for his lifetime, after which it would revert to the French crown. The dataset records a transition near Vermandois (coords 2.8E, 49.6N) within 1177-1188, reflecting this partition of the county.

citations.label: Philip I, Count of Flanders - Grokipedia

w4-600416.name: Pomeranian submission to Denmark (1185)
w4-600416.blurb: After Danish campaigns in 1184-1185, Duke Bogusław I of Pomerania (of the House of Griffin) was compelled to take his duchy as a fief from King Canute VI of Denmark in 1185, after the Pomeranian fleet was sunk in the Bay of Greifswald. By 1186 all of Pomerania was under Danish suzerainty. Denmark held overlordship of the southern Baltic coast, including Pomerania, until its defeat at the Battle of Bornhöved in 1227.

citations.label: Bogusław I, Duke of Pomerania - Wikipedia
Pomerania during the High Middle Ages - Wikipedia

w4-600418.name: Pisan commercial takeover of the Giudicato of Cagliari
w4-600418.blurb: Pisa and Genoa contended for control of southern Sardinia through the 12th century, working largely through the Giudicato of Cagliari. When open war erupted in 1187, the Pisans expelled the Genoese from Cagliari, and on 7 July 1188 papal legates of Clement III proclaimed a peace affirming Pisan supremacy over the giudicato and its rulers. This consolidated Pisan dominance over the Cagliari giudicato, which Pisa would oversee until the kingdom's dissolution in 1258.

w4-600419.name: Pisan seizure of the Giudicato of Cagliari and installation of William I (1188)
w4-600419.blurb: In 1188 a Pisan-backed coup captured Judge Peter of Cagliari and installed William I (Salusio IV) under Pisan patronage, turning the Giudicato of Cagliari into a Pisan client state. The coordinates (9°E, 39.6°N) match southern Sardinia; from=Giudicato of Cagliari, to=Republic of Pisa matches the 1177-1188 window.

w4-600421.name: Yadava overthrow of the Western Chalukyas (Bhillama V)
w4-600421.blurb: Bhillama V of the Yadava (Seuna) dynasty declared independence from the collapsing Western Chalukya Empire and seized its Deccan heartland, founding the kingdom of Devagiri around 1187. The Chalukyas, already weakened by the Kalachuris and Hoysalas, lost their core Karnataka–Maharashtra territories. This large transfer represents the Yadava conquest of the Chalukya domains.

w4-600425.name: Smolensk Absorption of Vitebsk (c. 1180s)
w4-600425.blurb: During the late 12th century, the Principality of Vitebsk repeatedly fell under the influence and effective control of the Principality of Smolensk, ruled by the expanding Rostislavich princes (a first episode occurred around 1165–1167). The princes of Polotsk and Chernigov reacted militarily against Smolensk, eventually re-establishing Polotsk control over Vitebsk by around 1195. The dataset window 1177–1188 covers this Smolensk encroachment period over Vitebsk.

w4-600426.name: Smolensk Encroachment into Polotsk Territory (late 12th century)
w4-600426.blurb: Concurrent with its absorption of Vitebsk in the 1180s, the Principality of Smolensk under the Rostislavich princes also encroached on adjacent Polotsk-held lands (near lng 29.1, lat 56). The two entries (600425 and 600426) record a roughly simultaneous re-attribution of this region — Vitebsk and adjacent Polotsk territories — to Smolensk, reflecting the fluid overlapping claims of these closely related Rurikid principalities. By c. 1195 a coalition of Polotsk and Chernigov princes reversed the Smolensk gains.

w4-600428.name: Saladin's annexation of the Jazira / Zengid Mosul lands
w4-600428.blurb: Saladin (Ayyubid Sultanate) campaigned against the Zengid principalities of Syria and the Jazira, capturing Aleppo in 1183 and bringing much of the Zengid realm under his suzerainty. The region of the upper Jazira/Khabur shifted from Zengid to Ayyubid control as Saladin consolidated his power before facing the Crusaders. This reflects Ayyubid absorption of Zengid territory.

w4-600433.name: Leonese frontier gains in Extremadura (Reconquista, Fernando II/Alfonso IX)
