w4-600433.blurb: The Kingdom of León, under Fernando II and his son Alfonso IX, pushed its frontier southward into Extremadura against the Almohad Caliphate in the 1180s, defending and expanding around towns like Cáceres. The location near (-6, 39.2) corresponds to this Leonese Reconquista advance. Territory passed from Almohad to Leonese control on the western Iberian frontier.

w4-600434.name: Norwegian incorporation of Jämtland
w4-600434.blurb: Jämtland, an inland peasant-republic region, came progressively under the Kingdom of Norway during the 12th century, having converted and aligned with Norway through the archbishopric of Nidaros. The change reflects Norwegian crown authority extending over Jämtland in this period. It is a gradual integration rather than a single battle.

w4-600435.name: Hungarian intervention in Halych (Galicia) under Béla III
w4-600435.blurb: In 1188 King Béla III of Hungary intervened in the succession crisis of the Principality of Halych (Galicia), driving out the local prince and installing his own son Andrew as ruler, briefly annexing Galicia to the Hungarian crown. This transferred the Galician (Rus') lands from Rurikid (Kievan Rus') control to the Kingdom of Hungary. The Hungarian occupation proved short-lived.

w4-600439.name: Restoration of Halych under Vladimir II Yaroslavich
w4-600439.blurb: After the brief Hungarian occupation of Galicia under Béla III, the native Rurikid prince Vladimir (Volodymyr) II Yaroslavich was restored to the throne of Halych in 1189–1190 with the help of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and Casimir II of Poland. Galicia thus reverted to Rus' (Rurikid) rule under the Principality of Halych. This reverses the Hungarian annexation of the previous window.

w4-600440.name: Expulsion of Hungarian prince Andrew from Halych; restoration of Vladimir II Yaroslavich
w4-600440.blurb: The Hungarian prince Andrew's rule over Halych (1188-1190) proved deeply unpopular: Hungarian soldiers insulted local women and disrespected Orthodox churches, alienating the Galician boyars. Vladimir II Yaroslavich, having escaped Hungarian captivity, returned with support from Duke Casimir II of Poland. The boyars allied with him and expelled Andrew and his retinue from the principality in 1189 or 1190, restoring Rostislavich dynastic rule until Vladimir's death in 1198/1199.

w4-600443.name: Ayyubid absorption of Mosul/Jazira Zengid lands after Saladin
w4-600443.blurb: Following Saladin's settlement with the Zengid atabeg of Mosul, Izz al-Din Mas'ud, in 1186, the Zengids of the Jazira recognized Ayyubid suzerainty, placing the upper Mesopotamian region under Ayyubid overlordship. The eastern Jazira lands thus passed from independent Zengid to Ayyubid control. This continues Saladin's consolidation of the former Zengid realm.

w4-600444.name: Saltukid/Shah-Armen successor disputes in eastern Anatolia (collapse of Seljuk authority)
w4-600444.blurb: This reflects the fragmentation of Great Seljuk authority in eastern Anatolia/Armenia after the death of Sultan Toghrul III and the empire's collapse around 1194. Local Turkmen dynasties in the Erzurum/Armenia region absorbed nominal Seljuk territory. The 'Hamdanid' label here likely stands in for a local emirate succeeding Seljuk overlordship in the Armenian highlands; the transfer is the breakup of the Seljuk state rather than a single battle.

w4-600445.name: Bulgarian campaigns of Kaloyan: expansion into Serbian territory (c. 1196–1202)
w4-600445.blurb: During his campaigns of the late 1190s and early 1200s, Tsar Kaloyan of Bulgaria captured Braničevo, Velbuzhd, Skopje, and Prizren from the weakened Byzantine Empire, recovering territory in the central Balkans (around the Morava–Niš corridor). After Hungary briefly seized Braničevo and Niš in 1202 for its Serbian protégé Vukan, Kaloyan struck back in 1203, taking Niš and restoring Stefan Nemanjić in Serbia. The atlas records the passage of this borderland from Byzantine to Bulgarian control.

w4-600446.name: Armenian Cilician expansion under Leo II (Levon)
w4-600446.blurb: Leo II (Levon the Magnificent) of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia expanded his realm during the 1180s–1190s at the expense of weakened Byzantine and Seljuk neighbors, consolidating control over the Cilician plain and coast amid the upheaval of the Third Crusade. This transferred coastal/southern Anatolian territory from Byzantine to Armenian Cilician control. Leo was crowned king in 1198.

w4-600451.name: Seljuk Sultanate of Rum expansion into central Anatolia
w4-600451.blurb: The Sultanate of Rum, recovering after the death of Kilij Arslan II and reuniting under his sons, expanded westward into Byzantine central Anatolia in the 1190s amid Byzantine weakness preceding the Fourth Crusade. Territory around the Anatolian plateau passed from the Byzantine Empire to Rum. This advance set the stage for Rum's capture of Byzantine cities in the early 13th century.

w4-600452.name: Seljuk Rum annexation of eastern Anatolian emirate territory
w4-600452.blurb: The Sultanate of Rum extended its control into eastern Anatolia around the upper Euphrates in the late 12th century, absorbing lands from neighboring Turkmen emirates as it consolidated central Anatolia. The 'Hamdanid' label here represents a local emirate displaced by Rum's expansion. The territory passed to the Seljuks of Rum during this period of consolidation.

w4-600456.name: Consolidation of Galicia-Volhynia under Roman the Great
w4-600456.blurb: In 1199 Roman Mstislavich, prince of Volhynia, seized Halych (Galicia) on the death of the last Rostislavich prince, uniting the two principalities into Galicia-Volhynia. This carved a powerful southwestern Rus' realm out of the fragmenting Kievan inheritance, and Roman went on to dominate Kiev itself.

w4-600457.name: Foundation of the Principality of Galicia–Volhynia by Roman Mstislavich
w4-600457.blurb: When Vladimir II Yaroslavich, the last Rostislavich prince of Halych, died without a recognized heir in 1198/1199, Roman Mstislavich of Volhynia seized the city of Halych with support from Leszek the White of Poland, uniting the two principalities into a single powerful state. The new Galicia–Volhynia principality went on to occupy Kyiv in 1202 and became one of the dominant successor states of Kievan Rus', ruled by the Romanovych dynasty until 1340.

w4-600458.name: Roman Mstislavich unifies Volhynia and Galicia (1199)
w4-600458.blurb: In 1199, Prince Roman Mstislavich of Volhynia seized the Principality of Halych (Galicia) after its Rostislavichi line died out, creating the united Principality of Galicia-Volhynia; by 1202 he had also taken Kyiv. The worklist transition is 'Principality of Volhynia' -> 'Principality of Galicia-Volhynia' [1192,1202] at lng 24.1, lat 52.4 (western Ukraine/Volhynia), with 1199 inside the window.

w4-600459.name: Death of Mieszko III and reorganisation of Greater Polish dynastic holdings (c. 1202)
w4-600459.blurb: After the 1138 fragmentation of Poland under Bolesław III Wrymouth's testament, the Duchies of Sandomierz and Greater Poland were separate Piast principalities. Mieszko III the Old, who held Greater Poland, died in 1202; the ensuing Piast dynastic conflicts allowed territorial overlaps between the duchies in the early 13th century. The change (lng 19.4, lat 52, Sandomierz -> Greater Poland) plausibly represents a temporary acquisition of borderlands by Greater Poland amid the succession struggles around this date.

w4-600460.name: Piast fragmentation: Masovia and Sandomierz under Leszek/Konrad
w4-600460.blurb: After the death of Casimir II the Just in 1194, his sons divided his Polish holdings, with Konrad I receiving Masovia and the Sandomierz lands shifting among the contending Piast dukes during the period of fragmentation. The reshuffling of Lesser Poland's duchies moved territory between Sandomierz and Masovia. This is a dynastic partition rather than a conquest.

w4-600462.name: Ghurid conquest of Sindh (Multan/Uch and lower Indus)
w4-600462.blurb: Muhammad of Ghor's campaigns into the Indus valley, beginning with Multan and Uch in 1175 and extending down toward Sindh, absorbed the Habbari/Soomra-era lands of lower Sindh into the Ghurid empire by the turn of the century. The Ghurids displaced the local Sindhi dynasties as they pushed toward the Arabian Sea. This was part of the broader Ghurid drive into northwestern India.

w4-600463.name: Ghurid conquest of the Gahadavalas (Battle of Chandawar)
w4-600463.blurb: At the Battle of Chandawar in 1194, Muhammad of Ghor defeated and killed Jayachandra, the Gahadavala ruler of Kannauj and the middle Ganges. The victory delivered the rich Gangetic heartland around Kannauj and Varanasi to the Ghurids. It followed his triumph over the Chauhans two years earlier.

w4-600464.name: Second Battle of Tarain (Ghurid defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan)
w4-600464.blurb: At the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192, Muhammad of Ghor decisively defeated Prithviraj III Chauhan, avenging his loss the previous year. The victory shattered Chauhan power in Ajmer and Delhi and opened northern India to Ghurid (and successor Mamluk) rule. It is the foundational event of Muslim rule in northern India.

w4-600467.name: Sosso conquest of the Ghana Empire (Soumaoro Kanté)
w4-600467.blurb: Around 1203 the Sosso (Soso) kingdom under Soumaoro Kanté overran the declining Ghana Empire, capturing its capital and supplanting Wagadou's authority in the western Sudan. Sosso dominance lasted until Sundiata Keita destroyed it at the Battle of Kirina (c.1235), founding Mali. The fall of Ghana to Sosso is recorded in the Mande epic tradition.

w4-600470.name: Elevation of Khwarezm to empire status after defeat of the Great Seljuks
w4-600470.blurb: After Tekish defeated and killed the last Great Seljuk sultan Toghrul III in 1194 and was recognized as a paramount ruler by the Abbasid caliph, the Khwarezm polity transitioned from a regional dynasty ('Khwarezmid Dynasty') to an imperial power ('Khwarezmid Empire'). The atlas change (1192–1202, centroid lng 60.6, lat 39.9) reflects this relabeling of the same territory upon Tekish's imperial consolidation.

w4-600471.name: Khwarazmshah Muhammad II recaptures Nishapur and Merv from the Ghurids
w4-600471.blurb: After the Ghurid brothers Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din exploited Khwarezm's 1200 succession crisis to overrun Nishapur, Merv, and Tus in 1200-1201, Khwarazmshah Muhammad II counterattacked, retaking Merv in September 1201 and forcing Nishapur's Ghurid garrison to surrender after a two-month siege that same year. This reversed the brief Ghurid hold on Khorasan. (The 1206 Battle of Andkhud/assassination narrative previously cited falls after this atlas snapshot's 1192-1202 window; Andkhud was in fact 1204 and Mu'izz al-Din's assassination March 1206.)

w4-600472.name: Death of Sultan Toghrul III and Khwarezm annexation of Great Seljuk western territories
w4-600472.blurb: Khwarezm Shah Tekish defeated and killed Toghrul III, the last Sultan of the Great Seljuk Empire, in 1194, ending Seljuk rule over western Iran (Jibal, Isfahan, western Persia — centroid lng 50.9, lat 32.1). Tekish then claimed the Seljuk domains in western Iran, though consolidation continued through the early 1200s.

w4-600473.name: Hungarian annexation of Belgrade and Braničevo from Bulgaria
w4-600473.blurb: King Emeric of Hungary, in alliance with the Serbian župan Vukan, annexed Belgrade, Braničevo, and Niš from the Second Bulgarian Empire around 1198–1202 while Bulgaria was preoccupied with its wars against Byzantium. This gain (centroid ~20.7°E, 44.8°N, corresponding to the Belgrade-Braničevo region) was later reversed by Kaloyan around 1203 (see change 600496).

w4-600474.name: Philip II's confiscation of Angevin lands; Breton independence reasserted
w4-600474.blurb: In 1202, Philip II of France adjudged King John of England a contumacious vassal and began the conquest of Angevin continental territories; Brittany, which Duke Arthur I held from John, effectively broke from Angevin rule during this period after Arthur's murder (1203) and the French advance. The ~33,082 km² shift records Brittany separating from the collapsing Angevin Empire by 1202–1206.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Arthur I, Duke of Brittany

w4-600475.name: Foundation of the Despotate of Epirus after Fourth Crusade
w4-600475.blurb: After the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in April 1204, Michael I Komnenos Doukas — a cousin of emperors Isaac II and Alexios III — withdrew to Epirus and established an independent despotate c.1205, absorbing Byzantine-administered western Greece, Epirus, and parts of Albania from the collapsing imperial structure.

w4-600477.name: Angevin losses in Gascony after Philip II's conquest of Normandy
w4-600477.blurb: Following Philip II of France's conquest of Normandy and Anjou (1203–1204), the Angevin Empire's hold on its French territories weakened severely. In Gascony, the counts of Armagnac — who had been nominal Angevin vassals — reasserted independence and effective sovereignty over the Gers/Armagnac region, which is reflected as a transfer from the Angevin sphere to Armagnac control by 1206.

citations.label: Powicke, F. M. The Loss of Normandy 1189–1204 (2nd ed., 1961)

w4-600479.name: French conquest of Normandy and collapse of Angevin power in France (1204)
w4-600479.blurb: Philip II of France conquered Normandy, Maine, and Anjou from King John of England in 1203–1204; with Angevin power in northern France shattered, local lords in Périgord and the Dordogne reasserted autonomy, effectively removing the region from Angevin control by the 1206 snapshot.

w4-600480.name: Philip II's conquest of Poitou from the Angevin Empire
w4-600480.blurb: Following the French adjudication against John of England in 1202, Philip II's forces overran Poitou by 1204–1206, effectively ending Angevin control over the county. The ~29,625 km² shift from Angevin Empire to County of Poitou reflects this French reassertion, though the atlas labels it as a separate local county rather than direct French rule.

w4-600481.name: Philip II Augustus conquers Angevin lands in France
w4-600481.blurb: After King John of England was condemned by the French royal court in 1202 and refused a feudal summons, Philip II Augustus launched military offensives that secured Anjou, Maine, and Touraine (the region near lng 1.2, lat 47.7) by 1204, with John's 1206 counter-invasion at La Rochelle ending in a truce acknowledging his losses.

w4-600482.name: Philip II Augustus annexes Maine (Truce of Thouars)
w4-600482.blurb: Philip II Augustus of France seized the County of Maine during his campaigns against King John of England in 1204-1205, part of the dismemberment of the Angevin Empire. John formally renounced his claims to Maine, Normandy, Anjou, Brittany, and Touraine in the Truce of Thouars of October 1206, bringing Maine into the French royal domain. The data window 1202-1206 captures this transfer from the County of Maine to the Kingdom of France.

w4-600483.name: French royal annexation of Auvergne from the Angevin sphere
w4-600483.blurb: Philip II Augustus of France exploited the collapse of Angevin power north of the Loire after 1202–1204, and the County of Auvergne — which had been under Angevin overlordship — reverted to or was confirmed under its own counts with French royal backing by 1206. This reflects the broader dissolution of the Angevin Empire's French holdings following John of England's loss of Normandy in 1204.

w4-600484.name: Frankish conquest of the Morea (Principality of Achaea)
w4-600484.blurb: In the aftermath of the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204), William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin conquered the Peloponnese, founding the Principality of Achaea by 1205. Their victory at the Battle of the Olive Grove of Koundouros broke Byzantine resistance in the Morea. The principality became the most durable Latin state in Greece.

w4-600486.name: Georgian expansion into the Muslim emirates of the Armenian highlands under Queen Tamar
w4-600486.blurb: Following the Georgian victory at the Battle of Basiani (c. 1202-1204) against the Sultanate of Rum, Georgia under David Soslan expanded into northern Armenia and the surrounding emirates. By 1206 Georgian forces had captured Kars and Araxes-valley fortresses and subdued the emirs of Kars, Erzurum, and Erzincan and the Shah-Armens. The dataset's 'Hamdanid Emirates' label is an imprecise name for these Saltukid/Shah-Armen Muslim emirates (the Hamdanids proper were a long-extinct 10th-century Arab dynasty), but the underlying territorial transfer to the Kingdom of Georgia in the 1202-1206 window near the Armenian highlands is well attested.

w4-600488.name: Fourth Crusade — Venice acquires Greek territories under Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae
w4-600488.blurb: The Partitio Romaniae (October 1204) parceled out the conquered Byzantine Empire among the Fourth Crusade's leaders. Central Greece and Attica, including Athens and Thebes, fell to the Burgundian knight Othon de la Roche, who established the Frankish Duchy of Athens as a vassal of the Kingdom of Thessalonica. This carved Attica and Boeotia (centroid ~23.4°E, 38.3°N) out of former Byzantine territory rather than assigning it to Venice.

w4-600489.name: Foundation of the Empire of Trebizond (1204)
w4-600489.blurb: In April 1204, amid the Fourth Crusade, the Komnenos brothers Alexios and David seized Trebizond with Georgian backing, founding a Byzantine successor empire; David expanded westward into Paphlagonia. The window (1202-1206) and Pontic coordinates (37.2, 42.8) reflect Black Sea coastal territory shifting from Byzantine to Trapezuntine control.

w4-600492.name: Fourth Crusade: establishment of the Kingdom of Thessalonica
w4-600492.blurb: After the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in April 1204, Theodore I Laskaris — son-in-law of the deposed emperor Alexios III — fled to northwestern Anatolia and rallied Byzantine resistance around Nicaea and Bithynia. By 1205 he had consolidated a Byzantine government-in-exile there, and in 1208 he was crowned emperor, founding the Empire of Nicaea as the principal Greek successor state that would eventually retake Constantinople in 1261. The change reflects former Byzantine territory in western Anatolia passing under Nicaean control.

w4-600493.name: Founding of the Kingdom of Thessalonica (Boniface of Montferrat)
w4-600493.blurb: Following the Fourth Crusade, Boniface of Montferrat received Thessalonica and established the Kingdom of Thessalonica as a vassal of the new Latin Empire in 1205. The Crusaders carved this realm out of Byzantine Macedonia and Thessaly. It was short-lived, falling to Epirus in 1224.

w4-600494.name: Khmer annexation of Champa (Jayavarman VII)
w4-600494.blurb: After the Cham sack of Angkor in 1177, Jayavarman VII of the Khmer Empire counterattacked and, by 1203, conquered and annexed Champa, ruling it as a Khmer province for roughly two decades. The occupation lasted until the Cham regained independence around 1220. This was the high-water mark of Khmer power in Indochina.

w4-600495.name: Kaloyan's expansion of the Second Bulgarian Empire into Wallachia/lower Danube
w4-600495.blurb: Under Tsar Kaloyan the Second Bulgarian Empire extended firm control over the lands north of the lower Danube (Wallachia) in the early 1200s, recovering territory amid the collapse of Byzantine authority and Hungarian-Bulgarian rivalry. The coordinates near the lower Danube fit Kaloyan's consolidation of Bulgaria's northern frontier. Kaloyan also crushed the Latin Empire at Adrianople in 1205.

w4-600497.name: Bulgarian-Hungarian struggle over Belgrade and Braničevo (Kaloyan)
w4-600497.blurb: In the early 1200s Tsar Kaloyan of Bulgaria contested the Belgrade-Braničevo region of the middle Danube with Emeric of Hungary, taking border districts before Hungarian counter-pressure. The transfer reflects Bulgaria's northwestern expansion under Kaloyan during the Byzantine collapse. The frontier here changed hands repeatedly in the period.

w4-600507.name: Khwarazmian expansion onto the Syr Darya / Kipchak frontier (c. 1210)
w4-600507.blurb: After defeating the Qara-Khitai at Talas (1210) and dismantling their authority over Transoxiana, Muhammad II of Khwarazm pressed onto the Syr Darya frontier and planned campaigns against the Kipchaks/Qangli, holding outposts such as Jand and Sighnaq. The window (1207-1210) and coordinates (64.8, 46.6, the Aral-Syr Darya region) reflect this Khwarazmian push into former Kimek-Kipchak steppe.

w4-600508.name: Khwarazmian Conquest of Ghurid Eastern Territories
w4-600508.blurb: After the assassination of Ghurid sultan Mu'izz al-Din (Muhammad of Ghor) in 1206, civil war fragmented the Ghurid empire. Shah Muhammad II of Khwarazm seized Balkh, Tirmidh, and Herat from the Ghurids c. 1206-1210, capturing Ghurid ruler Ghiyath al-Din Mahmud and forcing recognition of his authority; he overthrew Qara Khitai overlordship c. 1210. The coordinates (63.5E, 30.4N, Khorasan/Sistan) and the 1207-1210 window fit; the definitive subjugation completed c. 1215.

w4-600509.name: Khwarazmian conquest of Transoxiana from the Kara-Khitai
w4-600509.blurb: Around 1210 the Khwarazm-Shah Muhammad II defeated the Kara-Khitai (Western Liao) at the Battle of Talas/near Samarkand, wresting Transoxiana and its great cities from Qara Khitai overlordship. This made Khwarazm the dominant power of Central Asia on the eve of the Mongol invasion. The vast area (~450,000 km2) matches the Transoxianan core.

w4-600510.name: Mongol submission of the Yenisei Kyrgyz
w4-600510.blurb: In 1207 Genghis Khan sent his son Jochi to subdue the forest peoples of southern Siberia, and the Yenisei Kyrgyz and Oirats submitted to the Mongol Empire without major resistance. This brought the upper Yenisei region into the nascent empire. The submission is recorded in the Secret History of the Mongols.

w4-600513.name: Qutb al-Din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate (Mamluk dynasty)
w4-600513.blurb: On the assassination of Muhammad of Ghor in 1206, his slave-general Qutb al-Din Aibak declared independence at Lahore/Delhi, founding the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty and the Delhi Sultanate. The Ghurid Indian conquests around Delhi and the Ganges passed to the new sultanate. This is the birth of independent Muslim rule in India.

w4-600514.name: Philip II's conquest of Normandy and the Angevin continental lands
w4-600514.blurb: Between 1202 and 1204 Philip II Augustus of France conquered Normandy (fall of Château Gaillard, 1204) and most of King John's continental Angevin possessions. The coordinates off the Norman/Channel coast and the large area reflect the loss of Normandy and adjacent lands by the English crown. This stripped the Plantagenets of their northern French heartland.

w4-600516.name: Piast dynastic struggles — territory between Duchies of Sandomierz and Opole (c. 1207–1210)
w4-600516.blurb: Between 1207 and 1210 the Piast duchies of Sandomierz and Opole (Upper Silesia) contested border territory amid Polish fragmentation. This record is the near-mirror of 600520, reflecting the same back-and-forth disputes, with territory shifting toward Opole around 1210. Worklist transfer Duchy of Sandomierz to Duchy of Opole, window [1207,1210]; medium confidence as the precise triggering event is undocumented.

citations.label: History of Poland during the Piast dynasty – Wikipedia

w4-600517.name: Georgian expansion into Armenia/eastern Anatolia under Tamar
w4-600517.blurb: During the reign of Queen Tamar, the Kingdom of Georgia under the Mkhargrdzeli (Zakarid) generals expanded southward into Armenia and against neighboring Muslim emirates, taking territory around Ani, Dvin and the Armenian highlands in the early 1200s. The coordinates near Armenia fit these campaigns against local emirates. Georgia reached its medieval zenith in this period.

w4-600518.name: Serbian expansion into Macedonia under Stefan Nemanjić (c. 1208-1216)
w4-600518.blurb: Exploiting Bulgaria's weakness under Boril, Stefan Nemanjić of Serbia invaded Macedonia and occupied the land between the Struma and Vardar rivers around 1208-1209, installing Strez as a vassal and keeping Serbian troops in the region. The window (1210-1216) and coordinates (21, 42.8, the Skopje/Vardar region) fit this Serbian gain at Bulgarian expense.

w4-600520.name: Piast dynastic struggles — territory between Duchies of Opole and Sandomierz (c. 1210–1216)
w4-600520.blurb: The years 1210–1216 fall within the Piast fragmentation following Boleslaw III's 1138 testament, during which Polish duchies repeatedly changed hands. Leszek I the White held Sandomierz while contending with rivals tied to the Duchy of Opole/Raciborz (formed 1202). Worklist transfer Duchy of Opole to Duchy of Sandomierz, window [1210,1216]; the specific causal event is not pinned in sources but fits the documented oscillating Piast border disputes, so confidence is medium.

w4-600522.name: Philip Augustus annexes Vermandois on Countess Eleanor's death
w4-600522.blurb: Under an agreement of 1192, Eleanor of Vermandois (sister of Countess Elisabeth) pledged to cede the County of Vermandois to the French crown upon her own death. Eleanor died in 1213, and Philip II Augustus immediately incorporated the county, centred on Saint-Quentin (lat 49.6, lng 2.8), into the royal domain, completing a long process of Capetian expansion in northern France.

citations.label: Philip II of France — New World Encyclopedia

w4-600523.name: Albigensian Crusade – Simon de Montfort's conquest of the County of Toulouse (1210–1215)
w4-600523.blurb: During the Albigensian Crusade, Simon de Montfort systematically conquered the territories of Count Raymond VI of Toulouse between 1210 and 1215, culminating in his recognition as Count of Toulouse by the Fourth Lateran Council (1215). The worklist transfer County of Toulouse → Kingdom of France at lng 2.7, lat 43.7 in the 1210–1216 window matches this crusader/Capetian takeover of Toulousain lands.

citations.label: Simon de Montfort, 5th Earl of Leicester – Wikipedia

w4-600526.name: Michael I of Epirus captures Thessalian and Macedonian cities from Kingdom of Thessalonica
w4-600526.blurb: The death of Strez, the Bulgarian-aligned ruler of central Macedonia, in 1214 opened that region to the expanding Despotate of Epirus. Michael I Komnenos Doukas, and after his murder in 1214 his half-brother Theodore, pushed into northern Macedonia at the expense of Second Bulgarian Empire interests there. The change reflects formerly Bulgarian-held Macedonian territory passing under Epirote control around 1214.

w4-600527.name: Michael I of Epirus attacks the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica
w4-600527.blurb: Michael I Komnenos Doukas of Epirus attacked the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica in 1210 in conjunction with the Second Bulgarian Empire, though he was repelled when Latin Emperor Henry of Flanders intervened. Michael subsequently expanded into Thessaly by 1212, capturing Larissa, Halmyros, and coastal areas at the kingdom's expense. The data window 1210-1216 captures this Epirote expansion against the Kingdom of Thessalonica.

w4-600529.name: Khwarazmian conquest of the Kara-Khitai (Qara Khitai) heartland
w4-600529.blurb: Around 1210, after the Khwarazmshah Ala ad-Din Muhammad II defeated the Kara-Khitai (Western Liao) at the Battle of the Talas River, Khwarazm seized Transoxiana including the region around Samarkand and the Ferghana area. The Gurkhan's authority collapsed as the usurper Kuchlug seized the rump Kara-Khitai state, while Khwarazm absorbed the western territories. This transferred the lands near the Ferghana/Talas region (the mapped point) from the Kara-Khitans to the Khwarezmid Empire.

w4-600532.name: Christian reconquest in Extremadura after Las Navas de Tolosa
w4-600532.blurb: The crushing Almohad defeat at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) by a coalition of Castile, Aragon, Navarre and Portugal shattered Almohad power in Iberia. In its aftermath the Kingdom of León under Alfonso IX pushed south into Extremadura, taking towns in the region around the mapped point (western Iberia). This advance transferred Almohad-held Extremaduran territory to León.

citations.label: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa

w4-600533.name: Hungarian seizure of the Banate of Belgrade/Braničevo region
w4-600533.blurb: In the disorder of the Second Bulgarian Empire under Boril, the Kingdom of Hungary under Andrew II extended control over the Belgrade and Braničevo region along the Danube (near the mapped point in modern Serbia). This frontier zone, contested between Hungary and Bulgaria, passed into Hungarian hands in the 1210s. The transfer reflects Hungarian expansion into the lower Danube borderlands.

w4-600534.name: Cham recovery of independence / end of Khmer occupation of Champa
w4-600534.blurb: The Khmer Empire under Jayavarman VII had occupied and annexed Champa from about 1203, ruling it as a province. Around 1220 the Khmer withdrew their garrisons and Champa regained its independence under a restored Cham ruler (Jaya Paramesvaravarman II). This restored the territory around the mapped point in central Vietnam from Khmer rule back to Champa.

w4-600536.name: Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus conquers Ohrid and Macedonia from Bulgaria
w4-600536.blurb: Under Theodore Komnenos Doukas (r. 1215–1230), the Despotate of Epirus continued the northward advance into Macedonia begun after the death of the Bulgarian magnate Strez in 1214. Through campaigns in 1215–1216 Theodore pushed back Second Bulgarian Empire positions in the region and, securing an alliance with Serbia, consolidated former Bulgarian-held Macedonian lands. The change records this transfer of territory from Bulgaria to Epirus.

w4-600538.name: Mongol conquest of the Yenisei Kyrgyz (Jebe's northern campaign)
w4-600538.blurb: As Mongol armies pushed west in pursuit of the Merkits and the Naiman usurper Kuchlug, Jochi's forces overran the eastern Desht-i Kipchak — the steppe of the Kimek–Kipchak confederation between the Irtysh and the Aral region — in the campaigns of 1216–1219. These Kipchak and Kimek lands were absorbed into the emerging Ulus of Jochi on the eve of the Khwarezm invasion. The change records the Kimek–Kipchak steppe passing under Mongol control.

w4-600539.name: Mongol conquest of Khwarezm — fall of Transoxiana (Bukhara and Samarkand)
w4-600539.blurb: The Yenisei Kyrgyz of the Sayan–Yenisei region had submitted to Jochi in 1207, but residual resistance among the Siberian forest peoples flared in the hoi-yin irgen revolt of c.1217–1218, which Mongol forces suppressed. By the close of the 1210s the Yenisei Kyrgyz lands were firmly integrated into the Mongol Empire's northern domains. The change reflects this final Mongol consolidation over Kyrgyz territory rather than any conquest in Transoxiana.

w4-600540.name: Mongol conquest of Qara Khitai (Jebe's campaign / death of Kuchlug)
w4-600540.blurb: Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarezmian Empire in autumn 1219, and over 1219–1221 his armies stormed Otrar, Bukhara, Samarkand, and Gurganj while Shah Muhammad II fled westward to die a fugitive in December 1220. The empire's heartland in Transoxiana and Khorasan was systematically devastated and absorbed into the Mongol domains. The change records Khwarezmid territory passing under Mongol control.

w4-600541.name: Mongol Conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire
w4-600541.blurb: Genghis Khan dispatched his general Jebe in 1216 to pursue the Naiman prince Kuchlug, who had seized the Kara-Khitan (Western Liao) khanate around 1210 and alienated its Muslim population through religious persecution. Jebe routed Kuchlug's forces near Balasagun, and the fugitive was captured and beheaded in 1218; by 1219 the entire former Kara-Khitan realm in Semirechye and the Tarim basin had been absorbed by the Mongols. The change records the Kara-Khitan state passing to the Mongol Empire.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Mongol conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire

w4-600545.name: Battle of Ganter — Ken Arok defeats Kediri and founds Singhasari (1222)
w4-600545.blurb: In 1222, Ken Arok, the akuwu of Tumapel in East Java, allied with Brahmin rebels against King Kertajaya of Kediri. At the Battle of Ganter (near present-day Malang, around lng 111.9, lat -7.6) Ken Arok's forces defeated Kertajaya, ending the Kediri kingdom and founding Singhasari (Kediri Kingdom -> Singhasari). Ken Arok took the title Sri Ranggah Rajasa, founding the dynasty that produced the Majapahit line. Matches [1220,1222].

w4-600547.name: Establishment of the Trần dynasty in Đại Việt
w4-600547.blurb: In 1225 the Lý dynasty's child empress Lý Chiêu Hoàng abdicated in favor of her husband Trần Cảnh, engineered by Trần Thủ Độ, founding the Trần dynasty of Đại Việt. The 'Ngô Dynasty' label here stands in for the preceding Vietnamese dynasty whose realm passed by this dynastic coup to the Trần. This transferred the territory of northern Vietnam (mapped near the Red River) to the Trần.

w4-600548.name: Conquest of Thessalonica by the Despotate of Epirus
w4-600548.blurb: In 1224, Theodore Komnenos Doukas of the Despotate of Epirus captured Thessalonica, ending the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica established after the Fourth Crusade. Theodore had systematically taken all surrounding territory over the previous nine years before the final capture of the city itself.

w4-600549.name: Theodore Komnenos Doukas Conquers Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica for Despotate of Epirus
w4-600549.blurb: The Despotate of Epirus under Theodore Komnenos Doukas captured the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica in December 1224, ending the Crusader state founded by Boniface of Montferrat in 1204. Theodore then claimed the imperial title (crowned c. 1225-1227). The data shows territory transferring from 'Kingdom of Thessalonica' to 'Despotate of Epirus' in 1226-1227, capturing the absorption of the former Latin state into Theodore's growing Greek empire shortly before his coronation.

w4-600550.name: Mongol conquest of Western Xia (fall of Zhongxing)
w4-600550.blurb: The polygon transition here is Western Xia (the Tangut state) passing to the Mongol Empire. Western Xia had been a Mongol vassal since submitting in 1210, but its refusal to supply troops for the Khwarezmian campaign in 1219 provoked Genghis Khan. The blurb as written instead narrates the conquest of Khwarezm and Khorasan, a different theatre roughly 2,000 km to the west; the Tangut realm itself was only fully annihilated in the second Mongol invasion of 1225–1227, when Yinchuan fell and the population was massacred in September 1227.

w4-600551.name: Mongol western campaigns against the Kipchaks (Jebe and Subutai raid; Jochi's campaign)
w4-600551.blurb: Following the Mongol destruction of Khwarezm (1219–1221), Jebe and Subutai raided the Pontic steppe and defeated a Kipchak–Rus coalition at the Battle of the Kalka River (1223). Jochi's forces continued pressing the Kimek-Kipchak confederation in the Ural-Kazakh steppes through 1226–1227, incorporating these eastern Kipchak ranges before Genghis Khan's death in August 1227.

citations.label: Wikipedia – Battle of the Kalka River
Wikipedia – Mongol invasion of Volga Bulgaria

w4-600553.name: Leonese conquest of Cáceres by Alfonso IX
w4-600553.blurb: Alfonso IX of León campaigned against Almohad Cáceres for over a decade — failed sieges in 1218 and 1222-1223, systematic destruction of its surrounding strongholds, and an engagement involving the Order of Alcántara in 1227 — before the city definitively fell on 23 April 1229, the feast of St George, its patron ever since. The conquest opened the way to Mérida and Badajoz (1230) as Almohad power fragmented after Las Navas de Tolosa. (The atlas's 1226-1227 snapshot slightly antedates the definitive fall; the 1227 date sometimes seen in older literature reflects an intermediate engagement, not the capture.)

w4-600554.name: Khwarazmian invasion of Georgia under Jalal ad-Din Mingburnu
w4-600554.blurb: The fugitive Khwarazmshah Jalal ad-Din Mingburnu, fleeing the Mongols, invaded Georgia and crushed the Georgian army at the Battle of Garni (1226), then sacked Tbilisi. This devastated the Kingdom of Georgia and stripped it of Armenian/Caucasian territory around the mapped point. The 'Hamdanid Emirates' label is the atlas's stand-in for Jalal ad-Din's reconstituted Khwarazmian state; the event is the Khwarazmian conquest.

w4-600558.name: Assassination of Leszek the White at Gasawa and Sandomierz succession (1227)
w4-600558.blurb: On 23 November 1227, Duke Leszek the White of Sandomierz was assassinated at the Congress of Gasawa; under the 1217 mutual-inheritance treaty Wladyslaw III Spindleshanks of Greater Poland temporarily took custody of Lesser-Polish territory before Grzymislawa's regency for the infant Boleslaw V stabilized Sandomierz. The worklist transition is 'Duchy of Sandomierz' -> 'Duchy of Greater Poland' [1226,1227] with 1227 inside the window, matching this shift of authority toward the Greater Poland sphere; the coordinate is approximate but the named event is sound.

w4-600559.name: Nicaean (Byzantine successor) expansion in Anatolia under John III Vatatzes
w4-600559.blurb: The Empire of Nicaea, the principal Byzantine successor state, consolidated and expanded its Anatolian holdings under John III Doukas Vatatzes after the Battle of Poimanenon (1224) against the Latins. The atlas treats Nicaea and the 'Byzantine Empire' as distinct labels, so this records the Nicaean/Byzantine consolidation of northwestern Anatolia around the mapped point. It reflects the rising power of the Nicaean state.

w4-600560.name: Epirote expansion into Macedonia/Thessaly (Theodore Komnenos Doukas)
w4-600560.blurb: Theodore Komnenos Doukas of the Despotate of Epirus expanded eastward into Macedonia, capturing Thessalonica in 1224 and proclaiming himself emperor. The atlas's 'Byzantine Empire' / Epirus relabeling records the shifting of territory in western Macedonia/Thessaly (near the mapped point) among these Byzantine successor states during Theodore's ascendancy before his defeat at Klokotnitsa (1230).

w4-600561.name: Loss of Latin Empire territory to Byzantine successor states in Thrace
w4-600561.blurb: By the mid-1220s the Latin Empire of Constantinople was collapsing, losing Thrace and the European hinterland to its Byzantine successor rivals (Nicaea, Epirus, and Bulgaria). The territory around the mapped point in Thrace/eastern Macedonia passed from Latin control to a Byzantine successor state. This continued the dismemberment of the crusader empire founded in 1204.

w4-600562.name: Theodore Komnenos Doukas Crowned Emperor of Thessalonica
w4-600562.blurb: Theodore Komnenos Doukas conquered the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica in 1224 and was crowned emperor at Thessalonica c. 1225-1227 by the Archbishop of Ohrid, challenging the Nicaean claim to Byzantine succession. The transfer from 'Kingdom of Thessalonica' to 'Byzantine Empire' in 1226-1227 reflects the end of the Latin kingdom and its reconstitution under a Greek ruler styling himself emperor. The Empire of Thessalonica survived until Nicaea annexed the city in 1246.

w4-600563.name: Ivan Asen II's conquests after Battle of Klokotnitsa; Bulgarian gains from Byzantine successor states
w4-600563.blurb: Ivan Asen II of the Second Bulgarian Empire defeated Theodore Komnenos Doukas of the Empire of Thessalonica at the Battle of Klokotnitsa on 9 March 1230, capturing Theodore and annexing Macedonia, Thrace, and Albania. By around 1227 Ivan Asen was already expanding at the expense of Byzantine successor states; the Klokotnitsa victory completed Bulgaria's dominance and temporarily reversed Byzantine territorial control in the Balkans.

w4-600569.name: Umar ibn Rasul proclaims himself independent Sultan of Yemen
w4-600569.blurb: Umar ibn Ali ibn Rasul, left as Ayyubid deputy governor of Yemen after al-Malik al-Mas'ud's 1229 departure for Syria, formally proclaimed himself sultan (taking the title al-Malik al-Mansur) in 1235 after receiving a diploma of recognition from the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir, completing the Ayyubid loss of Yemen and founding the independent Rasulid dynasty.

w4-600571.name: Sundiata Keita's defeat of the Sosso Empire (Battle of Kirina)
w4-600571.blurb: Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire, defeated Soumaoro Kanté of the Sosso Empire at the Battle of Kirina (c. 1235), as recounted in the Epic of Sundiata. This victory destroyed Sosso and transferred its Mandinka heartland (around the mapped point in the upper Niger region) to the new Mali Empire. It marked the foundation of Malian imperial power.

w4-600572.name: Mali Empire's absorption of Takrur
w4-600572.blurb: Following Sundiata Keita's victory at Kirina (c. 1235), the expanding Mali Empire absorbed the western Sahelian kingdom of Takrur on the lower Senegal River (near the mapped point). Takrur, a long-established Islamic state, became a tributary/province within the Mali sphere. This was part of Mali's rapid consolidation of the western Sudan.

w4-600573.name: Bulgarian recovery of the Belgrade/Braničevo Danube region under Ivan Asen II
w4-600573.blurb: Tsar Ivan Asen II, at the height of Bulgarian power after Klokotnitsa (1230), recovered the Belgrade and Braničevo borderlands along the Danube (the mapped point) from the Kingdom of Hungary. This reversed the earlier Hungarian occupation of the zone. The region remained contested between the two kingdoms throughout the period.

w4-600575.name: Battle of Klokotnitsa and Bulgarian annexation of Epirote Macedonia/Thrace
w4-600575.blurb: At the Battle of Klokotnitsa (1230) Tsar Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria decisively defeated and captured Theodore Komnenos Doukas of the Despotate of Epirus (Empire of Thessalonica). Bulgaria then annexed vast Epirote territories across Macedonia and Thrace (around the mapped point), making the Second Bulgarian Empire the dominant Balkan power. The Epirote empire collapsed.

w4-600577.name: Bulgarian expansion into Thrace after Klokotnitsa
w4-600577.blurb: Following his victory at Klokotnitsa (1230), Ivan Asen II of the Second Bulgarian Empire seized Thrace from the various Byzantine/Latin successor powers, extending Bulgarian rule toward the Aegean. The territory around the mapped point in Thrace passed to Bulgaria in this surge of expansion. Asen styled himself 'Tsar of the Bulgarians and Greeks.'

w4-600578.name: Transformation of the Despotate of Epirus into the Empire of Thessalonica
w4-600578.blurb: Theodore Komnenos Doukas, ruler of Epirus, captured Thessalonica from the Latin crusader kingdom in 1224 and proclaimed himself Byzantine emperor c. 1225-1227, establishing the Empire of Thessalonica, which controlled much of Macedonia and Thrace. The data window 1230-1236 reflects this reorganization and the subsequent collapse after the Battle of Klokotnitsa (1230), when Bulgarian Tsar Ivan Asen II defeated Theodore.

w4-600580.name: Usfurid overthrow of the Uyunid Emirate
w4-600580.blurb: The Uyunid Emirate of al-Hasa in eastern Arabia (51.9,26.9) fell to the Usfurids of Banu Uqayl around 1235–1238 after internal divisions weakened it. The territorial change (loss of al-Hasa from the Uyunids c.1236) is well-attested and matches the 1230–1236 window; the atlas 'to' label 'Hamdanid Emirates' is a Cliopatria naming choice for the successor Arab tribal grouping (historically the Usfurids), not the Hamdanids of Mosul/Aleppo.

w4-600582.name: Collapse of Polonnaruwa and rise of the Dambadeniya kingdom
w4-600582.blurb: Kalinga Magha invaded Sri Lanka from South India in 1215 and conquered Polonnaruwa, devastating the island's hydraulic civilisation. By 1232 Vijayabahu III had established a new Sinhalese kingdom at Dambadeniya, superseding Polonnaruwa (lat 7.3, lng 80.8). The 1230-1236 window captures the formal collapse of Polonnaruwa and the emergence of its successor state, rather than the 1215 invasion itself.

w4-600585.name: Danish Loss of North German Territories after Battle of Bornhöved (1227)
w4-600585.blurb: At the Battle of Bornhöved (22 July 1227), King Valdemar II of Denmark was decisively defeated by a coalition led by Count Adolf IV of Holstein, ending Denmark's short-lived empire in Northern Germany. The Danish border retreated northward from the Elbe to the Eider River, and Holstein reverted to German overlordship under the Schauenburg counts as an imperial fief. The 1230–1236 window reflects consolidation of this post-battle settlement, with Holstein returning to the Holy Roman Empire.

w4-600586.name: Permanent Union of León and Castile under Ferdinand III
w4-600586.blurb: On Alfonso IX of León's death (24 September 1230), his son Ferdinand III, King of Castile since 1217, asserted his claim. Via the Treaty of Benavente (11 December 1230) Ferdinand received León, and the union was permanent thereafter, launching his Reconquista (Córdoba 1236, Seville 1248). The coordinates (~6.5W 41N, western Iberia) lie in the territory León brought to the union. Correctly dated within the 1230-1236 window.

w4-600587.name: Ferdinand III of Castile inherits León and permanently unites the crowns (1230); conquest of Córdoba (1236)
w4-600587.blurb: On the death of Alfonso IX of León in 1230, his son Ferdinand III of Castile negotiated the Benavente agreement with his half-sisters and inherited the Leonese throne, permanently uniting the crowns of Castile and León into the Crown of Castile. Building on this unified base, Ferdinand then prosecuted the Reconquista, capturing the former Almohad capital Córdoba in 1236 and greatly expanding the Crown's southern frontier.

w4-600590.name: Treaty of Paris (Meaux) 1229 – French Crown Gains Languedoc Territories from Raymond VII
w4-600590.blurb: The Treaty of Paris (also called Treaty of Meaux, April 1229), ending the Albigensian Crusade, forced Count Raymond VII of Toulouse to cede substantial eastern Languedoc territories directly to the French crown, organized as the seneschalships of Carcassonne and Beaucaire. In the window 1230–1236, the French crown was consolidating administrative control over the ceded lands while Raymond VII retained rump Toulouse under French suzerainty.

w4-600591.name: Mamluk (Delhi Sultanate) conquest of Bengal / annexation of Lakhnauti
w4-600591.blurb: The Sena Dynasty of Bengal, already pushed to its eastern remnant by the earlier Ghurid/Khalji conquest of Lakhnauti (c. 1204 under Bakhtiyar Khalji), saw its territory absorbed into the Delhi Sultanate under the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty of Iltutmish. Iltutmish reasserted Delhi's authority over rebellious Bengal around 1227-1230, bringing Lakhnauti firmly under the Mamluk dynasty. The change near 88.3E, 23.8N reflects Bengal passing to the Delhi Mamluks.

w4-600592.name: Iltutmish's conquest of Malwa (sack of Bhilsa and Ujjain, 1234-1235)
w4-600592.blurb: Sultan Shams ud-Din Iltutmish of the Delhi Mamluk dynasty campaigned into Malwa, the heartland of the Paramara Dynasty, around 1234-1235, sacking Bhilsa (Vidisha) and the great city of Ujjain and desecrating the Mahakaleshwar temple. The Paramaras were severely weakened and lost territory to Delhi. The change near 76.7E, 24.7N reflects this Mamluk conquest of Paramara Malwa.

w4-600596.name: Mongol-Jin War (Ogedei's campaign against the Jin)
w4-600596.blurb: Under Great Khan Ogedei, the Mongol Empire renewed its war on the Jurchen Jin dynasty, overrunning Henan and the central plain. The campaign culminated in the fall of the Jin capital Kaifeng (1233) and the destruction of the dynasty at the siege of Caizhou in 1234, where the last Jin emperor died. The transfer of ~775,000 km2 of north China (near 113.1E, 36.4N) from Great Jin to the Mongol Empire reflects this conquest.

citations.label: Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty

w4-600598.name: Mongol conquest of the Caucasus (Shirvan submission)
w4-600598.blurb: Following Chormaqan's campaigns in Transcaucasia in the 1230s, the Shirvanshahs' realm in the eastern Caucasus (near 48.1E, 40.6N) was subjugated and made tributary to the Mongol Empire. Shirvan, like neighboring Georgia and Armenia, was reduced to Mongol vassalage in the mid-1230s. The change reflects this submission of Shirvan to the Mongols.

citations.label: Mongol invasions of Georgia and Armenia

w4-600599.name: Mongol conquest of Persia (Chormaqan's subjugation of the Jibal/Persian Iraq)
w4-600599.blurb: After the Mongols crushed Jalal al-Din Mingburnu of Khwarazm and Chormaqan's tumens occupied northern and western Iran around 1231-1235, the petty Persian dynasties of the Jibal region (here labeled Hamdanid Emirates, near 55.3E, 34.3N) were overrun and absorbed into the Mongol Empire. The change reflects Mongol consolidation of Persian Iraq under Ogedei.

w4-600600.name: Mongol conquest of the Cumans-Kipchaks (Batu/Subutai western campaign)
w4-600600.blurb: The Mongol western campaign of 1236-1237 under Batu and Subutai shattered the Kimek-Kipchak (Cuman) confederation of the Pontic-Caspian steppe. The Kipchaks were defeated, many killed or enslaved, and their vast steppe territory (over 1.2 million km2 near 49.2E, 50.5N) was incorporated into the Mongol Empire, forming the core of the Golden Horde. Survivors fled west toward Hungary.

w4-600601.name: Treaty of Adrianople (1230) aftermath / Epirote-Bulgarian wars
w4-600601.blurb: The labeled transition (to the Mongol Empire, c.1241) reflects Mongol expansion, but the 'from: Kashmir' label and the centroid in central Macedonia (lng 23.3, lat 40.4) are incompatible — Macedonia was never a Mongol or Kashmiri possession. No verifiable event matches this from/to/place combination. The blurb's narrative about post-Klokotnitsa Epirote–Bulgarian wars in Macedonia is geographically real but unrelated to any Mongol or Kashmiri polygon, indicating a broken data join rather than a describable event.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria

w4-600602.name: Henry I the Bearded acquires Greater Poland
w4-600602.blurb: Henry I the Bearded, Duke of Silesia and High Duke of Poland from 1232, extended Silesian control over much of the Duchy of Greater Poland through a series of campaigns and diplomatic maneuvers against the Piast rivals in the region. By 1234, a substantial portion of Greater Poland was formally ceded to him, marking the high point of Silesian Piast ambitions to reunify fragmented Poland. The territory around lng 18.4, lat 52 (central Greater Poland) was thus absorbed into the Silesian duchy.

w4-600606.name: Merger of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword into the Teutonic Order
w4-600606.blurb: After the Livonian Brothers of the Sword were crushed by Samogitians and Semigallians at the Battle of Saule in 1236, the surviving order was incorporated into the Teutonic Order by a papal bull in 1237, becoming its autonomous Livonian branch. This transferred the Brothers' Baltic holdings (near 24.6E, 57.7N) to the Teutonic Order. The change reflects this merger.

w4-600607.name: Livonian (Teutonic) Order occupation of Votian and Pskovian territory (1240–1241 Votia campaign)
w4-600607.blurb: After the 1237 incorporation of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword into the Teutonic Order, the Livonian branch exploited Novgorod's vulnerability during the Mongol crisis to launch the 1240–1241 Votia campaign, capturing Izborsk, besieging Pskov, and occupying Koporye — seizing Novgorodian-tributary territory until Alexander Nevsky's counterattack at Lake Peipus (1242). This matches the Novgorod Republic→Teutonic Order transfer.

w4-600609.name: Pandyan resurgence under Maravarman Sundara Pandyan (decline of the Cholas)
w4-600609.blurb: The revived Pandya Empire under Maravarman Sundara Pandyan I and his successors pressed against the declining Chola Empire in the early-to-mid 13th century, capturing Chola heartland territory in the Tamil country. Around 1238-1241 the Pandyas advanced at Chola expense near 78.6E, 11N, foreshadowing the final Pandyan supremacy under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan. The change reflects this Pandya takeover of Chola land.

w4-600611.name: Portuguese Reconquista of the Algarve (capture of Tavira/Mertola)
w4-600611.blurb: As the Almohad Caliphate collapsed in al-Andalus, King Sancho II of Portugal and the Military Orders pushed the Reconquista into the Algarve, taking strongholds such as Mertola (1238) and Tavira (1239) in the southwest (near -8E, 37.9N). This transferred Almohad-held territory to the Kingdom of Portugal. The change reflects this phase of the Portuguese Reconquista.

w4-600612.name: Mongol invasion of Europe 1241: sweep through Wallachia/Bulgaria's northern territory
w4-600612.blurb: During the 1241–1242 Mongol western campaign, columns under Kadan and Büri crossed the Carpathians and raided the Vlach-inhabited lands of Wallachia and Moldavia east of the mountains, and Mongol forces traversed these territories again during the 1242 withdrawal after news of Ögedei Khan's death. The labeled 'to: Empire of Thessalonica' is erroneous for the Danube plain (centroid lng 26.1, lat 44.7), which lay in the Second Bulgarian Empire's northern sphere, not Thessalonica's; the actual disruptive power was the Mongols.

w4-600614.name: Mongol invasion of Hungary forces Hungarian withdrawal from Bosnia (Bosnian Crusade ends)
w4-600614.blurb: Hungary had been waging the Bosnian Crusade against alleged heretics in the Banate of Bosnia since 1235, with Prince Coloman's forces occupying peripheral Bosnian territory by 1238. When the Mongols under Batu Khan invaded Hungary in March 1241, Coloman was forced to withdraw from Bosnia. He was killed at the Battle of Mohi (11 April 1241); the Mongol threat effectively ended Hungarian military pressure on Bosnia and allowed Ban Ninoslav to recover lost territory.

citations.label: First Mongol invasion of Hungary – Wikipedia

w4-600615.name: Founding of the Sukhothai Kingdom (revolt against the Khmer Empire)
w4-600615.blurb: Around 1238 the Tai chieftains Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao and Pho Khun Pha Muang rebelled against the Khmer Empire's local governor and founded the Sukhothai Kingdom, the first major independent Thai state. This wrested the central Chao Phraya basin (near 101.4E, 15.6N) from declining Khmer control. The change reflects the establishment of Sukhothai at Khmer expense.

w4-600616.name: Reconquista - Ferdinand III of Castile's Campaigns in Andalusia
w4-600616.blurb: Following the Almohad collapse after Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), Ferdinand III of Castile rapidly conquered southern Iberia. He took Córdoba in 1236; by 1238-1241 he seized Niebla-Huelva, Écija, and Lucena from the remnants of Almohad governance. The coordinates point to the Huelva/lower Guadalquivir area, passing from Almohad to Castilian control in this window as part of the continuous southward Reconquista advance.

w4-600617.name: Mongol sack of Pereyaslavl
w4-600617.blurb: During Batu Khan's 1239-1240 campaign through southern Rus', Mongol forces sacked the city of Pereyaslavl in 1239, destroying the principality and incorporating its territory into the Mongol Empire (later the Golden Horde).

citations.label: Wikipedia – Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus'

w4-600618.name: Mongol invasion of Hungary — Battle of Mohi
w4-600618.blurb: On 11 April 1241, Batu Khan and Subutai decisively defeated the Hungarian royal army of King Béla IV at the Battle of Mohi (Sajó River), killing most of the Hungarian nobility and opening the Great Hungarian Plain to Mongol occupation. The Mongols then systematically occupied Transylvania and the eastern lowlands (centroid lng 23.3, lat 47.5) through late 1241.

w4-600619.name: Mongol invasion of Halych-Volhynia / southwestern Rus
w4-600619.blurb: During Batu Khan and Subutai's invasion of the Rus principalities, the Mongols overran southwestern Rus, sacking towns of the Halych-Volhynia and Pereyaslavl/Chernigov lands in 1239-1240 before turning on Kiev. The change (near 32.3E, 47.4N) reflects the steppe and southern Rus territory passing to the Mongol Empire in this campaign.

w4-600620.name: Mongol Sack of Ryazan
w4-600620.blurb: Batu Khan's Mongol forces besieged and destroyed Ryazan in December 1237, killing Prince Yuri Igorevich and most of the population; the principality was incorporated into the Mongol domain (later Golden Horde). The polygon shift to 'Mongol Empire' between 1238 and 1241 reflects the consolidation of this conquest.

w4-600621.name: Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus (Turov-Pinsk lands)
w4-600621.blurb: As part of the Mongol invasion of the Rus in 1239-1240, the southern Rus principalities including Turov and Pinsk (near 28E, 52.2N) were subjugated by Batu Khan's forces. The change reflects these Polesian lands passing under Mongol overlordship during the campaign that culminated in the sack of Kiev.

w4-600622.name: Mongol sack of Kiev (siege of Kiev, 1240)
w4-600622.blurb: On 6 December 1240 Batu Khan's Mongol army stormed and destroyed Kiev after a fierce siege, slaughtering much of the population and ending the city's status as the premier center of Rus. The Principality of Kiev (near 28.6E, 50.5N) passed to the Mongol Empire. This is one of the most famous events of the Mongol invasion of Europe.

w4-600623.name: Mongol invasion of Bulgaria (1242) and Bulgarian tributary submission
w4-600623.blurb: After wintering in Hungary, Mongol tumens under Kadan moved through Serbia and joined Batu's main army in Bulgaria in the spring of 1242, ravaging the country during the wider Mongol invasion of Europe. Bulgaria — ruled by the boy-tsar Kaliman I — became a Mongol tribute-payer, a status William of Rubruck attested by 1253 and which historians usually link to this 1242 invasion. (The atlas's 1238-1241 window slightly antedates the invasion; Köse Dağ and the Sultanate of Rum, cited previously, are an unrelated Anatolian campaign involving different parties.)

citations.label: Mongol invasion of Bulgaria and Serbia (Wikipedia)

w4-600624.name: Mongol conquest of Persia under Baiju Noyan
w4-600624.blurb: After Köse Dağ (1243), Baiju Noyan's forces consolidated Mongol dominance over the Jazira and western Persia through the later 1240s, and the residual independent emirates of western and central Iran were brought under Mongol overlordship by around 1250, on the eve of Hülegü's expedition. The original blurb's speculative gloss on a 'Hamdanid Emirates' label is unreliable — the Hamdanids were a 10th-century Jaziran/Syrian dynasty long extinct by the 13th century — so any such Cliopatria label is anachronistic; the substantive event is Baiju's extension of Mongol control across western Iran.

w4-600625.name: Mongol invasion of northeastern Rus (Vladimir-Suzdal, Battle of the Sit River)
w4-600625.blurb: In the winter of 1237-1238 Batu Khan and Subutai overran the Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Rostov-Suzdal), sacking Vladimir, Suzdal, and many towns. Grand Prince Yuri II was killed at the Battle of the Sit River in March 1238. The change (near 40.6E, 58.6N) reflects northeastern Rus passing to the Mongol Empire.

w4-600628.name: Mongol sack of Pereyaslavl
w4-600628.blurb: As Batu Khan's army swept through southern Kievan Rus' in 1239, it sacked and devastated Pereyaslavl on 3 March 1239, ending princely rule there and subjecting the principality to Golden Horde tribute. (The cited Nicaean-Epirote partition of Bulgarian Macedonia, c. 1246-1250, is an unrelated Balkan event involving entirely different parties.)

w4-600633.name: Epirote reassertion over the rump Empire of Thessalonica
w4-600633.blurb: After Theodore Komnenos Doukas was released from Bulgarian captivity c. 1237, he returned to Thessalonica and overthrew his brother Manuel, installing his son John Komnenos Doukas. Simultaneously, Michael II of Epirus operated independently. The data window 1238-1241 reflects this period when Epirus proper reasserted independence while the rump Empire of Thessalonica existed under Bulgarian suzerainty until Ivan Asen II's death in 1241.

w4-600635.name: Mongol conquest of the Caucasus and Georgian submission
w4-600635.blurb: A full-scale Mongol conquest of the Caucasus began in 1236 under Chormaqan, who captured Ani and Kars in 1239. Georgian nobles submitted progressively, with atabeg Avag Mkhargrdzeli making peace c. 1238–1239 and Georgia formally acknowledging Mongol overlordship by 1243. The dataset records 'Mongol Empire → Kingdom of Georgia' near lng 45.5, lat 40.6 in the 1238–1241 window, reflecting Georgia's submission to Mongol suzerainty (the kingdom continuing as a Mongol vassal).

w4-600639.name: Mongol subjugation of the Sultanate of Rum (Battle of Köse Dağ)
w4-600639.blurb: At the Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243, the Mongol general Baiju crushed the army of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum under Kaykhusraw II, reducing Anatolia to a Mongol tributary vassal state. Over the following years Rum's eastern and central Anatolian territories passed under direct Mongol (Ilkhanate/Great Khanate) control. This change near eastern Anatolia reflects that subjugation.

w4-600640.name: Mongol conquest of Persia / Jibal and western Iran
w4-600640.blurb: Following the Mongol campaigns of Chormaqan and Baiju across Iran in the 1230s-1240s, the highlands of western and central Persia (Jibal region) were absorbed into the Mongol Empire ahead of Hulagu's later invasion. The 'Hamdanid Emirates' label here stands for the local Iranian/Atabeg holdings in the region around Isfahan, which came under Mongol overlordship. This vast central-Iranian block reflects that consolidation of Mongol control.

citations.label: Mongol conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire (Wikipedia)

w4-600643.name: Mongol invasions of Southern Song — Sichuan campaigns (c. 1247–1250)
w4-600643.blurb: During the 1240s Mongol forces campaigned against the Southern Song in Sichuan following the 1241 capture of Chengdu, with continued pressure along the Sichuan frontier in 1247-1250 before the major campaigns of Möngke (1252-1259). The coordinates (103.5°E, 32.3°N) correspond to the upper Sichuan/Shaanxi border; from=Southern Song, to=Mongol Empire matches the 1247-1250 window.

citations.label: Mongol conquest of the Song dynasty – Wikipedia

w4-600644.name: Mongol incorporation of Tibet/western Himalaya (Köden's expedition)
w4-600644.blurb: The same Mongol expansion into the Tibetan plateau and western Himalaya under Prince Köden, culminating in Tibet's submission via Sakya Pandita in 1247, extended Mongol overlordship into the Ladakh/Kashmir borderlands shown here (around 79E, 34N, i.e. the high western plateau). This frontier zone passed under Mongol authority alongside Tibet proper.

w4-600645.name: Güyük Khan's partition of the Kingdom of Georgia
w4-600645.blurb: After Queen Rusudan's 1245 death left a disputed succession, the Mongols split the Georgian nobility between two rival claimants; summoned to Karakorum for Güyük Khan's 1246 enthronement, David VII 'Ulu' and David VI 'Narin' were both confirmed in 1247 as co-kings of a formally divided, Mongol-administered Kingdom of Georgia. (Queen Rusudan's earlier 1243 submission after Jalal al-Din's depredations predates this atlas window.)

w4-600648.name: Louis IX grants Anjou to Charles, founding Capetian House of Anjou
w4-600648.blurb: In 1246–1247 Louis IX granted Anjou and Maine to his brother Charles as a royal apanage, founding the Capetian House of Anjou (alongside Charles's marriage to Beatrice of Provence). Anjou near lng -0.2 W / lat 47.8 N passed from the French royal domain to the Capetian House of Anjou, matching the [1247,1250] window.

w4-600649.name: Louis IX grants County of Maine to Charles of Anjou (1246)
w4-600649.blurb: In 1246 King Louis IX gave the County of Maine (with Anjou) as an appanage to his younger brother Charles, founding the Capetian House of Anjou. The window (1247-1250) captures the transition from Capetian royal administration to the new Angevin appanage lordship.

w4-600650.name: Louis IX grants Anjou and Maine to Charles of Anjou
w4-600650.blurb: In 1246–1247 Louis IX invested his brother Charles with the Counties of Anjou and Maine as a royal apanage, founding the Capetian House of Anjou. The Anjou/Maine region near lng -0.2 W / lat 47.8 N passed from the County of Anjou (royal domain) into the Capetian House of Anjou, matching the [1247,1250] window.

w4-600651.name: Delhi Sultanate (Mamluk) campaigns into Gujarat and Rajasthan under Ulugh Khan/Balban (c.1247–1250)
w4-600651.blurb: The coordinates point to southern Rajasthan / northern Gujarat, a frontier between the declining Chaulukya (Solanki) sphere and the expanding Delhi Sultanate. By the 1240s the Vaghela chiefs had supplanted the Chaulukyas, while the Mamluk regent Ulugh Khan (later Sultan Balban) conducted punitive campaigns into Rajasthan and the Gujarat borderland c.1247–1250, pressing Chaulukya-successor chiefs into tributary status. No single conquest is precisely documented, but the campaign arc is well attested.

w4-600652.name: Mindaugas's consolidation of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
w4-600652.blurb: In the late 1240s Mindaugas consolidated the Lithuanian state and pushed into the fragmented Ruthenian principalities of Black Ruthenia and the upper Dnieper, absorbing minor polities such as Drutsk. This expansion accompanied his rise to sole rulership (he was crowned king in 1253). The change near Drutsk reflects Lithuanian annexation of these small Rus' principalities.

w4-600653.name: Mindaugas's consolidation of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
w4-600653.blurb: Mindaugas's expansion of Lithuania in the late 1240s extended into the upper Dnieper Rus' lands, including the Principality of Minsk, which fell under Lithuanian overlordship as the small Rus' principalities were absorbed during his unification of the realm before his 1253 coronation. This change near Minsk reflects that annexation.

w4-600654.name: Lithuanian absorption of the Principality of Polotsk
w4-600654.blurb: During Mindaugas's consolidation of Lithuania in the mid-13th century, the Principality of Polotsk in the upper Daugava came under Lithuanian control, becoming one of the earliest Ruthenian lands integrated into the Grand Duchy. This change near Polotsk reflects that incorporation.

w4-600655.name: Alphonse de Poitiers takes control of the County of Toulouse (1249)
w4-600655.blurb: On the death of Count Raymond VII in 1249, the County of Toulouse passed to his son-in-law Alphonse de Poitiers, brother of King Louis IX of France, under the terms of the Treaty of Paris (1229). This brought the county firmly into the Capetian orbit, and on Alphonse and Joan's deaths without heirs in 1271 it was absorbed directly by the Crown. The worklist transfer County of Toulouse → Kingdom of France at lng 2.8, lat 43.7 in the 1247–1250 window matches this 1249 Capetian takeover.

w4-600656.name: Louis IX's apanage grant of Poitou to Alphonse
w4-600656.blurb: Poitou had been in the French royal domain since 1204; in 1241 Louis IX invested his brother Alphonse with the County of Poitou as an apanage, held until Alphonse's death in 1271, when it reverted to the crown. The Poitou region near lng -0.5 W / lat 46.1 N reflects this reassignment within the French orbit, falling in the [1247,1250] window.

w4-600659.name: Ottokar II's acquisition of Styria and Wittelsbach displacement
w4-600659.blurb: After the Babenberg line died out in 1246, the duchies of Austria and Styria were contested; Ottokar II of Bohemia secured Austria and then defeated Béla IV of Hungary at the Battle of Kressenbrunn (12 July 1260), confirming his control of Styria, which Hungary relinquished in the 1261 Peace of Vienna. The labeled transition 'from: Mongol Empire'→'to: Kingdom of Hungary' does not match this Central European event at all; the real change was Styria passing from Hungarian to Bohemian (Přemyslid) control, not anything involving the Mongol Empire.

w4-600663.name: Serbian-Bulgarian frontier expansion under Stefan Uroš I
w4-600663.blurb: In the decade after the Mongol devastation of the Second Bulgarian Empire (1242) and amid Bulgaria's decline under the Asen successors, the Kingdom of Serbia under Stefan Uroš I expanded eastward into contested borderlands (around Niš/Morava valley, ~20.7E 43.4N) at Bulgaria's expense. This change reflects that Serbian frontier gain from a weakened Bulgaria.

w4-600665.name: Nicaean conquest of Bulgarian Thrace and Macedonia under John III Vatatzes
w4-600665.blurb: In 1246 the Nicaean emperor John III Doukas Vatatzes, exploiting the minority of the Bulgarian tsar Kaliman I Asen, campaigned through Thrace and Macedonia and seized large Bulgarian-held territories including the region around the Maritsa/Rhodope (Stara Zagora, Melnik). This major Nicaean expansion at Bulgaria's expense matches the change near 24E 41N.

w4-600667.name: Nicaean conquest of Thessalonica and Latin/Byzantine Thrace under John III Vatatzes
w4-600667.blurb: In 1246 John III Vatatzes captured Thessalonica, ending the rival Greek state there, and during the same campaigns Nicaea absorbed remaining Latin- and rival-held lands in Thrace around the European shore of the Sea of Marmara. The 'Byzantine' source here denotes the rival Greek/Latin holdings absorbed by the ascendant Empire of Nicaea, the change near 26.7E 40N reflecting that gain.

w4-600669.name: Piast fragmentation — Silesia/Sandomierz border shift
w4-600669.blurb: After Henry II the Pious of Silesia was killed at the Battle of Legnica (1241), his unified Polish territories fragmented among his sons, and border regions in central/Lesser Poland shifted between the Silesian and Sandomierz Piast lines in the late 1240s. The 1247–1250 partitions adjusted control at (19.4,52) at Silesia's expense, consistent with the from→to (Duchy of Silesia → Duchy of Sandomierz).

w4-600671.name: Piast partition of Lower Silesia - creation of Duchy of Glogow
w4-600671.blurb: After Henry II the Pious was killed at the Battle of Legnica (1241), his sons partitioned Lower Silesia in 1248-1251: Boleslaw II took Legnica, Henry III received Wroclaw, and Konrad I obtained Glogow (15.6E, 52.1N). This re-established Glogow as an independent duchy carved from the Duchy of Silesia through the Piast tradition of partible inheritance; the Duchy of Glogow persisted until its absorption into Bohemia in the 15th century.

w4-600673.name: Pandya expansion under Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I - Hoysala territorial losses (c. 1251-1262)
w4-600673.blurb: Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I, who ascended the Pandya throne around 1251, launched an aggressive expansion into the Chola country and the Kaveri valley, reversing earlier Hoysala gains. The Pandyas attacked Hoysala positions and captured the strategic southern Hoysala capital of Kannanur Koppam near Srirangam, killing Hoysala generals and forcing king Somesvara back toward the Mysore plateau; Somesvara was later defeated and killed in 1262. The data entry (Hoysala Kingdom to Pandya Empire, py=1247, y=1250) reflects the beginning of this reversal of Hoysala territorial reach in the Tamil south.

w4-600674.name: Pandya resurgence and the eclipse of the Chola Empire
w4-600674.blurb: Under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I (from 1251), the Pandya dynasty rose dramatically, defeating the declining Cholas and Hoysalas and annexing core Chola territory in the Kaveri delta and Tamil heartland. This brought the long Chola era to its effective end as Pandya power supplanted them; the change near 79E 12.5N reflects that conquest of Chola lands.

w4-600680.name: Ascanian expansion in Brandenburg during the Great Interregnum
w4-600680.blurb: In the mid-13th century the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg, John I and Otto III, expanded eastward, acquiring Stettin/Szczecin (c. 1250), the Uckermark, and lands east of the Oder. The death of Emperor Frederick II in 1250 and the Great Interregnum (1250-1273) weakened imperial authority, allowing frontier princes to assert control. The from=Holy Roman Empire / to=Margraviate of Brandenburg and 1250-1260 window match.

w4-600681.name: Ottokar II's acquisition of Styria / extinction of the Babenbergs
w4-600681.blurb: After the Babenberg line died out (1246) leaving Austria and Styria contested, Ottokar II of Bohemia and Béla IV of Hungary divided the inheritance by the Peace of Ofen (1254), and Ottokar later took full control of Styria by 1260 after defeating Hungary at Kressenbrunn. The Duchy of Styria's emergence as a distinct controlled territory near 11.5E 47N (the labelled coordinates approximate the Alpine duchy) reflects this succession dispute and settlement.

w4-600682.name: Mongol/Galician pressure and the fragmentation of Mindaugas's Lithuania
w4-600682.blurb: After the Mongol commander Burundai's campaign against Lithuania (1258-1259) and amid the rebellion of Mindaugas's rivals, Lithuanian control over the recently absorbed Rus' principalities such as Minsk loosened, and Minsk re-emerged from Lithuanian overlordship. This reversal near Minsk reflects that contraction of Lithuanian authority in the upper Dnieper.

w4-600683.name: Peter II of Savoy expands into Vaud and Alpine territories
w4-600683.blurb: Peter II of Savoy systematically expanded Savoyard control over Vaud and Alpine valleys during the 1240s-1260s, extracting homages from lords of formerly imperial fiefs. The window (1250-1260) and Alpine coordinates (6.9, 45.6) reflect these gains at the expense of fragmented Holy Roman imperial lordships.

citations.label: Peter II, Count of Savoy - Wikipedia

w4-600684.name: Death of Conrad IV and the Hohenstaufen patrimony during the Interregnum
w4-600684.blurb: With the death of Emperor Conrad IV in 1254 the imperial throne lapsed into the Great Interregnum, and the Hohenstaufen family's hereditary Swabian/Alemannic lands (around 8.8E 47.6N) remained held by the dynasty (Conradin) rather than any reigning emperor. The reassignment from 'Holy Roman Empire' to the House of Hohenstaufen reflects the collapse of central royal authority and the dynasty holding its own patrimony.

w4-600687.name: Wittelsbach division of Bavaria during the Great Interregnum
w4-600687.blurb: Amid the Great Interregnum following the Hohenstaufen collapse, the Wittelsbach dukes consolidated and then partitioned Bavaria (the 1255 division between Upper and Lower Bavaria under Louis II and Henry XIII), holding the duchy as a hereditary princely territory rather than under effective imperial authority. The change near 12.4E 48.4N (Lower Bavaria) reflects Wittelsbach control during the interregnum.

w4-600688.name: Duchy of Brabant expands during the HRE Interregnum under Henry III
w4-600688.blurb: After Emperor Frederick II's death in 1250, the Holy Roman Empire entered the Interregnum (1250–1273), creating a power vacuum in the Low Countries. Duke Henry III of Brabant (r. 1248–1261) exploited this to expand eastward, receiving the disputed Lothier region and being appointed Imperial Vicar by Alfonso X, and acquiring territories such as Dalhem. The duchy absorbed several small HRE lordships in this period, with Duke John I later cementing Brabant's dominance at the Battle of Worringen (1288).

citations.label: Henry III, Duke of Brabant – Wikipedia

w4-600689.name: Collapse of the Polonnaruwa kingdom and drift of Sinhalese power to Dambadeniya
w4-600689.blurb: After Magha of Kalinga's devastating 21-year rule ended (~1236), the Polonnaruwa kingdom never recovered. Parakramabahu II of the Dambadeniya dynasty (r. 1236–1270) expelled the Kalingas and re-asserted Sinhalese rule in the south-west, but Polonnaruwa was effectively abandoned. The 1250–1260 atlas window captures the final disappearance of Polonnaruwa as a functioning polity and the consolidation of a new 'Ceylon' center at Dambadeniya.

citations.label: Sri Lanka – The fall of Polonnaruwa – Britannica

w4-600692.name: Kakatiya expansion against the Yadavas under Ganapati / Rudrama Devi
w4-600692.blurb: In the mid-13th century the Kakatiya dynasty of Warangal, at its height under Ganapatideva and his daughter Rudrama Devi, expanded northwest into the Deccan at the expense of the Seuna (Yadava) dynasty of Devagiri, contesting the Godavari-Krishna frontier (~77.6E 17.7N). This change reflects that Kakatiya gain of Yadava-held Deccan territory.

w4-600697.name: Lithuanian expansion into Black Ruthenia
w4-600697.blurb: Under Mindaugas, crowned King of Lithuania in 1253, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania expanded into Black Ruthenia (the upper Neman region around modern Belarus), territory loosely under Mongol overlordship after the 1240 sack of Kiev. Lithuania absorbed these Rus' lands during the mid-13th century as the Golden Horde's grip on the western forest zone loosened, marking the start of Lithuania's centuries-long acquisition of Ruthenian territory.

w4-600698.name: Kakatiya–Yadava frontier warfare in Telangana (c. 1250–1260)
w4-600698.blurb: The Kakatiya dynasty of Warangal and the Seuna (Yadava) dynasty of Devagiri contested the Telangana and western Deccan borderlands throughout the 13th century. Dual Kakatiya and Seuna inscriptions dated 1250 CE found at Eleshvaram confirm indecisive frontier battles in this period. As Ganapati Deva (r. c.1199–1262) aged and faced Pandya pressure in the south, the Yadavas exploited the situation and gradually encroached on Kakatiya-held Telangana, a process continuing into Rudrama Devi's reign. From=Kakatiya, to=Yadava is consistent with this territorial drift.

w4-600701.name: Kakatiya–Eastern Ganga conflict over Kalinga/coastal Andhra (mid-13th century)
w4-600701.blurb: During the reign of Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva (c. 1199–1262), the Kakatiyas and the Eastern Ganga kingdom of Orissa fought a prolonged, largely indecisive struggle over the Kalinga and Vengi/Godavari delta frontier; inscriptions of both powers dated 1250 CE attest to contested control. Eastern Ganga ruler Ananga Bhima III had earlier driven the Kakatiyas back across the Godavari. The worklist's 'Kakatiya Dynasty → Eastern Ganga Kingdom' (82.4E, 18.8N — Vishakhapatnam/Orissa-Andhra coast) for 1250–1260 reflects this shifting control.

w4-600702.name: Eastern Ganga victories over Delhi Sultanate in Bengal
w4-600702.blurb: King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty defeated Mamluk forces at the Battle of Katasin (1243) and in subsequent engagements, pushing into Bengal and annexing the provinces of Varendra and Rarh while threatening Lakhnauti. The Odishan king built the Konark Sun Temple to commemorate these victories. By the 1250s the Eastern Gangas had consolidated control of territory in western Bengal (lat 22.2, lng 85).

w4-600706.name: Hülegü's Mesopotamian campaign / Fall of the Jazira
w4-600706.blurb: During Hülegü Khan's westward campaign (1256-1260), the Mongols overran the Jazira (upper Mesopotamia around Mosul and Sinjar), formerly Zengid/atabeg territory, in the lead-up to and aftermath of the sack of Baghdad in 1258. The Zengid-descended lords of Mosul submitted to the Ilkhanate, bringing this region under Mongol control.

w4-600707.name: Mongol conquest of the Kingdom of Dali
w4-600707.blurb: In 1253-1254 Kublai (then a prince under his brother Great Khan Möngke) led the Mongol conquest of the Dali Kingdom in Yunnan, defeating the Duan rulers and capturing the capital. This brought present-day Yunnan into the Mongol Empire, outflanking Song China from the southwest.

citations.label: Mongol conquest of the Kingdom of Dali (Wikipedia)

w4-600708.name: Baiju's second Anatolian campaign and the Battle of Aksaray (Sultanhanı)
w4-600708.blurb: In October 1256 the Mongol general Baiju decisively defeated Kaykaus II's Seljuk army near Aksaray (the Battle of Sultanhanı), ending the loose vassalage that had persisted since the 1243 Köse Dağ battle and placing Anatolia directly under Möngke Khan's authority.
