This 1256 campaign, not Köse Dağ itself (which lies outside this window), is the event that tightened Mongol administrative control and transferred central Anatolian territory from the Rum Seljuks to the Mongol Empire.

w4-600711.name: Mongol Suppression of the Kashmiri Revolt
w4-600711.blurb: Around 1254–1255, Kashmiris revolted against Mongol overlordship, and Great Khan Möngke despatched generals Sali and Takudar to reassert control. General Sali Noyan invaded Kashmir, killed the local king who had murdered the Mongol overseer Otochi, and suppressed the revolt; Kashmir remained subject to the Mongol Empire for years afterwards. The dataset's window (py=1250, y=1260) encompasses this episode, though the 'from' label 'Lohara Dynasty' is loose — the Lohara dynasty proper had ended by c.1171–1175, and by 1252 Kashmir was under the late Hindu kings (Ramadeva). The transfer represents the assertion of Mongol suzerainty over the Hindu Kashmir polity rather than a discrete conquest of the Loharas specifically.

w4-600712.name: Mongol reassertion over Kashmir (c. 1254–1260)
w4-600712.blurb: Kashmir was made a Mongol dependency after 1235 with a darughachi installed. The Kashmiris revolted c. 1254–1255, killing the Mongol administrator Otochi at Srinagar; Möngke Khan's general Sali then invaded, killed the Kashmiri king, and re-established Mongol suzerainty. By 1260 Kashmir was firmly within the Mongol sphere, matching the Kashmir→Mongol Empire change at (74.8°E, 34.9°N).

w4-600713.name: Ottokar II's acquisition of Austria and the Babenberg lands
w4-600713.blurb: After the extinction of the Babenberg line (1246) left the Duchies of Austria and Styria vacant, Přemysl Ottokar II of Bohemia was invited to take Austria in 1251, expanding the Kingdom of Bohemia southward into formerly imperial lands. His marriage to Margaret of Babenberg and subsequent gains made Bohemia the dominant power in the southeastern Empire during the Interregnum.

w4-600714.name: Partition of Bavaria between Ludwig II and Henry XIII (1255)
w4-600714.blurb: After Duke Otto II of Bavaria died in 1253, his sons Ludwig II and Henry XIII ruled jointly then partitioned Bavaria in 1255: Ludwig II took Upper Bavaria and the Palatinate (Munich), Henry XIII took Lower Bavaria (Landshut). The from=Holy Roman Empire / to=Duchy of Bavaria and 1250-1260 window bracket the division during the Great Interregnum.

w4-600715.name: Charles of Anjou and the County of Provence
w4-600715.blurb: Charles I of Anjou (Capetian House of Anjou), who acquired the County of Provence by marriage in 1246, consolidated his rule over Provence and Forcalquier through the 1250s, subduing the autonomous communes (Marseille, Arles, Avignon) by 1257. The coordinates in the lower Rhône/Provence region reflect this Angevin consolidation of formerly imperial (Arelat) territory.

w4-600716.name: Ascanian expansion in the Holy Roman Empire - Great Interregnum
w4-600716.blurb: During the Great Interregnum (1250-1273) the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg, John I and Otto III, expanded, acquiring Stettin (c. 1250), the Uckermark, and territories east of the Oder as central imperial authority collapsed. The from=Holy Roman Empire / to=House of Ascania and 1250-1260 window match.

w4-600720.name: Partition of the Sultanate of Rum under Mongol overlordship
w4-600720.blurb: Within the period of Mongol domination of Anatolia, the Seljuk sultanate was repeatedly partitioned among rival brothers (Kaykaus II and Kilij Arslan IV) under Mongol arbitration in the late 1250s, with the Ilkhanate restoring Seljuk vassal rule over parts of central Anatolia. This reverse transfer from Mongol to Rum reflects the Mongols reinstalling their Seljuk clients rather than ruling directly.

w4-600721.name: Marinid attacks on Zayyanid Tlemcen (mid-13th century)
w4-600721.blurb: The Zayyanid dynasty (from 1236) at Tlemcen faced repeated Marinid pressure through the 1240s–1260s, with Marinid attacks and territorial encroachment in western Algeria. The worklist 'Zayyanid dynasty → Marinid Sultanate' at 1.4E, 35.2N (Tlemcen region), py=1250 y=1260, reflects Marinid gains in this period before Zayyanid stabilisation. Real conflict, plausibly dated.

w4-600722.name: Yekuno Amlak overthrows the Zagwe dynasty; Solomonic restoration (1270)
w4-600722.blurb: In 1270 Yekuno Amlak, an Amhara nobleman backed by monastic clergy, killed the Zagwe emperor Yitbarek and established the Solomonic dynasty. The window (1260-1270) and Ethiopian highland coordinates (38.9, 12.3) mark territory passing from Zagwe to the new Ethiopian Empire.

w4-600724.name: Thessaly breaks away from Epirus under John I Doukas
w4-600724.blurb: On the death of Michael II Komnenos Doukas of Epirus c. 1268, his legitimate son Nikephoros I inherited Epirus proper while his illegitimate son John I Doukas received Thessaly as an appanage. John asserted full independence at Neopatras and was granted the Byzantine title sebastokrator c. 1272. The data window 1270-1272 captures Thessaly's separation from Epirote control.

citations.label: John I Doukas of Thessaly – Wikipedia

w4-600728.name: Norwegian annexation of the Greenland settlements
w4-600728.blurb: The Norse settlements in Greenland (Eystribyggð/Vestribyggð) accepted the sovereignty of King Haakon IV of Norway in 1261, ending the settlers' self-governance. This brought the Greenland Viking colonies under the Old Kingdom of Norway, part of Haakon's broader incorporation of the Norse North Atlantic.

w4-600729.name: Norwegian annexation of Norse Greenland (1261)
w4-600729.blurb: In 1261 the Norse Greenlanders submitted to King Haakon IV Haakonsson of Norway, surrendering their independent commonwealth-style governance in exchange for royal protection and trade. The Greenland colonies thereby passed under the Old Kingdom of Norway, the same northward consolidation that absorbed Iceland soon after.

w4-600730.name: Gamli sáttmáli (Old Covenant) — Iceland submits to Norway
w4-600730.blurb: By the Gamli sáttmáli (Old Covenant) of 1262-1264, the Icelandic chieftains, exhausted by the civil strife of the Sturlung Age, swore allegiance to King Haakon IV of Norway, ending the Icelandic Commonwealth. Iceland thus passed under the Old Kingdom of Norway, completing Norway's North Atlantic consolidation.

w4-600733.name: Ottokar II's acquisition of Styria and Carinthia
w4-600733.blurb: Přemysl Ottokar II of Bohemia gained Styria (confirmed after the 1260 Battle of Kressenbrunn against Hungary) and inherited Carinthia and Carniola in 1269 on the death of Duke Ulrich III. The southeastern Alpine lands (around lat 47.7) thus passed from the patchwork of imperial minor states to the Kingdom of Bohemia, making Ottokar's realm stretch from the Sudetes to the Adriatic.

w4-600740.name: Despot Nikephoros I submits to Angevin suzerainty
w4-600740.blurb: Charles I of Anjou (King of Sicily) had proclaimed himself King of Albania in 1272, seizing Durres and coastal Epirote territory. Facing Byzantine pressure, Despot Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas of Epirus formally accepted Charles's suzerainty on 14 March 1279, surrendering the castles of Sopot and Butrint. The coordinates (20.9E, 40.2N) correspond to western Epirus/Albania, the core Angevin-claimed territory. Angevin ambitions collapsed after the Sicilian Vespers (1282) and the Battle of Berat (1281).

w4-600743.name: Sandomierz passes to Leszek II the Black on death of Bolesław V the Chaste
w4-600743.blurb: Bolesław V the Chaste, Duke of Sandomierz and High Duke of Poland, died childless on 7 December 1279, having designated Leszek II the Black (Leszek Czarny) as his heir in his testament. Leszek duly took control of both Kraków and Sandomierz, becoming High Duke. The dataset records the Duchy of Sandomierz (lat 52.8, lng 18.8) passing to the broader 'Duchies of Poland' polity around 1272–1279, reflecting this succession and the administrative consolidation under Leszek.

w4-600744.name: Battle on the Marchfeld (Dürnkrut)
w4-600744.blurb: At the Battle on the Marchfeld (Dürnkrut and Jedenspeigen) on 26 August 1278, King Rudolf I of Habsburg, allied with Hungary, defeated and killed Přemysl Ottokar II of Bohemia. The victory stripped Ottokar of Austria, Styria, Carinthia and Carniola (the southeastern lands around lat 46.9), which Rudolf granted to his own sons in 1282, founding Habsburg power in the Alpine lands.

w4-600745.name: Pope Nicholas III secures Romagna from Rudolf I of Habsburg for the Papal States (1278–1279)
w4-600745.blurb: In 1278 Pope Nicholas III concluded a concordat with Rudolf I of Habsburg, who renounced imperial claims to the Romagna, Bologna, and the Exarchate of Ravenna, ceding them to the Papacy. The coordinates (~44.2°N) correspond to Romagna; from=Holy Roman Empire minor states, to=Papal States matches the 1272-1279 window.

w4-600746.name: Leszek II the Black inherits Kraków and Sandomierz (1279)
w4-600746.blurb: On the death of Bolesław V the Chaste (7 Dec 1279), Leszek II the Black inherited the duchies of both Kraków and Sandomierz, becoming High Duke of Poland. The coordinates are the Sandomierz/Kraków borderland in Lesser Poland, matching the recorded Sandomierz → Kraków transfer for 1272–1279.

w4-600753.name: Serbian conquests in Byzantine Macedonia under Stefan Milutin
w4-600753.blurb: After Stefan Uroš II Milutin took the Serbian throne in 1282, he launched campaigns into Byzantine Macedonia, seizing Skopje, Polog, Belasica, Porec, Kicevo, and Debar between 1282 and 1284. These gains at the expense of the weakened Byzantine Empire under Andronikos II were consolidated and later confirmed by the Treaty of 1299. The data window 1279-1285 captures this southward expansion from Byzantium to the Kingdom of Serbia.

w4-600754.name: Robert III of Flanders marries Yolande II of Nevers; Nevers passes to Flanders
w4-600754.blurb: In March 1272, Robert III of Flanders (future Count of Flanders) married Yolande II, ruling Countess of Nevers and heiress of the Dampierre line. This union transferred the County of Nevers into the Flemish Dampierre orbit. Robert co-administered Nevers from 1272/73, and after Yolande's death (c. 1280) Nevers was held by the counts of Flanders until the inheritance passed to Philip the Bold of Burgundy upon his wife Margaret's succession in 1384.

w4-600757.name: Philip IV of France acquires County of Champagne through marriage to Joan I of Navarre
w4-600757.blurb: Philip IV married Joan I of Navarre in 1284, bringing the County of Champagne (and Navarre) to the heir-presumptive. When he ascended the French throne in 1285, Champagne's governance merged with the royal domain (formal incorporation followed on Louis Hutin's accession in 1314). The atlas records this as a 1279–1285 transition, corresponding to Joan's inheritance through Philip's accession.

w4-600759.name: Habsburg–Tyrol partition under Meinhard II
w4-600759.blurb: After Rudolf I of Habsburg won at Marchfeld (1278) and reorganized the southeastern imperial lands, the County of Tyrol (around 11.3E, 46.8N) was confirmed to Meinhard II, who also received the Duchy of Carinthia from Rudolf in 1286. The reassignment from the House of Habsburg proper to a Holy Roman Empire minor state reflects Tyrol/Görz-Tyrol settling as a distinct comital principality under Meinhard rather than a directly Habsburg-administered domain in this window.

w4-600761.name: Decline of Srivijaya and rise of Malay mainland polities
w4-600761.blurb: The Malay Peninsula interior (102.5E, 3.6N) passed out of Srivijayan thalassocratic control as that empire collapsed in the late 13th century, squeezed by the Javanese (Singhasari's Pamalayu expedition of 1275–1292) and by Tai expansion. The peninsular Malay lands reorganized under local Malay rulers in the vacuum left by Srivijaya's disintegration, which the snapshot records as a transfer to 'Malaya.'

w4-600764.name: Byzantine recovery of Epirus/Albania from the Angevins after the Sicilian Vespers
w4-600764.blurb: The Angevins' Adriatic-Greek ambitions collapsed after the Sicilian Vespers (1282). With Charles' defeat, Nikephoros I of Epirus lost Albania to a Byzantine counteroffensive; by the early-to-mid 1290s the Byzantines had recovered much of the Albanian/Epirote interior (regaining Ioannina by 1296). The coordinates (21.2°E, 39.2°N) lie in Epirus, consistent with the House of Anjou-Sicily→Byzantine recovery in the 1285–1294 window.

w4-600768.name: Khalji Revolution (overthrow of the Mamluk dynasty of Delhi)
w4-600768.blurb: In 1290 Jalal-ud-din Firuz Khalji overthrew the last rulers of the Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty of Delhi, killing the boy-sultan Muiz ud din Qaiqabad's line and founding the Khalji Dynasty. This dynastic coup transferred the Delhi Sultanate's vast north Indian domains (centered near 79.2E, 27.8N) from the Mamluks to the Khaljis, matching the large area and the (1285,1294) window.

w4-600769.name: Isabella of Villehardouin restores Villehardouin rule in Achaea
w4-600769.blurb: In 1289, Charles II of Anjou returned the Principality of Achaea to Isabella de Villehardouin, daughter of the last Villehardouin prince, in exchange for her homage. Philip I of Taranto (son of Charles II) received suzerainty rights over Achaea in 1294. The atlas window 1285–1294 marks the transition from direct Angevin House of Anjou-Sicily rule back to a Villehardouin-held principality under Angevin suzerainty.

w4-600771.name: Scottish succession crisis / First Interregnum after death of Alexander III
w4-600771.blurb: When Alexander III of Scotland died in March 1286, the succession passed to his infant granddaughter Margaret, Maid of Norway, who died en route in 1290 uncrowned, triggering the First Interregnum (1286-1292) under the Guardians of Scotland, with John Balliol chosen king in November 1292. The dataset transfer (Kingdom of Alba -> Kingdom of Scotland, py1285/y1294) at lng-4.6/lat56.7 marks this transitional period and the Alba-to-Scotland naming continuity; note this is primarily a same-polity relabel tied to a genuine succession crisis rather than a territorial conquest.

w4-600775.name: Fall of Singhasari and founding of Majapahit
w4-600775.blurb: In 1292 the rebel Jayakatwang of Kediri killed Kertanegara and ended the Singhasari kingdom; Kertanegara's son-in-law Raden Wijaya then exploited the arriving Mongol (Yuan) expeditionary force, turned on it, and founded the Majapahit Empire in 1293. Eastern Java (111.9E, -7.6N) thus passed from Singhasari to Majapahit, the dominant successor state on the island.

w4-600776.name: Majapahit succession to Srivijayan Sumatra
w4-600776.blurb: With Srivijaya in terminal decline, the new Majapahit Empire under Raden Wijaya (founded 1293) and later Gajah Mada laid claim to the Sumatran and Strait of Malacca lands (103.9E, -1.6N) formerly under Srivijayan hegemony. The snapshot assigns this large maritime sphere from Srivijaya to Majapahit as the Javanese power inherited the archipelago's commercial primacy.

w4-600777.name: Vladimir-Suzdal under the Golden Horde yoke
w4-600777.blurb: The northeastern Rus' lands centered on Vladimir-Suzdal (41.1E, 58.4N) remained vassals paying tribute to the Mongols, but the snapshot transfers them from the undivided 'Mongol Empire' to the named Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal as the Jochid/Golden Horde overlordship is formalized over the Grand Principality. The period coincides with the Mongol-backed succession struggles among Alexander Nevsky's sons (Dmitry vs. Andrey) under Horde arbitration.

w4-600780.name: Shan ascendancy after the collapse of Pagan
w4-600780.blurb: The Mongol destruction of the Pagan Kingdom in 1287 allowed Shan (Tai) chiefs to seize the northern uplands of Burma (95.6E, 22N). The three Shan Brothers and other Tai leaders carved out principalities across the former Pagan north, which the snapshot records as a transfer from Pagan to the Shan States.

w4-600781.name: Establishment of the Ilkhanate as an autonomous Mongol successor state
w4-600781.blurb: After the death of Kublai Khan in 1294 the nominal unity of the Mongol Empire dissolved, and Hulagu's line ruling Persia (the Ilkhanate, centered near 49.2E, 33.6N) became fully independent. This snapshot reassigns the vast Iranian/Iraqi territory from the undivided 'Mongol Empire' to the Ilkhanate, reflecting the empire's formal fragmentation into four khanates.

w4-600782.name: Ilkhanate consolidation of suzerainty over Shirvan (late 13th century)
w4-600782.blurb: Shirvan had been under Ilkhanate suzerainty since Hulegu's conquest of the Caucasus (1250s–60s). Between 1285 and 1294 Ilkhans Arghun and Gaykhatu repelled Golden Horde incursions while tightening administrative control over Shirvan, whose rulers issued no independent coinage and paid tribute. This entry reflects the formalisation of Shirvan's transition toward direct Ilkhanate incorporation under Gaykhatu (1291–1295).

w4-600783.name: Georgia under Ilkhanate Suzerainty – Execution of Demetrius II
w4-600783.blurb: The Kingdom of Georgia was an Ilkhanate vassal supplying tribute and troops. Under Arghun Khan (r. 1284-1291), King Demetrius II became implicated in the Buqa conspiracy and, to spare his kingdom a punitive invasion, surrendered himself and was executed at Movakan in 1289. The coordinates (~44E 41N, eastern Georgia) reflect continued Ilkhanate control enforced through this submission. The execution is well-attested and falls within the 1285-1294 window.

w4-600784.type: Mongol absorption / end of vassal sultanate
w4-600784.name: Ilkhanate direct absorption of the Sultanate of Rum (c. 1285–1308)
w4-600784.blurb: The Sultanate of Rum had been an Ilkhanate vassal since Köse Dağ (1243). By the 1280s the sultans were puppets; under Mas'ud II and Mas'ud III the Ilkhanate exercised direct administrative control over central Anatolia, the sultanate dissolving entirely by 1308. This Sultanate of Rum -> Ilkhanate transition falls within the [1285,1294] window.

w4-600787.name: Myinsaing brothers' seizure of central Burma after Pagan's fall
w4-600787.blurb: Following the Mongol-induced collapse of Pagan (1287), the three Myinsaing Brothers (Athinkhaya, Yazathingyan, Thihathu) became the real power in central Burma, ruling the heartland around the Irrawaddy (96E, 20.8N) and deposing the Mongol puppet king Kyawswa in 1297. The snapshot transfers the Pagan core to the Myinsaing Kingdom they founded.

w4-600788.name: Mangrai's conquest of Haripunjaya and founding of Lan Na
w4-600788.blurb: In 1292 King Mangrai of the Tai Yuan conquered the Mon kingdom of Haripunjaya (centered on Lamphun, near 99.1E, 19.2N), absorbing it into his new realm. He founded Chiang Mai in 1296 as capital of the Lan Na Kingdom, to which this snapshot assigns the former Haripunjaya territory.

w4-600791.name: Independence of the Chagatai Khanate
w4-600791.blurb: With the fragmentation of the Mongol Empire after Kublai Khan's death in 1294, the descendants of Chagatai held Central Asia (Transoxiana and the Tarim basin, around 75.2E, 39.8N) as the autonomous Chagatai Khanate, reconstituted under Duwa and Kaidu. The snapshot reassigns this region from the undivided 'Mongol Empire' to the Chagatai Khanate.

w4-600793.name: Independence of the Golden Horde (Jochid Ulus)
w4-600793.blurb: The breakup of the Mongol Empire after Kublai Khan's death in 1294 confirmed the descendants of Jochi as independent rulers of the western steppe (the Golden Horde, centered near 55.3E, 47.7N). This snapshot transfers the enormous Pontic-Caspian and western Siberian expanse from the undivided 'Mongol Empire' to the Golden Horde.

w4-600794.name: Golden Horde overlordship of Caucasian Georgia
w4-600794.blurb: Georgia (42.3E, 42.9N) was a tribute-paying Mongol vassal; as the empire split, its northern/Caucasus frontier fell into the sphere of the Golden Horde, which long contested the Caucasus with the Ilkhanate. The snapshot records this borderland passing from the Kingdom of Georgia to the Golden Horde amid the post-1294 fragmentation and the chronic Horde–Ilkhanate war over the Caucasus.

w4-600795.name: Galician-Volhynian expansion into Transcarpathia under Lev Danylovych
w4-600795.blurb: Lev Danylovych of Galicia-Volhynia pushed the Carpathian frontier southward, annexing part of Transcarpathia (including Mukachevo) around 1280 and campaigning against Hungary in 1285, exploiting Hungarian dynastic instability. The coordinates (23.1, 48.6) lie in the Transcarpathian/Mukachevo region contested with Hungary; the window (1285-1294) fits this period of Galician-Volhynian gains at Hungarian expense.

w4-600797.name: Galicia-Volhynia as autonomous Mongol vassal under the Golden Horde
w4-600797.blurb: The Rus' principality of Galicia-Volhynia (23.8E, 50.5N) was a Mongol vassal under the Romanovich dynasty (Lev I and successors). As the empire fragmented after 1294, the snapshot reassigns this southwestern Rus' realm from the undivided 'Mongol Empire' to Galicia-Volhynia, which paid tribute to the Golden Horde while retaining internal self-rule.

w4-600798.name: Principality of Turov-Pinsk under Mongol fragmentation
w4-600798.blurb: The Principality of Turov-Pinsk in the Pripyat marshes (28.9E, 52.3N) was a minor Rus' realm under nominal Mongol overlordship. With the empire's post-1294 fragmentation the snapshot reassigns it from the undivided 'Mongol Empire' to the named Principality of Turov, then drifting toward Lithuanian influence.

w4-700005.name: Hungarian intervention in Galicia-Volhynia succession
w4-700005.blurb: Following the death of Lev II of Galicia-Volhynia and ensuing succession struggles in the 1290s–1300s, the Kingdom of Hungary under Charles Robert pressed claims over Galicia. Hungarian influence was intermittently asserted in the Carpathian foothills and eastern borderlands (~lng 23.6, lat 48.5, sub-Carpathian Galicia) in the period 1294–1305.

w4-700006.name: Moscow succession of Daniel Alexandrovich — absorption of Pereyaslavl (1302)
w4-700006.blurb: In 1302, Ivan I's father Daniel of Moscow inherited the Principality of Pereyaslavl-Zalessky from his childless nephew Ivan Dmitriyevich, the first major territorial addition to Moscow from the Vladimir-Suzdal system. The ~26,500 km² centred at lat 56.1 / lng 37.6 (the Golden Ring region northeast of Moscow) corresponds to these Pereyaslavl and adjacent Vladimir-Suzdal territories passing to the growing Muscovite principality.

w4-700007.name: Daniel of Moscow consolidates the Principality of Moscow
w4-700007.blurb: Daniel of Moscow (d. 1303) acquired Kolomna by force around 1300 and was bequeathed Pereslavl-Zalessky in 1302, substantially expanding Moscow at the expense of Golden Horde tributaries and neighbouring princes, establishing the principality's independent territorial base.

w4-700010.name: Philip IV of France absorbs County of Touraine into royal domain
w4-700010.blurb: Philip IV (the Fair) of France systematically reabsorbed Capetian appanages into the royal domain during his reign (1285–1314); Touraine, which had briefly been granted as a county, was drawn back under direct royal administration around 1300.

w4-700011.name: Foundation of the Candarid/Jandarid Beylik of Sinop
w4-700011.blurb: The Candar (Jandarid) dynasty was founded c.1291 when Şemseddin Yaman Candar Bey received Eflani; his son Süleyman I conquered Kastamonu and Sinop in the early 1300s, establishing effective autonomy from the weakening Ilkhanate. The beylik of Sinop thus emerged as a distinct polity c.1300–1309.

w4-700013.name: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia claims suzerainty over Silesia
w4-700013.blurb: Following the extinction of Piast male heirs in several Silesian duchies and Wenceslaus II's election as King of Poland (1300), he extended Bohemian suzerainty over multiple Silesian duchies around 1300–1305, exploiting dynastic vacuums to bring them under Přemyslid/Bohemian control.

w4-700014.name: Bohemian Dynastic Union with Hungary under Wenceslaus III
w4-700014.blurb: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia arranged the election of his son Wenceslaus (III) as King of Hungary (crowned as Ladislaus V in 1301), placing Hungarian Slovakia under effective Přemyslid/Bohemian control. The atlas shows this Bohemian ascendancy over northern Hungarian territories (centroid lng 19.2, lat 48.3, Slovakia) within the 1294–1305 window.

w4-700015.name: Bohemian acquisition of Upper Silesian duchies — Wenceslaus II purchase/feudal submission
w4-700015.blurb: Around 1300–1305, Wenceslaus II of Bohemia extended Bohemian overlordship over Upper Silesian duchies including Opole, which recognized Bohemian suzerainty through feudal submission. The centroid (18.1°E, 50.4°N) matches the Duchy of Opole area that came under Bohemian feudal lordship during this period of Bohemian expansion under the Přemyslid dynasty.

w4-700019.name: Kastamonu beylik emergence after Ilkhanate fragmentation (c. 1300)
w4-700019.blurb: By c.1301-1302 the Jandarid (Candarid) dynasty had consolidated effectively autonomous control over the Kastamonu region of Paphlagonia in north-central Anatolia, as the Ilkhanate's grip on its Anatolian dependencies loosened. The beylik emerged out of the Çobanid frontier marches under Şemseddin Yaman Candar and his successors, holding the territory under only nominal Mongol suzerainty.

w4-700020.name: Partition of Silesia — Głogów inheritance of Henry III
w4-700020.blurb: The Duchy of Głogów had been a distinct Silesian Piast appanage since the partition of 1274, and by c.1301 Duke Henry III had built it into one of the strongest Silesian principalities, styling himself "heir of the Polish Kingdom." The territory around Głogów (16.1°E, 51.7°N) on the central Oder was the core of this consolidated northern-Silesian polity, distinct from the other Piast duchies and pressing claims into Greater Poland.

w4-700023.name: Collapse of Ilkhanate authority in Anatolia and rise of Ahi Brotherhood
w4-700023.blurb: Following the death of Ilkhan Arghun (1291) and the weakening of Mongol control in central Anatolia, the Ahi Brotherhood—a Sufi-craft guild confederation based in Ankara—effectively governed central Anatolia as an autonomous entity (the so-called Ahi Republic of Ankara) by the early 1300s, filling the power vacuum left as Ilkhanate grip receded after 1299.

w4-700026.name: Early Ottoman expansion under Osman I
w4-700026.blurb: Osman I exploited the collapse of Ilkhanate authority in Anatolia c.1299–1305 to seize Byzantine frontier towns and Ilkhanid-nominally-controlled territories in northwest Anatolia (Bithynia). His victory at the Battle of Bapheus (1302) marked the practical end of Ilkhanate presence in that zone.

w4-700027.name: Death of Wenceslaus II and outbreak of Łokietek's revolt in Poland
w4-700027.blurb: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, who had held the Polish crown since 1300, died on 21 June 1305. His death broke Bohemian authority in Poland: Władysław Łokietek, who had re-entered Poland from exile in 1304, seized the duchies of Sandomierz, Sieradz-Łęczyca, and Brześć Kujawski by the end of 1305. The final reversal — Wenceslaus III's assassination (August 1306) and Łokietek's capture of Kraków — followed the next year, but the decisive break with Bohemian rule began with Wenceslaus II's 1305 death.

w4-700028.name: Reunification of Poland under Władysław I
w4-700028.blurb: Władysław I (Ladislaus the Short) progressively reunified the fragmented Polish duchies, taking Greater Poland by around 1296–1300 and Lesser Poland by 1305, consolidating them under a single ruling duke before his eventual coronation as King of Poland in 1320. The centroid (lng 18.8, lat 52.8, central Poland) reflects this gradual political unification of the Polish core lands within the 1294–1305 window.

w4-700029.name: Władysław Łokietek's entry into Poznań and absorption of Greater Poland
w4-700029.blurb: Around 1305 Greater Poland (Wielkopolska), centred on Poznań, was held by Henry III of Głogów, who had taken the province after the assassination of Przemysł II in 1296. Władysław Łokietek was at this point only beginning his recovery of the southern Polish lands; his entry into Poznań and the absorption of Greater Poland into his reunifying realm came later, after a 1314 knightly revolt against Głogów's heirs.

w4-700030.name: Death of Wenceslaus II and Władysław Łokietek's recovery of Sandomierz
w4-700030.blurb: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia died in June 1305, fatally weakening Bohemian control over the Duchy of Sandomierz. Władysław Łokietek, who had returned from exile in 1304 with Hungarian aid, swiftly occupied Sandomierz and Sieradz-Łęczyca, reincorporating them into the nascent Kingdom of Poland before the Přemyslid line ended entirely in 1306.

w4-700031.name: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia claims Galicia-Volhynia / Polish crown
w4-700031.blurb: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia was crowned King of Poland in 1300 and pressed claims over Galicia-Volhynia, bringing parts of the region under Bohemian-Polish overlordship before his death in 1305; the atlas reflects the contested frontier shifting toward Polish control during this interval.

w4-700036.name: Beylik of Saruhan's seizure of Byzantine western Anatolia
w4-700036.blurb: As Byzantine authority in western Anatolia collapsed after the failed Catalan Company campaign, the Turkmen chief Saruhan Bey carved out his beylik around Magnesia (Manisa), seizing the Lydian lands near the Aegean coast (27.5E, 38.5N) around 1313. The snapshot records this region passing from the Byzantine Empire to the Beylik of Saruhan.

citations.label: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty (Wikipedia)

w4-700038.name: Teutonic Order acquires Pomerelia (Treaty of Soldin / Kępno)
w4-700038.blurb: In 1308–1309 the Teutonic Order seized Pomerelia (Gdańsk Pomerania) from the Margraviate of Brandenburg, buying off Brandenburg's claims by the Treaty of Soldin (1309) for 10,000 marks. This gave the Order a large block of territory on the Baltic coast (around lng 17–18, lat 54) previously counted as HRE minor territory.

w4-700043.name: Lithuanian absorption of the Principality of Minsk
w4-700043.blurb: Under Grand Duke Vytenis (and continued by Gediminas), the Grand Duchy of Lithuania extended its rule over the western Rus' principalities of the upper Dnieper; the Polotsk lands were taken around 1307 and Minsk (28.3E, 55.1N) came under Lithuanian control in the same expansion. The snapshot records the Principality of Minsk passing to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

w4-700044.name: Battle of Bannockburn
w4-700044.blurb: On 23-24 June 1314, Robert the Bruce's Scottish army decisively defeated Edward II of England near Stirling at the Battle of Bannockburn. The victory expelled English forces and confirmed Robert I as King of Scots, reversing the English conquest Edward I had completed by 1305. The dataset transfer (Kingdom of England -> Kingdom of Scotland, py1305/y1314) at lng-4.6/lat56.4 reflects the Scottish reconquest, later formalized in the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton (1328).

w4-700045.name: End of Přemyslid claim to Hungary and Angevin consolidation under Charles I
w4-700045.blurb: After the death of King Andrew III of Hungary (the last Árpád) in 1301, the Přemyslid Wenceslaus III was elected and crowned king of Hungary, contested by the Angevin Charles I (Carobert). Wenceslaus renounced the Hungarian throne in 1305 (in favour of Otto of Bavaria); after Otto's imprisonment (1307) and abdication (1308), Charles I emerged as ruler and progressively secured the realm by around 1310–1312. The dataset records Slovakia/northern Hungary territory (lat 48.3, lng 19.2) transferring from Bohemian/Přemyslid-aligned to Hungarian Angevin rule as the Přemyslid claim collapsed.

w4-700047.name: Jaffna Kingdom expansion following Pandyan collapse (c. 1310-1314)
w4-700047.blurb: The Jaffna Kingdom (Arya Chakravarti dynasty) had been a tributary of the Pandyan Empire, but around 1310 the Delhi Sultanate's general Malik Kafur sacked Madurai, destroying Pandyan power. Freed from suzerainty, the Jaffna Kingdom expanded southward in Sri Lanka, exploiting the drift of Sinhalese political authority to the southwest. The dataset records territory at 80.5E, 8.9N (northern Sri Lanka) passing from 'Ceylon' to the 'Jaffna kingdom' around 1305-1314, consistent with this power shift.

w4-700049.name: Thihathu becomes sole ruler and moves the capital to Pinya
w4-700049.blurb: After the deaths of his elder brothers Athinhkaya and Yazathingyan, Thihathu became sole ruler of the central Burmese Shan state and in February 1313 relocated the capital from Myinsaing to Pinya, renaming the polity accordingly. This is a continuation of the same dynasty under a new capital, not a conquest by an outside power.

w4-700050.name: Louis I of Nevers Inherits County of Flanders (1322)
w4-700050.blurb: Robert III of Flanders, who also held the County of Nevers, died in 1322 and was succeeded by his grandson Louis I, uniting Nevers and Flanders under one ruler. The window 1314-1326 encompasses Robert III's death (1322) and Louis I's early rule. The coordinates sit in the Nevers region; the transfer from County of Nevers to County of Flanders reflects this dynastic union of the two counties under Louis I.

citations.label: Louis I, Count of Flanders - Wikipedia

w4-700051.name: Delhi Sultanate expeditions into South India - Pandya decline and Hoysala gains (1314-1326)
w4-700051.blurb: The Delhi Sultanate's expeditions into the Tamil south in the 1310s further devastated the Pandya Empire, already weakened by Malik Kafur's 1311 raid. The Pandya civil war between Vira Pandya and Sundara Pandya allowed the Hoysala king Veera Ballala III to occupy former Pandya territories and serve as a counterweight to Sultanate expansion in the far south. The Hoysala kingdom thus exercised control over territory previously under Pandya suzerainty in this period, matching the entry (from Pandya to Hoysala, py=1314, y=1326).

citations.label: Malik Kafur's invasion of the Pandya kingdom - Wikipedia

w4-700054.name: Aragonese conquest of Sardinia
w4-700054.blurb: The Crown of Aragon, enfeoffed Sardinia by Pope Boniface VIII in 1297, launched its military conquest in 1323 in alliance with the Giudicato of Arborea. Hugh II of Arborea became a vassal of James II on 11 April 1323, and a Catalan-Aragonese fleet landed at Palmas in June 1323. The Pisans were defeated and Castel di Castro (Cagliari) fell to Aragon in June 1326, establishing Aragonese control over most of Sardinia. The data window 1314-1326 captures the conquest.

w4-700056.name: Louis IV's Grant of Brandenburg to his son Louis V (Wittelsbach)
w4-700056.blurb: When the last Ascanian ruler of Brandenburg, Henry the Child, died without heirs in 1320, Holy Roman Emperor Louis IV of the House of Wittelsbach — himself Duke of Bavaria — claimed the margraviate as an imperial fief. In 1323 he granted it to his eldest son, the future Louis V of Brandenburg, transferring it into the Wittelsbach (Bavarian) family. The dataset's 'Duchy of Bavaria → Margraviate of Brandenburg' label and the window 1314–1326 encompass this transfer; the Wittelsbach held Brandenburg until 1373.

citations.label: Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor – Wikipedia

w4-700059.name: Establishment of the Sagaing Kingdom by Saw Yun
w4-700059.blurb: Saw Yun, son of Thihathu of Pinya, broke away from his father and founded a rival Shan kingdom centered on Sagaing on the west bank of the Irrawaddy around 1315. The split divided central Burma into two competing realms, Pinya and Sagaing, for the next four decades. This change reflects the secession of Sagaing's territory from Pinya.

w4-700060.name: Serbian conquest of Syrmia under Stefan Milutin (c. 1319)
w4-700060.blurb: Following the death of Stefan Dragutin, ruler of the semi-independent Kingdom of Syrmia, in 1316, his son Vladislav inherited the territory. King Stefan Milutin of Serbia invaded and defeated Vladislav around 1319, imprisoning him and annexing much of Dragutin's lands. The Syrmia region remained contested between Serbia and Hungary through the 1320s.

w4-700065.name: Tughlaq conquest of Devagiri / Annexation of Yadava Kingdom
w4-700065.blurb: In 1318 the Yadava (Seuna) kingdom centered on Devagiri was finally extinguished when its last ruler, Harapaladeva (Harapala), who had revolted to reclaim independence after Alauddin Khalji's death, was defeated, captured, and executed on the orders of Sultan Qutb al-Din Mubarak Shah Khalji. The campaign was led by the Delhi general Khusrau Khan, and a Delhi governor was installed at Devagiri, ending Yadava rule and bringing the northern Deccan permanently under the Delhi Sultanate; a decade later (1328) the Tughlaqs would make Devagiri their southern capital as Daulatabad.

w4-700067.name: Execution of Mubariz al-Din Mehmed and dissolution of the Eshrefid beylik
w4-700067.blurb: The Eshrefid beylik of Beysehir (Esrefogullari), a small post-Seljuk Turkmen principality in central-western Anatolia, was extinguished in 1326 when its ruler Mubariz al-Din Mehmed (the dynasty's most prominent bey) was put to death by Timurtash, the Chobanid governor of Anatolia acting under Ilkhanid authority. Wikipedia and the standard genealogies list the Chobanids, not the Karamanids, as the immediate successors to Eshrefid territory, though the Karamanid beylik later absorbed much of the region.

w4-700069.name: Karasid beylik expands into former Byzantine territory in northwestern Anatolia (c. 1314–1326)
w4-700069.blurb: The Karasid dynasty, based around Balıkesir and Bergama (classical Mysia), expanded into Byzantine territory in northwestern Anatolia in the early 14th century, exploiting Byzantine weakness after the failed 1302-1308 campaigns. The coordinates (27.4°E, 40°N) correspond to the Marmara/Aegean borderlands; from=Byzantine Empire, to=Beylik of Karasi matches the 1314-1326 window (Karasi Bey died c.1328).

w4-700071.name: Lithuanian conquest of Turov-Pinsk (c. 1320s)
w4-700071.blurb: During the expansion of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Grand Duke Gediminas in the early 1320s, the Ruthenian Principality of Turov-Pinsk (Polesia), which had been a dependency of the kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia, passed into the Lithuanian orbit. Sources indicate the principality was incorporated largely without major warfare as its dukes increasingly cooperated with Vilnius to escape Galician-Volhynian control, part of Lithuania's broader absorption of western Rus' lands around 1320-1321.

w4-700075.name: Rise of Ludwig IV the Bavarian and Wittelsbach consolidation
w4-700075.blurb: The Wittelsbach-ruled Duchy of Bavaria had been partitioned among branches since 1255. Ludwig IV of the House of Wittelsbach secured the German kingship in 1314 and consolidated his hold over Bavaria, defeating the Habsburgs at Muhldorf (1322). The worklist window (1314-1326) captures this consolidation of Wittelsbach Bavaria under Ludwig (coordinates 12.4E, 48.4N, Bavaria proper); the further reunification of Lower Bavaria came in 1340, outside this window.

citations.label: Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor - Britannica

w4-700076.name: Louis IV seizes the Margraviate of Brandenburg for the Wittelsbachs (1323–1326)
w4-700076.blurb: After the last Ascanian Margrave of Brandenburg, Henry the Child, died heirless in 1320, Holy Roman King Louis IV of Bavaria seized the margraviate and appointed his son Louis V as margrave in 1323. Pope John XXII condemned the grant, but the 1326 Treaty of Trausnitz with the Habsburgs stabilised Louis IV's position and confirmed Wittelsbach control, transferring Brandenburg from the old margraves to Bavarian Wittelsbach rule.

citations.label: Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor — Wikipedia

w4-700078.name: Angevin reassertion over the Principality of Achaea after Louis of Burgundy's death
w4-700078.blurb: After the death of Louis of Burgundy (husband of Matilda of Hainaut) on 2 August 1316, King Robert of Naples and Philip I of Taranto forced Matilda to marry Robert's brother John of Gravina, scheming to return Achaea to the House of Anjou. The principality's governance between 1314 and 1326 was contested among Burgundian claims, a usurper (Ferdinand of Majorca), and Angevin pressure; an Angevin baillie governed from 1318 and Angevin control was consolidated by 1322, with Achaea bestowed on John of Gravina.

w4-700084.name: Genko War and Siege of Kamakura – Kenmu Restoration
w4-700084.blurb: Emperor Go-Daigo launched the Genko War in 1331 against the Kamakura Shogunate and, after initial defeat and exile to the Oki Islands, escaped in 1333. With the support of defected Kamakura general Ashikaga Takauji and rebel commander Nitta Yoshisada, Go-Daigo's forces besieged and captured Kamakura in 1333, causing the mass suicide of the ruling Hojo clan and collapsing the shogunate. Go-Daigo returned to Kyoto and inaugurated the Kenmu Restoration, attempting to restore direct imperial rule for the first time since the twelfth century. The dataset records the transition (Kamakura Shogunate → Kenmu Restoration) over 1326–1333; the restoration lasted only until 1336, when Ashikaga Takauji rebelled and established the Muromachi Shogunate.

w4-700086.name: Odo IV acquires the Free County of Burgundy through Joan III (1330)
w4-700086.blurb: On 21 January 1330 Joan III of France, wife of Odo IV Duke of Burgundy, inherited the Free County of Burgundy (Franche-Comté) from her mother Joan II. Odo IV thus gained the county as consort, uniting it with the Duchy of Burgundy in personal union. The window (1326-1333) and Jura coordinates (6.2, 47.1) fit this shift to Burgundian comital control.

w4-700087.name: Extinction of Capetian House of Anjou and reversion to French Crown (1328)
w4-700087.blurb: By 1328 the House of Wittelsbach was consolidating its hold on the Margraviate of Brandenburg, granted in 1323 as an imperial fief to the young Louis V by his father, Emperor Louis IV, after the Ascanian margravial line had died out in 1319-1320. From 1328 Louis was drawn into a protracted war over neighboring Pomerania (which he claimed as a fief) that lasted until 1333, while contending with papal opposition to the grant and resistance from the Brandenburg nobility.

w4-700090.name: County of Anjou reverts to the French royal domain (1328)
w4-700090.blurb: When Charles IV of France died without male heirs in 1328, the County of Anjou (held as a Capetian apanage) reverted to the royal domain under the new Valois king Philip VI (who later granted it to his son John in 1332). The coordinates are the Loire valley, matching the recorded Anjou → Kingdom of France transfer for 1326–1333.

w4-700092.name: Revolt against Christopher II - mortgaging of Danish royal lands
w4-700092.blurb: In 1326, Danish magnates allied with Count Gerhard III of Holstein overthrew Christopher II, installing the young Duke Valdemar of Southern Jutland as king with Gerhard as regent. Crown lands across the realm - including the Danish dominion of Estonia (around 25.7E, 59N) - were mortgaged to German and Danish lords. The kingdom remained fragmented until Valdemar IV began reacquiring the mortgaged territories after 1340.

w4-700093.name: Magnus Eriksson's Norwegian-Swedish personal union (Greenland)
w4-700093.blurb: In 1319, the infant Magnus Eriksson was simultaneously elected King of Sweden and inherited the Norwegian throne from his grandfather Haakon V, creating a personal union of the two crowns that lasted until 1355. Norway's overseas territories, including Greenland (coordinates ~-49.8, 63), passed under this joint sovereignty. The dataset records a transition from 'Old Kingdom of Norway' to 'Kingdom of Sweden' around 1326-1333, reflecting Greenland falling under the Swedish-Norwegian personal union as Magnus came of age (1331-1332).

w4-700096.name: Creation of the Duchy of Bourbon as royal appanage
w4-700096.blurb: King Charles IV of France elevated the lordship of Bourbon-l'Archambault to a duchy on 30 December 1327 for Louis I, grandson of Louis IX. This created the Duchy of Bourbon as a royal appanage, separating the Bourbonnais territory (lat 46.2, lng 2.5) from direct crown domain. Louis I became the founding duke of the House of Bourbon, which would eventually produce the kings of France from 1589.

w4-700102.name: First Swedish–Norwegian Union under Magnus Eriksson
w4-700102.blurb: In 1319, the three-year-old Magnus Eriksson inherited the Norwegian throne from his maternal grandfather Haakon V and was simultaneously elected King of Sweden, creating the First Swedish–Norwegian Union under a regency. The dataset's 1326–1333 window corresponds to the period of disputed regency (Ingeborg's removal 1323–1326) and the First Norwegian Noble Rising (1331–1333) over Magnus's premature coming of age, culminating in the rebels' submission in 1333.

w4-700104.name: Ashikaga Takauji's revolt and founding of the Ashikaga Shogunate
w4-700104.blurb: Emperor Go-Daigo's Kenmu Restoration (1333) briefly restored direct imperial rule, but his former ally Ashikaga Takauji turned against him, seized Kyoto in 1336, installed a rival emperor, and issued the Kenmu Code, founding the Ashikaga (Muromachi) Shogunate. Go-Daigo fled to Yoshino, beginning the Nanboku-cho era. This transferred effective control of Japan from the Kenmu Restoration to the Ashikaga Shogunate.

w4-700105.name: Collapse of the Ilkhanate and Kartid independence
w4-700105.blurb: The death of Ilkhan Abu Sa'id in December 1335 without an heir triggered rapid fragmentation of the Mongol Ilkhanate; regional dynasts including the Jalayirids, Chobanids, Muzaffarids, and Kartids seized de facto independence. The Kartids, a Sunni Tajik dynasty ruling Khorasan from Herat since 1244 as Ilkhanate vassals, became effectively independent sovereigns after 1335 and endured until Timur's invasion in 1381. Under Mu'izz al-Din they defeated the Sarbadars at Zava (1342). The worklist window of 1336-1344 captures this Ilkhanate dissolution and Kartid assertion.

w4-700106.name: Ottoman expansion into Anatolia amid the collapse of the Ilkhanate
w4-700106.blurb: The Ilkhanate disintegrated after the death of Abu Sa'id in 1335, leaving its Anatolian territories to fragment among the beyliks. The Ottomans under Orhan exploited this vacuum to expand eastward into former Ilkhanid Anatolian lands. This change reflects Ottoman absorption of territory left ungoverned by the dissolving Ilkhanate.

w4-700107.name: Ottoman annexation of the Beylik of Karasi
w4-700107.blurb: Around 1345, Sultan Orhan annexed the neighboring Beylik of Karasi in northwestern Anatolia, exploiting a succession dispute among its rulers. The acquisition gave the Ottomans Karasi's coastline and fleet on the Dardanelles, providing the springboard for their crossing into Europe at Gallipoli in 1354. This transferred Karasi's territory to the Ottoman Empire.

w4-700110.name: Founding of the Shah Mir (Kashmir) Sultanate
w4-700110.blurb: Shah Mir, an adventurer who had served the Hindu rulers of Kashmir, seized power and founded the Kashmir Sultanate (Shah Mir dynasty) in 1339, ending Hindu rule in the valley. This established the first Muslim dynasty in Kashmir. The change reflects the transformation of the Hindu Kingdom of Kashmir into the Kashmiri Sultanate.

w4-700112.name: Injuid assertion of independence over Fars following Ilkhanate collapse (1336-1344)
w4-700112.blurb: The death of the last effective Ilkhan, Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, in November 1335 triggered the fragmentation of Ilkhanid authority. In Fars (Shiraz), the Injuid family, who had administered the Mongol crown lands (inju), seized de facto independence; Sharaf al-Din Mahmud Shah's sons divided Fars through the early 1340s. The worklist transition is 'Ilkhanate' -> 'Injuids' [1336,1344] at lng 51.4, lat 30.8 (Shiraz/Fars), with the 1336 onset inside the window.

w4-700114.name: Chobanid Takeover in Azerbaijan after the Ilkhanate's Collapse
w4-700114.blurb: The death of the last effective Ilkhan Abu Sa'id in 1335 dissolved the Ilkhanate. The Chobanids (Suldus clan) seized Azerbaijan and northwestern Persia; Hasan-i Kuchak consolidated power, installing puppet Ilkhanid claimants from 1336, and his brother Malek Ashraf secured full control by 1344. The coordinates (47.2E, 37.6N) lie in northwestern Iran/Azerbaijan. Transfer Ilkhanate -> Chobanids fits the 1336-1344 window.

w4-700115.name: Golden Horde seizure of Caucasian/Azerbaijani lands during the Ilkhanate's collapse
w4-700115.blurb: The coordinates lie near the western Caspian/Azerbaijan, long contested between the Ilkhanate and the Golden Horde in the Berke-Hulagu wars over Arran and Azerbaijan. After Abu Sa'id's death in 1335 dissolved the Ilkhanate, the Golden Horde pressed south to claim these long-disputed Transcaucasian territories. This transferred former Ilkhanid land to the Golden Horde.

w4-700116.name: Peter IV of Aragon's conquest of the Kingdom of Majorca (1343–1344)
w4-700116.blurb: Peter IV ('the Ceremonious') of Aragon invaded the Kingdom of Majorca in May 1343 after James III refused homage, and by September 1344 had incorporated the Balearics and Roussillon into the Crown of Aragon. James III fled and was killed at Llucmajor (1349), confirming Aragonese sovereignty. The 1336–1344 window captures the dispute and decisive conquest, matching Majorca→Crown of Aragon at (2.8°E, 40.8°N).

w4-700117.name: Valdemar IV Atterdag reclaims mortgaged Danish territories
w4-700117.blurb: Valdemar IV (Atterdag), crowned in 1340, systematically redeemed the lands mortgaged during the crisis of Christopher II's reign. He reasserted royal authority over the Danish dominion of Estonia (25.7E, 59N) before, lacking resources to hold it, selling it to the Teutonic Order in 1346 for 19,000 marks - revenue he then used to redeem Jutland, Funen, and Zealand. The worklist's Magnates-to-Denmark transition reflects this 1340s recovery of crown lands.

w4-700120.name: Isfendiyarid (Candarid) Consolidation of Kastamonu Region
w4-700120.blurb: The Candar dynasty (also Isfendiyarids) established control over Kastamonu in 1314 under Süleyman I Paşa after years of Ilkhanid vassalage. As the Ilkhanate disintegrated in the late 1330s, the beylik consolidated its independence and expanded around Kastamonu and Sinop on the Black Sea coast. The dataset records 'Kastamonu → Beylik of Isfendiyar' for the period 1336–1344, capturing this transition from nominal Ilkhanid-era administration to firm Isfendiyarid rule as the Mongol overlordship collapsed.

w4-700124.name: Samma dynasty's seizure of Sindh from the Tughlaqs
w4-700124.blurb: The Samma Rajputs overthrew the Soomra dynasty and asserted control over Lower Sindh (capital Thatta) in the 1330s, breaking away from Delhi Sultanate authority as Tughlaq power in the region waned under Muhammad bin Tughlaq. This established the independent Samma Sultanate of Sindh. The change reflects the transfer of Sindh from the Tughlaq Dynasty to the Samma dynasty.

w4-700125.name: Samma Dynasty Foundation amid Ilkhanate Collapse
w4-700125.blurb: The dissolution of the Ilkhanate by the 1330s created a power vacuum in Sindh, which had been nominally under Ilkhanid suzerainty. Around 1339, Jam Unar of the Samma tribe defeated the last Soomra ruler and established the Samma Sultanate of Sindh. Ibn Battuta, visiting c.1333, recorded the Sammas' rising power. The dataset window 1336–1344 captures the consolidation phase when the Sammas filled the territorial void left by the Ilkhanate's collapse in this region.

w4-700126.name: Byzantine reconquest of Epirus under Andronikos III
w4-700126.blurb: Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos, aided by John Kantakouzenos, brought the Despotate of Epirus back under direct Byzantine rule around 1337-1340, suppressing a local revolt by 1340. This reincorporated Epirus into the Byzantine Empire after decades of autonomy. The change reflects the transfer of Epirote territory to the Byzantine Empire.

w4-700128.name: Habsburg inheritance of Carinthia and Carniola (1335)
w4-700128.blurb: On the death of Duke Henry of Carinthia (Gorizia-Tyrol) in 1335 without male heirs, Emperor Louis IV enfeoffed the Habsburg dukes Albert II and Otto with the Duchy of Carinthia and the March of Carniola. The coordinates lie in the eastern Alps consistent with this acquisition. This transferred imperial territory to the House of Habsburg.

w4-700129.name: Ilkhanate collapse and Trebizond's recovery of autonomy (1335-1344)
w4-700129.blurb: After the death of Ilkhan Abu Sa'id in 1335, the Ilkhanate rapidly fragmented into rival successor states (Jalayirids, Chobanids, and others). The Empire of Trebizond, which had been an Ilkhanate vassal since 1243, regained its autonomy as Mongol power receded from Anatolia. The dataset records territory near northeastern Anatolia (39.6E, 40.6N) passing from the Ilkhanate to the Empire of Trebizond around 1336-1344, consistent with Trebizond reasserting independence during the Ilkhanate's dissolution.

w4-700131.name: Ivan I 'Kalita' of Moscow's encroachment on Novgorod's northern lands
w4-700131.blurb: In the 1330s Grand Prince Ivan I 'Kalita' of Moscow, leveraging his role as the Golden Horde's chief tribute-collector among the Rus' princes, pressed his authority over the Novgorod Republic, demanding additional payments such as the so-called 'Zakam'e silver.' When Novgorod refused, Moscow forces occupied the Novgorodian dependencies of Torzhok and Bezhetsky Verkh; mediation by Metropolitan Theognost produced an uneasy settlement, but friction over tribute and Novgorod's contacts with Lithuania persisted to the end of Ivan's reign.

w4-700132.name: Moscow's acquisition of Vladimir under Ivan I Kalita
w4-700132.blurb: Ivan I Kalita of Moscow secured the patent (yarlyk) for the Grand Principality of Vladimir from the Golden Horde and accumulated lands and tax-collection rights, making Moscow the dominant power in northeastern Rus by his death in 1340. This shifted the old Vladimir-Suzdal heartland into the Grand Principality of Moscow's orbit. The change reflects Moscow's absorption of Vladimir-Suzdal territory.

w4-700133.name: Muzaffarid conquest of central Iran after Ilkhanate collapse
w4-700133.blurb: In the power vacuum left across southeastern Anatolia by the collapse of the Ilkhanate after Abu Sa'id's death in 1335, the Turkmen chieftain Zayn al-Din Qaraja founded the Beylik of Dulkadir, taking Elbistan in 1337 and securing recognition as a Mamluk na'ib (deputy) from Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. Centered on the Elbistan-Maras region of the Taurus, the Dulkadirid principality became a buffer state between the Mamluk Sultanate and the rising powers of Anatolia.

w4-700135.name: Rise of the Muzaffarids following the collapse of the Ilkhanate
w4-700135.blurb: After the death of the last effective Ilkhan Abu Sa'id in 1335, the Ilkhanate fragmented rapidly. Mobarez al-Din Muhammad of the Muzaffarid dynasty seized Kerman in 1340 and Shiraz (from the Injuids) in 1353, establishing the Muzaffarid state across Fars and central Iran. The dataset's window of 1336-1344 corresponds to this initial Muzaffarid territorial consolidation out of Ilkhanate collapse; coordinates (56.1, 33.3) point to the Kerman/central Iran area.

w4-700136.name: Galicia–Volhynia Wars: Lithuania takes Volhynia from Poland
w4-700136.blurb: The Galicia–Volhynia Wars (1340–1366) pitted Poland under Casimir III against the Grand Duchy of Lithuania for the Galicia–Volhynia succession. After Casimir secured Galicia (1349), Algirdas and Kęstutis pressed the Lithuanian claim to Volhynia; the 1352 truce awarded Volhynia (Lutsk, Belz, Chełm) to Lithuania, matching the Galicia-Volhynia→Lithuania transfer at (25.1°E, 51.2°N).

w4-700139.name: Coronation of Stefan Dusan as Emperor (proclamation of the Serbian Empire)
w4-700139.blurb: Stefan Dusan, having vastly expanded the Serbian kingdom by conquering Byzantine Macedonia, Albania, and Epirus, was crowned 'Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks' at Skopje in 1346, elevating the Kingdom of Serbia to the Serbian Empire. This formalized the transformation of the realm into an empire at its territorial height. The change reflects the kingdom becoming the Serbian Empire.

w4-700142.name: Founding of the Ayutthaya Kingdom and incorporation of Lavo
w4-700142.blurb: Ramathibodi I (U Thong) founded the Ayutthaya Kingdom in 1351, and Lavo (Lopburi) was incorporated as its first major stronghold; the territory of Lavo was effectively merged into Ayutthaya at the kingdom's foundation, as Lavo's ruling class provided the administrative core of the new state.

w4-700143.name: Vijayanagara absorption of Hoysala territory
w4-700143.blurb: With the death of the last Hoysala king Veera Ballala III in battle against the Madurai Sultanate in 1343 and the subsequent collapse of Hoysala administration, the nascent Vijayanagara Empire under Bukka Raya I expanded to absorb Hoysala territories in the Kannada-speaking Deccan by 1346, positioning itself as the Hoysala's successor state.

w4-700144.name: Majapahit raid on Samudera Pasai
w4-700144.blurb: Majapahit attacked and looted Samudera Pasai in the mid-14th century (circa 1350), as attested in the Nagarakretagama (1365); the raid temporarily brought the area under Majapahit suzerainty as part of Hayam Wuruk's imperial expansion recorded by court poet Prapanca.

w4-700146.name: Polish Annexation of Galicia-Volhynia
w4-700146.blurb: Casimir III of Poland launched a campaign in 1349 that captured Galicia (including Lviv), and after further conflict with Lithuania the Treaty of Buda (1351) and subsequent diplomacy formalized Polish control over much of Galicia-Volhynia. The atlas window 1347–1352 captures this decisive Polish annexation of the last Rurikid principality in the region.

w4-700147.name: Polish annexation of Galicia / Treaty of 1352
w4-700147.blurb: After the extinction of the Galicia-Volhynia Rurikid dynasty (1323) and ensuing wars, Casimir III of Poland seized Galicia from Golden Horde suzerainty by 1349 and consolidated control via a partition agreement with Lithuania around 1352. The centroid (~lng 26.4, lat 48.9, Podolia/Galicia borderland) reflects Golden Horde-claimed steppe territory incorporated into the Polish sphere.

w4-700150.name: Denmark sells Duchy of Estonia to the Teutonic Order
w4-700150.blurb: On 1 November 1346, King Valdemar IV of Denmark sold Harria and Vironia (Danish Estonia) to the Teutonic Order for 19,000 Cologne marks of silver; the Teutonic Order transferred control to its Livonian branch, and Danish sovereignty over Estonia ended permanently.

w4-700151.name: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah unifies Bengal, independent of Delhi (1352)
w4-700151.blurb: By 1352, Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah had defeated the rival Bengali triad and unified all of Bengal, effectively ending Tughlaq Delhi Sultanate authority over the region; the independence of Bengal was subsequently confirmed by peace treaty after Delhi's failed invasion of 1353–1359. This ~78,000 km² represents former Tughlaq-attributed Bengal passing to the independent Sultanate of Bengal.

w4-700152.name: Ilyas Shah of Bengal conquers Orissa territories (c. 1350–1352)
w4-700152.blurb: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, founder of the Ilyas Shahi dynasty of Bengal, conducted aggressive campaigns westward and southward around 1350–1352, seizing territory from the Eastern Ganga Kingdom of Orissa and incorporating the Mahanadi delta region into the Sultanate of Bengal.

w4-700154.name: Valdemar IV recovers Danish crown lands
w4-700154.blurb: Valdemar IV Atterdag systematically repurchased or militarily recovered pledged Danish territories from Holstein nobles and Danish magnates throughout the 1340s and early 1350s, re-establishing royal domain over Jutland and Funen by c. 1350–1352.

w4-700155.name: Fa Ngum founds Lan Xang and conquers territories (1353)
w4-700155.blurb: Fa Ngum, backed by Khmer military support, founded the Lan Xang kingdom in 1353 and conducted campaigns along the middle Mekong that brought territories formerly under nominal Tran dynasty or Lan Na suzerainty into the new Lao polity; the 1352–1354 atlas window precisely captures this founding expansion.

w4-700156.name: Fa Ngum's Lan Xang expansion into Lan Na frontier territory (1353)
w4-700156.blurb: During Fa Ngum's founding campaigns of Lan Xang in 1353, forces extended northwestward into areas along the Nam Ou and upper Mekong that had been loosely held by the Lan Na kingdom, establishing a contested border zone absorbed into Lan Xang; the 1352–1354 atlas window maps this initial expansion.

w4-700157.name: Foundation of Lan Xang and conquest of Muang Sua region (1353)
w4-700157.blurb: Fa Ngum, backed by a Khmer army, founded the Kingdom of Lan Xang in 1353 and rapidly expanded northward and westward, incorporating the Muang Sua region and upper Mekong valley territories that had been loosely within the Sukhothai sphere; this ~116,000 km² reflects the atlas registering Lan Xang's initial territorial claim.

w4-700158.name: Foundation of the Principality of Moldavia under Bogdan I
w4-700158.blurb: In 1359 Bogdan of Cuhea crossed the Carpathians, expelled the Hungarian-installed Voivode Balc, and established an independent Principality of Moldavia, wresting the territory from the declining Golden Horde's sphere and Hungarian suzerainty simultaneously. The atlas registers this as a shift from Golden Horde to Moldavia in the 1354–1363 window.

w4-700159.name: Zayyanid recovery of Tlemcen after Marinid collapse
w4-700159.blurb: After the assassination of Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris in 1358 and the ensuing Marinid political crisis, the Zayyanids under Abu Hammu II recaptured Tlemcen around 1359, restoring their dynasty to their traditional capital and expelling Marinid authority from the central Maghreb.

w4-700160.name: Hafsid recovery of Tunis from Marinid occupation
w4-700160.blurb: The Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris had captured Tunis in 1347, briefly subordinating the Hafsids, but after Abu Inan's assassination in 1358 the Marinid grip on Ifriqiya collapsed. The Hafsids recovered their central Tunisian territories by around 1357–1360, re-establishing control over the region shown in the atlas.

w4-700164.name: John II of France grants Anjou to Louis I, founding House of Valois-Anjou
w4-700164.blurb: In October 1360, after the Treaty of Brétigny, John II elevated the County of Anjou to a duchy and granted it as an apanage to his son Louis I, founding the House of Valois-Anjou. The Anjou region near lng -0.2 W / lat 47.8 N passed from the French royal domain to the House of Valois-Anjou, matching the [1354,1363] window.

w4-700165.name: Creation of the Duchy of Anjou as a Valois apanage for Louis I
w4-700165.blurb: King John II of France, after his release from English captivity following the Battle of Poitiers, erected the Duchy of Anjou in 1360 as an apanage for his second son Louis. This transferred the Anjou region from direct royal French domain to the House of Valois-Anjou.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Louis I, Duke of Anjou

w4-700166.name: Chagatai (Moghulistan) encroachment on the Yuan as the dynasty collapsed
w4-700166.blurb: The coordinates lie in the Tarim Basin/eastern Turkestan frontier between the Yuan and Chagatai realms. As the Yuan Dynasty disintegrated amid rebellion in the 1350s-60s, the eastern Chagatai khanate (Moghulistan, consolidated under Tughlugh Timur from c.1347) expanded into the Yuan's far-western Central Asian holdings. The change reflects loss of these lands to the Chagatai Khanate.

w4-700171.name: End of Yuan (Mongol) overlordship of Tibet and the rise of the Phagmodrupa
w4-700171.blurb: Tibet had been administered under the Yuan-allied Sakya regime, but Changchub Gyaltsen of the Phagmodrupa overthrew Sakya dominance and established independent Tibetan rule by 1354, ending effective Yuan control as the Mongol dynasty collapsed in China. This restored Tibetan self-rule. The change reflects the transfer of the vast Tibetan plateau from the Yuan Dynasty to Tibet.

w4-700176.name: Treaty of Brétigny
w4-700176.blurb: The Treaty of Brétigny (8 May 1360) ended the first phase of the Hundred Years' War. Edward III of England received the Duchy of Aquitaine, including Gascony, Périgord, Limousin, Quercy, and surrounding territories in full sovereignty, free of homage to the French crown, in exchange for renouncing his claim to the French throne.

w4-700177.name: Treaty of Brétigny — English acquisition of Pyrenean territories
w4-700177.blurb: The Treaty of Brétigny (8 May 1360) transferred to Edward III, in full sovereignty, an enlarged Aquitaine that reached up to the Pyrenees, including Bigorre and Rouergue near the County of Foix. These southern lands, formerly held of the French crown, thereby passed to English sovereignty; the homage-free Gascon and Bigorre marches abutted Foix, whose count Gaston III Fébus nonetheless preserved his own autonomy through the upheaval.

w4-700179.name: Establishment of the Despotate of Vidin under Ivan Sratsimir
w4-700179.blurb: Following the death of Ivan Alexander's interest in dividing his realm, the Second Bulgarian Empire fragmented as his elder son Ivan Sratsimir was given the northwestern lands around Vidin to rule. By around 1356 the Despotate (Tsardom) of Vidin had broken off from the Tarnovo-based Bulgarian state, with Sratsimir styling himself an independent ruler. This partition weakened Bulgaria fatally on the eve of the Ottoman conquest.

w4-700180.name: Lithuanian expansion into the Smolensk lands under Algirdas
w4-700180.blurb: Under Grand Duke Algirdas (Olgierd), the Grand Duchy of Lithuania pressed eastward into the upper Dnieper region, absorbing principalities dependent on Smolensk such as Mstislavl (taken around 1359). The Principality of Smolensk was steadily reduced to vassalage and lost outlying territories to Lithuania during this period, presaging its full annexation in the early 15th century.

w4-700182.name: Jalayirid conquest of Azerbaijan from the Chobanids
w4-700182.blurb: Shaikh Uvais of the Jalayirid Sultanate seized Tabriz and Azerbaijan from the Chobanids after the Golden Horde's Jani Beg had briefly occupied and then withdrawn from the region. The last significant Chobanid ruler, Malik Ashraf, had been captured and executed by Jani Beg in 1357, and the Jalayirids filled the power vacuum, taking control of Chobanid Azerbaijan and Arran.

w4-700185.name: Muzaffarid conquest of Shiraz and Fars from the Injuids (1353-1357)
w4-700185.blurb: Mubariz al-Din Muhammad of the Muzaffarid dynasty besieged Shiraz in 1352-1353 and captured it from the last Injuid ruler, Abu Ishaq, who fled to Isfahan and was executed in 1357. The Muzaffarids then made Shiraz their capital. The worklist transition is 'Injuids' -> 'Muzaffarids' [1354,1363] at lng 51.4, lat 30.8 (Fars), with the conquest consolidation falling within the window.

w4-700187.name: Auvergne granted as appanage to John, Duke of Berry
w4-700187.blurb: By a royal grant of October 1360, King John II of France raised Auvergne to a duchy and granted it, together with Berry, to his third surviving son John of Valois as an appanage, partly compensating for territories ceded to England under the Treaty of Brétigny. The Duchy of Auvergne thus passed from the royal domain into the apanage of John, Duke of Berry, who held it until his death in 1416.

w4-700189.name: Rise of the Despotate of Dobruja under Balik and Dobrotitsa
w4-700189.blurb: The Black Sea region of Dobruja broke away from the Second Bulgarian Empire as a semi-independent principality led first by Balik and then by Dobrotitsa, from whom the region takes its name. By the late 1350s this Despotate of Dobruja was acting autonomously, part of the broader political fragmentation of Bulgaria into Tarnovo, Vidin, and Dobruja before the Ottoman conquest.

w4-700190.name: Treaty of Regensburg / Habsburg acquisition of Tyrol
w4-700190.blurb: Margaret 'Maultasch', countess of Tyrol, ceded the County of Tyrol to the Habsburgs (Rudolf IV of Austria) in 1363 after the death of her son Meinhard III, who had been tied to the Wittelsbach Dukes of Bavaria. The Wittelsbachs contested the transfer but ultimately renounced their claims in the Peace of Schärding (1369), giving the House of Habsburg control of Tyrol at Bavarian expense.

w4-700194.name: Treaty of Fürstenwalde – Charles IV Acquires Brandenburg
w4-700194.blurb: Emperor Charles IV of Luxembourg acquired the Margraviate of Brandenburg from the Wittelsbach margrave Otto V in 1373 via the Treaty of Fürstenwalde, attaching it to the Bohemian Crown and combining Brandenburg's electoral vote with Bohemia's. Territory (~13.8E/53.1N) moved from Margraviate of Brandenburg to Kingdom of Bohemia. Window [1363,1375], date 1373.

w4-700195.name: Founding of the Kingdom of Ava and absorption of Sagaing
w4-700195.blurb: In 1364 Thado Minbya founded the Kingdom of Ava, uniting the upper Burmese statelets after the Shan-led sack of Sagaing and Pinya. The kingdom of Sagaing, which had been raided and weakened by the Maw Shans, was absorbed into the new Ava polity, restoring a single dominant power in central Myanmar.

w4-700196.name: Founding of the Kingdom of Ava and absorption of Pinya
w4-700196.blurb: Thado Minbya founded Ava in 1364, consolidating the Pinya and Sagaing kingdoms after both had been devastated by Shan raids—Pinya having been sacked with Maw Shan involvement. By taking Pinya and then Sagaing, Thado Minbya reunified upper Burma under the new Ava Kingdom centered near modern Mandalay.

w4-700197.name: Ming conquest of China / fall of the Yuan Dynasty
w4-700197.blurb: Zhu Yuanzhang's rebel armies overthrew the Mongol Yuan Dynasty, capturing the Yuan capital Dadu (Beijing) in 1368 and forcing the court to flee north; Zhu proclaimed himself the Hongwu Emperor, founding the Ming Dynasty. Through campaigns into the 1370s the Ming took over the heartland of China proper, the territory shown passing from Yuan to Ming here.

w4-700199.name: Byzantine reconquest after the collapse of the Serbian Empire
w4-700199.blurb: After Stefan Dušan's death in 1355 the Serbian Empire fragmented; the decisive Battle of Maritsa (Chernomen) in 1371 destroyed the army of the Mrnjavčević brothers, accelerating Serbian disintegration. The Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologoi recovered territory in Macedonia and around Serres (held by the Serbian ruler Jovan Uglješa, killed at Maritsa) as Serbian power in the south collapsed.

w4-700200.name: Albert of Mecklenburg becomes King of Sweden (1364)
w4-700200.blurb: In 1363–64, Swedish nobles led by Bo Jonsson Grip invited Duke Albert of Mecklenburg (a Holy Roman Empire princeling) to replace the unpopular Magnus Eriksson as king. Albert was proclaimed King of Sweden on 18 February 1364 with backing from German dukes and the Hanseatic League. His accession aligned Mecklenburg-area HRE borderlands more closely with the Swedish crown, with German lords receiving Swedish offices. The dataset's HRE-minor-states → Sweden change near the Mecklenburg/Baltic coast reflects this dynastic shift.

w4-700201.name: Retreat of the Yuan court to Mongolia and founding of the Northern Yuan
w4-700201.blurb: When the Ming took Dadu in 1368, the Yuan emperor Toghon Temür fled north to Shangdu and then the Mongolian steppe, where the dynasty continued as the Northern Yuan. The Mongolian homeland and northern territories thus passed from the (defunct) Yuan to its rump successor, the Northern Yuan, which contested the Ming for decades.

w4-700202.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania's Eastward Expansion under Algirdas
w4-700202.blurb: Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania aggressively expanded into Ruthenia in the 1360s-1370s, incorporating Kyiv (1362, after the Battle of Blue Waters), Podolia, and Volhynia from weakened principalities contested with Poland. The 1366 treaty temporarily ceded part of Volhynia to Poland, but in 1370 Lithuania recaptured Volhynia including Volodymyr. The coordinates point to Volhynia/Podolia, where Lithuania absorbed former Polish-claimed Ruthenian borderlands within the 1363-1375 window; partition in the 1380s confirmed Lithuania's hold.

w4-700206.name: Arborean revolt — Marianus IV expels Pisan influence from Sardinia
w4-700206.blurb: As part of Marianus IV of Arborea's sweeping reconquest of Sardinia (1353–1375), the residual Pisan commercial and territorial presence on the island (inherited from the pre-Aragonese era) was also extinguished, with the Giudicato of Arborea absorbing those areas. Pisa had lost its main Sardinian base at Cagliari to Aragon in 1324 but retained minor interests that Arborea eliminated by 1375.

w4-700207.name: Fragmentation of the Serbian Empire into regional lordships
w4-700207.blurb: Following Stefan Dušan's death and the destruction of the central army at Maritsa in 1371, the Serbian Empire dissolved into competing principalities ruled by despots and lords such as Lazar Hrebeljanović, Vukašin's heirs, and the Zeta lords. The territory here reflects the empire's core passing to these regional Serbian despots/princes as imperial authority disintegrated.

w4-700208.name: Timur's early conquest of the Kartid lands (Herat region)
w4-700208.blurb: As Timur consolidated power in Transoxiana from 1370, he began subjugating neighboring dynasties, including the Kartids of Herat. The Kartid kingdom was reduced to tributary status in this period (campaigns culminating in the formal subjugation of Herat in 1381), with Khurasanian territory passing under Timurid control.

w4-700212.name: Qara Qoyunlu seizure of territory from the Jalayirids
w4-700212.blurb: The Qara Qoyunlu Turkoman confederation under Bayram Khwaja, based around Lake Van and Mosul, expanded at the expense of the Jalayirid Sultanate during the 1370s as Jalayirid power weakened after the death of Shaikh Uvais (1374). The Qara Qoyunlu took control of territory in the Mosul–Azerbaijan borderlands, beginning their long rivalry with the Jalayirids.

w4-700214.type: political fragmentation / emergence of new polity
w4-700214.name: Albanian Despotate of Arta established after fall of Serbian Empire
w4-700214.blurb: After Stefan Dušan's death in 1355, Serbian imperial authority over Epirus collapsed. Albanian clan leader Pjetër Losha seized Arta, and by the late 1360s two Albanian principalities had emerged: the Despotate of Arta (under the Shpata clan) and the Serbian Despotate of Ioannina under Thomas Preljubović. Gjin Bua Shpata unified these Albanian territories and launched an offensive on Ioannina by 1375, consolidating the Despotate of Arta as the successor to Serbian control of Epirus.

citations.label: Fall of the Serbian Empire – Wikipedia

w4-700215.name: Ayutthaya expansion against the declining Khmer Empire
w4-700215.blurb: The newly founded Ayutthaya Kingdom (established 1351 under Ramathibodi I) pressed against the decaying Khmer Empire, launching repeated invasions of its territory in the later 14th century, including an attack on Angkor around 1369. The Khmer lost the Khorat Plateau and western frontier lands to the rising Thai power during this period.

w4-700216.name: Ayutthayan campaign against Angkor (c. 1369–1373)
w4-700216.blurb: Ayutthaya mounted recurring assaults on the weakening Khmer Empire across the later 14th century, with a recorded Tai attack on Angkor in 1369 amid the contested succession after Ramathibodi I's death. These raids pressed the Khmer along the Chao Phraya frontier and extracted tribute, but Angkor was not permanently broken until the later sieges; the decisive Ayutthayan capture and the Khmer abandonment of Angkor came only in the 15th century (conventionally 1431).

w4-700221.name: Kartid conquest of Nishapur from the Sarbadars
w4-700221.blurb: Around 1375–1376 the Kartid ruler Ghiyas al-Din Pir 'Ali exploited internal Sarbadar strife to seize the city of Nishapur, extending Kartid control over significant Sarbadar-held territory in Khorasan. The Sarbadars had suffered from leadership conflicts, allowing the Kartids to outflank them. Both dynasties were soon absorbed by Timur, who invaded Khorasan from 1381 onward.

w4-700222.name: Kartid expansion into Khorasan at the expense of the Muzaffarid sphere
w4-700222.blurb: The Muzaffarids and Kartids were rival successor states to the Ilkhanate controlling Persia and Khorasan respectively. During the 1360s-1370s the Muzaffarids were weakened by internecine struggles (Shah Shuja deposed his father in 1358 and faced his brothers). Exploiting Sarbadar instability, the Kartid ruler Ghiyas al-Din Pir Ali seized Nishapur around 1375-1376 and clashed with Shah Shuja's Muzaffarids, extending Kartid control westward across the Kartid-Muzaffarid frontier in eastern Khorasan (the worklist coordinates, lat 32.8 lng 59, lie in Quhistan on that frontier). Note Nishapur itself had been Sarbadar-held; the broader Kartid push was at the expense of the Muzaffarid sphere.

w4-700226.name: Aragonese reconquest of Sardinian interior from Pisan lords
w4-700226.blurb: Following Aragon's initial conquest of Pisan Cagliari and Gallura in 1324, a prolonged struggle continued against Pisan-backed Sardinian lords and Genoese allies; by the late 1360s Aragonese forces under Peter IV had defeated the last major Pisan-allied resistance in Sardinia, consolidating the island's interior and displacing Pisan territorial claims.

w4-700228.name: Mamluk conquest of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia
w4-700228.blurb: The Mamluk Sultanate captured Sis (capital) in 1374 and the fortress of Gaban in 1375, where King Levon V had taken refuge, ending three centuries of Armenian rule in Cilicia and terminating the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. The from=Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia / to=Mamluk Sultanate and 1363-1375 window match.

w4-700231.name: Ming pacification of the Yunnan–Shan frontier
w4-700231.blurb: Following the Ming conquest of Yunnan from the Yuan loyalist prince Basalawarmi (1381–1382), the Ming Dynasty extended its authority over the Shan States of the Sino-Burmese borderlands, organizing them into native chieftaincy offices (tusi). Frontier Shan territory thus passed under Ming overlordship as the dynasty consolidated its southwestern border.

w4-700232.name: Moravian Margrave Wars: partition between Jobst and Prokop (1382–1385)
w4-700232.blurb: The Margraviate of Moravia, held under the Kingdom of Bohemia, was divided between the Luxembourg brothers Jobst and Prokop through negotiation in 1382, confirmed by further arrangements in 1385. The settlement established a contested partition of Moravian territories among the brothers and their cousin, King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia.

w4-700238.name: Tokhtamysh's campaigns in the Caucasus (Shirvan)
w4-700238.blurb: After reunifying the Golden Horde with Timur's backing, Khan Tokhtamysh launched aggressive campaigns into the Caucasus in the early 1380s, raiding Shirvan and Azerbaijan. Shirvanshah territory along the western Caspian passed under Golden Horde domination during these incursions, which soon brought Tokhtamysh into open war with his former patron Timur.

w4-700239.name: Tokhtamysh's invasion of Azerbaijan (Tabriz campaign)
w4-700239.blurb: In 1385 Tokhtamysh of the Golden Horde invaded Azerbaijan, sacking Tabriz and devastating the region then contested by the Jalayirids and Qara Qoyunlu. Territory in northwestern Iran/Azerbaijan held by the Qara Qoyunlu passed under Golden Horde control during this raid, a direct provocation that precipitated full war with Timur.

w4-700240.name: Tokhtamysh's reunification of the Golden Horde (White Horde)
w4-700240.blurb: Tokhtamysh, khan of the White Horde (eastern wing), with backing from Timur, defeated Mamai and reunited the eastern and western wings of the Jochid ulus into a restored Golden Horde by 1380-1381.
