The naming conventions for White/Blue Horde are notoriously confused in the sources, but this change reflects the eastern Jochid lands passing under the unified Golden Horde under Tokhtamysh, ending the 'Great Troubles' of internal division.

w4-700241.name: Tokhtamysh's reunification of the Golden Horde (Blue Horde / western wing)
w4-700241.blurb: After taking the eastern wing, Tokhtamysh marched west, overthrew Mamai (who was then defeated at Kulikovo by the Russians in 1380), and seized the western steppe wing, reuniting it with the rest of the Jochid ulus as the Golden Horde by 1381. This change captures the western Volga steppe passing under Tokhtamysh's restored unified Horde.

w4-700243.name: Mamluk recognition of Ramadanid Emirate in Cilicia (1381–1383)
w4-700243.blurb: The Ramadanid dynasty held Adana and the Cilician plain under Mamluk suzerainty from the mid-14th century. After Ibrahim I of the Ramadanids rebelled and was defeated near Marash in 1381, the Mamluks acknowledged his authority and appointed him na'ib (viceroy) of Adana in 1383. The territory around Adana thus remained formally within the Mamluk sphere while administered by the Ramadanids.

w4-700244.name: Ottoman conquest of Thrace and Macedonia — Murad I's Balkan campaigns (1383–1385)
w4-700244.blurb: Under Murad I, Ottoman forces pushed into the Balkans in the early 1380s, capturing Serres (1383) and Sofia (1385) and reducing Greek lords of Thessaly to vassalage; Thessaloniki fell in 1387. The coordinates (26°E, 40.6°N) correspond to Thrace/Macedonia; from=Byzantine Empire, to=Ottoman Empire matches the 1377-1385 window.

w4-700246.name: Joanna I of Naples adopts Louis I of Valois-Anjou
w4-700246.blurb: In 1380 Joanna I of Naples (Capetian House of Anjou) adopted Louis I, Duke of Anjou (House of Valois-Anjou) as her heir to Naples and Provence; she died in 1382 and Louis campaigned to enforce the claim. The Provence region near lng 6.3 E / lat 44.1 N reflects the transfer of Provençal claims from the Capetian to the Valois-Anjou line, within the [1377,1385] window.

w4-700248.name: Burgundian inheritance of Flanders and Peace of Tournai (1384–1385)
w4-700248.blurb: On the death of Count Louis II of Flanders in January 1384, his son-in-law Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, inherited the County of Flanders through his wife Margaret. The Peace of Tournai in 1385 ended the Flemish revolt (notably from Ghent) and consolidated Philip's authority. This union of Flanders with Burgundy formed the nucleus of the later Burgundian Netherlands.

w4-700249.name: Philip the Bold inherits County of Nevers with the Flemish succession
w4-700249.blurb: Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, had married Margaret of Dampierre (heiress to Flanders) in 1369. When her father Louis II of Flanders died in 1384, Philip inherited the Counties of Flanders, Artois, Nevers, and Rethel. The administrative consolidation of these territories was effected from 1384–1385, uniting Nevers with the Burgundian state. After Philip's death, Nevers was assigned to his younger son Philip II as an appanage.

w4-700252.name: Founding of the Joseon dynasty by Yi Seong-gye
w4-700252.blurb: In 1392 the general Yi Seong-gye (Taejo) deposed the last Goryeo king and founded the Joseon dynasty, ending nearly five centuries of Goryeo rule over the Korean peninsula. The dynastic change followed Yi's 1388 turnabout at Wihwa Island, when he refused orders to invade Ming China and instead seized power. The entire Korean realm passed from Goryeo to Joseon.

w4-700255.name: Ottoman annexation of the Despotate of Dobruja
w4-700255.blurb: During Sultan Bayezid I's Balkan campaigns in the early 1390s, the Ottomans absorbed the Despotate of Dobruja (the Black Sea coastal principality of Dobrotitsa and his son Ivanko), which had been contested between Wallachia and the Ottomans. The region between the Danube and the Black Sea passed under direct Ottoman control around 1393-1395.

w4-700256.name: Ottoman conquest of Byzantine Macedonia / Thessaly under Bayezid I
w4-700256.blurb: Sultan Bayezid I aggressively reduced the surviving Byzantine territories in the Balkans, annexing Byzantine and vassal holdings in Macedonia and Thessaly (centered near Thessalonica) in the early-to-mid 1390s, around the same time he laid siege to Constantinople (1394 onward). This change reflects remaining Byzantine Macedonian territory near Thessalonica falling to the Ottomans.

w4-700257.name: Ottoman subjugation of the Albanian principalities under Bayezid I
w4-700257.blurb: As part of Bayezid I's sweeping consolidation of the Balkans following the Battle of Kosovo (1389), the Ottomans subdued the fragmented Albanian principalities (the lords of the Albanian/Macedonian highlands) in the early-to-mid 1390s, reducing them to vassalage or direct control. This change reflects Albanian-held territory passing to the Ottomans.

w4-700258.name: Ottoman conquest of Dobruja under Ivanko
w4-700258.blurb: After Dobrotitsa's death (1386), his son Ivanko made a treaty of submission to the Ottomans; by 1395 Ottoman overlordship was effectively complete as Bayezid I consolidated control over the Danubian region following the defeat of Bulgarian resistance.

w4-700260.name: Jaunpur Sultanate's expansion into Bihar under Khwaja Jahan / Ibrahim Shah Sharqi
w4-700260.blurb: The Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur, founded in 1394 by Malik Sarwar (Khwaja Jahan) as the Tughlaq empire disintegrated, expanded eastward and seized Bihar and the upper Bengal frontier (the region near Patna) from the Sultanate of Bengal. This change reflects Bihar passing from Bengal to the rising Jaunpur Sultanate.

w4-700264.name: Ayutthaya Kingdom Absorbs Lavo (Lopburi) Kingdom
w4-700264.blurb: The Lavo (Lopburi) Kingdom, one of the oldest polities in mainland Southeast Asia, ended its independent existence in 1388. Founded in 1350 by Ramathibodi I (of Lavo/Uthong lineage), Ayutthaya progressively subordinated Lavo; in 1388, King Ramesuan marched from his Lopburi base to retake Ayutthaya, completing the absorption of the Lavo heartland into the Ayutthayan state, which then controlled the central Chao Phraya valley.

w4-700265.name: Muscovite annexation of Vladimir / the Grand Principality of Vladimir
w4-700265.blurb: The Grand Principality of Moscow under Vasily I formally absorbed the Grand Principality of Vladimir and acquired the principalities of Nizhny Novgorod, Gorodets, Murom and others by patent from Tokhtamysh around 1392. The grand-princely title of Vladimir, long held jointly with Moscow, was permanently merged into the Muscovite state, and the Vladimir-Suzdal lands passed to Moscow.

w4-700274.name: Timurid absorption of the Sarbadar state (Khorasan)
w4-700274.blurb: The Sarbadar state of Sabzevar in Khorasan had submitted to Timur in 1381, and by the early 1390s its territory was fully integrated into the Timurid Empire as Timur consolidated Khorasan and the eastern Iranian plateau. This change reflects the former Sarbadar lands of Khorasan passing under Timurid control.

w4-700278.name: Mrkša Žarković consolidates Valona
w4-700278.blurb: After the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Savra (1385) killed Balsha II and weakened the Balsha dynasty, Mrkša Žarković (later lord of Valona and Kanina) established control over the Valona-Kanina area in the early 1390s, effectively separating it from the broader constellation of Albanian principalities.

w4-700279.name: Formation of the Kalmar Union (Sweden)
w4-700279.blurb: In 1397 the Kalmar Union united the crowns of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under a single monarch, Eric of Pomerania, engineered by Queen Margaret I of Denmark. This change reflects the Kingdom of Sweden (including Finland) entering the personal union.

w4-700280.name: Formation of the Kalmar Union (Denmark / Norway-Atlantic)
w4-700280.blurb: The Kalmar Union of 1397 joined Denmark, Norway and Sweden under Eric of Pomerania, arranged by Margaret I. This change (centered in the North Atlantic) reflects Danish/Norwegian crown lands — including the North Atlantic possessions — entering the union.

w4-700282.name: Hồ Quý Ly's usurpation of the Trần dynasty
w4-700282.blurb: In 1400 the powerful regent Hồ Quý Ly deposed the last Trần emperor and founded the Hồ dynasty, ending Trần rule over Đại Việt (renamed Đại Ngu). The 'Ngô Dynasty' label here is a data mislabel for the Hồ dynasty, but the underlying event is Hồ Quý Ly's seizure of the Vietnamese throne from the Trần.

w4-700283.name: Tokhtamysh's recovery of the western steppe after Timur's withdrawal
w4-700283.blurb: After Timur devastated the Golden Horde in 1395 and sacked Sarai, Tokhtamysh and rival Jochid claimants fought to recover the western Volga steppe; by 1401-1402 portions of the western (Blue Horde) wing were re-incorporated into the Golden Horde as the Jochid lands were partly reconstituted. This change reflects western steppe territory passing back to the Golden Horde.

w4-700284.name: Golden Horde recovery of Caucasus-steppe frontier from Timur
w4-700284.blurb: Following Timur's withdrawal from the Pontic-Caspian steppe after his 1395 campaign and his turn toward Anatolia (culminating in the Battle of Ankara, 1402), the Golden Horde reoccupied frontier territory north of the Caucasus (near the lower Volga/Caspian) that Timur had overrun. This change reflects that steppe frontier returning from the Timurid Empire to the Golden Horde.

w4-700286.name: Oirat ascendancy over the Northern Yuan (Ugechi Khashikha)
w4-700286.blurb: Around 1399-1402 the Oirats (Four Oirats confederation), under leaders such as Ugechi Khashikha, revolted against and overthrew the Borjigin Northern Yuan khans, with Elbeg Khan killed and Mongol power shifting westward to the Oirats in the Altai/western Mongolia region. This change reflects western Mongolian territory passing from the Northern Yuan to the Four Oirats.

w4-700288.name: Cession of Samogitia to the Teutonic Order (Treaty of Salynas, 1398)
w4-700288.blurb: By the Treaty of Salynas in 1398, Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania ceded Samogitia (the region between Lithuania and Prussia) to the Teutonic Knights in exchange for the Order's support of his ambitions in the east. This change reflects Samogitian/Lithuanian frontier territory passing to the Teutonic Order.

w4-700289.name: County of Savoy acquires the Genevois (County of Geneva)
w4-700289.blurb: The direct male line of the Counts of Geneva became extinct in 1394. In 1401 Count (later Duke) Amadeus VIII of Savoy purchased the rural county of the Genevois from its remaining heirs, including Odo of Thoire-Geneva. With the further purchase of the Dombes in 1402, this consolidated Savoyard control over the western Alpine passes and the southern shore of Lake Geneva, converting scattered HRE minor fiefs into an integrated Savoyard domain. This matches the worklist transfer from HRE Minor States to the County of Savoy in 1401-1402.

w4-700292.name: Timur's sack of Aleppo and invasion of Mamluk Syria
w4-700292.blurb: In 1400 Timur (Tamerlane) invaded Mamluk Syria, sacking Aleppo after defeating the Mamluk garrison and then taking Damascus in 1401, which he brutally pillaged. This transferred northern Syrian territory from the Mamluk Sultanate to the Timurid Empire, matching the location near Aleppo (37.7E, 35.4N) in the 1401-1402 window.

w4-700293.name: Timur's campaigns against the Golden Horde / Khwarazm
w4-700293.blurb: Timur waged a series of devastating campaigns against Tokhtamysh and the Golden Horde, culminating in the victories at the Kondurcha (1391) and the Terek (1395), and seizing the Khwarazm region around the Aral Sea. The large transfer near 57E, 42N reflects Timurid control over former Horde lands in the Khwarazm/Aral steppe consolidated by the early 1400s.

w4-700296.name: Timur's conquest of Baghdad and Jalayirid Iraq
w4-700296.blurb: Timur conquered the Jalayirid Sultanate's heartland of Iraq, capturing Baghdad in 1393 and, after a Jalayirid restoration under Ahmad Jalayir, brutally sacking it again in 1401, when tens of thousands were massacred and towers built of skulls. This moved central Iraq (44.4E, 33N, the Baghdad region) from the Jalayirids to the Timurid Empire in the 1401-1402 window.

w4-700304.name: Timurid grant of Diyar Bakr to the Aq Qoyunlu
w4-700304.blurb: After his victory at the Battle of Ankara (1402) over the Ottomans, Timur redistributed Anatolian territory among allied Turcoman confederations. Qara Yülük Osman of the Aq Qoyunlu, who had aided Timur, received Diyar Bakr (upper Mesopotamia/southeastern Anatolia, ~lng 39.9, lat 38.0) as a reward, establishing the Aq Qoyunlu's first permanent territorial base.

w4-700307.name: Lithuanian Conquest of Smolensk under Vytautas
w4-700307.blurb: Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania captured Smolensk in 1404, ending the Principality of Smolensk's independence after it had briefly reasserted itself following the Lithuanian defeat at the Battle of the Vorskla (1399). This definitively incorporated Smolensk and its surrounding territory into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

w4-700310.name: Venetian terraferma conquest of the Veneto
w4-700310.blurb: Venice rapidly conquered the eastern Po plain (terraferma) in 1404–1405, taking Vicenza (1404), Verona (1405), and Padua (1405) from the Visconti and Carrara lords; these had previously been administered as minor HRE vassal lordships.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Republic of Venice – Terraferma expansion

w4-700311.name: Recovery of Delhi Sultanate territories after Timur's withdrawal
w4-700311.blurb: After Timur's devastating 1398–1399 invasion of the Delhi Sultanate, the Timurid forces withdrew and the reconstituted Tughlaq (and successor Sayyid) administration gradually reasserted control over the Doab and Delhi hinterland (centroid ~76°E 29°N, ~17,000 km²); Timur's death in 1405 ended any Timurid claim to these territories.

w4-700312.name: Battle of Ankara and Timurid withdrawal from Anatolia
w4-700312.blurb: At the Battle of Ankara in July 1402 Timur defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I. Timur restored the Anatolian beyliks and then withdrew eastward; as Timurid forces left, central Anatolian territory near Sivas (36.6E, 39.5N) reverted to Ottoman control during the 1402-1407 recovery under Mehmed I and the Ottoman Interregnum.

w4-700318.name: Aq Qoyunlu absorption of the Diyarbakır region under Kara Osman
w4-700318.blurb: After the Battle of Ankara (1402) and Timur's redistribution of power, Kara Osman (Uthman Beg) of the Aq Qoyunlu received custody of Amid (Diyarbakır) and consolidated Eastern Anatolia. The Artuqids of Mardin were extinguished c. 1408-1409 (by the Qara Qoyunlu), but the broader Diyarbakır region (lat 37.8, lng 39.6) had passed into Aq Qoyunlu hands by the early 1400s. Window 1407-1415.

w4-700319.name: Stefan Lazarević expands Serbian Despotate (c. 1407-1415)
w4-700319.blurb: After receiving the title of Despot from Byzantine Emperor Manuel II in 1402 and allying with Hungary, Stefan Lazarević began recovering and expanding Serbian territories. He received Belgrade and Golubac from Hungary and pursued a balancing policy between the Ottoman Empire and Hungary. The dataset records territory at 20.2E, 42.6N (Kosovo-Serbia region) passing from 'Serbian Despots' to 'Serbian Empire' around 1407-1415, likely reflecting Stefan's territorial consolidation, though the 'Serbian Empire' label is anachronistic (the empire proper ended in 1371).

w4-700320.name: Hohenzollern Acquisition of Brandenburg at the Council of Constance
w4-700320.blurb: After the extinction of the Ascanian ruling dynasty in Brandenburg and years of noble lawlessness, Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund appointed Frederick VI of Hohenzollern (Nuremberg) as governor in 1411. Frederick restored order by force against the 'robber barons' and was formally invested as Margrave and Prince-Elector Frederick I of Brandenburg at the Council of Constance on 30 April 1415. The formal purchase was completed in 1417 for 400,000 Hungarian guilders, marking the definitive transfer of Brandenburg to the Hohenzollern line. The atlas's from/to label (Brandenburg → HRE minor states) reflects the reorganization of the margraviate's status during this 1407–1415 transition.

w4-700321.name: Foundation of the Sayyid Dynasty at Delhi
w4-700321.blurb: The Tughlaq Dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, fatally weakened by Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398, collapsed and was supplanted by the Sayyid Dynasty when Khizr Khan, Timur's appointed governor of Multan, took Delhi in 1414. This moved the Delhi region (76.8E, 28N) from the Tughlaqs to the Sayyids, matching the 1407-1415 window.

w4-700324.name: Georgian recovery after Timur's death
w4-700324.blurb: The Kingdom of Georgia, repeatedly devastated by Timur's eight invasions between 1386 and 1403, reasserted control over its core territory around Tbilisi (44.1E, 41.2N) after Timur's death in 1405 under King George VII and his successors. The 1407-1415 window captures the reversion of these lands from the Timurid Empire back to Georgia as Timurid authority in the Caucasus collapsed.

w4-700328.name: Ottoman Interregnum — loss of eastern Anatolian frontier to Qara Qoyunlu
w4-700328.blurb: In the disorder following Timur's defeat of the Ottomans at Ankara (1402) and the Ottoman Interregnum, the Qara Qoyunlu under Qara Yusuf pushed into the upper Euphrates and Diyarbekir highlands. There they absorbed the remnants of the Artuqid principality of Mardin, whose last rulers had been Qara Qoyunlu tributaries; Qara Yusuf extinguished Artuqid rule and annexed the region around 1408-1410. The centroid in the upper Euphrates uplands marks this transfer of formerly Artuqid territory to the Qara Qoyunlu confederation.

w4-700331.name: Ottoman re-annexation of Saruhan under Mehmed I
w4-700331.blurb: After the Battle of Ankara (1402) Timur restored the Aegean Anatolian beyliks, including Saruhan (capital Manisa) and Menteshe (capital Milas, in ancient Caria), as buffers against the Ottomans. During and after the Ottoman Interregnum, Mehmed I and his successor Murad II reconquered these coastal principalities, with Menteshe finally annexed around 1424. The event records the reabsorption of one such southwestern Aegean beylik into the reunified Ottoman state.

w4-700332.name: Qara Qoyunlu seizure of Iraq after Timur
w4-700332.blurb: After Timur's death the Turkmen Qara Qoyunlu under Qara Yusuf defeated Timurid and Jalayirid rivals, capturing Baghdad in 1410 after the Battle of Tabriz and ending Timurid control of Iraq. The large transfer near Baghdad (45.3E, 33N) in the 1407-1415 window reflects Iraq passing out of the Timurid Empire; the Cliopatria 'Hashemite Arab Federation' label appears to be the dataset's anachronistic name for the Iraq polity that emerged.

w4-700333.name: Anthony of Burgundy inherits Brabant; killed at Agincourt
w4-700333.blurb: Anthony of Burgundy (House of Valois) inherited the Duchy of Brabant from his great-aunt Joanna in 1406 and became Co-Duke of Luxembourg in 1411, drawing numerous minor HRE lordships into the Brabantine sphere. He was killed at the Battle of Agincourt on 25 October 1415. His underage son John IV inherited Brabant under the Estates of Brabant, with the accumulated minor HRE territories (around lng 5.8, lat 49.8) remaining under Brabantine administration. This matches the worklist transfer from HRE Minor States to the Duchy of Brabant within 1407-1415.

w4-700335.name: Fall of the Ifat Sultanate and rise of Adal
w4-700335.blurb: The Ifat Sultanate was destroyed by the Ethiopian Empire under Dawit I and Yeshaq I, whose forces killed Sultan Sa'ad ad-Din II at Zeila around 1410-1415. The surviving Walashma dynasty regrouped to found the Adal Sultanate, inheriting Ifat's Muslim domains in the Horn of Africa near Harar/Zeila (42.8E, 10.3N), matching the 1407-1415 transfer.

w4-700341.name: Sale of the Giudicato of Arborea to Aragon (1420)
w4-700341.blurb: After a century of warfare, including the Aragonese victory at Sanluri (1409), the last Judge of Arborea, William II (Viscount of Narbonne), sold his remaining rights over the Giudicato to Alfonso V of Aragon for 100,000 gold florins on 17 August 1420. This ended the last independent Sardinian state and completed Aragonese control over the island.

w4-700343.name: Oirat expansion into the Chagatai/Moghulistan steppe
w4-700343.blurb: The Four Oirats (Western Mongols), rising in power in the early 15th century, expanded southwestward into the Dzungaria and eastern steppe (84.9E, 45.3N) at the expense of the fragmenting Chagatai Khanate / Moghulistan. The 1415-1422 transfer reflects Oirat dominance over these Central Asian steppe lands as Chagataid authority weakened.

w4-700344.name: Formation of the Livonian Confederation
w4-700344.blurb: CORRECTED: The junior researcher misattributed this to the Treaty of Melno (1422), which concerned Samogitia and the Prussian-Lithuanian border, not Livonia, and would not transfer territory at lng24.6/lat57.7 (Livonia, near Riga). The actual event matching the transfer Teutonic Order -> Livonian Conference (Confederation) at this location and window (py1415/y1422) is the formation of the Livonian Confederation: at the initiative of Archbishop Johannes Ambundii the Livonian Diet (Landtag) first gathered at Walk in 1419, organizing the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, the Livonian bishoprics, and towns into a distinct confederated polity (formed c.1419-1435). This formalized Livonia's separation from the main Teutonic Order following the Order's post-Grunwald decline.

w4-700346.name: Carlo I Tocco conquers the Despotate of Arta (1416)
w4-700346.blurb: Carlo I Tocco, Count of Cephalonia, was granted the title of Despot by Byzantine Emperor Manuel II in 1415. In 1416 he captured the city of Arta, executing the last Spata ruler, and reunited the Despotate of Arta with the broader Despotate of Epirus under his rule. From=Despotate of Arta, to=Despotate of Epirus matches; window 1415-1422 includes the 1416 capture.

w4-700347.name: Death of Duke Anthony of Brabant at Agincourt and succession crisis (1415–1422)
w4-700347.blurb: Duke Anthony of Brabant was killed at Agincourt on 25 October 1415, leaving two underage heirs; John IV (1415–1427) succeeded under estate supervision amid Burgundian–imperial rivalry. The 1415–1422 window corresponds to the unsettled Brabantian succession, during which border territories (at 5.8°E, 50.1°N) reverted toward imperial control before the 1422 'Nieuw Regiment' stabilised John IV's reign, matching the Brabant→HRE Minor States change.

w4-700352.name: Muscovite absorption of Vladimir-Suzdal territories under Vasily I (c.1415–1422)
w4-700352.blurb: The Grand Principality of Moscow under Vasily I (r. 1389–1425) steadily absorbed the remaining sub-principalities of the old Vladimir-Suzdal domain. After the major annexation of Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal (1392), residual territories around Kostroma, Yaroslavl, and the upper Volga continued to be incorporated through Vasily I's later reign, including the Kostroma–Vologda region in this 1415–1422 window.

w4-700353.name: Le dynasty conquest of Cham territory / Lam Son campaigns
w4-700353.blurb: As Le Loi's Lam Son uprising expelled the Ming and founded the Le dynasty (Later Le, proclaimed 1428), Dai Viet reasserted and extended control over the central coast bordering Champa around Quang Nam (108.2E, 15.4N). The 1422-1429 transfer from Champa to the Le Dynasty reflects Vietnamese consolidation of these contested northern Cham lands as the Le state was established.

w4-700355.name: Lam Son uprising and expulsion of the Ming from Dai Viet
w4-700355.blurb: Le Loi's Lam Son uprising (1418-1427) drove the Ming Dynasty out of occupied Dai Viet, culminating in the victory at Tot Dong-Chuc Dong and the siege of Dong Quan (Hanoi), after which the Ming withdrew in 1427-1428 and Le Loi founded the Le dynasty. This transferred northern Vietnam (106.1E, 19.7N) from the Ming to the Le Dynasty, matching the 1422-1429 window.

w4-700358.name: Ottoman annexation of the Beylik of Teke
w4-700358.blurb: The Beylik of Teke in southwestern Anatolia around Antalya (30.2E, 36.9N), restored as an independent emirate after Timur's defeat of Bayezid I in 1402, was reconquered and definitively annexed by the Ottoman Empire under Murad II in the early 1420s as the Ottomans reabsorbed the Anatolian beyliks. This matches the 1422-1429 transfer.

w4-700360.name: Eric of Pomerania's reintegration of Sweden into the Kalmar Union
w4-700360.blurb: The Kalmar Union, ruled by Eric of Pomerania, bound Sweden, Denmark and Norway under a single monarch. The transfer of northern Swedish territory (around 64.7N, near the Gulf of Bothnia) to the Union reflects the consolidation of Swedish crown lands under Union administration before the Engelbrekt rebellion of 1434 fractured it. This is a data-model recoding of Sweden as part of the Kalmar Union rather than a military conquest.

w4-700362.name: Philip the Good acquires the County of Namur
w4-700362.blurb: In 1421 Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, purchased the indebted County of Namur from the childless John III, Marquis of Namur, for 132,000 golden crowns, with formal Burgundian possession taking effect on John III's death in 1429. The county bordered Brabant and Luxembourg (around lng 5.8, lat 49.8), and Cliopatria codes the gain into the Burgundian-Luxembourg complex, matching the worklist transfer from HRE Minor States to the Duchy of Luxembourg within 1422-1429. This was a peaceful commercial transaction extending Burgundian control in the Low Countries.

w4-700363.name: Elisabeth of Görlitz acquires County of Namur and adjacent territories
w4-700363.blurb: Elisabeth of Görlitz, widow of Anton of Brabant and heiress of the Luxembourg line, held the Duchy of Luxembourg in pledge from Emperor Sigismund from 1411 and accumulated rights over adjacent Low Countries lordships in the Meuse region. The County of Namur, however, had already been sold by Count John III to Philip the Good of Burgundy (effective 1421, with Philip taking possession on John's death in 1429). The centroid in the Namur-Meuse area reflects a transitional assignment of these middle-Meuse territories to the Luxembourg domain before they devolved to Burgundy.

w4-700365.name: English Occupation of Brittany (Lancastrian Phase, Hundred Years War)
w4-700365.blurb: After Henry V's 1422 death, the Duke of Bedford pressed the Duke of Brittany (John V) into the English-Lancastrian camp. By the Treaty of Amiens (13 April 1423) John V recognized Henry VI as King of France and joined the Anglo-Burgundian alliance; after wavering, he was forced back to vassal status and reaffirmed his recognition of Henry VI on 8 September 1427. This period of Breton allegiance to the English-Lancastrian crown effectively ended with the French resurgence following Joan of Arc's 1429 relief of Orléans.

citations.label: John V, Duke of Brittany – Wikipedia

w4-700367.name: Saxe-Wittenberg electorate granted to House of Wettin
w4-700367.blurb: On the death of the heirless Ascanian Elector (Albert III/IV) on 12 Nov 1422, Emperor Sigismund granted the Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg and the electoral dignity to Frederick I of Meissen (House of Wettin) on 6 January 1423, rewarding his loyalty in the Hussite Wars. This ended Ascanian rule over Electoral Saxony and united Saxe-Wittenberg, Meissen, and Thuringia under the Wettins. Coordinates are the Wittenberg region.

w4-700368.name: Lithuanian Civil War (1431–1435) / Polish–Lithuanian conflict over Podolia and Volhynia
w4-700368.blurb: After Grand Duke Vytautas died in 1430, the succession dispute between Švitrigaila and Sigismund Kęstutaitis triggered the Lithuanian Civil War. Poland under Władysław II Jagiełło seized the contested borderlands of Podolia and Volhynia (the region near 27.4E, 49.1N), which had long been disputed between the two states of the Polish–Lithuanian union. The Lutsk War of 1431 was part of this struggle.

w4-700369.name: Philip the Good Inherits Duchy of Brabant
w4-700369.blurb: Philip of Saint-Pol, Duke of Brabant, died without heirs on 4 August 1430. Brabant (with Limburg and the Margraviate of Antwerp) passed to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, incorporating it into the growing Burgundian Netherlands. The window 1429-1431 captures this transfer from Duchy of Brabant to Duchy of Burgundy, ending over three centuries of Brabant's separate existence.

w4-700370.name: Ottoman Conquest of Ioannina and Fall of the Despotate of Epirus
w4-700370.blurb: The Despotate of Epirus under the Tocco dynasty lost Ioannina to the Ottomans in 1430; the city surrendered peacefully to avoid the fate of Thessaloniki, sacked only months before. Carlo II Tocco remained as vassal lord of Arta, but the main Epirote territories fell to Ottoman control. The window 1429-1431 captures the fall of Ioannina (1430), ending Greek Christian rule of the Epirote interior.

w4-700371.name: Death of Duke Charles II of Lorraine; succession of René d'Anjou
w4-700371.blurb: Duke Charles II of Lorraine died in 1431 without male heirs; the duchy passed through his daughter Isabelle to her husband René I (René d'Anjou) of the House of Valois-Anjou, triggering a succession dispute with Antoine de Vaudémont (settled at the Battle of Bulgnéville, 1431, though René was captured). Coord 6.2E/48.7N is in Lorraine. The dataset's 1429–1431 'HRE Minor States → Duchy of Lorraine' shift reflects the Anjou succession; event real and correctly dated.

w4-700372.name: Byzantine (Despotate of the Morea) conquest of the Principality of Achaea
w4-700372.blurb: The Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, led by Constantine Palaiologos (the future last emperor) and Thomas Palaiologos, conquered the remaining Frankish Principality of Achaea in the Peloponnese. The fall of Patras (1430) and the surrender of the Latin principality brought nearly all of the Morea (around 22.3E, 37.4N) under Byzantine control, ending two centuries of Crusader rule there.

w4-700373.name: Oirat (Four Oirats) expansion under Toghon into Hami and the western frontier
w4-700373.blurb: The Four Oirats, consolidated under Toghon Taishi in the 1430s, expanded eastward and southward, pressuring the Ming frontier garrisons and the Hami oasis region (around 93.3E, 43N). This western Gansu/Hami corridor passed from Ming influence to Oirat control as the Oirats grew into the dominant Mongol power that would later crush the Ming at Tumu in 1449.

w4-700375.name: Joseon's Four Forts and Six Garrisons frontier expansion under King Sejong
w4-700375.blurb: Under King Sejong the Great, Joseon expanded its northern frontier against the Jurchens along the Yalu and Tumen rivers, establishing the Four Forts (Sagun, 1416–1443) and Six Garrisons (Yukjin, 1434–1443). This pushed the Korean border to its modern line, absorbing territory near 128.2E, 41.8N that had been nominally under Ming/Jurchen control.

w4-700376.name: French recovery of Maine and Anjou from English occupation
w4-700376.blurb: René of Anjou, head of the House of Valois-Anjou and brother-in-law of Charles VII, succeeded to the Duchy of Anjou and County of Maine on his brother Louis III's death in 1435. Through French military pressure and diplomacy in the later 1430s and 1440s, Valois-Anjou and crown forces rolled back the English position in these western provinces, which England had claimed since the Treaty of Troyes (1420); Maine was finally surrendered by treaty and retaken by 1448. The event records the consolidation of Maine and Anjou under Valois-Anjou control.

w4-700378.name: Death of Louis III of Anjou; René of Anjou inherits Maine
w4-700378.blurb: Louis III of Anjou, Count of Maine, died childless in Cosenza on 12 November 1434. Maine and the Valois-Anjou appanage passed by fraternal succession to his brother René of Anjou. The window (1431-1440) reflects René's assumption of the county; 'House of Valois-Anjou' is the correct successor polity.

w4-700382.name: Treaty of Arras and French Reconquest of Central France
w4-700382.blurb: The Treaty of Arras (1435) ended the Anglo-Burgundian alliance, and French forces under Charles VII swiftly recovered Paris (1436) and much of central France (including the Loire valley region shown by the centroid) over the following years. England's position in France collapsed without Burgundian support, and by 1440 large swaths of the Loire heartland had reverted to French control.

w4-700383.name: Foundation of the Khanate of Kazan by Ulugh Muhammad
w4-700383.blurb: Ulugh Muhammad, a former Khan of the Golden Horde who had been expelled from the western steppe, established the Khanate of Kazan around 1437–1438 by seizing the city of Kazan with the support of local nobility. This carved out a new independent khanate from the disintegrating Golden Horde's northeastern territories in the middle Volga region.

w4-700384.name: Aq Qoyunlu expansion into Iraq/Jazira under Qara Yuluk Uthman and successors (1430s–1440s)
w4-700384.blurb: The Aq Qoyunlu (White Sheep Turkoman) confederation, based in Diyarbakir, expanded eastward into the Jazira and upper Mesopotamia during the 1430s, exploiting the civil wars within the rival Qara Qoyunlu. Qara Yuluk Uthman Beg was killed fighting the Qara Qoyunlu near Erzurum in 1435, but his successors continued pressing into the Iraq-Jazira corridor. By the late 1440s the Aq Qoyunlu had absorbed significant territory in upper Mesopotamia previously under Jalayirid or Qara Qoyunlu control.

w4-700386.name: English withdrawal from Breton territories following the Congress of Arras and Breton realignment
w4-700386.blurb: After Duke John V of Brittany's alliance with England lapsed and the Congress of Arras (1435) realigned French nobles against England, Breton territories that English forces had occupied or influenced reverted to Ducal Breton control. English military presence in the Breton borderlands was gradually abandoned through the late 1430s.

w4-700388.name: Vijayanagara–Bahmani Wars: Treaty of 1450 / Vijayanagara gains in the Deccan
w4-700388.blurb: In the 1440s, Vijayanagara under Devaraya II and then Mallikarjuna Raya engaged in prolonged warfare with the Bahmani Sultanate over the Tungabhadra Doab and Raichur; a peace settlement around 1446–1450 confirmed Vijayanagara's gains in the disputed territory east of the Tungabhadra river.

w4-700389.name: Frederick III's guardianship of Ladislaus Posthumus over Hungary
w4-700389.blurb: After the death of Władysław I of Hungary at Varna (1444), the young Habsburg claimant Ladislaus Posthumus (son of Albert II) came under the guardianship of Emperor Frederick III, giving the Habsburgs effective control over Hungarian royal affairs from 1446 until Ladislaus assumed direct rule in 1453. The atlas reclassifies Hungarian territory to reflect Habsburg dominance during this interregnum.

w4-700390.name: Foundation of the Crimean Khanate under Hacı I Giray
w4-700390.blurb: Hacı I Giray, a Genghisid claimant who had waged a decades-long struggle against the Golden Horde, established the independent Crimean Khanate around 1441–1449, drawing the Crimean peninsula and adjacent steppe north of the Black Sea out of Golden Horde control. The atlas captures this separation in the 1444–1450 window.

w4-700391.name: Founding of Crimean Khanate under Hacı I Giray (1449)
w4-700391.blurb: After warring for independence from the Golden Horde/Blue Horde since c. 1420, Hacı I Giray secured his position as founder-Khan of the Crimean Khanate by 1449, establishing the capital at Qırq Yer; the khanate is formally dated to 1441. The ~27,000 km² centred at lat 45.2 / lng 34.5 (Crimea and northern Black Sea steppe) represents territory that thereby separated from the decaying Blue Horde into the new Crimean polity.

w4-700393.name: French conquest of Normandy — Battle of Formigny
w4-700393.blurb: On 15 April 1450 French forces crushed the English army at the Battle of Formigny in Normandy, breaking English military power in the region. Caen fell in June and Cherbourg in August 1450, completing the French reconquest of Normandy from England.

w4-700394.name: Formalization of Nogai Horde independence under Edigu's heirs
w4-700394.blurb: The Manghit-led confederation that became the Nogai Horde had operated as a quasi-autonomous western Jochid wing since Edigu's ascendancy in the 1390s-1410s. Sources place its formal separation from the disintegrating Golden Horde broadly in the 1440s, consolidated under Edigu's descendants — notably his grandson Waqqas Biy, then a leading beg allied with Abu'l-Khayr Khan; the northern Caspian steppe (near 51.4E, 50.7N) is consistently identified as Manghit-dominated by this point. Exact-year precision is elusive in the sources, but the mid-1440s formalization falls within this window.

w4-700397.name: Casimir IV Jagiellon elected King of Poland
w4-700397.blurb: After Władysław III died at the Battle of Varna (1444), his brother Casimir IV was elected and crowned King of Poland on 25 June 1447, already holding the Grand Duchy of Lithuania since 1440. The atlas reclassifies Polish territory from 'Kingdom of Poland' to 'House of Jagiellon' to mark this dynastic union under a single ruler.

w4-700398.name: Casimir IV Jagiellon elected King of Poland
w4-700398.blurb: After Władysław III died at the Battle of Varna (1444), his brother Casimir IV—already Grand Duke of Lithuania since 1440—was elected and crowned King of Poland on 25 June 1447, uniting both crowns under the Jagiellonian dynasty. The atlas reclassifies the Grand Duchy territory from 'Grand Duchy of Lithuania' to 'House of Jagiellon' to reflect this dynastic union.

w4-700399.name: Aragonese Conquest of Naples
w4-700399.blurb: Alfonso V of Aragon besieged Naples from November 1441 and entered the city on 26 February 1443, defeating René of Anjou's claim and uniting the Kingdom of Naples with the Crown of Aragon. The atlas shows this change between 1444–1450, reflecting the consolidation of Aragonese rule following the conquest.

w4-700401.name: Death of Christopher of Bavaria and election of Christian I
w4-700401.blurb: Christopher of Bavaria, ruler of the three Kalmar Union realms, died childless in January 1448, breaking the union. Sweden's nobility elected Karl Knutsson Bonde as King Karl VIII in June 1448, while Denmark separately elected Christian I of the House of Oldenburg. The 'to' label here marks the Danish-led Oldenburg succession, but for the Swedish (Kingdom of Sweden) portion the crown passed to Karl Knutsson, not Oldenburg, and Sweden left the union rather than coming under Oldenburg rule.

w4-700402.name: Ottoman capture of Arta (fall of Despotate of Epirus)
w4-700402.blurb: Ottoman forces under Turahan Bey captured Arta in 1449, the capital of the Despotate of Epirus, effectively ending the Despotate's control over the region around lng 21.7, lat 39.2 (Thessaly/Epirus). The Despotate had already been reduced after Ottoman conquests following the 1430 fall of Ioannina.

w4-700403.name: Philip the Good purchases Duchy of Luxembourg from Elisabeth of Görlitz
w4-700403.blurb: Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, had advanced Elisabeth of Görlitz a series of loans beginning in the 1430s; in 1443 he occupied Luxembourg militarily and Elisabeth formally sold him the duchy, completing the Burgundian absorption of the Low Countries.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Duchy of Luxembourg – Burgundian period

w4-700407.name: Establishment of the Qasim Khanate
w4-700407.blurb: Around 1452, Vasily II of Moscow granted Kasimov (Gorodets Meshchersky) and surrounding territory to Qasim Khan, a Tatar prince who had aided him, creating the Qasim Khanate as a client state. This territory (centroid lng 41.0, lat 54.8) on the Oka River had previously been under Golden Horde suzerainty and was ceded out of Golden Horde control as Muscovite power grew.

w4-700408.name: Abdication of Alam Shah in favour of Bahlul Lodi
w4-700408.blurb: On 19 April 1451, the ineffectual last Sayyid sultan Ala-ud-Din Alam Shah voluntarily abdicated the throne to Bahlul Khan Lodi, governor of Sirhind, who had gradually accumulated enough military power to dominate Delhi; Alam Shah retired to Badaun, completing a peaceful transfer of the Delhi Sultanate to the Lodi dynasty.

w4-700411.name: René of Anjou consolidates control of Lorraine after the War of the Succession of Lorraine
w4-700411.blurb: René of Anjou (House of Valois-Anjou) had contested the Duchy of Lorraine for decades; by 1453 he had definitively secured his position as duke, and territories that had been disputed between Anjou and Lorraine were mapped under Lorraine in Cliopatria's dataset.

w4-700414.name: Battle of Castillon (1453): France retakes Gascony, ending the Hundred Years' War
w4-700414.blurb: At the Battle of Castillon (17 July 1453) French forces under Jean Bureau defeated the English and killed John Talbot; Bordeaux surrendered on 19 October 1453, ending over 300 years of English rule in Gascony and the Hundred Years' War. Coord 0.9W/44.5N is in Gascony (Aquitaine), the region England lost (retaining only Calais). The dataset's 1450–1453 'England → France' shift matches; event real and correctly dated.

w4-700415.name: Habsburg regency over Bohemia under Ladislaus the Posthumous
w4-700415.blurb: Ladislaus the Posthumous, a Habsburg, was the boy-king of Bohemia (and Hungary), with his guardianship under Emperor Frederick III. The 1450–1453 period saw Bohemia (around 15.7E, 50.5N) formally recognized under Habsburg/Ladislaus rule before George of Poděbrady consolidated power as regent. This is a dynastic/administrative reattribution rather than a conquest.

w4-700421.name: Tahirid Sultanate's overthrow of the Rasulid Dynasty in Yemen
w4-700421.blurb: The Tahirid dynasty supplanted the declining Rasulid dynasty as rulers of Yemen in the mid-15th century, taking the capital and the lowlands around Aden and the Yemeni highlands (near 47.3E, 15.9N). The Rasulids collapsed amid internal succession strife and plague, and the Tahirids formally took power around 1454, governing Yemen until the Mamluk and Ottoman conquests of the early 16th century.

w4-700422.name: Decline of Majapahit and the rise of Palembang under Chinese-Muslim leadership
w4-700422.blurb: The Javanese Majapahit empire entered steep decline after the Paregreg civil war (1404–1406) and the death of Hayam Wuruk, losing its grip over Sumatra. Palembang (near 105.7E, 2.9S) emerged as an autonomous polity, associated with the Chinese-Muslim community and figures like Gan Eng Cu / the later Palembang sultanate, breaking from Majapahit suzerainty by the mid-15th century. This reflects gradual loss of Majapahit's outer dependencies rather than a single battle.

w4-700423.name: Election of Matthias Corvinus as King of Hungary
w4-700423.blurb: After the death of the Habsburg Ladislaus the Posthumous in 1457, the Hungarian Diet elected Matthias Corvinus (son of John Hunyadi) as King of Hungary in January 1458, ending Habsburg rule there. This restored an independent national Kingdom of Hungary (centered near 20.4E, 46.5N), wresting some 333,000 km2 from Habsburg control, though Frederick III contested the crown until the Treaty of Wiener Neustadt (1463).

w4-700424.name: Death of Alfonso V of Aragon and separation of Naples from the Crown of Aragon (1458)
w4-700424.blurb: Alfonso V (the Magnanimous) died on 27 June 1458, having ruled both the Crown of Aragon and the Kingdom of Naples since conquering Naples in 1442. In his will he separated the two: the Crown of Aragon passed to his brother John II, while the Kingdom of Naples went to his illegitimate son Ferrante (Ferdinand I), crowned in 1459. This severed Naples from Aragonese control at lng 15.7, lat 40.4 (Crown of Aragon -> Kingdom of Naples), within the [1453,1459] window.

w4-700425.name: Christian I of Denmark inherits Schleswig and Holstein (Treaty of Ribe)
w4-700425.blurb: Christian I of Denmark inherited Schleswig and Holstein following the death of his maternal uncle Duke Adolphus VIII in 1459; the Estates of both territories confirmed his succession at Ribe on 5 March 1460, transferring these HRE-affiliated duchies to the Kalmar Union crown.

w4-700428.name: Election of George of Poděbrady as King of Bohemia
w4-700428.blurb: Following the death of the Habsburg king Ladislaus the Posthumous in 1457, the Bohemian estates elected George of Poděbrady as King of Bohemia in March 1458, ending direct Habsburg rule. This transferred the Kingdom of Bohemia (around 15.7E, 50.5N, roughly 128,000 km2) from the House of Habsburg to a native Hussite-aligned monarch.

w4-700430.name: Muscovite absorption of the Vladimir-Suzdal lands (Yaroslavl/Suzdal principalities)
w4-700430.blurb: The Grand Principality of Moscow under Vasily II and Ivan III progressively absorbed the old Vladimir-Suzdal appanage principalities. Around 1463 the Principality of Yaroslavl was annexed to Moscow, with the Suzdal-Nizhny Novgorod lands (near 39.9E, 58.2N) likewise falling under Muscovite control, part of Moscow's gathering of the Russian lands.

w4-700432.name: Timurid (Abu Sa'id) campaigns against the Qara/Aq Qoyunlu in western Persia
w4-700432.blurb: The Timurid ruler Abu Sa'id Mirza campaigned westward into Persia and Iraq in the early 1460s, contesting the Turkmen confederations. The transfer of territory near Khuzestan/lower Iraq (48.9E, 31.5N) from the Aq Qoyunlu to the Timurid Empire reflects Abu Sa'id's temporary expansion before his disastrous 1469 invasion of Azerbaijan, where Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu captured and executed him.

w4-700433.name: Songhai expansion under Sunni Ali at the expense of the Mali Empire
w4-700433.blurb: Sunni Ali Ber became ruler of the Songhai Empire in 1464 and rapidly expanded along the Niger bend, seizing the river-trade heartland (near 0.4W, 16.2N, around Gao/Timbuktu) from the declining Mali Empire. The capture of Timbuktu followed in 1468, marking Songhai's supplanting of Mali as the dominant West African power.

w4-700435.name: Partition of the Chagatai Khanate / Moghulistan and the rise of Yarkand (Eastern Turkestan) under Yunus Khan
w4-700435.blurb: The eastern Chagatai successor state, Moghulistan, fragmented in the mid-15th century, with the Tarim Basin oases (around 83.2E, 40.3N) coalescing into a distinct Eastern Turkestan / Altishahr polity. The vast transfer (over 1 million km2) reflects the data model splitting the old Chagatai/Moghul realm into Moghulistan proper and the settled Eastern Turkestan domains under rulers descending from Esen Buqa II and Yunus Khan.

w4-700439.name: Ottoman annexation of the Beylik of Isfendiyar (Candaroğlu) and capture of Sinop
w4-700439.blurb: In 1461 Sultan Mehmed II annexed the Jandarid (Isfendiyaroğlu/Candar) beylik of Kastamonu and Sinop on the Black Sea coast (around 34.2E, 41.1N), as part of the same campaign that conquered the Empire of Trebizond. The last emir, İsmail Bey, surrendered Sinop without a fight, ending the independent Beylik of Isfendiyar.

w4-700442.name: Foundation of the Kazakh Khanate by Janibek and Kerei
w4-700442.blurb: Around 1465–1466 the sultans Janibek and Kerei broke away from Abu'l-Khayr Khan's Uzbek confederation and migrated into the lands of Moghulistan in Semirechye (the Zhetysu, around 73.4E, 44N), where the Moghul khan Esen Buqa II granted them refuge. This founding of the Kazakh Khanate transferred the steppe territory from Moghulistan's orbit to the new Kazakh polity.

w4-700446.name: Battle of Paravani — Samtskhe-Saatabago separates from Kartli
w4-700446.blurb: In 1465 Qvarqvare II Jaqeli, Atabeg of Samtskhe, defeated and captured Georgian King George VIII at Paravani Lake, triggering the collapse of the unified monarchy. Samtskhe separated from Kartli as an independent principality within the 1465-1468 window. Well attested.

w4-700447.name: Georgian civil war – Kartli under Bagrat VI (c. 1466–1468)
w4-700447.blurb: During the Georgian civil war (1463–1490), Bagrat VI briefly consolidated rule over both eastern (Kartli) and western Georgia in the mid-1460s before renewed challenges. The coordinates are the Kartli/Tbilisi region; the recorded Kartli → Georgia change reflects the oscillation of Kartli between unified-Georgia and separate-Kartli polity labels in this period.

citations.label: Collapse of the Georgian realm – Wikipedia

w4-700448.name: Formation of the Astrakhan Khanate from the disintegrating Golden Horde (c. 1466)
w4-700448.blurb: As the Golden Horde (Great Horde) fragmented throughout the 15th century, Mahmud bin Küchük Muhammad, based at Astrakhan on the lower Volga, established what became the Astrakhan Khanate around 1465–1466. After his defeat by the Crimean Khan Hajji Giray in 1465, Mahmud's descendants consolidated a separate khanate at Astrakhan, and the territory around the lower Volga effectively separated from the Great Horde.

citations.label: List of khans of the Golden Horde – Wikipedia

w4-700451.name: Georgian Civil War - Mingrelia Elevated to Autonomous Principality
w4-700451.blurb: The Georgian civil war of 1463-1490 fragmented the unified Kingdom of Georgia. After Bagrat of Imereti defeated King George VIII at the Battle of Chikhori (1463) and was crowned king of western Georgia, he rewarded his allies - including Liparit I of Mingrelia - by elevating them to the rank of mtavari (prince), creating semi-independent principalities. The coordinates are the Mingrelia/Kolkheti coast, consistent with territory shifting from Kartli's nominal control to autonomous Mingrelian governance in the 1465-1468 window.

w4-700453.name: Molon Khan's accession and Eastern Mongol reassertion over Oirat-held territory (1465–1466)
w4-700453.blurb: Following the decline of Oirat power after Esen Taishi's death in 1454, Molon Khan (Tögüs Mengke) of the Borjigin line became Khagan of the Northern Yuan in 1465, briefly reasserting Eastern Mongol authority over territories the Four Oirats had dominated. Molon Khan was assassinated by warring Mongol nobles in 1466, leaving a roughly decade-long interregnum before Manduul Khan was crowned in 1475. The Cliopatria dataset's transfer of this large Mongolian territory from 'Four Oirats' to 'Mongol Khanate' across [1465,1468] most plausibly reflects this brief Borjigin reassertion, though detailed sourcing for the precise 1465–1468 territorial change is sparse.

w4-700455.name: Fall of the Marinid Sultanate and rise of the Wattasid dynasty
w4-700455.blurb: In April 1465 the last Marinid sultan Abd al-Haqq II was overthrown and killed in a Fez revolt; after a Sharifian interregnum the Wattasids consolidated power as independent sultans by 1472. The Marinid-to-Wattasid transition (31.9N) is within the window (1465-1468).

w4-700461.name: Lê dynasty conquest of Champa (1471); Cham contraction and refugee absorption
w4-700461.blurb: In 1471, Emperor Lê Thánh Tông of Đại Việt invaded Champa, sacking Vijaya and reducing Champa to a rump state, with many Cham refugees fleeing toward Cambodia. As Champa contracted, the Khmer kingdom absorbed Cham populations and influence in former buffer zones during this period. The worklist transfer Champa → Khmer Empire at lng 108.1, lat 12.3 (south-central Vietnam highlands) in the 1468–1475 window reflects this contraction; the coding is approximate but tied to a real, correctly dated collapse of Cham power.

w4-700463.name: Charles the Bold of Burgundy conquers Duchy of Lorraine
w4-700463.blurb: After years of conflict with Duke René II of Lorraine, Charles the Bold of Burgundy captured Nancy in November 1475 and occupied the duchy; he was killed at the Battle of Nancy in January 1477, ending Burgundian control, but within the window 1468–1475 this change reflects his conquest.

w4-700466.name: Inca conquest of the Chimú Empire by Topa Inca Yupanqui (c. 1470)
w4-700466.blurb: Around 1470 the Inca prince Topa Inca Yupanqui conquered the Chimú Empire (Chimor), the last major Andean kingdom able to resist Inca expansion. Emperor Minchançaman was taken to Cuzco and Chan Chan fell under Inca rule. The coordinates (~78°W, ~7.5°S) match the northern Peruvian coast; from=Chimu, to=Inca matches the 1468-1475 window.

w4-700468.name: Champa–Đại Việt War (1471) — Fall of Vijaya
w4-700468.blurb: In January-March 1471 Lê Thánh Tông of Đại Việt invaded Champa, stormed the Cham capital Vijaya (near modern Bình Định, lat 13.9, lng 108.4) in early March, killed King Trà Toàn, and razed the city. The Lê Dynasty annexed the northern Cham territories, ending Champa as a significant state. Window 1468-1475.

w4-700469.name: Yunus Khan seizes Aksu and reasserts Moghulistan over East Turkestan (c. 1468–1475)
w4-700469.blurb: After Dost Muhammad Khan of eastern Moghulistan died of illness in 1468/1469, Yunus Khan (backed by the Timurids) immediately seized the oasis city of Aksu and drove out Dost Muhammad's young heir, consolidating control over western Moghulistan and the Tarim oases. The dataset reflects expansion of 'Moghulistan' over former 'East Turkestan' territory in the 1468–1475 window.

w4-700471.name: Songhai conquest of Timbuktu and Djenné from Mali Empire
w4-700471.blurb: Sunni Ali of Songhai seized Timbuktu in 1468 after its leaders requested help against the occupying Tuareg, then besieged and captured Djenné around 1473–1475. These conquests transferred the key trans-Saharan trade cities from Mali's residual control to the expanding Songhai Empire,

w4-700475.name: Swedish (Kalmar Union) encroachment into Novgorodian Karelia; Olavinlinna founded (1475)
w4-700475.blurb: In 1475 Sweden, then part of the Kalmar Union, built Olavinlinna (Olofsborg) castle on the Novgorodian side of the 1323 Treaty of Nöteborg border in eastern Finnish Karelia (matching the coordinate lng 29, lat 62.8). Novgorod regarded this as a breach of the border, and the move asserted Kalmar-Union/Swedish control over contested Novgorodian frontier territory. This frontier encroachment supports a Novgorod → Kalmar Union shift at this location, though it was a fortified push rather than a formal cession.

w4-700476.name: Kingdom of Sweden reintegrated into Kalmar Union after Karl Knutsson's final deposition
w4-700476.blurb: Karl Knutsson (Charles VIII of Sweden) died in May 1470 after his third reign as Swedish king. The following year, Danish King Christian I attempted to reassert direct Kalmar Union control over Sweden but was defeated at the Battle of Brunkeberg (1471) by Swedish regent Sten Sture the Elder. Sweden was thus under a Swedish regent nominally within the Kalmar Union framework. The 1468–1475 window captures this turbulent period of reintegration.

w4-700477.name: Foundation of the Kazakh Khanate and Death of Abulkhair Khan
w4-700477.blurb: The Kazakh Khanate was founded around 1465 when sultans Janibek and Kerei broke from Abulkhair Khan's Uzbek Khanate. In 1468 Abulkhair Khan was killed during a campaign against the Kazakh rebels, collapsing Uzbek control over the Syr Darya basin and the Central Asian steppe north of the Timurid Empire. The Kazakhs expanded rapidly to fill this power vacuum across the period 1468-1475 as the Timurid realm contracted.

w4-700479.name: County of Périgord inherited by House of Albret (Count of Foix)
w4-700479.blurb: The death of Francis Phoebus, Count of Foix and King of Navarre, in January 1483 without male heirs passed his titles to his sister Catherine de Foix, who married Jean d'Albret on 27 March 1484. The House of Albret thereby unified Foix and Navarre with existing Albret holdings including Périgord (lat 45.1, lng 0.9), which had been acquired by the Albrets in 1470 through Françoise de Périgord.

w4-700482.name: Prome Kingdom breaks from Ava
w4-700482.blurb: Following the death of the governor of Prome (Mingyi Swa) in 1482, Governor Thado Minsaw seized the city and declared independence from the weakening Kingdom of Ava, which was consumed by the Yamethin rebellion and Shan incursions. Ava dispatched an army but failed to retake Prome, and the breakaway kingdom (lat 18.6, lng 95.7) survived as an independent state for six decades before falling to the Toungoo Empire in 1542.

w4-700483.name: Inca conquest of the Chimú Empire under Tupac Inca Yupanqui (c. 1470–1476)
w4-700483.blurb: Tupac Inca Yupanqui (Topa Inca) led the Inca armies northward against the Chimú Empire (Chimor) in the 1470s, defeating the last Chimú emperor Minchançaman, reportedly by cutting off Chan Chan's water supply. Minchançaman was taken to Cuzco and Chimú territory along the northern Peruvian coast (near lng -79.2, lat -7.3) was incorporated into Tawantinsuyu (Chimú Empire -> Inca Empire), matching the [1475,1482] window.

w4-700485.name: Ottoman conquest of Herzegovina (final phase, 1481–1482)
w4-700485.blurb: After the Ottoman conquest of the Kingdom of Bosnia (1463), the Duchy of Saint Sava (Herzegovina) under the Kosača continued as an Ottoman vassal. Ottoman forces progressively took its fortresses; the last fell in 1481–1482, when Vlatko Hercegović was expelled, completing the absorption of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian lands. This matches the Kingdom of Bosnia→Ottoman transfer at (18°E, 43.1°N) in the 1475–1482 window.

citations.label: Ottoman conquest of Bosnia and Herzegovina – Wikipedia

w4-700486.name: Ottoman conquest of Albania after the League of Lezhë
w4-700486.blurb: Following Skanderbeg's death in 1468, the League of Lezhë fragmented under sustained Ottoman pressure. The Ottomans captured Krujë in 1478 and Shkodër in 1479, at which point Venice ceded the Albanian coastal towns by treaty and Albanian resistance collapsed. By 1482 even the last holdouts had submitted, ending over three decades of Albanian resistance and incorporating Albanian territories (lat 41.5, lng 20.1) into the Ottoman Empire.

w4-700492.name: Kazakh Khanate steppe expansion amid Sibir dynastic turmoil (c. 1475–1482)
w4-700492.blurb: In the late 1470s–early 1480s the Kazakh Khanate (under descendants of Janibek and Girey) expanded into forest-steppe zones, while the Shaybanid Ibak Khan killed the Taibugid ruler Mar of Sibir (between 1464 and 1480) and seized Chimgi-Tura, creating overlapping claims over poorly-defined steppe. The dataset's large 'Khanate of Sibir' → 'Kazakh Khanate' transfer (window 1475–1482) reflects this dynastic turmoil rather than a single treaty or battle; the boundaries are loosely defined.

w4-700497.name: County of Maine reverts to the French crown on death of Charles IV of Anjou
w4-700497.blurb: Charles IV of Anjou, Count of Maine, died on 10 December 1481 without legitimate heirs, bequeathing Maine, Anjou, and Provence to his cousin King Louis XI of France. Maine was formally incorporated into the French royal domain in 1482, ending the last quasi-independent Angevin holding. The data window 1475-1482 captures this reversion to the Kingdom of France.

citations.label: Charles IV, Count of Maine – Wikipedia

w4-700498.name: Kazakh Khanate expansion against the Khanate of Sibir in the 1480s
w4-700498.blurb: In the 1480s, after the Golden Horde's breakup, the Kazakh Khanate under Kerey and Janibek expanded into the forest-steppe of the Irtysh/Ishim/Tobol basin contested with the Khanate of Sibir. The Sibir-to-Kazakh transition (73.4E, 52.1N) plausibly records such a frontier gain; date set within the window (1482-1487).

w4-700502.name: Death of Mary of Burgundy; Burgundian Netherlands pass to Habsburg rule under Maximilian I
w4-700502.blurb: Mary of Burgundy died on 27 March 1482 after a fall from her horse, and her Burgundian inheritance — including Flanders, Brabant, Holland, and other Low Country territories — passed to her infant son Philip the Handsome under the regency of her husband Maximilian I of Habsburg. This transition began Habsburg rule over the Burgundian Netherlands. The worklist coordinates lie in the Low Countries, and the House of Habsburg → Habsburg Monarchy coding reflects the consolidation of these lands under Habsburg authority across the 1480s.

w4-700504.name: Darbazi partition of the Kingdom of Georgia (1490)
w4-700504.blurb: In 1490, after decades of civil war (1463–1490), King Constantine II and the royal Darbazi council formally recognized the division of the Kingdom of Georgia into the kingdoms of Kartli, Kakheti, and Imereti (plus the principality of Samtskhe). Constantine retained Kartli, centred on Tbilisi, matching the recorded Georgia → Kartli transfer.

citations.label: Collapse of the Georgian realm – Wikipedia

w4-700506.name: War of the Hungarian Succession — Maximilian I seizes Austrian territories from Hungary
w4-700506.blurb: On the death of Matthias Corvinus in April 1490, the Habsburg Archduke Maximilian I immediately invaded and recaptured the Austrian territories (including Vienna and Styria, lat 47.7, lng 15.1) that Matthias had conquered. The Hungarian nobility then elected Vladislaus II of Bohemia as king; the Peace of Pressburg (1491) formalised Habsburg succession rights to Hungary and confirmed their territorial recovery. The dataset records Austria-area territory transferring from the Kingdom of Hungary to the House of Habsburg.

citations.label: War of the Hungarian Succession – Wikipedia
Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor – Wikipedia

w4-700509.name: Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk founds the Berar Sultanate (1490)
w4-700509.blurb: As the Bahmani Sultanate disintegrated after the execution of Mahmud Gawan (1481), provincial governors declared independence in succession. Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, governor of Berar (centred on Ellichpur/Achalpur, near lng 78.2, lat 20.1), proclaimed the independent Imad Shahi dynasty in 1490, one of the five Deccan Sultanates (Bahmani Sultanate -> Berar Sultanate), matching the [1490,1492] window.

w4-700510.name: Marriage of Anne of Brittany to Charles VIII of France
w4-700510.blurb: After French military pressure dissolved Anne of Brittany's proxy marriage to Maximilian I, she married King Charles VIII of France at Langeais on 6 December 1491, with papal validation in February 1492. Charles became Duke of Brittany jure uxoris and imposed a Royal Governor. The from=Duchy of Brittany / to=Kingdom of France and 1490-1492 window match this first step toward Brittany's annexation (Edict of Union 1532).

citations.label: Union of the Duchy of Brittany with the Crown of France - Wikipedia

w4-700512.name: Reversion of the Bohemian crown lands (Moravia, Silesia) to Vladislaus II of Bohemia after the death of Matthias Corvinus (1490)
w4-700512.blurb: Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary, had conquered the Bohemian crown lands of Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia in the 1470s and held them until his death on 6 April 1490. Upon his death these lands reverted to Vladislaus II, King of Bohemia, who was then also elected King of Hungary on 15 July 1490, reuniting the Bohemian crown lands under the Bohemian crown. The Peace of Pressburg (7 November 1491) settled the residual Habsburg claims. The coordinates lie in Moravia/Bohemia, matching the Kingdom of Hungary -> Kingdom of Bohemia transition: the formerly Hungarian-held Bohemian lands returning to Bohemia.

w4-700513.name: Founding of the Sultanate of Bijapur
w4-700513.blurb: Yusuf Adil Shah, governor of Bijapur (coords 75.4E/16.7N) under the weakening Bahmani Sultanate, declared de facto independence in 1490, founding the Adil Shahi dynasty — one of several tarafdars to break away simultaneously (Ahmadnagar did likewise). The Bahmani Sultanate formally collapsed by 1518.

w4-700516.name: Division of Moghulistan after the death of Yunus Khan
w4-700516.blurb: Yunus Khan of Moghulistan died in 1487 and his realm split between his sons: Sultan Mahmud held the Tashkent area while Sultan Ahmad controlled the eastern steppe (Turpan, Aksu, Kucha). By c. 1490-92 the unified entity had dissolved into rival successor polities historians label 'Eastern Chagatai Khanate'. From 'Moghulistan' to 'Eastern Chagatai Khanate'; window py=1490, y=1492 fits.

w4-700517.name: Foundation of the Bidar Sultanate by Qasim Barid I
w4-700517.blurb: The Bahmani Sultanate fragmented after the execution of minister Mahmud Gawan in 1481. By 1490 Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, and Berar had declared independence; in c. 1492 Qasim Barid I, the powerful Bahmani prime minister, established the Bidar (Barid Shahi) Sultanate as a fifth successor state centred on Bidar. He seized de facto control of the rump Bahmani state, placing the last sultans under his guardianship and absorbing their remaining revenues and territory.

w4-700519.name: Muhammad Shaybani's campaigns against the Kazakh Khanate
w4-700519.blurb: In the mid-1490s, Muhammad Shaybani Khan conducted campaigns pushing the Kazakh Khanate northward off their winter pastures and grazing lands in the Syr Darya basin (centroid lng 66, lat 40.2). Shaybani temporarily seized Timurid-held Transoxiana including areas the Kazakhs had occupied, before his own conquests of Samarkand (1500) reshaped the regional order.

w4-700520.name: County of Armagnac reverts to France on death of Charles of Armagnac
w4-700520.blurb: Charles of Armagnac, the last count, died in December 1497 without legitimate heirs, and the County of Armagnac was united to the French crown under Charles VIII. This culminated decades of royal pressure on the house of Armagnac following the death of Count John V (1473) and Charles's imprisonment. The data window 1492-1497 captures this reversion to the Kingdom of France.

citations.label: Charles IV, Count of Maine – Wikipedia

w4-700522.name: Muscovite–Lithuanian War and Treaty of 1494
w4-700522.blurb: Ivan III of Moscow launched military operations against Lithuania in 1492–1494, capturing principalities in the upper Oka basin including Vyazma. A peace treaty signed on 5 February 1494 formalized these gains, with Lithuania ceding the Principality of Vyazma and surrounding territory. A second war (1500–1503) further expanded Muscovite gains, transferring Chernigov, Novgorod-Seversk, and other areas — collectively about a third of Lithuanian territory.

w4-700524.name: Battle of Sharur – Ismail I defeats the Aq Qoyunlu and founds the Safavid dynasty (1501)
w4-700524.blurb: On 17 July 1501, Ismail I's Qizilbash forces defeated the Aq Qoyunlu under Sultan Alvand at the Battle of Sharur, near the Aras River in modern Azerbaijan. Ismail then captured Tabriz and proclaimed himself Shah of Iran, founding the Safavid dynasty. Over the next few years (to 1502 and beyond) the Safavids eliminated remaining Aq Qoyunlu resistance and absorbed their territory in Azerbaijan, Iran, and Iraq.

w4-700526.name: French conquest of Naples during the Italian Wars (1501)
w4-700526.blurb: The Treaty of Granada (November 1500) between Louis XII of France and Ferdinand of Aragon secretly partitioned the Kingdom of Naples. France occupied the northern half (Naples, Abruzzo, Terra di Lavoro) in 1501, giving it territorial control of the area around lng 15.7, lat 40.4 (Kingdom of Naples -> Kingdom of France). Disputes over the unassigned central provinces sparked war in 1502; Spanish forces under Gonzalo de Córdoba later expelled the French by 1504, but the data window [1497,1502] captures the French takeover.

w4-700527.name: Muhammad Shaybani's conquest of Transoxiana
w4-700527.blurb: Muhammad Shaybani Khan led the Uzbek Shaybanids in a series of campaigns that expelled the Timurids from Transoxiana, capturing Samarkand and Bukhara by 1500–1501. The Kazakh Khanate lost territory in the Syr Darya region as Shaybani pushed them back while consolidating control over the settled agricultural lands of modern Uzbekistan.

w4-700529.name: Muhammad Shaybani's Conquest of Timurid Transoxiana
w4-700529.blurb: Muhammad Shaybani Khan led Uzbek forces across the Syr Darya and captured Samarkand from the Timurids in 1500, consolidating Bukhara and the rest of Transoxiana by 1501. The coordinates (~68E 40N, Transoxiana) are the heart of the former Timurid realm. Babur's attempts to reclaim Samarkand failed and the Shaybanids replaced Timurid rule. Correctly dated within the 1497-1502 window.

w4-700531.name: Toungoo Expansion amid Ava's Succession Crisis (c. 1497–1502)
w4-700531.blurb: Mingyi Nyo of Toungoo conquered the Pyinmana area near Toungoo in the 1490s and, exploiting Ava's severe 1501–1503 succession crisis (the death of Minkhaung II and accession of Narapati II amid Shan pressure), expanded into contested Upper Burma territory. By 1502 Mingyi Nyo had decided to break away from Ava, spurning Narapati's offer of the Kyaukse granary. Though formal independence came in 1510, Toungoo absorbed Ava-administered lands in this 1497–1502 window.

w4-700533.name: Portuguese First Contact with Ceylon and Establishment of Trade Presence
w4-700533.blurb: In 1505, Lourenço de Almeida's fleet was blown off course to the southwest coast of Ceylon (Sri Lanka), making the first Portuguese contact with the island and the Kingdom of Kotte. The Portuguese concluded a trade agreement and were later permitted to build a fort at Colombo (1518). The 1502–1507 window reflects Portugal's initial presence on the island, though formal Portuguese Ceylon dates from the early 16th-century fort-building phase rather than from territory seized by conquest.

w4-700534.name: Funj Sultanate conquest of Alodia
w4-700534.blurb: Around 1504-1505, the Christian Nubian kingdom of Alodia (Alwa), with its capital at Soba on the Blue Nile, was destroyed by a combination of Arab tribal forces under Abdallah Jammah and the emerging Funj people under Amara Dunqas. The Funj Sultanate of Sennar was founded circa 1504 and absorbed Alodia's territory along the Nile. The exact sequence and relative roles of the Arabs and Funj remain debated, but the territorial transition occurred in this narrow window.

w4-700536.name: Muhammad Shaybani's conquest of the Timurid Empire (1499–1507)
w4-700536.blurb: Muhammad Shaybani Khan of the Uzbek Shaybanids conquered Transoxiana from 1499, capturing Samarkand and Bukhara in 1500 and Herat (the last major Timurid capital) in 1507, ending Timurid rule and establishing the Khanate of Bukhara. The dataset records the Timurid Empire → Shaybanids transfer in the 1502–1507 window.

w4-700538.name: Portuguese establishment of Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gué (Agadir fortress) and expansion along Moroccan Atlantic coast
w4-700538.blurb: Portugal built the fortress of Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gué (Agadir) in 1505 and brought Safi under Portuguese influence by 1508, extending Portuguese Africa's coastal foothold in Morocco at the expense of the Wattasid sultanate. The centroid at -7.3°, 34° corresponds to the Safi/Azemmour littoral where Portugal established these fortified trading posts.

w4-700542.name: Death of Philip I (the Handsome) and appointment of Margaret of Austria as regent of the Low Countries (1506–1507)
w4-700542.blurb: Philip I 'the Handsome', Duke of Burgundy and Habsburg ruler of the Low Countries, died suddenly on 25 September 1506, leaving his six-year-old son Charles (the future Charles V) as nominal heir. Maximilian I appointed his daughter Margaret of Austria as regent in April 1507 after a brief interregnum. The shift from 'Habsburg Monarchy' to 'House of Habsburg' in the data likely reflects this transfer from Philip's personal composite administration to a broader dynastic regency arrangement centered at the Low Countries.

w4-700543.name: Muscovite–Lithuanian War – truce of 1503 cedes a third of Lithuania to Moscow
w4-700543.blurb: The Muscovite–Lithuanian War (1500–1503) ended with a six-year truce in 1503 in which the Jagiellonian Grand Duchy of Lithuania ceded roughly one-third of its territory—including key towns of the upper Dnieper and Oka regions—to the Grand Principality of Moscow. When Sigismund I Jagiellon became Grand Duke in 1506–1507, he immediately sought to reverse these losses, but the territorial shift established by the truce persisted.

w4-700544.name: Babur's Conquest of Kabul (including Kapisa)
w4-700544.blurb: In October 1504, Babur — the last Timurid ruler, driven from Central Asia by the Uzbek Muhammad Shaybani — crossed the Hindu Kush and captured Kabul from the Arghun chieftain Mukim Beg, encompassing the Kapisa region (coords 69.6E/35.1N) north of Kabul. He assumed the title padshah of the Timurid line, consistent with the 'to=Timurid Empire' label, and used Kabul as the base from which he later founded the Mughal Empire.

w4-700545.name: Foundation of the Khanate of Khiva (Arabshahid dynasty)
w4-700545.blurb: After Muhammad Shaybani Khan was killed by Shah Ismail I of the Safavids at Merv in December 1510, Safavid forces briefly occupied Khorezm. In 1511, the Safavid garrison was expelled and Ilbars I, of the Arabshahid branch of the Shaybanids, established himself as the first Khan of the independent Khanate of Khiva (Khorezm). This territory thus separated permanently from the Shaybanid main body and became the long-lived Khanate of Khiva.

w4-700547.name: Collapse of western Moghulistan under Shaybani Uzbek pressure (1503-1508)
w4-700547.blurb: Muhammad Shaybani Khan defeated the Moghul khans Mahmud and Ahmad Alaq at the Battle of Akhsi, forcing the surrender of Tashkent and Shahrukhiya; Ahmad Alaq died soon after and Mahmud Khan was executed by Shaybani near Khujand in 1508. This ended Chagatayid power in the west and left the eastern remnant (Turpan/Uyghuristan) under Mansur Khan. The dataset's Eastern Chagatai Khanate -> Moghulistan transition reflects the reassertion of the rump Moghul identity over the eastern remnant within the 1507-1512 window. (Eastern Chagatai Khanate and Moghulistan are largely synonymous, so this is partly a relabeling.)

w4-700548.name: Vasily III's annexation of the Pskov Republic (1510)
w4-700548.blurb: In January 1510, Grand Prince Vasily III of Moscow pressured the Pskov Republic into dissolving its ancient veche (democratic assembly) and submitting to Muscovite rule, declaring Pskov his hereditary domain (votchina). The veche bell was removed and transported to Moscow on 13 January 1510, symbolizing the end of Pskov's autonomy. Around 300 wealthy Pskovian families were deported and their estates redistributed to Muscovite servitors.

w4-700549.name: Babur's recovery of Samarkand (brief Timurid restoration)
w4-700549.blurb: After Shah Ismail I killed Muhammad Shaybani at the Battle of Merv in 1510, the Timurid prince Babur, allied with the Safavids, recaptured Samarkand and Farghana in October 1511, a momentary Timurid restoration in Transoxiana. At the Battle of Ghijduvan (Dec 1512) the Shaybanids retook the region. The transition Shaybanids -> Timurid Empire (1507-1512) reflects this Baburi reconquest.

w4-700551.name: Battle of Merv; Safavid conquest of Khorasan
w4-700551.blurb: On 2 December 1510, Shah Ismail I of the Safavid dynasty defeated and killed the Shaybanid khan Muhammad Shaybani at the Battle of Merv (Marv). The Safavids absorbed the province of Khorasan, including Herat and Merv, from the Shaybanids, matching the worklist transition Shaybanids -> Safavid Dynasty (1507-1512) in eastern Iran.

w4-700553.name: Vasily III captures Smolensk from Lithuania (1514)
w4-700553.blurb: Grand Prince Vasily III of Moscow captured the strategically vital city of Smolensk from the Grand Duchy of Lithuania on 31 July 1514, after two earlier failed sieges in 1512–1513. Although Muscovy was defeated at the Battle of Orsha in September 1514, it retained Smolensk; a 1522 truce confirmed Russian control, ending Lithuanian (Jagiellon) suzerainty over the city and surrounding region.

w4-700554.name: Death of Ferdinand II and Accession of Charles I — Birth of the Spanish Empire
w4-700554.blurb: Ferdinand II of Aragon died on January 23, 1516, and his grandson Charles was proclaimed King of Castile and Aragon jointly with his mother Joanna on March 14, 1516. Charles's inheritance of Castile (with the Americas), Aragon, the Netherlands, and later the Holy Roman Empire (1519) transformed the Crown of Castile into the core of the Spanish Empire. Coordinates (−32.5, 22.4) suggest Atlantic/Canary-adjacent territory under this merged structure; the [py=1512, y=1516] window brackets the accession.

citations.label: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor – Wikipedia

w4-700555.name: Mongol recovery of steppe territory from the Ming under Dayan Khan
w4-700555.blurb: In the early 16th century Dayan Khan reunited the eastern Mongols and reasserted pastoral control over the Inner Mongolian frontier (coordinates 118.2E, 43N) as the Ming retreated behind the Great Wall. The Ming-to-Mongol Khanate transition is within the window (1512-1516).

citations.label: Ming dynasty in Inner Asia – Wikipedia

w4-700556.name: Charles I Inherits Spain and the Burgundian Netherlands
w4-700556.blurb: On the death of Ferdinand II on 23 January 1516, the Crown of Aragon — Aragon proper, Catalonia, Valencia, and the Aragonese Mediterranean realms of Naples, Sicily, and Sardinia — passed to his grandson Charles of Habsburg, who ruled jointly with his mother Joanna. United in personal union with Castile under a single sovereign, the Aragonese territories were thereafter administered as part of the composite monarchy that contemporaries began to call the Kingdom of Spain.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor

w4-700557.name: Death of Ferdinand II and accession of Charles I — unification of the Spanish Crown
w4-700557.blurb: Ferdinand II of Aragon died on 23 January 1516, leaving his grandson Charles I (later Holy Roman Emperor Charles V) as sole ruler of Castile and Aragon. This personal union created the composite Kingdom of Spain, with Castile's territories formally passing under the new crown.

w4-700558.name: Spanish conquest of Upper Navarre
w4-700558.blurb: Ferdinand II dispatched the Duke of Alba into Navarre on 19 July 1512; Pamplona surrendered within days and the whole of Upper (Iberian) Navarre was occupied. The Navarrese Parliament accepted Ferdinand as king in 1513, and Navarre was formally incorporated into Castile in 1515.

w4-700559.name: Spanish conquest of the Kingdom of Navarre (1512)
w4-700559.blurb: In July 1512 Ferdinand II of Aragon invaded the Kingdom of Navarre; Spanish forces captured Pamplona and most of Iberian Navarre, which was annexed to Castile by 1515. From=Kingdom of Navarre, to=Kingdom of Spain matches the 1512-1516 window.

citations.label: Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre – Wikipedia

w4-700560.name: Mamluk conquest of the Tahirid Sultanate of Yemen
w4-700560.blurb: The Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt sent a naval expedition under Husain al-Kurdi to Yemen in 1515–1516. After defeating the Tahirid sultan Az-Zafir, al-Kurdi captured the treasury and beheaded the sultan near Sana'a on 15 May 1516; the Tahirid realm fell to the Mamluks. Matches the Tahirid Sultanate → Mamluk Sultanate transfer in the 1512-1516 window.

w4-700561.name: Shaybanid recovery of Transoxiana; Battle of Ghijduvan
w4-700561.blurb: After briefly losing Transoxiana to the Timurid-Safavid coalition in 1511, the Shaybanids under Ubaydullah Khan decisively defeated the coalition at the Battle of Ghijduvan on 12 November 1512. Babur was expelled and Transoxiana came permanently under Shaybanid control, forming the basis of the Khanate of Bukhara. Matches worklist transition Timurid Empire -> Khanate of Bukhara (1512-1516).

w4-700566.name: Battle of Chaldiran – Ottoman conquest of eastern Anatolia
w4-700566.blurb: On 23 August 1514, Sultan Selim I decisively defeated Shah Ismail I of the Safavids at the Battle of Chaldiran in eastern Anatolia. The Ottomans sacked Tabriz and permanently annexed Eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia from Safavid control. The dataset window (Safavid Dynasty -> Ottoman Empire, py1512/y1516) at lng41.4/lat39.8 (eastern Anatolia) encompasses the battle and subsequent consolidation.
