w4-700567.name: Accession of Charles I of Spain
w4-700567.blurb: When Ferdinand II of Aragon died in January 1516, his Habsburg grandson Charles inherited both Castile and Aragon, ruling as Charles I. The accession brought the Spanish realms under the House of Habsburg, binding them into the wider dynastic monarchy that would also encompass the Burgundian Low Countries and, after 1519, the Holy Roman Empire under Charles V.

w4-700569.name: Final Division of Moghulistan into Turpan and Yarkent Khanates
w4-700569.blurb: Around 1514-1516 the last unified Moghulistan was permanently split between two Chagatayid brothers: Mansur Khan held the Turpan (eastern) khanate and Sultan Said Khan founded the Yarkent (western) khanate at Kashgar. By 1519 the steppe of Moghulistan proper (~85E 43N, Ili valley) was absorbed by Kazakh and Kyrgyz tribes. The dataset records this as a transfer to a successor 'Mongol Khanate' designation, within the 1516-1519 window.

w4-700573.name: Golconda Sultanate consolidation of Telangana from Bidar
w4-700573.blurb: In 1518 Quli Qutb Shah established the effectively independent Golconda Sultanate, breaking from the disintegrating Bahmani Sultanate and consolidating control over Telangana (lat 18.4, lng 79.2). The Bidar Sultanate (Barid Shahis), the smallest Deccan successor, lost effective control of the eastern Telangana zone to Golconda during this period. Window 1516-1519.

w4-700575.name: Charles I of Spain elected Holy Roman Emperor (Charles V)
w4-700575.blurb: Charles, already King of Spain (from 1516) and holder of the Burgundian inheritance including the Low Countries and Franche-Comte (5.5E, 47N), was elected Holy Roman Emperor as Charles V on 28 June 1519 following Maximilian I's death, also inheriting the Austrian Habsburg lands. This united the Spanish Crown, the Burgundian territories, and the Austrian lands in a single Habsburg personal union; the worklist's Spain-to-Habsburg-Monarchy coding reflects this 1519 consolidation.

citations.label: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor - Wikipedia

w4-700578.name: Muscovite capture of Smolensk (Muscovite–Lithuanian War)
w4-700578.blurb: During the fourth Muscovite–Lithuanian War (1512–1520), Grand Prince Vasili III of Moscow besieged Smolensk three times before the city capitulated in late July 1514, annexing it from the Jagiellonian-ruled Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Although the Lithuanians won a major counter-victory at the Battle of Orsha on 8 September 1514, they could not retake Smolensk, and the 1522 truce confirmed Muscovite possession.

w4-700579.name: Permanent division of Moghulistan — Sultan Said Khan conquers Kashgar (1514), peace 1516
w4-700579.blurb: In 1514 Said Khan conquered Kashgar, Yarkand, and Khotan from the Dughlat ruler Abu Bakr, establishing himself in the western Tarim Basin. A 1516 peace divided Moghulistan: Said Khan ruled from Kashgar (Yarkent Khanate) while his brother Mansur Khan ruled from Turfan (Eastern Moghulistan/Turpan Khanate). The dataset records this split as the 1516–1519 window.

w4-700581.name: Division of Moghulistan between Mansur Khan and Said Khan (1516)
w4-700581.blurb: In 1516 Mansur Khan (ruling Turpan/eastern Moghulistan) and his brother Said Khan reached a peace agreement that formalized the permanent division of Moghulistan. Said Khan had conquered Kashgar, Yarkand and Khotan in 1514, founding the Yarkent Khanate (Western Moghulistan), and nominally submitted to Mansur. The split into eastern (Turpan) and western (Yarkent) khanates proved permanent. The from->to (Moghulistan -> Western Moghulistan) matches this division within the 1516-1519 window.

w4-700582.name: Foundation of the Khanate of Khiva after Shaybani's death
w4-700582.blurb: After Muhammad Shaybani (khan of the Uzbek/Bukhara khanate) was killed by the Safavids at the Battle of Merv in 1510, the Safavid garrison in Khwarazm was expelled in 1511 by Ilbars I, who founded the Arabshahid dynasty and the Khanate of Khiva. The Khwarazm region near 62.1E, 42.9N thus broke away and became the independent Khanate of Khiva.

w4-700583.name: Foundation of the Sultanate of Maguindanao
w4-700583.blurb: The Sultanate of Maguindanao emerged in Mindanao around 1515-1521 as Sharif Kabungsuwan, a Muslim missionary from the Ba'Alawi sada of Johor, introduced Islam to the Cotabato Valley and married into local chiefly families. This coincided with the twilight of Brunei's influence over Mindanao; by the time of Magellan's 1521 expedition, Maguindanao was consolidating its own distinct Islamic sultanate separate from Brunei's sphere. The data change from Brunei to Maguindanao reflects this shift of suzerainty over coastal Mindanao during the 1519-1521 window.

w4-700584.name: Portuguese conquest of Bahrain – defeat of the Jabrid (Bahrani) dynasty (1521)
w4-700584.blurb: In 1521, a joint Portuguese–Hormuzi force under António Correia invaded Bahrain after the Jabrid king Muqrin ibn Zamil refused tribute to Hormuz, defeating and killing Muqrin and capturing Qal'at al-Bahrain. This began roughly 80 years of Portuguese control via Hormuzi governors. The worklist transfer Bahrani Dynasty → Kingdom of Portugal at lng 52.1, lat 26.5 (Bahrain) in the 1519–1521 window matches this conquest.

w4-700586.name: Early Golconda Sultanate expansion at expense of Vijayanagara
w4-700586.blurb: The Golconda Sultanate was established around 1518 by Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk, breaking from the Bahmani Sultanate. In the early 1520s the newly independent Golconda consolidated territories in the Krishna-Godavari delta contested with Vijayanagara. The worklist coordinates point to coastal Andhra, consistent with the Vijayanagara → Golconda border shift in the 1519–1521 window.

w4-700587.name: Vasily III annexes the Principality of Ryazan
w4-700587.blurb: In 1520 Vasily III summoned Grand Prince Ivan Ivanovich of Ryazan to Moscow and had him arrested; when Ivan fled to Lithuania in 1521, Vasily annexed the principality directly to Moscow. Ryazan (coord 39.5E/54.6N) was the last major autonomous Russian principality absorbed. The dataset's 1519–1521 'Ryazan → Grand Principality of Moscow' shift matches; event real and correctly dated.

w4-700588.name: Fall of Tenochtitlan
w4-700588.blurb: Hernán Cortés and a coalition of Spanish troops and Tlaxcalan and other indigenous allies completed an 80-day siege of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan; the last emperor Cuauhtémoc was captured on August 13, 1521, ending the Aztec Triple Alliance and transferring its ~205,000 km² heartland to Spanish imperial control. The victory opened the entire Valley of Mexico and surrounding territories to colonization under the newly proclaimed Captaincy General of New Spain.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

w4-700589.name: Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire - Fall of Tenochtitlan
w4-700589.blurb: Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico in 1519 and, with a large coalition of indigenous allies (especially Tlaxcalans) who resented Aztec domination, laid siege to Tenochtitlan from May to August 1521. The combined effects of the siege, smallpox epidemics, and the destruction of Aztec supply lines forced the surrender of Emperor Cuauhtemoc on 13 August 1521, ending the Aztec Triple Alliance and incorporating its territory into the Spanish Empire as New Spain.

citations.label: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire - Wikipedia

w4-700594.name: Kazakh Khanate Absorption of Western Moghulistan under Kasym Khan
w4-700594.blurb: Under Kasym Khan (r. c. 1511-1521) the Kazakh Khanate reached its greatest extent, pushing into northwestern Moghulistan including Taraz, Sairam, and Semirechye (~77E 44N). Moghulistan was simultaneously losing its steppe hinterland to Kazakh and Kyrgyz tribes; Kasym's death c. 1521 marks the peak before internal decline. The transfer of steppe territory falls within the 1519-1521 window.

w4-700597.name: County of Nevers passes to François de Clèves (1521)
w4-700597.blurb: On the death of Charles II of Nevers (10 August 1521), the County of Nevers passed by inheritance to his five-year-old son François de Clèves, of the Cleves-Nevers line, held under French royal suzerainty. Francis I of France erected Nevers into a duchy-peerage in 1539. The 1521 inheritance is a real, well-dated dynastic transition consolidating the county within the French realm.

citations.label: Francis I, Duke of Nevers – Wikipedia

w4-700600.name: Uzbek–Safavid Wars: Shaybanid conquest of eastern Khorasan
w4-700600.blurb: Following the death of Shah Ismail I and the accession of the young Tahmasp I in 1524, Uzbek Khan Ubayd Allah launched repeated invasions of Khorasan. In 1526 the Shaybanids captured Balkh and swept across eastern Khorasan, annexing it from the Safavids. This represents a high point of Khanate of Bukhara territorial gains in Khorasan during the Persian–Uzbek Wars,

w4-700601.name: Dissolution of the Kalmar Union — Swedish War of Independence
w4-700601.blurb: Gustav Vasa led a Swedish war of independence against the Danish-dominated Kalmar Union, sparked in large part by outrage at the Stockholm Bloodbath (November 1520) in which Danish King Christian II executed Swedish nobles. Gustav Vasa was crowned King of Sweden on 6 June 1523, ending the Kalmar Union. Denmark and Norway continued as a personal union (Denmark-Norway). The Treaty of Malmo (1524) formalized Denmark's renunciation of its claim to Sweden.

w4-700604.name: Swedish War of Liberation; Gustav Vasa elected King of Sweden
w4-700604.blurb: Following the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520, Gustav Vasa led a rebellion against Danish King Christian II of the Kalmar Union. On 6 June 1523 the Swedish riksdag at Strängnäs elected him King of Sweden, ending the Kalmar Union for Sweden; the Treaty of Malmö (1524) gave Danish recognition. Matches worklist transition Kalmar Union -> Kingdom of Sweden (1521-1526); coords lng 20.8 lat 63.6 are in northern Sweden.

w4-700606.name: First Battle of Panipat - Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi
w4-700606.blurb: On 21 April 1526 Babur, the Timurid ruler of Kabul, defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat using field artillery and the tulughma formation, ending Lodi (Delhi Sultanate) rule over northern India and founding the Mughal Empire. The from=Lodi Dynasty / to=Timurid Empire (Babur's Timurid line, the nascent Mughals) and 1521-1526 window match.

w4-700607.name: Secularization of the Teutonic Order and Treaty of Kraków
w4-700607.blurb: In April 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach converted to Lutheranism and, under the Treaty of Kraków, dissolved the Monastic State of the Teutonic Order, transforming it into the secular Duchy of Prussia held as a Polish fief. Albert became first Duke of Prussia, retaining Königsberg. Prussia (lat 54.4, lng 20.8) thereby passed from the Teutonic Order to the House of Hohenzollern. Window 1521-1526.

citations.label: State of the Teutonic Order – Wikipedia

w4-700608.name: Establishment of the Madurai Nayak dynasty by Viswanatha Nayaka
w4-700608.blurb: In 1529, Emperor Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara appointed Viswanatha Nayaka as governor of Madurai and the Tamil provinces, founding the Madurai Nayak dynasty. The Nayaks, though nominally subordinate to Vijayanagara, exercised de facto independent rule and became a distinct polity over the following two centuries. The worklist transfer Vijayanagara → Nayaks of Madurai at the Tamil south in the 1526–1529 window matches this devolution.

w4-700609.name: Safavid reconquest of Khorasan: Battle of Jam (1528)
w4-700609.blurb: After Uzbek forces occupied much of Khorasan in 1526, Shah Tahmasp I personally led the Safavid army into Khorasan and defeated Ubayd Allah Khan at the Battle of Jam (Khosrowjerd) on 24 September 1528. This Safavid victory drove the Uzbeks out of most of Khorasan, restoring Safavid control though Balkh remained Uzbek. Matches the Bukhara → Safavid transfer in the 1526–1529 window.

w4-700610.name: Shan Confederation sack of Ava
w4-700610.blurb: In 1527, the Confederation of Shan States led by the Mohnyin saophas, in alliance with the Kingdom of Prome, sacked the Ava Kingdom and placed Thohanbwa on the Ava throne as a Shan puppet. This ended Burman control of Upper Burma and fragmented the Kingdom of Ava, with much of its territory falling under Shan overlordship. Burman refugees fled south to the Toungoo kingdom, which used this influx to build the power base for its later conquests. The coordinates (96 degrees E, 21 degrees N) point to the upper Irrawaddy valley and the Ava / Shan States border region.

citations.label: Min-gyi-nyo and the Shan Invasions of Ava – Academia.edu

w4-700612.name: Spanish conquest of the Mayan lowlands – Montejo's Yucatán expedition and Alvarado's Guatemala campaigns
w4-700612.blurb: Francisco de Montejo received a royal capitulación on 8 December 1526 to conquer Yucatán, launching his first entrada in 1527–1529. Simultaneously, Jorge de Alvarado's 1527–1529 campaign in Guatemala finally consolidated Spanish authority over the K'iche' and Kaqchikel Maya kingdoms. Together these campaigns brought the Later Maya city-states of the Yucatán and highland Guatemala under Spanish imperial control, though resistance in Yucatán persisted until 1697.

citations.label: Spanish conquest of the Maya – Wikipedia

w4-700614.name: Habsburg consolidation of Low Countries territories (Pragmatic Sanction / Charles V)
w4-700614.blurb: Charles V, already Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, progressively consolidated Habsburg control over the Low Countries in the late 1520s. The centroid (~lng 5.5, lat 51.3, Guelders/Overijssel region) corresponds to territory that Charles V absorbed from the local HRE minor states into the Habsburg Netherlands domain through purchase, treaty, or inheritance during 1524–1528.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor

w4-700616.name: First Battle of Panipat — Mughal conquest of the Delhi Sultanate
w4-700616.blurb: Babur, Timurid prince and ruler of Kabul, defeated and killed Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat on 21 April 1526, ending the Delhi Sultanate and establishing the Mughal Empire. The territory around lng 70.6, lat 33.1 (Punjab–Kabul region) passed from the Timurid label (Babur's Kabul domain) to the new 'Mughal Empire' polity; Babur followed up by taking Delhi and Agra shortly after.

w4-700617.name: First Battle of Panipat and Mughal Conquest of Northern India
w4-700617.blurb: Babur, the last significant Timurid prince ruling from Kabul, defeated the Lodi Sultanate at the First Battle of Panipat on 21 April 1526, killing Sultan Ibrahim Lodi and seizing Delhi and Agra. He subsequently defeated the Rajput confederacy at Khanwa (1527) and the eastern Afghans at the Ghaghra River (1529), consolidating Mughal control over the Indo-Gangetic plain and eastern Afghanistan. This transformed the remnants of the Timurid Empire in the east into the nascent Mughal Empire.

w4-700618.name: Battle of Mohács
w4-700618.blurb: On 29 August 1526, Suleiman the Magnificent crushed the Hungarian army at Mohács, killing King Louis II; the Ottomans occupied Buda and controlled much of central Hungary, with further consolidation in the 1526–1529 period as rival claimants fought over the throne.

w4-700619.name: Battle of Mohács and Ottoman occupation of Hungary
w4-700619.blurb: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács on 29 August 1526, killing King Louis II. Ottoman forces occupied Buda in September 1526, then withdrew. The Ottomans returned in 1529, installing John Zápolya as a vassal king and occupying the Hungarian plain (lat 46, lng 17.4). This tripartition of Hungary into Royal Hungary, Ottoman pashalik, and Transylvania persisted until 1699.

w4-700625.name: Founding of the Sultanate of Johor
w4-700625.blurb: After the Portuguese destroyed the exiled Malaccan court's base at Bintan in 1526 and Sultan Mahmud Shah died at Kampar in 1528, his son Alauddin Riayat Shah II established the Sultanate of Johor (c. 1528–1530) on the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, inheriting territorial claims over the region formerly held by Malacca.

w4-700626.name: Portuguese destruction of Bintan and founding of Johor Sultanate (1526-1528)
w4-700626.blurb: In 1526, the Portuguese razed the capital of exiled Sultan Mahmud Shah of Malacca on the island of Bintan, forcing him to flee to Kampar in Sumatra where he died around 1528. His son Alauddin Riayat Shah II then founded the Sultanate of Johor on the Malay Peninsula around 1528, re-establishing Malay sovereignty in the Strait of Malacca region. The dataset records territory passing from the 'Portuguese Empire' to the 'Sultanate of Johor' in 1526-1529, corresponding to this transition.

w4-700627.name: Bohemian–Hungarian election of Ferdinand I of Habsburg
w4-700627.blurb: Following the death of Louis II of Hungary and Bohemia at the Battle of Mohács (August 1526), the Bohemian Diet elected Ferdinand I of Habsburg as King of Bohemia in October 1526. This brought the Kingdom of Bohemia under Habsburg rule; the atlas labels this as 'Kingdom of Spain' because Charles I of Spain was Ferdinand's brother and the Habsburgs were a unified dynastic block in the source data.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor

w4-700628.name: Habsburg Inheritance - Ferdinand I Becomes King of Bohemia
w4-700628.blurb: After Louis II of Bohemia and Hungary was killed at the Battle of Mohács (29 August 1526), the Bohemian Diet elected Ferdinand I of Habsburg as king on 24 October 1526, incorporating Bohemia into the Habsburg dynastic conglomerate. The dataset's 'to' label of 'Kingdom of Spain' is a Cliopatria quirk: Ferdinand's brother was Emperor Charles V, and Cliopatria represents the unified Habsburg bloc under the Spanish label. The underlying event - Habsburg acquisition of Bohemia in 1526-1529 - is well attested.

citations.label: Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor - Wikipedia

w4-700630.name: Ottoman intervention and establishment of the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom after Battle of Mohács
w4-700630.blurb: The Battle of Mohács (29 August 1526) destroyed the unified Kingdom of Hungary; King Louis II was killed and the realm fractured. John Zápolya, backed by Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I, was crowned king but contested by Ferdinand of Habsburg. By 1529, Ottoman forces returned to expel Ferdinand from Buda and back Zápolya, leading to the partition that created the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom in Transylvania and eastern Hungary. The dataset captures the transfer of Transylvanian territory (lat 46.5, lng 24.4) from the unified Hungary to the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom polity.

w4-700633.name: Lê restoration — Nguyễn Kim enthrones Lê Trang Tông against the Mạc dynasty
w4-700633.blurb: After the Mạc dynasty usurped the Vietnamese throne in 1527, loyalist general Nguyễn Kim rallied the exiled Lê royal family and in 1533 enthroned Lê Trang Tông in Thanh Hóa (southern territory), launching the Revival Lê dynasty and the Lê–Mạc War. By 1534 Ming China was pressuring the Mạc as illegitimate; the Lê controlled the south while the Mạc held the north (Đông Kinh/Hanoi), creating the de facto split of Đại Việt that characterised the century-long civil war.

w4-700634.name: Sevappa Nayak appointed governor of Thanjavur by Achyuta Deva Raya
w4-700634.blurb: In 1532 CE, Vijayanagara Emperor Achyuta Deva Raya granted Sevappa Nayak — a trusted Telugu commander and his relative by marriage — the governorship of Thanjavur under the nayankara system. Sevappa founded the Thanjavur Nayak kingdom, ruling autonomously (though still nominally under Vijayanagara suzerainty) until 1580. The kingdom became fully independent after Vijayanagara's catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565.

w4-700635.name: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (Gragn) conquers the Ethiopian highlands (1529-1534)
w4-700635.blurb: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi of the Adal Sultanate, armed with Ottoman firearms, overran the Amhara and Shewa highlands by 1532-1534 and invaded Tigray in 1534, at its height controlling roughly three-quarters of the Ethiopian Empire. The from->to (Ethiopian Empire -> Adal Sultanate) at 39.7, 10.5 in the 1532-1534 window matches this conquest.

w4-700637.name: Accession of Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah and Hussain Shahi succession crisis in the Bengal Sultanate
w4-700637.blurb: The Hussain Shahi dynasty was founded in 1494, but the worklist window 1532–1534 corresponds to a real in-Bengal succession crisis: the short-reigning Alauddin Firuz Shah II (c. 1532–33) was assassinated by his uncle, who took the throne as Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah (r. 1533–1538), the last Hussain Shahi sultan. His usurpation alienated nobles and triggered the defection of frontier governors, and Bengal's military prestige was broken at the Battle of Surajgarh against Sher Shah in March 1534. The worklist's Sultanate of Bengal → Hussain Shahi Dynasty relabeling (lat 24.2°N, lng 87.6°E, Gaur region) reflects this dynastic consolidation, not the 1494 founding originally named.

w4-700639.name: Spanish conquest of Michoacán / execution of the Cazonci
w4-700639.blurb: The Tarascan (Purépecha) state of Michoacán submitted to Hernán Cortés in 1522, but its conquest was completed by Nuño de Guzmán, who had the last Cazonci Tangaxoan II burned alive on 14 February 1530, marking the formal end of the pre-Spanish kingdom. By 1531-1534 the region was governed as Nueva Galicia. The dataset transfer (Michoacán -> Spanish Empire, py1532/y1534) at lng-102.2/lat19.1 corresponds to the final consolidation of Spanish administration over former Michoacán territory.

w4-700644.name: French occupation of Savoy (1536)
w4-700644.blurb: In February 1536, Francis I of France invaded and occupied the Duchy of Savoy and Piedmont, claiming suzerainty over the territories of Charles III of Savoy; French troops held Savoy for nearly 23 years until the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559). The ~30,000 km² centred at lat 45 / lng 6.7 corresponds to the Alpine Savoy territories seized in this French military campaign.

w4-700645.name: French invasion of Piedmont and Truce of Nice
w4-700645.blurb: After Francesco II Sforza died without heirs in November 1535, Francis I of France refused to accept Habsburg succession to Milan and launched an invasion in early 1536. French forces under Philippe de Chabot captured Turin and occupied most of Piedmont and Savoy by April 1536; the Truce of Nice (1538) confirmed France's retention of Turin and its Piedmontese holdings.

w4-700647.name: Tripartition of Hungary and Formation of the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom
w4-700647.blurb: After John Zápolya's death in 1540, his infant son John Sigismund was proclaimed king. Sultan Suleiman I intervened militarily, captured Buda in 1541, and divided Hungary into three zones: central Hungary under Ottoman control, Royal Hungary under the Habsburgs, and the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom (later Principality of Transylvania) under Zápolya's heirs as Ottoman vassals. Transylvania and the eastern counties became the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom administered from 1541 onward.

w4-700650.name: Lê–Mạc War; Revival Lê dynasty gains territory
w4-700650.blurb: After Mạc Đăng Dung usurped the Vietnamese throne in 1527, Lê loyalists under Nguyễn Kim launched a restoration; in 1539–1540 they entered Đại Việt from Laos and captured Thanh Hóa (coord 105.5E/20.7N), establishing a southern Lê-controlled zone, while the Mạc made humiliating concessions to Ming China in 1540. The dataset's 'Đại Việt (Mạc) → Lê Dynasty' shift in central Vietnam reflects this partition; event real and correctly dated.

w4-700653.name: Toungoo–Hanthawaddy War (1534–1541)
w4-700653.blurb: King Tabinshwehti of Toungoo launched invasions against the weakened Hanthawaddy Kingdom from 1534. A decisive campaign in 1538–1539 caused King Takayutpi to abandon his capital Pegu, which Toungoo seized; Tabinshwehti moved his capital there in 1539. By 1540–1541, the fall of Martaban completed the conquest of Lower Burma, ending Hanthawaddy and transferring its territory to the First Toungoo Empire.

w4-700655.name: Sher Shah Suri conquers Bengal and founds the Sur Empire (1538-1540)
w4-700655.blurb: Sher Shah Suri defeated the Bengal Sultanate's Hussain Shahi rulers, capturing the capital Gaur in 1538 and driving out the last sultan Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah, and after defeating Humayun at Kannauj in 1540 formally founded the Sur Empire. The from->to (Hussain Shahi Dynasty -> Sur Empire) at 87.6, 24.2 in the 1534-1540 window matches this conquest.

w4-700656.name: Ottoman occupation of Buda and central Hungary
w4-700656.blurb: After John I Zápolya's death (1540), the Habsburgs besieged Buda (1541) to claim the kingdom; Suleiman intervened, seized Buda on 29 August 1541, and converted central Hungary into the eyalet of Budin. The 1534–1540 worklist window corresponds to the period when Ottoman-backed John I consolidated his hold over the territory, expanding the Ottoman vassal footprint at the Kingdom of Hungary's expense.

w4-700657.name: Altan Khan's consolidation of the Tümed and assertion of dominance over the Mongolian steppe
w4-700657.blurb: After the death of the Mongol Khagan Bodi Alagh Khan around 1547, Altan Khan of the Tümed forced Bodi Alagh's successor Darayisung Küdeng Khan to flee eastward, making Altan the de facto master of the Right Wing of the Mongols and the Inner Mongolian steppe centred on the Ordos. The Tümed reached the peak of their power under his rule. The dataset transition from 'Mongol Khanate' to 'Tümed' in window [1540,1547] reflects this power shift.

w4-700660.name: Spanish Conquest of Yucatán and Itza Maya Consolidation
w4-700660.blurb: Spanish forces under Francisco de Montejo completed the conquest of the northern Yucatán Peninsula's city-states by 1546, defeating the Great Maya Revolt of November 1546. As the northern coastal polities collapsed and many Maya fled south, the Itza Maya of the Petén interior (around Lake Petén Itzá) consolidated control over a wider territory, remaining the last independent Maya kingdom until 1697. The 1540s represent the period when the Itza emerged as the dominant interior Maya power.

w4-700661.name: Sher Shah Suri defeats Humayun: founding of the Sur Empire
w4-700661.blurb: Sher Shah Suri defeated Mughal Emperor Humayun at Chausa (June 1539) and decisively at Kannauj/Bilgram (17 May 1540). Humayun fled to Persia, and Sher Shah took Delhi, Agra, and Lahore, establishing the Sur Empire over most of northern India until Humayun's reconquest in 1555. Matches the Mughal → Sur Empire transfer in the 1540-1547 window.

w4-700664.name: Toungoo conquest of Prome
w4-700664.blurb: King Tabinshwehti of the First Toungoo Empire besieged Prome (Pyay) through 1541–1542, with forces under General Bayinnaung defeating relief armies from the Shan Confederation and Mrauk U. The Prome king Minkhaung accepted amnesty and surrendered on 19 May 1542, bringing all of central Burma under Toungoo control. Ava formally ceded remaining central Burmese territory between Pagan and Prome by 1545 peace treaty.

w4-700665.name: Ottoman capture of Buda and partition of Hungary
w4-700665.blurb: In 1541 Sultan Suleiman I captured Buda, partitioning Hungary into Royal Hungary (Habsburg), Ottoman Hungary, and vassal Transylvania; the Peace of Edirne (1547) formalised the arrangement. The coordinates (19.7,46.3) on the central Hungarian plain came under Ottoman control, matching the from→to (Kingdom of Hungary → Ottoman Empire) in the 1540–1547 window.

w4-700666.name: Coronation of Ivan IV as Tsar of All Russia
w4-700666.blurb: On 16 January 1547 Ivan IV ('the Terrible') was crowned Tsar of All Russia in the Cathedral of the Dormition in Moscow, transforming the Grand Principality of Moscow into the Tsardom of Russia. This was more than a title change: Ivan claimed the imperial succession of Byzantium and adopted the two-headed eagle, signalling a new political identity for the expanding state. The date falls within the dataset window [1540,1547]; the Tsardom shortly thereafter took Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556.

w4-700670.name: Ottoman consolidation of central Hungary and the 1547 truce
w4-700670.blurb: After John Zápolya's death in 1540, Suleiman the Magnificent occupied Buda in 1541 under the pretext of protecting Zápolya's infant son John Sigismund. The Ottomans directly incorporated central Hungary while the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom continued as a vassal state in Transylvania. Further campaigns in 1543–1547 secured additional fortresses and territory in eastern Hungary (lat 47, lng 21.6, the Tisza region). A truce in 1547 confirmed Ferdinand of Habsburg's recognition of this settlement with annual tribute.

w4-700671.name: Demak succession crisis and emergence of Pajang (1547–1554)
w4-700671.blurb: The worklist labels a central Java polity as 'Sultanate of Malacca,' which here refers to the Demak Sultanate / its successor Pajang (the real Malacca fell in 1511 far to the northwest). In 1547 Arya Penangsang seized Demak after assassinating Sultan Prawoto; by 1554 he was defeated by Hadiwijaya of Pajang, who later moved the Demak regalia to Pajang (1568). This entry reflects that internal succession transition.

w4-700672.name: Altan Khan's Tumed Expansion and Displacement of Eastern Mongol Factions
w4-700672.blurb: Altan Khan of the Tumed Mongols emerged as the dominant power on the eastern steppe after Bodi Alagh Khan died in 1547, forcing his successor to grant Altan the title of Khan. Between 1547 and 1552 Altan consolidated Tumed control over Inner Mongolia north of Shanxi, launched major raids into northern China (including a siege of Beijing in 1550), and absorbed territory previously claimed by the fragmented Northern Yuan / eastern steppe polities. The 'Golden Horde' label in this entry refers to the remnant Northern Yuan rather than the western Golden Horde.

w4-700673.name: Toungoo-Mrauk U War (1545-1547)
w4-700673.blurb: The First Toungoo Empire under Tabinshwehti and later Bayinnaung repeatedly attempted to conquer the Kingdom of Mrauk U (Arakan), launching major campaigns in 1545-1547 and again in 1580-1581. Despite winning open-field battles, the Toungoo forces were unable to overcome the heavily Portuguese-assisted fortifications at the capital Mrauk U, and both invasions ended in withdrawal. Mrauk U thus remained the only major post-Pagan kingdom not absorbed by the Toungoo dynasty. The territorial change reflected in the data (py=1547, y=1552) corresponds to a final withdrawal of Toungoo forces and reversion of border territory to Mrauk U control around 1547-1552.

w4-700675.name: Conquest of Kazan — Qasim Khanate territory incorporated into Russia
w4-700675.blurb: The feature centred near Kasimov (lng 41.1, lat 54.7) is the Qasim Khanate (Kasimov Khanate), a small Tatar buffer principality that had served as a Muscovite client since the mid-15th century. It was a distinct entity from the Khanate of Kazan, whose capital Ivan IV stormed on 2 October 1552. Kazan's fall sharply curtailed any independent role for the Qasim khans, and although the Qasim Khanate persisted nominally until 1681, from 1552 it functioned as a fully dependent Russian appanage rather than an autonomous khanate.

w4-700676.name: Ivan IV's conquest of the Khanate of Kazan
w4-700676.blurb: Ivan IV (the Terrible) made failed attempts on Kazan in 1547 and 1549–50, then built the fortress of Sviyazhsk in 1551 as a forward base. On 2 October 1552 Russian forces stormed and sacked Kazan, ending the Khanate and absorbing its territories—including lands formerly associated with the Qasim Khanate—into the Tsardom of Russia. The atlas entry 1547–1552 encompasses the entire campaign that culminated in this decisive siege.

w4-700677.name: Abdication of Charles V - transfer of Habsburg Netherlands to Spain
w4-700677.blurb: Between October 1555 and January 1556, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V abdicated his multiple crowns, passing the Seventeen Provinces (Netherlands) and the Spanish kingdoms to his son Philip II of Spain, while the Imperial title and Austrian lands went to his brother Ferdinand I. The territories around modern Belgium/Netherlands thus shifted from the unified Habsburg Monarchy under Charles to the crown of the Kingdom of Spain under Philip II. This split the House of Habsburg into its Spanish and Austrian branches.

citations.label: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor - Wikipedia

w4-700678.name: Russian conquest of the Astrakhan Khanate
w4-700678.blurb: After a 1554 campaign installed the puppet Khan Dervish Ali, Ivan IV's forces returned in 1556 when Dervish Ali allied with Russia's enemies. Russian troops occupied Astrakhan without significant resistance and formally annexed the khanate, giving the Tsardom control of the Volga to the Caspian. The dataset transfer (Astrakhan Khanate -> Tsardom of Russia, py1552/y1556) at lng47.5/lat46.4 matches, following the 1552 annexation of Kazan.

citations.label: Russian conquest of the Astrakhan Khanate – Wikipedia
Ivan the Terrible Annexes Astrakhan – EBSCO Research Starters

w4-700679.name: Second Battle of Panipat
w4-700679.blurb: On 5 November 1556 the young Mughal emperor Akbar, guided by regent Bairam Khan, defeated Hemu (Hem Chandra Vikramaditya), commander of the remnant Sur forces, at the Second Battle of Panipat. Hemu was struck by an arrow and his army routed, restoring Mughal control over Punjab and the Indo-Gangetic plain (~239,575 km2) and effectively ending Sur (Afghan) rule. The 1556 date sits at the upper edge of the 1552-1556 window; transfer Sur Empire -> Mughal Empire is correct.

w4-700680.name: Bayinnaung's conquest of the Shan States (1556-1557)
w4-700680.blurb: King Bayinnaung of the Toungoo dynasty launched a comprehensive campaign against the Shan states in late 1556; the show of force caused most cis-Salween Shan states to submit by March 1557, bringing them under Toungoo suzerainty. The worklist transition is 'Shan States' -> 'First Toungoo Empire' [1552,1556] at lng 96, lat 22 (Upper Burma / northern Shan States), with 1556 at the edge of the window.

w4-700681.name: Abdication of Charles V — Division of Habsburg Domains
w4-700681.blurb: Between 1554 and 1556 Charles V divided the Habsburg empire: Spain and its empire passed to his son Philip II (1556), while the Austrian lands (coords 13.9E/48.3N) within the Holy Roman Empire passed to his brother Ferdinand I (abdication August 1556). This created the separate Spanish and Austrian Habsburg lines, with the Austrian domains forming the Habsburg Monarchy distinct from the Kingdom of Spain.

citations.label: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor – Wikipedia

w4-700683.name: Turgut Reis's recapture of Mahdia and Ottoman encirclement of Hafsid Ifriqiya (1554)
w4-700683.blurb: Through the 1550s, Ottoman-aligned corsairs under Turgut Reis (Dragut) progressively eroded Hafsid coastal authority: Spain seized Mahdia in 1550, but Turgut recaptured it in 1554, while Tripoli had fallen to the Ottomans in 1551. The worklist transition is 'Hafsid Dynasty' -> 'Ottoman Empire' [1552,1556] at lng 6.5, lat 35.8 (eastern Algeria / Constantine area, the western flank of Hafsid lands), capturing this phase of progressive Hafsid loss to Ottoman forces before the final Ottoman conquest of Tunis in 1574; 1554 falls within the window.

w4-700684.name: Safavid reconquest of Kandahar after Humayun's death (1556)
w4-700684.blurb: When Mughal Emperor Humayun died in January 1556, Safavid Shah Tahmasp I exploited the power vacuum and seized Kandahar, which Humayun had held since 1545. The worklist transition is 'Mughal Empire' -> 'Safavid Dynasty' [1552,1556] at lng 65.2, lat 32.8 (the Kandahar/southern Afghanistan contested zone), with 1556 at the edge of the window.

w4-700687.name: County of Foix Inherited by the House of Bourbon (via Jeanne d'Albret)
w4-700687.blurb: Henry II of Navarre, Count of Foix, died on 25 May 1555, leaving his titles — including the County of Foix, Kingdom of Navarre, and Béarn — to his daughter Jeanne d'Albret, who had married Antoine de Bourbon in 1548. Through this marriage the County of Foix came under Bourbon dynastic control. Their son, Henry of Bourbon, eventually became Henry IV of France in 1589, formally uniting Foix with the French Crown.

w4-700694.name: Bayinnaung deposes King Mekuti — direct Toungoo control of Lan Na
w4-700694.blurb: Lan Na had been a Toungoo vassal since Bayinnaung took Chiang Mai in 1558, but it was re-subjugated during the Burmese-Siamese War of 1563, and when King Mekuti (Mae Ku) refused to join Bayinnaung's campaign against Ayutthaya — treated as rebellion — he was deposed in 1564 and exiled to Pegu, with Wisutthithewi installed as queen regent under Burmese oversight. These 1563-64 events, not the trans-Salween Kengtung campaign further north, brought this core Lan Na parcel under direct Toungoo control.

w4-700695.name: Bayinnaung's conquest of the Shan States (1557-1563)
w4-700695.blurb: Bayinnaung, king of the First Toungoo Empire, conquered the cis-Salween Shan states in 1557 and the trans-Salween Shan states (including Kengtung and the Chinese Shan states) by 1563. The dataset window 1561-1564 (Shan States -> First Toungoo Empire at 97.3, 23.2 in the Shan highlands) corresponds to the final phase of these campaigns.

w4-700702.name: Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis and Treaty of Lausanne
w4-700702.blurb: The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559) ended the Italian Wars and restored the Duchy of Savoy to Duke Emmanuel Philibert, who had been expelled by France since 1536. France withdrew from Savoy and most of Piedmont, though it retained Turin until 1562. The Treaty of Lausanne (1564) between Savoy and the Swiss further refined boundaries, Savoy recovering Chablais and Genevois. The window 1561-1564 captures the final French withdrawal from Savoy (lat 45, lng 6.8).

w4-700706.name: Final Songhai absorption of western Mali territory
w4-700706.blurb: Songhai expansion at Mali's expense began under Sunni Ali (r.1464-1492) and Askia Muhammad (r.1493-1528), and continued through the mid-16th century as Mali was pushed back toward the upper Senegal/Niger (lat 13.5, lng -12.9). The 1561-1564 window corresponds to the late-stage collapse of residual Mali authority in this western zone rather than the earlier main conquests; the directional transfer Mali-to-Songhai is attested, though the dominant conquests predate the window.

w4-700707.name: Papal bull elevates Duchy of Florence to Grand Duchy of Tuscany (1569–1570)
w4-700707.blurb: Pope Pius V issued the bull Pontifex Maximus on 27 August 1569, elevating Cosimo I de' Medici from Duke of Florence to Grand Duke of Tuscany, with coronation in Rome on 5 March 1570. The dataset's 'Republic of Florence' destination label is an anachronism (the Republic ended in 1532); the actual transition was Duchy of Florence to Grand Duchy of Tuscany. The underlying titular/territorial event is well-attested.

w4-700708.name: Abdication of Tirumala Deva Raya; Vijayanagara partitioned, Mysore rises
w4-700708.blurb: In 1572 Tirumala Deva Raya, founder of the Aravidu dynasty and first crowned Vijayanagara emperor (r. 1570–1572), abdicated and divided the surviving empire among his three sons — the Kannada country (including Srirangapatna, near coord 76.8E/12.2N) going to his son Rama. The Wodeyar Kingdom of Mysore, a Vijayanagara vassal, exploited this fragmentation to assert effective independence and expand over formerly Vijayanagara Kannada territory. Event real and correctly dated; the dataset's 'Vijayanagara → Mysore' shift captures Mysore's emergence from the partition.

w4-700709.name: Haqnazar Khan reunifies the three Kazakh Hordes (c. 1569–1572)
w4-700709.blurb: Haqnazar Khan (r. 1538–1580), the last son of Kasym Khan to rule, successfully reunified the Great, Middle, and Little (Small) Hordes of the Kazakh Khanate after decades of fragmentation and civil war. His c. 1570 victory over Nogai/Manghit forces consolidated the western steppe under Kazakh authority, absorbing the Small Horde's territories back into the unified Kazakh Khanate.

w4-700710.name: Bijapur consolidation after Battle of Talikota
w4-700710.blurb: The Battle of Talikota (January 1565) saw the Deccan Sultanate coalition - led by Bijapur, Ahmednagar, Golconda, and Bidar - crush the Vijayanagara Empire and sack its capital Hampi. In the years 1570-1572, the Bijapur Sultanate under Ali Adil Shah I moved rapidly to annex former Vijayanagara territories in the northern Deccan and Krishna-Tungabhadra doab region. Vijayanagara persisted as a much-diminished rump under Tirumala at Penukonda but lost the contested lands to Bijapur during this 1570-1572 window.

w4-700712.name: Crimean Khan Devlet I Giray's burning of Moscow (1571)
w4-700712.blurb: In May 1571, Crimean Khan Devlet I Giray led approximately 40,000 Tatar horsemen and Ottoman troops around Russia's southern defenses, burned Moscow, and took as many as 60,000-150,000 captives. Taking advantage of Russia's entanglement in the Livonian War, the raid resulted in temporary Crimean territorial gains in southern Russia. Ivan IV was forced to disband the Oprichnina as a result of the military humiliation.

w4-700715.name: Trịnh Tùng consolidates power as Trịnh Lord
w4-700715.blurb: On Trịnh Kiểm's death in 1570, Trịnh Cối was outmanoeuvred and defected to the Mạc, leaving Trịnh Tùng as the new Trịnh lord and de facto ruler in the Lê dynasty's name; he briefly took Hanoi in 1572. The Thanh Hóa/Nghệ An region passed from nominal Lê control to effective Trịnh lords' administration within the 1570-1572 window. Well attested.

w4-700716.name: Banten Sultanate conquests of Sunda Kingdom territories (c. 1570-1579)
w4-700716.blurb: After Sultan Hasanuddin of Banten died in 1570, his successor Maulana Yusuf continued the conquest of the weakened Hindu Sunda Kingdom. By the late 1560s, Banten had already seized most Sunda ports; Maulana Yusuf launched a final offensive culminating in the sacking of Pakuan Pajajaran, the Sunda capital, on 8 May 1579. The seizure of the sacred enthronement stone disabled surviving Sunda royalty from crowning a new king, effectively ending the thousand-year Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of West Java.

w4-700719.name: Burmese conquest of Lan Xang
w4-700719.blurb: King Bayinnaung of the Toungoo Empire repeatedly invaded Lan Xang, finally pursuing King Setthathirath after he went missing c. 1571–1572 during a campaign against the Khmer. A Burmese expedition in 1574 occupied Vientiane and installed Maha Oupahat (Voravongsa I) as a Toungoo vassal king on 16 April 1575. Territory around lat 19, lng 101.6 (the Vientiane plain / Lan Xang heartland) thereby passed under Toungoo suzerainty.

w4-700720.name: Treaty of Speyer (1570): Eastern Hungarian Kingdom becomes Principality of Transylvania
w4-700720.blurb: The Treaty of Speyer (1570, ratified 1571) ended the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom's claim to the Hungarian throne: John Sigismund Zápolya abdicated as 'King of Hungary' and was recognised as 'Prince of Transylvania and Lord of the Partium' by Maximilian II. The western/northern portions of the former Eastern Hungarian Kingdom passed to Habsburg Royal Hungary, matching the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom→Habsburg Monarchy change at (21.6°E, 48.2°N) in 1570–1572.

w4-700721.name: Pajang absorbs former Demak territories in Central Java (c.1568–1572)
w4-700721.blurb: This central Java entry again labels the polity 'Sultanate of Malacca,' meaning Pajang or a Demak-successor (the real Malacca had fallen to Portugal in 1511). Around 1568–1572 Hadiwijaya of Pajang consolidated control over former Demak coastal territories, becoming suzerain over most of northern and central Java; the 'Malacca' to 'Pajang' label reflects this transition in the Cliopatria source.

w4-700724.name: Capture of Tunis (1569) - Uluc Ali ends Hafsid rule
w4-700724.blurb: In 1569 Uluc Ali (Occhiali), the Ottoman Beylerbey of Algiers, marched on Tunis with janissaries and Kabyle cavalry, defeated the Hafsid sultan at Beja, and by the end of 1569 entered the Kasbah unopposed, ending over three centuries of Hafsid rule and bringing Tunis under Ottoman suzerainty. He installed a governor, minted coins in Selim II's name, and garrisoned the city, though La Goletta remained Spanish. Spain briefly retook Tunis in 1573 before the final Ottoman conquest of 1574; the 1569 capture is the in-window event matching the Hafsid-to-Ottoman transition (1570-1572). Corrected from the original blurb's misdated 1574 event.

w4-700729.name: Russian conquest of Livonian territories (Livonian War)
w4-700729.blurb: During the Livonian War (1558–1583), Ivan IV of Russia established the puppet Kingdom of Livonia under Magnus of Denmark in 1570 and continued military operations to seize former Livonian Confederation lands in the eastern Baltic (roughly modern Latvia/Estonia). The centroid at ~lng 25.7, lat 57.7 corresponds to central Livonia (around Dorpat/Tartu area), territory that came under Russian or Russian-vassal control by 1570–1572.

w4-700730.name: Livonian War - Russian Gains in the Eastern Baltic
w4-700730.blurb: During the Livonian War (1558-1583) Ivan IV's Russia fought for control of Livonia against Sweden, Poland-Lithuania, and Denmark. The 1570-1572 sub-period saw intensified fighting: Russia besieged Reval (Tallinn) in 1570-1571, captured smaller towns, and raided as far as Finland. The coordinates point to the eastern Baltic / Livonia, where Russian forces temporarily held territory from the dissolving Livonian Confederation previously classified under 'Holy Roman Empire Minor States'.

w4-700731.name: Treaty of Speyer — Eastern Hungarian Kingdom becomes Principality of Transylvania
w4-700731.blurb: On 16 August 1570, John Sigismund Zápolya and Habsburg Emperor Maximilian II signed the Treaty of Speyer, by which John Sigismund renounced his royal title as King of Hungary, acknowledged Maximilian as sole king, and adopted instead the new title 'Prince of Transylvania and Lord of Parts of the Kingdom of Hungary.' This formally transformed the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom into the Principality of Transylvania. John Sigismund died on 14 March 1571 shortly after ratifying the treaty.

w4-700733.name: Patani's assertion of independence from Ayutthaya amid Burmese domination (1569–1572)
w4-700733.blurb: When the Burmese sacked Ayutthaya in 1569 and installed a vassal king, Patani under Sultan Manzur Shah (r. 1564–1572) exploited Siamese weakness to assert virtual independence. The 1570–1572 window corresponds to Patani's de facto autonomy from the collapsed Ayutthaya tributary system, matching the Ayutthaya→Patani transfer at (101.5°E, 6.3°N).

w4-700734.name: Banten-Cirebon conquest of the Sunda Kingdom (fall of Pakuan Pajajaran)
w4-700734.blurb: Under sustained pressure from the Islamic Sultanates of Banten and Cirebon, the last Hindu-Buddhist kingdom in western Java—Sunda (Pajajaran)—fell when Sultan Maulana Yusuf of Banten overran its capital Pakuan Pajajaran on 8 May 1579. The royal regalia were evacuated to Sumedang Larang. The atlas records this as a 1572–1579 transition, the final decade of Sunda's collapse under Islamic sultanate pressure, with Cirebon playing a key role as co-belligerent.

w4-700735.name: Dutch Revolt — Union of Utrecht
w4-700735.blurb: The Eighty Years' War (1568–1648) saw the northern Netherlands rebel against Philip II of Spain. After the Sea Beggars established Protestant bases in 1572, the rebellious northern provinces forged the Union of Utrecht on 23 January 1579, a military alliance that became the foundation of the Dutch Republic. The dataset records 'Kingdom of Spain → Union of Utrecht' for this Dutch coastal corridor in 1572–1579, reflecting the progressive Revolt-era transfer of effective sovereignty from Spain to the rebel provinces.

w4-700736.name: Ahmadnagar annexation of Berar
w4-700736.blurb: In 1572 Murtaza Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar exploited internal strife in Berar to invade; by 1574 he had imprisoned and executed the regent Tufal Khan and the last Berar ruler Burhan Imad Shah, annexing the sultanate. The dataset records this change as py1572/y1579 at lng78.2/lat20.3 (the Berar region), spanning invasion through consolidation, and the conquest brought Ahmadnagar to its territorial zenith among the Deccan sultanates.

w4-700737.name: Battle of Molodi (1572) - Russian recovery
w4-700737.blurb: In July-August 1572, Prince Mikhail Vorotynsky decisively defeated Devlet I Giray's 120,000-strong Crimean-Ottoman horde at the Battle of Molodi, roughly 50 km south of Moscow. The Crimeans lost the vast majority of their forces and never again mounted a campaign to conquer Russia outright. Russia recovered the southern territories that had been overrun in 1571, permanently halting Crimean ambitions to succeed the Golden Horde.

w4-700738.name: Toungoo conquest of Lan Xang (Bayinnaung's 1574 campaign)
w4-700738.blurb: King Bayinnaung of the First Toungoo Empire campaigned against Lan Xang in 1574; Vientiane was abandoned and Bayinnaung entered on 6 December 1574, installing a Burmese-loyal king. A 1579 campaign crushed a rebellion and installed Sen Soulintha as vassal. Lan Xang remained a Toungoo vassal until 1591. Matches the Lan Xang → First Toungoo Empire transfer in the 1572-1579 window.

w4-700740.name: Mughal Conquest of Bengal (Karrani Sultanate)
w4-700740.blurb: The Mughal conquest of Bengal was a series of campaigns (1574–1612) against the Karrani Afghan dynasty, the successors of the Sur Empire in Bengal (hence the dataset 'from' label Sur Empire). Akbar's general Khan Jahan / Munim Khan defeated Daud Khan Karrani at the Battle of Tukaroi (1575) and the decisive Battle of Raj Mahal (1576), after which Daud Khan was captured and executed, ending Karrani rule. By the late 1570s Akbar had appointed subahdars to administer Bengal, though the Bara-Bhuiyan zamindars under Isa Khan resisted for decades. The dataset window of 1572–1579 captures the transition from Sur/Karrani-held Bengal to Mughal provincial control.

w4-700743.name: Iberian Union — Portuguese possessions pass to Philip II of Spain
w4-700743.blurb: Following the death of King Sebastian I of Portugal at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir (1578) and the extinction of the Aviz line, Philip II of Spain was recognized as king of Portugal after his victory at the Battle of Alcântara (25 August 1580) and formal ratification at the Cortes of Tomar (1581), merging Portuguese overseas territories in West Africa (including the Gulf of Guinea islands) under the Spanish Crown.

w4-700744.name: Iberian Union — Philip II of Spain becomes Philip I of Portugal (1580–1581)
w4-700744.blurb: Following the death of King Sebastian of Portugal at Alcacer Quibir (1578) and Cardinal Henry's death in 1580, Philip II of Spain claimed the Portuguese throne and was recognized as Philip I of Portugal by the Cortes of Tomar in 1581. This personal union placed all Portuguese overseas territories — including Ceylon and the Estado da India — nominally under the Spanish Crown.

w4-700745.name: Spanish reconquest of parts of the northern Netherlands
w4-700745.blurb: Under the Iberian Union proclaimed in 1580–1581, Portugal's overseas possessions came under the Spanish Crown through a personal union of the two kingdoms. Portuguese Africa — the West African trading factories and the Gulf of Guinea islands — accordingly passed to Spanish sovereignty while continuing to be administered by Portuguese officials, the arrangement that the Iberian Union would maintain until 1640.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma

w4-700747.name: Spanish (Iberian Union) military advances into the Union of Utrecht territories
w4-700747.blurb: Following the Iberian Union (1580) under Philip II, Spanish forces under the Duke of Parma (Alexander Farnese) pressed their reconquest against the Union of Utrecht. Parma captured Breda in 1581 and, with an army of 61,000 by October 1582, made further advances into Gelderland and Overijssel in 1582 (his lieutenant Verdugo taking Steenwijk). The data window 1579-1582 captures these gains over the northern Netherlands.

w4-700749.name: Death of Altan Khan and Tümed succession crisis
w4-700749.blurb: Altan Khan, ruler of the Tümed Mongols and dominant power of the Mongol right wing, died on 13 January 1582. His death ended the political cohesion he had maintained over the western Mongols since the 1540s, and steppe territory around the Khalkha region reverted to the broader Mongol political sphere that the dataset designates 'Golden Horde'. The transition reflects local Mongol authority re-asserting itself after Tümed overlordship waned.

w4-700755.name: Truce of Plussa
w4-700755.blurb: The Truce of Plussa (10 August 1583) ended Russia's participation in the Livonian War, ceding Narva, Ivangorod, Jama, and most of Ingria to Sweden. The Ingria region near lng 27.1 E / lat 59.9 N passed from the Tsardom of Russia to the Kingdom of Sweden, matching the [1582,1588] window.

w4-700756.name: Eighty Years' War - Duke of Parma Recovers Southern Netherlands for Spain
w4-700756.blurb: During the Eighty Years' War, the Union of Utrecht (1579) united the northern provinces in rebellion and the Act of Abjuration (1581) declared independence, but the Duke of Parma's campaigns from 1578 reconquered much of the southern Low Countries for the Iberian Union. The dataset's 1582-1588 transfer from 'Dutch Republic' to 'Iberian Union' near lng 4.9, lat 52.1 reflects areas still under or returned to Habsburg control before the Dutch Republic fully consolidated. Note: this coordinate is in the Holland heartland, which Parma never recovered, so the precise placement is somewhat dubious even though the underlying reconquest is real.

w4-700757.name: Rise of Mataram Sultanate under Panembahan Senapati
w4-700757.blurb: After the death of Sultan Hadiwijaya of Pajang, Sutawijaya of Mataram and Prince Benowo attacked and defeated Pajang (1586). Sutawijaya proclaimed the independent Mataram Sultanate in 1587 as Panembahan Senapati, absorbing former Pajang and Demak territory and rapidly dominating central Java. The 'Sultanate of Malacca' from-label is a Cliopatria artifact; the affected territory (central Java, ~110.8E/-7.4N) is the displaced Pajang/Demak polity, not the historic Malacca (which fell to Portugal in 1511). Window [1582,1588] captures the conquest.

w4-700759.name: Panembahan Senopati conquers Pajang and founds the Mataram Sultanate (1586–1588)
w4-700759.blurb: After Sultan Hadiwijaya of Pajang died in 1582 a succession crisis erupted. Danang Sutawijaya (Panembahan Senopati), lord of Mataram, allied with Prince Benawa against the usurper Arya Pangiri; by 1586–1587 Pajang was defeated and Benawa submitted, merging Pajang into the nascent Mataram Sultanate. Resistance was suppressed by 1588, making Mataram the dominant power in Central Java.

w4-700764.name: Lan Xang regains independence from First Toungoo Empire
w4-700764.blurb: After Bayinnaung's death in 1581, the First Toungoo Empire rapidly fragmented. Lan Xang exploited internal Burmese conflicts and, in 1591, Prince Nokeo Koumane was crowned in Vientiane, reunited Luang Prabang and the central provinces, and formally declared Lan Xang's independence from the Toungoo Empire. The dataset window 1582–1588 captures the early phase of de facto Toungoo withdrawal from Laotian territory before the formal 1591 declaration.

w4-700766.name: Mughal Conquest of Kashmir under Akbar
w4-700766.blurb: Akbar dispatched armies to Kashmir in 1585-1586 against the Chak dynasty's Yusuf Shah Chak, who was lured to court and imprisoned in February 1586; his son Yaqub's resistance was crushed at the Battle of Hastivanj (October 1586), when the khutba was read in Akbar's name. The coordinates (~76E 33N) are in the Kashmir Valley, added to Akbar's realm within the 1582-1588 window.

w4-700768.name: Truce of Yam-Zapolsky ends the Livonian War
w4-700768.blurb: The Truce of Yam-Zapolsky, signed 15 January 1582 between Ivan IV's Russia and Stephen Báthory's Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, ended the Livonian War. Russia renounced all claims to Livonia and Polotsk, while the Commonwealth returned occupied Russian cities, restoring substantial eastern-Baltic territory to Commonwealth control. The data window 1582-1588 captures this transfer from the Tsardom of Russia to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

w4-700771.name: Mughal Conquest of Orissa — Akbar's Eastern Campaigns
w4-700771.blurb: Akbar's governor Raja Man Singh launched the Mughal conquest of Orissa (Odisha) in 1590–1592, defeating the Afghan Sur successor Nisar Khan Lohani by April 1592 and annexing Orissa to the Bengal Subah. This completed the Mughal absorption of the former Sur Empire's eastern territories. The dataset records 'Sur Empire → Mughal Empire' for the eastern coastal corridor (lng 85.5, lat 19.9 — Odisha coast) in 1588–1595, consistent with this campaign.

w4-700775.name: Dutch Revolt / establishment of the Dutch Republic (1588)
w4-700775.blurb: After the 1581 Act of Abjuration, the States General formally constituted the Dutch Republic in 1588. Under Maurice of Nassau the republic recaptured Breda (1590), Zutphen, Deventer, Nijmegen (1591) and Groningen (1594). The window (1588-1595) and Dutch heartland coordinates (5.3, 52.5) capture the republic displacing Iberian Union control.

w4-700776.name: Henry IV's accession and consolidation of France (1589–1595)
w4-700776.blurb: Henry of Navarre became the first Bourbon king of France as Henry IV upon the assassination of Henry III in August 1589, but faced resistance from the Catholic League and Spain. His conversion to Catholicism at Saint-Denis on 25 July 1593 proved decisive; he was crowned at Chartres in 1594 and absolved by Pope Clement VIII in 1595. These steps merged the Bourbon hereditary lands around lng 1.7, lat 44.7 (central/southern France) into the royal domain (House of Bourbon -> Kingdom of France), within [1588,1595].

w4-700777.name: Moroccan Invasion of the Songhai Empire — Battle of Tondibi
w4-700777.blurb: Ahmad al-Mansur's Saadi army under Judar Pasha crossed the Sahara and on 13 March 1591 routed the Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi (Niger Bend, lng -2.5, lat 15.7), then sacked Gao, Timbuktu, and Djenné, collapsing the Songhai Empire. The Songhai-to-Saadi transfer fits the py1588-y1595 window.

citations.label: Moroccan invasion of the Songhai Empire — Wikipedia

w4-700778.name: Imjin War — Japanese Invasion of Korea
w4-700778.blurb: Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched a massive invasion of Joseon Korea in May 1592 with over 150,000 troops, quickly occupying large portions of the peninsula including Gyeongsang and Chungcheong provinces. The dataset records 'Joseon → Warring States Japan' for this corridor in the window 1588–1595, capturing the height of Japanese occupation. Chinese Ming intervention and Korean naval resistance under Yi Sun-sin ultimately expelled Japanese forces by 1598.

w4-700780.name: Battle of Nong Sarai – Ayutthaya Defeats Toungoo
w4-700780.blurb: King Naresuan of Ayutthaya, having renounced Toungoo vassalage in 1584, routed the last Toungoo invasion at Nong Sarai (18 January 1593), killing crown prince Mingyi Swa. Ayutthaya then counter-attacked, seizing Tavoy and Tenasserim (the Tenasserim coast, ~97.6E/16.1N) by 1595, ending Toungoo's reach into the region. Window [1588,1595], date 1593; territory from First Toungoo Empire to Ayutthaya.

w4-700781.name: Trịnh lords retake Hanoi from the Mạc dynasty (Lê–Mạc War)
w4-700781.blurb: The Lê–Mạc War was a prolonged civil conflict in Đại Việt between the restored Lê dynasty (backed by the Trịnh lords) and the Mạc dynasty. In 1592, Trịnh Tùng's forces decisively defeated the Mạc, and in 1593 Emperor Lê Thế Tông returned to the capital Đông Kinh (modern Hanoi, lat 21.7, lng 106). The Mạc were expelled from the lowland heartland and confined to the northern mountain province of Cao Bằng. The Trịnh lords became the effective rulers of northern Đại Việt in the period 1588–1595.

w4-800001.name: Treaty of Lyon (1601)
w4-800001.blurb: Signed 17 January 1601 to end the Franco-Savoyard War of 1600–1601, the Treaty of Lyon had France relinquish Saluzzo to Savoy and in return gain Bresse, Bugey, Valromey, and Gex — the territories at lng 5.5, lat 46 — which were incorporated into the French crown under the military government of Burgundy.

w4-800002.name: Dissolution of Michael the Brave's Union — Wallachia Reconstituted
w4-800002.blurb: Michael the Brave's brief 1600 union of Wallachia, Transylvania, and Moldavia collapsed after his assassination by Habsburg general Giorgio Basta's forces in August 1601; Wallachian territory (centroid at lng=25.3, lat=44.6) that had been nominally subsumed under the union was reconstituted as the separate Principality of Wallachia.

w4-800003.name: Battle of Sekigahara
w4-800003.blurb: On October 21, 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern Army decisively defeated the Western Army under Ishida Mitsunari at Sekigahara in Mino Province, giving Tokugawa nominal control over all of Japan; Ieyasu was formally appointed shogun by the emperor in 1603, completing the transition from the Warring States (Sengoku) era to the Tokugawa shogunate that would rule Japan for 265 years.

w4-800004.name: Battle of Mirăslău — Michael the Brave loses Transylvania
w4-800004.blurb: Michael the Brave held Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia in personal union from May 1600, but Transylvanian nobles allied with Habsburg general Giorgio Basta defeated him at the Battle of Mirăslău on 18 September 1600, ending his control of Transylvania and reverting it to separate princely rule — distinct from his assassination in August 1601, a later, separate episode.

w4-800006.name: Union of the Crowns 1603
w4-800006.blurb: On 24 March 1603, James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne as James I following the death of Elizabeth I (last Tudor), creating a personal union of the English and Scottish crowns; Scotland remained a separate kingdom with its own Parliament, but the atlas conventionally reassigns Scottish territory to the English polity frame in this snapshot.

w4-800013.name: Treaty of Nasuh Pasha (1612) — Ottoman cession of Kartli to Safavid sphere
w4-800013.blurb: The Treaty of Nasuh Pasha (November 1612) ended the Ottoman–Safavid War of 1603–1618; it reaffirmed the terms of the 1555 Peace of Amasya, requiring the Ottomans to withdraw from Kartli and Kakheti (lat ~42°, lng ~43.8°) and restoring Safavid/Georgian suzerainty over these kingdoms.

w4-800014.name: Ottoman-Safavid War 1603–1612 — Safavid recovery of Azerbaijan and Armenia (Treaty of Nasuh Pasha)
w4-800014.blurb: Following Shah Abbas I's reconquest of Tabriz (1603) and a series of Safavid victories, the Treaty of Nasuh Pasha (1612) returned Ottoman-held Azerbaijan, Shirvan, and parts of Armenia to the Safavids. The centroid (lng ~47, lat ~39.7) corresponds to the Azerbaijan/Armenia region recovered by the Safavids.

w4-800017.name: Nyaungyan/Restored Toungoo reconquest of Lan Na under Anaukpetlun
w4-800017.blurb: After the first Toungoo Empire's collapse in the 1590s, Lan Na drifted into semi-independence and nominal Siamese suzerainty. King Anaukpetlun of the Nyaungyan/Restored Toungoo dynasty intervened militarily in Lan Na in 1614 following a request by the lord of Nan, defeated Chiang Mai's ruler and installed a Burmese-aligned ruler, restoring Burmese suzerainty. The dataset records the 1612–1619 transition from Lan Na to Toungoo (here labelled 'First Toungoo').

w4-800018.name: Burmese–Siamese War (1613–1618) – Restored Toungoo Recovers Tavoy and Lan Na
w4-800018.blurb: After King Anaukpetlun reunited Burma under the Restored Toungoo (Nyaungyan) dynasty, he invaded Ayutthayan-held territories from 1613. Burmese forces captured Tavoy (Dawei) in 1613 and conquered Lan Na (Chiang Mai region) by 1614–1615. Fighting continued until a peace treaty in 1618 confirmed Burmese sovereignty over Lan Na and northern Tenasserim, while Ayutthaya retained the southern Tanintharyi coast.

w4-800022.name: Bijapur Sultanate Annexation of Bidar
w4-800022.blurb: The Bidar Sultanate (Barid Shahi dynasty), the smallest of the five Deccan Sultanates, was conquered and absorbed by the Bijapur Sultanate (Adil Shahi dynasty) in 1619. Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur defeated Amir Barid III, the last Bidar ruler, ending the Barid Shahi dynasty. Bidar's territory was incorporated into the expanding Bijapur Sultanate.

w4-800024.name: Iberian Union — Portuguese Ceylon under the Spanish Crown (1580)
w4-800024.blurb: The Iberian Union of 1580, in which Philip II of Spain claimed the Portuguese crown, brought Portuguese overseas territories including Portuguese Ceylon under the Spanish Habsburg monarchy until 1640. From=Portuguese Ceylon, to=Spanish Empire reflects this nominal union; the 1612-1619 worklist window likely captures an atlas lag rather than the 1580 union date itself.

w4-800025.name: Portuguese (Iberian Union) conquest of French Maranhão (France Équinoxiale)
w4-800025.blurb: France Équinoxiale, a French colony established in 1612 at São Luís in modern Maranhão, was attacked by Portuguese-Tabajara forces under Alexandre de Moura. After the Battle of Guaxenduba (November 1614), French resistance collapsed and the fort at São Luís surrendered on 1 November 1615. Portugal (then under the Iberian Union) expelled the French; control was consolidated by 1619. The data window 1612-1619 captures this conquest.

w4-800029.name: Regrouping of the Oirat Confederation in the Junggar Basin (c. 1619–1620)
w4-800029.blurb: After conflicts with the Khalkha Altan Khan, the Choros and allied Oirat tribes (Dörbet, Khoid) regrouped around the Black Irtysh and Ili Valley c.1619–1620 under Khara Khula, reconstituting the Oirat Confederation that controlled the Junggar Basin; this was the precursor to the formal Dzungar Khanate (Erdeni Batur, 1634). The dataset's Junggar-Basin transition to 'Oirat Confederation' in the 1612–1619 window reflects this reorganisation, though the polity labels are partly anachronistic.

w4-800033.name: Later Jin capture of Liaoyang and Shenyang
w4-800033.blurb: Following the decisive Later Jin victory at the Battle of Sarhu (1619), Nurhaci's forces captured Liaoyang (March 1621) and Shenyang (April 1621), the two principal Ming administrative and military centers in Liaodong, effectively transferring control of the entire Liaodong region to Later Jin and forcing the Ming to retreat behind Shanhai Pass; Nurhaci relocated his capital to Liaoyang and then Shenyang.

w4-800035.name: Electoral transfer of the Upper Palatinate to Bavaria (1621–1622)
w4-800035.blurb: After Frederick V of the Palatinate's defeat at the Battle of White Mountain (November 1620), Emperor Ferdinand II transferred Frederick's electoral dignity and the Upper Palatinate to Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria by the Treaty of Munich (October 1619) and formally by imperial decree in 1621–1623. Bavaria thus gained the Upper Palatinate as reward for its military support of the Emperor. The centroid is in the Upper Palatinate.

w4-800038.name: Peace of Nikolsburg (1621)
w4-800038.blurb: Bethlen Gabor of Transylvania invaded Royal Hungary in 1619 in alliance with the Bohemian rebels. After the Habsburg victory at the Battle of White Mountain (1620), Bethlen negotiated the Peace of Nikolsburg (31 December 1621), by which he renounced the Hungarian crown but received seven counties of Upper Hungary (northeast Royal Hungary) and the fortress of Munkács. The centroid corresponds to northeastern Royal Hungary (Zemplén/Ung county area) ceded to Transylvania.

w4-800040.name: Safavid capture of Kandahar (First Mughal-Safavid War over Kandahar)
w4-800040.blurb: Shah Abbas I besieged Kandahar beginning May 1622 and captured it on 22 June 1622 after a 45-day siege; the Mughal garrison was too small and Prince Khurram refused to lead a relief expedition, resulting in a decisive Safavid victory and transfer of the city and surrounding region (centroid lat ~32.1°, lng ~65.7°) to Safavid Iran.

w4-800042.name: Foundation of the Yarubid Imamate
w4-800042.blurb: In 1624, Nasir bin Murshid al-Yarubi was elected Imam at Rustaq, founding the Yarubid (Ya'aruba) Imamate and launching the unification of interior Oman. He rapidly seized Rustaq, Nakhal, and Nizwa from rival Omani factions, transferring these approximately 2,600 km² of hinterland territory from the Iberian Union's sphere of influence to the new Yarubid polity — decades before his successor Sultan bin Saif completed the coastal expulsion by taking Muscat from the Portuguese in 1650.

w4-800043.name: Later Jin Liaodong campaigns (1622–1625)
w4-800043.blurb: Between 1622 and 1625, Nurhaci's Later Jin forces consolidated control over remaining Ming-held territory in Liaodong, including coastal and inland areas north of Shenyang; the Liaodong Peninsula and associated territory fell to Later Jin by 1625, halted only by the Ming defensive victory at Ningyuan in February 1626 where Yuan Chonghuan's artillery repulsed the Jin assault.

w4-800044.name: Spanish-Moro campaigns of the late 1620s
w4-800044.blurb: Spain conducted repeated expeditions against the Moro sultanates of the southern Philippines in the 1620s to suppress piracy and extend colonial control. In 1628–1629, a major Spanish expedition attacked Maguindanao and Sulu territories in the Visayas, shifting nominal control of islands in the Brunei sphere to Spain.

w4-800045.name: Ming counteroffensive after Battle of Ningyuan — Yuan Chonghuan's recovery of Jinzhou corridor
w4-800045.blurb: After Ming commander Yuan Chonghuan repulsed Nurhaci's assault at Ningyuan (February 1626) — the first major Ming victory against Later Jin — he exploited Later Jin's disarray following Nurhaci's death (September 1626) to push north, refortifying Jinzhou and recovering a strip of territory in the Liaoxi corridor between Shanhai Pass and Jinzhou, which briefly returned to Ming control.

w4-800046.name: Treaty of Lübeck (1629)
w4-800046.blurb: The Treaty of Lübeck (22 May 1629) ended Denmark's intervention in the Thirty Years' War; Christian IV withdrew from German affairs and relinquished claims over the northern German bishoprics and territories he had occupied, which reverted to their HRE princes and minor states. The centroid near Wolfenbüttel/Lower Saxony reflects this restoration of imperial territory.

w4-800048.name: Treaty of Lübeck (1629)
w4-800048.blurb: The Treaty of Lübeck (22 May 1629) ended Denmark's intervention in the Thirty Years' War; Denmark-Norway agreed to withdraw from the war and renounced its claims over the northern German bishoprics (Verden, Schwerin, Halberstadt, Minden) it had occupied. These territories returned to imperial/Habsburg authority, representing ~24,500 km² in northern Germany.

w4-800051.name: Treaty of Lübeck (1629); imperial restoration of Jutland to Denmark
w4-800051.blurb: In the Danish phase of the Thirty Years' War, Wallenstein's imperial forces occupied Jutland, Schleswig and Holstein in 1627-1628. The Treaty of Lübeck (May/June 1629) ended Danish involvement and restored these territories to Christian IV of Denmark-Norway. The window (1629-1632) and Jutland/Schleswig coordinates (9.8, 54.3) fit this Habsburg withdrawal and restoration to Denmark. (The original blurb's reference to the 'Convention of Klosterzeven' was an error - that belongs to the 1757 Seven Years' War.)

w4-800055.name: Li Zicheng's rebel campaigns in Shaanxi/northern Shanxi (1631–1632)
w4-800055.blurb: Li Zicheng joined the peasant rebel coalition under Gao Yingxiang in the late 1620s. By 1631–1632 rebel forces had seized extensive territory in northern Shaanxi and adjacent Shanxi/Ordos areas (~110°E, 38°N), the collapse of Ming frontier defense having been accelerated by the 1628–1631 famines. This polygon records Ming losing this region to Li Zicheng's (and allied rebel) forces during their campaigns in that period.

w4-800056.name: Thirty Years War — Swedish invasion of the Holy Roman Empire (1630–1632)
w4-800056.blurb: Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania in June 1630 and swept south through the Holy Roman Empire, winning the Battle of Breitenfeld (1631) and the Battle of the Lech (1632). The centroid at lng 8, lat 49.4 (Palatinate/Rhine-Main area) reflects Swedish military control of territory previously under Iberian Union (Spanish) Habsburg suzerainty as Swedish forces advanced into western Germany 1631–1632.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Swedish intervention in the Thirty Years' War

w4-800057.name: Swedish invasion of Bavaria (Thirty Years' War)
w4-800057.blurb: In spring 1632, Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden crossed the Danube and invaded Electoral Bavaria, forcing Elector Maximilian I to flee Munich; Swedish forces occupied most of Bavaria, accounting for this large transfer of Bavarian territory into Swedish control during the Thirty Years' War.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Thirty Years' War – Swedish phase

w4-800059.name: Swedish intervention in Thirty Years' War — Pomerania occupied (1630)
w4-800059.blurb: Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania in June 1630 and concluded the Treaty of Stettin (10 July 1630) with the Pomeranian duke, giving Sweden occupation of Pomeranian ports and territory. Brandenburg, which had dynastic claims on Pomerania, was forced to yield control of Pomeranian territory to the Swedish military. The centroid corresponds to Pomerania, the contested zone.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Swedish intervention in the Thirty Years' War

w4-800060.name: Swedish Invasion of Saxony / Thirty Years' War (Swedish Phase)
w4-800060.blurb: Following the Treaty of Bärwalde (1631) and the Battle of Breitenfeld (September 1631), Sweden and Saxony formed an alliance against the Emperor, and Swedish forces under Gustavus Adolphus swept across central Germany into Bavaria and the surrounding regions by 1632. The Cliopatria record reflects Swedish military control over the Electoral Saxon/Thuringian heartland that Sweden occupied during 1631–1632.

w4-800061.name: Swedish invasion of the Holy Roman Empire / Battle of Breitenfeld
w4-800061.blurb: Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus intervened in the Thirty Years' War in 1630 and won the decisive Battle of Breitenfeld (September 1631) against the Catholic League and Habsburg forces, enabling Swedish armies to overrun much of Saxony, Bohemia, and adjacent Habsburg territories by 1632.

w4-800064.name: Dzungar (Oirat) expansion into Western Moghulistan/Yarkent Khanate borderlands (1630s)
w4-800064.blurb: The Dzungar Khanate under Erdeni Batur expanded westward from its base near the Tarbagatai Mountains in the mid-1630s, pressing into the Ili valley and eastern portions of the Yarkent (Western Moghulistan) sphere around the Tian Shan. The centroid (lng ~76.8, lat ~40.7) corresponds to the Ili-Tarim basin transitional zone overrun in these early Dzungar campaigns.

w4-800065.name: Oirat / Early Dzungar Consolidation of Semirechye
w4-800065.blurb: In the 1630s the Oirat Confederation under Khara Khula and his son Erdeni Batur (who assumed the Hongtaiji title in 1634 and relocated to the Ili valley by 1636) consolidated power across Dzungaria and western Moghulistan (~77E 41N, Semirechye). Remnant Moghul authority was displaced as Erdeni Batur unified the Oirats into what became the Dzungar heartland, within the 1632-1636 window.

w4-800066.name: Qasimid-Zaydi Expulsion of the Ottomans from Yemen
w4-800066.blurb: The Zaydi Imam al-Mu'ayyad Muhammad (Qasimid dynasty) drove the Ottomans from Yemen, capturing Zabid (1634) and letting the last Ottoman forces depart Mocha by 1636, ending the first Ottoman period in Yemen. The coordinates (44.9E, 15.9N) lie in central Yemen, the Qasimid heartland. Transfer Ottoman Empire -> Qasimids fits the 1632-1636 window.

w4-800067.name: Spanish offensive into northern France (Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand's campaign)
w4-800067.blurb: In 1636, Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand led a Spanish Netherlands army deep into northern France, capturing Corbie and briefly threatening Paris before being driven back. The atlas centroid (lng 4, lat 49.2, Ardennes/Luxemburg fringe) reflects the Iberian Union's Spanish Netherlands forces temporarily controlling territory that France had claimed or contested along the frontier.

w4-800070.name: Manchu Conquest of Inner Mongolia and Proclamation of the Qing Dynasty
w4-800070.blurb: Hong Taiji, ruler of the Later Jin dynasty, completed the conquest of Inner Mongolia through three successive campaigns against Ligdan Khan's Northern Yuan. Ligdan Khan's son Ejei surrendered the Yuan imperial seal to Hong Taiji in 1635. In April 1636 Mongol, Manchu, and Han notables proclaimed Hong Taiji Emperor, and the dynasty was renamed from Later Jin to Great Qing. Forty-nine Mongol tribal leaders attended the enthronement; their tribes were reorganized into the leagues and banners of Inner Mongolia.

citations.label: Qing dynasty in Inner Asia - Wikipedia

w4-800071.name: Later Jin invasion of northern China / Battle area around Xuanfu–Datong corridor (1632–1636)
w4-800071.blurb: Between 1632 and 1636, Hong Taiji's Later Jin (renamed Qing in 1636) launched repeated raids deep into Ming northern China, including the 1632 campaign past the Great Wall into Shanxi and the 1634 incursion through Xuanfu and Datong. The centroid (~117°E, 41°N — the Zhangjihakou/Xuanhua area north of Beijing) falls in the corridor where Qing forces repeatedly overran Ming frontier defenses, and the atlas records this zone shifting to Later Jin control by the 1636 snapshot.

w4-800072.name: Second Manchu (Qing) invasion of Joseon – Treaty of Samjeondo
w4-800072.blurb: In December 1636 Hong Taiji invaded Korea; King Injo surrendered in January 1637 (Treaty of Samjeondo), compelling Joseon to break with Ming and become a Qing tributary. The northwestern Korean border zone near lng 125.9 E / lat 39.5 N reflects the resulting Qing-aligned realignment, within the [1632,1636] window (the 'Later Jin'/Qing being the same emergent power).

w4-800075.name: Dutch WIC Settlement of the Guiana Coast (Essequibo region)
w4-800075.blurb: The Dutch West India Company (WIC) extended its formal jurisdiction over the Guiana coast settlements — principally the Essequibo trading post region — in the early 1630s under the States-General's WIC charter. This area (the Guiana coast near lng -52.4, lat 1.8) had nominally fallen within Spain's claimed domain. The Dutch establishment of permanent posts at the Essequibo, Berbice, and Pomeroon rivers between 1632 and 1636 effectively displaced Spanish nominal sovereignty. The atlas labels this Dutch WIC holding as 'New Netherland,' its umbrella term for WIC territory.

citations.label: Dutch colonisation of the Guianas – Wikipedia

w4-800076.name: Li Zicheng's Rebellion (Late Ming Peasant Uprising)
w4-800076.blurb: Li Zicheng rose as rebel leader after Gao Yingxiang's death in 1636, proclaiming himself Chuang Wang (Dashing King) and controlling much of Shaanxi while expanding into neighboring provinces. The coordinates (111.6E, 37.6N) lie in Shanxi, consistent with mid-1630s expansion; he captured Beijing in 1644. Transfer Ming Dynasty -> Li Zicheng fits the 1632-1636 window.

w4-800088.name: Swedish military occupation of Lusatia during Thirty Years' War
w4-800088.blurb: Swedish forces under Field Marshal Johan Banér raided deep into Saxony and Bohemia in 1639–1640, temporarily occupying Lusatia (centroid lng 14.8, lat 51.1, Görlitz area) as part of the Swedish offensive phase of the Thirty Years' War. The atlas records this as a temporary transfer from Habsburg to Swedish control before the region was recovered.
