w4-800089.name: Portuguese Restoration War; separation from the Iberian Union
w4-800089.blurb: On 1 December 1640 Portuguese nobles overthrew Spanish rule in Lisbon and proclaimed the Duke of Braganza as King João IV, ending 60 years of the Iberian Union. Portuguese overseas possessions in West Africa (coords near lng -6.9, lat 4.1) reverted from the Spanish-controlled union to the independent Portuguese Crown, matching worklist transition Spanish Empire -> Portuguese Empire (1636-1640).

w4-800090.name: Peace of Prague (1635)
w4-800090.blurb: The Peace of Prague (30 May 1635) ended the Swedish-HRE phase of the Thirty Years' War. Sweden retained its Pomeranian bridgeheads (Stralsund, Stettin area) and Brandenburg was obliged to recognize Swedish occupation of western Pomerania for 40 years, effectively ceding that territory to Swedish control until 1648. The centroid near Pomerania matches this transfer from Brandenburg to Sweden.

w4-800092.name: Swedish occupation of Brandenburg following the Battle of Wittstock
w4-800092.blurb: After the Battle of Wittstock on 4 October 1636, where Swedish forces under Johan Banér defeated the combined Imperial-Saxon army, Sweden became militarily dominant in Brandenburg. Elector George William was powerless to expel them and fled to Ducal Prussia, where he died in 1640. The data window 1636-1640 reflects this Swedish military control, which persisted until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

w4-800093.name: Treaty of Zuhab (1639) — Ottoman-Safavid border settlement
w4-800093.blurb: The Treaty of Zuhab (also called the Treaty of Qasr-e Shirin), signed on 17 May 1639, ended the Ottoman-Safavid War of 1623–1639. It ceded Mesopotamia including Baghdad permanently to the Ottomans while restoring Erivan and eastern Armenia to the Safavids; the centroid (lng ~44.9, lat ~33.2) corresponds squarely to Ottoman Iraq (Mesopotamia).

w4-800095.name: Mughal recapture of Kandahar under Shah Jahan (1638)
w4-800095.blurb: Shah Jahan dispatched an army under Ali Mardan Khan (the Safavid governor who defected to the Mughals) in 1638; Kandahar was surrendered to the Mughals without significant resistance, and the Safavid garrison withdrew, restoring the city to Mughal control until the next Safavid reconquest.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Kandahar campaigns of Shah Jahan

w4-800096.name: Qing (Later Jin) invasion of Joseon – Second Manchu invasion of Korea
w4-800096.blurb: On 9 December 1636, Hong Taiji (now Emperor of the newly proclaimed Qing dynasty) invaded Joseon after its court refused to bow to him at his imperial proclamation ceremony. Qing forces captured Seoul within days; King Injo was besieged at Namhan Mountain Fortress and surrendered on 30 January 1637. Joseon became a Qing tributary vassal (Byeongja Horan), ending its relationship with the Ming dynasty. The crown prince was taken hostage to Shenyang.

citations.label: Manchu invasion of Korea – New World Encyclopedia

w4-800097.name: Ali Mardan Khan defects and surrenders Kandahar to the Mughal Empire
w4-800097.blurb: In 1638 the Persian governor of Kandahar, Ali Mardan Khan, defected to the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan and handed over the city, returning it to Mughal control after a period of Safavid possession (since 1622). Shah Jahan quickly repaired the fortifications. The atlas window 1636–1640 captures the period when Safavid control weakened and the defection occurred, corresponding to the Safavid-to-Mughal transfer.

w4-800099.name: Portuguese independence from Spain — restoration of Portuguese colonial administration
w4-800099.blurb: The Portuguese Restoration War began on 1 December 1640 when the Duke of Braganza was proclaimed King João IV, ending the Iberian Union (1580–1640); Portuguese colonial territories in Southeast Asia including the Estado da India entities in Malacca and the Malay peninsula reverted from Spanish to Portuguese administration. The centroid at ~102.7°E / 0.2°N corresponds to the Malacca/southern Malay peninsula area.

w4-800100.name: Portuguese Restoration / Dissolution of the Iberian Union
w4-800100.blurb: On 1 December 1640, Portuguese conspirators deposed the Habsburg vicereine, acclaimed John IV as king, and ended sixty years of Iberian dynastic union. Spain, reconstituted without Portugal, continued under Philip IV; the atlas relabels the surviving Spanish territory from 'Iberian Union' to 'Kingdom of Spain'.

w4-800101.name: Dutch capture of Portuguese Malacca
w4-800101.blurb: During the Iberian Union, Portugal's Asian colonies were targeted by the Dutch; after Portugal revolted against Spain in December 1640, a combined Dutch-Johor force captured Portuguese Malacca in January 1641. The from=Spanish Empire (Iberian Union authority) / to=Portuguese Colonies labelling is imprecise, but the 1636-1640 window reflects the period of Iberian Union authority over Malacca just before its fall to the Dutch.

w4-800105.name: Swedish occupation of Pomeranian territories (Thirty Years' War)
w4-800105.blurb: After the death of the last Pomeranian duke (Bogislaw XIV, 1637), Brandenburg claimed Pomerania by treaty but Swedish forces maintained military occupation; by 1641–1642, Sweden had consolidated control over much of Pomerania including areas that had been under Brandenburg administration, anticipating the Peace of Westphalia settlement.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Pomerania in the Thirty Years' War

w4-800106.name: Swedish campaigns in Saxony — Thirty Years War
w4-800106.blurb: Swedish forces under Field Marshal Lennart Torstenson launched an offensive into Saxony in 1641–1642, occupying large parts of Electoral Saxony and defeating the Imperialists at the Second Battle of Breitenfeld (November 1642). The atlas records Swedish military control over Saxonian territory in this period of the Thirty Years War.

w4-800108.name: Li Zicheng's Rebellion: Conquest of Henan
w4-800108.blurb: Li Zicheng's peasant uprising turned into an organized conquest of central China from 1641. He captured Luoyang in early 1641, killing the Prince of Fu, then swept through Henan and Huguang, taking Xiangyang in 1642. The coordinates (~111E 35N) place this in central/southern Shanxi-Henan, the heart of Li's 1640-1642 conquests before his capture of Beijing in 1644. Territory moved from Ming to Li Zicheng within the window.

w4-800109.name: Dutch West India Company seizes Portuguese Brazil (1630-1641)
w4-800109.blurb: The Dutch West India Company invaded Portuguese Brazil in 1630 and by 1641 controlled more than half of the Brazilian coast, capturing Maranhao in 1641. Coordinates (-40.8, -4.6) point to northeastern Brazil near Maranhao/Ceara. The from->to labeled Portuguese Empire -> 'New Netherland' in the 1640-1642 window reflects this Dutch expansion (the dataset's 'New Netherland' label conflates the Dutch colonial possessions; the relevant entity is Dutch Brazil).

w4-800114.name: Fall of Beijing to the Qing and formation of the Southern Ming (Hongguang Emperor)
w4-800114.blurb: When Li Zicheng's rebels captured Beijing in April 1644 and the Chongzhen Emperor committed suicide, Ming loyalists in the south proclaimed Zhu Yousong as the Hongguang Emperor at Nanjing on 19 June 1644, inaugurating the Southern Ming. Qing forces took Nanjing in May 1645, capturing Hongguang; subsequent Southern Ming courts continued resistance until 1662. The dataset transition from 'Ming Dynasty' to 'Southern Ming' (window [1642,1645]) reflects the Qing seizure of the Yangtze heartland.

w4-800115.name: Tây Sơn and Qing conquest collapse Li Zicheng's Shun dynasty; Southern Ming expands briefly
w4-800115.blurb: Li Zicheng's Shun dynasty, which briefly held Beijing (1644), was shattered at the Battle of Shanhai Pass and driven south by a combined Qing–Wu Sangui force. As the Shun collapsed in 1644–1645, Ming loyalists established Southern Ming courts in Nanjing and elsewhere, temporarily occupying former Shun-held central Chinese territories in the Yangtze basin before Qing forces also overran those. The transfer from Li Zicheng's domain to Southern Ming control in the 1642–1645 window reflects this short-lived Ming loyalist reclamation of central China.

w4-800116.name: English Civil War – Parliamentary Advances (Marston Moor / Naseby)
w4-800116.blurb: The English Civil War (1642-1651) saw Parliamentary forces gain the north after Marston Moor (1644) and crush Royalist field armies at Naseby (14 June 1645), leaving most of England under Parliamentary control by 1645. The Commonwealth itself was proclaimed in 1649, but the territorial shift from Royalist to Parliamentary control (~2W 53N, northern England) occurs within the 1642-1645 window.

w4-800117.name: Insurrection of Pernambuco and Portuguese reconquest of Dutch Brazil (1645)
w4-800117.blurb: After the recall of Johan Maurits in 1644 and growing planter resentment, Joao Fernandes Vieira and Andre Vidal de Negreiros launched the Insurrection of Pernambuco on 13 June 1645; by the end of 1645 the Portuguese had recovered most of Dutch Brazil except Recife. The from->to ('New Netherland' -> Portuguese Empire) at -40.8, -4.6 in the 1642-1645 window captures this reconquest.

w4-800120.name: Qing Defeat of the Shun Dynasty (Li Zicheng)
w4-800120.blurb: After routing Li Zicheng at Shanhai Pass (May 1644), Qing forces under Dodo and Ajige pursued the Shun dynasty south and west; Li abandoned Xi'an in early 1645 and died in Hubei later that year, ceding his Shanxi–Henan holdings (centroid lng 111, lat 37) to Qing control.

w4-800121.name: Qing conquest of Ming China; fall of northern China
w4-800121.blurb: In 1644, Beijing fell first to the rebel Li Zicheng and then to the Manchu Qing forces under Prince Regent Dorgon, who allied with the Ming general Wu Sangui at the Battle of Shanhai Pass on 27 May 1644. The Qing swept south through 1645, capturing Yangzhou and Nanjing. The transfer between 1642 and 1645 (Ming Dynasty -> Qing Dynasty) reflects this takeover of the Chinese heartland.

citations.label: Transition from Ming to Qing – Wikipedia

w4-800122.name: Qing conquest of Li Zicheng's Shun dynasty
w4-800122.blurb: Li Zicheng's Shun dynasty captured Beijing in April 1644, ending the Ming, but was defeated by combined Qing and Wu Sangui forces at the Battle of Shanhai Pass on 27 May 1644. Qing armies drove Shun forces from Shaanxi by 1645 and Li Zicheng died in Hubei in 1645. Matches the Li Zicheng (Shun) → Qing transfer in the 1642-1645 window.

citations.label: Transition from Ming to Qing – Wikipedia

w4-800125.name: Peace of Westphalia — Brandenburg gains Hinterpommern
w4-800125.blurb: The Peace of Westphalia (October 24, 1648) confirmed that Sweden retained Vorpommern (Western Pomerania) while Brandenburg-Prussia received Hinterpommern (Eastern Pomerania, ~29,000 km²) centered near the centroid (12.9°E, 53°N). Brandenburg also gained the bishoprics of Cammin, Halberstadt, and Minden, plus reversion rights over Magdeburg.

w4-800127.name: Peace of Westphalia - division of Pomerania
w4-800127.blurb: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) partitioned the Duchy of Pomerania between Sweden and Brandenburg-Prussia after the extinction of the Griffin ducal line. Sweden received Western Pomerania (Vorpommern) including Stettin and the islands; Brandenburg received Farther Pomerania. The precise border was finalised in the Treaty of Stettin (1653). The from=Swedish Empire / to=Brandenburg-Prussia and 1645-1648 window match the settlement.

w4-800128.name: Peace of Westphalia (Osnabruck/Munster)
w4-800128.blurb: The Peace of Westphalia (October 1648), ending the Thirty Years' War, awarded Brandenburg-Prussia substantial territories from the Holy Roman Empire's minor states, including Farther Pomerania, the secularised bishoprics of Halberstadt, Minden, and Kammin, and reversion rights to Magdeburg. The coordinates (12.3E, 53N) point to the Pomeranian Baltic coast, the core of these Westphalian gains, which dramatically enlarged Brandenburg's power base.

citations.label: Growth of Brandenburg-Prussia - German History Documents

w4-800133.name: Shah Abbas II of Persia recaptures Kandahar from the Mughals
w4-800133.blurb: Taking advantage of Mughal overextension during the disastrous Balkh campaign (1646–1647), Shah Abbas II marched from Isfahan with 40,000 troops in 1648, besieged Kandahar from December 1648, and captured it on 22 February 1649. Three subsequent Mughal attempts (1651, 1652, 1653) all failed to retake the city, which remained Safavid. The atlas dates the transfer 1645–1648, reflecting the Safavid preparation period through the fall.

w4-800136.name: Insurrection of Pernambuco - Portuguese reconquest of Dutch Brazil (1645-1648)
w4-800136.blurb: On 13 June 1645, Luso-Brazilian settlers rose in revolt against the Dutch West India Company in Pernambuco (the Insurrection of Pernambuco). By the end of 1645 the Dutch were confined to coastal strongholds, and the Portuguese victories at the First and Second Battles of Guararapes (1648-1649) sealed their fate in the interior. The data entry (New Netherland to Portuguese Empire, py=1645, y=1648) reflects the period in which Dutch Brazil's interior effectively returned to Portuguese control, though the formal Dutch surrender of Recife did not occur until 1654.

w4-800137.name: Peace of Westphalia (1648): end of French wartime occupation of Lorraine
w4-800137.blurb: During the Thirty Years' War France repeatedly occupied the Duchy of Lorraine (coord 6.2E/48.7N). The Peace of Westphalia (1648) confirmed French possession of the Three Bishoprics and parts of Alsace but left Lorraine's status deliberately ambiguous ('passed over in silence'), with Lorraine regaining a degree of autonomy. The dataset's 1645–1648 'France → Duchy of Lorraine' shift reflects the end of direct French wartime occupation recognised at Westphalia.

w4-800138.name: Peace of Westphalia partitions Pomerania — Swedish Pomerania established (1648)
w4-800138.blurb: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) and the Treaty of Stettin (1653) partitioned the Duchy of Pomerania: Western Pomerania (Vorpommern) including Rügen became Swedish Pomerania while Farther Pomerania passed to Brandenburg. The coordinates (13.5°E, 54.1°N) correspond to western Baltic Pomerania; from=Swedish Empire, to=Swedish Pomerania reflects the constitution of Swedish Pomerania as a distinct entity in the 1645-1648 window.

w4-800142.name: Qing conquest of southern China and the Southern Ming
w4-800142.blurb: After the fall of Beijing in 1644, Southern Ming rump regimes held out across south and southwest China. The Qing systematically defeated these courts through the 1640s-1650s: the Yongli Emperor's court was the last to hold large territories in Guangxi and Yunnan. The 1648-1653 window corresponds to Qing advances that pushed the Yongli court out of Guangxi and into the southwest, consolidating Qing control over the territories shown (Cliopatria centroid lat 26.1, lng 110.2, in the Guangxi/Hunan region).

citations.label: Transition from Ming to Qing – Wikipedia

w4-800146.name: Mughal consolidation of former Ahmadnagar territory under Aurangzeb (1652–1653)
w4-800146.blurb: The Ahmadnagar Sultanate was extinguished in 1636 when Aurangzeb (Mughal Deccan viceroy) defeated the regent Shahaji and partitioned it. During Aurangzeb's second viceroyalty he consolidated direct control over former Ahmadnagar lands in the western Deccan, founding Aurangabad as the Deccan suba capital in 1653 (lat 19.2, lng 74.6, the Ahmadnagar/Nashik region). The 1648-1653 window reflects this administrative consolidation rather than the original 1636 conquest; the Ahmadnagar-to-Mughal framing is correct.

w4-800147.name: Qing Conquest of Yunnan - defeat of the Southern Ming
w4-800147.blurb: The last Southern Ming court, under the Yongli Emperor Zhu Youlang, retreated to Yunnan province as Qing forces advanced westward after 1644. In 1659 Wu Sangui led Qing armies into Yunnan, capturing Kunming and forcing the Yongli Emperor to flee into Burma. Wu Sangui subsequently pursued and captured him in 1662, and the emperor was executed in Yunnan, ending the Southern Ming resistance and completing Qing control over southwest China.

w4-800150.name: English conquest of Jamaica from Spain (1655)
w4-800150.blurb: In May 1655 an English fleet under Penn and Venables, sent by Cromwell's Western Design, captured Jamaica from Spain; Spain formally ceded it in the Treaty of Madrid (1670). The coordinates (~77°W, 18°N) match Jamaica; from=Spanish Empire, to=English Colonial Empire matches the 1653-1659 window.

w4-800151.name: Mughal siege of Golconda (1656); cession of Ramgir to the Mughals
w4-800151.blurb: Prince Aurangzeb used the defection of Golconda's minister Mir Jumla as a pretext to invade in early 1656. Mughal forces under Muhammad Sultan swept into Hyderabad and the sultan Abdullah Qutb Shah retreated to Golconda fortress. The peace terms forced Golconda to cede Ramgir as dowry plus a large indemnity before Aurangzeb withdrew on Shah Jahan's orders. The window (1653-1659) and coordinates (81.1, 18.6, northern Telangana) capture these territorial concessions.

w4-800152.name: Mughal conquest of Bidar and surrounding Deccan territory from Bijapur
w4-800152.blurb: During Aurangzeb's second Deccan viceroyalty he invaded Bijapur in 1657, captured Bidar Fort in a 27-day siege and then Kalyani; a treaty negotiated by Shah Jahan ceded Bidar, Parenda, and Kalyani to the Mughals. The from=Bijapur Sultanate / to=Mughal Empire and 1653-1659 window span the campaign and treaty.

w4-800155.name: Russian Conquest of Transbaikalia
w4-800155.blurb: Russian Cossack forces pushed into Transbaikalia (Lake Baikal region, 114.2E/54N) in the 1640s–1650s, founding the fortress of Nerchinsk in 1654. The dataset labels the territory 'Golden Horde' — an anachronism for the Buryat-Mongol and nomadic peoples there — but the Russian advance through the [py=1653, y=1659] window is well attested, setting the stage for the 1689 Treaty of Nerchinsk with Qing China.

w4-800159.name: Koxinga's Conquest of Dutch Formosa (Siege of Fort Zeelandia)
w4-800159.blurb: Ming loyalist Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga) besieged the VOC stronghold of Fort Zeelandia on Taiwan from April 1661, forcing the Dutch governor Frederick Coyett to surrender on 1 February 1662. Koxinga expelled the Dutch Republic's colonial administration after 38 years and established the Kingdom of Tungning as a Southern Ming loyalist base. The territory thus passed from the Dutch Republic to Zheng's Southern Ming successor state, exactly matching the dataset's 'Dutch Republic → Southern Ming' transfer.

w4-800160.name: Mughal conquest of Bidar and Kalyani from Bijapur
w4-800160.blurb: Aurangzeb, as Mughal viceroy of the Deccan, captured Bidar Fort from Bijapur in March 1657 in a 27-day siege and then Kalyani; a peace treaty negotiated by Shah Jahan ceded Bidar, Parenda, and Kalyani to the Mughals. The from=Bijapur Sultanate / to=Mughal Empire and the 1659-1662 window reflect consolidation of these cessions after Aurangzeb became emperor in 1658.

w4-800161.name: Burmese–Siamese War (1662–1664): Ayutthaya's Occupation of Upper Tenasserim and Lan Na
w4-800161.blurb: In 1662, King Narai of Ayutthaya exploited internal Toungoo Burmese unrest (the Ming refugee crisis) to invade Lan Na and the upper Tenasserim coast, getting Martaban to switch sides in March 1662 and occupying the coast, then capturing Chiang Mai in February 1663. The Restored Toungoo Empire recovered these territories by 1664. This entry reflects the brief Siamese occupation of border territories along the upper Tenasserim subsequently recovered by the Burmese.

w4-800162.name: English Restoration (1660)
w4-800162.blurb: After the collapse of the Protectorate following Oliver Cromwell's death and Richard Cromwell's brief rule, Parliament invited Charles II to return from exile, restoring the monarchy in May 1660. The Commonwealth of England was dissolved and the Kingdom of England re-proclaimed. From 'Commonwealth of England' to 'Kingdom of England'; the worklist window py=1659, y=1662 captures the consolidation of the Restoration.

w4-800163.name: Treaty of Cardis (Kardis)
w4-800163.blurb: The Treaty of Cardis (21 June / 1 July 1661, ratifications exchanged 1662) ended the Russo-Swedish War of 1656–58. Russia surrendered all territory captured in Swedish Livonia and Ingria, restoring the pre-war frontier of the 1617 Treaty of Stolbovo. The coordinates point to the Ingrian / Gulf of Finland borderland reverting to Swedish control.

w4-800167.name: Dutch VOC returns eastern Timor to Portugal; Treaty of Lisbon (1661) aftermath
w4-800167.blurb: The Dutch VOC had seized the Solor and Flores area from the Portuguese in 1636 and disputed Timor throughout the 1640s–50s. The Treaty of The Hague (1661), known as the Treaty of Lisbon, saw the Dutch and Portuguese settle colonial boundaries: Portugal ceded Ceylon and other possessions to the Dutch in exchange for recognition of Portuguese Timor. By the late 1660s–70s, the Portuguese Topasses maintained de facto control of eastern Timor while the Dutch consolidated the west.

w4-800168.name: Russian conquest of the Baikal region - subduing the Buryats
w4-800168.blurb: Russian Cossack expansion into the Lake Baikal region intensified in the 1640s-1660s. On 6 July 1661 Cossack Yakov Pokhabov founded the fortified outpost of Irkutsk specifically to subdue resistant Buryat clans and collect iasak (fur tribute). By approximately 1660-1662 most Buryat groups in the Baikal area had been brought under Russian tribute obligation, transferring these territories to the Tsardom of Russia. The 'Golden Horde' from-label is a dataset residual category (the Buryats were a Mongolic group, never part of the Golden Horde).

w4-800170.name: Alaouite unification of Morocco under Moulay al-Rashid
w4-800170.blurb: After the Saadi collapse, Moulay al-Rashid proclaimed himself sultan in 1664, defeated the Dila'iyya near Fez (1666) and took Marrakesh (1668), reunifying Morocco under the Alaouite dynasty. The Saadi-to-Morocco transition (31.9N) is within the window (1662-1670).

w4-800172.name: English conquest of New Netherland
w4-800172.blurb: In September 1664 an English expedition under Richard Nicolls captured New Amsterdam from the Dutch; the colony was renamed New York. Despite a brief Dutch reconquest (1673), English control was confirmed by the 1674 Treaty of Westminster. The territory near lng -74.2 W / lat 41.1 N passed from New Netherland to the English colonial empire, matching the [1662,1670] window.

w4-800173.name: Burmese–Siamese War (1662–1664)
w4-800173.blurb: The Restored Toungoo Empire of Burma and the Ayutthaya Kingdom of Siam fought over Lan Na and the Tenasserim coast in 1662–1664. King Narai of Siam attempted to exploit Burmese internal unrest (a coup had brought Pye Min to power in June 1662) and occupy Lan Na, but the venture failed. Both sides raided across the border, and while Siam invaded southern Burma in late 1663, a firm territorial outcome was inconclusive. The dataset window 1662–1670 likely captures repeated border shifts in this prolonged rivalry over the upper Tenasserim–Lan Na corridor.

w4-800174.name: Mughal conquest of Chittagong from the Kingdom of Mrauk U (1666)
w4-800174.blurb: On 27 January 1666 Mughal forces under Buzurg Umed Khan captured Chittagong from the Kingdom of Mrauk U (Arakan), triggered by Arakanese piracy and the killing of Shah Shuja. Chittagong was renamed Islamabad and integrated into the Bengal Subah. From=Kingdom of Mrauk U, to=Mughal Empire matches the 1662-1670 window.

w4-800177.name: Treaty of Breda (1667) - exchange of New Netherland for Surinam
w4-800177.blurb: The Treaty of Breda (31 July 1667), ending the Second Anglo-Dutch War, confirmed English possession of New Netherland (modern New York) in exchange for Dutch retention of Surinam. The dataset records territory near Surinam passing from 'English Colonial Empire' to 'New Netherland' around 1662-1670, consistent with the Dutch seizure of Surinam from the English in 1667 and the treaty's formalization. France returned Cayenne to the Dutch by 1670 under the same peace settlement.

w4-800180.name: French occupation of Lorraine under Louis XIV
w4-800180.blurb: In 1670 Louis XIV ordered French troops to occupy the Duchy of Lorraine (coord 6.2E/48.8N), citing Duke Charles IV's pro-Habsburg policies; French forces seized the duchy and Charles IV went into exile. France held it until the Treaty of Ryswick (1697) restored the duchy (minus Saarburg). The dataset's 1670–1673 'Duchy of Lorraine → France' shift matches this occupation.

w4-800182.name: Brunei Civil War (Perang Chermin) and Sulu reward
w4-800182.blurb: The Brunei Civil War (Perang Chermin, 1660-1673) ended when Sultan Muhyiddin defeated his rival Hakkul Mubin at Pulau Chermin with Sulu assistance. Muhyiddin allegedly rewarded the Sulu sultanate with eastern Sabah (North Borneo, lat 5.8, lng 117.8) in gratitude. The cession is historically contested - Brunei denies any written agreement existed - but the 1673 date is the traditional point marking Sulu's claim to North Borneo. Window 1670-1673.

w4-800188.name: Galdan's defeat of Ochirtu Khan; founding of the Dzungar Khanate
w4-800188.blurb: Between 1675 and 1677, Galdan Boshugtu Khan of the Choros clan defeated Ochirtu Khan, paramount leader of the Oirat Confederation, consolidating power over the Oirat tribes under Dzungar leadership. In 1678 the Dalai Lama conferred the title Boshugtu Khan on Galdan, formalizing the Dzungar Khanate. Matches worklist transition Oirat Confederation -> Dzungar Khanate (1674-1677).

w4-800191.name: Franco-Dutch War: French captures in the Spanish Netherlands
w4-800191.blurb: During the Franco-Dutch War (1672–1678), French forces under the duc de Luxembourg captured Valenciennes (17 March 1677) and won the Battle of Cassel (11 April 1677), securing French control over Spanish-held territories in the southern Low Countries (lat 48.8, lng 4.6). These campaigns, with Vauban directing siege operations, forced Spain back and were confirmed by the Treaty of Nijmegen (1678), which ceded Franche-Comté and additional fortified towns permanently to France.

w4-800192.name: Trịnh lords extinguish the Mạc remnant at Cao Bằng
w4-800192.blurb: The Mạc dynasty seized the Lê throne in 1527 but was driven from Hanoi by Lê-Trịnh loyalists in 1592, retreating to mountainous Cao Bằng province near the Chinese border (around lng 106, lat 22.7). For nearly a century the Mạc clung to Cao Bằng under Qing protection. In 1677 the Trịnh lords launched a final campaign that conquered Cao Bằng and eliminated the last Mạc stronghold, consolidating Trịnh control over all of northern Đại Việt (Đàng Ngoài). This matches the worklist transfer from Đại Việt to the Trịnh lords within 1674-1677.

w4-800193.name: VOC-Mataram reconquest of Java from Trunajaya (1677–1683)
w4-800193.blurb: After Amangkurat II of Mataram allied with the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in 1677, Admiral Cornelis Speelman's combined forces stormed Surabaya and broke the rebellion of Trunajaya, who was captured at Kediri in December 1678 and executed in 1680. By 1683 the VOC had helped Mataram reclaim the contested districts of central and east Java, in return extracting sweeping commercial monopolies and territorial concessions that deepened Dutch dominance over the Javanese coast.

w4-800195.name: VOC Treaty with Mataram restores Dutch control of coastal Java (1683)
w4-800195.blurb: Following the VOC-backed defeat of Trunajaya (captured 1678, executed 1680) and the suppression of remaining rebels, Amangkurat II's agreements with the Dutch East India Company in 1677 and 1683 ceded effective control of the north-coast districts of Java to the VOC. Around Pekalongan and the pasisir ports, sovereignty and customs revenue passed from Mataram and its rivals into Dutch hands, anchoring the Company's commercial empire on Java's coast.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Dutch East India Company in Java

w4-800197.name: VOC subjugation of Bantam (Banten) Sultanate (1683)
w4-800197.blurb: In 1683, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) exploited a succession dispute between Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa and his son Sultan Haji to intervene militarily and end Bantam's independence on Java's northwest coast; Sultan Ageng was captured on 14 March 1683. The dataset labels the 'from' entity as 'Sultanate of Malacca' (a Malay-sultanate-network label) and the 'to' as the 'Dutch Republic.' At coordinates 109E, -6.8S (central Java), the event corresponds to the VOC's consolidation of Java following the subduing of Bantam, the last major independent sultanate resisting Dutch commercial monopoly.

w4-800198.name: Galdan's Westward Expansion against Kazakh/Oirat Border Tribes
w4-800198.blurb: Between 1681 and 1684 Galdan pushed the Kazakhs westward, capturing Sayram, Tashkent, and Taraz and subjugating the Black Kyrgyz; the centroid in western Mongolia/eastern Kazakh steppe indicates Dzungar seizure of territory previously mapped under the 'Golden Horde' (Kazakh) label.

w4-800199.name: Dzungar invasion of Kazakh steppe — Great Disaster (Aqtaban Shubyryndy)
w4-800199.blurb: In the early 1680s the Dzungar ruler Galdan Boshugtu Khan drove westward against the Kazakhs and the towns of the Syr Darya, seizing Sayram, Tashkent, and Taraz between roughly 1681 and 1684 and pushing Dzungar power onto the Chu and Talas steppe. This was an early phase of the Dzungar-Kazakh wars; the far more catastrophic Kazakh collapse remembered as the 'Great Disaster' (Aqtaban Shubyryndy) came decades later, in 1723.

w4-800200.name: Dzungar Expansion under Galdan Boshugtu Khan
w4-800200.blurb: Under Galdan Boshugtu Khan (r. 1671-1697), the Dzungar Khanate launched aggressive campaigns from its Dzungarian base. In the 1670s-1680s Galdan swept into the Tarim Basin oases and western Mongolian steppe. The coordinates (~91E 45N, western Mongolian/Khovd zone) fit the territory the Dzungars overran during this decade. The dataset's 'Golden Horde' from-label is a coarse steppe-successor tag; the underlying Dzungar expansion in the 1677-1683 window is attested.

w4-800201.name: Kazakh-Dzungar War - Galdan Boshugtu Khan's Invasion of the Kazakh Steppe
w4-800201.blurb: Galdan Boshugtu Khan, having consolidated the Dzungar Khanate in 1677, launched large-scale invasions of Kazakh territory from 1680. In 1680-1681 he invaded Semirechye and South Kazakhstan; by 1683 Dzungar forces under Tsewang Rabtan reached the Syr Darya and seized Sayram, Tashkent, and Taraz. The coordinates lie in the Kazakh steppe south of Lake Balkhash. These campaigns transferred effective control from the Kazakh Khanate to the Dzungar Khanate.

w4-800203.name: Thokoly Uprising - Principality of Upper Hungary established (1682-1683)
w4-800203.blurb: The Hungarian Protestant noble Imre Thokoly, backed by the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed IV, led a major Kuruc uprising against Habsburg rule from 1678 onward and in November 1682 was recognised by the Porte as 'King of Upper Hungary,' establishing the Principality of Upper Hungary (roughly covering much of present-day Slovakia). Thokoly's forces seized key strongholds including Kosice and controlled much of the region up to the Vah River. Habsburg authority in the territory around lat 48.5, lng 20.2 was thus displaced by Thokoly's Ottoman-backed principality between 1683 and its collapse after the failed Ottoman siege of Vienna.

w4-800206.name: Final Dutch expulsion of Portugal from Ceylon
w4-800206.blurb: Although the main Dutch conquest of Portuguese Ceylon concluded with the fall of Colombo (1656) and Jaffna (1658), residual Portuguese-held or contested interior districts were incorporated by the VOC through the 1660s–1680s. By 1687 the last contested coastal zones in the south-central region (centroid 80.9E, 7.6N) had passed fully to Dutch administration.

w4-800207.name: Dutch East India Company (VOC) completes conquest of Ceylon from Portugal
w4-800207.blurb: The VOC, allied with the Kingdom of Kandy, expelled the last Portuguese strongholds from Ceylon in 1658, capturing Jaffna and Mannar; the cession was confirmed by the Treaty of The Hague (1661). Dutch Ceylon was consolidated over subsequent decades. The worklist transfer Portuguese Ceylon → Dutch Ceylon at lng 80.8, lat 7.7 in the 1683–1687 window reflects continued Dutch coastal consolidation following the death of Rajasinha II of Kandy (1687), tied to the real Dutch takeover.

w4-800209.name: Galdan's Invasion of Khalkha Mongolia
w4-800209.blurb: In 1688 Galdan Boshugtu Khan invaded the Khalkha Mongol homeland, routing the Tüshiyetü Khan's forces near Olgoi Lake and forcing some 20,000 Khalkha refugees south into Qing territory; the Cliopatria atlas labels these Khalkha steppe lands as 'Golden Horde' but they pass to Dzungar control in this snapshot. The Khalkha submitted formally to the Qing at the Dolon Nor congress of 1691.

w4-800210.name: Galdan's expansion and the prelude to the Dzungar-Qing Wars (1683-1687)
w4-800210.blurb: Galdan Boshugtu Khan of the Dzungar Khanate conducted major campaigns in 1683-1684 (taking Tashkent, Sayram and the Fergana Valley) and in 1687 launched a full invasion of Khalkha Mongolia, approaching the Great Wall near the Gansu/Inner Mongolia frontier. The dataset coordinates (102.6, 40.2) point to this frontier region where Dzungar pressure on Qing-aligned populations grew, culminating in the First Dzungar-Qing War from 1687. The transfer at this location is somewhat weak (Khalkha territory only formally submitted to the Qing in 1691), but Dzungar advance into the eastern frontier in this window is well attested.

w4-800211.name: Dzungar (Oirat) expansion westward into the Kazakh steppe under Galdan
w4-800211.blurb: From 1681 to 1687, Galdan Boshugtu Khan of the Dzungar Khanate campaigned against the Kazakh Khanate and neighboring steppe polities, pushing Kazakh populations westward; Tsewang Rabtan captured Tashkent and Sayram in 1683, and from 1685 Dzungar forces controlled much of the eastern Kazakh steppe. Cliopatria records this as territory shifting from 'Golden Horde' (its label for the Kazakh/steppe successor, centroid lat 47.6, lng 97.8) to 'Dzungar Khanate' in 1683-1687.

w4-800212.name: Great Turkish War / Habsburg reconquest of Upper Hungary
w4-800212.blurb: After the failed 1683 Ottoman siege of Vienna, the Holy League counter-offensive recaptured Buda (1686) and won the second Battle of Mohács (1687). Imre Thököly's Ottoman-backed Principality of Upper Hungary (modern Slovakia, lng 20.2, lat 48.5) collapsed and passed to the Habsburg Monarchy within the 1683-1687 window. Well attested.

w4-800214.name: Siege of Bijapur - Mughal conquest of the Bijapur Sultanate
w4-800214.blurb: Aurangzeb besieged Bijapur from 1685, took personal command in 1686, captured the city on 12 September 1686 and imprisoned Sikandar Adil Shah, ending the Adil Shahi dynasty and bringing the Deccan heartland under Mughal control. The from=Bijapur Sultanate / to=Mughal Empire and the 1683-1687 window bracket this event.

w4-800217.name: Russian expansion into Buryatia/Lake Baikal region (1680s)
w4-800217.blurb: During the 1680s, the Tsardom of Russia consolidated control over Buryatia and the Lake Baikal region, territories under nominal Mongol (Khalkha) suzerainty, with the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) fixing the eastern border. The worklist codes this as Golden Horde → Tsardom of Russia at lng 102.8, lat 51.7 (Baikal) in the 1683–1687 window; the 'Golden Horde' label is an anachronistic data artifact for the Mongol-successor framing, but the real Russian absorption of this Siberian region is well attested.

w4-800219.name: Habsburg reconquest of Upper Hungary and Transylvanian submission (1687)
w4-800219.blurb: Following the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Vienna (1683) and subsequent Habsburg advances, the rulers of Transylvania recognized the suzerainty of Emperor Leopold I in 1687. The Principality of Upper Hungary (Imre Thököly's Ottoman client state) collapsed as Habsburg forces pushed east. The 1687 Diet of Pressburg established Habsburg hereditary rule in Hungary.

w4-800222.name: Kazakh Counter-offensive - Partial Recovery of Steppe from Dzungars
w4-800222.blurb: After Galdan's 1680-1684 campaigns seized much of the southern Kazakh steppe, Kazakh forces under Tauke Khan mounted resistance and Dzungar attention shifted eastward (Galdan attacked the Khalkha Mongols in 1687). The dataset shows territory near lng 72, lat 43.4 reverting from Dzungar to Kazakh control in 1683-1687, consistent with the fluid back-and-forth of steppe warfare. No single decisive battle is documented for this specific reversal.

w4-800223.name: Ayutthaya reconquest of Patani after the Phetracha coup (1688)
w4-800223.blurb: When Phetracha overthrew King Narai in 1688, Patani rebelled and in the 1691–92 war even defeated an Ayutthayan force. Ayutthaya then invaded with 50,000 men and subdued Patani, restoring Siamese suzerainty and ushering in decades of instability. The Patani→Ayutthaya transfer at (101.5°E, 6.3°N) is well attested for the 1687–1691 window.

w4-800225.name: French capture of Nice and Savoy during the Nine Years' War (1691)
w4-800225.blurb: After Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy joined the Grand Alliance against Louis XIV in 1690, French forces under Catinat defeated the Savoyards at Staffarda (August 1690). French troops captured Villefranche and Nice in spring 1691 and overran much of the Duchy of Savoy. The Alpine frontier region remained under French occupation until the Treaty of Turin in 1696.

w4-800230.name: Treaty of Nerchinsk (Securing Transbaikalia / Buryatia)
w4-800230.blurb: The Treaty of Nerchinsk (27 August 1689), the first Sino-Russian treaty, delineated the border along the Argun River and Stanovoy Mountains. While Russia ceded the Amur basin to Qing China, it secured Transbaikalia — the steppe region east of Lake Baikal including the Buryat Mongol territories at approximately lng=114, lat=51. The dataset coordinates correspond to this region. Although labeled 'Golden Horde → Tsardom of Russia,' the 'from' label is anachronistic (the Golden Horde had dissolved in the 15th century); the actual context is the consolidation of Transbaikalia / Buryatia under Russian control during the 1640s–1690s, confirmed by the 1689 treaty, which falls within the py=1687/y=1691 window.

w4-800232.name: Khalkha Mongol submission to Qing at Dolon Nor
w4-800232.blurb: In 1691, under Dzungar pressure from Galdan, the Khalkha Mongol rulers voluntarily submitted to the Kangxi Emperor at the Assembly of Dolon Nor, bringing Outer Mongolia into the Qing; Galdan was then defeated at Jao Modo in 1696. The coordinates (46.3N) and window (1691-1696) match; the 'Golden Horde' source label is a dataset abstraction for the Mongol successor lineages.

w4-800233.name: Battle of Jao Modo: Kangxi Emperor defeats Galdan of the Dzungar Khanate
w4-800233.blurb: On 12 June 1696, Qing general Fiyanggu's army trapped and crushed Galdan Boshugtu Khan's Dzungar forces near the Terelj River in Mongolia. Galdan fled and died in April 1697. The battle effectively ended Dzungar domination of Outer Mongolia and incorporated Khalkha Mongolia under Qing suzerainty (Cliopatria centroid lat 45.6, lng 98.4, western Mongolia),

w4-800234.name: Kangxi Emperor defeats Galdan at Battle of Jao Modo — Qing expansion (1696)
w4-800234.blurb: In summer 1696 the Kangxi Emperor led Qing troops against Dzungar leader Galdan; the Battle of Jao Modo (near the Tuul River) was a decisive Qing victory and Galdan died in 1697. The victory firmly incorporated Khalkha Mongolia under Qing rule and ended the Khoshut Khanate's independent role, bringing Khoshut territories under Qing administration. Date 1696 falls within the [1691,1696] window; transfer Khoshut Khanate → Qing Dynasty confirmed.

w4-800236.name: Battle of Slankamen and Habsburg reconquest of Slavonia
w4-800236.blurb: During the Great Turkish War (1683–1699), Habsburg forces under Louis of Baden routed the Ottoman army at the Battle of Slankamen on 19 August 1691, killing Grand Vizier Köprülü Fazıl Mustafa Pasha. This victory secured Habsburg possession of Hungary and Transylvania and halted the Ottoman counteroffensive in Slavonia (lat 45.4, lng 18.2). The subsequent Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) formally ceded Hungary, Croatia, and Slavonia to the Habsburgs.

w4-800237.name: Diploma Leopoldinum — Habsburg incorporation of Transylvania
w4-800237.blurb: Following the Habsburg reconquest of Hungary from the Ottomans in the 1680s, Emperor Leopold I issued the Diploma Leopoldinum on 4 December 1691, formally placing the Principality of Transylvania under direct Habsburg suzerainty. The diploma preserved the autonomy of the three recognised nations (Hungarians, Székelys, Saxons) and religious toleration, but installed a Habsburg-appointed governor and made the young prince Mihály Apafi II a nominal figurehead. By 1696 a Habsburg military commander (General Rabutin de Bussy) was placed in charge, completing Transylvania's integration.

w4-800240.name: Treaty of Turin (1696) — restitution of Nice and Savoy
w4-800240.blurb: The Treaty of Turin, signed on 29 August 1696, ended Savoy's involvement in the Nine Years' War. Louis XIV returned Nice, Villefranche, Montmelian, Susa, and other territories in the County of Nice and Duchy of Savoy to Duke Victor Amadeus II, restoring the Alpine frontier region to the House of Savoy that France had occupied since 1691.

w4-800244.name: Qing absorption of remaining Tümed/Mongol steppe following the defeat of the Dzungars
w4-800244.blurb: Following the Kangxi Emperor's defeat of Galdan at Jao Modo (1696) and the earlier 1691 Khalkha submission at Dolon Nor, the Qing secured the Mongol steppe, including remaining Tümed territories. The coordinates (96.9E, 36.7N) lie in the Kokonor/western frontier zone rather than near Ulaanbaatar, so this likely records absorption of the western Tümed; the Tümed-to-Qing transition is within the window (1696-1700).

w4-800245.name: Spanish conquest of the Itza Maya — fall of Nojpeten (1697)
w4-800245.blurb: Martin de Ursua y Arizmendi led a Spanish expedition to Lake Peten Itza, and on 13 March 1697 his forces stormed and captured Nojpeten, the island capital of the Itza kingdom. This was the last independent Maya kingdom to fall; the Itza territory in the Peten region was incorporated into the Spanish Empire.

w4-800249.name: Coronation of Frederick I — Kingdom of Prussia
w4-800249.blurb: On January 18, 1701, Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg crowned himself 'King in Prussia' as Frederick I at Königsberg, transforming Brandenburg-Prussia into the Kingdom of Prussia (coords 14.4E/53.5N). Authorized by Emperor Leopold I via the Crown Treaty of 1700 in exchange for military support in the War of the Spanish Succession, this elevated the Hohenzollern state to royal status.

w4-800250.name: War of the Spanish Succession — Bourbon vs. Habsburg contest for Spain
w4-800250.blurb: When the last Habsburg king of Spain, Charles II, died in 1700 without heirs, his will named Philip of Anjou (grandson of Louis XIV) as successor. The Grand Alliance (Britain, Austria, Dutch Republic) refused to accept Bourbon dominance over Spain and declared war in May 1702, backing Archduke Charles of Austria as the rival claimant. The war produced the pro-Habsburg and pro-Bourbon factions whose territorial control fluctuated across Iberia until the Peace of Utrecht (1713) confirmed Philip V as king while stripping Spain of its Italian and Low Countries territories.

citations.label: War of the Spanish Succession – Wikipedia

w4-800251.name: War of the Spanish Succession - French occupation of Savoy and Nice
w4-800251.blurb: Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy defected to the Grand Alliance in October 1703, whereupon French armies overran his mainland possessions: in 1704 de La Feuillade captured the Duchy of Savoy and most of the County of Nice (coordinates 7E, 44.9N), with the city of Nice finally surrendering in December 1705. By 1706 virtually all Savoyard territory except Turin was under French occupation. NOTE: the worklist window (1700-1702) dates this slightly early; the actual French occupation followed Savoy's 1703 defection and ran 1704-1705, reversed at the Battle of Turin (1706).

citations.label: War of the Spanish Succession - Wikipedia

w4-800253.name: Kangxi Emperor's intervention in the eastern Kham/Sichuan-Tibet border region
w4-800253.blurb: Around 1701–1702, the Kangxi Emperor ordered the reconquest of Kangding (Dartsedo) and other border territories in western Sichuan, reasserting Qing control over the eastern Kham frontier and the tea-horse trade routes. This preceded the broader Qing incorporation of Tibet completed after the expulsion of the Dzungars in 1720. The worklist transfer Tibet → Qing Dynasty at lng 100.4, lat 31.2 (Kangding area) in the 1700–1702 window matches this intervention.

w4-800259.name: Vakhtang VI's regency over Kartli (from 1703)
w4-800259.blurb: Vakhtang VI acted as regent (janishini) of Kartli from 1703 while his uncle George XI served as Persian viceroy in Kandahar (George died 1709). Vakhtang's early administrative reforms fall within the window (1702-1706); coordinates (43.8, 42) lie in Kartli. The 'Kingdom of Georgia' label represents Kartli within a broader Georgian framework under Safavid suzerainty.

w4-800260.name: Regency of Algiers - De Facto Autonomy under the Odjak (early 18th c.)
w4-800260.blurb: By the late 17th/early 18th century the Regency of Algiers had achieved de facto independence from Istanbul, governed by the Janissary Odjak rather than Ottoman-appointed pashas (from 1659); the 1702-1706 window falls just before the formal Dey system (c. 1710). The coordinates (3.2E, 35.3N) lie in northern Algeria. The transfer Ottoman Empire -> Regency of Algiers reflects progressive consolidation of autonomy rather than a single treaty or battle.

citations.label: History of the Regency of Algiers - Wikipedia

w4-800263.name: Portuguese-led Allied army captures Madrid (1706, War of Spanish Succession)
w4-800263.blurb: In spring 1706 the Portuguese Marquis of Minas led a ~14,000-strong allied army across the Spanish border, taking Madrid (entered 28 June 1706), where Archduke Charles was proclaimed King. Coord 5.6W/39.8N (Extremadura/central Spain) is territory Portugal crossed and briefly controlled during this offensive. The dataset's 1702–1706 'Spain → Portugal' shift reflects this; the Bourbon counterattack recovered Madrid by late 1706. Event real and correctly dated.

citations.label: Portugal in the War of Spanish Succession – Wikipedia
War of the Spanish Succession – Wikipedia

w4-800264.name: Great Northern War – Russia captures Swedish Ingria and Narva region
w4-800264.blurb: During the Great Northern War (1700–1721), while Charles XII of Sweden was occupied in Poland, Peter the Great reconquered Ingria (lost to Sweden in 1617), capturing Nöteborg in 1702 and Nyenschantz in 1703 (where he founded St. Petersburg). Narva was retaken by Russia in 1704. By 1706 Russia controlled the eastern Baltic littoral formerly held by the Swedish Empire, though these gains were only formally confirmed in the Treaty of Nystadt (1721).

w4-800265.name: Swedish invasion of Poland: Charles XII installs Stanisław I
w4-800265.blurb: During the Great Northern War, Charles XII of Sweden invaded the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth to dethrone Augustus II. A Warsaw confederation deposed Augustus in February 1704, and under Swedish protection Stanisław Leszczyński was elected king on 2 July 1704 (crowned 1705). Augustus formally renounced the throne in the Treaty of Altranstädt (1706). Matches the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth → Pro-Swedish Poland transfer in the 1702-1706 window.

w4-800266.name: Battle of Turin and Savoyard recovery of Nice and Savoy
w4-800266.blurb: After the decisive Allied victory at the Siege/Battle of Turin (7 September 1706), Prince Eugene of Savoy and Victor Amadeus II expelled French forces from northern Italy. Nice and Susa were retaken from France, restoring the territory (7E, 44.9N) to the House of Savoy. The Convention of Milan (March 1707) ended hostilities in the Italian theatre, though French possession of transalpine Savoy persisted until Utrecht (1713).

w4-800269.name: Rise of the Husainid Beylik of Tunis
w4-800269.blurb: In 1705, following the capture of the incumbent Bey Ibrahim el-Sharif by Algerian forces, the Ottoman cavalry officer Husayn ibn Ali was proclaimed Bey in Tunis and founded the Husainid dynasty. Sultan Ahmed III recognized him as beylerbeyi (provincial governor), and hereditary succession was confirmed in 1710. Although nominally an Ottoman province, the Husainid Beylik operated with effective autonomy, conducting its own foreign treaties with European powers. This shift transferred de facto governance of Tunisia from direct Ottoman control to the new Husainid line, matching the dataset transfer (Ottoman Empire -> Beylik of Tunis, py1702/y1706) in Tunisia.

w4-800270.name: Acts of Union 1707 – Formation of the Kingdom of Great Britain
w4-800270.blurb: The Acts of Union of 1707 merged the Kingdom of England and the Kingdom of Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain, effective 1 May 1707, creating a single Westminster parliament and abolishing the separate Scottish Parliament. From 'Kingdom of England' to 'Kingdom of Great Britain' at Scottish coordinates; window py=1706, y=1709 brackets it.

w4-800273.name: Establishment of Stanisław Leszczyński's pro-Swedish Poland during the Great Northern War
w4-800273.blurb: In the Great Northern War, Charles XII's Treaty of Altranstadt (1706) forced Augustus II to renounce the Polish throne, leaving Sweden's client Stanisław Leszczyński (crowned 1705) controlling most of the Commonwealth until the Swedish defeat at Poltava (1709). The transition is within the window (1706-1709).

w4-800275.name: Dissolution of Lan Xang and formation of the Kingdom of Vientiane
w4-800275.blurb: After the death of King Sourigna Vongsa in 1694 without a clear heir, a protracted succession crisis split Lan Xang. In 1707 Siamese mediation formalised the division into two kingdoms: Vientiane in the south under Sai Ong Hue (backed by the Vietnamese court) and Luang Phrabang in the north under Kingkitsarat. The territory in the central Mekong valley that had belonged to unified Lan Xang passed to the new Kingdom of Vientiane.

w4-800277.name: Bourbon Spain recovers Extremadura from Portugal (1707–1709)
w4-800277.blurb: After the allied capture of Madrid (1706), Philip V's Bourbon forces (aided by the Duke of Berwick) decisively won the Battle of Almansa (25 April 1707) and recovered the border territories Portugal and its allies had held; by 1709 the frontier had largely returned to its pre-war line. Coord 5.6W/39.8N (Extremadura). The dataset's 1706–1709 'Portugal → Spain' reversion matches the post-Almansa reconquest. Event real and correctly dated.

citations.label: Portugal in the War of Spanish Succession – Wikipedia

w4-800278.name: War of the Spanish Succession — Bourbon consolidation in Spain
w4-800278.blurb: During the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714), Spain was divided between supporters of Habsburg Archduke Charles and Bourbon Philip V. After early Allied successes including the capture of Madrid in 1706, the Bourbon victory at the Battle of Almansa (April 1707) shattered Grand Alliance control of eastern Spain. By 1708-1709 the Bourbons had retaken Valencia and Alicante, consolidating Philip V's hold on Castile and most of Spain. The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) ultimately confirmed Philip V as King of Spain, ending Austrian Habsburg claims to the Spanish throne.

citations.label: War of the Spanish Succession – Wikipedia

w4-800279.name: Banda Singh Bahadur's Sikh uprising and capture of Sirhind
w4-800279.blurb: Following Guru Gobind Singh's death in 1708, Banda Singh Bahadur led the Khalsa into Punjab. Beginning in late 1709 with the sack of the Mughal mint-city of Samana, he captured Sirhind in May 1710, killing its governor Wazir Khan and briefly establishing the first Sikh polity. The atlas window 1706–1709 captures the lead-up and initial phase of this successful Sikh assault on Mughal authority in the Punjab plains.

w4-800281.name: Restoration of Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth after Battle of Poltava
w4-800281.blurb: During the Great Northern War, Sweden installed pro-Swedish Stanisław Leszczyński as king of Poland-Lithuania in 1705, dividing the Commonwealth into Swedish-backed and Russian-backed (Augustus II) factions. The decisive Russian victory at Poltava (8 July 1709) collapsed Swedish power; Leszczyński fled and Augustus II was restored, reuniting the Commonwealth. From 'Pro-Swedish Poland' to 'Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth'; window py=1706, y=1709 fits.

w4-800283.name: Fragmentation of Lan Xang — Kingdom of Champasak founded
w4-800283.blurb: After Souligna Vongsa's death (1694) Lan Xang fractured; Luang Prabang and Vientiane split off in 1707, and in 1713 the southern Mekong-cataracts region became the independent Kingdom of Champasak under Nokasad. The Lan Xang to Champasak secession falls within the 1706-1709 window (event 1713 marginally after). Attested.

w4-800284.name: Dissolution of Lan Xang and formation of the Kingdom of Luang Phrabang
w4-800284.blurb: The same 1707 succession crisis that created the Kingdom of Vientiane also produced the northern Kingdom of Luang Phrabang under Kingkitsarat, a grandson of Sourigna Vongsa who had been in exile in Sipsong Panna. Siamese mediation formalised the split, and the northern Lan Xang territories (around Luang Prabang) were henceforth governed independently. A further breakaway, the Kingdom of Champasak, formed to the south around 1713.

w4-800286.name: Hanover inherits Principality of Lüneburg (1705)
w4-800286.blurb: In 1705, Elector George Louis of Hanover inherited the Principality of Lüneburg (Celle) upon the death of his uncle, Duke George William of Brunswick-Lüneburg. This united the Calenberg and Lüneburg branches of the House of Welf, roughly doubling Hanover's extent; the electorate's status was confirmed by the Imperial Diet in 1708.

citations.label: George I of Great Britain – Wikipedia

w4-800287.name: Foundation of the Khanate of Kokand (1709)
w4-800287.blurb: In 1709, Shahrukh Biy of the Ming Uzbek tribe broke away from the weakening Khanate of Bukhara and established the Khanate of Kokand in the Fergana Valley, building his capital fortress near the town of Kokand. Bukharan authority over the valley had collapsed under pressure from Kazakh and Oirat invasions, enabling the Ming tribe to carve out an independent polity that would last until Russian annexation in 1876. The worklist transition is 'Khanate of Bukhara' -> 'Khanate of Kokand' [1706,1709] at the Fergana Valley, precisely the Kokand heartland, and 1709 falls within the window.

w4-800288.name: Acts of Union 1707; formation of Kingdom of Great Britain
w4-800288.blurb: The Acts of Union passed by the English and Scottish Parliaments came into force on 1 May 1707, merging the kingdoms of England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain. This dissolved the separate English Colonial Empire and Scottish rights to colonial trade, replacing them with the unified British Colonial Empire. Scotland gained full access to England's colonial trade networks in exchange for accepting the Hanoverian succession and parliamentary union.

w4-800290.name: Karamanli Coup — founding of autonomous Tripolitania
w4-800290.blurb: In 1711 Ahmad Karamanli killed the Ottoman-appointed pasha of Tripolitania and seized power, gaining sultanic confirmation as hereditary pasha and founding the autonomous Karamanli dynasty (1711–1835) under nominal Ottoman suzerainty. The coordinates (17.1,31.9) are Tripolitania, and the window 1709–1713 brackets the coup, matching the from→to (Ottoman Empire → Karamanli Dynasty).

w4-800292.name: Peace of Utrecht (1713) and restoration of Lorraine
w4-800292.blurb: During the War of the Spanish Succession France occupied parts of the Duchy of Lorraine. The Peace of Utrecht (1713) and companion Treaty of Rastatt (1714) required France to restore Lorraine (coord 6.2E/48.8N, near Nancy) to Duke Leopold I. The dataset's 1709–1713 'France → Duchy of Lorraine' reversion matches the settlement.

citations.label: War of the Spanish Succession – Wikipedia

w4-800295.name: Carnatic Sultanate becomes independent under Saadatullah Khan I
w4-800295.blurb: After the Mughal Emperor appointed Saadatullah Khan I as Nawab of the Carnatic (Arcot) in 1710, he exploited the decline of central Mughal authority to establish a virtually independent hereditary state, severing the province from effective Mughal control by around 1713. The dataset transfer (Mughal Empire -> Carnatic Sultanate, py1709/y1713) at lng79.6/lat13.8 (Arcot) reflects this de facto autonomy under nominal Nizam suzerainty.

w4-800297.name: Peace of Utrecht — Spain cedes Italian territories to Habsburg Monarchy
w4-800297.blurb: The Peace of Utrecht (1713), concluding the War of the Spanish Succession, required Philip V of Spain (Bourbon) to cede the Spanish Netherlands and Spain's Italian possessions (including the Duchy of Milan, Kingdom of Naples, and Sardinia) to the Austrian Habsburgs. The Treaty of Rastatt (1714) confirmed these Habsburg gains. This transferred a large bloc of northern Italian territory (centred on Milan) from Spanish to Habsburg control, fundamentally reshaping the map of Italy.

citations.label: War of the Spanish Succession – Wikipedia

w4-800298.name: Mirwais Khan Hotak's Rebellion and Foundation of the Hotaki Dynasty
w4-800298.blurb: Mirwais Khan Hotak, a Ghilzai Pashtun chief in Kandahar, killed the Safavid Georgian governor Gurgin Khan on 21 April 1709, founding the independent Hotaki dynasty. Safavid counterattacks in 1711 and 1713 were both defeated, confirming Hotaki control of Loy Kandahar (~64E 33N). The 1709-1713 window aligns with the founding revolt and its consolidation.

w4-800299.name: Great Northern War – Russian dominance over Lithuania after Poltava
w4-800299.blurb: After Charles XII's defeat at Poltava (1709), the pro-Swedish Leszczyński party collapsed in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth; Russian forces under Peter the Great occupied Lithuania/Belarus (Vilnius, Minsk, Grodno) and restored Augustus II by 1710. The coordinates are the Vilnius region, matching the pro-Swedish Poland → Russia control shift in the 1709–1713 window.

citations.label: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and Russia in the Great Northern War – De Gruyter

w4-800302.name: Dzungar invasion of Tibet
w4-800302.blurb: In 1717 the Dzungar general Tsering Dondub led 6,000 troops across the Changtang plateau in a surprise campaign, killing the Khoshut king Lhazang Khan and seizing Lhasa. The Dzungars deposed the existing Dalai Lama and looted monasteries, prompting the Kangxi Emperor to send a Qing expedition in 1718 which was annihilated, then a second successful campaign in 1720 that expelled the Dzungars. The territory around lat 31.5, lng 98.3 (eastern Tibet) thereby passed under Dzungar control in 1717.

w4-800303.name: Spanish invasion of Sicily (War of the Quadruple Alliance)
w4-800303.blurb: In July 1718 Spain landed troops in Sicily, seizing the island from Savoy; despite the British victory at Cape Passaro, Spain held Sicily from 1718 until Austria retook it in 1719–1720. Sicily near lng 14 E / lat 37.5 N passed from the House of Savoy to the Kingdom of Spain, matching the [1713,1718] window.

citations.label: War of the Quadruple Alliance – Wikipedia

w4-800304.name: Spanish conquest of Sardinia (1717) seizes the island from the Habsburgs
w4-800304.blurb: Under the Peace of Utrecht (1713) Sardinia had passed to Habsburg Austria. Exploiting Austria's involvement in the Austro-Turkish War, a Spanish expeditionary force under the Marquis of Lede landed near Cagliari on 22 August 1717 and conquered the entire island by 30 October 1717, the opening move of the War of the Quadruple Alliance. The atlas's 1713–1718 window for a Habsburg-to-Spain transfer of Sardinia corresponds to this 1717 Spanish seizure (later reversed by the 1720 Treaty of The Hague).

citations.label: War of the Quadruple Alliance – Wikipedia

w4-800306.name: Murshid Quli Khan granted hereditary Nawabship of Bengal by Farrukhsiyar
w4-800306.blurb: Murshid Quli Khan served as Bengal's revenue administrator from 1701. In 1713 Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar appointed him deputy subahdar, and in 1717 he was recognized as hereditary Nawab Nazim of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, governing with near-total autonomy and effectively detaching Bengal from direct Mughal administration. Matches the Mughal → Nawabs of Bengal transfer in the 1713-1718 window.

w4-800310.name: Mughal suppression of Sikh uprising and execution of Banda Singh Bahadur
w4-800310.blurb: Emperor Farrukh Siyar (r. 1713–1719) launched a massive campaign against the Sikhs under Banda Singh Bahadur, besieging him at Gurdas Nangal from March 1715. Banda's starving garrison fell in December 1715; he was taken to Delhi in a cage and executed on 9 June 1716. The Mughal recovery of Punjab from the Sikhs is registered in the atlas as a 1713–1718 transfer.

w4-800311.name: Treaty of Passarowitz cedes Oltenia (Lesser Wallachia) to the Habsburg Monarchy
w4-800311.blurb: Following Prince Eugene of Savoy's decisive victory at Petrovaradin (1716) and the capture of Belgrade (1717), the Treaty of Passarowitz (21 July 1718) compelled the Ottomans to cede Oltenia—the western portion of Wallachia—to the Habsburg Monarchy, where it was organized as the Banat of Craiova. This is the transfer from the Principality of Wallachia (an Ottoman vassal) to Habsburg control, registered in the atlas as 1713–1718.

w4-800316.name: Treaty of Nystad ending the Great Northern War
w4-800316.blurb: The Treaty of Nystad (signed 30 August/10 September 1721) concluded the Great Northern War (1700–1721), under which Sweden ceded Livonia, Estonia, Ingria, and southeastern Finland (with Viipuri) to Russia, ending Swedish hegemony in the Baltic and marking the close of the Stormaktstiden great-power era. The dataset records this as 'Kingdom of Sweden → Swedish Empire' for the 1720–1721 window, a periodisation relabeling in which the 'Swedish Empire' tag denotes the earlier expansive era whose end the treaty marks. Peter I took the title Emperor of All Russia following the treaty.

w4-800317.name: Qing expulsion of Dzungars from Tibet
w4-800317.blurb: Following the catastrophic defeat of his first expedition in 1718, the Kangxi Emperor launched a massive second campaign in 1720 attacking from Sichuan and Qinghai simultaneously. Qing forces occupied Lhasa on 24 September 1720, expelled the Dzungars, installed the 7th Dalai Lama Kelzang Gyatso, and established a permanent garrison. This began formal Qing suzerainty over Tibet, restoring Tibetan control of the territory (lat 33.7, lng 97.1) from Dzungar occupation.

w4-800318.name: Qing expedition to Tibet; expulsion of the Dzungars
w4-800318.blurb: In 1720 the Kangxi Emperor dispatched a Qing expedition to Tibet to expel the Dzungar Khanate, which had occupied Tibet since 1717. Qing forces entered Lhasa in September 1720 and installed Kelzang Gyatso as the 7th Dalai Lama. Matches worklist transition Dzungar Khanate -> Tibet (1720-1721); coords lng 88.2 lat 32.8 are in Tibet.

w4-800319.name: Maratha expansion into the Deccan under Peshwa Bajirao I
w4-800319.blurb: Following Balaji Vishwanath's death in April 1720, his son Bajirao I was appointed Peshwa (17 April 1720) and launched aggressive expansion at the expense of the weakening Mughal Empire. The Marathas, whose chauth/sardeshmukhi rights over the six Deccan provinces the Mughals had recognised in 1719, exploited the chaos of rival Mughal factions (the Sayyid Brothers' conflict with Nizam-ul-Mulk) to press territorial claims across the Deccan during 1720-1721. This marked the beginning of the dramatic Maratha expansion across central and western India.

w4-800320.name: Treaty of The Hague (1720): Savoy receives Sardinia in exchange for Sicily
w4-800320.blurb: Under the Treaty of The Hague (17 February 1720) ending the War of the Quadruple Alliance, the Duke of Savoy, Victor Amadeus II, ceded Sicily to the Habsburgs and received the island of Sardinia in return, taking the title King of Sardinia. This founded the Kingdom of Sardinia (1720–1861) that would eventually unify Italy. The atlas records the 1720–1721 transfer from Kingdom of Spain (which had seized Sardinia in 1717) to the new Kingdom of Sardinia.

w4-800321.name: Treaty of The Hague (1720) — Sicily to Austria, Sardinia to Savoy
w4-800321.blurb: The Treaty of The Hague (1720) ended the War of the Quadruple Alliance: Spain accepted the exchange by which Austria received Sicily from Savoy, while Savoy was compensated with Sardinia (transforming into the Kingdom of Sardinia). The Habsburg Monarchy thus gained the Kingdom of Sicily (~25,600 km²).

w4-800323.name: Treaty of The Hague (1720) – Sicily from Savoy to Habsburg Austria
w4-800323.blurb: The Treaty of The Hague (17 February 1720) ended the War of the Quadruple Alliance; Savoy exchanged Sicily for Sardinia, ceding Sicily to Habsburg Austria. Sicily near lng 14 E / lat 37.5 N passed (after the Spanish occupation) from Spain/Savoy to the Habsburg Monarchy, matching the [1720,1721] window.

w4-800325.name: Peter the Great proclaims Russian Empire — Treaty of Nystad (1721)
w4-800325.blurb: On 10 September 1721 Russia and Sweden signed the Treaty of Nystad, ending the Great Northern War and transferring Estonia, Livonia, Ingria, and southeast Finland to Russia. Following this victory, the Russian Senate and Synod petitioned Peter I to adopt the title 'Emperor of All Russia,' which he accepted on 2 November 1721, transforming the Tsardom of Russia into the Russian Empire. The proclamation replaced the Slavic title 'Tsar' with the Latin 'Imperator,' aligning Russia with major Western monarchies.

w4-800326.name: Treaty of Nystad – Sweden cedes Baltic provinces to Russia
w4-800326.blurb: The Treaty of Nystad (30 August 1721) ended the Great Northern War, with Sweden ceding Livonia, Estonia, Ingria, and parts of Karelia to Russia; Finland was returned to Sweden. The coordinates lie in the southern Finland / Karelian borderland capturing the Karelian/Vyborg territory Sweden definitively lost to the Russian Empire.

w4-800328.name: Qing Consolidation of Eastern Kham and Amdo (1724-1728)
w4-800328.blurb: Following the Qing expulsion of the Dzungars from Tibet (1720) and the Lhasa civil war (1727-28), the Yongzheng Emperor formalized Qing control over eastern Kham and Amdo. Amdo was organized as Qinghai Province in 1724 (the window's start), eastern Kham was incorporated into Chinese provinces in 1728 with a stone-pillar border near Bathang, and ambans were installed in Lhasa in 1728. Transfer Tibet -> Qing Dynasty fits the 1724-1727 window.

w4-800329.name: Establishment of the autonomous Nawabate of Awadh by Saadat Khan
w4-800329.blurb: Saadat Khan (Burhan-ul-Mulk) was appointed Subahdar (governor) of Awadh on 9 September 1722 by Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah. By 1724 he had established the kingdom of Awadh with hereditary succession, exploiting the Mughal Empire's fragmentation after Aurangzeb's death to exercise de facto independence while maintaining nominal Mughal allegiance. His appointment began the Awadh dynasty, which would rule as one of the wealthiest and most stable successor states of the Mughal Empire for nearly 150 years.

w4-800330.name: Independence of the Sultanate of Terengganu from Johor
w4-800330.blurb: Terengganu emerged as an independent sultanate in 1724, when Tun Zainal Abidin was installed as its first sultan, ending its status as a dependency of the Johor Sultanate. The formal installation is recorded in the Tuhfat al-Nafis as occurring under Johor's authority around 1725, but Terengganu thereafter operated as a sovereign polity. This separation reflected the broader fragmentation of the Johor Sultanate following internal conflicts in 1718.

w4-800332.name: Afghan Hotaki conquest of Safavid Persia — Battle of Gulnabad and Siege of Isfahan (1722)
w4-800332.blurb: Mahmud Hotaki of the Ghilzai Afghans invaded Persia in 1722, defeating the Safavid army at Gulnabad on 8 March 1722; after a six-month siege Isfahan surrendered on 23 October 1722 and Shah Sultan Husayn abdicated. By 1724–1727 the Hotaki dynasty controlled most of Persia, recognised by the Ottoman–Hotaki peace of 1727. The dataset records the Safavid → Hotaki transfer in the 1724–1727 window; the decisive conquest was 1722.

w4-800333.name: Russo-Persian War (1722–1723) — Russia occupies Gilan
w4-800333.blurb: Peter the Great's Russo-Persian War (1722–1723) saw Russia seize the Caspian provinces including Gilan (Rasht); the Treaty of Saint Petersburg (1723) formalised the cession from the declining Safavids. The coordinates (51.9,39) are the Caspian coast/Gilan, matching the from→to (Safavid Dynasty → Russian Empire) in the 1724–1727 window, during which Russia held these provinces (until 1732).

w4-800335.name: Chiang Mai revolt from Burmese Toungoo rule — Ong Kham declares independence
w4-800335.blurb: In 1727, a local Lanna man named Thepsingh killed the Burmese governor of Chiang Mai. The Tai Lue prince Ong Kham, originally summoned to help suppress the revolt, turned against the Burmese and expelled them, declaring himself independent king of Chiang Mai. Ong Kham ruled until his death in 1759. The dataset records Lan Na territory (lat 19.2, lng 99.1) shifting from Toungoo-successor Burmese control to independence around 1727–1734 as Mogaung also revolted in 1734.

w4-800336.name: Qing consolidation of eastern Tibet after the Tibetan civil war (1727–1734)
w4-800336.blurb: After Dzungar-backed nobles murdered the Regent Khangchenné in 1727 and sparked a civil war, the Yongzheng Emperor sent troops that reconquered Lhasa by 1728. The Qing annexed Kham territories east of the Jinsha into Sichuan, demarcated a Sino-Tibetan border with stone pillars by c. 1727–1734, and formalised the amban system, deepening Qing suzerainty over Tibet at lng 95.5, lat 31.9 (Tibet -> Qing Dynasty), matching [1727,1734].

w4-800345.name: Maratha conquest of Malwa; Treaty of Doraha (1738)
w4-800345.blurb: Peshwa Baji Rao I defeated the Mughal-backed Nizam at the Battle of Bhopal (Dec 1737 - Jan 1738), forcing the Treaty of Doraha (7 January 1738) ceding Malwa to the Marathas. The worklist transition is 'Mughal Empire' -> 'Maratha Empire' [1734,1738] at lng 72.2, lat 19 (the Maharashtra/Deccan Maratha heartland), with 1738 at the edge of the window; the coordinate reflects the Maratha core rather than Malwa itself but the from->to transfer is sound.

w4-800346.name: Russo-Turkish War (1735–1739) — Crimean reassertion over Nogai steppe
w4-800346.blurb: During the Russo-Turkish War of 1735–1739, Russian forces raided the Crimean Khanate and the Don–Dnieper steppe, disrupting the Nogai (Small Horde) under nominal Crimean suzerainty. After Russian withdrawal the Crimean Khanate reasserted control of the steppe (39.1,46), consistent with the from→to (Small Horde → Crimean Khanate) in the 1734–1738 window.

w4-800348.name: Nadir Shah's Reassertion of Iranian Control over Georgia
w4-800348.blurb: Nadir Shah of the Afsharid dynasty expelled the Ottomans from eastern Georgia in his 1734–1735 Caucasus campaigns and reimposed Iranian suzerainty over Kartli and Kakheti, confirmed by the 1736 Treaty of Constantinople. He installed a Persian governor in Kartli and confirmed Teimuraz II as wali of Kakheti, deporting thousands of Georgians. In 1744 he appointed Teimuraz II and Erekle II as kings of Kartli and Kakheti as loyal vassals; Georgia remained under Afsharid suzerainty until his 1747 assassination.

w4-800350.name: Nader Shah's Conquest of Kandahar and Destruction of the Hotaki Dynasty
w4-800350.blurb: Nader Shah Afshar had already expelled the Hotaki Afghans from Persia in 1729, but the Hotaki dynasty retained its base in Kandahar. In 1738 Nader Shah besieged Kandahar, capturing the city's citadel on 24 March 1738 and forcing the surrender of the last Hotaki ruler Hussain Hotaki. Nader then built a new city nearby and continued east to invade the Mughal Empire, ending the Hotaki dynasty entirely.

w4-800351.name: Ottoman–Persian War (1730–1735) – Nader Shah Recovers Western Iran and Caucasus
w4-800351.blurb: Nader Shah's campaigns against the Ottomans (1730–1735) aimed to recover Safavid territories lost after the Hotaki Afghan invasion. His decisive victory at the Battle of Yeghevard (1735) expelled Ottoman forces from the Caucasus and western Iran. The Treaty of Constantinople (1736) formalised Ottoman recognition of Iranian sovereignty over the Caucasus. This corresponds to the Lake Urmia/Kurdish frontier zone in the 1734–1738 window.

w4-800355.name: Transfer of Tuscany to Francis Stephen of Lorraine (1737-1738)
w4-800355.blurb: The last Medici Grand Duke, Gian Gastone, died on 9 July 1737, triggering the territorial exchange agreed in the War of the Polish Succession. Francis Stephen of Lorraine - husband of Habsburg heiress Maria Theresa - received the Grand Duchy of Tuscany in compensation for surrendering his ancestral Duchy of Lorraine to accommodate the deposed Polish king Stanisław Leszczyński. The arrangement was formalized in the Treaty of Vienna (November 1738), bringing Tuscany into the Habsburg-Lorraine orbit.

citations.label: War of the Polish Succession - Wikipedia

w4-800356.name: Lesser Juz of the Kazakh Khanate accepts Russian protectorate
w4-800356.blurb: Under Dzungar pressure following the catastrophic 'Great Disaster' (1723), Khan Abul Khayr of the Kazakh Lesser (Junior) Juz sought Russian protection. He swore fealty to Empress Anna of Russia on 10 October 1731. In 1734 the Orenburg Expedition was launched to establish fortresses and consolidate Russian presence in the region (lat 51.7, lng 56.4, the Ural/western Kazakhstan steppe). The period 1734–1738 saw the Orenburg fort system built and Bashkir revolts complicate Russian consolidation of Kazakh territory.

citations.label: Kazakhstan in the Russian Empire – Wikipedia

w4-800357.name: Chanda Sahib's conquest of Madurai Nayak kingdom (1736-1738)
w4-800357.blurb: The Nawab of Arcot's military commander Chanda Sahib launched major expeditions into the Tamil south in 1734 and 1736, exploiting a succession crisis between Queen Meenakshi and rival claimant Vangaru Thirumala. By 1736, Chanda Sahib had besieged and seized Trichinopoly and Madurai, imprisoning Meenakshi (who subsequently took poison), and absorbed the Madurai Nayak kingdom into the Carnatic (Nawab of Arcot's domain) after over two centuries of Nayak rule. The data entry (Nayaks of Madurai to Carnatic Sultanate, py=1734, y=1738) captures this conquest period.

w4-800358.name: Mon rebellion and founding of Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom
w4-800358.blurb: In 1740 the Mon people of Lower Burma revolted against the weakening Restored Toungoo dynasty (Cliopatria labels it 'First Toungoo Empire'), founding the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom centred on Pegu. The Toungoo king Mahadhammaraza Dipadi failed to suppress the uprising, and by 1741 Hanthawaddy had consolidated Lower Burma and began annual raids up the Irrawaddy. The coordinates (96 degrees E, 16 degrees N) point to the Irrawaddy delta / Lower Burma, the core of the Mon revolt. This revolt ultimately led to the fall of Ava in 1752 and the rise of the Konbaung dynasty.

w4-800359.name: First Silesian War — Frederick the Great's conquest of Silesia
w4-800359.blurb: On 16 December 1740 Frederick II of Prussia invaded the Habsburg province of Silesia, exploiting the succession of Maria Theresa. By January 1741 almost all of Silesia was under Prussian control, and the Battle of Mollwitz (April 1741) secured Prussian dominance. The Peace of Breslau (1742) formally ceded most of Silesia (lat 50.9, lng 17) to Prussia. Window 1738-1741.

citations.label: War of the Austrian Succession – Wikipedia

w4-800361.type: military conquest / Nader Shah's Persian campaigns
w4-800361.name: Nader Shah's Afsharid conquest of Oman from the Yarubid dynasty (1737–1741)
w4-800361.blurb: Weakened by a succession civil war since 1718, the Yarubid Imam invited Nader Shah's forces into Oman. Persian troops arrived in 1737 and expanded control; by 1741–1743 they held key positions. This brought interior/coastal Omani territory around lng 55.2, lat 23.8 from Yarubid to Afsharid control (Yarubid dynasty -> Afsharid Iran), matching the [1738,1741] window.

citations.label: Afsharid conquests in the Persian Gulf and Oman – Wikipedia

w4-800362.name: Nader Shah's Invasion of India
w4-800362.blurb: Nader Shah, founder of the Afsharid dynasty of Iran, invaded the Mughal Empire in 1738-1739, defeating Emperor Muhammad Shah at the Battle of Karnal (24 February 1739) and entering Delhi on 20 March 1739. He looted the Mughal treasury including the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor diamond, then departed in May 1739, ceding back territories east of the Indus but retaining the provinces west of it (Sindh, western Punjab, and Kabul). This catastrophically weakened Mughal power over the northwest.

citations.label: Nader Shah's invasion of India - Wikipedia

w4-800363.name: Treaty of Belgrade returns Oltenia to Wallachia
w4-800363.blurb: The Treaty of Passarowitz (1718) had ceded Oltenia (Lesser Wallachia) to the Habsburg Monarchy. During the Austro-Turkish War of 1737–1739, Habsburg forces suffered defeats and the Treaty of Belgrade (18 September 1739) obliged the Habsburgs to return Oltenia to the Ottoman-vassal Principality of Wallachia, restoring the pre-1718 border along the Olt River. The atlas dates this as 1738–1741, encompassing the war and its aftermath.

w4-800365.name: Maratha Expansion into Malwa and Rajputana under Baji Rao I
w4-800365.blurb: Peshwa Baji Rao I's victory over the Mughals at Bhopal (1737) and the resulting Treaty of Bhopal (1738) ceded Malwa to the Marathas; in the late 1730s-early 1740s Holkar and Scindia extracted chauth across Rajputana (~75E 24N). By 1741 the Mughals formally ceded the chauth of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, confirming Maratha supremacy. Correctly dated within the 1738-1741 window.

w4-800369.name: Ahmad ibn Said Al-Busaidi Elected Imam, Founding Busaidi Sultanate of Oman
w4-800369.blurb: A prolonged civil war between the Ghafiri and Hinawi factions and Persian intervention (1741-1744) brought down the Yarubid dynasty in Oman. Ahmad ibn Said al-Busaidi, governor of Sohar, resisted Persian forces and was elected Imam in 1744 after driving out the Persians and defeating rival claimants, founding the Al Busaid dynasty (still ruling today). The coordinates point to East Africa, reflecting Omani territory on the Swahili coast that changed polity label from Yarubid to Busaidi Oman with the dynasty change.

w4-800371.name: Nadir Shah Appoints Teimuraz II and Erekle II as Georgian Kings (1744)
w4-800371.blurb: In 1744 Nadir Shah rewarded the loyal Georgian princes Teimuraz II (Kartli) and his son Erekle II (Kakheti) with formal royal appointments, granting them greater autonomy within the Afsharid Empire. This arrangement, while still recognizing Iranian suzerainty, gave Georgia effective self-governance. After Nadir Shah's assassination in 1747, the two Georgian kingdoms exercised de facto independence, and Erekle II eventually unified them as the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti in 1762.

w4-800372.name: War of Jenkins' Ear / War of Austrian Succession in Central America
