w4-900401.blurb: After Japan's victory in the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95) and the assassination of Queen Min (1895), King Gojong of Joseon proclaimed the Great Han (Korean) Empire on 12 October 1897, taking the title of Emperor and renaming the state to assert independence. The coordinates (127.5E, 38.1N) lie on the Korean peninsula. Transfer Joseon -> Korean Empire fits the 1895-1898 window.

w4-900403.name: Portuguese-Dutch Timor Mixed Boundary Commission Agreement
w4-900403.blurb: A Portuguese-Dutch mixed boundary commission working in 1895-1898 agreed on most of the land border between Portuguese Timor and Dutch Timor (coordinates lng 124.3, lat -9.6). The 1898 agreement resolved the main frontier issues, though some points required the 1904 Hague Convention and the 1914 Permanent Court of Arbitration award. The dataset's 1895-1898 window captures this demarcation, shifting borderline territory between the two colonial polities.

w4-900405.name: South African Republic protectorate over Swaziland lapses; Boer War begins
w4-900405.blurb: The 1894 London Convention placed Swaziland (coord 31.4E/-26.6N) under the South African Republic (Transvaal) as a protectorate. When the Second Boer War broke out in October 1899, the SAR administration of Swaziland collapsed as Boer administrators withdrew, and by 1900 the SAR could no longer govern it. The dataset's 1898–1900 'South African Republic → Swaziland' shift captures this transition to an interregnum before Britain assumed the protectorate in 1903.

w4-900409.name: Battle of Omdurman and Anglo-Egyptian reconquest of Sudan
w4-900409.blurb: General Herbert Kitchener led an Anglo-Egyptian expeditionary force south along the Nile, culminating in the decisive Battle of Omdurman on 2 September 1898, where the Mahdist army of Khalifa Abdallahi was crushed. Khartoum was retaken on 4 September 1898, ending the Mahdist State that had controlled Sudan since 1885. The territory was subsequently administered as the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium, consistent with the window [1898,1900].

w4-900412.name: Division of the Omani Empire (1856) and adoption of 'Sultanate of Muscat and Oman' name
w4-900412.blurb: Following the death of Sultan Said bin Sultan in 1856, the Omani Empire split: Thuwaini bin Said became Sultan of Muscat and Oman, formalising the dual name distinguishing the Arabian coast from the interior. The dataset codes territory at lat 23.3, lng 57.6 transitioning from 'Sultanate of Oman' to 'Sultanate of Muscat and Oman' around 1898–1900, a lag in map-label updating relative to the 1856 formal naming that became entrenched through the British protectorate relationship formalised in 1891. The event is real but the coded date trails the substantive change by decades.

w4-900414.name: U.S. military occupation of Cuba after Spanish–American War
w4-900414.blurb: Following the decisive U.S. victory in the Spanish–American War, Spain signed the Treaty of Paris (10 December 1898) ceding Cuba, which under the Teller Amendment could not be annexed by the U.S. The United States Military Government in Cuba was established from 1 January 1899, administering the island (lat 21, lng -76.4) until 20 May 1902. The Platt Amendment (1901) gave the U.S. the right to intervene militarily in Cuba even after formal independence, making it a de facto protectorate.

w4-900422.name: Franco-German Cameroon-Nigeria Boundary Convention (1902-1906)
w4-900422.blurb: Around 8-9E, 9.5N on the Yola-to-Lake-Chad frontier, the boundary between British Northern Nigeria and German Kamerun was clarified by the Anglo-German Convention of 19 March 1906, building on the 1893 delimitation of the Rio del Rey-Cross River-Benue-Lake Chad line. The agreement adjusted contested stretches of the Nigeria-Kamerun border north of the Benue and was confirmed by further accords in 1909 and 1913. The principals here were Britain and Germany, not France; the centroid sits on the British-German, not a Franco-German, boundary.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Franco-German boundary agreements in West Africa

w4-900423.name: German Adamawa Wars — conquest of Sokoto-affiliated territory in Kamerun
w4-900423.blurb: The Adamawa Wars (1899–1907) were German colonial campaigns against Fulani/Hausa states linked to the Sokoto Caliphate in northern Kamerun. Key actions include the Battle of Miskin-Maroua (January 1902) in which Hans Dominik defeated Sokoto Emir Zubairu's forces, and the Anglo-German partition formalised in 1903 following the British conquest of Sokoto itself. German forces consolidated control over the Lake Chad region and northern Kamerun by 1905, extinguishing Sokoto's territorial authority in the area.

w4-900424.name: Franco-German Cameroon–Nigeria border delimitations c. 1902–1905
w4-900424.blurb: In the early 1900s Franco-German boundary commissions delimited the frontier between French West/Equatorial Africa and German Kamerun in the Lake Chad hinterland and northern Cameroon. The coordinates lie in this northern Cameroon–Nigeria borderland where the protocols adjusted the French Africa / German Africa line.

w4-900425.name: End of First US Occupation — Cuban independence (1902)
w4-900425.blurb: On 20 May 1902, the United States concluded its first military occupation of Cuba (which had begun after the Spanish-American War of 1898) and transferred sovereignty to the Republic of Cuba under President Tomas Estrada Palma. Military Governor Leonard Wood handed over control at noon in Havana. Cuba's independence was conditioned on accepting the Platt Amendment, incorporated into its constitution, which allowed US intervention and established the Guantanamo Bay naval base. By 1905, US investors owned 60% of Cuban rural properties, reflecting ongoing economic dependence despite formal independence.

w4-900426.name: Dutch annexation of the Sultanate of Jambi
w4-900426.blurb: The Sultanate of Jambi on Sumatra was brought under full Dutch East Indies control after the death of the last resisting Sultan, Taha Saifuddin, on 27 April 1904, and reconstituted as a Dutch Residency by 1906. The from=Sultanate of Jambi / to=Dutch East Indies and 1902-1905 window span the final resistance and annexation.

w4-900430.name: Treaty of Peace and Friendship between Bolivia and Chile (1904/1905)
w4-900430.blurb: The Treaty of Peace and Friendship signed on 20 October 1904 (ratifications exchanged March 1905) formally ended the War of the Pacific between Bolivia and Chile. Bolivia permanently ceded the Atacama littoral to Chile, becoming landlocked. The worklist transition is 'Bolivia' -> 'Republic of Chile' [1902,1905] at lng -69, lat -21.7 (the Atacama/Antofagasta ceded territory), with 1904 inside the window.

citations.label: Treaty of Peace and Friendship (1904) – Wikipedia

w4-900431.name: First Saudi–Rashidi War: Ibn Saud's Qasim campaign
w4-900431.blurb: After Ibn Saud retook Riyadh in January 1902, he launched the First Saudi–Rashidi War (1903–1907) to recapture Nejd from the Rashidi Emirate of Jabal Shammar. Despite Ottoman-backed Rashidi counterattacks in 1903–1904, Ibn Saud secured Qasim by 1906 after the Battle of Rawdat Muhanna, in which the Rashidi emir was killed. Matches the Jabal Shammar → Nejd transfer of Qasim territory in the 1902-1905 window.

w4-900434.name: Belgian annexation of the Congo Free State
w4-900434.blurb: King Leopold II of Belgium had ruled the Congo Free State as his personal property since 1885, but mounting international outrage over atrocities documented by E.D. Morel, Roger Casement, and others forced him to cede the territory to the Belgian state. The Belgian Parliament formally annexed the Congo on 18 October 1908, renaming it the Belgian Congo, matching the dataset window [1907,1908]. This transferred Africa's largest colonial holding from private royal control to a colonial state.

w4-900435.name: Second US Occupation of Cuba (Platt Amendment invoked)
w4-900435.blurb: Following the disputed 1905 re-election of President Estrada Palma and a Liberal armed revolt in August 1906, Palma resigned and invoked the Platt Amendment requesting US intervention. On 29 September 1906 Secretary of War William Howard Taft declared himself Provisional Governor, beginning the Second Occupation of Cuba. Some 5,000 American troops occupied the island, with Charles Magoon serving as provisional governor. The occupation lasted until 28 January 1909 when Jose Miguel Gomez was inaugurated as Cuban president.

citations.label: Second Occupation of Cuba – Military Wiki

w4-900436.name: Franco-Siamese Treaty of 1907
w4-900436.blurb: The Franco-Siamese Treaty of 23 March 1907 required Siam (the Rattanakosin Kingdom) to cede the Cambodian provinces of Battambang, Siem Reap, and Sisophon to French Indochina, in exchange for France returning Trat and Dan Sai to Siam. The ceded territories included Angkor Wat and the heart of ancient Khmer civilization (lat 12.6, lng 103.6, near Siem Reap/Battambang). This was the last major territorial expansion of French Indochina and completed French control of Cambodia.

w4-900439.name: Portuguese revolution of 1910 / end of Portuguese monarchy
w4-900439.blurb: The Portuguese revolution of 5 October 1910 overthrew the monarchy and established the Portuguese Republic, changing the governing entity for all Portuguese colonial territories. The atlas records the Malay Peninsula Portuguese territory (100°E/6.4°N = Portuguese Malacca area) transferring from 'Portuguese Colonies' to 'Portuguese Republic' between 1908 and 1911, an administrative relabelling consequent to the political change in Lisbon.

w4-900442.name: Anglo-French Wadai-Darfur Boundary Agreement
w4-900442.blurb: The 1899 and subsequent Anglo-French boundary conventions delimited the frontier between British Sudan (Darfur) and French Equatorial Africa (Chad/Wadai) in the region around 22.9°E, 12.8°N (the Wadai-Darfur border zone); the 1911 Anglo-French Convention finalized adjustments that transferred some territory from British to French administration in this borderland.

w4-900443.name: Morocco–Congo Treaty (Neukamerun)
w4-900443.blurb: The Morocco-Congo Treaty of November 4, 1911, which resolved the Agadir (Second Moroccan) Crisis, required France to cede approximately 275,000 km² of French Equatorial Africa (parts of Middle Congo and Ubangi-Shari) to German Kamerun — the territory known as Neukamerun — in exchange for Germany recognizing the French protectorate over Morocco.

w4-900444.name: Union of South Africa Act 1909 / Formation of Union of South Africa
w4-900444.blurb: The Colony of Natal (the successor territory to the original Natalia Republic area) joined the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910 under the South Africa Act 1909. The atlas polygon labelled 'Natalia Republic' at this period likely represents Natal Colony, which was absorbed into British Africa's broader administrative framework as one of the four founding provinces.

w4-900445.name: Agadir Crisis settlement: France cedes Neukamerun to Germany
w4-900445.blurb: During the Agadir Crisis of 1911, the Franco-German Convention of 4 November 1911 had France cede over 107,000 sq mi of the French Congo to German Kamerun (Neukamerun) in exchange for German recognition of France's protectorate over Morocco. Matches the French Africa → German Africa transfer in the 1908-1911 window.

w4-900446.name: Formation of the Union of South Africa
w4-900446.blurb: The Colony of Natal (which had absorbed the former Boer Natalia Republic in 1843 and Zululand in 1897) was united with the Cape Colony, Transvaal, and Orange River Colony on 31 May 1910 to form the Union of South Africa under the British Crown, pursuant to the South Africa Act 1909. The 1908–1911 window reflects the period from the National Convention (1908–1909) through the establishment of the Union and its first census (1911). (The worklist's 'from' label 'Natalia Republic' is a Cliopatria carryover for the Natal territory.)

w4-900448.name: End of Second US Occupation of Cuba
w4-900448.blurb: After restoring order and holding elections in November 1908, the United States ended the Second Occupation of Cuba when President Jose Miguel Gomez was inaugurated on 28 January 1909 and the provisional US administration withdrew. Cuba regained effective sovereignty under the Platt Amendment framework, though the US retained the right to intervene and maintained its Guantanamo Bay naval base. US economic and political influence remained dominant through the following decades until the Platt Amendment was abrogated in 1934.

citations.label: Second Occupation of Cuba – Military Wiki

w4-900450.name: Mexican Revolution — Maderista Uprising and Fall of Porfirio Díaz
w4-900450.blurb: Francisco I. Madero's Plan of San Luis Potosí (November 1910) called for armed revolt against dictator Porfirio Díaz. Through spring 1911, Maderista forces under Pancho Villa, Pascual Orozco, and others swept through northern Mexico, capturing Ciudad Juárez on 10 May 1911. The Treaty of Ciudad Juárez (21 May 1911) forced Díaz to resign and go into exile; Mexican federal control of the northern interior (near lng -106.6, lat 28.4, Chihuahua) gave way to revolutionary forces. The dataset window 1908–1911 captures this transition.

w4-900451.name: Japan-Korea Annexation Treaty (1910)
w4-900451.blurb: Japan formally annexed the Korean Empire on 29 August 1910 under the Japan-Korea Annexation Treaty, following the 1905 protectorate. Emperor Sunjong was forced to sign, dissolving the Korean Empire (~220,163 km2) into the Empire of Japan as the colony of Chosen. Transfer Korean Empire -> Empire of Japan fits the 1908-1911 window.

w4-900452.type: political consolidation / restoration of federal control
w4-900452.name: Madero Elected President; Revolutionary Territory Reintegrated into Mexico
w4-900452.blurb: After Porfirio Díaz's exile in May 1911, the interim government of Francisco León de la Barra governed until elections in October 1911, when Madero won by an overwhelming majority. As his government consolidated its administration across northern Mexico, the areas (near lng -106.6, lat 28.4, Chihuahua) that had operated under Maderista revolutionary authority were formally reintegrated into the Mexican state. The dataset records this 1911–1912 back-transfer of Maderista-controlled territory to Mexico, mirroring the previous entry.

w4-900454.name: Italo-Turkish War — Italy conquers Ottoman Libya and signs Treaty of Ouchy (1912)
w4-900454.blurb: Italy declared war on the Ottoman Empire on 29 September 1911 and landed in Tripolitania and Cyrenaica; under Balkan War pressure the Ottomans signed the Treaty of Ouchy (18 October 1912), ceding Tripolitania and Cyrenaica to Italy. The territory became Italian Libya, administered as 'Italian Africa'. The dataset records the Ottoman Tripolitania → Italian Africa transfer in the 1911–1912 window.

w4-900456.name: Xinhai Revolution / Abdication of the Xuantong Emperor
w4-900456.blurb: The Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 triggered a cascade of provincial defections from the Qing Dynasty; the Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 January 1912, and the six-year-old Xuantong Emperor (Puyi) issued his abdication edict on 12 February 1912, ending the Qing Dynasty and over two millennia of Chinese imperial rule.

w4-900457.name: Treaty of Fez: establishment of the French Protectorate in Morocco
w4-900457.blurb: On 30 March 1912 Sultan Abd al-Hafid signed the Treaty of Fez under duress, establishing a French protectorate over Morocco's foreign policy, military, and economy. The Agadir Crisis (1911) had paved the way. Matches the Morocco → French Africa transfer in the 1911-1912 window.

w4-900458.name: Mongolian Revolution of 1911 / Bogd Khanate declaration of independence
w4-900458.blurb: On 1 December 1911, the Provisional Government of Khalkha Mongolia issued a proclamation ending Qing suzerainty and establishing an independent theocratic state under the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu (Bogd Khan) as head of state. The Qing garrison in Urga was expelled, creating the Bogd Khanate of Mongolia (the 'Great Mongol State' in the atlas).

w4-900460.name: Mongolian Revolution of 1911 and proclamation of the Bogd Khanate
w4-900460.blurb: As the Qing Dynasty collapsed during the Xinhai Revolution, Outer Mongolian nobles convened and on 29 December 1911 proclaimed independence with the 8th Jebtsundamba Khutughtu (Bogd Khan) as theocratic ruler. The new Bogd Khanate (called 'Great Mongol State' in Cliopatria, centroid lat 46.9, lng 103.8) immediately appealed to Russia for support,

w4-900462.name: Albanian Declaration of Independence (Vlorë Proclamation)
w4-900462.blurb: On 28 November 1912, as Balkan League armies advanced to partition Ottoman Albania, an All-Albanian Congress in Vlorë declared Albanian independence. The declaration was driven by fear that Serbia, Greece, and Montenegro would divide Albanian-populated territories among themselves following Ottoman defeats in the First Balkan War. The Great Powers recognised Albanian independence de facto on 17 December 1912, though final borders were set by the Treaty of Bucharest (1913).

w4-900463.name: Hague Arbitration on Timor border (1913); Manufahi revolt context
w4-900463.blurb: The boundary between Dutch East Indies and Portuguese Timor was long disputed. The 1904 treaty adjusted some enclaves, but the major Manufahi revolt of 1911–12 prompted cross-border refugee movements and diplomatic pressure. The landmark Delimitation arbitration signed at The Hague on 3 April 1913 drew the formal border separating Dutch West Timor from Portuguese East Timor. The dataset records the 1911–1912 window, which reflects the pre-arbitration period of contested authority before the border was fixed.

citations.label: IBRU Boundary Briefing on East Timor

w4-900465.name: Treaty of Constantinople (1913) — Ottoman recovery of Eastern Thrace
w4-900465.blurb: While Bulgaria was fighting Serbia and Greece in the Second Balkan War (June–August 1913), the Ottoman Empire recaptured Adrianople (Edirne) and eastern Thrace; the Treaty of Constantinople (29 September 1913) between Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire confirmed Ottoman sovereignty over the region, establishing approximately the modern Turkish–Bulgarian border in Thrace.

w4-900466.name: Ibn Saud's Conquest of al-Ahsa (Eastern Arabia)
w4-900466.blurb: In May 1913 (4-6 May) Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, ruler of the Third Saudi State (the Emirate of Riyadh, soon styled the Emirate of Nejd and Hasa), led a surprise assault on the Ottoman province of al-Ahsa (al-Hasa), storming the Kut fortress at Hofuf and expelling the Ottoman garrison. The conquest gave the Saudis the Persian Gulf coast and its lucrative date-palm and customs revenues, and the Ottomans subsequently recognized Ibn Saud's rule over Nejd and al-Hasa.

w4-900467.name: Ibn Saud's conquest of Al-Hasa from the Ottomans (1913)
w4-900467.blurb: In April-May 1913, Abdulaziz ibn Saud exploited Ottoman preoccupation with the Balkan Wars to overrun the Ottoman garrison in the Al-Hasa oasis of eastern Arabia, capturing Hofuf and folding the region into the Emirate of Nejd and Hasa. The worklist transition is 'Ottoman Empire' -> 'Emirate of Nejd' [1912,1913] at lng 49.7, lat 26.5 (eastern Arabia / Al-Ahsa region), and 1913 falls within the window.

w4-900468.name: Treaty of London (1913) / Conference of Ambassadors
w4-900468.blurb: The Treaty of London (30 May 1913) ended the First Balkan War, ceding Ottoman Europe west of the Enos-Midia line to the Balkan League but leaving Albania's borders to the Great Powers, who had recognized Albanian independence (declared 28 November 1912). The subsequent Conference of Ambassadors in London demarcated the new Principality of Albania's frontiers, forcing Montenegro - which had taken Shkoder (Shkodra) after a long siege in April 1913 - to evacuate the city, which was assigned to Albania.

w4-900470.name: Ibadi revolt and establishment of the Imamate of Oman
w4-900470.blurb: In May 1913, tribal leaders in the Omani interior elected Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi as Imam at Tanuf, launching a rebellion against the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman backed by British influence. Imamate forces captured Nizwa (June 1913) and Izki, establishing control over the interior. The Sultan sought British military support to defend the coast. This de facto partition between the coastal Sultanate and the interior Imamate was formalised by the Treaty of Seeb (1920), and the Imamate was only suppressed militarily during the Jebel Akhdar War of 1954-1959.

w4-900473.name: Russian Protectorate over Uryankhay (Tannu Tuva)
w4-900473.blurb: After the 1911 Xinhai Revolution, Tuvan nobles petitioned Tsar Nicholas II for protection. On 17 April 1914 Russia formally proclaimed the Uryankhay Krai protectorate, absorbing the former Qing vassal territory (~94E 52N, modern Republic of Tuva) into Yenisei Province. This ended Tuvan subordination to the collapsing Qing/Republic of China. Correctly dated within the 1913-1914 window.

w4-900474.name: End of the Aceh War
w4-900474.blurb: The Aceh War (1873-1914) was one of the longest colonial conflicts in Southeast Asia. By 1903 the Acehnese sultan had surrendered, but guerrilla resistance continued until 1913-1914, with the Gayo highlands the last area pacified. In 1914 the Dutch declared the Aceh Sultanate fully incorporated into the Dutch East Indies. Window 1913-1914.

w4-900480.name: Russian capture of Eastern Galicia (Battle of Galicia, WWI Eastern Front 1914)
w4-900480.blurb: In autumn 1914, Russian forces under Generals Brusilov and Ruzsky defeated Austro-Hungarian armies in the Battle of Galicia, capturing Lemberg (Lviv) and occupying Eastern Galicia for roughly nine months. The Gorlice-Tarnów Offensive of May 1915 later pushed Russia back, but the py1914/y1915 window captures this temporary passage of the large Austro-Hungarian territory to Russian control, matching the dataset transfer (Austria-Hungary -> Russian Empire) at lng23/lat49.2.

w4-900481.name: British occupation of southern Persia (WWI)
w4-900481.blurb: During World War I, despite Iran's declared neutrality, British forces occupied Bushehr (Bushire) on 8 August 1915 to secure the Mesopotamian campaign supply lines and oil interests in Khuzestan. A broader British presence extended through southern and western Persia, with the South Persia Rifles established in 1916 under Percy Sykes to counter German and Ottoman influence. The wartime Anglo-Russian understanding allowed direct British control of southern Qajar territories.

w4-900484.name: WWI Cameroon Campaign — French advance from AEF
w4-900484.blurb: Following the outbreak of World War I, French forces from French Equatorial Africa invaded German Kamerun in August 1914, advancing from the south and east. By 1915, French troops had occupied southern Kamerun (the area around lng 4.8, lat 7.5), with the last German garrison at Mora surrendering in February 1916.

w4-900485.name: British/Belgian Conquest of German East Africa (WWI)
w4-900485.blurb: During World War I, British and Belgian forces invaded German East Africa; by late 1916 the main German garrison had been expelled from most of the territory after the fall of Dar es Salaam (September 1916) and Tabora (September 1916). Britain assumed administration of the territory under a military occupation that was later formalized by the League of Nations mandate in 1922.

citations.label: Wikipedia: East African campaign (World War I)

w4-900486.name: WWI Kamerun Campaign: Anglo-French partition of German Kamerun
w4-900486.blurb: Following the conquest of German Kamerun (completed February 1916 with the fall of Mora), Britain and France partitioned the former colony under the Milner-Simon Agreement (July 10, 1919, retroactive to military occupation); the British sector near the centroid (~9°E, 4.6°N, southern Cameroon coast/hinterland) was separated from the French zone.

w4-900487.name: World War I East African Campaign — British forces capture German East Africa (1916)
w4-900487.blurb: In 1916 a large Allied force (British, South African, Belgian, Congolese) invaded German East Africa, capturing the central railway corridor and most urban centres while von Lettow-Vorbeck retreated into guerrilla warfare. Britain assumed military administration over most of the territory, later the League of Nations 'Tanganyika Territory' mandate from 1922. The dataset records the German Africa → British Africa transfer in the 1915–1916 window.

citations.label: East African campaign (World War I) — Wikipedia

w4-900492.name: Allied conquest of Neukamerun – French takeover (1916)
w4-900492.blurb: In 1911 France had ceded the 'Neukamerun' strip to Germany during the Agadir Crisis settlement. During the Kamerun campaign, Belgian and French troops occupied most of Neukamerun in 1915, and after German forces collapsed the territory passed to French administration in 1916. The southernmost Neukamerun salient bordered the Belgian Congo near the equator; this area reverted to French Equatorial Africa, now part of Chad, the Central African Republic, and the Republic of the Congo.

w4-900493.name: Kamerun campaign; Allied conquest of German Cameroon
w4-900493.blurb: The Kamerun campaign was an Allied offensive into the German colony of Kamerun running from August 1914 to March 1916. British, French, and Belgian forces forced the German Schutztruppe to surrender on 10 March 1916 after the last garrison at Mora fell. The colony was partitioned between France and Britain. Matches worklist transition German Africa -> French Africa (1915-1916); coords lng 13.9 lat 5.8 correspond to Cameroon.

w4-900494.name: Gorlice-Tarnow Offensive and the Great Retreat of 1915
w4-900494.blurb: The Austro-German Gorlice-Tarnow Offensive (May–September 1915) broke the Russian front in Galicia, forcing the Great Retreat; by autumn 1915 Austria-Hungary had recaptured eastern Galicia (centroid ~lng 22.4, lat 49.4, the Przemyśl–Rzeszów corridor) from Russia, reversing Russian gains of 1914–15.

w4-900495.name: Austro-Hungarian conquest of Serbia (October–November 1915)
w4-900495.blurb: Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Bulgaria launched a coordinated invasion of Serbia in October 1915. Overwhelmed on three fronts, the Serbian army retreated through Albania to the Adriatic. By late November 1915 Austro-Hungarian forces had occupied Serbia, imposing military administration over ~55,000 km² of Serbian territory.

w4-900496.name: Gorlice–Tarnów Offensive and the 'Great Retreat' (1915)
w4-900496.blurb: On 2 May 1915 German-Austro-Hungarian forces under Mackensen launched the Gorlice–Tarnów Offensive in Galicia against a Russian army short of ammunition. The Russian 3rd Army was shattered and Russian forces began the 'Great Retreat,' abandoning Galicia (including the Przemyśl region) to Austro-Hungarian control — the largest Central Powers operation on the Eastern Front.

w4-900497.name: Bulgarian occupation of Greek Macedonia (World War I)
w4-900497.blurb: Bulgaria entered World War I on the side of the Central Powers in October 1915 and rapidly overran Greek (and Serbian) Macedonia in 1916, occupying the region including Drama, Kavala, and Serres; Greece under King Constantine I maintained a disputed neutrality, allowing Bulgarian forces to advance into areas nominally under Greek sovereignty.

w4-900498.name: Bulgarian-German Invasion of Romania / Occupation of Southern Dobruja (1916)
w4-900498.blurb: After Bulgaria joined the Central Powers and Romania entered the Entente in August 1916, a combined Bulgarian-German force under General von Mackensen invaded Southern Dobruja in September 1916, overrunning Romanian (formerly Wallachian) territory and placing it under Bulgarian occupation.

citations.label: Romania in World War I — Wikipedia

w4-900499.name: Surrender of Fort Roupel and Bulgarian occupation of Eastern Macedonia (1916)
w4-900499.blurb: Following the surrender of the Greek Fort Roupel to German-Bulgarian forces in late May 1916 (with the acquiescence of the pro-German royal Greek government during the National Schism), Bulgarian troops occupied Greek Eastern Macedonia — Kavala, Drama, and Serres — through summer 1916, a direct Greece-to-Bulgaria transfer matching this record.

w4-900501.name: Bulgarian Occupation of Serbia in World War I
w4-900501.blurb: Bulgaria joined the Central Powers on 14 October 1915 and immediately invaded Serbia alongside German and Austro-Hungarian forces in a coordinated offensive. By late November 1915 all of Serbia was occupied; Bulgaria administered eastern and southern Serbia (including most of Macedonia and Kosovo) as the Military Inspection Areas of Morava and Macedonia. The dataset records 'Kingdom of Serbia → Bulgaria' for 1915–1916 in the Macedonian corridor.

citations.label: Bulgarian occupation of Serbia (World War I) – Wikipedia

w4-900502.name: Hongxian Monarchy — Yuan Shikai proclaims Empire of China
w4-900502.blurb: On 12 December 1915, President Yuan Shikai declared the restoration of the monarchy and accepted the imperial throne, renaming the Republic of China the 'Empire of China' and designating 1916 as 'Hongxian Year 1.' A monarchist lobbying campaign backed by Yuan had assembled a facade of popular consent through the Plan for Peace Association. The empire collapsed within 83 days as provinces rebelled under the National Protection War, and Yuan abdicated on 22 March 1916 before dying of kidney failure in June 1916.

w4-900503.name: United States military occupation of the Dominican Republic (1916–1924)
w4-900503.blurb: On 29 November 1916, the United States established a military government over the Dominican Republic, after Marines landed in May 1916, citing instability, debt, and World War I strategic concerns. The occupation lasted until September 1924. The worklist transfer Dominican Republic → United States at lng -70.3, lat 18.8 in the 1915–1916 window matches the onset of the occupation.

citations.label: Military Government of Santo Domingo – Wikipedia

w4-900504.name: United States occupation of Haiti – Haitian-American Treaty of 1915
w4-900504.blurb: US Marines landed in Haiti on 28 July 1915, and the Haitian-American Treaty (signed 16 Sept 1915, ratified 1916) gave the United States control over Haiti's finances, customs, and constabulary, effectively transferring sovereign control. The coordinates are Haiti, matching the recorded Haiti → United States shift for 1915–1916.

citations.label: United States occupation of Haiti – Wikipedia
U.S. Invasion and Occupation of Haiti, 1915–34 – history.state.gov

w4-900506.name: Russian military occupation of northern Iran during World War I
w4-900506.blurb: During WWI Russia conducted the Persian campaign, advancing into nominally neutral Qajar Iran to counter Ottoman/German influence. From late 1915 General Baratov's forces occupied Hamadan, Kermanshah, and other parts of northern/western Iran. The 1915–1916 window matches the peak Russian occupation of Qajar territory at (47.2°E, 37.9°N) in northwestern Iran.

w4-900507.name: Gorlice-Tarnow Offensive and the Great Retreat of Russia (1915)
w4-900507.blurb: The Gorlice-Tarnow Offensive launched by Germany and Austria-Hungary in May 1915 broke the Russian lines and triggered the Russian 'Great Retreat'. By autumn 1915 Germany had occupied Congress Poland, Lithuania, and much of Courland. The coordinates (22.7E, 53.8N) lie in central Lithuania/Belarus, squarely within the 1915 advance. Transfer Russian Empire -> German Empire fits the 1915-1916 window.

w4-900508.to: United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia
w4-900508.name: Romanian invasion of Transylvania (August 1916)
w4-900508.blurb: Romania entered WWI on 27 August 1916 and immediately invaded Austria-Hungary's Transylvania, occupying territory before the Central Powers counteroffensive under Falkenhayn and Mackensen reversed these gains from September onward. The originally cited 'fall of Bucharest' counteroffensive describes the opposite direction of territorial flow (Central Powers gains, not Romanian ones) and cannot explain an Austria-Hungary-to-Romania transfer.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Romania during World War I

w4-900512.name: February Revolution and Reaffirmation of the Emirate of Bukhara's Status (1917)
w4-900512.blurb: After the Russian February Revolution of 1917, Emir Alim Khan signed a manifesto (7 April 1917) endorsing the Provisional Government, which reaffirmed Bukhara's independence and territorial integrity in March 1917; the emir suppressed the Young Bukharan reformers. The dataset records the change between 1916 and 1917, reflecting the shift of the protectorate relationship to the new Russian Republic. (Full Soviet conquest came in 1920.) Transfer Emirate of Bukhara -> Russian Republic fits the window as a status change.

w4-900513.from: United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia
w4-900513.name: Bulgarian occupation of Romanian Dobruja during World War I
w4-900513.blurb: Bulgaria, motivated by its loss of Southern Dobruja in the Second Balkan War (1913), entered World War I on the side of the Central Powers and invaded Southern Dobruja on 2 September 1916 following Romania's declaration of war. The Dobruja Campaign ended in a Central Powers victory, and Bulgarian forces occupied the region to the Danube by January 1917. The data window 1916-1917 captures this occupation; Romania ceded Dobruja under the Treaty of Bucharest (1918), reversed after the war.

citations.label: Romania in World War I – Wikipedia

w4-900516.name: Brusilov Offensive and subsequent Austrian counteroffensive recovery (1916-1917)
w4-900516.blurb: The Brusilov Offensive (June–September 1916) was Russia's greatest feat of arms in WWI, capturing most of Eastern Galicia and northern Bukovina. However, after the Russian Revolution weakened the Eastern Front, Austria-Hungary, with German support, recovered much of this lost territory during the Kerensky Offensive's failure and subsequent Austro-German counteroffensives in 1917.

w4-900518.name: Jabal Shammar raids on the Hejaz during WWI
w4-900518.blurb: In 1917 the Emirate of Jabal Shammar (an Ottoman ally) launched raids against the Hashemite Kingdom of Hejaz (around 39E, 27.5N, the Hejaz highlands near Medina/Yanbu), targeting the British-backed Arab Revolt and the Hejaz Railway, temporarily contesting border territory. British-supported Ibn Saud of Nejd increasingly pressured Jabal Shammar, leading to its surrender in 1921.

w4-900520.name: Austrian-German Counteroffensive after Brusilov Offensive / Russian Collapse 1917
w4-900520.blurb: General Brusilov's 1916 offensive (June–September 1916) drove deep into eastern Galicia and Bukovina, bringing Russian forces into territory previously held by Austria-Hungary. By late 1916 and through 1917, a combination of German reinforcements, Russian exhaustion, and the political collapse of the Russian imperial state following the February and October Revolutions of 1917 led to the reversal of most Russian gains. Austria-Hungary re-occupied Galician and Bukovinan territories near Chernivtsi, culminating in the armistice and Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918). The dataset captures the 1916–1917 transition.

w4-900521.from: United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia
w4-900521.name: Central Powers Occupation of Romania (1916–1917)
w4-900521.blurb: Romania entered WWI on August 27, 1916, invading Transylvania, but was overwhelmed by a Central Powers counteroffensive. German, Austro-Hungarian, Bulgarian, and Ottoman forces captured Bucharest on December 6, 1916, occupying most of Wallachia and Dobruja by early 1917, with only Moldavia (coords 25.3E/45.9N) under Romanian and Russian control. Austria-Hungary stands here for the occupying Central Powers.

citations.label: Romania in World War I – Wikipedia

w4-900522.name: Russian withdrawal from Persia following the February Revolution
w4-900522.blurb: During World War I, Russia occupied large parts of northwestern Persia (Qajar territory), fighting the Ottomans in the Persian campaign. The February Revolution of 1917 triggered the rapid disintegration of the Russian Caucasus Army through 'democratization' measures, causing troops to desert en masse. By late 1917, Russian forces had effectively withdrawn from Persia, and the Armistice of Erzincan (December 1917) ended Russian-Ottoman fighting. The power vacuum in northern Persia was filled by Qajar authority, British forces (Dunsterforce), and later Ottoman incursions.

w4-900525.name: Collapse of the Hongxian Empire and onset of the Warlord Era
w4-900525.blurb: Yuan Shikai's abdication on 22 March 1916 and his death on 6 June 1916 left China without a unifying authority. His former Beiyang generals fragmented into competing military cliques — Fengtian, Zhili, Anhui, and others — inaugurating the Warlord Era (1916–1928). The nominal Republic of China government in Beijing remained but held no real control, while Sun Yat-sen's Kuomintang established a rival government in Canton in 1917. The dataset records territory nominally re-attributed to the Kuomintang faction around this period of fragmentation.

w4-900526.name: Idrisid Emirate declares independence from Ottoman Empire
w4-900526.blurb: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi had been fighting Ottoman rule in Asir since 1909 and entered into a British alliance treaty in April 1915. As the Arab Revolt weakened Ottoman control across Arabia in 1916–1917, al-Idrisi consolidated an effectively independent Emirate of Asir with British recognition; the Ottoman collapse in 1918 cemented this independence. A splinter Sheikdom of Upper Asir had already broken away in August 1916.

citations.label: Timeline of the Emirate of Asir – Wikipedia

w4-900527.name: Ibn Saud's expansion into former Ottoman-Rashidi territory during World War I (1916–1917)
w4-900527.blurb: During World War I Ibn Saud of the Emirate of Nejd (allied to Britain by the 1915 Treaty of Darin) campaigned against the pro-Ottoman Rashidis and expanded into frontier territories previously under Ottoman suzerainty. The coordinates (42.3°E, 22°N) lie in the southern Hejaz/Asir borderlands; from=Ottoman Empire, to=Emirate of Nejd matches the 1916-1917 window.

w4-900528.name: Proclamation of the Alash Autonomy
w4-900528.blurb: Following the collapse of the Russian Empire after the February Revolution, the Second All-Kazakh Congress held at Orenburg in December 1917 proclaimed the Alash Autonomy, a Kazakh proto-state covering the steppes of present-day Kazakhstan (Cliopatria coordinates lat 50.3, lng 66.9). Led by Alikhan Bukeikhanov, it sought national self-determination amid the Russian Civil War, The autonomy aligned with White Russian forces but was absorbed by Soviet power by 1920.

w4-900534.name: Khanate of Khiva reasserts independence after Russian Revolution
w4-900534.blurb: After the 1917 Russian Revolution dissolved the Russian Empire's protectorate (in force since 1873), the Khanate of Khiva regained nominal autonomy, but real power passed to the Turkmen Yomut chieftain Junaid Khan, who installed Sayid Abdullah as a figurehead khan from October 1918. The fragile state did not consolidate genuine independence: anti-monarchist and Turkmen factions allied with the Bolsheviks, and by early February 1920 the Red Army had defeated Junaid Khan's forces, with Sayid Abdullah abdicating on 2 February 1920 - ending the khanate and creating the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic.

w4-900536.name: Vardar Offensive / Allied breakthrough and Bulgarian armistice, WWI
w4-900536.blurb: Bulgaria occupied most of Vardar Macedonia (including the area near Skopje/Bitola at 21.4E, 41.6N) after joining the Central Powers in 1915. The Vardar Offensive (15 September 1918) saw French and Serbian forces shatter Bulgarian lines at Dobro Pole; Bulgaria signed the Armistice of Thessaloniki on 29 September 1918, the first Central Power to capitulate. Bulgarian forces evacuated all Serbian and Macedonian territory, restoring it to Serbia (later Yugoslavia).

citations.label: Bulgarian occupation of Serbia (World War I) - Wikipedia
Bulgaria during World War I - Wikipedia

w4-900538.name: British Military Occupation of Nyasaland / Portuguese East Africa Border Zone (WWI)
w4-900538.blurb: During WWI, Lettow-Vorbeck's German forces crossed into Portuguese Mozambique in late 1917 (Battle of Ngomano, 25 November 1917), and British forces from Nyasaland and Rhodesia pursued them into the Portuguese territory. Britain temporarily administered areas of northern Mozambique during this period; the centroid (lat -14.1, lng 37.7) corresponds to the Shire Highlands / Nyasa border zone occupied during operations against the German column.

citations.label: Wikipedia: East African campaign (World War I)

w4-900540.name: German East Africa campaign — von Lettow-Vorbeck invades Portuguese Mozambique
w4-900540.blurb: In November 1917 German Schutztruppe commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck crossed the Rovuma into Portuguese East Africa (Mozambique), defeating a Portuguese force at Ngomano (25 November 1917) and seizing supplies. German forces ranged through the Mozambican interior (lat -16.6, lng 37.5) during 1918 before returning north - a brief German military occupation. Window 1917-1918.

citations.label: East African campaign (World War I) – Wikipedia

w4-900541.name: British Operations in Portuguese Mozambique (Lettow-Vorbeck Campaign)
w4-900541.blurb: On 25 November 1917, German Schutztruppe commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck crossed the Rovuma River into Portuguese East Africa (Mozambique), destroying the Portuguese garrison at Ngomano. In response, British forces (the Port Amelia Force / PAMFORCE, King's African Rifles) landed at Port Amelia in January 1918 and operated across northern Mozambique through 1918 pursuing the Germans. The dataset records approximately 213,388 km² passing from the Portuguese Republic to British Africa at lng=37.7, lat=-14.1 (northern Mozambique), reflecting the British military operations/effective control in this zone during the campaign, prior to the post-armistice restoration to Portugal in 1919.

citations.label: Portuguese campaign in Mozambique (World War I) – Wikipedia

w4-900542.name: WWI East Africa Campaign - Allied takeover of German East Africa
w4-900542.blurb: During the World War I East African campaign, British and allied forces under General Jan Smuts progressively occupied German East Africa (modern Tanzania) from 1916 onward. By 1917 the Germans under Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck had been pushed into the southern and Portuguese territories. At the war's end in November 1918 Germany surrendered its forces; the 1919 Treaty of Versailles assigned the bulk of German East Africa to Britain as the League of Nations mandate territory of Tanganyika.

citations.label: East African campaign (World War I) - Wikipedia

w4-900544.name: Danish–Icelandic Act of Union — Iceland becomes sovereign Kingdom
w4-900544.blurb: The Danish–Icelandic Act of Union, signed on 1 December 1918 and approved by 92.6% of Icelandic voters in a referendum, recognised Iceland as a fully sovereign state in personal union with Denmark, sharing only the monarch (Christian X). Iceland gained its own flag, declared neutrality, and took control of domestic affairs, while Denmark retained management of foreign affairs and defence by agreement. This effectively ended Denmark's centuries-long direct rule over Iceland.

w4-900546.name: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk — Central Powers occupation of the SW borderlands
w4-900546.blurb: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March 1918) ended Soviet Russia's war participation, ceding Ukraine and the western borderlands; Central Powers forces (German and Austro-Hungarian) occupied these regions in 1918. The coordinates (28.2,47.1) lie in the Bessarabia/Moldova borderland that passed out of Russian control into the Central-Powers/Austro-Hungarian occupation zone, consistent with the from→to (Russian Republic → Austria-Hungary) in the 1917–1918 window.

w4-900549.to: Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus
w4-900549.name: Declaration of the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus (11 May 1918)
w4-900549.blurb: Following the February Revolution of 1917, the North Caucasian peoples formed the Union of the Peoples of the Northern Caucasus. With the Bolshevik seizure of power making union with Russia incompatible with their aspirations, they declared full independence on 11 May 1918 at the Batum Peace Conference, forming the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus, which claimed the former Terek Oblast and Dagestan Oblast territories of the Russian Republic.

citations.label: Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus – Wikipedia

w4-900550.name: Proclamation of the Kuban People's Republic
w4-900550.blurb: During the Russian Revolution's chaos, the Kuban Cossack Rada proclaimed the Kuban People's Republic on 28 January 1918 and declared independence on 16 February 1918, covering the territory of the former Kuban Oblast. The republic struggled between full independence (favored by the Chernomortsy faction seeking union with Ukraine) and federation with the White Army under Denikin. It was de facto occupied by Denikin's forces in November 1919 and finally absorbed by the Soviet Red Army in spring 1920.

w4-900551.name: Czechoslovak declaration of independence (28 October 1918)
w4-900551.blurb: Czechoslovakia declared independence from Austria-Hungary on 28 October 1918 and progressively asserted control over Bohemia, Moravia, Slovakia, and Czech Silesia in the following months; borders were later confirmed by the Treaty of Saint-Germain (1919). The Treaty of Trianon text previously cited describes Hungary's losses, not Czechoslovakia's formation, and its 1920 date is outside this window.

w4-900552.from: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
w4-900552.name: Post-WWI Allied territorial awards to Greece (Paris Peace Conference, 1919)
w4-900552.blurb: At the Paris Peace Conference (May 1919) the Allied Supreme Council, backed by Lloyd George, authorised the Greek occupation of Smyrna (15 May 1919), beginning the Greek presence in western Anatolia later formalised at Sèvres (1920). The coordinates (24.8°E, 39.9°N) lie in northern Greece (Macedonia), territory consolidated under Greece via the post-WWI settlement, consistent with the UK→Hellenic Republic transfer in the 1918–1919 window.

w4-900553.name: Collapse of Austria-Hungary and Romanian Annexation of Transylvania
w4-900553.blurb: Austria-Hungary dissolved in October–November 1918 following military defeat in WWI; Romania occupied Transylvania and Bukovina in late 1918, and the Treaty of Trianon (4 June 1920) formally ceded these territories — totaling roughly 280,000 km² — to the Kingdom of Romania.

w4-900554.name: Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine (1919)
w4-900554.blurb: The Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine, signed on 27 November 1919, imposed territorial losses on Bulgaria as a defeated Central Power. Southern Dobruja was ceded to Romania, restoring the 1913 border. The territory near Dobruja passed from Bulgarian control to Romanian sovereignty as part of the post-WWI settlement.

w4-900555.name: Romanian occupation and union of Transylvania (Treaty of Trianon, 1920)
w4-900555.blurb: Following Austria-Hungary's defeat in World War I, Romanian forces occupied Transylvania from November 1918 and the Romanian National Assembly declared union with Romania on 1 December 1918. The Treaty of Trianon (4 June 1920) formally transferred Transylvania to Romania. The dataset window 1918-1919 (Austria-Hungary -> Kingdom of Romania at 25.4, 46.2 in eastern Transylvania) captures the military occupation phase preceding the formal treaty.

w4-900556.name: Ottoman withdrawal from Yemen - Yemeni independence after WWI
w4-900556.blurb: The Ottoman Empire signed the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918, ending its participation in World War I and requiring evacuation of remaining forces from Yemen. Imam Yahya entered Sana'a and declared independence, proclaiming the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen. Although the Ottoman garrison in Sana'a delayed full withdrawal for several weeks, Yemeni independence was effectively established by November 1918 and the Imam began consolidating northern Yemen.

w4-900559.name: Brest-Litovsk and recognition of the Ukrainian People's Republic (1918)
w4-900559.blurb: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk between the Ukrainian People's Republic and the Central Powers (9 Feb 1918), reinforced by the Soviet-German treaty (3 March 1918) requiring Russia to recognize Ukrainian independence, established UPR sovereignty over eastern Ukraine; the area was contested again as the treaties collapsed after Germany's defeat. The coordinates are eastern Ukraine (Donbas/Kharkiv), matching the recorded Russian Republic → Ukrainian People's Republic shift.

w4-900560.name: Collapse of Austria-Hungary and Ukrainian People's Republic proclamation
w4-900560.blurb: The collapse of Austria-Hungary in November 1918 led Ukrainian Galicians to proclaim the Western Ukrainian People's Republic, which merged with the Ukrainian People's Republic (UPR) in January 1919. The region centred on eastern Galicia (lat 48.4, lng 26.6) briefly fell under UPR control before Polish forces expelled the West Ukrainian army across the Zbruch River by July 1919. The py/y window (1918-1919) captures the brief transfer from Habsburg to Ukrainian administration before the subsequent Polish conquest.

w4-900564.name: Armenian-Azerbaijani War (1918-1920) - dispute over Karabakh and Zangezur
w4-900564.blurb: Following independence in May 1918, Armenia and Azerbaijan fought over Karabakh, Zangezur, and Nakhchivan (45.8E, 39.9N, the Karabakh-Zangezur region). In 1919 the fighting and shifting control around these contested districts saw Armenian and Azerbaijani forces vie for the area until Soviet forces conquered both republics in 1920, with the NKAO eventually assigned to Soviet Azerbaijan.

w4-900566.name: Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine (1919) / Allied relinquishment of Macedonian occupation zone
w4-900566.blurb: Following the Armistice of Thessaloniki (September 1918) and the collapse of Bulgaria, Allied (including French) occupation forces in Macedonia withdrew as the territory was assigned to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia) under the Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine (November 1919).

w4-900570.name: Armistice of Mudros and British occupation of Ottoman Mesopotamia and Levant (1918)
w4-900570.blurb: On 30 October 1918, the Ottoman Empire signed the Armistice of Mudros, ending its participation in World War I. British forces, which had already taken Baghdad (1917) and much of the Levant, extended their occupation northward, seizing Mosul on 14 November 1918 in defiance of the armistice lines. This transferred large swathes of former Ottoman territory in the Fertile Crescent to British military administration pending a peace settlement.

citations.label: Partition of the Ottoman Empire – Wikipedia

w4-900572.name: Estonian War of Independence — Estonia gains control from German Empire
w4-900572.blurb: After German occupation under Brest-Litovsk, the Kaiser's abdication and the November 1918 Armistice ended German rule; administration was handed to the Estonian provisional government on 11-19 November 1918. Estonia passed from German Imperial occupation to the restored Republic of Estonia within the 1918-1919 window. Well attested.

citations.label: German occupation of Estonia during World War I – Wikipedia

w4-900577.name: Dissolution of Austria-Hungary / Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye
w4-900577.blurb: With the defeat of the Central Powers, Austria-Hungary dissolved in October–November 1918 and the German-Austrian core was reconstituted as the Republic of German-Austria, proclaimed in Vienna on 12 November 1918. The Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye (10 September 1919) recognized the successor Republic of Austria, fixed its reduced borders, and forbade union with Germany. This transition reattributes the Cisleithanian Austrian heartland from the Habsburg monarchy to the new Austrian republic — not to Poland, as the original 'to' label (Second Polish Republic) erroneously stated.

w4-900579.name: Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye - dissolution of Austria-Hungary
w4-900579.blurb: The Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye (10 September 1919) formalized the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, recognizing the Republic of Austria as the successor state to the Austrian half of the Dual Monarchy. Austria was stripped of non-German territories (Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Poland, South Tyrol to Italy) and forbidden from uniting with Germany. The Habsburg Law (3 April 1919) had already exiled the Habsburg dynasty.

w4-900581.name: Post-WWI Restoration of Mozambique to Portugal
w4-900581.blurb: Following the end of World War I (armistice 11 November 1918) and the German surrender in East Africa (Lettow-Vorbeck surrendered at Abercorn on 25 November 1918), British forces withdrew from the areas of Portuguese Mozambique they had operated in during the pursuit of the Schutztruppe. The dataset records approximately 211,248 km² reverting from 'British Africa' to the 'Portuguese Republic' between py=1918 and y=1919, at coordinates matching northern Mozambique. This represents the post-war territorial restoration rather than a fresh annexation, consistent with Portugal's status as a WWI Allied co-belligerent.

citations.label: East African campaign (World War I) – Wikipedia
Portuguese campaign in Mozambique (World War I) – Wikipedia

w4-900582.name: German occupation of Crimea and Soviet re-establishment of control
w4-900582.blurb: Under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918) Russia ceded Ukraine, and German-Ukrainian forces occupied Crimea (April-May 1918), installing a puppet government. After the November 1918 armistice and German withdrawal, Crimea passed to White and then briefly Bolshevik control in April-June 1919, with Soviet/Russian control made permanent in late 1920. The from=German Empire / to=Russian Republic and 1918-1919 window capture the German-to-Russian transition; 'Russian Republic' loosely denotes the Soviet/Bolshevik side.

w4-900589.name: Treaty of Versailles and end of the German Empire
w4-900589.blurb: The Treaty of Versailles, signed 28 June 1919 and in force 10 January 1920, formally ended World War I and stripped Germany of roughly 13% of its prewar European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine (to France), Posen and West Prussia (to Poland), North Schleswig (to Denmark), and the Saar (to League administration). The German Empire had already collapsed in the November 1918 revolution, giving way to the Weimar Republic. The worklist transfer (German Empire to Weimar Republic, 1919-1920) matches.

citations.label: Territorial losses of Germany in the 20th century – Wikipedia

w4-900590.name: Latvian War of Independence and Soviet–Latvian Peace Treaty (1920)
w4-900590.blurb: During WWI Latvia was under the German Empire's Ober Ost military administration. Latvia declared independence on 18 November 1918. A complex struggle ensued against Bolshevik forces and German Freikorps (von der Goltz's troops, who held Riga into mid-1919). Latvian forces, aided by Estonia, Allied naval support, and Poland, defeated all opponents; German troops fully withdrew by December 1919. Soviet Russia recognised Latvian independence in the Treaty of Riga on 11 August 1920. The dataset captures the transition of Latvian territory (lat 57, lng 24.4) from German Empire occupation to the Republic of Latvia.

w4-900591.name: Treaty of Sèvres — Ottoman cession of western Anatolia/Smyrna zone to Greece
w4-900591.blurb: The Treaty of Sèvres (10 August 1920) awarded Greece administration over the Smyrna (İzmir) enclave in western Anatolia and Eastern Thrace, where Greek forces had been present since May 1919. Under the treaty, the Smyrna zone would remain nominally Ottoman but be administered by a Greek-controlled local parliament with a plebiscite after five years. The Greek advance into western Anatolia in summer 1920 extended the zone considerably, though Turkish nationalist forces under Mustafa Kemal refused to recognise the treaty and ultimately expelled the Greeks by 1922.

w4-900592.name: Treaty of Trianon (1920)
w4-900592.blurb: The Treaty of Trianon, signed on 4 June 1920, dismembered the Kingdom of Hungary as a defeated WWI power. Slovakia and Sub-Carpathian Ruthenia were assigned to Czechoslovakia. Hungary lost roughly two-thirds of its pre-war territory and three-fifths of its population.

w4-900594.name: Japanese occupation of northern Sakhalin (1920)
w4-900594.blurb: In April 1920, following the Nikolayevsk-on-Amur Incident in which Bolshevik forces massacred Japanese residents and garrison troops, Japan launched a military operation to occupy the Russian (northern) half of Sakhalin Island as part of its Siberian Intervention. Japan maintained this occupation of northern Sakhalin-which had been Russian territory since 1875-until the Soviet-Japanese Basic Convention of January 1925, when Japan agreed to withdraw in exchange for oil and coal concessions. The data entry (Russian Republic to Empire of Japan, py=1919, y=1920) reflects this seizure.

w4-900595.name: Franco-Italian Border Adjustments in North Africa (1919)
w4-900595.blurb: After WWI, under Article 13 of the 1915 London Agreement, France and Italy signed the Franco-Italian Arrangement on 12 September 1919, ceding Saharan territory along the Algeria-Libya border; the Anglo-French Convention of 8 September 1919 delimited the Libya-Chad boundary. These transferred strips of Saharan territory (~12E 26N, Fezzan region) from French Africa to Italian Libya. Correctly dated within the 1919-1920 window.

w4-900597.name: Soviet Conquest of Ukraine (1919–1920)
w4-900597.blurb: In the Soviet–Ukrainian War the Red Army overwhelmed the forces of the Ukrainian People's Republic, retaking Kiev and defeating the Directory; by early 1920 the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic was consolidated across most of central and eastern Ukraine. This transition therefore reattributes that territory from the Ukrainian People's Republic to Soviet (Ukrainian SSR) control. The separate Polish settlement — the Peace of Riga (March 1921), which partitioned the western Ukrainian lands — was a distinct later event and should not be conflated with the Soviet conquest depicted here.

w4-900600.name: Formation of Soviet republics / RSFSR Constitution (1918) and consolidation of Bolshevik control
w4-900600.blurb: As the Bolsheviks won the Russian Civil War (1918–1921), the Russian SFSR was established under the 1918 constitution and allied Soviet republics (Ukrainian SSR, Byelorussian SSR, Azerbaijani SSR, etc.) were constituted by 1920, replacing the transitional Russian Republic with a set of nominally separate Soviet republics. The atlas reflects this reorganization of the former Russian state into constituent Soviet republics prior to formal USSR unification in 1922.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic

w4-900601.name: Red Army invasion of Armenia and establishment of Armenian SSR
w4-900601.blurb: On 29 November 1920, the Soviet 11th Army invaded the First Republic of Armenia, and Armenian Bolsheviks declared the Armenian SSR. The republic surrendered on 2 December 1920, and Soviet troops entered Yerevan on 4 December. The territory near 45.2E, 40N thus passed from the independent Armenian Republic to the Soviet system. Armenia joined the Transcaucasian SFSR in 1922 before becoming a distinct Soviet republic in 1936.

citations.label: Red Army invasion of Armenia – Wikipedia

w4-900602.name: Bukharan Revolution and Red Army Conquest of the Emirate of Bukhara
w4-900602.blurb: In August-September 1920 the Red Army under Mikhail Frunze, allied with Bukharan revolutionaries, invaded and conquered the Emirate of Bukhara; Old Bukhara fell on 2 September 1920 and Emir Alim Khan fled to Afghanistan. The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic was proclaimed over the ~218,688 km2 emirate. Transfer Emirate of Bukhara -> (Soviet) republics fits the 1919-1920 window.

w4-900603.name: Russian Civil War — Bolshevik victory and Sovietisation (1917–1921)
w4-900603.blurb: Following the October Revolution of 1917, the Bolsheviks fought a devastating civil war against the White Army and foreign interventionists. By 1920–1921 the Red Army had defeated the main White forces and Sovietised most of the former Russian Empire, establishing Soviet republics in Ukraine, Byelorussia, the Transcaucasus, and Central Asia. The RSFSR (Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic), renamed from the Russian Republic in July 1918, co-existed with these newly formed Soviet republics before they merged into the USSR in 1922.

citations.label: Formation of the Soviet Union – Lumen Learning

w4-900604.name: Italy evacuates Albania / Vlora War ends Italian protectorate claims
w4-900604.blurb: After World War I Italy had occupied much of Albania under the secret Treaty of London (1915) and claimed a protectorate. Albanian resistance forces attacked Italian garrisons in June 1920 (Vlora War), and after fighting Italy signed the Treaty of Tirana (2 August 1920), withdrawing from Valona/Vlora. This ended Italian territorial control and restored Albanian sovereignty, recorded in the atlas as a 1919–1920 transfer from Kingdom of Italy to Albania.

citations.label: Italian campaign in Albania (World War I) – Wikipedia

w4-900606.name: British Mandate for Mesopotamia (San Remo, 1920)
w4-900606.blurb: Following WWI, the British Empire acquired League of Nations mandates over former Ottoman territories. The coordinates point to the Iraq-Syria border region, consistent with the British Mandate for Mesopotamia (Iraq), confirmed at the San Remo Conference in April 1920. The dataset labels this territory shifting from 'British Africa' to 'British Colonial Empire', a relabeling reflecting the reorganization of British imperial administration as new Middle Eastern mandates were added.

w4-900607.to: French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon
w4-900607.name: San Remo Conference and French Mandate for Syria (1920)
w4-900607.blurb: The San Remo Conference (25 April 1920) assigned France the League of Nations mandate for Syria and Lebanon, and French forces under General Goybet defeated Faisal's Arab army at the Battle of Maysaloun (24 July 1920), ending the Arab Kingdom of Syria. The centroid in Syria/Lebanon was thus transferred from the Hashemite-controlled territory (nominally linked to the Kingdom of Hejaz) to French Mandate administration.

w4-900610.to: French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon
w4-900610.name: San Remo Conference and French Mandate for Syria
w4-900610.blurb: The San Remo Conference (April 1920) assigned the Class A League of Nations mandate over Syria and Lebanon to France, superseding the short-lived Arab Kingdom of Syria under Faisal (son of Hussein of the Kingdom of Hejaz). Gouraud's victory at Maysalun (July 1920) established direct French control. The Levantine territory near lng 36.8 E / lat 33.1 N passed from the Hejaz-backed Arab administration to French mandatory authority, matching the [1919,1920] window.

citations.label: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon – Wikipedia

w4-900611.name: Treaty of Seeb — partition of Oman between Imamate interior and Sultanate coast
w4-900611.blurb: Following the anti-Muscat rebellion led by Imam Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi (1913–1920), an uneasy stalemate left the Sultanate of Muscat controlling the coast and the Imamate of Oman controlling the interior. The Treaty of Seeb, signed 25 September 1920 with British mediation by Ronald Wingate, formally codified this division: the Sultan ruled Muscat and the coastal provinces while Imam Isa bin Salih al-Harithi governed the interior, with each party pledging non-interference in the other's affairs.

w4-900613.name: Collapse of the Anglo-Persian Agreement of 1919 and British Withdrawal
w4-900613.blurb: The Anglo-Persian Agreement of August 1919 would have made Iran a de facto British protectorate. It was never ratified by the Iranian Majlis; PM Moshir al-Dawla suspended it in June 1920 and it was annulled in 1921. British forces withdrew from northern Iran, restoring nominal Qajar sovereignty (~48E/35N). The 'British Africa' from-label is a Cliopatria overlapping-label artifact; this and id 900612 record the same withdrawal restoring Qajar control. Window [1919,1920], date 1920.

w4-900614.name: Bolshevik creation of the Far Eastern Republic as a buffer state
w4-900614.blurb: With Bolshevik forces controlling Siberia west of Lake Baikal but Japan occupying the Pacific coast including Vladivostok, Lenin ordered the creation of the Far Eastern Republic on 6 April 1920, centred on Chita, as a nominally independent buffer state to avoid direct Soviet–Japanese conflict during the Russian Civil War. It was controlled de facto by the Bolsheviks. The dataset records the transition in window [1919,1920].

w4-900615.name: Red Army Invasion of Georgia
w4-900615.blurb: On 12 February 1921 the Soviet Red Army invaded the Democratic Republic of Georgia; Tbilisi fell on 25 February 1921, the Georgian SSR was proclaimed, and Georgia was incorporated into the USSR in 1922. The coordinates (43.4,42.3) are Georgia, matching the from→to (Georgia → USSR) in the 1921–1922 window.

citations.label: Red Army invasion of Georgia – Wikipedia

w4-900616.name: Treaty on the Creation of the USSR
w4-900616.blurb: On 30 December 1922, the Russian SFSR, Ukrainian SSR, Byelorussian SSR, and Transcaucasian SFSR signed the Treaty and Declaration on the Creation of the USSR, formally merging the Soviet republics into the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. The Congress of Soviets ratified both documents, dissolving the separate republican structures into a single federal union under Bolshevik leadership. This followed the Red Army's victory in the Russian Civil War and the consolidation of Soviet power across the former Russian Empire.

citations.label: Treaty on the Creation of the USSR – Wikipedia
Declaration of the Creation of the USSR – Wikipedia

w4-900618.name: Treaty of Seeb (Treaty of Al-Sib) - 1920
w4-900618.blurb: On 25 September 1920 Sultan Taimur bin Feisal of Muscat concluded the Treaty of Seeb with the Imam of Oman's interior tribes, brokered by British mediator Ronald Wingate. The treaty formalized a de facto division of Oman: the coastal Sultanate retained the name 'Muscat and Oman' and managed external affairs, while the interior Imamate gained autonomous self-governance. This administrative partition and naming convention accounts for the dataset's entity transition.

w4-900619.name: Uqair Protocol / British Trucial States boundary settlement
w4-900619.blurb: During 1921–1922 Britain reorganized its treaty relations along the lower Persian Gulf, where the Trucial States (centroid ~56.5°E, 21.6°N, near Fujairah/Ras al-Khaimah) were bound to Britain by exclusive agreements rather than to Muscat and Oman. Several coastal parcels previously mapped under Muscat were thus realigned under direct British Trucial-Coast jurisdiction. This is distinct from the Uqair Protocol of November 1922, which Percy Cox negotiated to fix the Nejd–Kuwait and Nejd–Iraq frontiers far to the west and which did not concern the Trucial Coast.

w4-900620.name: Egyptian independence — Kingdom of Egypt recognised (1922)
w4-900620.blurb: Britain unilaterally declared Egyptian independence on 28 February 1922, converting its protectorate into the nominally sovereign Kingdom of Egypt under King Fuad I, though British troops remained under a residual treaty relationship. The dataset records the British Africa → Kingdom of Egypt transfer in the 1921–1922 window.

w4-900621.name: Turkish recovery of western Anatolia — Smyrna Catastrophe (1922)
w4-900621.blurb: Greece had occupied western Anatolia (including Smyrna / İzmir) from May 1919. Mustafa Kemal's nationalist forces launched the Great Offensive on 26 August 1922, routed Greek armies at Dumlupınar, and recaptured Smyrna by 9 September 1922. The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) recognised Turkey's sovereignty over Anatolia around lng 28, lat 38.7. Matches First Hellenic Republic -> Ottoman Empire in [1921,1922] (the surviving Ottoman/Turkish state regaining the area).

w4-900622.from: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
w4-900622.name: Anglo-Irish Treaty; Irish Free State and renaming of the UK
w4-900622.blurb: The Anglo-Irish Treaty (signed 6 December 1921) established the Irish Free State, which came into being on 6 December 1922; twenty-six Irish counties left the United Kingdom. The state was renamed 'United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland' by the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act 1927. Matches worklist sovereignty rename United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland -> United Kingdom (1921-1922); coords lng 25.2 lat 36.7 (eastern Mediterranean) are a spurious geocoding of an empire-wide relabel.

citations.label: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland – Wikipedia

w4-900625.from: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
w4-900625.name: Anglo-Irish Treaty — Establishment of the Irish Free State
w4-900625.blurb: The Anglo-Irish Treaty (signed 6 December 1921) ended the Irish War of Independence; the Irish Free State came into legal existence on 6 December 1922, separating 26 counties from the UK. The coordinates (-8.2,53.4) match the from→to (United Kingdom → Irish Free State) in the 1921–1922 window.

w4-900627.name: Saudi Conquest of Ha'il (Third Saudi-Rashidi War)
w4-900627.blurb: Ibn Saud's forces and their Ikhwan allies besieged the Rashidi capital Ha'il through 1921. Emir Muhammad bin Talal Al-Rashid surrendered on 2 November 1921, ending the Emirate of Jabal Shammar. The territory (~241,500 km2) was incorporated into the Emirate/Sultanate of Nejd. Transfer Jabal Shammar -> Nejd fits the 1921-1922 window.

w4-900628.name: Ibn Saud captures Ha'il and expands Nejd's borders
w4-900628.blurb: In November 1921 Ibn Saud's forces captured Ha'il from the Rashidi emirs, ending their dynasty and consolidating the Emirate of Nejd's control over central Arabia, bringing Nejd to the Hejaz borderlands near coord 38.9E/27N. The Hejaz itself was not conquered until 1924–25; the dataset's 1921–1922 change reflects Nejd absorbing Rashidi territory adjacent to Hejaz. The 'Kingdom of Hejaz → Emirate of Nejd' label captures this frontier shift.

w4-900629.name: League of Nations Class-B Mandate for Ruanda-Urundi awarded to Belgium (1922)
w4-900629.blurb: Belgian forces occupied Ruanda and Urundi (former German East Africa) in 1916. The post-war settlement gave Germany's East African territories to Britain (Tanganyika) and Belgium (Ruanda-Urundi). On 20 July 1922 the League formally awarded Ruanda-Urundi to Belgium as a Class-B Mandate, a distinct territory administratively separated from the Belgian Congo.

w4-900630.name: Dissolution of the Far Eastern Republic and absorption into Soviet Russia
w4-900630.blurb: Once the People's Revolutionary Army of the Far Eastern Republic retook Vladivostok on 25 October 1922, expelling the last Japanese forces, the buffer state's purpose disappeared. On 15 November 1922 the FER government dissolved itself and transferred authority to Moscow, merging into the RSFSR, which became a founding member of the USSR on 30 December 1922. This falls within the dataset window [1922,1924]; the 'to' field 'Union of Soviet Socialist Republics' reflects the territory's absorption into the Soviet polity.

w4-900633.name: Treaty of Lausanne; proclamation of the Republic of Turkey
w4-900633.blurb: The Treaty of Lausanne, signed 24 July 1923, settled the post-WWI partition of the Ottoman Empire and recognized the new Republic of Turkey as successor state; the republic was proclaimed 29 October 1923. Matches worklist transition Ottoman Empire -> Republic of Turkey (1922-1924); coords lng 35.5 lat 39.1 are in Anatolia.

w4-900634.name: Treaty of Lausanne and Greco-Turkish Population Exchange
w4-900634.blurb: The Treaty of Lausanne (24 July 1923) resolved the Greco-Turkish War (1919–1922) and established the boundaries of the Republic of Turkey, including Eastern Thrace, which passed from Greek control to Turkey. The accompanying Convention on Population Exchange (30 January 1923) transferred approximately 1.2 million Greek Orthodox from Anatolia to Greece and 400,000 Muslims from Greece to Turkey. The treaty came into effect on 6 August 1924.

citations.label: Population exchange between Greece and Turkey – Wikipedia

w4-900635.name: United States withdrawal from the Dominican Republic (Hughes–Peynado Accord, 1922–1924)
w4-900635.blurb: The Hughes–Peynado Accord of June 1922 set a roadmap for ending the U.S. military occupation; a provisional government formed in October 1922, elections were held in March 1924, and U.S. forces withdrew on 18 September 1924, restoring Dominican sovereignty. The worklist transfer United States → Dominican Republic at lng -70.3, lat 18.8 in the 1922–1924 window matches this withdrawal.

citations.label: Military Government of Santo Domingo – Wikipedia

w4-900636.name: Reza Khan's coup and abolition of the Qajar Dynasty
w4-900636.blurb: Reza Khan led a military coup on 22 February 1921, deposing the Qajar government and eventually becoming prime minister. In October 1925 the Majlis formally deposed Ahmad Shah and declared the Qajar dynasty ended; Reza Khan was proclaimed Reza Shah Pahlavi. The Cliopatria window of 1922-1924 (Qajar Dynasty to Pahlavi Dynasty at lat 32.4, lng 53.7, central Iran) reflects the period of Reza Khan's consolidating control after the 1921 coup but before the formal 1925 dynastic change.

w4-900640.name: Saudi (Nejdi) expansion into the Emirate of Asir
w4-900640.blurb: After the death of Muhammad al-Idrisi in 1920 the Emirate of Asir weakened amid internal rivalries and pressure from Ibn Saud's expanding Sultanate of Nejd. Following the 1920 border treaties that gave Nejd the Asir al-Sarah mountain tribes, the Sheikdom of Upper Asir was occupied and annexed by Nejd in 1923, bringing significant Asir territory under Nejdi control in the 1922-1924 window. This culminated in the 1926 Mecca Agreement (Saudi protectorate), a 1930 administrative integration, and formal annexation in 1934 by the Treaty of Taif.

w4-900641.name: Proclamation of the Second Hellenic Republic
w4-900641.blurb: Following Greece's defeat in the Greco-Turkish War (Asia Minor Disaster 1922) and King Constantine I's exile and death in 1923, Alexandros Papanastasiou proclaimed the Second Hellenic Republic on March 25, 1924, ratified by plebiscite. The dataset's 'First Hellenic Republic' label (Athens, 23.4E/38.3N) denotes the preceding Kingdom-of-Greece era polity; the change captures the monarchy-to-republic transition.

citations.label: History of the Hellenic Republic – Wikipedia

w4-900642.name: Treaty of Jaghbub (1925) — Anglo-Italian cession of Jarabub Oasis to Italian Libya
w4-900642.blurb: Italy had been promised territorial compensation in Africa under Article XIII of the Treaty of London (1915). Egypt and Italy signed the Treaty of Jaghbub on 6 December 1925, ceding the Jaghbub (Jarabub) oasis and surrounding desert district from British-aligned Egyptian administration to Italian Libya. Italian forces took physical control of Jaghbub in early 1926. The dataset records 'British Africa → Italian Africa' for 1924–1926 near the Libyan Desert, consistent with this cession.

w4-900644.name: Amanullah Khan proclaims the Kingdom of Afghanistan
w4-900644.blurb: On 9 June 1926, Emir Amanullah Khan elevated his title from Amir to Padshah (King), transforming the Emirate of Afghanistan into the Kingdom of Afghanistan, following the 1919 Treaty of Rawalpindi that secured Afghan independence. Matches worklist transition Emirate of Afghanistan -> Kingdom of Afghanistan (1924-1926); coords lng 67.7 lat 33.9 confirm Afghanistan.

w4-900645.name: Soviet-backed Mongolian People's Republic proclaimed
w4-900645.blurb: After the death of Bogd Khan on 20 May 1924, Soviet-backed Mongolian revolutionaries abolished the theocracy and on 25 November 1924 proclaimed the Mongolian People's Republic, adopting a Soviet-style constitution. Mongolia (Cliopatria centroid lat 46.9, lng 103.8) became the world's second communist state, transitioning from the Bogd Khanate ('Great Mongol State') to communist rule, matching the 1924-1926 window.

w4-900646.name: Soviet-Japanese Basic Convention (1925) - withdrawal from northern Sakhalin
w4-900646.blurb: The Soviet-Japanese Basic Convention, signed in Peking on 20 January 1925, established formal diplomatic relations between the USSR and Japan. Under its terms Japan agreed to evacuate its forces from northern Sakhalin, which it had occupied since 1920, in exchange for oil and coal concession rights in that territory. Japan's withdrawal was completed by May 1925, returning northern Sakhalin to Soviet control. The data entry (Empire of Japan to USSR, py=1924, y=1926) records this transfer.

w4-900647.name: Saudi Conquest of the Hejaz
w4-900647.blurb: Ibn Saud's forces besieged Jeddah and Medina through 1925; King Ali bin Hussein surrendered and Jeddah fell on 17 December 1925. The Hejaz was annexed by Nejd, and in January 1926 Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of the Hejaz, creating the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd (later Saudi Arabia, 1932). Transfer Kingdom of Hejaz -> Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd fits the 1924-1926 window.

w4-900648.name: Saudi conquest of Hejaz — Ibn Saud captures Mecca, Medina, and Jeddah (1924–1926)
w4-900648.blurb: After Britain withdrew subsidies, Ibn Saud launched his campaign against Sharif Hussein in August 1924; Saudi-Ikhwan forces took Mecca in October 1924, Medina in December 1925, and Jeddah on 8 January 1926, when Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of Hejaz, merging it with his Emirate of Nejd to form the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd. The dataset window of 1924–1926 matches.

citations.label: Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd — Wikipedia

w4-900650.name: Timor Border Adjustment Following 1904 Hague Convention and 1914 Arbitration Award
w4-900650.blurb: The 1904 Hague Convention and the 1914 Permanent Court of Arbitration award (effective 1916) finalised the land border between Dutch and Portuguese Timor, including the cession of Maucatar to Portugal and Noimuti to the Netherlands. The dataset's 1924-1926 window reflects administrative implementation of these adjustments. The 'Estado Novo' label is anachronistic (that regime was established only in 1933), used retroactively by Cliopatria for the Portuguese state.

citations.label: Boundaries in the Island of Timor, Award, 25 June 1914 - Jus Mundi

w4-900653.name: Establishment of the Jinggangshan Soviet base (KMT-CCP split)
w4-900653.blurb: At the Hunan-Jiangxi border near 114.4E, 27.3N (the Jinggang Mountains), the data records control passing from the Kuomintang to the Chinese Communists in 1927-1928. After the April 1927 Shanghai Massacre ended the First United Front and the failed Autumn Harvest Uprising (September 1927), Mao Zedong led the surviving Communist forces into Jinggangshan in October 1927, establishing the CCP's first rural revolutionary base. In April-May 1928 Zhu De's troops joined to form the Fourth Red Army, and the base held off KMT suppression campaigns. So at THIS coordinate the Communists did seize and hold rural territory from KMT/local control, matching the data direction (corrects the earlier blurb, which mistakenly described the Communists being expelled — that applied to the cities, not this base area).

w4-900656.name: Kuomintang / Sichuan Warlord Control of Eastern Kham (Xikang)
