Guangdong and most of southern China fell by late 1949–1950. By 1953 virtually all mainland territory had passed from ROC to PRC control, with the ROC confined to Taiwan and small offshore islands. The dataset records 'Republic of China → People's Republic of China' for interior southern China during this consolidation phase.

citations.label: History of the People's Republic of China – Wikipedia

w4-900925.name: Chinese People's Liberation Army enters Tibet (1950) — Tibet incorporated into PRC
w4-900925.blurb: On 7 October 1950 the PLA invaded Tibet, defeating Tibetan forces at the Battle of Chamdo; the Seventeen Point Agreement of 23 May 1951 formalised Tibet's incorporation into the People's Republic of China. The dataset records the Tibet → PRC transfer in the 1950–1953 window.

citations.label: Annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China — Wikipedia

w4-900926.name: Libyan Independence and Creation of the Kingdom of Libya
w4-900926.blurb: Following a UN General Assembly resolution of 21 November 1949 requiring Libyan independence before 1 January 1952, the United Kingdom of Libya was proclaimed on 24 December 1951, becoming the first country to gain independence through the United Nations. The French-administered Fezzan region was unified with British-administered Tripolitania and Cyrenaica under King Idris I. France evacuated the Fezzan, ending its post-WWII administration of the region.

w4-900927.name: Independence of Libya — UN trusteeship to Kingdom of Libya (1951)
w4-900927.blurb: After the Allied defeat of Italy in North Africa, British and French forces administered Tripolitania, Cyrenaica, and Fezzan. Under UN Resolution 289 (1949), King Idris declared Libya's independence on 24 December 1951, making it the first country to gain independence via the United Nations. The dataset records British Africa transferring to the Kingdom of Libya in the 1950–1953 window.

w4-900930.name: Cambodian independence from France
w4-900930.blurb: After King Norodom Sihanouk's 'Royal Crusade for Independence,' France - weakened by the deteriorating First Indochina War - progressively transferred sovereignty: the judiciary and police in August-September 1953, then full military command in October 1953. Full independence was celebrated on 9 November 1953 and later confirmed by the 1954 Geneva Accords, which recognized Sihanouk's government as the sole legitimate authority and required withdrawal of all foreign forces from Cambodian soil.

w4-900931.name: Geneva Accords (1954) and establishment of the Republic of Vietnam
w4-900931.blurb: The Geneva Accords of 21 July 1954 ended the First Indochina War and temporarily divided Vietnam at the 17th Parallel. French forces withdrew from Indochina (last troops departing April 1956), and the southern zone became the Republic of Vietnam under Ngo Dinh Diem. This transferred administrative authority over southern Vietnam from French Indochina to the nascent Republic of Vietnam.

w4-900932.name: Tunisian independence from France (20 March 1956)
w4-900932.blurb: Following decades of nationalist agitation led by Habib Bourguiba's Neo-Destour party and France's post-Dien Bien Phu reassessment of colonial policy, France granted full independence to Tunisia on 20 March 1956. The French protectorate established by the Bardo Treaty (1881) was dissolved, and the territory of Tunisia transferred from French Africa to the newly independent Republic of Tunisia.

w4-900934.name: British expulsion of Saudi forces from Buraimi Oasis (1955)
w4-900934.blurb: This mirrors id 900933, recording the British-organised expulsion of Saudi forces from the Buraimi Oasis in October 1955, restoring the Sultanate of Oman's claim to oasis villages. The 'Sultanate of Oman → United Kingdom' label reflects the British protectorate relationship under which Britain exercised external affairs; window py=1954, y=1956 fits.

w4-900936.name: Moroccan independence from France
w4-900936.blurb: The Franco-Moroccan Joint Declaration of 2 March 1956 ended the French Protectorate established by the Treaty of Fez in 1912. Sultan Mohammed V, exiled in 1953, returned in November 1955 and negotiated independence; the US recognized Morocco on 7 March 1956 and Spain on 7 April 1956. Matches the French Africa → Morocco transfer in the 1954-1956 window.

w4-900937.name: Geneva Accords Partition of Vietnam
w4-900937.blurb: The 1954 Geneva Accords, after France's defeat at Dien Bien Phu, ended the First Indochina War and partitioned Vietnam at the 17th parallel: the Democratic Republic of Vietnam under Ho Chi Minh held the north, French/South Vietnamese administration the south. French forces withdrew by April 1956 (~105E 20N, Red River Delta). Planned 1956 reunification elections were blocked. Correctly dated within the 1954-1956 window.

w4-900940.name: Hungarian Revolution of 1956
w4-900940.blurb: The Hungarian Revolution began on 23 October 1956 as a popular uprising against Soviet-backed communist rule. Within days, Imre Nagy became premier, announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, and declared neutrality. Revolutionary forces briefly held national territory (represented as 'Hungarian Nationalists'), ousting the People's Republic government across essentially all of Hungary for approximately two weeks.

w4-900941.name: Hungarian Revolution of 1956 - territory held by revolutionaries
w4-900941.blurb: Alongside the People's Republic label change, the dataset tracks the same territory under 'Hungary' shifting to 'Hungarian Nationalists' during the 1956 revolution, reflecting the dual authority crisis during the uprising. The revolutionary government under Imre Nagy briefly controlled essentially the entire country, repudiating the communist system and Soviet alliance before being crushed by Soviet intervention on 4 November 1956.

w4-900943.name: Ghana Independence
w4-900943.blurb: The Gold Coast Colony became independent as Ghana on 6 March 1957, the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence, under Prime Minister Kwame Nkrumah, following the 1956 plebiscite that joined British Togoland to the new state. The dataset records the change between 1956 and 1958, straddling the March 1957 date. Transfer Gold Coast Colony -> Ghana is correct.

w4-900944.name: Egypt–Syria union forms the United Arab Republic (1958)
w4-900944.blurb: On 1 February 1958 Egypt and Syria merged to create the United Arab Republic under Nasser; Egypt continued to use the UAR name even after Syria's 1961 secession until 1971. The dataset records the name change from 'Republic of Egypt' to 'United Arab Republic' in the 1956–1958 window, consistent with the 1958 proclamation.

w4-900945.name: Formation of the United Arab Republic
w4-900945.blurb: On 1 February 1958 Syrian President Shukri al-Kuwatli and Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser signed a union pact forming the United Arab Republic, ratified by plebiscite on 22 February 1958. Syria became the 'Northern Region' of the UAR, formally merging its territory with Egypt under Nasser's presidency. The union was driven by Syrian Ba'athists and officers seeking protection against both communist influence and Western interference.

w4-900946.name: Israeli Withdrawal from Sinai after the 1956 Suez Crisis
w4-900946.blurb: Israel seized the Sinai Peninsula during the Suez/Sinai War of October–November 1956, in coordination with British and French operations. Under intense U.S. and Soviet pressure, Israel withdrew its forces from the Sinai by March 1957, and the territory reverted to Egypt (which became the United Arab Republic in February 1958). The dataset's 1956→1958 window captures both the Israeli conquest and the completion of Egyptian/UAR control.

citations.label: Israeli occupation of the Sinai Peninsula – Wikipedia

w4-900947.name: Soviet suppression of the Hungarian Revolution
w4-900947.blurb: On 4 November 1956, the Soviet Red Army launched Operation Whirlwind, rolling tanks into Budapest to crush the Hungarian Revolution. Soviet forces installed Janos Kadar as leader of a restored Hungarian People's Republic. By mid-November the major fighting was over; the 'Hungarian Nationalists' were suppressed and the People's Republic was fully restored by 1958.

w4-900950.name: Formation of the Arab Federation of Iraq and Jordan
w4-900950.blurb: On 14 February 1958, King Faisal II of Iraq and King Hussein of Jordan proclaimed the Arab Federation, a Hashemite union of their two kingdoms formed in direct response to the Egypt-Syria United Arab Republic announced days earlier. Under the federation, foreign policy was unified while each kingdom retained domestic governance; Nuri al-Said became premier of the federation. Jordan's territory was thus nominally incorporated into the Arab Federation. The federation lasted only six months before the 14 July 1958 Iraqi revolution dissolved it.

citations.label: When Jordan and Iraq United – Arab America

w4-900951.name: Formation of the Hashemite Arab Federation
w4-900951.blurb: On 14 February 1958, King Faisal II of Iraq and King Hussein of Jordan merged their Hashemite kingdoms into the Arab Federation, a confederation with Baghdad as capital, explicitly countering the Nasserist United Arab Republic. Each kingdom retained its monarch while sharing institutions under Nuri al-Said. The worklist transfer (Kingdom of Iraq to Arab Federation, 1956-1958) reflects this merger.

w4-900954.name: 1958 French constitutional referendum — establishment of the Fifth Republic
w4-900954.blurb: On 28 September 1958 citizens of metropolitan France and its overseas territories voted overwhelmingly (82.6% in favour) to adopt a new constitution proposed by Charles de Gaulle, establishing the French Fifth Republic and ending the Fourth Republic. African territories that voted 'yes' became autonomous republics within the new French Community rather than directly administered colonies, fundamentally reorganising the legal relationship between France and its African possessions. Guinea alone rejected the constitution and became immediately independent; the remaining French African territories subsequently gained full independence by 1960.

w4-900959.name: Indonesian suppression of Darul Islam rebellion and integration of Aceh
w4-900959.blurb: The Sultanate of Aceh had maintained a de facto separate Islamic identity through the Darul Islam/NII rebellion (1953-1959) led by Daud Beureueh. A 1959 settlement granted Aceh special autonomous province status with rights for Islamic law, effectively reintegrating it into the Republic of Indonesia. By 1960 the Darul Islam movement was militarily broken, completing the administrative consolidation of Aceh into the Indonesian state. Window 1958-1960.

w4-900960.name: Madagascar Independence from France
w4-900960.blurb: Madagascar formally gained independence from France on 26 June 1960, following a referendum in September 1958 in which the territory voted to become an autonomous republic within the French Community as the Malagasy Republic. After negotiations, full sovereignty was granted and Philibert Tsiranana became the first president. The transition followed decades of French colonial rule and the suppressed 1947 Malagasy Uprising.

w4-900961.name: Independence of the Mali Federation from France
w4-900961.blurb: The Mali Federation, formed on 4 April 1959 from French Sudan and Senegal, became fully independent from France on 20 June 1960. The federation fragmented when Senegal withdrew on 20 August 1960; French Sudan then renamed itself the Republic of Mali on 22 September 1960. Cliopatria records this as French Africa (the French Fifth Republic, centroid lat 17.6, lng -6.6 in the Mali/Sahara region) transferring to the Mali Federation in 1958-1960.

w4-900966.name: Congolese independence from Belgium
w4-900966.blurb: Amid the wave of African decolonisation and following the Brussels Round Table Conference, Belgium granted the Belgian Congo independence on 30 June 1960, whereupon it became the Republic of the Congo (Léopoldville), later the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Patrice Lumumba became the first Prime Minister. The date falls within the dataset window [1958,1960] and the territorial extent was unchanged from the Belgian Congo.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Democratic Republic of the Congo — History

w4-900967.name: 14 July Revolution and dissolution of the Arab Federation
w4-900967.blurb: On 14 July 1958, the Free Officers under Abd al-Karim Qasim and Abdul Salam Arif launched a coup against the Hashemite monarchy in Baghdad, killing King Faisal II and Nuri al-Said. The coup proclaimed the Republic of Iraq and on 2 August 1958 formally dissolved the six-month-old Arab Federation with Jordan. The worklist transfer (Arab Federation to Iraqi Republic, 1958-1960) reflects this transition.

w4-900968.name: Dissolution of the Arab Federation
w4-900968.blurb: The Arab Federation of Iraq and Jordan, formed on 14 February 1958 as a Hashemite response to Egypt-Syria's United Arab Republic, was dissolved on 2 August 1958 after the 14 July Revolution in Iraq. Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim's Free Officers coup overthrew and killed King Faisal II and proclaimed an Iraqi republic, terminating Jordan's union with Iraq after only six months. Jordan, now isolated, requested and received British military support. The Jordanian territory reverted to the independent Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.

w4-900969.name: Cuban Revolution
w4-900969.blurb: On 1 January 1959, Fidel Castro's 26th of July Movement overthrew the Batista dictatorship after a guerrilla campaign from the Sierra Maestra. Castro entered Havana on 8 January 1959 and became Prime Minister. Through 1959-1960 Cuba was progressively transformed: large US-owned properties were nationalised, communists were appointed to key ministries, and a Soviet-Cuban trade agreement was signed in February 1960. By 1960 Cuba had become a de facto communist state aligned with the USSR, severing ties with the United States, which broke off diplomatic relations in January 1961.

w4-900971.name: Republic of the Congo (Brazzaville) independence from France
w4-900971.blurb: The Republic of the Congo (Congo-Brazzaville) gained full independence from France on 15 August 1960, proclaimed from French Equatorial Africa, with Fulbert Youlou as first president; it had been an autonomous republic within the French Community since November 1958. Matches the French Fifth Republic → Republic of the Congo transfer in the 1960-1961 window.

citations.label: Republic of the Congo – Office of the Historian

w4-900973.name: 1961 Syrian coup - dissolution of the United Arab Republic
w4-900973.blurb: On 28 September 1961 Syrian military officers staged a coup in Damascus, announcing Syria's withdrawal from the United Arab Republic. Nasser, unwilling to use force, recognized Syrian independence on 5 October 1961. Syria re-emerged as the Syrian Arab Republic under a civilian government, effectively ending the three-year union with Egypt and restoring Syria as a separate territorial entity.

w4-900974.name: Independence of Tanganyika from British Africa (1961)
w4-900974.blurb: Tanganyika gained independence from British administration on 9 December 1961 under Prime Minister Julius Nyerere, becoming a republic on 9 December 1962. The dataset records this as a 1960–1961 transition from 'British Africa'. Tanganyika later merged with Zanzibar to form Tanzania in 1964.

w4-900975.name: Kuwait Independence from Britain
w4-900975.blurb: On 19 June 1961, Kuwait terminated its protectorate status with Britain when Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah exchanged memoranda with the British Political Resident cancelling the 1899 Anglo-Kuwaiti Treaty. Kuwait became an independent sovereign state (coordinates lng 47.5, lat 29.5), with Sheikh Abdullah as its first Emir. Iraq immediately threatened to annex Kuwait, prompting British Operation Vantage, but independence was sustained and Kuwait joined the Arab League and United Nations.

w4-900976.name: Independence of Kuwait from British Protectorate
w4-900976.blurb: On 19 June 1961 an exchange of notes between Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah and British Political Resident Sir William Luce terminated the Anglo-Kuwaiti Treaty of 1899, making Kuwait a fully sovereign state. Iraq challenged the independence and threatened invasion, but British troops (Operation Vantage) and Arab League support deterred aggression. Kuwait was admitted to the United Nations on 14 May 1963.

w4-900977.name: Sierra Leone independence from Britain (27 April 1961)
w4-900977.blurb: Sierra Leone, a British possession since the Crown Colony of 1808 and Protectorate of 1896, became independent on 27 April 1961 following the 1960 Lancaster House negotiations. Sir Milton Margai became the first Prime Minister. The territory transitioned from British Africa to the independent state of Sierra Leone within the Commonwealth, matching [1960,1961].

w4-900978.name: British African territorial reclassification during East African decolonization
w4-900978.blurb: The coordinates fall in central-southern Africa. The recorded relabelling from 'British Africa' to 'British East Africa' in 1960–1961 reflects a Cliopatria reclassification of British-administered territory as the accelerating decolonisation of the era split British holdings into distinct successor categories; Tanganyika itself became independent on 9 December 1961. This is a label/administrative reclassification rather than a discrete conquest, and the coordinates are imperfectly centred, so confidence is medium.

w4-900979.name: Central African Republic Independence from France
w4-900979.blurb: The Central African Republic formally gained independence from France on 13 August 1960, as part of the broad wave of African decolonization that year. The territory had been administered as Ubangi-Shari within French Equatorial Africa; autonomy within the French Community had been proclaimed in December 1958, and full sovereignty followed in 1960 with David Dacko as first president. France had retained administrative authority until independence took effect.

citations.label: History of the Central African Republic - Wikipedia

w4-900980.name: Independence of Côte d'Ivoire from France
w4-900980.blurb: Côte d'Ivoire became fully independent from France on 7 August 1960, leaving the French Community under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who became its first president. The transition was largely peaceful; France retained close ties through the Françafrique framework. From 'French Fifth Republic' to 'Republic of Côte d'Ivoire' at coordinates within the country; window py=1960, y=1961 fits.

w4-900982.name: Independence of Chad from France
w4-900982.blurb: Chad was granted independence from France on 11 August 1960, transitioning from a territory of French Equatorial Africa under the French Fifth Republic to the sovereign Republic of Chad. François Tombalbaye became the first president. The dataset window of 1960–1961 reflects the lag between formal independence and updated atlas boundaries.

w4-900984.name: 1961 British Cameroons plebiscite - reunification with Republic of Cameroon
w4-900984.blurb: A UN-supervised plebiscite held on 11 February 1961 asked voters in British-administered Southern and Northern Cameroons whether to join Nigeria or the Republic of Cameroon. Southern Cameroons voted 70.5% to join Cameroon, and on 1 October 1961 the Federal Republic of Cameroon was proclaimed, with former British Southern Cameroons becoming West Cameroon. This is the event behind the territory passing from British Africa to the Republic of Cameroon at the given coordinates.

w4-900985.name: Independence of Dahomey from France
w4-900985.blurb: On 1 August 1960, the Republic of Dahomey (present-day Benin) gained full independence from France, as part of the broader wave of decolonization across French West Africa. Dahomey had become self-governing within the French Community on 4 December 1958, and Hubert Maga became its first president upon independence. France's 1960 decolonization resulted from post-WWII nationalist pressure, the costs of the Indochina War, and the political restructuring of the French Community. The territory passed from French Fifth Republic administration to the new Republic of Dahomey.

w4-900987.name: Independence of Mauritania from France
w4-900987.blurb: Mauritania became independent from the French Fifth Republic on 28 November 1960 during the 'Year of Africa', with Moktar Ould Daddah as first leader. Morocco initially contested the new state, but Mauritania joined the UN in 1961. The dataset window of 1960–1961 matches.

w4-900988.name: Independence of Upper Volta (later Burkina Faso) from France (1960)
w4-900988.blurb: Upper Volta became fully independent from France on 5 August 1960. The dataset uses 'Burkina Faso' as the modern retronym for the entity that was officially the Republic of Upper Volta until Thomas Sankara renamed it in 1984. The 1960-1961 transition (Republic of Upper Volta -> Burkina Faso) reflects independence from French colonial administration, not the 1984 renaming.

w4-900989.name: Independence of Niger from France
w4-900989.blurb: Niger gained independence from the French Fifth Republic on 3 August 1960, transitioning from French West Africa to the sovereign Republic of the Niger under President Hamani Diori. One of the 'Year of Africa' states. The dataset window of 1960–1961 reflects atlas update lag.

w4-900990.name: Kenyan Independence from Britain
w4-900990.blurb: Kenya gained independence from Britain on 12 December 1963 under the Kenya Independence Act 1963, with Jomo Kenyatta as the first Prime Minister. The transition followed the Mau Mau Uprising (1952-1960) and Lancaster House constitutional negotiations. Kenya had achieved internal self-government in June 1963 before full independence; it became a republic on 12 December 1964.

w4-900991.name: Rwandan independence from Ruanda-Urundi (1962)
w4-900991.blurb: On 1 July 1962, Belgium granted independence to the two halves of the UN trust territory of Ruanda-Urundi, creating the independent Republic of Rwanda and Kingdom of Burundi. The Rwandan Revolution of 1959–1961 had overthrown the Tutsi monarchy, and the Belgian government, under UN pressure, divided and decolonized the territory. Rwanda was admitted to the UN in 1963.

w4-900992.name: Jamaica gains independence from Britain (1962)
w4-900992.blurb: Jamaica achieved independence from the United Kingdom on 6 August 1962, after withdrawing from the West Indies Federation following a September 1961 referendum. From=British Colonial Empire, to=Jamaica matches the 1961-1963 window.

w4-900994.name: 1963 Ba'ath Party coup in Syria
w4-900994.blurb: On 8 March 1963 Ba'athist military officers overthrew the civilian Syrian government of President Nazim al-Qudsi, one month after a parallel Ba'ath coup in Iraq. The new regime dissolved remaining institutional links to the UAR era and established an Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party one-party state. This transferred Syrian territorial control from the post-UAR republic to the Ba'ath-ruled Syrian Arab Republic.

w4-900995.name: Syrian Ba'ath Party coup of 23 February 1966
w4-900995.blurb: The same 1966 neo-Ba'ath coup that swept out Jadid's rivals also ended any residual association with the defunct United Arab Republic (Egypt-Syria union, dissolved 1961); the dataset registers the successor entity as the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party controlling Syria from 1966.

w4-900996.name: Formation of Malaysia (Malaysia Agreement 1963)
w4-900996.blurb: On 16 September 1963 the Federation of Malaysia was formed when the British territories of North Borneo (renamed Sabah), Sarawak, and Singapore joined the existing Federation of Malaya under the Malaysia Agreement (MA63) signed in London. Britain formally relinquished sovereignty over the Bornean territories, integrating them into the new Malaysian state. The coordinates (~111E, 4N) correspond to Sarawak/Borneo, the formerly British territory incorporated into Malaysia.

w4-900997.name: Formation of Malaysia (Malaysia Agreement 1963)
w4-900997.blurb: On 16 September 1963 the Federation of Malaya merged with Singapore, Sarawak, and North Borneo (Sabah) to form Malaysia, following the Malaysia Agreement signed in London on 9 July 1963; Tunku Abdul Rahman proclaimed the federation on Malaysia Day. The coordinates (~102E 4N) are the Malayan heartland. Singapore left in 1965. Correctly dated within the 1961-1963 window.

w4-900999.name: Burundi independence from Ruanda-Urundi Belgian trusteeship
w4-900999.blurb: The UN terminated the Belgian Trusteeship Agreement over Ruanda-Urundi on 1 July 1962, on which date the Kingdom of Burundi and the Republic of Rwanda emerged as two independent states. Burundi joined the UN on 18 September 1962. The atlas window 1961–1963 captures the pre-independence elections (1961), the independence itself (1962), and the immediate post-independence period.

w4-901000.name: Dissolution of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland; Zambian independence
w4-901000.blurb: The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland was dissolved on 31 December 1963. Northern Rhodesia became the independent Republic of Zambia on 24 October 1964 under President Kenneth Kaunda. Matches worklist transition Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland -> Zambia (1963-1964); coords lng 27.8 lat -13.2 correspond to Zambia.

citations.label: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland – Wikipedia

w4-901001.name: Malawi independence from the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland
w4-901001.blurb: The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland was formally dissolved on 31 December 1963 following African nationalist pressure and Britain's recognition of the right of its constituent territories to secede. Nyasaland achieved internal self-government in February 1963 under Hastings Banda and became fully independent as Malawi on 6 July 1964.

citations.label: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland - Wikipedia

w4-901002.name: Union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar forms Tanzania (1964)
w4-901002.blurb: After Zanzibar's January 1964 revolution, Presidents Nyerere and Karume signed the Articles of Union on 22 April 1964, proclaiming the United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar on 26 April 1964, renamed the United Republic of Tanzania on 29 October 1964. The dataset records this as a Tanganyika → Tanzania transfer in the 1964–1965 window.

w4-901003.name: Six-Day War — Israel captures Sinai and Gaza from Egypt (UAR)
w4-901003.blurb: In the Six-Day War (5–10 June 1967) Israel destroyed Egypt's air force and advanced across the Sinai Peninsula and Gaza Strip, holding both to the Suez Canal by 10 June. The coordinates (34.1,30.6) are the Sinai/Gaza area, matching the from→to (United Arab Republic → State of Israel) in the 1965–1967 window.

w4-901006.name: Brazilian Constitution of 1967 (military regime)
w4-901006.blurb: After the 1964 military coup that ousted President João Goulart, the Brazilian military dictatorship progressively dismantled the 1946 democratic constitution through a series of Institutional Acts. In 1967, the regime promulgated a new constitution that formally centralised power in the executive and federal government, effectively replacing the federated democratic republic with a state dominated by the military presidency. The 1967 constitution ratified by a purged Congress reflected the regime's authoritarian reorganisation of Brazilian governance.

w4-901008.name: Independence of Lesotho
w4-901008.blurb: Basutoland became the independent Kingdom of Lesotho on 4 October 1966, ending British protection in force since 1868, with a full constitutional handover under King Moshoeshoe II. The dataset records the territorial change between 1965 and 1967, consistent with the legal transfer of sovereignty.

w4-901009.name: Independence of Guyana
w4-901009.blurb: British Guiana became independent as the Co-operative Republic of Guyana on 26 May 1966, the first English-speaking country in South America to gain independence. The coordinates (-59W, 4.8N) lie in Guyana. The dataset records the change between 1965 and 1967, straddling the 1966 date. Transfer British Colonial Empire -> Guyana is correct.

w4-901011.name: 1966 Syrian Ba'ath internal coup - Salah Jadid seizes power
w4-901011.blurb: On 23 February 1966 the 'regionalist' (qutri) military faction of the Syrian Ba'ath Party under Salah Jadid overthrew the 'nationalist' (qawmi) civilian leadership of Michel Aflaq and Amin al-Hafiz in a violent internal coup. Jadid's faction, allied with Hafez al-Assad, installed a new neo-Ba'athist government committed to radical socialism. This transferred Syrian state power from the earlier Ba'athist administration to the new Jadid-led government.

citations.label: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party - Syria Region - Wikipedia

w4-901014.name: Greek Coup d'état of 1967 (Regime of the Colonels)
w4-901014.blurb: On April 21, 1967, right-wing army officers led by Colonels George Papadopoulos, Nikolaos Makarezos, and Brigadier Stylianos Pattakos seized power in Athens (coords 23.9E/38.3N) weeks before scheduled elections, suspending the constitution and banning political parties. The junta, the Regime of the Colonels, ruled Greece until July 1974.

w4-901015.name: 1969 Libyan coup d'état (Gaddafi's Revolution)
w4-901015.blurb: On 1 September 1969, Colonel Muammar Gaddafi and the Free Officers Movement staged a bloodless coup while King Idris I was in Turkey for medical treatment. Within hours the monarchy was abolished and the Libyan Arab Republic proclaimed (Cliopatria centroid lat 26.4, lng 17.3, central Libya). This matches the Kingdom of Libya to Libyan Arab Republic transfer in the 1967-1969 window.

w4-901016.name: British withdrawal from Aden and independence of South Yemen
w4-901016.blurb: Britain withdrew from the Aden Protectorate and Colony on 30 November 1967. The National Liberation Front took control and proclaimed the People's Republic of South Yemen (later People's Democratic Republic of Yemen), covering modern southern Yemen. From 'United Kingdom' to 'People's Democratic Republic of Yemen' at southern-Yemen coordinates; window py=1967, y=1969 fits.

citations.label: People's Democratic Republic of Yemen – Wikipedia

w4-901018.name: Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia and Soviet 'normalisation' (1968–1969)
w4-901018.blurb: On the night of 20–21 August 1968, roughly 200,000 Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia to suppress the Prague Spring. Dubček was forced out in April 1969 and replaced by Gustáv Husák under 'normalisation,' with Soviet troops remaining until 1991. The data records Bohemia transitioning Czechoslovakia -> Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (effective control), matching the [1967,1969] window.

citations.label: Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia – Wikipedia

w4-901019.name: Swaziland independence from Britain
w4-901019.blurb: The Kingdom of Swaziland (coord 31.4E/-26.6N, Eswatini) achieved full independence from Britain on 6 September 1968 under King Sobhuza II after 65 years as a British High Commission Territory. The dataset's donor label 'British East Africa' is wrong (Swaziland was administered via the British High Commissioner for South Africa, not East Africa) but the location is precisely Eswatini and the independence event is real; the dataset's 1967–1969 window brackets it.

w4-901021.name: 1970 Cambodian coup d'etat - Lon Nol overthrows Sihanouk
w4-901021.blurb: On 18 March 1970, while Prince Norodom Sihanouk was abroad, Prime Minister Lon Nol and his ally Sirik Matak orchestrated a parliamentary vote removing Sihanouk as head of state. With tacit US support, Lon Nol formed a new government and formally proclaimed the Khmer Republic on 9 October 1970, abolishing the monarchy. This transferred Cambodian territorial authority from the Kingdom of Cambodia to the US-aligned Khmer Republic.

w4-901024.name: Guinea-Bissau Unilateral Declaration of Independence (1973)
w4-901024.blurb: The African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC) declared the independence of Guinea-Bissau on 24 September 1973, following a decade-long guerrilla war against Portugal's Estado Novo colonial regime. The PAIGC had established 'liberated zones' that Portuguese forces could not retake. The UN General Assembly recognized the new state in November 1973; Portugal formally acknowledged independence in September 1974 after the Carnation Revolution.

w4-901026.name: Egypt renamed Arab Republic of Egypt (1971)
w4-901026.blurb: After Nasser's death on 28 September 1970, Anwar Sadat adopted a new constitution and the official name 'Arab Republic of Egypt' on 2 September 1971, replacing the United Arab Republic name. Territory was unchanged; only the state's name and constitutional structure changed. The dataset window of 1970–1973 brackets this.

w4-901027.name: Hafez al-Assad's Corrective Movement coup and 1973 constitution
w4-901027.blurb: On 13 November 1970 Defense Minister Hafez al-Assad launched a bloodless coup (the 'Corrective Movement') against Salah Jadid's radical Ba'athist government, imprisoning Jadid and President Nur al-Din al-Atassi. Assad consolidated power, reopened parliament, and in 1973 promulgated a permanent constitution designating the Ba'ath Party as the state's vanguard, converting Syria from the Jadid-era party-state into the Assad family-dominated authoritarian republic labeled here as 'Syria'.

w4-901028.name: Fiji independence from Britain
w4-901028.blurb: Fiji (coord 178.6E/-17.7N) achieved independence from Britain on 10 October 1970, becoming a Commonwealth realm under PM Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara. The dataset's py=1970/y=1973 window captures the post-independence period; the 'British Colonial Empire → Republic of Fiji' direction is correct (the donee label anticipates Fiji's later republican status). Event real and correctly dated.

w4-901029.name: 1973 Afghan coup d'état; Daoud Khan abolishes the monarchy
w4-901029.blurb: On 17 July 1973, General Mohammad Daoud Khan launched a bloodless coup against King Mohammad Zahir Shah, ending the monarchy and establishing the Republic of Afghanistan with himself as president; the king abdicated on 24 August 1973. Matches worklist transition Kingdom of Afghanistan -> Republic of Afghanistan (1970-1973); coords lng 67.7 lat 33.9 confirm Afghanistan.

w4-901032.name: Qatar–Saudi Arabia boundary crystallisation at Qatari independence (1971–1973)
w4-901032.blurb: When Qatar became independent in 1971 the land border with Saudi Arabia, partly delimited by the 1965 Dammam agreement, crystallised, with hinterland territory mapped to Saudi jurisdiction. From=Qatar, to=Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reflects this boundary settlement in the 1970-1973 window. (Note the cited Jordan-Saudi border article is not the relevant source.)

w4-901033.name: Qatar declares independence from British protectorate (1971)
w4-901033.blurb: On 3 September 1971 Qatar declared independence from Britain, ending decades as a British protectorate. From=Qatar, to=State of Qatar matches the 1970-1973 window of independence and formal statehood.

w4-901034.name: British withdrawal from the Trucial States and formation of the UAE
w4-901034.blurb: Britain announced in 1968 it would end its protectorate over the Trucial States, and on 1 December 1971 the protection treaties were terminated. On 2 December 1971 six of the seven Trucial sheikhdoms united as the United Arab Emirates; Ras al-Khaimah joined on 10 February 1972. The dataset transfer (United Kingdom -> United Arab Emirates, py1970/y1973) at lng54.1/lat24.4 spans this handover; the UAE joined the UN on 9 December 1971.

citations.label: Foundation of the United Arab Emirates – Wikipedia

w4-901038.name: Proclamation of the People's Republic of Benin
w4-901038.blurb: Following the 1972 coup by Mathieu Kerekou, the Republic of Dahomey was renamed the People's Republic of Benin on 30 November 1975, as Kerekou formally adopted Marxism-Leninism. The name 'Benin' was chosen as a politically neutral designation derived from the Bight of Benin, to avoid privileging the Fon-dominated legacy of the Kingdom of Dahomey. This name change represented the culmination of Kerekou's ideological reorientation of the state. The country subsequently became the Republic of Benin in 1991 upon democratic transition.

w4-901042.name: Greek Metapolitefsi — Restoration of the Hellenic Republic
w4-901042.blurb: The Greek military junta collapsed on July 23–24, 1974, following its disastrous role in the Cyprus coup. Konstantinos Karamanlis returned from exile as Prime Minister, and a December 1974 referendum (69% for republic) abolished the monarchy, establishing the Third Hellenic Republic with a new constitution in 1975. Coords (23.9E/38.3N) = Athens; window [py=1973, y=1976] brackets the transition.

w4-901043.name: Angolan War of Independence and proclamation of the People's Republic of Angola
w4-901043.blurb: Portugal's Estado Novo colonial regime was overthrown in the Carnation Revolution of April 1974, triggering rapid decolonisation of Angola. After a transitional period marked by civil war between rival liberation movements, the MPLA proclaimed the People's Republic of Angola on 11 November 1975, with full international recognition and the end of Portuguese jurisdiction by 1976. The dataset window of 1973–1976 brackets this transfer from Estado Novo to the People's Republic of Angola.

w4-901044.name: Mozambique independence
w4-901044.blurb: After a decade-long liberation war by FRELIMO and the Carnation Revolution that overthrew Portugal's Estado Novo regime in April 1974, Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975 under President Samora Machel. The Lusaka Accord (Sept 1974) transferred power to FRELIMO. Matches worklist transition Estado Novo -> Mozambique (1973-1976); coords lng 35.5 lat -18.7 confirm Mozambique.

w4-901046.name: Spanish Transition to Democracy (La Transicion)
w4-901046.blurb: Francisco Franco died on 20 November 1975 after 36 years in power, and King Juan Carlos I, whom Franco had designated as his successor, facilitated a peaceful transition to constitutional democracy. Adolfo Suarez was appointed Prime Minister in 1976; the Political Reform Act was approved by referendum in December 1976; free elections were held in June 1977; and Spain's democratic constitution was ratified by referendum in December 1978. The Kingdom of Spain formally replaced the Francoist state.

w4-901050.name: Yom Kippur War: Israeli salient across the Suez Canal (1973)
w4-901050.blurb: During the Yom Kippur War (October 1973) Israeli forces crossed the Suez Canal and encircled Egypt's Third Army, briefly holding ground on the canal's west bank in addition to the Israeli-occupied Sinai. The coordinates (lat 29.6, lng 33.6, Gulf of Suez/Sinai) and the 1973-1976 window capture this Israeli-held salient before the Sinai I (1974) and Sinai II (1975) disengagement agreements progressively returned the ground to Egypt.

w4-901053.name: Carnation Revolution and Portuguese democratic transition
w4-901053.blurb: The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 ended nearly five decades of the Estado Novo authoritarian regime, founded by Salazar and continued by Caetano. The Movimento das Forcas Armadas (MFA) staged a peaceful coup in Lisbon, triggering a rapid transition to democracy formalized in the 1976 Constitution. The coordinates point to the Azores, which became an autonomous region under the new constitution - reflecting the formal reclassification of Estado Novo territory under the new democratic Portuguese Republic.

w4-901054.name: Proclamation of the Central African Empire
w4-901054.blurb: On 4 December 1976, President Jean-Bedel Bokassa dissolved the Central African Republic's government and, at a MESAN congress, promulgated a new constitution transforming the republic into the Central African Empire, with himself as Emperor Bokassa I. The regime change was inspired by Napoleon I and accompanied by an extravagant coronation ceremony in December 1977. The empire lasted until French paratroopers ousted Bokassa in September 1979, restoring the republic.

w4-901059.name: Iranian Revolution: fall of the Pahlavi Dynasty and establishment of the Islamic Republic
w4-901059.blurb: Mass protests beginning in 1977-1978 forced Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi to flee Iran on 16 January 1979. Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile on 1 February 1979 and the Pahlavi regime formally collapsed on 11 February. A March 1979 referendum established the Islamic Republic of Iran (Cliopatria centroid lat 32.4, lng 53.7),

w4-901060.name: Solomon Islands independence from Britain
w4-901060.blurb: The Solomon Islands gained full independence from Britain on 7 July 1978 under the Solomon Islands Act 1978, becoming independent within the Commonwealth with Peter Kenilorea as first Prime Minister. The British Solomon Islands Protectorate had been established in 1893. The from=British Colonial Empire / to=Solomon Islands and 1976-1979 window match.

w4-901061.name: Saur Revolution — PDPA Coup in Afghanistan
w4-901061.blurb: On 27-28 April 1978 the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA) staged the Saur Revolution, a violent coup that overthrew President Mohammad Daoud Khan (who had himself established the Republic of Afghanistan in 1973) and killed him along with his family. Nur Muhammad Taraki of the PDPA became head of state, renaming the country the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan. This Soviet-aligned government's policies triggered nationwide insurgency and ultimately the Soviet invasion in December 1979.

w4-901062.name: Independence of Djibouti from France (1977)
w4-901062.blurb: On 27 June 1977, the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas became the independent Republic of Djibouti following a May 1977 referendum that overwhelmingly voted for independence. Djibouti was France's last African colony to gain independence. Hassan Gouled Aptidon became its first president. French forces remained in Djibouti under a defence agreement. The dataset records a transition from 'French Fifth Republic' to 'Republic of Djibouti' around 1976-1979.

w4-901063.name: Zimbabwe independence following the Lancaster House Agreement
w4-901063.blurb: The Lancaster House Agreement (December 1979) ended the Rhodesian Bush War; after February 1980 elections won by ZANU, Southern Rhodesia became the independent Republic of Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980 under Robert Mugabe. The Zimbabwe Rhodesia-to-Zimbabwe transition (-19.1N) is within the window (1979-1980).

w4-901065.name: Independence of Vanuatu from the New Hebrides Condominium (1980)
w4-901065.blurb: The New Hebrides, administered since 1906 under an Anglo-French Condominium, achieved independence as the Republic of Vanuatu on 30 July 1980. The transition was complicated by a secessionist uprising on Santo island, suppressed by Vanuatu police and Papua New Guinean troops. From=New Hebrides, to=Vanuatu matches the 1980 independence.

w4-901066.name: Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty (1979) – Israeli Withdrawal from Sinai
w4-901066.blurb: Following the Camp David Accords (September 1978) brokered by President Carter, Egypt and Israel signed their peace treaty on 26 March 1979. Israel agreed to a phased withdrawal from the Sinai, completed on 25 April 1982 when the last Israeli soldiers and settlers left. The data window (1980→1983) corresponds to the phased Israeli withdrawal during which Egypt progressively recovered Sinai territory.

w4-901069.name: Soviet-Afghan War - Mujahideen territorial gains
w4-901069.blurb: By 1986-1987 the Mujahideen, equipped with US-supplied Stinger missiles, controlled large swathes of the Afghan countryside, limiting Soviet/government control to cities and garrisons. On 20 July 1987 the USSR announced its intent to withdraw; the 1988 Geneva Accords formalised the withdrawal completed by February 1989. The from=USSR / to=Mujahideen and 1983-1987 window capture this transfer of territorial control.

w4-901070.name: Soviet-Afghan War — Mujahideen territorial gains mid-1980s
w4-901070.blurb: During the Soviet-Afghan War (1979-1989), the Afghan Mujahideen — backed by the United States, Pakistan, and others — controlled much of the Afghan countryside while Soviet and government forces held cities. By the mid-1980s, following the introduction of Stinger surface-to-air missiles (1986) and expanded CIA covert support (NSDD-166 of 1985), Mujahideen forces substantially expanded their territorial control across rural Afghanistan.

w4-901072.name: Brazil — return to civilian rule (New Republic) and National Constituent Assembly (1985–1987)
w4-901072.blurb: Brazil's transition back to a democratic republic occurred within this window: the electoral college chose civilian Tancredo Neves as president on 15 January 1985, ending 21 years of military rule, and after his death José Sarney was inaugurated as the first civilian president since 1964, inaugurating the 'New Republic' (Nova República). A National Constituent Assembly was elected and convened on 1 February 1987 to draft a new democratic charter. (Note: the worklist [py=1983,y=1987] window predates the actual promulgation of the 1988 'Citizen Constitution' on 5 October 1988, which fully entered effect in 1990; the in-window transition is the 1985 return to civilian rule and the 1987 Constituent Assembly.)

citations.label: Brazil Returns To Civilian Rule – The Washington Post (16 Mar 1985)

w4-901073.name: Romanian Revolution of 1989
w4-901073.blurb: The Romanian Revolution of December 1989 overthrew the communist dictatorship of Nicolae Ceausescu, executed on 25 December 1989. The Socialist Republic of Romania was dissolved and replaced by Romania as a democratic republic. The dataset registers the label change between 1987 and 1990, consistent with the 1989 revolution. Transfer Socialist Republic of Romania -> Romania is correct.

w4-901078.name: Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan (Geneva Accords, 1988)
w4-901078.blurb: Under the 1988 Geneva Accords (signed 14 April 1988), the Soviet Union agreed to withdraw all forces from Afghanistan over nine months. The withdrawal began 15 May 1988 and was completed on 15 February 1989. Mujahideen forces progressively retook Afghan territory the Soviet troops and the Najibullah government had controlled. The 1987–1990 window reflects accelerating Soviet disengagement and Mujahideen territorial gains.

w4-901079.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
w4-901079.blurb: With the formal dissolution of the Soviet Union on 25 December 1991, the Republic of Lithuania completed its restoration of full sovereignty. Lithuania had been the first Soviet republic to declare the re-establishment of its independence, on 11 March 1990, and the USSR's State Council recognized that independence on 6 September 1991 after the failed August coup in Moscow. By the union's end Lithuania (~lng 23.9, lat 55.2) was an internationally recognized sovereign state, reversing the 1940 Soviet annexation.

w4-901082.name: SLORC renames Burma to Union of Myanmar
w4-901082.blurb: After the SLORC military junta seized power in September 1988, on 18 June 1989 it renamed the country from Burma to the Union of Myanmar. This is a renaming rather than a territorial transfer, so the large area reflects the whole country changing administrative identity. Matches worklist transition Burma -> Union of Myanmar (1987-1990); coords lng 96.6 lat 19.3 confirm Burma.

citations.label: State Peace and Development Council – Wikipedia

w4-901083.name: German Reunification (Deutsche Wiedervereinigung)
w4-901083.blurb: On 3 October 1990 the German Democratic Republic formally acceded to the Federal Republic of Germany, reunifying the country after 45 years of division. The dataset records the label shift from 'Federal Republic of Germany' to 'Federated Republic of Germany' (a minor variant) as the unified state took on its full extent (~245,000 km2). The Two Plus Four Treaty (12 September 1990) between the two German states and the four wartime Allied powers paved the legal way. Fits the 1990-1991 window.

citations.label: Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany - Wikipedia

w4-901085.name: Fall of communism in Albania - proclamation of Republic of Albania
w4-901085.blurb: Student protests from December 1990 and multi-party elections on 31 March 1991 accelerated the collapse of communist rule. On 29 April 1991 the People's Socialist Republic of Albania was renamed the Republic of Albania, with Ramiz Alia as first president; the Democratic Party's 1992 victory completed the transition. The from=People's Socialist Republic of Albania / to=Republic of Albania and 1990-1991 window match.

citations.label: Fall of communism in Albania - Wikipedia
People's Socialist Republic of Albania - Wikipedia

w4-901086.name: Bulgarian transition to democracy and renaming to Republic of Bulgaria
w4-901086.blurb: Following Todor Zhivkov's removal on 10 November 1989 after 33 years in power, Bulgaria transitioned to multiparty democracy. On 15 November 1990 the Grand National Assembly renamed the state from 'People's Republic of Bulgaria' to 'Republic of Bulgaria'. A new democratic constitution was adopted on 12 July 1991, formally establishing a parliamentary republic. The Bulgarian Communist Party rebranded as the Bulgarian Socialist Party and won the first free elections in June 1990, though it was later replaced by a coalition government.

w4-901089.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union — Latvia regains independence
w4-901089.blurb: Latvia declared the restoration of full independence on 21 August 1991 after the failed Moscow coup; the USSR recognised it on 6 September 1991. The coordinates (24.6,57) are Latvia, matching the from→to (USSR → Republic of Latvia) in the 1991–1992 window.

citations.label: Occupation of the Baltic states – Wikipedia

w4-901090.name: Kazakhstan declares independence from the Soviet Union
w4-901090.blurb: On 16 December 1991, the Supreme Soviet of the Kazakh SSR passed the Constitutional Law 'On the State Independence of the Republic of Kazakhstan,' signed by President Nursultan Nazarbayev. Kazakhstan was the last Soviet republic to declare independence, doing so ten days before the Soviet Union formally dissolved on 25 December 1991. The new state retained its vast territory (the world's ninth-largest country) and subsequently joined the Commonwealth of Independent States via the Alma-Ata Protocol.

citations.label: On the State Independence of the Republic of Kazakhstan – Wikipedia

w4-901092.name: Chechen Republic of Ichkeria declares independence
w4-901092.blurb: After the failed August 1991 Moscow coup, Dzhokhar Dudayev was elected president of Chechnya on 27 October 1991 and proclaimed sovereignty on 1 November 1991, establishing the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria as de facto independent from the dissolving USSR (which formally ended 25 December 1991). Coord 45.6E/43.3N is in Chechnya. Chechnya operated as a de facto independent state 1991–1994. Event real and correctly dated.

w4-901095.name: Breakup of Yugoslavia – Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) declared (1992)
w4-901095.blurb: After Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia declared independence in 1991–1992, the two remaining republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia—Serbia and Montenegro—proclaimed the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27 April 1992. This effectively transferred the rump territory of the former SFRY to a new Serbia-Montenegro federation, though the international community did not immediately recognise its claim to SFRY succession.

w4-901096.name: Slovenia declares independence from Yugoslavia
w4-901096.blurb: Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991 following a 23 December 1990 referendum in which 88.2% voted for separation. A ten-day war with the Yugoslav People's Army followed but ended quickly with the Brioni Agreement (7 July 1991). The EU recognized Slovenia in January 1992 and it joined the UN on 22 May 1992, making the 1991–1992 window the transition from Yugoslav to Slovenian sovereignty.

citations.label: Ten Days that Ended Yugoslavia – ZOIS Berlin

w4-901097.name: Mongolian democratic revolution and adoption of the 1992 Constitution
w4-901097.blurb: Following the collapse of Soviet influence, Mongolia's 1990 democratic revolution led to multiparty elections and a new constitution adopted on 13 January 1992, entering force on 12 February 1992. The country's official name changed from 'Mongolian People's Republic' to simply 'Mongolia' (Cliopatria centroid lat 46.9, lng 103.8), matching the transition Cliopatria records as 1991-1992.

w4-901099.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union - Kyrgyz independence
w4-901099.blurb: The Kyrgyz Soviet Socialist Republic declared independence on 31 August 1991 following the failed Moscow coup attempt, becoming the Republic of Kyrgyzstan. With the formal dissolution of the USSR on 25-26 December 1991, Kyrgyzstan inherited the territory of the Kirghiz SSR as an internationally recognized sovereign state and a founding member of the Commonwealth of Independent States.

citations.label: Dissolution of the Soviet Union - Wikipedia

w4-901100.name: Dissolution of Czechoslovakia ('Velvet Divorce') – creation of Slovakia
w4-901100.blurb: The Dissolution of Czechoslovakia, effective 1 January 1993, peacefully divided the Czech and Slovak Federative Republic into the independent Czech Republic and Slovakia, sealed by the November 1992 constitutional acts negotiated by Klaus and Mečiar. The worklist transfer Czechoslovakia → Slovakia at lng 19.6, lat 48.7 (central Slovakia) in the 1991–1992 window captures the legislative process culminating in the split.

w4-901101.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union / Azerbaijan independence
w4-901101.blurb: Azerbaijan declared independence on 30 August 1991 and adopted a Constitutional Act of State Independence on 18 October 1991, as the Soviet Union disintegrated. The USSR formally ceased to exist on 26 December 1991. Azerbaijan was admitted to the United Nations in March 1992. The dataset transfer (USSR -> Republic of Azerbaijan, py1991/y1992) at lng47.6/lat40.2 reflects the end of the Azerbaijan SSR and the emergence of the independent Republic of Azerbaijan.

citations.label: Dissolution of the Soviet Union – Wikipedia
Azerbaijan – Office of the Historian, U.S. State Department

w4-901103.name: Dissolution of Czechoslovakia (Velvet Divorce)
w4-901103.blurb: Following the June 1992 elections that brought incompatible Czech and Slovak leaderships to power, the Federal Assembly passed laws dissolving the Czech and Slovak Federative Republic, effective 31 December 1992. The Czech Republic and Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993 in the peaceful 'Velvet Divorce', with no public referendum. The dataset transfer (Czechoslovakia -> Czech Republic, py1991/y1992) at lng15.5/lat49.8 matches the 1992 dissolution.

w4-901104.name: Macedonia declares independence from Yugoslavia
w4-901104.blurb: On 8 September 1991 the citizens of the Socialist Republic of Macedonia voted 95% in favor of independence in a referendum; independence was declared on 25 September 1991. Macedonia was the only Yugoslav republic to leave without armed conflict with Belgrade. International recognition followed through 1992, with Bulgaria recognizing it in January 1992 and UN admission (as the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia) in 1993.

w4-901105.name: Eritrean Independence
w4-901105.blurb: The Eritrean People's Liberation Front defeated Ethiopian forces and took control of Eritrea (coords 39.8E/15.2N) in May 1991 as the Derg regime collapsed. An internationally observed referendum (April 1993) produced a 99.83% vote for independence, formally declared May 24, 1993. The [py=1991, y=1992] window reflects the EPLF's de facto assumption of control.

w4-901106.name: Uzbekistan independence from the Soviet Union
w4-901106.blurb: Uzbekistan declared independence from the USSR on 31 August 1991 after the failed Moscow coup, confirmed by a December 1991 referendum; Islam Karimov became first president. The transition (41.4N) is within the window (1991-1992).

w4-901108.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union – Moldova independence
w4-901108.blurb: Moldova declared independence from the USSR on 27 August 1991 after the failed Moscow coup, with broad international recognition by 25 December 1991 and UN membership on 2 March 1992. The coordinates are the Republic of Moldova, matching the recorded USSR → Republic of Moldova shift for 1991–1992.

w4-901109.name: Ukrainian Declaration of Independence and Dissolution of the USSR
w4-901109.blurb: Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union on 24 August 1991 in the aftermath of the failed Moscow coup attempt. A referendum on 1 December 1991 confirmed independence with over 90% in favor, and the Soviet Union formally dissolved on 26 December 1991 following the Belovezh Accords signed by Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus. Ukraine assumed sovereignty over the territory of the former Ukrainian SSR.

citations.label: Declaration of Independence of Ukraine - Wikipedia
Dissolution of the Soviet Union - Wikipedia

w4-901111.name: Turkmenistan declaration of independence from the USSR
w4-901111.blurb: On 27 October 1991, the Supreme Soviet of Turkmenistan formally declared independence following a referendum the previous day with overwhelming support. This was part of the broader wave of Soviet republic independence declarations during the dissolution of the USSR, formally completed on 31 December 1991. Saparmyrat Niyazov, former Communist Party first secretary, became the country's first president. The worklist transfer (USSR to Turkmenistan, 1991-1992) matches precisely.

w4-901113.name: Taliban capture of Kabul and seizure of Afghanistan
w4-901113.blurb: The Taliban emerged in Kandahar in 1994 under Mullah Omar during the Afghan civil war among rival Mujahideen factions. With Pakistani support the movement swept across southern and western Afghanistan, capturing Herat in September 1995. On 27 September 1996 the Taliban seized Kabul from President Burhanuddin Rabbani's forces and declared the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. The worklist transfer (Mujahideen to Taliban, 1992-1996) captures this takeover.

w4-901115.name: UNTAC transition - restoration of the Kingdom of Cambodia
w4-901115.blurb: The Paris Peace Accords of October 1991 ended Cambodia's civil war and established UNTAC to oversee a transition from the People's Republic of Kampuchea/State of Cambodia to a constitutional monarchy. UN-supervised elections were held 23-28 May 1993 with roughly 90% turnout; the Kingdom of Cambodia was formally restored on 24 September 1993 when a new constitution was promulgated and Norodom Sihanouk was reinstated as king. The dataset range 1992-1996 spans UNTAC deployment through the new government's consolidation.

w4-901117.name: First Congo War and fall of Mobutu — restoration of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
w4-901117.blurb: The First Congo War (1996–1997), led by Laurent-Désiré Kabila and backed by Rwanda and Uganda, rapidly toppled Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year dictatorship. Kabila entered Kinshasa on 17 May 1997 and immediately renamed Zaire back to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The dataset window py=1992 / y=1996 captures the war's onset; the formal renaming occurred in 1997 following Mobutu's overthrow.

citations.label: Wikipedia: Democratic Republic of the Congo

w4-901119.name: Dayton Accords and Bosnian War Territorial Settlement
w4-901119.blurb: Following the 1992–1995 Bosnian War, the General Framework Agreement for Peace (Dayton Accords) was signed on 21 November 1995, formally separating Bosnia and Herzegovina from Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia-Montenegro) control. The agreement created two entities within Bosnia — the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska — and the IEBL became effective in 1996, consolidating Bosnian territorial sovereignty.

w4-901121.name: Taliban conquest of Afghanistan
w4-901121.blurb: The Taliban, emerging from Pashtun madrasas with Pakistani backing, swept through Afghanistan from 1994 and captured Kabul on 27 September 1996, establishing the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. By 1998 they had taken Mazar-e Sharif and by 2001 controlled approximately 90% of the country, leaving only the Northern Alliance in Badakhshan and parts of the north. The Taliban imposed a strict interpretation of sharia and hosted al-Qaeda. Their rule ended with the US-led invasion following the September 11, 2001 attacks.

w4-901122.name: Kosovo War and UN administration of Kosovo under UNSC Resolution 1244 (1999)
w4-901122.blurb: Following the 1998-99 Kosovo War, NATO's air campaign forced Serbian forces to withdraw from Kosovo in June 1999. UNSC Resolution 1244 established UNMIK, placing Kosovo under international administration separate from Serbian control. From=Serbia-Montenegro, to=Kosovo captures this 1999 transfer within the 1996-2000 window.

citations.label: United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo – Wikipedia

w4-901123.name: First Chechen War and Khasavyurt Accord
w4-901123.blurb: Russia invaded Chechnya on 11 December 1994; after two years of fighting the Khasavyurt Accord (31 August 1996), signed by Alexander Lebed and Aslan Maskhadov, ended hostilities and withdrew Russian troops, granting Chechnya (coord 45.6E/43.3N) de facto independence with final status deferred to 2001. The dataset's 'Russian Federation → Chechen Republic' shift after 1996 captures this. Event real and correctly dated.

w4-901124.name: British Overseas Territories reclassification (1999 White Paper / 2002 Act)
w4-901124.blurb: Britain's 1999 White Paper 'Partnership for Progress and Prosperity' set out the reclassification of the remaining 'British Dependent Territories' (the Falklands and others), formalised by the British Overseas Territories Act 2002, which renamed them 'British Overseas Territories' and restored British citizenship. The coordinates (-50.3, -11.2) point to the mid-Atlantic/central Brazil rather than the Falklands, a likely dataset artefact. NOTE: the worklist window (1996-2000) brackets the 1999 White Paper; the Act itself came in 2002, just after the window.

w4-901126.name: Second Chechen War; Russia restores control
w4-901126.blurb: Russia launched the Second Chechen War in August–September 1999 after the Dagestan incursion and apartment bombings. Under Putin, Russian forces captured Grozny by February 2000 and imposed direct Kremlin rule over Chechnya (coord 45.6E/43.3N) in May 2000, installing Akhmad Kadyrov. The dataset's 'Chechen Republic → Russian Federation' shift 2000–2006 captures this reconquest. Event real and correctly dated.

w4-901127.name: East Timor independence from Indonesia
w4-901127.blurb: After a UN-supervised referendum in August 1999 (78.5% for independence), UNTAET governed the territory until formal independence on 20 May 2002; East Timor joined the UN on 27 September 2002. The from=Republic of Indonesia / to=East Timor and 2000-2006 window reflect the transitional independence process.

w4-901128.name: Montenegro independence referendum and dissolution of Serbia and Montenegro
w4-901128.blurb: On 21 May 2006, Montenegro held an independence referendum in which 55.5% voted for independence, exceeding the EU-mandated 55% threshold. Montenegro's parliament declared independence on 3 June 2006, and Serbia declared itself the successor state on 5 June 2006, dissolving the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. The data window 2000-2006 captures Montenegro's separation from the union.

w4-901129.name: Montenegrin independence referendum and dissolution of Serbia and Montenegro
w4-901129.blurb: On 21 May 2006, Montenegro held an independence referendum in which 55.5% voted for independence, narrowly exceeding the EU-required 55% threshold. Montenegro declared independence on 3 June 2006, and Serbia recognised it two days later, dissolving the 2003 State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. The dataset transfer (Serbia-Montenegro -> Serbia, py2000/y2006) at lng20.8/lat44.2 reflects Serbia reverting to its post-secession borders.

w4-901130.name: 2011 Libyan Civil War and fall of Gaddafi regime
w4-901130.blurb: The 2011 Libyan Civil War, part of the Arab Spring, began in February 2011 with protests against Gaddafi's regime. NATO air support enabled the National Transitional Council to take Tripoli in August 2011; Gaddafi was captured and killed at Sirte on 20 October 2011. The NTC declared liberation, transitioning Libya (Cliopatria centroid lat 26.4, lng 17.3) from the Libyan Arab Republic/Jamahiriya to the State of Libya, matching the 2011-2014 window.

w4-901133.name: Syrian Civil War — rebel/ISIS territorial expansion
w4-901133.blurb: During the Syrian Civil War (2011–), rebel and jihadist factions (Mujahideen/ISIS) seized large areas of central and northern Syria from the Assad government. The coordinates (39.1,34.8) point to central Syria (Deir ez-Zor/Euphrates valley), consistent with territory lost by Damascus to rebel/Mujahideen forces in the 2011–2014 window, matching the from→to (Syria → Mujahideen).
